Tuesday, 11th March, 1924.
The Fourth Session of the First Parliament
of Northern Ireland, appointed to meet 11th
March, 1924, in the fourteenth year in the
Reign of King George V, was opened by the
Governor (His Grace the Duke of Abercorn,
K.P.) in person.

The House met at Ten Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock. Mr. Speaker (Right
Hon. Hugh O'Neill, D.L., M.P.) in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. D. H. Hackett, D.S.O.) was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman
Usher said; His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three of
the Clock, and then resumed.
LOCAL BILLS.
Mr. SPEAKER laid upon the Table Report
from the Examiner of Petitions for Local
Bills, that he has certified that the Standing
Orders have been complied with in the
following cases:
Belfast Corporation,
Londonderry Corporation,
Belfast Water,

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are returned for two or more places in any part of
Northern Ireland do make their Election for
which of the places they will serve, within
one week after it shall appear that there is
no question upon the Return for that place;
and if anything shall come in question
touching the Return or Election of any
Member, he is to withdraw during the time
the matter is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been elected or returned a Member of this House or endeavoured so to be,
by Bribery, or any other corrupt practices,
this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against all such persons
as shall
have been wilfully concerned in such Bribery
or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been tampering with any
Witness in respect of his evidence to be
given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any person
from appearing or giving evidence, the same
misis declared to be a high crime or
demeanour; and this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in any
case before this House, or any Committee
thereof, this House will proceed with the
utmost severity against such offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary do take care that,
during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets leading to this
House be kept free and open, and that no
obstruction be permitted to hinder the pas
sage of Members to and from this House,
and that no disorder be allowed in the precincts of or in the passages leading to this
House, during the Sitting of Parliament,
and that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at Arms
attending this House do communicate this
Order to the Commissioner of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings and
Records of this House be printed, being first
perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do
appoint the printing thereof; and that no
person but such as he shall appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges
be appointed.

KING'S SPEECH.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have to acquaint the
House that the House has this day attended
in the Senate to hear his Grace's Speech,
on behalf of the Crown, to both Houses of
Parliament; of which I have for greater accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is as
follows:
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
When a year ago I first had the privilege
of addressing this House as Governor of
Northern Ireland I expressed the hope that
respect for the law would prevail and that
the good order which had recently been
established in the Province might continue,
King's Speech.
King's Speech.
11 MARCH 1924.
I am glad to be able to state that this
expectation has been most happily realized
by the experience of the past twelve
months.
This
Shortly after their assumption of office
I received and transmitted a suggestion
from the new Imperial Government that
there should be a Conference to consider
the Boundary question and certain other
matters outstanding between Northern
Ireland and the Irish Free State.
suggestion was accepted and the Government was represented at a Conference
which took place with three Members of the.
Imperial Government and three Members
of the Free State Government by the Prime
Minister of Northern Ireland, the Minister
of Education and the Attorney-General.
After two preliminary meetings the Conference was postponed for a month, but
owing to the ill-health of the Prime
Minister, which I am sure we all greatly
deplore, a further postponement has been
requested.
There are indications of a revival in
trade, and in the Linen Industry an improvement has already occurred which has
exceeded general expectation. This is likely
to have
salutary effect
a
on other
Industries. In other directions, however,
I fear that the position is still abnormal
and exceptional measures are still required
for relieving the graver cases of distress
among our people. I am happy to note that
the Local Authorities have realized the
continued seriousness of the situation and
are doing their utmost, with the assistance
of the Government, to promote most useful
work to meet the difficulties created by
unemployment. The success of the Loans
Guarantee Act has been of such a character
as to render it very desirable that further
steps should be taken in this direction.
Accordingly, your assent will be invited to
proposals seeking for authority to issue
guarantees over and above the existing
limit in respect of loans to be applied
towards the carrying out of capital undertakings calculated to create employment in
Northern Ireland. Legislation dealing with
Unemployment Insurance will be introduced to make the necessary provision a
regards unemployment benefit for the latter
part of the current year.
I take this opportunity of endorsing the
appeal which has recently been made by
the Government on behalf of unemployed
disabled ex-Service men, and I trust that
every employer who has not yet enrolled
on the King's National Roll of Honour will
take immediate steps to qualify for enrolment by employing the requisite number of
ex-Service men.
I would also appeal to every firm to do
all it can to provide work for the large
number of persons, both men and women,
whose return to their normal employment
is so essential.
I am glad that the relations of employers
and employed in Northern Ireland continue on such harmonious lines, and it is
my earnest hope that this satisfactory state
of affairs may be maintained in order that
there may be no injury to the reviving
industry of the Province.
The Commission on Development, to
which I referred last year, has been actively at work and has already presented
Reports on which the Government intends
to take action during the present session.
The reports of the Reformatory and Industrial Schools Committee, and of the
Committee which investigated the Jury
system have been received and are receiing careful consideration
I am glad to learn that it is intended
to appoint very shortly a Commission to
inquire into the suitability and cost of the
existing local administrative machinery in
connection with Local Government, Public
Health, Poor Law and the allied Services.
Steps have been taken to put into operation the Education Act which was passed
last session. An Order in Council was
issued on the 27th of September last appointing the 1st October, 1923, as the date
on which the whole of the Act should take
effect so far as relates to the exercise of
powers and the performance of duties in
the general administration of education by
King's Speech.
King's Speech.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
the Minister of Education or any other
Minister under the Act. The same date
was appointed for the commencement of
the local administration of education in
the County Boroughs, those sections of the
Act being brought into operation which
have enabled the Councils of the County
Boroughs to set up the necessary machinery. The administration of the Act, so
far as it is at present in operation, has
proceeded smoothly, and it is hoped to extend its scope in the County Boroughs at
an early date. The extension of the operation of the Act to the Counties in the
Autumn is under consideration. Certain
Rules and Regulations will be laid forthwith before Parliament under the provisions of the Act.
. The absence of facilities in Northern
Ireland for higher education in agriculture
has for some time been a source of anxiety
to those concerned with agricultural development. The authorities of the Queen's
University of Belfast, acting in conjunction with the Ministry of Agriculture, have
now decided to establish a Faculty of Agriculture within the University, so that
henceforth in the matter of agricultural
education in all its branches Northern Ireland will be an independent unit. At the
moment the development of the scheme is
handicapped by lack of suitable buildings
and equipment, but provision is being
made in the estimates of the Ministry of
Agriculture for a contribution towards the
cost of the requisite buildings and equipment.
In my speech on the prorogation of your
Parliament last November I stated that a
Bill dealing with the subject of Rent and
Mortgage Interest Restrictions would be
placed in the forefront of your legislation
in the ensuing session. A Bill is being prepared accordingly, but it has been thought
advisable to postpone its presentation until
consideration has been given to the measure now being introduced in the Imperial
Parliament on this subject.
If our agricultural produce is to hold its
own in face of increasing competition from
overseas it is essential that increased attention should be paid to the condition in
which commodities are placed on the market. The Minister of Agriculture is fully
cognizant of this matter and is taking steps
accordingly.
A measure will also be laid before you
which will provide for the disposal of the
sum granted by the Imperial Government
to the Government of Northern Ireland,
in final satisfaction of the claims made by
the Northern Government under the terms
of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920,
for the provision of buildings other than
Parliament Buildings or Departmental
Headquarter Offices.
This measure
will also contain proposals regarding the
expenditure from the Exchequer of
capital moneys necessary for the construc.
tion and renovation of Constabulary Barracks in Northern Ireland, the dilapidated
condition of which has been a source of
constant anxiety to my Ministers, as well
as being detrimental to the health and
efficiency of the Police.
In accordance with Section 14 of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, the Parliament of Northern Ireland will have
power at the end of three years after the
date of its first meeting to alter the qualification and registration of the electors and
the distribution of members among the
constituencies. This period will expire on
the 5th of June next and the subject of
making such alterations is receiving the
careful attention of the Government.
Other important measures which will
engage your attention will include:-
An Illegitimate Children (Affiliation
Order) Bill, the object of which is to
make the putative father of an illegitimate child liable to contribute towards
the maintenance of the child.
A Pharmacy Bill to establish a Phar
maceutical Society for Northern Ireland,
and to carry out some necessary amendments in the existing Pharmacy laws.
A Bill to extend the principal sections

Mrs. CHICHESTER: I beg to move:
"That an humble Address be presented
to His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland, as followeth :
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal
subjects the Commons of Northern Ireland,
in Parliament assembled, beg leave to offer
our humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament."
Before touching upon the matters of public
interest and public welfare which have been
embodied in the King's Speech I would like
to express my appreciation and my realisation of the honour which has been conferred upon me to-day in asking me to move
this Address. I fully realise that it is not
a personal honour, but that it is, first of
all, a compliment to the city and county of
which I am one of the representatives, and
also that it is a tribute-if I may take it
as such-to the sex to which I belong. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I believe I am
correct in saying that I am the first woman,
at any rate in the British Empire, who has
had this privilege-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) and I take it as a recognition of the
altered position of our sex in the councils
of the Empire (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) and also, coming nearer home, as a
recognition, perhaps, of the work which has
been accomplished by the women of Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
As such I need not say that I value it most
highly.

After the remarks of the Member for
County Derry I do not intend to dwell at
length on the several matters alluded
to in the King's Speech. That Speech deals
with a variety of subjects, and I fancy it
is sufficiently comprehensive to please even
the most exacting critic. Of course the role
of critic is very easy. I have sometimes
adopted that role myself. It is hard,however,
for the critic to estimate the difficulty with
which this Government, and indeed, all
Governments, have been struggling during
the past few years. Apart from anything
else a great deal of adaptability is necessary.
For a long period we had to strain every
nerve towards putting down crime and outrage. We succeeded, and a serious
handicap to industry was thus removed.
Public confidence has been restored, and it
is now recognised throughout the world that
trade can be carried on with Ulster with
the same trust and uniformity as with the
rest of the United Kingdom. We are now
bending every effort towards reconstruction
and building up, and it can hardly be
doubted that we are winning through, slowly
but surely, to stability and prosperity. Law
and order prevail within our borders and
the people realise and appreciate the advantages of firm and impartial government.
I am glad to see the reference in the King's

matter

that has attracted widespread attention, and

The Loans Guarantee Act passed last year

to note that this House will be invited to

In order to provide for those who are
still unfortunately unemployed the provisions
of the Unemployment Insurance Acts have
been applied to Northern Ireland on precisely the same terms as in Great Britain.
Since the 1st January, 1922, a sum of about
£3,100,000 has been paid in Unemployment
Benefit. For the week ended 22nd February
last the sum paid amounted to £28,675.
Those are large figures, and indicate how
the Government is endeavouring to cope
with the problem. I may say that the
administration of this Unemployment Benefit
has been greatly improved by the association
with each Employment Exchange of a Local
Employment Committee, consisting of representatives of employers, workers, and the
general public in each area. Benefit is now
paid only to those who are entitled to it.
I would like to join in the appeal on behalf
of the unemployed disabled ex-Servicemen,
and I hope that employers throughout our
area will qualify for enrolment on the
King's National Roll of Honour. It is their
duty to do so, and I trust they will not
confine themselves to the necessary
percentage.
As the House knows, the Government has
appointed a strong representative Commission consisting of employers, workers and
experts to inquire into the natural and
industrial resources of the Province with a
view to creating new industries and taking
further measures for removing unemployment. This Committee is hard at work, and
there is no doubt that its activities will
have an important bearing on the industrial
future of Ulster. They have already presented reports in regard to special subjects,
and upon these the Government intends to
take action during the present Session.
The Government has striven to preserve
industrial peace, and it can truthfully be
asserted that as a result of the reasonableness of both employers and workers, and a
sympathetic understanding of each other's
points of view, Ulster has been singularly
free from industrial troubles. Long may
that happy state of affairs continue.
It is the intention of the Government to
appoint very shortly a Commission to inquire into the suitability and cost of the
existing local administrative machinery in
connection with Local Government, Public
Health, Poor Law and the Allied Services.
I think such a Commission is absolutely
necessary, and I trust that the outcome of

think I need add to the reference in the
King's Speech to the Education Act. We
had the whole matter fully discussed last
Session, and I notice that it is still a fruitful subject of controversy and debate.

We are to have a Bill dealing with rent

I do not altogether approve of that. Hon.

I cannot agree with this procrastination.
I sincerely hope that when the Bill is introduced into this House the tenants will receive

I am pleased to see that steps are to be

Among other matters that will engage the

Laws,
the existing Pharmacy
and to

Measures of this description will meet with

Lastly, allusion is made to the recently
published report of the Colwyn Committee.
This Committee, as you know, was set up
to deal with the financial relations between
the Imperial Government, and the Government of Northern Ireland. I do not feel
competent to criticise such a complicated
document at present, but it is not difficult
to see that in some respects we have been
unfairly treated. Take for instance our
claim to 40 per cent of the Irish Grant,
under the Provision for Soldiers and Sailors
Act, 1919. This was a War relief measure.
Under Lord French's recruiting scheme
and as
an additional inducement to men
to join up, plots of land and houses were
to be provided for ex-servicemen. Twenty
eight per cent of these plots and houses
have been allofted to Ulster apparently on
the ground that this represents the ratio
of population in the six counties to the rest
of Ireland, but it should not be forgotten
that the recruits from Northern Ireland
were at least 50 per cent of the whole. If
the allocation is not to be on the basis of
recruiting, then what other basis is there
that can have the least regard to fairplay?
Yet our claim to 40 per cent is disallowed.
The Committee has cut down by £200,000
the £500,000 unemployment relief grant.
That is also an injustice, but I am
pleased that our Northern Government has
decided to provide the £200,000 so that the
original amount of £500,000 will remain.
The claim to £1,000,000 contribution towards
malicious injuries since January, 1922, the
date when administration powers were
transferred, has been reduced to £500,000.
As a matter of equity and justice the Imperial Treasury ought to meet all the
malicious injuries awards up to the restoration of law and order by the Northern
Government, because the Imperial Government was alone responsible as a Government
for the destruction of life and property in
Northern Ireland. I shall not further
discuss the report as it will take some time
to digest it, but I am sure that the Minister
of Finance, who revels in figures, will enlighten us upon all these statistical matters.
I am afraid I have wearied you with a
somewhat uninteresting speech, and I shall
conclude with the hope that we may have
a useful and fruitful Session.

Now the first thing in connection with

mind. I am very glad to find myself in
agreement with the hon. Member who has
just sat down (Mr. Grant) in regard to this
matter. May I be permitted to say that for
a considerable time I have been of the
opinion that there has been a desire shown
by the Government too slavishly to follow
every movement of the British legislature?
(Mr. McGuffin: Hear, hear.) I know there
are many questions and many measures in
which it is absolutely essential that we
should have similarity and uniformity, but
I am surprised that it has been suggested
that this matter should be postponed. And
postponed for what reason? We appointed
a Committee to inquire into the whole
matter, and a report has been made to the
Department concerned. I take leave to say
that they have got all the information that
can be possibly given to them, and the time
has come for the Government to legislate on
their own account. Are they really serious
in thinking that in the coming days they
are going to adopt all the measures that
any Government that may be in power at
Westminster is going to pass? Are they
serious in suggesting that on questions of
Housing and Rent Restriction, and other
matters, we must wait to see what the
Government in power there is going to do,
and then that we are going to say "ditto"
to their measures? I protest against the
principle involved here, and I sincerely hope
that the Government will immediately
proceed to implement the report that was
presented to them by their own Committee,
and allow the House to come to its own
conclusions in regard to this Rent Restriction measure.
There are two other matters that I should
like to refer to before I sit down. Probably
they are the most important matters that
could be referred to, and they are subjects
that the people we represent are thinking
about constantly. First of all there is the
question of the Boundary. I am not going
to argue that particular subject-it has been
done by the hon. Member (Mr. Grant) who
has just sat down-but I would like to make
one or two observations upon it. Sometimes
we find a good deal of criticism, a good of
scepticism, is expressed by people outside in
regard to this whole subject. I think that
this matter can be safely left with those who
have handled the question, and handled it so
successfully, up to the present moment.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I think that
the House will have the utmost confidence in
those who are representing them and that
the people of the Six Counties may rest
assured that the Prime Minister, and those
that are working with him, will see that
the interests of this Parliament and the Six
Counties will be protected to the fullest
possible extent. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
I come now to a familiar subject, the
importance of which I think every member
of this House will recognise. I hope that
all the Members have studied the report
presented by the Colwyn Committee. There
is plenty of material there for consideration
in their quiet moments, and I think the
conclusions that the Committee have arrived
at on many subjects lie at the very root and
foundation of the efficiency of this Parlia-
.ment. I hope we recognise that. I
have no intention of going into detailmatters of detail can be dealt with when we
come to the Estimates-but there are a few
questions I wish to put to the Minister of
Finance upon this subject. Most of you will
recollect that when the Act of 1920 was
passing through the British House of Commons we were assured by British Ministers
that Ulster would probably have a surplus
of close on £2,000,000 to play with. Has
that promise been fulfilled? As far as I
can read the report, nothing of the kind has
been accepted. If I am wrong in the
opinions I have formed from this report, the
Minister of Finance can correct me.
The Committee have laid down the principle
--and I assume the British Treasury will act
upon it in the coming years-that the contribution from Ulster for Imperial purposes
-and we know what those Imperial purposes are shall be the balance remaining
over after we have paid our way. I think
that is roughly the principle laid down.
They have laid down the further principle
that we as a Government will receive what
might be considered to be our normal expenditure, and I think I am right in
assuming, too, that they are not going to
give us credit for any new Services or
improvements in existing Services.
No one in this House will say for a
moment that the condition of this Province,
when we took over the administration of
affairs, was such as any progressive community-and I hope we are considered a progressive community-could possibly be satisfied with. But what had the Colwyn
Committee done? They have laid
down this principle that all these
increased charges for improving the Services
in Northern Ireland must in future be
borne by the Ulster taxpayer himself. I
consider that that is neither reasonable nor
fair treatment to give us.

However, they have done one thing which

Those annuities, roughly speaking, come to

do that with will be the £600,000 of land

naturally enough, has a bearing upon the

Committee is that it is going to be £5,892,000.
We are going to have a margin there, but

£7,600,000, speaking roughly, and he calculated that OUT contribution towards

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: So that the
£5,900,000, will be reduced during 1923-24 to

That is roughly the position of affairs as we

I am sorry that I have had to deal with

Hear, hear). From the very outset, when

The past few years have confirmed them in

This has been a wonderful speech that we

country.

Before I touch upon the matters raised by
the hon. Member (Sir Robert Anderson) who

variety of matters which naturally emerge
from the Gracious Speech to which we have
listened to-day. The first matter which was
touched upon was a congratulatory reference
to the restoration of peace and order in our
community. Under normal conditions, of
course, such 2. reference would be unnecessary, and perhaps really unnatural.
but, although the Government has succeeded
in eradicating the turbulent element which
disturbed our Province so greatly in the
past, and in reinstating respect for law
and order, there is no disguising the fact
that if we are to enjoy a full and permanent
measure of that peace and security to which
we are entitled the mentality of many of our
neighbours in Southern Ireland must
undergo a radical change, and there must
be something of a human consciousness that
there are other people in the world who have
equal rights with themselves and who are
equally determined to maintain those rights.
Therefore, I should say now, almost at the
outset of my remarks, that watchfulness on
the part of the Govenment is just as necessary
now as it has ever been, and I think it is

the trust which has been laid upon the
Government in that respect.
Following upon that, reference is made in

refer, of course, especially to the Special
Constabulary. The House may perhaps recall that a year ago the Prime Minister (Sir
James Craig), standing in the position 1
occupy to-day, paid a tribute to the fairness
of the Imperial Government in making the
necessary financial grants to enable us to
carry on the full strength of our Special
Constabulary to the end of the present
financial year, that is the 31st of the present
month. The amount so voted at that time
was £1,500,000, and hon. Members will also
recall that we supplemented that grant oy
a sum of £80,000. These grants have been
sufficient to maintain our force in strength
up till the 31st of this month, but we must
now begin to look about for arrangements
for the coming year. The late Government
entered into an undertaking that £1,000,000
would be provided towards the maintenance
of the force for the year ending on the 31st
of March, 1925, that is the year from now,
and, as the present Government have stated
that they are prepared to honour the undertakings of their predecessors, I know we can
rely and I am sure we can rely fully-on
this undertaking being implemented. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). In view of recent
events the Government feel that a great
responsibility has been thrown upon them
and they would regard it as a betrayal of
their trust to weaken at this moment the
defensive forces of the State. I am quite
certain that the intentions of the Southern
Government are entirely pacific and that Mr.
Cosgrave and his colleagues do not entertain
any schemes of positive aggression against
this Province, out it is well known that
there are strong contingents of intransigent
elements in the South of Ireland which even
the Government of the Free State itself is
unable to control. Therefore, it becomes
additionally necessary that we should adopt
all precautions for any contingency that
might arise out of the conditions that have
been developing.
Now, I leave these purely political matters,
if I may so describe them, which weigh very
heavily indeed at the present time upon the
Government, and I come to touch upon those
grave economic and social problems which
so greatly affect our national welfare. The
depression in trade, which has hung like a
pall for such a time over the kingdom, has
not yet been entirely relieved. The outward
and visible manifestation of the condition
of trade is really the condition of employment. Indeed I may say that the rise or
fall of unemployment provides a sort of
barometrical index of the prosperity of the
country. In Great Britain generally, and
even to some extent in our own Province,
the glimmerings of the dawn of healthier
business conditions are apparent, but it will
require the sun to rise to a much higher
altitude, I am afraid, before we can consider
that we have returned to anything like
healthy or normal conditions. The first
signs of local trade revival, as has been referred to to-day by the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Grant), is in the linen
trade. If only a full and adequate supply
of raw material-and I wish to impress this
upon hon. Members from the country-could
be provided at the present time, it may be
stated that every mill and factory in
Northern Ireland would be going on full
time. This is a matter of considerable
interest to the farming elements of the
country. If the farmers of Ulster could only
realise how greatly their own welfare is
bound up with the welfare of the staple industry of the country, we should have a
much larger sowing of flax than we have had
in recent years. Certainly the outlook for
flax growing was never more promising than
it is at the present moment, and I am sure
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale) beside
me here has taken full cognisance of that
fact, and will endeavour, if it is possible,
greatly to increase the acreage under raw
material for our staple trade in the season
on which we have just entered.

Government to correct an unfair condition

Now, if I am not transgressing too long
upon the time of the House I come to a subject that has been a matter of considerable
attention, namely, education, and I propose
for a moment to touch upon it, because I
think it is necessary that the Government
should make its position clear. It is not unnatural, perhaps, that the magnum opus of our
last Parliamentary Session should continue to
form a subject of animated debate and discussion. It is quite obvious that a scheme
of education transforming a century-old
centralised State system to the direct control
of the people themselves, could hardly be
carried out without criticism of some of its
features. And what part was likely to be
more vulnerable to difference of opinion than
that of religion? Has there been a period in
the world's history when religious differences
have not provided material for quarrels,
great and small, for colossal wars, as well as
family jars? And so it has proved in the
case of our small but ambitious education
scheme. I do not wish to say a word to
increase the feeling aroused in connection
with the discussion on the religious clauses of
this Act, but it is my duty, as well as my
anxiety, to defend the position of the Government in its provision of a scheme of popular
education, which has met, in my judgment
and within my knowledge, with more general
approval than any similar effort that, at any
rate, I am familiar with. Clergymen of the
different Protestant denominations have
declared their intention of refusing to take
full advantage of the Act unless a different
method of providing religious instruction is
set up. I have especial and personal reasons
for feeling regret at this decision. When the
Clause dealing with this subject was
originally drafted exception was taken to its
wording by the heads of the Protestant
37 Debate on the Address.

Debate on the Address.
Churches. With a view of meeting their
scruples, a new Clause was drafted, and it
happened that I was the Minister commissioned to submit the amended wording to the
clergymen. Toward this end, I attended a
meeting which was held in the Assembly's
Buildings, at which were present the heads
of the different Protestant Churches. They
were fully represented, and, without a
dissentient, the new Clause was approved
and warmly welcomed as satisfying all the
claims of the Churches in respect of the
method of providing religious instruction in
the schools. The exact wording of that
Clause, without the change of a single line,
appears as Number 26 of the Education Act
to-day, and this is the Clause around which
has ranged the whole of the controversy.
I am convinced myself-it is only a matter
of personal opinion-that their forebodings of
evil are largely imaginary; but I do not propose to argue the merits or demerits of the
case of the Churches, as this is not a suitable
moment. I feel, however, that our Government has some ground of complaint, that,
having gone so far to satisfy the Churches,
it is now subject to such, I think, unmerited
abuse. We have good grounds to know that
the mass of the laity is not at all in
sympathy with the clerical agitation-(an
Hon. Member: Question)-and we have seen
that in the ranks of the clergy themselves
there are moderate and sensible men who
realise the fatuity of the opposition to the
measure. Only the other day we read a
speech delivered by a very well-known
Presbyterian professor of Magee College,
Londonderry, and I had better read a few
words to give an idea-
Mr. COOTE: What about the Grand
Orange Lodge of Ireland?
Mr. POLLOCK: To let you know what a
Presbyterian clergyman thinks on the subject.
Professor Semple said-
"He ventured to think that that provision was wider, more generous, and more
far-reaching in its scope than they had ever
experienced in that land. .
Some
defects and shortcomings might be developed in this Act when it was put into
operation, but it would be churlish and
ungrateful on their part to belittle and
thwart a measure which did not perhaps
conform in every particular to some
cherished standard of our own. It would
be criminal to strangle a child in its
cradle because we thought it had inherited
some vicious tendency. It would be better
to allow it to grow and develop its limbs
and energies, and then the parental rod
might be wisely used to correct its faults
and amend its failures."
This is the spirit which we had hoped
would have animated the Churches. No one
that I know of wishes to divorce the Bible
from the schools. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Even on lower or secular grounds, the
Bible as one of the great classics of the
world's literature must find its natural place
in the education of the children. But from
the higher or ethical point of view, it is
essential that every boy and girl should be
familiarised with the Bible story. It is the
only hope for the regeneration of the world.
Therefore, we say, in Dr. Semple's wise
words-"Don't strangle the child in its
cradle." Give it a chance for life, and if it
should develop any vicious tendency this
Parliament which brought it into being can
provide the necessary remedy to be applied.
That is the view this Government takes of
this Measure, and I think that if the
Regulations are properly framed all this
dissatisfaction will probably disappear, and
the value of the Act will be fully realised.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Is it contemplated to
issue an Order in Council with respect to
this matter, and, if so, when?
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not quite follow my
hon. Friend. I do not know that an Order
in Council has any application.
I come now to somewhat smaller, but
rather interesting, matters upon which the
House, I think, will be glad to have information. It is a matter of very great satisfaction to me to be able to announce that
the arrangements for the provision of the
new Law Courts, and such administrative
offices as require to be located in the centre
of the city, have been concluded with the
British Treasury, after negotiations extending over one year and eight months. The
accommodation for the courts, with all their
adjuncts, has been satisfactorily settled with
the judges, barristers and solicitors on the
one hand and the Treasury on the other.
The difficulty of finding a suitable site for
such pretentious buildings in a central position in Belfast was very great, as the choice
of suitable sites was exceedingly limited.
But the difficulty has at last been overcome
by the purchase of a sufficient area of ground
from the Corporation, in Chichester Street,
facing the Police Courts, and we expect that
the erection of the imposing structure will
be undertaken forthwith. I am bound to
bear testimony to the generous spirit in which
we were met in regard to the finance of this
matter by Mr. Graham, the new Financial
Secretary to the Treasury, on the one hand,
whilst on the other hand, I wish to pay this
compliment to the Corporation, that they
have acted in an exceedingly public-spirited
way and have relieved us of very great difficulty in respect of the provision of these
courts. I have only to add that if the Belfast Corporation has no statutory powers to
transfer the ground for the purposes I have

indicated, I have given an undertaking that

I had intended to deal with some other
matters, but I think they can be properly
left over, as time is running on. Speaking
generally of the results attained by the Government and Parliament in the year that has
just passed, I may say that sometimes I think
our people do not fully realise all the advantages that have accrued from the transfer of
local government to the province. Nor do
they seem to show much appreciation of the
results of the legislation which has been
passed by the labours of this Parliament, as
well as by the administrative work that has
been carried out. Reforms long overdue have
been effected by the earnest labours of this
Parliament from which not only this generation but also the generation that follows us
will reap considerable benefit. Much public
money has been well used by grants to local
authorities, and it is estimated that through
the assistance thus provided, a sum of at
least £2,500,000 has been spent on relief works.
This matter was referred to by my hon.
Friend who seconded the Address (Mr.
Grant), and it is of some interest to know
that it was through the action of this Government that that enormous sum of money has
been spent in the province. I would like to
know if any other part of the Kingdom could
show greater sympathy with suffering and
distress, or give more practical evidence of its
interest in the welfare of its people than this.
I should again remind the House that the decentralisation of the Government departments
from Dublin and their establishment in Belfast has been the means of circulating during
the past two or three years a vast sum of
money hitherto spent elsewhere. With all
these advantages then, do not let us dissipate
our strength by internal dissensions on small
and relatively trivial matters. We may need
all our strength. Let us bear in mind that
the safety of States does not necessarily depend on the justice or righteousness of their
cause. All history, indeed, gives complete
evidence of this. But let me say this, I do
not believe there is any danger to our
national safety so long as we remain true
and loyal to ourselves, as we have always
done when danger threatened us in days gone
by. (Hon. Members: "Hear, hear.")

"Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal

Question again proposed.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: According to ancient
custom in rising to speak on the Address the
first word that one has to utter is a word of
congratulation to the mover and seconder of
the Address. Sometimes it is a mere
formality, simply an act of courtesy, but in
this case I can say most sincerely that I have
listened to the moving and seconding of
the Address with the greatest possible
pleasure. The mover of the Address (Mrs.
Chichester) was making history, I think, yesterday, because, as she rightly pointed out,
she is the first lady Member of any Parliament in the British Empire, and possibly in
the world, who has had the privilege of
moving an Address such as she moved yesterday; and I am sure I carry the House with
me when I say she lived up to the occasion.
The speech was logical, it was forcible, it was
eloquent. But the hon. Member for Derry
her
(Mrs. Chichester) has already
Parliamentary spurs, and it was only the sort
of speech we would expect from her. The
same remark might be made with regard to
the seconder of the Address (Mr. Grant), who,
in his own outspoken way always says what
he thinks, and even when seconding the
Address he was not at all averse from using
some criticism of the Government that he is
commending to the House. I think this
House has every right to be proud of the
fact that the moving and the seconding of
the Address yesterday were so well done.
won
The only other point on which I would like
to say a word is with regard to the length
of the Speech. I have seen many Speeches
from the Throne in my time, but I have
never come across one in which so many
words were used to say so little, and I would
commend to the consideration of the Government the advisability of curtailing these
Addresses very considerably. If I were a
member of the Government I would curtail
them for the very selfish reason that the
broader the target the more chance there is
for one to get a shot at it.
I am sure every hon, Member of the House
regrets the absence of the Prime Minister,
and we all sincerely hope that he will soon be
restored to health again, and take his
accustomed place in this House. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I followed with great interest the speech of
the Minister of Finance-a very interesting
speech, if I may say so. At the very beginning of it he emphasised how much has been
done by way of restoring law and order in
this Province. I think people are apt to
forget how much the Government and how
much this Parliament have had to do in the
way of bringing order out of chaos during
the last two years. These things are easily
forgotten, and we have not forgotten, and we
ought not to forget, that the conditions very
near to our own border are not so settled at
the present time that we can afford to go to
sleep. We wish well to our neighbours in the
South, but we realise the difficult conditions
under which they are living, and at any
moment, it appears to me, such conditions
may arise that the Government in the South,
with the best will in the world, may not be
able to control their own people. Therefore,
it is the business of our Government to be
watchful, and to be prepared for any and
every emergency that may arise. In that
connection I would join with the Minister of
Finance in expressing the hope that the
Imperial Prime Minister will carry out the
pledge that has been given with regard to
the Special Constabulary. A million is a
large sum for a small Province like this to
have to raise, and I think we can rightly
contend that we are carrying out Imperial
work with the Special Constabulary in
Northern Ireland at the present time, and
that, therefore, we are justly entitled to the
money that has been promised to us.
The Minister of Finance asked us to use
restraint with regard to the Boundary
question. I cordially agree with him. There
is very little that we can say here that can
have any effect on it; and we might rashly
say something that would hamper the hands
of the Government. Our attitude as a House
and as a people is well known from the beginning. From that attitude we have not
departed in the slightest, and we have no
intention of departing. Beyond that I do not
intend to say anything more on the Boundary
question.
It is pleasant to hear the Minister of
Finance saying that trade is in a much
healthier condition. We are all delighted to
know that it is. But there is one point that
he made yesterday which I am afraid is not
generally known, and that is that if there was
more raw material-that is, flax-in the
Province every mill and factory in the city
could be running full time. I join most
heartily with the Minister of Finance in the
appeal that he has made to the farmers of
Northern Ireland to grow more flax this year.
It is essential that there should be a large
supply of flax in their own interest and in
our interest as an industrial community as
well, because the two are absolutely linked
together, and we should look not at what is
going to benefit the farmer only, or what is

going to benefit the manufacturer, or what is
going to benefit the worker in Belfast, but
what is going to benefit the whole community,
and it is in the interest of the community
that we should have plenty of raw material.
I believe that the Minister of Finance has
said that it will pay our farmers to provide
raw material, and in that way provide more
employment. In that connection I would
like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Archdale) on the fact that he is
going to establish a Faculty of Agriculture in
Northern Ireland. That is something that
has been long overdue. I am sure it will be
of the greatest benefit in Northern Ireland.
We wish it all success, and we hope that
there will be no red tape to stand in the way
of carrying out the establishment of this
Faculty of Agriculture.
With regard to unemployment-and I am
sorry the Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) is
not here it is interesting to know that if we
could get the number of unemployed reduced
by 10,000 we would be able to make ends meet.
We have spent very large sums on unemployment, and sometimes I ask myself whether
we have spent most of this money wisely or
not-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-because
we have spent so much, and yet what have we
to show for it? It is necessary, of course, that
our people should not be allowed to starve. I
think the seconder of the Address (Mr. Grant)
said yesterday, and said rightly, what the
people in Northern Ireland want is not the

Hear, hear.) If we could provide them with

in this House on several occasions last year
that we ought to go in for a large scheme of
road improvement and road development in
Northern Ireland. (Hon Members: Hear,
hear.) No one who knows this province
of ours has
any doubt with regard
to the bad condition of our roads.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Why
ought we not to utilise, at the
present time, when there are so many people
out of employment, these men for improving
the roads? When trade improves, as it is
improving and as we hope it will improve,
and we get back to something like normal
conditions, that will not be the time to take
men for the purpose of improving roads. We
ought to do it with the men unemployed,
who might be utilised for that purpose.
throw out the suggestion again, and I hope

re-
With regard to his reference to the Colwyn
Report, there, again, he has asked for
straint, and, as one who knows a good deal
of what is going on behind the scenes at
Westminster, I would emphasise what the
Minister of Finance has said on this point.
We might easily do a great deal of harm, but
to those Members who do not know all that
has been going on, I would say that the cause
of Ulster could not be in better hands from
a financial point of view than in the hands
of the Minister of Finance. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Those of us who know the
battles he has fought with the Treasury in
London, and who know how successful he has
been, are anxious that not a single word
should be said that would hamper him in
that work he is carrying on.
Now, with regard to education, that is
question I am only going to touch on briefly,
because it has been dealt with pretty fully by
the Minister of Finance and in another place
yesterday. There has been a good deal of
misunderstanding, and a good deal of unnecessary heat which always arises from misunderstanding, with regard to this education question. I think it might be taken that the
whole differences on the education question
narrow themselves down to two points, simple
Bible teaching in the school, and Protestant
teachers for Protestant children. With
regard to the simple Bible teaching if anyone

that
Religious instruction (including Bible

That read in connection with the Regulations

the past. I think with a little goodwillall

rather propose to address myself to a different aspect of the case from any I have

we exist as a Parliament, and have a perfect

have always maintained that the school is

there are persons who suffered considerable

else, one penny of compensation. When they
I went to the Courts they were told that these

Sir ROBERT LYNN: As I pointed out
early in the debate to-day I want to raise,
and raise calmly and without any feeling,
the question of the dismissal of District-
Inspector Nixon. I want at the outset to
say that so far as I am concerned in taking
this step I am not influenced in the slightest
degree by anything that has taken place recently at public meetings in my own constituency or elsewhere. As a matter of
fact, a week ago I had intimated
to the

were
Minister of Home Affairs that I would raise
this question as soon as the House met, and
I am doing so now. First of all an Orange
Lodge was set up with the approval of the
Ministry of Home Affairs of which members
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
eligible to become members. I know there
are differences of opinion with regard to
whether the police should be allowed to be
members of any organisation of that sort o
not. I have my own feelings, being an
Orangeman naturally sympathetic feelings,
and I see nothing in the Orange Institution
to prevent a policeman being an Orangeman
and being a good policeman at the same
time. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Nothing
whatever. At any rate, this Lodge was set
up with the approval and with the benediction of my right hon. Friend the Minister
of Home Affairs, and it appears that District-
Inspector Nixon was Master of that Lodge.
In the month of January, I think the 28th
or 29th January, I forget which-
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The 29th.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: On 29th January
District-Inspector Nixon attended an Orange
meeting at which he made a brief speech
in reference to the boundary question, which
was then being discussed in public and
in the public Press. He is alleged
to have made some reference to conditions
that prevailed in the Free State on the
border of Ulster. As a result of that speech,
which appeared in the newspapers, District-
Inspector Nixon was summoned before a disciplinary court. This court sat, and I understand that the charges made against him
were the charges that appeared in the newspapers, but if my information is correct no
evidence whatever was produced to show
that the statements in the newspapers were
correct. After the court had sat for some
days it was suddenly abolished. Afterwards
District-Inspector Nixon was brought before
his superior officers and questions were put
to him which he naturally refused to answer
as they were questions that would incriminate himself. The result was that some days
afterwards the Minister of Home Affairs
dismissed the District-Inspector. I think I
have put the main facts of the case fairly-
Mr. POLLOCK: The Governor dismissed
him.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: It is the Governor,
of course, acting on the advice of his regular
Ministers. That we take for granted.
I am not standing here to justify anything
in the form of indiscipline. In a police
force or any other force you have got to have
discipline and to enforce discipline. There
can be no two opinions on that point; but
the question which I want to ask the Government is this: Was the punishment not too
great for the crime, supposing there was a
crime? First of all, why was not
the District-Inspector dealt with by this
Court? If the Court had given its
decision then the public and this
House would have been in a different
position to the position they are in now.
They would have had some information.
The Court would have told us why they had
recommended the dismissal of the officer or
any other punishment that you like. I
would like to know from the Minister of
Home Affairs, firstly, why the Court was not
allowed to proceed and secondly, why after
the court had ceased to function the Government recommended the extreme course that
was taken. There is a feeling undoubtedly
amongst the public that the Government have
treated this officer harshly-
Mr. POLLOCK: What public?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: The general public.
I am only giving you the impressions that
have reached me. There is a feeling that
this officer has been treated harshly. So far
as this House is concerned, I am sure that
what they want to do is to see that justice
is done to the humblest man in the service of
this House. The Minister of Home Affairs
may have information that I have not got.
It may be that there is no justification for
the feeling that is abroad, but undoubtedly
there is the feeling that this officer has been
harshly dealt with. If he had been indiscreet
-surely dismissal is a very severe punishment for indiscretion? If everyone of us
was dismissed because we were indiscreet, I
am afraid a great many of us would be dismissed often. I would ask the Government,
because, after all, it is not a sign of weakness in a Government if they think they have
done something that ought to be rectified,
to look into this whole question in a sympathetic frame of mind, not to be influenced
by people who try to terrorise, or people who
try to cajole, but to ask themselves plainly end
squarely: "Have we done the right thing?
Are we justified in the course we have taken?
Can we justify our action before Parliament
and before the country, and prove that we
have done the right thing?" If the Government have a shade of a shadow of doubt that
they have taken a more extreme course than
they ought to have taken, then it is not a
sign of weakness to retrace their steps. On
the contrary, it is a sign of greatness. If
people find they have made a mistake they
can go back on it and rectify that mistake.
I do ask the Government to go into this
whole question in a sympathetic manner.

force, of which Mr. Nixon was fully aware,

Mr. COOTE: Question.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There are very
few people in this House and very few people
in the city of Belfast, who have not read
that speech, and a great many people outside
Ulster have read it. I think what attracted
a good deal of attention to it was not that
it was a political speech, but that it was a
political speech made by a policeman. I
think the vast majority of readers can come
to no other conclusion than that a more
mischievous and misleading statement could
not have been made by anyone who had the
peace of the community in his keeping. The
Inspector-General then proceeded to exercise
the right that he had as Commanding Officer
of the Force. He framed a charge against
Mr. Nixon, and formed a Court of Inquiry.
The charges were disobedience of orders, and
infringing the Code. Following on that
the Inspector-General suspended Mr. Nixon
from duty.
On the eve of the first sitting of the Court
of Inquiry, a demonstration took place in
the heart of Mr. Nixon's own district, with
banners and bands and placards. These
placards contained demands for the instant
dismissal of the Inspector-General, the
instant dismissal of the Commissioner of
Belfast, my own dismissal, and, incidentally,
the reinstatement of Mr. Nixon. That demonstration was organised and took place in
the heart of Mr. Nixon's district, and I do
not think anyone in this House will disagree
with me when I say that without Mr.
Nixon's active approval and support that
demonstration could not have taken place.
But worse followed-a campaign of intimidation-intimidation in its worst form.
Persons connected with the Inquiry and
Members of the Government received letters
threatening their lives, and when that did
not avail to stop the Inquiry, the intimidation was then directed against the witnesses
necessary to prove the specific charges made
against Mr. Nixon.

Reference has been made to the Press

Mr. BEST: After the very exhaustive
statement that was made earlier in the afternoon by my right hon. Friend the Minister
of Home Affairs, I really thought it would

I would like to bring right hon. and hon.
Members back to the inception of a constabulary in Ireland. I would like to bring
them back for a moment to the year 1836,
when the Royal Irish Constabulary were
established by Act of Parliament. The
people of the day thought it was absolutely
essential that a constabulary force should
take no side in politics, and accordingly not
only were they debarred from taking any
part in politics, but the members of the force,
from the officers down to the humblest constable, were all debarred from even voting
at an election. Furthermore, they were not
allowed, any of them, to vote at an election
until they were out of the force for six
months. That was a provision of Section 18
of the Act of 1836.
Further, the oath which these members had
to take was down in the schedule to the Act,
and the effect of it may be taken to be this,
that no society that could be called or construed as being secret was eligible to these
men as members, with the one sole exception
of the Society of Freemasons. That exception itself was done away with in the year
1916 by the Constabulary Police Act of that
year, and the result of the thing was that
from 1916 up to the time of the disbandmeut

of the Royal Irish Constabulary no

That was a step which went a tremendous
distance from what had been the practice
before. That was a great privilege, to my
mind. I am not afraid to say I think it was
a proper step. Others think it was not. I
always like to have the courage of my convictions, and I say here publicly that I think
it was right. It was a great privilege, but
it was a privilege that ought not to have
been abused. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It has been abused, sadly abused, by Mr.
Nixon. This was no speech made when, perhaps, the wine flowed too freely or in an
unguarded moment. This was a deliberate
speech, deliberately made in disobedience to
strict orders, made for the express purpose
of challenging the Government and having
a row over it. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
What happened? Mr. Nixon made a speech
of this character on the 4th of January this
year. Immediately after that-namely, on
the 17th January-the Inspector-General
did what he had an absolute right
to do under the code. This will answer one
of the points made by the hon. Member sitting opposite me, the hon. Member for Tyrone
and Fermanagh (Mr. Coote). Why has this
regulation not been embodied in the final
form? The answer is this: Circulars issued
from time to time to the force are of two
kinds—namely, those of a temporary character intended to answer an immediate
purpose, and those of a more permanent
character to be afterwards embodied in
whole or in part in the standing orders of
the force. The order is for the time-being
temporary, but it will be made into a permanent order.
Mr. Nixon, who had served so long and, I
say, so splendidly-(Hon. Members: Hear.
hear)-I do not deny it. But he knew that
code; he knew that an order of this kind
from a superior officer must be obeyed so
long as it was in existence. If he objected
to the order he could have had a question
raised by hon. Members in this House, when
the matter could be debated, and if the
pressure had been sufficient the Government
might have withdrawn the order.
But so
long as the order was in existence it was
his bounden duty to obey it. What happened? That order was sent to him on 17th
January. On the 29th January he made this
speech. Oh, we are told we never proved
that he made it. I will put a question to

deny it.

Mr. DONALD: He is quite safe in his

Unless the situation in the country be

quote a few words by a far greater man than

You talk of the first principles of liberty
which you have laid down. This officer has
a right to be brought within those principles of liberty. This officer has no right
to be broken by any authority, however
great, unless he has had a fair trial.
That is what we are asking for this afternoon. We are asking that this officer should
have a fair trial. Not a solitary word has
been said here with regard to the other men
who have got notices of transfer. I want to

with District-Inspector Nixon in danger's
time when, as my hon. Friend (Mr. McGuffin)
said, some others were sleeping in their beds?
Is it because these men were associated with
him that their homes are to be broken up?
They are all married men. Is it because of
that that their wives and families are to be
put to this inconvenience? Some of them
have from 23 to 28 years' service, and they
are to be transferred to the County of Antrim
and other counties. The thing is intolerable;
it is absolutely ridiculous. Arising out of
the Nixon affair, the homes of these other

the same thing applies at the other end.
Some men have been told off for duty in the
city of Belfast. What does that mean to
those men? It means reducing men to send
them from the city to the country. We are
not going to tolerate that; it is pushing the
thing a little too far. Not only do you want to
penalise one officer, but you say in effect that
all the members of the Force who are members of this Orange lodge will have to leave
the city, the object being to break up the
lodge. This is a challenge to the Orange
Order. Do not forget it. I am an Orangeman, and I accept that challenge in spite of
any Government. If it is a challenge to the
Orange Order, then I say to those men: “Go
to your lodge; sit in your lodge; stick to
your lodge." It was these men who stood up
for Ulster, and not the Englishmen that
have been imported. It was Ulstermen who
helped to save the Empire, and who were
they? They were Orangemen, like my right
hon. Friend.
The right hon. Gentleman seemed to make
a good deal of the demonstration that was

I want the House to understand this, and
I want the right hon. Gentleman to take a
note of what I am going to say now. On
Sunday last there was an excursion from
Belfast to Waterford, and it was after
Curfew hours when that excursion returned.
Instructions were issued by the Commissioner
that these men were not to be intefered with
on their arrival at Belfast on Monday morning. I want to ask the right hon. Gentleman
how many, over and above the number that
went away, came back with that excursion,
and how many had arms. He seems to smile
at that, but it is the absolute truth. Gunmen
came into Belfast last Sunday evening, and
had District-Inspector Nixon, or men like
him, been on the spot, in spite of the instructions of the Commissioner or the
Inspector-General, a search would have been
made and the arms would have been found.
What is the object of all this? I hold no
brief for District-Inspector Nixon. I scarcely
know the gentleman at all, but I am out for
fair play. I was at the inquiry on the first
day, when it was proved to the hilt that the
Court broke down owing to the stupidity of
the Government.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Certainly; it could not
have been worse.
Mr. DONALD: When I left the Court that
morning I said "Your Court is a farce." The
Government could not establish a solitary
charge. Then they come here, when they have
had weeks in which to make up their brief
and to engineer the thing. It is not going
to end here to-day, and I want to tell the
Government this, that they have done the
worst day's work they ever did since this
Parliament was set up. I regret it. I regret
this discussion. I have not thrown any heat

and classes. What about those men whose

want to know what is to become of them if

Is that transfer due to the fact that they
were friendly to this officer? I leave the
whole matter at that. It will not finish the
case. The Government have got to prove
their case. If they prove it, then I, for one,
will say they have a right to take whatever
action they feel free to take, but until they
prove their case there will be further discussion in this House.

Colonel WOODS: I will only keep the

speech. A good many hon. members of this

those conditions and on that understanding.

say.
Mr. MEGAW: I have listened to the debate

I think this affair has taken an altogether
exaggerated importance, because the only
thing that is involved is the case that a
police officer misconceived what police duty
was. He thought at the same time that he
could act as a policeman and as a politician.
Now, that is a thing that cannot be admitted
for one moment, because a policeman's duty
is entirely different from that of a politician.
What is all right in a politician is not what
is required in a policeman at all. However,
the matter gets an importance from another
point of view-that is, that the policeman
had courted the populace to intimidate the
Government, and the question became one
whether the Government would yield to
popular clamour that was largely fostered
in the interests of the policeman himself?
If such a thing could be tolerated it would
be an end to government. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) As our system of government
is constituted we cannot have members of
our Judiciary as politicians. If a member
of our Judiciary were to make a political
speech it is entirely contrary to his position.
In the same way a policeman may not interfere and may not take part in politics,
especially in cases where a precise instruction has been given against it.
government is by the people, through the
people, and for the people, it is not the

voice of the people. The people has its

members. Until the voice of the populace
is declared in that way, then it cannot prevail. We cannot have vociferations by

99 Dismissal of Dist.-Inspr. Nixon. HOUSE OF COMMONS. Dismissal of Dist.-Inspr. Nixon. 100
Mr. DONALD: Shame! That is not fair.
He became no leader.
Mr. MEGAW: All the demonstrations held
are based on the right of the man to make
the speech he did.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Fudge.
Mr. MEGAW: Supposing it were permitted
to become general-and my right hon. and
learned Friend (Mr. Best) has already drawn
attention to the fact that if one side can make
speeches another is entitled to do so-we would
soon find District-Inspectors throughout
Ulster at different times giving vent to their
political opinions at meetings with reporters
present. What would the end be ? How
could there be any confidence in the impartiality of the force if such a thing were done?
Suppose this offence had been allowed to pass
without the severest censure no crities would
have been louder in their accusations against
the Government than the hon. Gentlemen
who have raised this matter to-day. They
would have attacked us and said "How can
you have a police force when speeches of that
kind are permitted ?"
A good deal has been said about Mr. Nixon
not having an opportunity to defend himself.
That is one of the gravest charges that could
be made against us. When he was called up
by the Inspector-General, as he was by the
direction of the Government, as they were
entitled to, to have certain specific questions
put to him why could not he have taken the
opportunity, as any honourable man would
have done, and say, "I did not say that. I
did not mean that," and if he had any explan
ation to offer let him offer it? At no time
has he ever made any statement. If Mr.
Nixon at the time had said he had made a
mistake, had expressed his contrition, and had
said that the matter would not cccur again
the case would have borne a different aspect
altogether. But, so far from that being the
case, he does nothing of the kind. When
those questions are put to him he practically
declines to answer, and we can only draw our
own conclusions.
As I have said, the whole accusation was met
with two voices. One was that he did not
make the speech at all, and the other glories
in the speech and regards it as the utterance
of a patriot. These two are entirely inconsistent, but we still have the tenour of them
running through all the speeches from the
opposite side of the House this afternoon.
At one stage they say he has been wrongly
convicted that he did not make the speech,
and then on the other hand they say that he
did make the speech but that the punishment
is too hard. No other course was open to
the Government in the situation that arose,
because, instead of having submitted himself
to discipline in the ordinary way, or expressed
any contrition for his breach of discipline, he
gloried in the speech, has done so openly, and
has not, as I have said, made one expression
of regret for what has occurred. The policeman who is to uphold the law and carry out
orders appeals from his superior to all sorts
of irregular assemblages and attempts to
throw the machinery of Government and of
administration out of gear. if the Government were to yield to that it would mean an
end of government altogether.
Was there ever outside Mexico such a
meeting as took place before the Court of
Inquiry? We had speakers at that meeting
who desired to remain anonymous, and who
directed the Press that if they knew the
names of the speakers they were not to
publish them. The House will recollect that
in the Press the next day there appeared the
statement that the speakers desired to remain
anonymous and not one name of a speaker
was given. We had also threatening letters
conveyed to members of the Government aud
to others. This made the position absolutely
plain. It is absolutely impossible to yield to
popular clamour, and now here in this House
we have dragged in that fine body of men the
Orange Order. Why was the Orange Order
introduced here? What have we to do
with it here. We have to do with the conduct of a policeman. Who is to judge the
conduct of a policeman ? Is it his superior
officer or is it the mob of people outside? We
say that, so long as we are a Government,
policemen must be subject to discipline and
to their superior officers, and we decline to
be overawed by any of these Soviet assemblages that take place and have taken place
in regard to this case.

The pressure of work in the Ministry at
this period is exceptionally severe, and
unless the hon. Member presses for the
information on grounds of public interest
I would hesitate to authorise the expenditure
which the preparation of the return would
involve.

COTTAGES FOR EX-SERVICE MEN.
8. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he will state the total number of cottages at present allotted or contemplated under the Irish Land (Provision for
Sailors and Soldiers) Act, the number at
present erected and occupied, and the number in course of erection, in each
County respectively, including Belfast and
Londonderry?
Sir DAWSON BATES: As the admini.
stration of the Act referred to by the hon.
Member is one reserved by the Imperial
Government, all questions regarding it
should be raised in the Imperial Parliament.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask my right hon.
Friend does he not misunderstand me?
Question No. 10? It is as to the building of
ex-Service men's houses.
Mr. SPEAKER: I understand it is a
reserved matter. It now belongs, I think,
to this Trust that has been set up.
Mr. DONALD: Is my right hon. Friend
aware that I asked a question in this House
on the same subject, and I merely want to
know how the building of these houses is
advancing. The Trust has been set up.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Trust is formed under the Imperial Government and the
Imperial Government is responsible for that
Trust. I cannot undertake to hold myself
or the Government responsible for anything
that this Trust may do. For that reason I
suggest to my hon. Friend that he should
arrange to have a question put down in the
Imperial House.
Mr. DONALD: This raises a new point,

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid the
hon. Member misunderstands the matter.
The Ministry of Finance and the Home
Office acted as agents for the Imperial

GRANTS FOR EX-SERVICE MENTAL
PATIENTS.
10. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance whether his attention has been
drawn to the decision of the Imperial Exchequer and the Ministry of Pensions with
regard to ex-Service Mental Patients, to the
effect that, under the provisions of Article
7 (2) of the Royal Warrant, where their mental
condition has been decided neither to be attributable to nor aggravated by war service, a
special grant is being provided in the estimates, 1924-25, to meet the special circumstances of these cases, thus removing
them from the ambit of the Poor Law; and
whether this arrangement will be applicable
to patients in Northern Ireland?
Mr. POLLOCK: The service administered
by the Ministry of Pensions is an Imperial
Service in accordance with Section 4 of the
Government of Ireland Act. Any question,
therefore, on this subject should properly be
put in the Imperial Parliament. I may add
that I possess no information, either official
or otherwise, on the point put by the hon.
Member, and I regret therefore that I am
unable to give him the information he desires.
Mr. DONALD: I am sorry.
DISMISSAL OF PORTADOWN TEACHER.
11. Mr. McGUFFIN asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education
whether his attention has been drawn
to the dismissal of a teacher in the
Edenderry N.S., Portadown, on the ground
of approaching maternity; and if so, will he
state the rule governing procedure in such
cases; also whether the Ministry has reviewed the case in question, and approved
the decision of the patron or manager; and
if so, is such decision to become a precedent
in determining all similar cases in future;
also whether a distinctive order should be
issued to regularise procedure in such cases,
or whether it would be advisable to introduce
a new clause to the recent Act to protect the
teacher from capricious decisions in such
cases?
Mr. POLLOCK: Perhaps I may be permitted
to reply to my hon. Friend in the absence of
my hon. Friend the Parliamentary Secretary
(Mr. McKeown).
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
13 MARCH 1924.
The attention of the Ministry of Education
has been drawn to the case referred to by the
hon. Member.
Under the Rules of the Commissioners of
National Education, which are still in force,
married women teachers appointed for the
first time subsequent to 30th June, 1911, are
required to absent themselves from their
schools for two months continuously during
the period preceding and succeeding childbirth and to provide substitutes at their
own expense, but there is no rule governing
the dismissal of a teacher in the circumstances in question. The appointment
and dismissal of teachers in public elementary schools has always rested with the
managers, and the terms on which teachers
hold their positions are set forth in the agreements entered into between the parties concerned.
The Ministry has fully considered all the
circumstances of this case and has decided
not to interfere with the discretion of the
manager.
I cannot within the limits of Question and
Answer deal with the large question of the
employment of married women teachers.
That is a question
on which the views of
educational authorities are much at variance.
The absence of general agreement amongst
perfectly fair-minded persons on this subject
seems to the Ministry to constitute a strong
reason for declining to lay down any hard
and fast rule in regard to it.
Under Section 68 of the new Educational
Act teachers are protected against unreasonable dismissal, but the Ministry is not prepared to hold that that section of the Act
should be applied so as to restrict the discretion of managers in cases of this kind.
I may add that the Government do not
propose to introduce further legislation on
this subject.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Arising out of this
answer, may I inquire is the action of the
Ministry in this matter not calculated to
prejudice the interests of the teachers concerned? If it is established as a general
principle are we to take it that the Ministry
will in future decide as they have done in
this matter in respect of other cases that
may crop up?
Mr. POLLOCK: My hon. Friend raises in
his inquiry, if I may say so, the general
question which is and always has been a
very debatable one, and I could not pretend
in reply to a question to enter into all the
arguments either for or against the pursuance of any particular policy in regard to
the matter. I did say in the formal reply
I gave that the Ministry objected, seeing that
there was strong reason for it, to lay down
any hard and fast rule in regard to it, the
presumption being that the managers of
schools, those who are responsible for their
organisation, should have some discretion in
matters of this kind, because I think it must
be clear to hon. Members that circumstances
often vary in different cases, and they have,
therefore, to be treated by different methods.
For that reason the Ministry has come to
the conclusion that it would not be wise to
lay down any definite ruling in regard to how
matters should be conducted in these circumstances.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I further inquire,
is the action of this manager not absolutely
without precedent? It appears to be not
only cruel but autocratic. Is the Government going to sanction a course
with respect to a teacher which has
never been adopted in connection with any
other case?
taken

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Court of
Inquiry set up to investigate the charges
preferred against Inspector Nixon was dissolved under circumstances which
matters of common knowledge. It was not
by reason of the fact that the Court made
no finding that the Inspector was dismissed.
Mr. Nixon had every opportunity of making
his defence before his superior officers, of
which he did not elect to avail himself. He
was dismissed from the Force on the recommendation of the Government, who satisfied
themselves that his disobedience of orders
rendered his continued employment a menace
to peace and good order amongst the general
community.
The reasons which led to Inspector Nixon's
dismissal have been published in the Press,
the accuracy of which is not denied.
Under the circumstances of the case the
Government is not prepared to reconsider
its decision.
I may add that the Inspector is now in
enjoyment of the full pension to which he
would have been entitled had he completed
his service in the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
