LOANS GUARANTEE ACT.
13. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the amounts
of money advanced under the Loans Guarantee Act to the firm of Harland and Wolff,
Limited, and how many extra men were
employed in consequence of the subsidy.
Mr. POLLOCK: The hon. Member would
appear to be under a misapprehension regarding the facilities provided by the Loans
Guarantee Acts. No advances or grants are
made by the Government under the terms
of this legislation, but guarantees are given
and nothing more. No immediate charge on
public funds is involved and it is hoped
that no ultimate charge will result. Firms
taking advantage of these facilities must
raise the money in the ordinary way in the
open market, and in so doing they are assisted by Government credit. Up to the
present date Messrs. Harland and Wolff
have received guarantees in
respect of
capital undertakings up to an amount of
£248,000, and, in addition, guarantees of
£2,190,000 have been given to various
large shipowning Companies in connection
with the construction of ships in the Yards
of Messrs. Harland and Wolff, Ltd., Belfast,
making in all a total of £2,438,000.
I may add that returns have already been
laid upon the Table of the House showing
the guarantees which the Government have
undertaken to give up to the end of September, 1923, and a further return for the six
months ending the 31st instant will be presented to Parliament after the close of the
present financial year.
In reply to the latter part of the question,
the average number of men employed in connection with the construction of these
vessels during February, 1924, was 5,500.
Mr. DONALD: Hear, hear.

That an Humble Address be presented

Question again proposed.
Mr. DONALD: In the first place I should
like to express my regret, and I am sure I
am voicing the feelings of every Member of
the House, at the absence of our Prime
Minister. I feel, at any rate, that the front
Government Bench is not complete without
him.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Hear, hear.
Mr. DONALD: The first question to which
reference is made to His Grace's Speech
is with regard to the boundary, and
like my hon. Friend, the Member for North
Belfast (Mr. McGuffin), I can say there are
certain suspicions abroad in regard to this
very complex question. To some extent these
suspicions are aroused in view of the fact
that this matter is being brought continually
before the Imperial House. I noticed in the
paper yesterday that a question will be
asked there with reference to this conference.
That, to some extent, arouses suspicion in
the minds of our people here. There is
something to be said with regard to what
my hon. Friend said yesterday that we at
least should know something from time to
time as to what takes place at these conferences in order to allay these suspicions.
When I say that I cannot help thinking
about a reference that was given by the
Noble Marquess, Lord Londonderry, at the
Reform Club the other night. He said that
we should be loyal to the Government. I
could not help wondering was the Government loyal to itself, and that is why I am
referring to this matter. Very often
suspicions are aroused through misunderstandings, but the people should at least
know something of what is going on.
Secondly, the Noble Marquess referred to
hon. Members, and said they should devote
a great deal of time in their constituencies
talking to their people. That is exactly the
thing that I feel a great difficulty about.
When I go into my constituency, I am
approached about this very thing, and I
cannot tell any of my people what is going
on. I merely mention that to show that we
should be told something from time to time
as to what is going on at this conference.
Personally, I am satisfied with the statement made by the Prime Minister at the close
of the last Session, and I am going to refer
to the very able speech which he made on
7th December in which he touched upon this
question. I, for one, am satisfied that there
has been no change as regards our position,
and I have every confidence in our Prime
Minister and those who with him represent
us at that conference. The Prime Minister
said with regard to the boundary question:-
"The whole thing is that if Mr.
Cosgrave and his representatives claim the
whole of Fermanagh and Tyrone, and if I

The next question is the revival of the

myself to this extent-

of that our unemployment is increasing on

not doing an honest day's work for an honest

(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) If
The next matter is with regard to education and the establishment of a building for
the teaching of agriculture, that is the
University. I was taught the elementary
stages of agriculture in the elementary
school, and why that system should be departed from I cannot tell. It is the greatest
industry in our country, and why we have
departed from the teaching of this in our
elementary schools I cannot understand. It
was most useful to our young people to learn
at least something with regard to the farm.
This will be a splendid thing, but all these
people will have to come to Belfast in order
to get the training.
Mr. POLLOCK: No.
Mr. DONALD: I hope not. If it is to be developed that way I would be satisfied. The
next important question in the Speech is
with regard to rent restrictions. I think the
Government are well advised to postpone
this matter, although I am not in agreement
with other hon. Members. We could have
taken this question up, but a difficulty might
have arisen by our deciding one thing and
the Imperial Government deciding another.
It is a most difficult question. Yesterday it
developed into rents with houses. These two
are linked together, and, in my judgment,
the whole trouble arose through the Imperial
Government having restricted rents at all.
That was where the mischief was first
created. They restricted rents at a time
when the people were really able to pay a
fair increase on a sliding scale, in keeping
with their income at that time. But a most
unnatural thing is taking place to-day.
Rents are high and wages are low. The
people are not in a position to pay the rents.
That is the position we are confronted with
at the present time, due, I say, to Government interference. There is too much
Government interference (hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-not only with rents but with
housing. I want to see the private builder
getting in, for until the private builder gets
in we are not going to get houses. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
That is apparent, because somehow or other
I have a feeling, because I have learned
during the war that a private builder or a
private contractor could get a job through
much more quickly than with Government
interference and with their roundabout ways
of doing things. I have always found that
we get greater production when we are relieved from this kind of suspicion that gets
into the minds of the people "Well, we
know the money is all right. We will do as
little as we can." I am against that system.
I regretted very much to hear the speech and
the reference yesterday about output. Surely
our people will come to see the stupidity of
the working classes take that narrow view
they are their own enemies, because I am
convinced if we put our shoulders to the
wheel we could relieve the situation and get
houses very speedily. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) There is something more at the back
of the minds of the working classes. They
feel that there are "rings" holding up the
cost of other things. Undoubtedly that is
true. They say: "After all why should we
give everything and other people profiteer."
I could not help taking note of a speech I
read, and which I think dealt very
clearly with this subject. It was by a very
able Minister, and one whom I appreciated
when he was Minister of Health in the
Imperial House. He is one who has held
high place, but has now resigned owing to
ill-health. I refer to Sir Auckland Geddes.
Sir Auckland Geddes dealing with this
question referred first to prices. He said the
rise was due to the fall in the value of gold
and the unavoidable paper inflation which
accounted for 20 per cent. to 25 per cent. of
the increase; scarcity values; the diminished
utilisation of capital, the result in the main
of labour readjustment. Thank God we
have no labour readjustment in this part of
the country! Also to the diminished use of
shipping. We regret that also. My right
hon. Friend has given us an idea that freights
are going up. We trust they will go up; that
they will result in a revival in trade and
help the shipbuilding industry. He also said
it was due to unreasonable individual profitmaking. I say there is still unreasonable
individual profit-making in house building,
and that these "rings" that are holding up
cement, timber, and other materials that go
to the building of houses should be broken up
by some means. The right hon. Gentleman
said the cure for all this was increased production, increased export and import. I
agree with him.
The next matter on the paper is with
regard to the grants, or rather the financial
settlement where I see a sum of money will
be devoted to the renovation of our police
barracks. My right hon. Friend has left the.

The next question that I want to refer to

we are only going to get £300,000; that the

oney must be spent in a certain way." Now

Mr. DONALD: Thanks very much. That
puts our people on a par with those on the
other side. I do not see any necessity for

regard to the financial end. Of course that
is an important matter. I do not wish to go

hon. Friend who has charge of that end is
more capable of dealing with that question
than I am.
But I am very anxious about our
final settlement. I hope it will be good for
us, but the reason I am anxious is this. It
is in view of our position. I think we have
control of affairs here, yet we have not
control of our finances. Ninety per cent. is
supposed to be collected by the Imperial
authorities. We have only control of something like 10 per cent. That places us in a
very difficult position, and that is the reason
why I am impressed with this idea, that
that is why we cannot go on or develop these
schemes because we have not the money to
do it, nor have we the means of raising a
considerable amount of money. £14,000,000
have again been voted for relief of unemployment by the Imperial Government, not to
speak of all the development which will run
into £100,000,000 that is to be expended by
arrangement. I am sure this Government
will keep the obligations arranged by the late
Government.
The railways companies are going to do
tremendous work. I want to know has our
Government in contemplation any practical
scheme for the spending of this money on
the relief of unemployment over and above
these twopence-halfpenny schemes that are
going on. Why, there are only a few thousand people employed. Unless something is
done in the very near future for the relief
of unemployment you will have a serious
state of affairs arising here. Furthermore,
the unemployed on the other side are in a
much better position than the unemployed
here, because there is what is known as the
hybrid system for all unemployed in England,
Scotland, and Wales. These people get as
much unemployed benefit as our people, and
over and above that they get relief from another source. That has never been dealt
with in this part of the country.
As far as I

understand a Bill has been introduced to

Mr. CRAWFORD: I want to trespass upon
the time of the House for two or three
minutes in order to make one charge against
the Government, and two requests of them
on matters relevant to the Speech. The
Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock) in the
admirable speech which he delivered spoke
of the state of employment as being the
barometer of trade, and left the impression
on me, and I am sure on other hon. Members
of the House, that the Government is exceedingly anxious to reduce the number of
unemployed. I can only speak for the town
and district from which I come, when I say
that I think the Government are somewhat
responsible for the number of unemployed in
our midst. They seem to have an exceedingly
peculiar and hidebound way of passing plans
and things of that description in such a
manner as to keep back the work in the
various districts. I am not trying to clear
the people who send in the plans. Sometimes they do not send them in as accurately
as they ought to, but I venture to say that
any Government Department which gets the
plans of houses from a rural district and
does not look at them at all for two or three
weeks is failing in its duty. Even though
those plans are not correct they ought to be
looked at at a much earlier date, and the
errors in them pointed out so that the unemployed people might be employed
in rural and urban districts. It
is unreasonable that a Government official
should go down to an urban district and hold
an inquiry on the 20th day of December
regarding the expenditure of a considerable
sum of money, which would create employment for a great number of people who are
at present drawing the dole, and that from
the 20th December till the 11th March no
word should come from the Government as to
whether the application made at the inquiry
was favourably considered or not.
I know there are difficulties and considerable differences of opinion as to whether the
thing should be granted or not, but I think
the Government should not be so hidebound,
but should be more elastic in their methods
of doing things, and that this long time
should not be allowed to elapse between the
holding of the inquiry and the receipt of some
word. If the Government had been more
alert there would be less unemployment in
the district from which I come. I leave this
matter before the Government, and trust that
the Ministry of Home Affairs will see to it
that less time is wasted on matters of this
description in time to come. I was speaking
to a legal gentleman this morning, who sometimes looks at things from a humorous point
of view, and he said he was hopeful when this
new Explosives Bill passes that we would get
some way of stirring up the Government
officials. I would not go so far as that, but
I do hope that less delay will take place in
the future. I know the fault might be attributed, perhaps, to the errors in the plans,
and I know what the answer is likely to be,
but I hold that such errors should be pointed
out much earlier and the mistakes rectified
in order that the unemployed might be put
to work.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock)
also referred to the improvement in
the linen trade. I rejoice to hear of it, but
is that improvement not of a somewhat
fictitious nature? Is it not to be attributed
somewhat to the abnormally high price of
cotton that at present exists, and is that high
price of cotton not to be attributed to the
somewhat short crop last year, and also to
the action of a number of speculators, who
are holding up the cotton, and not allowing
it to find its way on to the open market? It
may be that this increase occurs not in the
ordinary course of supply and demand, but
from the fact that cotton is now nearly as
dear as linen. I would like the Minister of
Finance to assure the House and the farmers
that there is some hope that this increase is
a legitimate increase, and that the farmers
would be justified in producing more flax.
I have a pretty extensive knowledge of
farming, although I am a business man, and
Debate on the Address.
Debate on the Address.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Crawford]
I have taken out here an exact copy of the
amount it costs a farmer to produce fourteen
pecks of flax, that is, a bag sown on two
statute acres of land. I have the figures
a
here, and if it will not weary the House I
will give them, as I think they will be very
instructive. If you take for taxes, rent, and
interest on capital the sum of £5, which
would not be at all an adequate amount; if
you take for ploughing the fields the sum of
£2 for two statute acres, and it would not
pay it if a man had to hire horses and
plough; if you take £2 for making the ground
ready, and it takes an immense amount of
work to make the ground ready for flax after
it is ploughed; if you allow £5 to buy a bag of
seed-it will cost from sixty to sixty-five shillings now-and the artificial manure which is
necessary to grow flax; if you hire a man to
sow it in a scientific manner it will cost 10s;
if you allow £2 for harrowing the field and
rolling it afterwards; if you allow 10s for
weeding, £5 for pulling the flax after it is
grown, and £2 for carting it up a steep laneway to be steeped in the dams, and it would
not do it at all; if you allow £1 for putting
it into the dams, putting stones upon it,
examining it every day according to the
temperature of the weather, and trying to
discover if the flax is getting steeped
properly; if you allow £1 for throwing it out,
and I have seen it thrown out.
I have seen
a relative of my own in the water almost to
his waist throwing flax out when he could
not get a man to do it, and he has pointed
to a man a short distance away, and asked me
did I know what that man was doing, and
when I said I did not he has told me that he
was watching lest a drop of water from his
dam should escape into a burn and kill a
trout. It is a fact. A man was buried
some time ago. He could not get seven pecks
of flax thrown out of the dam unless he paid
35s for it, so he went into the water and
threw it out himself. He was a pretty
elderly man, and he contracted a cold which
resulted in his death. I know another man
who has three daughters, who help sometimes
to work on the farm as well as in the house,
and he was asked such an extravagant price
for the throwing of his flax out of the dam
that those girls said to their own father, "We
will never pay it," and they got up at three
o'clock in the morning, those three women,
and one of them went in to the flax dam up
to her waist and threw out the flax while her
sisters pulled it along the ground across the
field. I am only putting £1 down here, and
I would not take £50 and throw out a dam of
flax at three o'clock in the morning. For
carrying the flax from the dams to the field
allow £2; for spreading, a filthy job, allow
£2, for lifting it when it is dry allow £1, for
putting it into stooks, hovels, or stacks allow
£3, and it would not do it; for carting it to
the mill, perhaps four or five miles along a
country road, allow £2, for taking it to the
market £2, and for scutching it allow £8 8s.
When I total that up I find it comes to
£46 8s for fifty-six stones of flax. He sold it
in the open market for 12s 6d a stone, and
got £35 into his pocket for it, and at the
miserable prices I have quoted here it cost
him £46 8s. Finally, at the next Petty
Sessions Court he was fined 20s and costs
because he had allowed a little drop of water
to escape out of his flax dam. I can stand
over those figures, and I have submitted them
to the most eminent judge of agriculture in
this House, and he said I had underestimated
if anything. In the face of those figures,
unless the Government are prepared to do
something for the farmers that will give
them an opportunity to get a price for their
flax, I do not think you need ask the farmers
of Northern Ireland to grow flax. They get
less than a shilling per pound at the average
of fourteen shillings per stone, which is a
high average.
I was sitting the other day on a Board
which was accepting contracts for a large
institution in County Antrim, and I was
greatly struck by the fact that the prices
quoted for linen-thread was 16s, I think, per
pound. I am speaking from memory and
cannot say exactly whether it was 15s or 16s,
but I would point out to the House that the
farmer, who produces the flax and sells it in
the market at less than one shilling per
pound, loses a matter of £11, and that every
other person who touches the flax from the
time the farmer sells it until it reaches the
consumer is paid, as he ought to be, a decent
wage. The directors and shareholders of the
mills and factories can make a good profit,
pay a good dividend, and build up a reserve
fund, while the poor farmer who produces
the flax does it at a loss, and the Government ask him now to continue doing it and
to produce more. I blame no manufacturer,
I blame no worker. They all have the right
to good wages and a good profit, but I say
again that unless you are prepared to do
something for the farmers you cannot expect
them to produce the raw material. What
can you do? The Government say they have
established a Faculty of Agriculture and
appointed a professor in the city of Belfast,
in connection with the University, to lecture
upon agriculture. How many of our small
farmers are going to send their sons to the
University for these things?
Mr. POLLOCK: It is for research purposes.
Mr. CRAWFORD: It is not going to be of
tremendous use. Then you say you will send
instructors round the country and have
classes in that way. That is an admirable
thing, but what are you doing by that work?
You are educating the young people, and in

connection with one denomination alone in

Are they able to promise the farmers that

an important thing. Can you do anything at

The farmers are the salt of the earth. They
are producing food and everything that we
require, and they must get something. What
can you do for them in order to give them a
chance to produce things for us at a price
that will give the people employment? I
hope the Government will see to it that some
subsidy is given to the farmers, especially in
this matter of flax, so that they may be able
to produce the raw material and reduce the
unemployment that exists in the factories and
mills of the country. Having said so much
about the farmers, I hope the Minister of
'Agriculture will give us some hope in this
matter.
I see that a good deal of money is to be
spent in the construction and renovation of
police barracks throughout the country, and
I want to draw the attention of the Government to one portion of the country that the
police were removed from some time ago.
There are eighty square miles of the County
of Antrim in which there are no policemen
at all. It is immensely creditable to the
people of the Templepatrick district that
they are so peaceful and law-abiding. I
remember reading in Holy Writ of a district
that was so peaceable that there was neither
magistrate in the land nor bar nor bolt in
the doors. The peace and prosperity of that
part of the country attracted a band of people
who were looking for booty, and they came
and took advantage of the peace and prosperity of the place, ousted the inhabitants,
and took possession of their crops and stocks.
I do not want that to occur in the peaceful
district of Templepatrick, and I ask the
Government is eighty square miles of country
not too large an area to be left without a
police barracks? I will tell you of something that happened in the case of a respectable clergyman. A gang in a motor-car came
to his door and demanded to be put up for
the night. He was compelled to let them
take refuge in a loft, and he afterwards discovered that one of the men, who was
wanted for a serious crime, escaped to
America. I say the Government is not doing
its duty when it allows eighty square miles
of country to go without a policeman, and in
connection with this construction and renovation work I hope to get an assurance that
Templepatrick and Parkgate will have a
police barracks as was the case for many
years. A magistrate told me that, like
Othello, his occupation was gone. It is not
the thing to appoint magistrates, and not
give them something to do. I hope the
Government will see to this matter. There
are some other things to which my attention
has just been drawn in the matter of flax,
but I will leave them to be dealt with by
another speaker.
Mr. ROBB: I want to make only one or
two observations in regard to the Speech from
the Throne and the statement of the Minister
of Finance. I agree with those Members of
the House who expressed a good deal of impatience at the delay in the introduction of
the Rent Restrictions Act. The Prime
Minister at the end of last Session promised
that the first measure that would be brought
before us this Session would be a Rent
Restrictions Bill for Northern Ireland, and
now, in the Speech from the Throne we are
told that we have to wait on England. Why
should we wait on England? (Hon. Members:
"Hear, hear.") Is this House to be committed definitely to the policy of always waiting until the House of Commons in London
passes an Act? And, if we are to wait, is
this House to be bound slavishly to follow
every such Act? Our conditions are not, or
at any rate may not be, the same as in England. We have here the material and the
machinery for making our own laws upon
this subject, and I cannot understand at all
why it is necessary, when our conditions are
not the same, to wait for the passing of an
Act in London for Great Britain. Surely we
can do these things for ourselves.
There is another matter I would like to
mention. Arising out of the reference in the
Gracious Speech to an improvement in the
linen trade, the Minister of Finance made an
appeal to the farmers to grow flax. It might
be that what the Minister of Finance said
would be interpreted as in some way blaming
the farmer.
Mr. POLLOCK: No.

Dr. MORRISON: I would like to make a
remark or two in connection with the speech
of the hon. Member for the County of
Antrim (Mr. Crawford). I cannot
with him that the Government Offices in
Northern Ireland need an explosive to waken
them. My experience of them is that they
attend to any business that is put
before them with a great amount
of ability, and I think, if my
experience is uniform, there is no reasonable ground of complaint. I speak specially
of Finance, Home Affairs, and Labour. 1
sympathise a good deal with the picture that
he has drawn of the difficulties that face the
farmer, but the remedy that he suggests is
not to my mind adequate. I think that something might be done. I met two very clever
men, I think representing spinning, in the
city two nights ago, and one of them told me
that an important society in Ulster, the Agricultural Research Society, is carrying out
very valuable experiments in an English
county, and that there is a difficulty in financing the undertaking. He says the seed they
are purchasing and trying to grow in sufficient quantity will practically, in his opinion,
revolutionise the product of fibre from the
flax grown, and that it will be necessary for
the Government to help them. I think any
scheme like that, which offers a good prospect,
will meet with a hearty response from this
Government of Northern Ireland. We have
now an organised Agricultural Society that
can speak with authority for the farmers of
Northern Ireland. I see one of the leading
members in this House to-day, and I tell him,
and I tell the other members of these societies
that if they formulate a policy-which they
are quite capable of doing-and put it before
this Government and before this House I am
sure it will receive sympathetic consideration,
and that if anything can be done it will be
done by the Government and by the members
of the House.
But I did not get up to speak on
this
matter. I wanted to say a few things with
regard to the Speech from the Throne. It
covers very many points. There is one point
of which I think notice should be taken. It
has already been referred to by my colleague
from the University. That is, the friendly
attitude that the Labour Government have
shown to Ulster. I think that many of us
had doubts in our mind as to how we would
be treated if a Labour, or even a Liberal,
Government got into office. It should be a
great satisfaction to all of us that they have
approached this question not from a party
standpoint but from the great, broad
principle that Ulster is a loyal, prosperous,
and industrious unit in the Empire, and deserves the support of all parties irrespective
of politics. In connection with that I think
there is a corresponding obligation on us.
In my opinion it would be a wise course if we
as a party remained neutral in party controversies across the water, and we did not interfere in English elections. I can imagine
that if our Prime Minister went to the
Prime Minister of a Labour Government,
and the Prime Minister of the Labour

he would think it was very unfair. I merely

What I wish to speak specially about is
this Illegitimacy Bill, which is mentioned in
the King's Speech. In connection with that
I would like to congratulate the Minister of
Home Affairs and his Deputy, and I think I
should include in my congratulations the
very able official who looks after Local
Government Board work in the Home Office,
namely, Major Harris. A good deal of condemnation and criticism has been expended
on the Ministry of Home Affairs. Some of
it is probably deserved, but I am certain a
great deal of it is undeserved. I think that
by and by, when these controversies have
subsided and disappeared, it will be found
when the history of Ulster is written, that
the Minister of Home Affairs has immortalised himself by placing a Bill of this nature
on the Statute Book of Northern Ireland.
It removes a stain that unfortunately has
lain upon this Province for a long time. It
is inconceivable to the average mind that for
fifty years the girls in Ireland have been
without the protection that their sisters in
England have. For those fifty years these
girls have been outside the law, but now the
question is viewed by us and by every reasonable man from a new standpoint.
We believe that the ideal of womanhood
lies neither in the fair saint nor fair sinner.
The female type of character is neither worse
nor better than the male, only weaker. Women
are meant to be neither men's guides nor
their play things, but their comrades, their
fellows, and their equals so far as nature
puts no bar to that equality. In potential
motherhood nature has put a bar, and seeing
that this is her lot she is found to be fearfully weighted in the race of life. It is, therefore, the duty of men to see that not one
ounce is put upon that load beyond what

Captain MULHOLLAND: It is a matter of
great regret that my right hon. Friend, the

to bring up the question of agriculture at

opening for my right hon. Friend to reply.
It is unnecessary for me to tell the House
once more of the importance of agriculture.
It is fully recognised by everyone that our
great industries of linen and shipbuilding
rest on the position of agriculture in this
country.
Hon. Members are perhaps feeling rather
anxious as to what subjects I am going to
discuss, and I would like to ease their minds
immediately by saying that the one subject
I am not going to discuss this afternoon is
the subject of goats. (Laughter.) I had intended to enter into the question of flax, but
my hon. Friend the Member for Antrim (Mr.
Crawford) has dealt with that question very
fully. It is a very important matter to us
in the country districts that we should grow
large crops of flax. My right hon. Friend
the Minister of Finance, in his admirable
speech on Tuesday, made use of these words:
If only a full and adequate supply of raw
material can be guaranteed, every mill in
the Province can return to full time work.
That is a very wide statement, and if it is
true, as I have no doubt it is, it points to a
great future for our farmers in the country
districts. But I would say to my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Pollock) that either he or my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Agriculture
(Mr. Archdale) should go a good deal further
into this matter. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). After all you cannot tell farmers or
advise farmers to grow flax just as you might
advise a man to grow mustard and cress in
his garden As my hon. Friend the Member
for Antrim (Mr. Crawford) has pointed out
it is a speculative crop, and unless you have
very strong indications that the price of
flax will be remunerative to farmers
you will not get them to grow flax
throughout the Six Counties. It is difficult to offer suggestions as to how farmers
would have an adequate price, but it is
possible that the other gentlemen interested
in the trade might get together and buy flax
in advance or else give guarantees that the
farmers would get a reasonable price.
What I would like the Minister of Agriculture to tell us is the various indications of
prosperity in the agricultural industry. I
would like to get some information about the
potato trade this year. It is within the
recollection of hon. Members that last year
potatoes could not be sold, and some farmers
were giving them away in order to get the
land clear. I would like the Ministry of
Agriculture to give some information as to
the varieties of potato that have been grown
in the past year, and as to whether they are
considered suitable for the Bristol Channel
ports. I would also like to know whether
the restricted areas have been extended or
decreased, and how the black scab disease
has been progressing. As everybody knows,
the millennium of the potato farming
industry in this country is that the whole of
the Six Counties should grow immune
varieties, and as to how far that has progressed the Ministry of Agriculture might be
able to inform us later on. Another point of
great importance is the milk recording stations,
and also the registration of bulls. I would
like to know how far the scheme has progressed, and whether it has proved a success.
Hon. Members will agree that it costs as
much to feed a cow producing 300 gallons of
milk as it costs to feed a cow that produces
900 gallons. It is almost staggering to the
imagination to realise that if we could only
raise the average in the Six Counties up to
600 or 700 gallons per cow the output would
be so enormous that it would bring a great
deal of employment to our population.
Then there is the question of poultry. The
hen is an animal which is very often laughed
and sneered at. Hon. Members will laugh
and sneer at hens, but they will eat eggs at
breakfast each morning with the greatest of
relish-if they are eggs in a reliable form.
The hen has now become a machine, a
machine which enables the foreigner to
import every year into the British Isles eight
million pounds sterling of eggs in the shell.
That is a market the greater portion of
which we can grasp if farmers would only
realise one or two facts about poultry. The
Ministry of Agriculture might be able to
do and I believe they are doing to a certain
extent a great deal of good in this direction.
I understand more money will be available
for this purpose, and I hope they will con-

It is not everyone who knows that from the
Cockerel descends three-fourths of the producing qualities of the egg. It is not everyone
who knows that the egg-laying propensities
descend from the Cockerel to the female and
not from the female to females. In other
words a well-considered scheme of registering Cockerels or else of spreading Cockerels
throughout the Six Counties and not
allowing bad Cockerels to be used
in flocks would result in an enormous increase in the eggs we export from this country. I am not exaggerating when I say that
if attention was paid to that point, and that
point only, we could easily double our output within one year. At the present moment,
take the average farmer who takes no
particular trouble about this subject. You
will find that the average number of eggs
laid by his hens during the year would not
amount to more than 40 or 50. It is a matter
easily within the practical possibility of any
farmer to have a flock which would average
at least 160. At the present day there are
flocks in Northern Ireland averaging 180
eggs per hen. It may sound a small thing,
but when you take the thousands and thousands of hens that exist in Northern Ireland
I can assure you that the eight million
pounds worth of eggs imported into the
British Isles could be very easily met now
to a great extent by Northern Ireland.
There is a great future for the egg-laying
industry, and I would commend this subject
to the Ministry of Agriculture.

the Ministry of Agriculture are fully alive to

Mr. MARK: I would like to add a few remarks to those of the hon. Member (Captain
Mulholland) on the question of agriculture.
The hon Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford)
has given very interesting figures, which I
had the opportunity of seeing just before I
entered this House, and I can assure hon.
Members that he is really within the price
when he quotes the figures he has given with
regard to the production of flax. No farmer
to-day, at the present rate of wages in the
country, could grow one acre of flax, or two
acres or ten acres, to pay for the cost of
production. But that is nothing very strange
in the agricultural world to-day, because I
do not believe for a moment that a farmer
can grow any crop now which would pay for
the cost of production. Last year, undoubtedly we had potatoes going to waste. One farmer told me he had 100 tons of potatoes that
went to waste. He bought cattle to eat them.
They managed that part all right, but
when the slump in the prices of cattle came
he only got the cost price of the cattle. He
lost £8 per head on the cattle. This year no
farmer has any potatoes to sell. I saw a man,
whom I knew to be a summons server, going
round a country district the other day carrying a huge bag. I saw him serving a summons on an individual. I asked him, "What
are you doing? Are you giving him something?" He said he was. He was burdened
with summonses for the payment of rates by
the agriculturists of Northern Ireland.
Where that state of affairs exists it will, I
am sure, be evident to hon. Members that
agriculture has reached a very low ebb.
I came across one particular case recently,
where a man bought a small farm for £700.
He had a small overdraft at the bank. His
wife got a little money left her by a friend
who died, and they sold out the shares and
paid off the overdraft. Notwithstanding
very frugal management the farmer got into
debt again; and only a few weeks ago they
had to sell out. They sold in time to pay
their debts, and now they are left without a
penny. That state of affairs will be brought
more to our attention during the next two
years. We heard in reply to a question that
this Government is going to follow in the

people to speak, but it was suggested to me
there were one or two matters in which I
was greatly interested and on which I should
say a few words, particularly as these two

Before touching on these two matters, I
would like for a few minutes to say something
on what I consider the sin of omission in
the speech, and that is what has been referred to by the hon. Member for the University
Dr. Morrison), and on which he and I
worked together a good deal last year. I had
hoped that in the Gracious Speech from the
Throne we should have a promise that before
the Education Act was put into force in the
counties there would have been an Amending
Act. The Education Act in the counties is
entirely different from what it has been in
the cities. It is not to come into operation
till 1st October next, and in connection with
that I would like to dissociate myself
from some remarks that fell from a colleague of mine which suggested that
the Government were afraid to put the
Act into force in the counties. I was
one of those who advocated both in
public, in this House on the Third
Reading of the Bill, and in private
with the Minister of Education and the
Prime Minister that this Education Act
should not be put into force in the counties
until after the Local Government elections,
so that the people should have a say at those
elections as to who should represent them
on these councils, which, for the first time,
should take over education. The Government conceded that, and for that reason I
do not like it to go abroad that it was the
fault of the Government, because the
Government were merely doing what a good
many of us who represent the country districts asked them to do.
I am sorry that the Government could not
see their way to fall in with the suggestion
that has been made all over the country
about Section 66, sub-Section 3. The
Minister of Finance in all the time that he
devoted to the Education Act, in his speech
the other day went altogether on one point.
That was the point of religious teaching, and
my hon. Friend, the Member for the University (Dr. Morrison) to-day, went mostly
on that point too. I do not intend to touch
that point at all. I suppose I should be
honest; I am not in the least deceived
by the Minister of Finance. Everything that
the Minister of Finance says I am very sure
happened. I was not at the meeting, but 1
met the Minister of Finance coming out
and I had at that time four amendments to
that particular clause to be proposed that
afternoon. When I went into the meeting,
which was still sitting, I was asked to withdraw my four amendments, and that is the
reason I am taking no more part in that
controversy. I was told by the representatives of the Churches that they were
satisfied with what the messenger of peace
who had come from the Government had
said, and I withdrew those amendments.
I was not the least deceived, and for that
reason I do not want to touch the thing at
all because, so far as I am concerned, it is
over. It is the other point that has created
such consternation in the country. I was
at a meeting in my own constituency a week
ago, and this question came up for consideration, and a resolution was passed asking me
to vote against the Government. Even if
my vote would put the Government out I
was asked to vote against them. Why?
Because of this Section 66, sub-Section 3.
The country is alarmed and indignant, and
I really cannot understand the mentality of
the Government who seem to me to be rushing down the steep place into the Sea of
Destruction on this matter. I do not believe
that in my part of the country if there was
an election the Government candidate
would get as many men as would nominate
him, and he certainly would lose his £150
deposit.

I take it that the Government will do

where is our industry to come from? (Hon.

was wondering what inducement the farmer

myself could the Government, through the
able Minister of Agriculture, in some shape
or form bring the spinners and the Farmers'

with the understanding that when it

the Minister of Agriculture gets upon the
floor of the House-as I hope he will very
soon be restored to his former health-he
may be able to work out some scheme which

for the welfare of our people.
Everybody knows that there has been a

But what was the actual condition in
which we took over? We were suffering
from a world-racking war which had shaken
every civilised community and taxed every
resource of men and governments, taxed the
patience of every population and every
country in the world, wearied them at times
to. a feeling of exasperation at the wholesale
disturbance of commerce, business, and industry, and then the sudden throwing back
into the ordinary course of commerce of a large
number of men who had been called out to
the defence of their country.
Apart from
these general conditions which prevailed over
the world, we in Ireland had added to it a
condition practically of rebellion. At all
times there was a feeling of dissension between
the two parties of our country, and unfortunately to the two parties who had
always existed in Ireland, there was added
a third party at that time. I refer to the
Republican Party, who seemed absolutely
opposed to any form of recognised government, and opposed to any sense of loyalty or
attachment to England which even might
exist in the Southern part of this island.

Then again there was this condition of unemployment. I really think sufficient stress
has not been laid upon the peculiar conditions
which attached to our Province here. I do
not say unfortunately. I think every one of
us regard it as a fortunate thing that the
great productions of our industries here
were matters of vital importance in the conduct of the war. There is no doubt that in
our shipyards and in our linen industries we
had two absolutely indispensable factors in
carrying on and in the preservation of our
country. This had different results. One
was that it caused these businesses to be more
subject to Government interference and
Government regulations than industries of a
less essential character. It had also the effect
of drawing into this part of the world a very
large additional number of working poeple to
those who were in the ordinary habit of
living about here. A large number of loyal
men went out to the front, and not only
were the places of these men filled by men
who had not felt called to the defence of
their country as strongly as ours had, but our
shipbuilding yards during those few years of
the war added to their capacity nearly as
much as was the accumulated growth of their
previous existence. Such an expansion in our
industry really could hardly have been conceived. Those in our industry, for the
ordinary products of which we enjoyed
world-wide reputation, were practically prohibited from manufacturing them. The
work of the spinners and weavers had to be

A number of the matters which have been
Idealt with in the course of this Debate on
the Address are matters necessarily which
might possibly have been more fruitfully
dealt with had they been raised at Westminster. They were the actions of the Parliament at Westminster in some respects
which have been most severely criticised.
For instance, there is that sum of £500,000,
which is so familiar to us all. We must
remember that that was in the nature of a
free gift to this part of the country, more
or less without counterpart in any expenditure of the United Kingdom. It was made
to us at a time when we were struggling
with difficulties over here. It was volunteered by the Imperial Parliament, or by
the Government of the time, and at the time
it was given conditions were attached to it.
I think our Prime Minister and our Minister
of Labour, instead of being criticised for the
way in which we were bound to administer
this fund once it was given to us, deserve
our thanks. The sense of gratitude seems
to have vanished. We owe a great deal to
those two right hon. Gentlemen for getting
that money and making it available in this
part of the world; but, whatever we may
feel, everyone of us must entertain a sense
of disappointment. Although I do not like
to dwell upon the sense of injustice to Ireland, this affords an instance of treatment
to which really one is almost justified in
giving that name. We certainly were led
to expect that we would get this £500,000.
It was handed over to our Minister of
Labour, and he very properly wished to see
that that money, although it was given for
the relief of unemployment, was spent upon
some justifiable, some useful object. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) It has been said
here that our working people do not want
money if they possibly can help it.
Mr. McGUFFIN: The dole.
Mr. BARBOUR: They do not want
charity, which is the same thing. If my
hon. Friend (Mr. McGuffin) will permit me
to finish the sentence, they want to feel that
they are trying to give value for whatever they
receive. In order to get this money laid out
it was necessary to interest our large public
bodies to institute schemes. These were then
submitted to a Committee, and the schemes
approved of or not as that Committee thought
right. It was only after the money had
actally been spent that we were able to draw
on that £500,000 from England. The
schemes necessarily were of a character
that took a long time to complete. The Committee did
they could to try to ensure
schemes would be completed with the least
everything

In spite of what I have said I would not
like any hon. Member to think that this
Government, having referred the settlement
of matters of this kind to the Colwyn Committee, are not going to accept loyally the
findings of that Committee. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). We certainly would not wish

On the matter of education I would like
hon. Members to listen to me more in my
individual capacity, but still as one who is
keenly interested in education. It struck
me that this House had unanimously accepted the principle that our Education Act
should be of a non-sectarian character. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). We realised that
we have in this Province people holding
very conflicting views, and so it was the
attitude of this House that, in dealing with
an Act which affected every family throughout the Six Counties, we should try to make
it sufficiently elastic that it would be
possible in one way or another for every
member of all the communities in the Six
Counties to take advantage of the facilities
which existed and yet not to do violence to
his religious or conscientious scruples. I
think the Act accomplishes this. If there
is any reluctance to transfer schools there
certainly is no object in transferring them
at the present time, and I would not call
any man disloyal, or say that he was in
any way attempting to thwart the proper
working of this Act, if he did delay in
transferring a school in order to see how
the Act is going to work out. We must
remember that it is possible to retain control of your own school, to carry on
practically under the old conditions and yet
receive 95 or 96 per cent. of the cost of
conducting your school from the Government under this Act. Therefore, whatever
party, or body, or individual, who retains
what he sets such store on, namely the
appointment of teachers and the management of his schools, is able to do that at
a cost of, say, three or four per cent. of
the total cost of running the school. That, I
think, is very generous support.
Another thing which has been repeatedly
affirmed in this House-I daresay some are
more enthusiastic in their support than
others--is that this is a democratic age, and
we want to try to get control of all public
activities more and more under democratic
lines. The object of the Education Act is
to decentralise, to make the control of a
more and more popular character, and in
this, again, I believe that if people, instead
of showing ruffled feelings where, perhaps,
their old rights have been encroached upon
in some way, if they have the real interests
of education at heart, approach this by
saying "Well, here is this Act, which places
more money at our disposal than ever before;
let us see if we cannot improve on it, and take
hold of it with the determination to make it
as efficient as possible," we will have a better
system of education than ever before. It is
not so long to wait, so I would appeal to
everybody, both in this House and outside, to
give the Act a fair trial and try to make it
the success we would like to see it.
Comment has been made about the expenditure which has taken place in the city of
Belfast as compared with the Counties. Those
who bear the weight of public affairs con-

where the Imperial Parliament is concerned,

The question of land purchase had been
brought up to the point when it was practically ready for submission to the Imperial
House, when unfortunately the Government
under Mr. Baldwin was defeated. In the
course of negotiations which have taken place
the new Government have informed us-and
we must accept their word-that they will
honour any commitments into which their
predecessors entered. That is the present state
of the negotiations.
Mr. POLLOCK: If non-controversial.
Mr. BARBOUR: If non-controversial. So
I think we can count with a fair measure of
confidence on that Bill being passed through
Westminster if we agree, and if the farmers
and landowners in the Six Counties accept
the Bill as provisionally drawn up. I believe
that every Member of this House will do the
farmers throughout the Six Counties a good
service if he will do his very best to persuade
hem to accept the Bill which has been drawn
up to try to do justice between the parties,
and thus to ensure that it will be passed.
Otherwise it will be thrown back, and I am
afraid this much-desired reform will be delayed many years.
Reference has been made in the Governor's
Gracious Speech to another thing which is of
considerable importance to the country districts, that is the improvement of the police
barracks. It is intended, as soon as this work
can be taken up, to spend between £400,000
and £500,000 in the remodelling of the police
barracks throughout the Six Counties. This
will be financed by means of a sinking fund
extending over a period of 20 years, so that,
while we hope to derive immediate benefit in
the shape of employment and better accommodation for our Constabulary, the burden
will not be too oppressive at the start.
THE
PARLIAMENTARY
SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw): It falls to my lot to reply to
some of the comments that have been made in
regard to matters that are specially associated with the Ministry of Home Affairs. The
Member for West Belfast (Sir R. Lynn), who
always approaches matters in the most
common-sense way, if I may say so, drew
attention to the housing question. It is, as
he said, one of the most important questions
affecting us at present, and he naturally asked
for information as to how the Act that was
passed last year was working, and how many
schemes had been passed under the provisions
of that Act. The position of the Ministry of
Home Affairs with regard to that matter is
this they have prepared and published regulations under which the amounts voted will be
given, and it has been fully explained to
the various Councils concerned how they
may take advantage of the provisions of this
measure. Under the Act it is necessary for
the various local authorities to pass resolutions putting the scheme into operation, so
that the amount of the free loan may be
made available for them. I am glad to say
that resolutions have been already passed by
upwards of thirteen urban district councils
and one rural district council. These have
indicated their desire to make grants
corresponding to the £60 given in respect of
each house by this Government. Twentyfour other authorities have the matter under
their consideration. It has not fructified yet,
but the Ministry of Home Affairs hopes that
before very long these bodies will also have
passed resolutions making the scheme available for themselves. While the Ministry regrets that certain bodies are holding back,
it feels, all the same, that they are likely to
come in, and that the undoubted advantages
given by the Act passed last year will be
taken advantage of. It is evident, on the
face of it, how much this would be to the
advantage of the local authorities themselves.
Take a case where a scheme for 100 houses is
passed. £40 advanced by the local authoritv
in respect of each house would mean they
would be liable for a sum of £4,000. According to the scheme available, that amount
would be repayable over forty years, and on
the terms on which they could get money it
would involve in respect of each house that
a payment of £2 6s 0d a year would have to
be made by the local authority. When one
takes into consideration the amount of rates
and taxes that would be payable, as well as
the great advantage that is given to the
community, it is absolutely clear that it
would be of very great advantage to those
bodies themselves to put into force the provisions of the Act.

His remarks on that subject are certainly well

A few other questions were touched upon
by some of the members in the course of the
debate on the Address in reply to the
Governor's Gracious Speech. My colleague
for County Antrim (Mr. Crawford) occupied

have to make with regard to the criticism
that he offered. He is a very rigid economist
in the abstract, but when he gets on his
feet for practical purposes no man is more

police, that 3,000 in the Royal Ulster Constabulary was out of all proportion to the

the men to come from? Are we going to take
them away from the Border and other places
where they are needed in order to have an
ornamental force? Those who have control
of the force have done their best to try to
establish the police in the places that
they are most needed, and we are very
glad to learn that there is such an area in

The hon. Member for Antrim then took exception to what the Ministry had done in
regard to some works that he said were badly
needed about Ballymena. I have looked into

points that he raised. He took exception to

furnished were entirely sketch plans,

the houses proposed to be built, with the

New plans have been forwarded now by the

were
Another point he mentioned was in regard
to the Town Hall of Ballymena, and he complained of great delay that had taken place
in sanctioning the expenditure. What are
the facts? An inquiry was held on the 20th
December of last year, but the notes of the
evidence taken at the inquiry were not received till the 7th January. These local
bodies often say that, instead of having an
official reporter, they can get a reporter on
the spot. They did so in Ballymena, and the
notes that were furnished were not quite full,
and in some parts they were mistaken. Some
delay was caused in regard to that, but the
inspector reported on the 8th February, and
the Ministry on the 8th March, after dealing
with the plans, and after studying the report
of their inspector, wrote to the Ballymena
Urban District Council with regard to it. I
do not see how the thing could have been done
more quickly, unless there had been a greater
staff employed by the Ministry of Home
Affairs, which is very busily engaged in a
great many other matters as well as the
housing question. Of course, if we have a
larger staff, and no objections are taken to
that, we can deal with the matters very much
more expeditiously.
I do not think that the other criticisms of
various Members dealt very much with matters that come under the purview of the
Ministry of Home Affairs, except the remarks
of the Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh
(Mr. Miller). He made reference to the inquiry into Poor-law reform. I am glad to
say that that inquiry is awakening so much

about the chairman, but once a chairman has
been arranged I think the Committee will

Loans Guarantee (Money).
Considered in Committee.
(Mr. MOLES in the Chair).
Motion made and Question proposed :-

'That it is expedient to amend the Loans
Guarantee Acts, Northern Ireland, 1922 and
1923-
(i) by increasing from £3,500,000 to
£5,000,000 the limit on the aggregate capital
amount of the loans, the principal or interest of which may be guaranteed by the
Ministry of Finance thereunder; and
(ii) by extending to the 31st day of March,
1925, the period within which guarantees
may be given under the Loans Guarantee
Act, Northern Ireland, 1922;
and to charge on the Consolidated Fund of
Northern Ireland any moneys required for
fulfilling any such guarantees."
Mr. BARBOUR: This is a Money Resolution preparatory to the bringing in of a Bill
to amend the Loans Guarantee Act. The
whole effect of the Amending Bill will be to
extend the amount from three-and-a-half
millions to five millions, and to extend the
period to 31st March, 1925. The object of the
Bill is also to charge on the Consolidated
Fund of Northern Ireland any moneys required for borrowing under such guarantees,
but the Committee who have charge of granting these sums exercise the greatest caution,
and it is not expected that any charge will
eventually fall on the Consolidated Fund of
Northern Ireland. I should like to give the
slight additional information desired by hon.
Members on the Second Reading of the Bill.
I will now confine myself to moving accordingly.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I inquire if it is
proposed in respect of this matter to restrict
the guarantees in present limitations, not to
exclude, for instance, the linen industry or
other cognate industry that might very well,
and in the interests of the country, look for
support or for credit?
Mr. BARBOUR: We do not in this
amending Bill propose to introduce any new
principles or new features. The guarantees
are restricted absolutely to purposes of a
Capital nature,

THE DISMISSAL OF DISTRICT-
INSPECTOR NIXON.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn."-(Captain
Dixon).
Mr. GRANT: I would just like to take this
opportunity of raising a question which
was discussed in this House yesterday, but
I hope that the discussion will not be on
the same lines as it took yesterday; that is,
that there will not be any heat engendered
in the discussion, because I rather regret
that even from the Government benches,
as well as from other parts of the House,
there was too much feeling introduced into
the matter. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I want to say at the outset that I do not agree
personally with everything that has been
said regarding the Nixon case in this House.
I do want to tell the members of the Government that there is a strong feeling outside
the House that this man has not been fairly
dealt with, and I want to approach the
matter rather with the object of holding out
the olive branch, to see if something cannot
be done to settle matters. I want to remind
the members of the Government that in the
South of Ireland a number of officers of
high position perpetrated a worse crime
than that-
Mr. DONALD: On a point of order, it is
rather unfortunate that during this discussion
there is not present a representative of the
Home Office.
Mr. SPEAKER: Yes, one is here.
THE PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw) rose.
Mr. DONALD: I beg your pardon.
Mr. GRANT: In the South of Ireland a
number of very high officers of the Free State
Army have committed a very serious crimethe crime of mutiny, the punishment for
which is death. I understand that these
men are willing to apologise, and that Mr.
Cosgrave, the President of the Free State, is
prepared to accept their apology, so I presume there is to be no further punishment
for these officers, I think under the circumstances and owing to the great feeling there
is in Northern Ireland to-day the Government
should reconsider this question-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and that Mr. Nixon
should be asked to apologise. I make this
suggestion in the interests of peace because
those who are supporters of Mr Nixon are
good loyalists and those who are supporters
of the Government are equally good loyalists.
I think that all of them have done their
bit in helping to preserve Ulster from an
invasion by Sinn Fein. I think Mr. Nixon
should be asked to apologise for any indiscretion of which he may have been guilty,
call it want of discipline if you like, and once
that apology has been tendered I think the
Government should be generous and receive
it and reinstate Mr. Nixon. If they do so
I am quite certain the Government will have
vindicated their position. No good will come
of making a victim of any man, and
there is a feeling that Mr. Nixon has been
a victim, but at the same time no good will
come from any official defying the Government.
It was mentioned by the hon. Member
(Mr. Coote), whose absence we regret to-day,
that my position in this House is that of an
apologist on behalf of the Government, or
otherwise a maid-of-all-work. I think if I am
able to do something to clear up this mess I
will be fully entitled to the name put upon
me yesterday. In all seriousness I appeal to
the Government to take the long and the
broad view of this matter, and to do everything they possibly can in the interests of
peace. I know that some Members of the
Ministry of Home Affairs rather lost their
tempers yesterday in this discussion-that is
to be regretted-and they actually replied to
the discussion before they had heard the
points put up. I hope they will not let anything that occurred in the House yesterday
interfere with them now, and I appeal to the
Government and I appeal to hon. Members
of the House in the interests of the peace of
our community to do all they possibly can to
have this matter agreeably settled, so that
both sides may be satisfied and the good feeling which exists amongst our people may be
carried on in the future.

much to sympathise with the case that has

Colonel WOODS: I wish to repeat what I
said yesterday, and that is, that the Government when they authorised the police to have
an Orange Lodge of their own knew the
consequences of their action, and that political speeches would be made in the Orange
Lodge. I hold that a misunderstanding exists
in regard to the matter. Mr Nixon made
his first speech on the 4th January, I believe,
and after that an instruction was issued by
the Inspector-General that no political
speeches were to be made. I have seen that
circular, and a very reasonable one it is.
But I hold that it was a private speech made
in an Orange Lodge, and that Mr. Nixon did
not know that it would be published. Therefore, so far as that circular was concerned,
it was not a political speech in the ordinary
sense of the word. A misunderstanding exists
in that respect. If the Government can
prove that Mr. Nixon knew it was to be made
public, then I hold there is no excuse for Mr.
Nixon, and the Government is perfectly
justified in its action; but if he did not
know the speech was to be published, then
I hold it was a misunderstanding and a
mistake upon the part of the Government.

18 MARCH, 1924.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 18th March, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
OLD AGE PENSIONS AND WORKHOUSE
INMATES.
1 Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether old age pensioners who,
through sickness enter a Union Hospital,
have their pensions cancelled; if so, on what
conditions; and whether, after being discharged from hospital, a fresh claim has to
be made for their old age pensions?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): Under Section 3 (1) of
the Old Age Pension Act of 1919 a person who
has become an inmate of any workhouse or
other Poor-Law institution for the purpose of
obtaining medical or surgical treatment is
not disqualified for receiving or continuing to
receive an old age pension during a period of
three months from the date on which he or
she enters the workhouse or institution as
long as such medical or surgical treatment is
required. If the person remain in the institution for a longer period than three months,
then, under the provisions of the Section, he
or she would become disqualified, and would
have to make a fresh claim for pension on
leaving the institution.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman
if he does not consider that the old age pensioners have a grievance inasmuch as they
would have to re-apply for the pension? They
find it very difficult at any time to make the
claim, and I suppose they would find it even
more difficult to ask that it should be renewed.
Could the right hon. Gentleman, therefore,
not abolish this procedure?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not think there
would be any great difficulty, because the
facts would already be before the Old Age
Pension Committee, and they could deal with
a case very rapidly.
Mr. DONALD: My object in putting the
question was to ascertain the existing law on
the matter, and I am quite satisfied with my
right hon. Friend's answer.
DEPARTMENTAL COMMITTEE ON
VALUATION.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance whether the Departmental Committee on Valuation have concluded their
labours; if so, whether a final report will be
issued, and whether it is proposed to introduce legislation dealing with this matter?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am informed that the investigations of the Departmental Committee on
Valuation have been completed and that the
Committee now have under discussion the
terms of their final report.
Before the issue of that report it would be
premature to anticipate whether or not
legislation might be necessary or desirable.
EX-SERVICE MEN'S HOUSES IN
CLEEMISH ISLAND.
3. Mr. MILLER (for Mr. Cooper) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs if he is aware
that a very good scheme for ex-soldiers has
been carried out on Cleemish Island, County
Fermanagh, over a dozen houses having been
built and good farms acquired, but that no
means have been provided to enable these
men to get to their homes; and if he can
state what is the difficulty about providing
a right-of-way and a bridge to the island,
or how it is proposed to remedy this great
drawback to an otherwise excellent scheme.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The question of the
provision of holdings for ex-Servicemen
under Sections 1 to 3 of the Irish Land (Provision for Sailors and Soldiers) Act, 1919, is
one entirely for the Imperial Government,
and all such schemes under the Act are administered by the Land Purchase Commission (Northern Ireland).
It is understood, however, that that Department, which is an Imperial Department,
has already made provision for the establishment of a ferry to provide communication
between the Island and the mainland.
.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Payment of Members of the Senate.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That in the opinion of this House, as and
from the beginning of the current Financial
Year, provision shall be made for the payment at the rate of £2 2s 0d per diem to
each Member of the Senate who has subscribed to the necessary Oath and taken his
seat, in respect of incidental expenses and
expenses incurred in travelling from the
country to Belfast for attendance at meetings of the Senate or Committees, excluding
any Member who is for the time being in
receipt of a salary as an officer of the Senate
or a member of the Government; provided
that the total of such payments of £2 2s Od
per diem made to any Member of the Senate
shall not exceed the sum of eighty guineas
in any one year.
Mr. BARBOUR: I feel that it is not necessary for me to say very much to hon. Members of this House concerning this Resolution
Hon. Members will, of course, be aware that
those Members who have fulfilled the necessary conditions are entitled to receive in
respect of their expenses in the discharge of
their Parliamentary duties during the present
financial year the sum of £200, and it has
been considered only right that similar
arrangements should be made in the case of
Members in another place. The scheme of
payment, however, is not quite on the same
lines as is provided in the case of hon. Members of this House. Speaking generally, the
length of Sessions in the Senate is very much
shorter. Last year the actual days of sitting
in the Senate only numbered 33. And so it
has been considered that a daily rate, rather
than an annual sum, would better meet the
conditions obtaining in the case of Members of
that House. It has consequently been proposed to fix a payment of two guineas per day
in respect of incidental expenses, subject, however, to a maximum sum of eighty guineas
being paid to any Member in any one year;
and, in addition thereto, first-class railway
fare should be allowed in the case of Members
living outside Belfast who have not permanent
businesses or other offices in Belfast. The
Resolution also proposes to make this retrospective to the 1st April, 1923.
I would like to draw your attention to the
word "and" (" and expenses incurred in
travelling ") in the fifth line of the Resolution
as printed, and to ask your permission that
for "and" may be read "together with," so as
to make it perfectly plain that the sum of two
guineas does not include the expenses of
travelling to Belfast. The additional charge
which is expected to fall on public funds as a
result of this Resolution is estimated in one
year to amount to about £500. The expenditure in question is of a somewhat special
character, and so it has been deemed a more
appropriate way to bring this matter forward
by means of a Resolution rather than that it
should appear for the first time in the Estimates. I beg to move.

Mr. McGUFFIN: The principle underlying this resolution is, in my opinion, very
much similar to that which governed a
resolution submitted in this House for the

really relevant to the issue before the House.
The proposal is, in my opinion, a democratic
measure That may sound strange. It is
a democratic measure in so far as it would
be impossible for what we call democracythe working classes-to have representation
in the House without the financial support
contained in a similar proposal. There was
a time when it was not of much importance
what Member represented a constituency.
The only qualification that seemed necessary
at the time was that he had sufficient money,
and it did not matter what intellect or
integrity he had in connection with his
purpose as a Member of Parliament. But,
as the Franchise became extended, it became
inevitable that something of this sort would
have to be done. There was a time when
there was no Labour representation in the
House. It is not so long ago-about twentyfive years ago.
Up to 1832, when the great Enfranchisement Bill was introduced, there was no representation of the industrial classes, nor was
there any likelihood of there being any; but
when the franchise was extended it made a
way for Labour representation in the House,
with the almost inevitable consequence that
provision would have to be made for them.
I know there are many people in the community who would demur to the Government
supporting representation of that description,
but if there is no other means
by which Labour can be represented
than through the financial support
of this House I do not think it should
be a deterrent on this House to provide the
necessary money. The workers require representation, and if they have not the representation they are inclined to favour they
may be driven to other extremes, and to
adopt other shibboleths and other creeds
they have not hitherto accepted. As to the
need of a Second Chamber and its claim for
financial support, that is a very different
matter; but, after all, a Second Chamber
is absolutely necessary, because if I remember aright, when the Education Bill passed
through this House and was committed to
the Senate for revision, it came back a very
different Bill. I remember sitting beside my
right hon. Friend the Chairman of Committees (Mr. Moles), and we were just interchanging opinions as to the number of emendations and revisions that took place in connection with that Bill. If the Senate is
not necessary as a check upon extravagant
expenditure in this House, it is certainly
necessary as a means of revision of the indiscretions and mistakes that we frequently
make in this House. I do not know how far
those are chargeable upon the Law Officers
who are responsible for the Bills presented
here, but certainly it does not reflect much
credit on us as a House if we allow a Bill
to pass in such a shambling way that it has
to be returned to the House, and we scarcely
know it because of the number of emendations made.
I subscribe to the principle of the resolution, but my difficulty is that the financial
procedure proposed in connection with this

Mr. BARBOUR: When this Resolution
was originally brought before the House, it
was at a late hour, and I said I would be
happy to afford hon. Members some additional information, which I thought they
would like to have, before the final voting
of this Resolution. The position at the
present time is that, under the Acts already
passed, the sum guaranteed amounts to
£3,340,500, and the balance available in
respect of guarantees under these Acts
at the present time is £159,500. The object of
this Resolution, which will form the basis
of a Bill to be brought in, would be to extend the limit on the aggregate capital
amount of the loans by the sum
of one and a half millions-(Mr. Donald :
"Hear, hear.")-making an aggregate amount
of £5,000,000. The second part of the
Resolution deals with the period during
which guarantees may be given. It is felt
very desirable to keep a close check on these
facilities, and to restrict the period of them
to the ensuing financial year. So it is proposed to make the period during which such
guarantees may be given terminate on 31st
March, 1925.
It is
I should like also to explain, if I may, to
hon. Members the way in which these guarantees are given. It is not quite fully understood, I think, by members of the outside
public, however fully hon. Members may
understand it, that it is not the function of
the Government under this Act to advance
any money or even to arrange loans.
entirely the duty of whatever firm or group
of persons wishing to take advantage of this
Act to make their own arrangements with
their bankers or whatever business houses they
may be able to arrange with for the actual
advance to be made. All that the Government does under this Act is that when that
arrangement is made, if the Committee
appointed to deal with these guarantees
consider the security offered is ample, and
that the terms of the loan are reasonable,
they then give their guarantee both as to
principal and interest to the banker or other
financial house that actually makes the loan.
These facilities cannot be regarded in any
sense of the word as a grant or subsidy: they
are merely lending the State credit to the
trader or firm who is able to arrange his
own loan. Seeing that this Committee are
dealing with the credit of the community,
they see that the security offered is of such
a character that it is only by a very remote
chance that any burden may ultimately fall
upon the Exchequer; in fact, some hon.
Members or members of the outside public
might possibly think that the conditions
which this Committee imposed are of too
onerous a character, or are conditions such
as might possibly restrict the extent to which
advantage might be taken of the facilities
offered under this Act; but, of course, the
reply to that is, that in spite of those conditions and in spite of the ample security
demanded, we have come to the House the
second time, and we have now come to the
House the third time, to have the amount
of the sum which we may guarantee increased. Therefore, it is undoubtedly proving
of very great advantage to those firms who
take advantage of it; and in reply to a
Question in the House the other day information was given as to the number of men who
have been employed directly in consequence
of the facilities given under the previous
Acts. I beg to move.

I can remember when this matter was first
discussed in this House, that I tried to
approach it from different angles. Some
people thought I was stupid or silly or something, or that I was advocating the subsidising of industries. There was nothing further
