Sir DAWSON BATES: This Bill, which I
have the honour to submit for the consideration of this House, is one which I think will
meet with the approval of most of the
Members who have, on several occasions,
given expressions of opinion as to their desire
that such a Bill should be introduced.
The main object of this Bill is to remove a
long-standing grievance, and to make the
putative father of an illegitimate child liable
for its maintenance up to 14 years of ageand in some cases 16 years of age; for the
expenses incidental to its birth, or, in case of
the child's death, for its funeral. The law at
the present time in Ireland is such that no
liability attaches to the father of an illegitimate child, except where the child becomes
a burden upon the rates, and the result is
that where the unfortunate mother (as is
only natural) maintains the child out of her
own earnings, the father goes entirely scot
free.
The Bill mainly follows the existing law in
England, where, for many years past, the
liability of the putative father for the maintenance of the child has been recognised. Hon.
Members will realise how a child (the innocent victim) must suffer in point of view of
health, being brought up by the unfortunate
mother who has not the means to provide the
infant with the proper nourishment, and the
consequence is that as a result of the father's
action a burden is ultimately thrown upon
the ratepayer.
I do not think there is any necessity to
dwell upon the equity of making the father
pay for his child's support. I can only express my amazement that whereas provision
has long since been made in England and
Scotland to meet such a case, up to the
present the unfortunate mothers of illegitimate children in Ireland have been left so
long to bear this intolerable burden. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) It may be said that
this opens the door to blackmail, but I think
hon. Members on looking carefully into the
measure will find there are sufficient provisions to reduce the possibility of this danger
to a minimum.
Turning to the particular provisions of the
Bill, the Court, which is one of Summary
Jurisdiction--that is, the ordinary Magistrates-is given power on the application of
the mother or, if the mother or
illegitimate child is in receipt of
relief from the rates, on the application of
the Guardians, to order the father to pay a
sum not exceeding 20/- a week for the maintenance of the child. The Order remains in
force until the child reaches the age of 14
years, but may be extended on a subsequent
application to a period not exceeding 16
years of age. In order to try to guard
against the possibility of any miscarriage of
justice it is provided that before a Summons
is issued the mother has got to make an
Information on Oath and in writing; (2) the
evidence of the mother must be corroborated;
(3) a limit of time is fixed within which the
application has to be made, and (4) an appeal
can be taken by either side to the County
Court Judge.
It is also provided that the Order can be
varied from time to time on the application
of either side, and if default is made in payment, the Court is given the same power of
enforcing payment (including imprisonment)
as if default was made in payment of a penal
Power is also given to attach
pension of the father, where such pens
could otherwise be legally attached; and a
discharge in bankruptcy, unless expressly so
stated, will not release the father from
liability under the Order.
sum.
B
It is proposed to appoint Collecting Officers
for the County Boroughs and Petty Sessions
Districts, whose duty it will be to collect the
sum ordered from the father, and pay it over
to the mother or other person entitled to it,
and such officer can, at the request of the
mother, proceed to recover arrears. In the
County Boroughs the Collecting Officer will
be appointed by the Ministry of Home
Affairs, and in all other places the Collecting
Officer will be the Petty Sessions Clerk of the
267 Illegitimate Children Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
District, who will be paid a sum of money
out of the Petty Sessions Clerks Fund to meet
the cost of such collection.
Finally, power is given to the Lord Chief
Justice to make rules as regards forms, &c.,
and the Minister of Home Affairs to make
rules to give the necessary effect to the Act.
I had hoped, as I indicated some time ago in
this House, that it might have been possible
to have dealt with the legitimation of
illegitimate children by a subsequent marriage, but this question is still a subject of
debate in the Imperial House. Questions of
property in both Great Britain and Ireland
may be involved, and I think for this
reason alone it is necessary that we should
await the result of legislation on the other
side of the Channel, as it will be obvious to
Hon. Members that difficult questions, involving that of domicile, would arise by a
different law on this side from that existing
in England.
I can only say this, that this Bill means the
removal of a gross injustice that has existed
too long, and gives a tardy measure of justice
to a class who are frequently "more sinned
against than sinning." I am sure the
measure will receive sympathetic consideration at the hands of hon. Members of this
House. I beg to move.

Mrs. CHICHESTER: May I first of all
congratulate the right hon. Gentleman (Sir
Dawson Bates) who has introduced this Bill?
It will be welcomed by everyone not only in
this House but in the Six Counties, and I
cannot conceive that anyone could possibly
oppose the Bill as a whole. The right hon.
Gentleman has taken very long stride
towards righting what has been a very cruel
wrong, towards remedying an injustice which
has been endured by erring, weak, unfortunate women in Northern Ireland, women who
have never been placed on the same footing
as the same class of women on the other
side of the water. They have sinned, but
they have had to bear the burden of their
sins alone and unaided, in pain, and shame,
and sorrow, and bitter suffering for their
actions.
The Minister of Home Affairs has done
more than help them. He has brought in a
Bill which will change-absolutely changethe lives of many unfortunate, weak, and
helpless children, who may now in the future
be properly cared for, properly clothed,
properly educated-that is to say outside the
workhouse, where hitherto they have found
refuge and without the stigma which
attaches, as, unfortunately, it cannot fail to
attach to a certain extent, to the workhouse
child. These children have been doomed in
most cases to the life of the absolutely unwanted encumbrance, brought into the world,
as I have said, in sorrow and despair, and in
some cases only kept alive, and just kept
alive, by the unaided struggle of their
mothers. In other cases they have been
thrown a burden on the rates, deadened,
dulled, devoid of all life, of the joy of living
and of the joy of childhood, fatherless,
motherless. What chance have they ever
had to make good, being brought up under
what to all of us is the brand of illegitimacy?
if our Minister of Home Affairs never brings
in another Bill he will at any rate with this
one have accomplished a very great work.
I congratulate him most heartily.
Although welcoming the Bill, as I have
said, and looking upon it as a very good one,
there are certain remarks I should like to
make. I hope that we will not go from one
extreme to the other in this question.
Whilst helping the children as the greatest
sufferers and, perhaps, saving the mother
from plunging more deeply into the mire, we
must remember that there is another side of
the case, another aspect with which the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) has dealt
to-day in passing. I refer to the possibility
-and there is undoubtedly a possibilityof unscrupulous and immoral women using
the opportunity given to them by a measure
of this kind for blackmail. In this respect
one can readily conceive that many decent
men, completely innocent of the charges
brought against them-I put this forward
as a suggestion and as a query-might be
inclined to pay rather than undergo the publicity involved through having to face the
Court in one of these actions. I wonder
whether the right hon. Gentleman would
consider the advisability of having these
cases heard privately, in camera, or even
in the Children's Court where this exists.
I put this forward because it seems to me
that it might provide a certain safeguard in
this direction. I believe the plan is adopted
in Australia, and I know that in a draft Bill,
which I saw printed by the Society for the
Prevention of Cruelty to Children, this was
the suggestion made. I think I have it here
now. The suggestion was that all orders and
proceedings should be made in private, and
that no privilege should attach to the publication of such order or of the facts upon
which it was based. That is one suggestion
I would like to make.
In this connection also I hope that the
Clause dealing with the evidence is strong
enough, and that it lays sufficient stress upon
the vital necessity of other evidence-very
material evidence than that to be given by
the mother. Then there is one other point.
I raise it very diffidently because I am afraid .
I know what the answer will be before I have
made the suggestion. First of all I would
like to say that I am very glad of the 20imposed under the Bill, but I wish that a
minimum could possibly have been defined.
I am very much afraid of what might take

perfectly well that he is liable to be transferred from station to station during the

the estimate where provision is made-for
the payment from time to time of the expenses of the transfer of these men and
their families from a station to a
new
station to which they may be ordered by the
Inspector-General. Therefore, so far as regards the hardship, it is perfectly true that
if a man has a nice station I am sure he
does feel it a hardship that he is ordered to
go to another place where he may not feel
quite so much at home.
But I can assure hon. Members that if the
principle was to be laid down, which so far
as I can
understand the hon. Member
suggests, that once a policeman comes into
the city of Belfast he is never to be moved,
all I can say is that a great injustice would
be done to other members of that force by
reason of the fact that they would know
that until a vacancy occurred in the police
force in Belfast by retirement, none of them
could hope to come into Belfast. I would
remind hon. Members that more than onethird of the police force are stationed in
Belfast and to adopt the suggestion of my
hon. Friend, I think, would be to extinguish
the ambition of the junior members of the
police force who are just as anxious to get
into Belfast as other members are to remain
there. It has been suggested here that
these particular transfers are for the purpose of inflicting punishment upon these
men. I can only say that if these transfers
were being carried out as a disciplinary
measure these men would be transferred at
their own expense. These men will be
transferred entirely at the expense of the
State, and all I can say is that probably the
Inspector-General, in the course of movements that are bound to take place, may
order these men back to Belfast.
But there is another underlying principle
which is involved in this matter, and that
is the question to what extent the Government are to interfere with the ordinary
discretion of the Inspector-General in regard
to movements of police. He is responsible
to the Government and the Government is
responsible to this House for the efficiency
of the policemen. I can only say this that
it would be a great mistake in my opinion
if this House is to lay down the principle
that before any member of this force of 3,000
men of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
could be transferred from one station to
another the Government should be consulted
and as a result of that a debate should take
place in this House. I say that would
weaken the authority of the Inspector-
General. The Inspector-General is responsible for seeing that the efficiency of the
force is kept up to the mark. He has got
the peace of the community to a large extent in his keeping. I say that the Government should be very slow to interfere with
the discretion that he exercised with regard
to the movements of the police.

officers. These are the facts as I understand
them. On the part of the Government I
Mr. ROBB: I do not wish to take one side

Oral Answers to Questions.
MUD-SPLASHING BY MOTOR VEHICLES.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether, in the public interest.
he would consider the advisability of issuing
regulations or enforcing the existing regulations, affecting the compulsory fixing to
heavy motor vehicles of devices for the prevention of mud-splashing.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The question of the
prevention of mud-splashing by heavy motor
vehicles has been engaging the attention of
the Ministry for some time past, and also of
the Ministry of Transport in Great Britain.
Exhaustive tests were carried out on behalf of that Ministry by the Royal Automobile Club with a view to ascertaining the
effectiveness of the various appliances available for this purpose, but the result of these
tests established beyond doubt that there
were no suitable appliances on the market
which are capable of dealing effectively with
the problem of mud-splashing.
The question was also referred to the
Roads Advisory Committee for Northern
Ireland, and following their recommendations, and having regard to the reasons given
above, the Ministry have decided that it is
not expedient to put into force compulsory
regulations in the absence of satisfactory
evidence that suitable appliances are available.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
reply, has the right hon. Gentleman's attention been drawn to the appliance used by
the Belfast Fire Brigade, which has been
found to be very satisfactory, and is very
cheap?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is a matter
of opinion. I prefer to go by the opinion of
the Royal Automobile Association in England who have had a great deal of experience and have devoted a great deal of time
and money in trying to get an effective
appliance to prevent mud-splashing.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Is my right hon.
Friend aware that that is the great grievance that exists at the present time, and is
ho not also aware that even an imperfect
arrangement would be better than the
present arrangement?
Mr. DONALD: As a member of the Roads
Advisory Committee is my right hon. Friend
aware that the Roads Advisory Committee
were not unanimous in their decision with
regard to this matter, but still have it under
consideration, and may I ask my right hon.
Friend will he consider the advisability of
offering a prize? You will find an efficient
splash protector can be put on the market.
DRINKING BARS IN CLUBHOUSES.
2. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of Home
Affairs if he can state (1) whether an
Athletic Club registered under the Registration of Clubs (Ireland) Act, 1904, as amended
by the Intoxicating Liquor Act, 1923, is at
liberty to open as many bars as it likes in
different and separate buildings within its
own grounds; (2) if so, whether an attendant
K
Supply.

Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Grant]
must be in charge of each bar; (3) whether a
statement, printed in plain type, must be conspicuously displayed in each clubhouse where
a bar is situate, showing the hours during
which intoxicating liquor may be supplied on the premises; and (4) whether a
Visitors' Book must be kept and signed in
connection with each bar.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am not aware of
any restrictions on the number of bars which
may be opened on the premises of a Registered Club.
The reply to the second and third paragraphs is in the affirmative.
As regards the last paragraph, a visitor can
only be supplied with liquor on the invitation
of and in the company of a member, and the
member must upon the admission of a visitor,
or immediately upon his being supplied with
liquor, enter his own name and the name and
address of the visitor in a book kept for the
purpose.
IMPROVEMENT OF RAILWAY COM-
MUNICATIONS.
3. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of Commerce if anything has been done in connection with the promise of the Prime Minister
that railway communications in the Six
Counties should be improved, and that more
importance should be given to the East and
West communications than the North and
South.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): I nave no knowledge of the pro-
Imise to which the hon. Member refers. For
his information, however, I would point
out that the administration of Northern Ireland railways rests with the Imperial
authority. Nevertheless my Department has
endeavoured, and will continue to endeavour,
to keep in close touch with all matters relating to the provision of railway facilities
in Northern Ireland and, where the circumstances appear to warrant such a course, will
be prepared to make representations in the
proper quarter for any needed improvements.
Mr. MILLER: Arising out of that reply,
is the right hon. Gentleman aware-perhaps
from sad experience that the railway facilities between the North-West and the North-
East are simply wretched for business purposes?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I quite agree with the
hon. Member. I have been doing my best
for some time to get them improved.
PENALTIES IN POTEEN CASES.
4. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he will state what is the
maximum penalty for the manufacture or sale
of poteen; whether the Magistrates who
adjudicate in such cases are fully aware of
the desirability of imposing as far as possible
the maximum penalties; and what are the
penalties generally imposed in Northern
Ireland.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The maximum
penalty for the manufacture or sale of poteen
in Northern Ireland is that imposed by the
Finance Act, 1923, i.e., "a penalty not exceeding £500, or imprisonment for a term not
exceeding 12 months or both such penalty and
imprisonment."
The Government cannot interfere with the
discretion of Magistrates in imposing
sentences in such cases which may be brought
before them, but I have no doubt that the
Resident Magistrates (before whom such cases
must be tried) are fully aware of the desirability of putting a stop to this traffic, and
their attention was specially directed to the
provisions of the above Act in this respect.
I regret I have no statistics regarding the
penalties recently imposed, but if the hon.
Member desires, I shall obtain these particulars for him.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Arising out of that
reply, is my right hon. Friend aware that so
far as small fines are concerned it pays these
people to make poteen ?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I quite imagine so.

case
Mr. McGUFFIN: The purpose of this Bill
is to remove a serious injustice in respect of
the womanhood of the Six Counties, and as
such will claim the approval and support,
I am sure, of every Member of this House.
It is to an extent an adaptation of an Act
existing at the present time in the Imperial
Parliament, and though we do sometimes
rather regret the habit of the Government
in imitating certain Bills that may
be introduced in the Imperial Parliament I think in this particular
rather
the Government is
to be
congratulated on introducing a Bill dealing with such an important subject. It does
not propose to control the public morals of
the community in respect of the evils of
illegitimacy. These evils spring from a common tendency of our own which education,
perhaps, may assist us to control, but which
human laws can do nothing to remedy or
cure. The public morals of a community are
regulated to a very large extent by what is
called the social conscience, and the social
conscience itself, is in a very large degree
dependent upon the efforts and influences of
the leaders of thought and opinion. A very
eminent authority of the last century said
that among societies of men it is always
those spirits of stronger will that morally
support the less, and as the scale of realised
excellence ascends, the conscience of us all
becomes ashamed to linger, and eventually
rises, too. I suppose it was exactly due to
those influences that to-day we have this Bill
introduced here in the House.
Of course, the standards of morals vary
with the times in the country in which one
is sojourning. I think it was Mr. Lecky, in
his "History of European Morals," who expresses the opinion that a man is only immoral who does not practice the morality of
his own country. I do not know that that is
a dictum that we are inclined to accept.
However, we are dealing in respect of this
Bill with the conditions that obtain here in
the Six Counties, and respecting which we
have a right to legislate as we think proper.
We create standards ourselves by our own
actions, and having created the standards
it is necessary for us then to regulate our
legislation according to the needs of the case.
This Bill provides for the support and
protection of the unfortunate mother and
child. We had three very good speeches
made here last Thursday in connection with
the second reading. One was by the hon.
and learned Member for Antrim (Mr.
Hanna), and the other by the hon. Member
for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Cooper). I
think he prefers that he should be designated the Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone,
but whatever way it is proper to refer to
him these two speeches were of a trenchant
nature, and dealt with the clauses, in my
opinion, not in a hypercritical way, but in a
very faithful way. I am sure when the
Government come to reply to those criticisms
they will find it necessary to meet in a very
adequate fashion the criticisms that have
been put up, and the objections that have
been made with regard to these clauses. 1
was more particularly. struck with the
speech of the hon Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester). The purpose of her speech, as
it appeared, was on behalf of the unfortunate
mother. No person who has been associated with industrial work can fail to recognise the justice of the plea that the hon.
Member put up on behalf of these women.
I myself have had experience of them for
many years in my industrial occupation,
and many a time I felt a poignant sorrow
at what these women were compelled to
endure. For months prior to maternity they
were working hard, and compelled to resume
their occupation only a few weeks after that
event, and to struggle on from month to
month and from year to year in support of
the offspring whose birth is always feared
and never welcomed. I feel very acutely in
sympathy with the hon. Member (Mrs.
Chichester) in the case she put up on their
behalf, and I think she has not exceeded by
one word what it is right should be said on
their behalf.
295 Illegitimate Children Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading.
[Mr. McGuffin]
But while I agree absolutely with regard
to that I want to intimate to the House
that my chief concern is on behalf of the
unfortunate child who comes into the world.
What I regret most in connection with this
matter is that this child unfortunately
comes into the world under a stigma, and
passes through life with that stigma
attached to it, and is excluded from many
of the recognised institutions of our nation
by reason of the fact that it cannot be called
legitimate. I may be thought perhaps to
be a little heteredox in support of my
opinion in this matter, but I utterly and
absolutely demur to a distinction being
drawn between what is called the legitimate
and illegitimate child. Life, as I understand it, is sacred in respect of every individual-(hon. Members: Hear, hear) and I
go further and say that life whatever its
character, humanly speaking, proceeds from
the great Author and Giver of all life, Who,
in my opinion, would make no distinction
between one and the other. I am not sure that
the social conscience of the nation was
always what it is to-day with respect to these
illegitimate children. One of the most
hideous, and in my opinion ugly words in
our language is the term "bastard." I wish
it was expurgated from our dictionaries
altogether, and the use for it had absolutely
disappeared. I am not without hope that
in the development of civilisation something
of that description will come about if
it is not hastened by the intervention of Christian thought and feeling. The
plea on behalf of the bastard is put up by
Edmund, who is the bastard, in the great
play of King Lear, and he asks himself "Why
bastard, wherefore base?" and he proceeds
to argue from physical, moral, and
mental reasons that he himself is in no way
inferior to Edgar, whom he describes as
"honest madam's issue." I wish to take that
view of the matter and import into our
intercourse more respect and some sympathy
for these unfortunate children who come
into the world, as Shakespeare says under
conditions
"Whereupon they are not guilty since
Nature cannot choose their origin."
We should exercise more sympathy for
them and our laws should be framed and
modified in such a way as to do more justice
to their claim.
Now, coming to the Bill itself I would like
to ask am I justified in thinking that the
first clause of the Bill provides that the
mother may upon her mere allegation and
unsupported before the magistrate have a
claim to what is called the affiliation order?
Dr. MORRISON: No.
Mr. McGUFFIN: The Bill reads as if that
were the case.
"Where a man is alleged by the mother
to be the father of her illegitimate child
and has been summoned in accordance with
the provisions of this Act. . . . . the
Court shall have power, after hearing all
the circumstances of the case, to adjudge
the man to be the putative father of the
child."
But I think there is another clause in the
Bill where it states that corroborative evidence of a material character must be
offered. If there is such a discrepancy or
contradiction between one and the other can
we proceed on the one clause and simply by
the unsupported evidence of the mother make
the affiliation order? It may be from a
slovenly reading of the Bill I have come
to that conclusion, but in the one case
it is insisted upon and in the other it is
not. I am absolutely with my hon. and
learned Friend, the Member for Antrim (Mr.
Hanna), in his contention that a Court of
Summary Jurisdiction is not the proper
Court for this class of case to be heard. I even
go so far as to agree with him when he suggests that on many occasions they are subject
to collusion. Such an assembly should not
be the Court before which a man alleged to be
the father of an illegitimate child should have
come. I am absolutely opposed to that idea,
because it should be, as far as possible,
a
Court above suspicion. I know that
is the feeling I have about it, and
others are of the same opinion.
suggest, in the interests of all concerned,
that the Court should be, as far as possible,
free from any such suspicion.
I am very much in sympathy with the contention of the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester). Perhaps she did not bring it
forward as a contention. She made, however,
a serious and solemn suggestion that
there should be a minimum observed with
respect to the award. If you do not adopt a
minimum you may not improve the circumstances of the child. It would be open to the
magistrate according as he may determine,
to vary the award in such a way as not to
make it to the advantage of the applicant in
the case. There is another item in connection
with this, and it is that part of Clause 1, that
enables a married woman to take advantage
of this Act. Surely it was never intended
that married woman should be included in
this matter.
And, so far as is necessary, to enable a
married woman to take proceedings under
this 'Act.
A more preposterous or more outrageous
thing was never introduced in a Bill of this
sort. There is a provision for people in
married life who are found in such a predicament, but that is the Divorce Court. I
do not see that any honourable man who
might be the husband of such a woman
under the circumstances, could take any other
297 Illegitimate Children Bill-

25 MARCH, 1924.
Second Reading.
course, and I do not think we should accommodate a woman of this sort to the extent
of making provision by which she can proceed
against a man for doing a thing which she
was lawfully bound to avoid for her own
honour, and to which, for the honour of her
husband, she was bound never to submit.
The hon. and learned Member for Antrim
(Mr. Hanna) and the hon. Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr. Cooper) also put it
forward that this Bill should not admit, as
it does, a series of applications made by the
same woman with regard to similar claims.
Where a woman has to appear twice or three
times before the Court with regard to the
same thing I would say of her that her sin
was not accidental, but that it was a trade.
We should be very careful indeed under the
circumstances not to condone such an act as
that, or enable a woman to take such advantage of the Bill as practically to establish a
trade in immorality, which the Government,
if not condoning, would be at least conniving
at. I hope that particular portion of the
Bill will not be pressed.
With regard to blackmail, there is always
the possibility of blackmail in connection
with cases of this sort. You cannot introduce a reformative Bill of this nature without
incurring that liability, but I think, even in
the face of that, it would be well to stress
this and to make it as hard as possible under
the provisions of the Bill for anyone possibly to blackmail any person against whom a
false allegation might be set up.
I was rather pleased in respect of one
matter in the Bill, and that is that there is
to be a Court collector appointed for the collection of these awards. That is a very fine
and a very necessary provision. Instead of
a woman seeking her award from week to
week in some appointed place, under this Bill
it will be paid to her at her own home by a
responsible official, to whom she can complain
if necessary but who is responsible for the
gathering in of the money. The Bill on the
whole is a good Bill. It is open to these two
or three serious objections, upon which we
probably will be enlightened by the hon. and
learned Gentleman (Mr. Megaw) who will
reply to this debate. I am only too glad to
be able to congratulate the Government on
introducing the Bill, which in my opinion
will serve a very useful purpose, and will be a
source of great alleviation in respect of the
circumstances of many a home where at the
moment, for want of this provision, there is
privation and even destitution.
Dr. MORRISON: I am afraid there is not
a great deal of time, otherwise I would be
disposed to follow somewhat minutely the
eloquent speech we have had from the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin).
I must, however, deny myself that pleasure.
He has led us through Shakespeare and Lecky,
i
and the evolution of the conscience. These
are all very interesting questions, but I do
not think they bear altogether on the matter
in hand. I would simply say that it seems
to me a rather extraordinary thing that we in
Northern Ireland have been fifty years longer
in evolving this conscience, that was to set
right these terrible wrongs, than they were
across the Channel in England, Scotland and
Wales. It is a reproach to us which this Bill
will remove for ever.
I think the Bill is a good Bill. Unfortunately
I was not present for the opening of the
debate on the Second reading, but I saw a
brief report in the papers which gave me an
idea of what the objections to the Bill are. I
have been working for thirty years in a pro
fession which has brought me in contact with
cases of this sort, and I know the whole of
the details, the whole of the troubles, the
whole of the sufferings, and the whole of the
miseries which follow the absence of this law.
Therefore, I would ask the House to listen to
me somewhat patiently while I put the case
before them. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
The hon. Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester)
suggested that these cases should be heard
in camera. There is a good deal to be said
in favour of that. We might get rid of these
very nasty details, which appear in the Press
sometimes, in connection with cases of sex
relations. I think it would be wise if we
adopted the system on which the Roman
Catholic Church insists and tried to exclude
these things from the public gaze, for undoubtedly they lessen and lower the moral
tone of the community. However, that is a
matter which, I am sure, the Government
will leave to the decision of the House.
Certain remarks were made by the hon.
and learned Member for Antrim (Mr. Hanna)
to which I would like to reply. I am sure
he has been brought up against these cases,
as everyone practising at the Quarter Sessions
and Petty Sessions Courts has been, although these cases never appeared
before the Petty Sessions Courts
before, and he must have seen the
very serious difficulties. He objects to the
Petty Sessions Court as the Court at which
these cases should be heard. That would
constitute a great obstacle when you come to
deal with a poor, stranded woman. One of
the greatest advantages which you can confer
upon her is to give her a cheap Court where
she can have her case tried.
Mr. HANNA: The Quarter Sessions is
cheaper than the Petty Sessions.
Dr. MORRISON: If that is so then have
it so. The Quarter Sessions involves. I think,
the retention of a lawyer-a solicitor and
possibly a barrister. You can have these
things decided at a Petty Sessions Court
with no legal representatives at all, more
or less. In the past these cases were all

determined at Quarter Sessions, because, as

and so these unfortunate people were bound

to retain lawyers. No injustice can be done

The mere fact of this law being in existence

fairer.
As a
The hon. and learned Member (Mr. Hanna)
and my hon. Friend (Mr. McGuffin) also
objected to that Clause defining the married
woman. I thought myself that there was
some ambiguity about it. On the face of it
it looks as if when a woman is married she
should not have to bring a charge of this
sort, but there are exceptional cases.
matter of fact during the war, when soldiers
were away perhaps for one year or two years,
they came home and found their wives with
children. That is a fact about which there
can be no dispute. Does either the hon. and
learned Member (Mr. Hanna) or the hon.
Member (Mr. McGuffin) demand that the
soldier, who was away fighting for his
country, should support an illegitimate child,
and that the father should go free? The
thing in itself is clearly an absurdity. Suppose, as sometimes happens, a man marries
a woman who has the reputation of being a
decent woman, and a couple of months
after he is married she has a child of which
he knows he is not the father; suppose he
leaves that woman, as he naturally would be
disposed to do, and the woman is exposed, is
she to be debarred from the protection which
this law would give if she then confesses and
says "I unfortunately had connection with
such a man on such a date," and produces
confirmatory evidence? Is it not absolutely
right and proper that special cases like that
should be provided for? This can only
happen occasionally, I know, but the absence
of provision for such cases in this Bill might
lead to injustice. I do not think it will be
found, when these things come to be discussed
in Committee, that there is any special injustice in having the Clause as it is in the Bill
passed by this House.
As I have already pointed out the Petty
Sessions Court is the cheapest Court to which
a woman like this has access. The hon. and
learned Member (Mr. Hanna) will tell you
that it has been practically the unanimous
practice for the judge at Quarter Sessions to
give a decree for £10, £20, or £25 for the
support of a child, and that ends the whole
transaction. The sum on the face of it is
absolutely inadequate, and the reason the
judge gives it is that he knows that if he imposes a heavier penalty it will never be paid.
The hon. and learned Member (Mr. Hanna)
must have seen these cases work out in this
injustice. The judge gives a small decree
because he knows that if he does not give a
small decree there is no hope whatever of
it ever being paid.
Mr. HANNA: I am afraid my hon. Friend
(Dr. Morrison) is rather misrepresenting me.
I did not suggest at all that I knew of cases
in the Courts where decrees of ten pounds
had been given for the upkeep of an illegitimate child. What the hon. Member (Dr.
Morrison) is trying to get at is decrees given
in seduction cases to the parents of the
seduced woman, or to a person standing in
loco parentis.
Dr. MORRISON: It is six of one and half
a dozen of the other. It is the only penalty
that is being inflicted upon the father. I
can tell you a little of the law, and the hon.
and learned Member (Mr. Hanna) knows the
law. Here is a case that happened in Co.
Antrim under Judge Orr, a clear-headed and
wise legal luminary. A case was brought
by a girl against the farmer who had employed her for seduction. No, she brought
an action against the son for seduction. It
came before the County Court Judge, who dismissed the case, and said it was wholly
wrong, and that the man who should have
been sued was not the father of the child at
all but the employer of the girl in question.
He dismissed the case on that point of law.
My hon. and learned Friend (Mr. Hanna)
smiles, but that is quite true. I leave, however, these little questions of law to the
lawyers. They make a handsome income out
of discussing them, and I have no objection
at all. What I want, and what I think this
House wants, is that we should get to the
root of the matter, punish the guilty man,
make him pay the penalty and support his
child.
A lawyer, a solicitor practising, came to me
on one occasion and said: "I have a client
who lives in County Londonderry. She was
hired by a farmer in County Antrim.
She is about to have a child, and she
wants to sue the man." She was a minor
and she could not plead; but at any rate what
she had to do was to sue through her father
who was the employer. She said she did

round corners as well as doctors, and the

solicitor said to me "This girl went home 1
every Saturday and stayed till Sunday night.
Would you get her to say she baked bread
when she went home, that she carried water
and made the beds, so as to qualify her to
sue the father of her child?" I think that
to all right-thinking men such anomalies in
a plain elementary matter are monstrous,
disgusting and nauseating. The whole law
in regard to this matter is a fraud; I say
that advisedly. As a result of thirty years'
experience, I say here that girls no longer
seek any protection from the law, because
there is practically no protection in the
law, and that the system that has prevailed
for fifty years in Ulster is setting a premium
on blackguardism and immorality and on
this dreadful thing of deliberately seducing
girls, for the simple reason that these seducers in effect have a guarantee that they
will not be prosecuted and punished.
The evils of this thing are very wide
and very far-reaching. Nobody knows that
better than I do. As my hon. and learned
Friend. the Member for Antrim (Mr. Hanna)
can tell you, you have cases of infanticide
and of concealment of birth. I suppose infanticide and murder are the same. You
have Coroners' inquests, the whole machinery
of the law is set in motion at the inquests
and before the magistrates and these people
are returned for trial at the assizes. Very
often the judge dismisses the case or sets
the woman free, and nothing further is done;
but a great deal of expense to the State is
involved in these proceedings. I want the
House to understand the sort of a case that a
doctor sometimes meets.
I came across this case in my capacity as
a Coroner. A girl who found herself in
this unfortunate position went away to Belfast to be confined, and she had made
arrangements in a local town for someone to
meet her on her return and to nurse the
child. She had been at service, and she had
to return to work. She went to this little
place-Castlerock- and when she came
out of the train she wandered about
looking for the woman who was to take the
child, but the woman did not turn up. Just
picture what that poor girl suffered.
Think, in the first place, of her
nine months of bad health during
pregnancy, then of the worry, anxiety and
dread as to what was to happen, and again
of the suffering and pain associated with her
confinement. Then, having made arrangements for someone to nurse the child, which
she was prepared to support, because there
was no other remedy for her, she goes down
to the village, but the woman does not turn
up. and she is faced with the prospect of
returning to her home with the child. The
girl was distracted. She had some cotton
wool which is used in attending to the
child, and she pushed this cotton
wool into the child's throat and smothered
it. She then got her ticket to go to Derry, she
got into the train, and she threw the child
into the tunnel at Downhill.
A man gave evidence before me, and as I
was acting in a judicial or semi-judicial
capacity I had to be careful that I expressed
my opinion in a wise and serious fashion, but
I had very great difficulty in refraining from
expressing my mind in regard to his conduct.
He saw this woman wandering about looking
for some place of refuge. He suspected that
she had a child in her arms. He saw her
going into the train, and he actually took
a ticket and followed her, charging her at
Downhill with having thrown the child out
of the window when the train was passing
through the tunnel. The matter came before
me I think it was in this instance-and
the jury at my request passed a unanimous
resolution calling for action by this House
in such cases. At any rate the jury did so
in another case at Castlerock. That woman
went before a judge. The Grand Jury
brought in a true bill not for murder but
for manslaughter, and the judge sent her
home. Her mistress, an elderly woman who
was the widow of a clergyman, wrote to me
stating that she was one of the finest girls
who had ever been in her service. As I
have pointed out to you, that involved great
trouble to the girl herself and great cost to
the ratepayers.
If a woman finds herself in a position like
that she is perhaps refused admission to her
own house, and she goes to the workhouse,
but the law is that if a woman having an
illegitimate child leaves the workhouse she
must take her child with her. That works
out this way, that large numbers of these
able-bodied females are imprisoned in the
workhouse, for the simple reason that they
cannot get out without taking the child
with them; they cannot get a place for the
child, and have no way of making provision
for it.
Provision is made in some cases through
foster parents, and that suggests another
serious grievance. Every Board of Guardians
in Ulster has a special officer appointed
under the Children Act for the purpose of
looking after these boarded-out children. That
is an item of cost to the ratepayers. But no
matter how kindly the foster mother may be
if she is called upon to provide a child with
milk and with food she may not be able to
do it, and the consequence often is that the
milk provided is not of the most suitable
quality and the child gets gastritis, and it
pines away until there is nothing left but
skin and bone. I knew a case of a decent
woman who nursed some of these children,
and who, so far as I could hear and understand, nursed them faithfully. But in the

case of a child brought up on the bottle
perhaps its stomach goes wrong, it gets

get them suffering from this digestive

and vigorous children, but weak and

a report of the Malone Rescue and Reform
Home in Belfast, which is the only institution
that we have in Northern Ireland for dealing
with these cases. I think it is a great credit
to the philanthropic people of Belfast who
run this home that they have done so much
to meet this urgent need in their district. I
believe the number of births of illegitimate
children in Belfast-I have the figures
in my pocket-exceeds 500 a year. Νο
provision is made for those children
except the workhouse and this home.
In this home last year there were
110 births, and 5 babies were still born. There
you have, before these children appear in the
world at all, the result of the hardships to
which their mothers are subjected. Here
under proper care, and with the best medical
skill that can be given, you have five children
still born out of 100. This Home is doing a
great work, and I am glad to know that they
are rebuilding the premises. The House will
also be glad to know that they want a grant,
and that the Minister of Labour and the
Minister of Home Affairs were most sympathetic and helped them in every possible
way. I want to establish that fact.
There was another case I was greatly
impressed by; it shows the position as I have
seen it, and as any man who is brought into
contact with these cases is bound to see it.
It would vex, worry and annoy any man to
see the injustice that is being done to these
helpless girls and their children. I do not
take up the position in this House of a
purist. I know, as the Member for North
Belfast (Mr. McGuffin) has said, the limitations of human nature; but what always
appealed to me was the scandalous injustice
that was done by putting the whole burden
on the woman. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
A little girl came into my office in Coleraine.
She was not more than 23 years of age;
possibly she was not that. She was very
badly clad; her clothing was wholly insufficient-boots, dress, everything-and she
was in charge of an elderly woman who
called herself a nurse, but was not really
qualified, although she had some special
knowledge. Said I, "How does it come you
have not sufficient clothes?" "Well," said
the girl, "I had to give them for the child."
I inquired into the facts of the case, and 1
found that when she was perhaps sixteen
she became pregnant. Her parents would
not allow her into their house. She went to
the workhouse and came out with the child
in her arms, and at this time she had been
paying for seven years £16 a year for the
support of the child. She had to deny
herself the ordinary decencies that any girl
is entitled to, and as she told me she was
looking forward to the child becoming old
enough to look after the house while she
worked for a farmer outside. We have had
Harriet Beecher Stowe preaching to the
American people and to the whole civilised
world about the cruelties that were inflicted
on the negro. I think we would have needed
during the past fifty years some writer like
that who would have preached about the
terrible evils that are associated with this
business. If we had had someone to do that
I am
sure the conscience of the publie

I welcome the Bill as one of the most

pass.

The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw) Considering the way that this
Bill has been met by the various critics it is
a very easy matter for me to reply. I am
very glad to learn that the Members of this
House have given such a reception to this
measure as they have done. The criticism
that has been offered has been of a helpful
nature, and such criticism has always been
welcomed by the Government.
I shall say
just at the beginning of the few observations
I have got to make that the Government will
be very glad to receive any suggestions from
the Members of this House as to the improvement of the Bill during its passage
through Committee. They are not wedded
to the precise language or the particular
Clauses that are there. What we want is as
perfect a measure as can be obtained. We
cannot close our eyes to the fact that no
Bill and no Act that is passed can entirely
remove the evils that are inherent in matters
of this kind. We may pass measures, but the
grief and the evils will very often still
remain. We cannot remove by a measure
of this kind the stigma that attaches, and
will attach according to the ideas of society,
to illegitimacy; but we can do something at
any rate to equalise the burden and to make
the person who is primarily responsible for
it bear his part of the burden.
The first criticism that was offered was
by the hon. Member for Londonderry (Mrs.
Chichester) and it was suggested by her that
cases of this kind should be heard in camera.
The hearing of cases in camera is alien to
the system of justice that has commended
itself to the people in the British Isles, and
cases are certainly regarded with very
great suspicion that are heard in camera.
It enables evils to be hushed up, and publicity is a very important affair in all
administration of law. Of course there are
cases where the publication of details have
a bad effect, but the Press, as a rule in this
country, does not lend itself to some of the
particular evils that are incident to the
cases on the other side of the Channel; and
until we really find that there is that
publicity-and those evils arising from
publicity-I think the attitude of the
Government will be to maintain the system
of jurisprudence that has held for so far and
to have the cases heard in courts in the
ordinary way.
Now so far as the court is concerned the
suggestion has been made that the petty
sessions is not a good tribunal. I think it
was mentioned by the hon. Member for
Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Cooper) and I
think by my hon. and learned Colleague for
Antrim (Mr. Hanna) that there were obvious
objections to having cases determined by the
ordinary courts of petty sessions. I think
I may say on behalf of the Government that
if it is the feeling of this House the Government will adopt the same system as is
applicable to some of the other cases that
come before petty sessions, and have the
matter determined by resident magistrates.
The Government have an open mind on the
matter, and if there is a feeling of that
kind the Government will be very glad to
adopt it, so far as the Bill goes. We may also
say that the same difficulty might apply to
quarter sessions in the ordinary sense. In
quarter sessions there is not only the County
Court Judge there, but magistrates, and
there would be danger of the bench of
magistrates being crowded to hear a particular case. The same system as has been
adopted in regard to Licensing Act cases,
where the Appeal is heard before the
County Court Judge sitting alone, will be
adopted by the Government if that is
thought right.
The hon. Member of Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Cooper) in his criticism of the
Bill did what I think there is too much of
a tendency to do-to sympathise with the
wrong-doer. He told of the tremendous
damages that a man might have to bear, and
said that in some cases he might have to pay
£52 a year for sixteen years. But why should
the wrong-doer in a case of the kind not
have to have the same obligations of fatherhood that a married man would have?
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). A married
man has got to support his children, but because an unmarried man has got a girl into
trouble he is to be sympathised with for the
reason that he has to bear some part of the

obligation that a married man has to bear by

which show that there is that old tendency
to look rather at the difficulties that may be
imposed on the man and the dangers that

who is the injured party. Some criticism
was made with regard to the provision in
the Bill as to the story of the claimant and
to claim of the claimant requiring to be
corroborated. Corroboration cannot be given
when the claim is made. It is not in the
making of the claim; it is in the hearing
of the claim, the evidence to support the
claim, and before any claim is passed there
requires to be corroboration by this Bill.
I think I have met most of the criticisms
mentioned As I have said, the Government
are not going to try to shut out criticism or
to resent anything in the nature of amendments. Every amendment that is offered by
hon. Members will be heard and will be considered with the greatest sympathy, and if
we all set out with the one purpose, namely,
to make as good a Measure as possible for the
future of illegitimate children, and to make
the position as equitable as possible, I am
sure we shall succeed in bringing to perfection an Act that will do credit to our own
community.

Married Women Teachers.
"That
STATEMENT BY MR. MCKEOWN.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I beg to move
in the opinion of this House, no disability
should attach to a married woman teacher
by reason of her marriage or maternity."
It will probably be a relief to
hon. Members to know that in introducing this Resolution there is not the
slightest intention on my part-perhaps I
may go further and say on the part of those
who will probably support this resolutionof impugning the Government or in any way
offering serious criticism to anything they
have done in respect of the case from which
this resolution has originated. The resolution arose from a question put down by
me with regard to a case that occurred in
Edenderry School, Portadown. The nature of
that case I did not then cite. I asked a few
questions with regard to it, and though the
reply was in every sense adequate it was
not, to my mind satisfactory in view of the
fact that the Ministry either ignored or
evaded responsibility as to the decision.
The case, in short, is this: Mrs. Lyske,
Assistant Teacher, Edenderry National
School, Portadown, was married in April,
1922. Her manager raised no objection at
the time of her marriage, and said he was
quite willing that she should continue teaching until she qualified for pension. That is
a very important part of the case and I would
have the hon. Gentleman who will reply on
behalf of the Ministry take a note of the fact
that by agreement with her manager she
got married. In September, 1923, as she was
about to become a mother, she asked for permission to appoint a substitute, and take
two months' leave of absence, as the Rules
of the Ministry make provision for. In reply
she got a three months' notice of dismissal.
An appeal was made to the Ministry under
Section 68 of the Education Act, and the
Ministry decided not to interfere in the case.
311 Married Women Teachers. HOUSE OF COMMONS
Married Women Teachers. 312
[Mr. McGuffin]
This, in short, is the ground upon which
this resolution has been submitted to the
House. It reads, as I have already shown,
that "no disability should attach to
a married teacher by reason of her marriage
or maternity." The Ministry's reply may
have been without prejudice so far as they
are concerned, but I am very much afraid
it suggests that it may become a precedent
and that, for instance, local authorities
might be entitled to act similarly to the case
of the manager in Portadown who rather in
disregard of the arrangement he had made
with the teacher actually took the summary
course of dismissing her when she applied
for leave. It will be a very important thing
for the House to know what the intention of
the Ministry is with respect to such cases.
Up to the present we have not heard anything that would entitle us to come to the
conclusion that the Ministry is taking
either one side or the other. Is it not a fact
-I rather think it is-that women teachers
have had an assurance with respect to the
retention of their positions in the case of
marriage? That assurance is practically
provided for by an arrangement of the old
National Board by which a teacher when
she married was not subject to a penalty
and even on approaching maternity had
accommodation made with respect to the
occasion by having liberty to provide a locum
tenens who would act in her place and for
the engagement of whom she herself was responsible.
What we ask in this case is: "Does the
Ministry propose to disturb the assurance
that has hitherto obtained with regard to
the married teacher?" She acts in the good
faith that the Ministry will continue the
arrangement that has been in force under the
National Board. Opinions may differ, and
probably do differ, amongst teachers themselves as to the desirability of married
women being retained in the service, and
upon that I am not going to take up any
very decided position because I have not adequately considered the whole matter, but the
point that we have really to concentrate
upon, and upon which we would require the
hon. Gentleman who will reply on behalf of
the Ministry to make some specific announcement, is whether the Ministry is going to
regard such women as ineligible for service
even under circumstances where hitherto
they have had permission to make use of
the provisions that are laid down. On
appeal to the Ministry this case has been
decided against the applicant with the result
that this married woman has been dismissed
from the service, in all probability never
to be reinstated. What we would like to ask
the hon. Gentleman is, if other cases are
submitted to him will the Ministry decide
similarly? That is really the gravamen of
the case at the moment. We do not want to
emphasise the decision in this specific case
so much as to obtain from the Ministry some
idea of what its proceeding will be in respect
of similar cases. Then I would like to put
the question to the hon. Gentleman if he
really thinks that the period of approaching
maternity is an opportune moment to make
an intimation of that description to the
teacher. If you do propose to disturb the

it should be on the intimation of her marriage rather than on the intimation of
maternity. I need not suggest to the hon.
Gentleman for he is quite well aware what

weigh it in that particular regard when the

that is taken in any future decisions he may
make with respect to this matter.
Now, there are two considerations with
respect to this question that we are considering at the moment. The first is in favour
of the course that it is desirable that married
women should be retained in the service.
Against that we have to put up this objection that it unnecessarily and perhaps
unjustifiably handicaps young aspirants who
are being trained in the hostels and training
colleges when they are in quest of situations.
I do not know, but perhaps the hon. Gentleman (Mr. McKeown) can tell us what the
proportion of married female teachers in
the service is. I have not been able to get
the figures. To tell the truth I did not exert
myself too much about it. I heard that it
was somewhere between 30 and 40 per cent.
If it is as high as that it furnishes a grave
problem for the Ministry, and I hope they
will deal with it accordingly. On the other
hand if you deny their right to continue
after the epoch of marriage that unnecessarily and unjustifiably discourages marriage
amongst teachers, and you have to choose
between the one and the other. In one case
you make more appointments for young
aspirants, and in the other case you prevent
probably a teacher from getting married.

There is one point that arises here in connection with this matter. It is scarcely
pertinent to the resolution, but at the same

said there were about 90 in the training college at the moment. Ninety would

you create these it will be necessary for you
to make vacancies for them, and I would

Dr. MORRISON: That is the question the
House has got to determine. Secondly, I
would like the House to express an opinion
as to the necessity of having a definite

Dr. MORRISON: This resolution is clear
and distinct.
That, in the opinion of this House, no
disability should attach to a married
woman teacher by reason of her marriage
or maternity.
The line that we took up, and the course I
think that should commend itself to this
House, is this, that if a lady has entered the
service and she has to retire when confinement approaches it would be an unjust and
unfair thing to make an arbitrary rule, and
I think that is what the Ministry decided
not to do. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
They thought it was unwise to make an
arbitrary rule, and, therefore, they took
refuge in the middle course, which I think
after all was the easiest avenue for them to
travel, and left it to public opinion to
determine what the proper course should be.
But I think it is not fair: If a person enters
on a profession such as teaching with
precedents established for many long years
I think it would be unfair to introduce any
legislation that would be retrospective and
would affect people who had entered under
circumstances that were wholly different.
My opinion is that it would be proper and
right for the House to take any action with
regard to this matter that they think wise.
Ladies who have entered the profession
should be secure against dismissal in cases
like this. Let the House, if it thinks wise
or if the Ministry thinks wise, make a rule
with regard to the position of women in this
important matter.
I think that this is perhaps the first evidence we have had of the rare and refreshing
fruit that this new Education Act is going
to have. The Minister of Education (The
Marquess of Londonderry) referred in the
Senate at the opening of Parliament to the
fact that the clergy by their selfish attitude
in this matter had built a chasm between
themselves and the teachers. I do not think
that is correct. I think it showed an absence
of tact, even if it were correct, on the
part of the Minister to make that remark,
and it showed an absence of statesmanship;
but be that as it may I deplore the fact that
there is more or less friction between the
teachers and the managers-I mean the
managers who are clerical men. That was
one of the dangers I saw when this Bill was
introduced, and I was anxious to have it
avoided. There is no reason why the manager
of the school, who is a clerical manager,
should be blamed in this matter. I do not
know the facts. Any facts I have I have got
from the teachers, and the teachers are inclined to think that the principal teacher
of the school is perhaps more to blame than
the manager. We have not in any case got
the second side, and I am long enough in the
world to know that there are always two
sides to a question. Before you come to a
decision it is better to hear the two sides.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I have spoken here on behalf of the
managers, and I would like to say a word
about the teachers. I know the Ulster
Teachers' Union, which represents the great
bulk of the teachers in the Northern area,
I was at the birth, if I may say so, of that
association and I have helped it as far as I
was able in its successful career. It speaks
for the united voice of the whole teachers of
Ulster. I perhaps do not see eye to eye with
them on one or two questions, one being the
managerial question, and another being the
widely vaunted, but I fear sadly defective,
Regional Committee. 1 say this, however,
that the men comprising the Executive Committee of this Teachers' Union are very
intelligent, very fair-minded, and very level
headed men, and I am certain also that if
it were left to them and to the managers to
evolve a system of education that would
satisfy the teachers, managers and people of
Ulster, the thing would be done and there
would be no dissension. I am an optimist,
but I am not an optimist with regard to the
successful working of this Education Act
which the Member for West Belfast (Sir R.
Lynn) had so much to do in forcing on the
people of Ulster in opposition to the Bill
that he drew and embodied in the Lynn
Committee Report.
What the teachers suggest-and this is
evidence of the moderation of the teachers--
what the Secretary of the Teachers' Union
says to me is "We will loyally accept any
ruling of the Ministry, provided that--as the
London County Council did when deciding
this question a few months ago-they make
the rule applicable to all future entrants into
the profession." That is a very fair proposal. Make the rule uniform Let it be
either that they must be unmarried, or, what
ever rule you make, make it uniform for all
future persons coming into the teaching
profession. Leave these people, so long as
they hold their present position guarantee
them that position. If they lose their
position then it is open to the education
authority to retain them or not. That is a
very fair proposal, and it is one which cer-

and when a woman marries she should devote herself to her home and the raising

A man who is in a good school and is attending to his work can keep his wife in decency
and in comfort. So far as the body of men
for whom I speak are concerned they are

I was very interested in a letter which appeared yesterday in the "Northern Whig" in
this connection. With part of this letter I
agree most heartily, and I should like to
read a paragraph from it, because it expresses

"The question is a very important one,
far more so than appears on the surface.
We are told that the work of a schoolteacher is a strenuous and nerve-racking

work in a satisfactory manner. It would
be interesting to obtain medical opinion on

think it should have been taken as a separate

Education, the rules which I understand we
are working under at present. Marriage
and maternity, as I have said, are admitted,
I believe under rule 92J, which lays down

fulfils certain regulations. Those regulations are that she shall be absent for two
months, one month before the birth of her
child, and presumably one month after, and
that she will provide and pay for a substitute for that period of time. The lady
whose case has been raised to-day served,
I believe, about ten years in this particular
case. I understand that she gave complete
satisfaction in every way during that time
both to the manager and to the inspectors.
Before her marriage, which took place in
1922, she approached her manager, and she
was given to understand that he had no
objection whatsoever to her marriage, and
that he hoped she would continue to teach
in the school. In spite of this understanding with the manager, when he said that he
did not object to her marriage, and to all
that her marriage necessarily implied, he
dismissed her when she fulfilled all the
obligations laid down under the rules
at a time when it was particularly
heartless that she should have been
dismissed. It must be obvious to any hon.
Member that a shock at that particular time,
such a shock as the prospect of losing a great
part of her means of livelihood, was calculated to do her far greater harm than at
any other time.
It seems to me that that is the managerial
action in the case, and to my mind nothing
has ever provided a stronger argument
against the managerial system which I hope
will soon be a thing of the past. It is for
that reason that I feel called upon to ask
for enlightenment on this particular issue
from the Ministry, and that I feel disposed
to criticise them more than I have ever done
in the past. I understand that they were
appealed to, and that they refused to interfere. The practice of the Commissioners, as
I understand, has been for ten years or more
to refuse to recognise a successor to a
teacher dismissed by a manager unless they
were satisfied that the dismissal was the result of inefficiency or misconduct. Was
there inefficiency or misconduct in this case?
Did this woman teacher not fulfil all the
regulations? The Ministry have reinstated
other teachers who were dismissed and who
appealed. They have reinstated a woman in
one case, and men in other cases. 1 understand that absolutely no fault is
alleged against this woman. She has
the right of appeal under the rules,
but she has been refused an
appeal. At present there are no rulesthat is my point-to prevent a married
woman teacher carrying on her duties provided that she complies with the regulation
that I have mentioned. It is the present
that we are discussing; it is not the future;
it is not what may be settled after the
debate to-day, or what may be settled by
the Ministry in the future-that is quite
another point.
I have expressed my views on that subject briefly, but I want to impress upon the
hon. Members here that this opens up a
great moral question. She was not dismissed when she married; she was not
advised not to marry; she was not warned;
but she is dismissed when she is about to
become a mother. Action such as that
taken by this manager is obviously-and 1
have tried to put it as fairly as possiblecalculated to do great moral harm, and to
encourage methods which will eventually
prove detrimental to the State. Bring in
legislation, make rules if you like, to the
effect that woman teachers may not marry-
I would support that as long as the interests
of those already married are safeguardedbut until those rules are brought in I ask
that the Ministry will protect these women
teachers and wipe out what seems to me,
until I have been clearly shown to
the contrary, a stain upon their chivalry.

before the House at this moment. My idea
was that we were not discussing the grievances of any individual case.

-have the rules and regulations governing

it is not a good thing for the married woman

manager comes into this particular case.
Having been a manager myself, I am not
inclined to blame the Education Department
in connection with this matter at all. I take

Bill
the Education
was passing
through this House, I was one of those who
fought and fought tenaciously, to have it
laid down that where a teacher was unreasonably dismissed, fair play should be done
by the Ministry, and that if an unjust dismissal took place, the salary of the teacher
should not be jeopardised pending his or her
obtaining another position. The whole question that we are discussing here this afternoon deals with the broad question of
whether married women shall continue to be
teachers or not. That is the problem, and
I want to know exactly what are the views
of those who represent the Education Department. I agree with the hon. Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison) that the position of teachers is very different from what
it was thirty or forty years ago, when it was
often essential for women teachers to do all
the work they possibly could in order to
assist their husbands and to keep their families. That is done away with, and there is
no reason why the position should be as pictured here this afternoon. Whether it
applies to appointments in connection with
education, or whether it deals with labour
matters, I hope the time will come when
society will be so arranged, and when the
economic position of the country will be such,
that it will not be necessary for any married
woman to go out and earn her living. I hope
the social order will improve in that direction, so that such a thing will be possible.
What I do support, and support most
heartily in connection with this Motion, is
that some principle should be laid down for
future guidance as to whether a Woman
teacher is to be deprived of her position on
her marriage or whether she is to be permitted to continue. The Ministry of Education naturally can have a say in connection with this whole matter, and I hope that
they have ideas in regard to this subject
that they will place before the House this
afternoon. Up to the present, as far as I
have been able to form a conclusion, the
Ministry as a Ministry could have taken no
other atttitude than they have taken, but
the future is another matter altogether, and
what is going to direct and guide us upon
this very interesting and important subject
is for them to inform us.

The second question upon which this debate

The wording of the Motion is a little bit
unfortunate. It does not mean what it says.
Under the present regulations there is a disability. There is the necessity for a married
woman on her approaching maternity to
cease from teaching in her school for two
months, and at her own expense to provide a
substitute. I have not heard from any hon.
Member of the House any quarrel with that
provision. Consequently the wording of the
Resolution is too wide in the first instance.
It does not mean no disability, but no further
disability than at present attaches.

Oral Answers to Questions.
POLICE FUNCTIONS WITHIN PRIVATE
PROPERTY.
1. COLONEL WOODS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs if he will give powers to the
Police to exercise their functions within
private property, such as football club
grounds, and bring Northern Ireland into
line with Great Britain in this respect?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): I understand the Police
in Great Britain-who, it must be remembered, are local forces-attending football matches are paid for by the owners of
the grounds. Our Police, when they attend
solely for the preservation of the peace and
enforcement of the criminal law, are not paid
for. I am not aware that there is any difference between the powers of a Police Constable
on private property in Great Britain and in
Northern Ireland.
While the Government is anxious to assist
as far as practicable the promoters of these
meetings, they feel it is not desirable the
Police should act under the orders of any
unofficial body, or undertake duties which
should be discharged by the servants or
officials of the promoters. To do this might
lead to friction with the public, and interfere
with the discharge of the principal duty for
which the attendance of the Police is required-the preservation of the peace.
KING'S NATIONAL ROLL OF HONOUR.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Labour if he can state how many firms are
now on the "King's National Roll of Honour,"
and how many disabled ex-Service men are
now employed in Northern Ireland?
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The Ministry of Labour in
Northern Ireland became responsible for the
administration of the King's National Roll of
Honour Scheme in Northern Ireland in
January, 1922, and at that date there were on
the Roll 105 firms employing 1,508 disabled
ex-Service men. To-day 573 firms are on the
Roll and they employ in all 3,268 disabled
ex-Service men.

Dr. MORRISON: I beg to move the motion
of which I have given notice, and in doing so
I wish to state that with the exception of
two great questions I am perfectly satisfied
with the Education Act.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Hear, hear.
Dr. MORRISON: I understand that practically everybody in Ulster is satisfied with
the Education Act except on these two points.
These Regulations deal with these two points.
The Regulations deal with religious instruction, and religious instruction is very
intimately associated with the question of the
appointment of teachers. What I want to see
in this House, or in Northern Ireland, is that
we shall avoid controversy on religious
questions, and I think that can only be done
by having it laid down clearly and distinctly
that Protestant teachers will be appointed to
Protestant schools. I think also that that
carries with it the appointment of Roman
Catholic teachers for Roman Catholic schools.
That is essentially fair and moderate and full.
I venture to say that if we can secure the
support and the approval of the large number
of influential Roman Catholics who have a
stake in the country and desire to see a
prosperous and settled condition of things in
our State, it is clearly our duty, if we can do
it without a sacrifice of principle, to try to
I
meet them and to take them with us.
consider it not only my duty but my privilege
and pleasure to follow the golden rule and do

PRIVATE BUSINESS.
Londonderry Corporation Bill.
(By Order.)
Order for Second Reading read.
The CHAIRMAN OF WAYS AND
MEANS (Mr. Moles): I propose to address
the House for just a moment or two, and my
reason for so doing is founded on the fact
359 Londonderry Corporation Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS

Second Reading.
[The Chairman]
that when this motion last stood on the
Order Paper the hon. Member for Tyrone
and Fermanagh (Mr. Miller) objected to the
Bill. I think it would be well for this House,
consisting as it does of quite a number of
new Members-that they should get clearly
into their minds what is involved in giving
a Second Reading to a Private Bill. A public Bill is founded upon reasons of State
policy, and in giving assent to the Second
Reading the House gives its assent to those
reasons. A Private Bill, on the other hand,
is founded upon certain allegations of fact
contained in that Bill which yet remain to
be proved before the Committee to which the
Bill ultimately stands referred, so that in
giving a Second Reading to a Private Bill
no hon. Member of this House, nor the
House itself as a whole, parts in any degree
with its jurisdiction, or its final and complete control of the measure. What it does
do is to conform to a mere ceremonial which
permits the Bill to be passed on to the Committee which receives all the evidence pro
and con, and sits at once as a legislative and
also as a judicial tribunal.
I would ask the House, therefore, to give
this Bill a Second Reading for that reason,
and for this further and weighty reason. The
preparation of a Bill of this kind involves
a large degree of labour. Parliamentary
agents have to be instructed, draughtsmen
engaged, and the Bill put in the form in
which it is transmitted to the Committee.
All that involves a large measure of expense.
Plans and specifications have got to be prepared, and the other authorities opposing the
Bill commit themselves also to a large measure of cost in lodging petitions and taking
the steps necessary to oppose the Bill before
the Committee. All that expense would be
thrown away if the moment it comes before
this House for the purpose of getting the
technical conformity of procedure it should
be blocked and finally rejected. I feel quite
sure that the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Miller)
does not know it would have involved these
authorities in such expense, but that it is
his wish rather that the merits of this Bill
may be investigated by the Committee, and,
having been reported upon, the Third Reading will afford him the opportunity, if he
feels it his duty, to invite the House to reject
the Bill. In the meantime, no representatives in this House are in any degree prejudiced by the Second Reading. For these
reasons, I beg to move the Second Reading..

inside their own city. It does not lead from

Tyrone. This bridge accommodates the
people of Derry. They send out their

As I have said before in this House I was
