Belfast is a city practically of mushroom
growth, the result of a century and a half
of labour and industry on the part of its
citizens, and it suffers, I think, in comparison with many of the older cities such as
Dublin, London, Edinburgh and Glasgow, in
the fact that the medical staff of Belfast and
the philanthropic people of Belfast have been
taxed to meet a great want that has suddenly sprung up and which has more or less
overwhelmed them. It is the same with
regard to the churches. Nevertheless the
task has been done, and done well, but
Belfast is more or less handicapped by these
conditions.
When you come to the immediate subject of
my resolution, and that is the recent discoveries of the beneficial influence of X-ray,
I would draw your attention to several points.
Superficial X-Ray has been in force for quite
a long time, and it has done wonderful
things for superficial cancer, that is cancer
on the outside of the body and the skin, but
it is not so far as we know able to deal with
cancer that is deep seated, and in the development of X-Ray scientific men have views that
by intensifying the power of the ray, multiplying it enormously, they have been able to
deal with tumours deeply seated in the body
that otherwise were beyond their reach. Let
ine give an example of what I know was the
experience of a friend. A concrete case sometimes brings home a matter like this with
more force than a whole argument. This
friend is a very intellectual man, a man of
wide influence and of wide popularity. He
got ill six years ago. The disease was obscure. He developed dropsy in his abdomen.
He was tapped six times, and after the sixth
time he was brought to Belfast and operated
on.
When his abdomen was opened it was
found that the condition was such that no
advantage could be gained by further surgical
interference. The wound was stitched up
and he was sent to London for treatment by
radium. The radium treatment helped him,
and he came home much benefited and improved for two years. But a year ago
the disease returned, and that man seeing that all other agencies were useless was
recommended to try this modern plan of deep
or intensified X-Ray therapy. He was sent
to a hospital in Dublin, and I saw him shortly
after he came back. He said that it would
take months before the beneficial result of
that treatment developed, but he was quite
sanguine as to the result. I met him last
week walking about Belfast. He can walk
more quickly than I can. He seems a better
man physically than I am, and I hope and
believe, as he hopes and believes, that he is
finally cured of his disease. (Hon. Members :
Hear, hear).
Now, I tell this House, and any medical
man will tell you, that that man by all past
experience was certain to die if this intense
X-Ray had not been applied, and if it had
not had the results of which I have now informed you.
I told the House about three
months ago that I travelled from this House
one morning with one of the most distinguished surgeons in Belfast. We talked
over diseases and the efforts the medical profession were making to combat them. He
spoke of cancer and the results of intense
X-Ray treatment. He told me of two cases
that he had been called upon to deal with,
one of them cancer of the rectum and the
other cancer of the womb. He said according
to his knowledge these were not expected
to live, and he sent them to London.
They were treated by deep X-ray therapy,
and he tells me that apparently both are
cured. I brought that before the House, and
I suggested it was a matter that should be
taken into consideration by this House with
the object of developing that treatment here
in the North of Ireland. There has been
published in Dublin a "Cancer Journal,"
and I find in that "Cancer Journal" that
have been sent by leading surgeons
from Belfast to the Cancer Hospital in
Dublin. At least two cases have been sent
there from Belfast, and there have also been
cases sent from Ballycastle, Coleraine and
Derry. They say plainly in their report
that it is too early to speak of the permanent results of the treatment, and it is
undoubtedly true that the profession may be
disappointed in these cases as they have been
in the past, and that given a sufficient time
the disease will reappear. But whether that
is so or not, with the knowledge that I have
of these cases, I say that so far as I can
judge the results are extraordinarily satisfactory, and that in my opinion we are on
our way to solving the problem of this
terrible scourge that has afflicted the human
cases
race.
With regard to the cost of treatment, that
becomes an important thing in connection
with what I propose to do. The cost of
treatment, I am told-and I speak with
hesitation, because I know it only approximately and the fees may vary according to the
special conditions of the case-is £50 in
Dublin, and £100 in London. As to the cost
of the apparatus, I wrote to the Secretary of
the Cancer Hospital in Dublin, and I have
his reply here, dated 17th November, 1922.
He says:-
I am in receipt of your letter of the 14th
inst., and in reply I beg to state that if
the apparatus referred to is intended for

deep work the cost will be about £1,000,
and if for superficial work 300 guineas.
It is obvious that no poor person can pay
£50 for treatment, and in this matter I speak
only for the poor. The rich are able to
provide for themselves, and do not need our
help. They can go to Dublin or London or
Vienna; our poor people cannot.
I go
further and I say that it is the first duty
of this House, as it is the first duty of every
Government, to provide for the poor, and to
help them.
Now I come to the second point of my
resolution, and that is the treatment by insulin. In 1922 there were 142 people in the
Six Counties who died of diabetes. A new
discovery has taken place with regard to
that malady, a discovery that, if it does
not make a cure certain, goes so far as this,
that a man or a woman who is doomed to a
life of invalidism is enabled by this treatment to resume his or her ordinary work and
to discharge his or her ordinary avocation
for an indefinite time. But in order that it
may be effective a central institution is required in Belfast for both these diseases.
Regarding insulin, work is already being
carried out in this respect in the Royal
Victoria Hospital, and the young surgeon
who is carrying it out tells me that in his
opinion there should be a central clinic in
the city for dealing with this matter of insulin. You want to train the patients to
test the sugar in their blood and in their
urine. You want to show them how to use
insulin, so that they can go home with a
hypodermic syringe, graduate the test, and
keep in a condition of health. He tells me
what I think is an appalling state of things
to announce in this civilised community of
Northern Ireland, that two of the patients
that he had under treatment, and whom he
had taught how to treat themselves, died
since owing to the fact that they had no
means of getting the necessary insulin with
which to cure themselves.
Mr. POLLOCK: How recently?
Dr. MORRISON: He mentioned that to me
a month ago. I do not know how long ago
it is, but the fact remains that two people
died through their inability to get the insulin that was necessary for their health.
What I want to point out to this House is
that in the meantime the whole field is clear
in the Six Counties. By and by some hospital
-Ballymena, Coleraine or Larne will be
establishing a system of deep X-Ray therapy,
and perhaps it will be building a wing for
the purpose. I think it would be far better
for the Government to come to the aid of
the people of Ulster, and especially of the
poor of Ulster, by taking this matter into
their own hands and building or fitting up
in the centre of Belfast a hospital that would
meet this want and would provide for this
intense X-ray treatment for those who unfortunately suffer from cancer, and insulin
for the many people in the Six Counties who
suffer from diabetes. Clearly in the meantime Boards of Guardians cannot do this; for
them to send patients to Belfast and to
Dublin, and to pay these fees, is impossible.
Therefore, I think, seeing that that is the
position of affairs, and that the field is comparatively limited for the Government, it is
clearly the duty of this House to pass the
Motion that I have the honour to put before
them, and to ask the Government to make
provision to meet this want and to provide
for these unfortunate people.
I feel that to allow this matter to linger,
and not to bring it before the House for twelve
months, puts a responsibility more or less
upon me. I had hesitation in bringing it
forward-hesitation that, as you know, has
only been really overcome now. I knew that
this thing was possible, but I was waiting
for developments and to see if some provision would not be made to meet this want.
But now that I have put these facts before
the House the responsibility for the matter
rests on the Members of this House, and it
rests on the Government of this State of
ours. If we are animated by the principles
which I am sure animate every Member of
this House and animate the whole body of
the Government, something will be done to
meet this case. I have talked over the matter
with the Minister of Finance. He has a
clear head, he has a sympathetic heart, he
is open to any argument that you can bring
forward. He and I discussed this thing, and
he received my advances in a very favourable manner. The difficulty was finance. 1
think, when you look at the amount of money
that we expend, the sum of £10,000 can be
easily provided. When you look at the
enormous amount of suffering that this thing
involves, owing to the impossibility of bringing relief to these poor suffering creatures
unless something like this is done, I think
you will see that this is a matter for Government action, and I hope you will support
me by passing this Motion. Then it becomes
not a Departmental matter; it becomes a
matter for the Government, and I am sure
that if you pass this Motion the Government
will consider it as favourably as they can
and see that something is done to meet this
urgent need and to bring about this very
necessary reform. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)

and that we regard as low enough. I do not

There is no question at all that deep
X-Ray treatment does produce very considerable ameliorative effects. It procures for the
time being a more or less complete disappearance of the tumour, but that tumour
in practically every instance recurs again
and again until the patient finally dies.
There is no question that the life of a man
who is condemned to death in six months'
time with inoperable cancer may be prolonged two, or three, or even four years by
deep X-ray therapy. That is a most
excellent result to the credit of deep X-Ray
therapy from the point of view of amelioration and sometimes the prolongation of life.
There is that very great advantage in deep
X-Ray therapy, but that is very different
from the question whether cancer is cured
or not cured. At the present time no
surgeon considers that a case of cancer is
cured until five years have elapsed, and no
return
has taken place. Deep X-Ray
treatment has been in practice in this
country very little more than five years
altogether, consequently no surgeon would
claim as cures any cases of deep X-Ray
therapy in this country. Certainly there are
a number of cases in the Cancer Hospital in
Dublin which was established at the
beginning of last year, but it is
impossible to talk about a
cure
in a case of cancer simply because
you do not see the cancer at the end of six
months. If we could give a record of cancer
cases assured at that period, the percentage
would be 90 instead of probably 20 or 25.
This question is a rather interesting
little sidelight on
international politics
and the reason why deep X-Ray
therapy has been boomed to such
extent is because it is a German invention.
A good many years ago now a very able
French woman, a genius practically, Madame
Curie, discovered radium. Radium is
instrument which has been used very widely
an
an
in the treatment of cancer with results very
comparable with those obtained by deep
X-Ray therapy. I have seen a case myself
where a patient had been condemned three
years before as being an inoperable case of
cancer. She received the radium treatment.
and was still alive, her condition being very
little the worse to all appearance than at
the commencement of the three years. As
far as we know deep X-Ray therapy cannot
do very much more than that. But it was
discovered, of course, that radium produced
this effect by very highly-penetrative gamma
rays. The Germans, who were always
scientific and anxious not to be outdone,
looked for something which would be more
powerful and produce greater effects than
radium.
They discovered the X-Ray and consequently boomed the X-Ray as against
radium exactly in the same way
as they boomed Koch as against
Pasteur when bacteriology was so much to
the front in medical thought and science.
That is the principal reason why X-Rays are
being boomed at the present time. And remember deep X-Rays are not without danger,
for patients have died after treatment with
X-Rays both in Germany and in London.
They do produce a very pronounced effect
upon the tissues of the body.
Now it is suggested that the only way to
get deep X-Ray treatment in Northern
Ireland is by the intervention of the Government. But the expense of deep X-Rays is
not such a tremendous matter that it cannot
be brought over to Northern Ireland. As a
matter of fact I know one very excellent
radiologist in Belfast who is having a deep
his house next
X-Ray plant installed in
month or so.
The question has been repeatedly considered as to whether deep X-Ray plant
should be installed in the hospital with

that it has not been afforded to the poor

on the advice of our radiological expert.
As I say there was a conference in London
on this subject of the treatment of cancer
by deep X-Ray and the general opinion, not
only of the surgeons and general medical men,

but of radiologists and of the men who were

Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask does the hon.

Has it never accomplished a cure?
Mr. JOHNSTONE: I do not say so. I say
a sufficient time has not elapsed to say

What I really would like to see if the

What I should recommend to the Government is to purchase a certain amount of
radium, which could be brought to Belfast
and utilised here, because there is no
question that radium is useful not only in
cancer but in many other diseases. At
present we have to get radium sent from
London and Liverpool and across the water.
Radium is used in radium emanation tubes.
That is the most economical way of using it.
It requires to be put under the care of a
skilled physicist. I suggest if the Government feel inclined to spend a sum of money
that they should spend it in buying radium,
and that they should put it in charge of a

As for insulin, I should like to press that

It is not because I am anxious to see the

Government distributing drugs free, but I

'control where disease is treated. Now

As I understand the London hospitals provide this treatment. These hospitals are
maintained by voluntary contributions; and
let me say this, that, although there are very
great hospitals to be found in London, some

the necessary funds to carry on the work
we in Belfast have been able to do a

With regard to the cure of this particular
disease we have been discussing, namely

has been suggested, can be achieved by the

to bear on the authorities in the

Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: It is quite obvious that it

suggest to hon. Members that it is

A central institution was suggested. Well
I think professional opinion, so far as I
can gather, is opposed to the provision of a

Minister decides that the applicant cannot

Supposing the members of a Local Authority

2 APRIL, 1924.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Wednesday, 2nd April, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
SALARIES OF TECHNICAL TEACHERS.
1. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he is now in a position
to make a pronouncement with regard to
the revision of the salaries of principals
and teachers engaged by Technical Instruction Committees in Northern Ireland, as
promised in this House on November 6th,
1923.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown) : A Departmental Committee
has been considering the question of
the salaries of teachers in Technical
Schools and has recently made a report containing their recommendations
to the Minister. These recommendations are
now being examined by the Ministry of
Education and the Ministry of Finance, and
I hope it will be possible to make a definite
pronouncement at an early date.
ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Local Government (Financial
Provisions) [Money]
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That for the purpose of any Act of the
present Session amending the provisions of
Section 10 of the Local Government Act (Northern Ireland), 1923, it is expedient to
authorize a charge upon moneys provided by
Parliament-
(a) in respect of such sums as may be
certified to be payable under sub-section (1)
of the said Section, as amended by such Act,
to or on behalf of County Councils, County
Borough Councils, District Councils, and
Boards of Guardians of Poor-law Unions, as
the equivalent of the average of the payments which were made out of the Local
Taxation (Ireland) Account to or on behalf
of such Councils and Boards in or in respect
of the three Financial Years ended on the
31st day of March, 1918,, the 31st day of
March, 1919, and the 31st day of March,
1920:
(b) of such sum to or on behalf of a
County Council or Urban District Council,
as may (notwithstanding anything in the
said sub-section as amended by any such
Act) be certified to be ninety per cent, of
one-half of the sum by which the amount
required to be raised in any Financial Year
for the purpose of meeting a railway or
harbour charge exceeds or would exceed a
sum equal to sixpence in the pound on the
rateable value of the area to be rated for
that purpose."
THE PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The Resolution which I am now called upon
to move relates to Clause 2 of the Local
Government (Financial Provisions) Bill,
which Honourable Members will observe
appears in italics, pending the påssing of this
Money Resolution. The first part of the
Resolution is identical, except for the addition of the words "or in respect of," with
the Money Resolution agreed to by the House
in connection with the passing of the Local
Government Act of the last Session. The
reason why it is considered desirable to
amend the Act of 1923 by the addition of
these words has already been explained by
my right honourable Friend, the Minister of
Home Affairs, in the course of the Second
Reading yesterday. I would remind honourable Members, however, that under the 1923
Act certain grants to Local Authorities were
to be based on the average of the payments
actually made from the Local Taxation
Account in the years 1918, 1919 and 1920, and
the intention of this Resolution, and the
Clause to which it is a preliminary, is that
this average shall be based on the payments
made in respect of those three years, whether
made within the years in question or subsequently. This is only fair to the Local
Authorities as in two of these years the payments made by the Imperial Government
were belated owing to the general chaotic
position of Local Government administration
throughout a large part of Ireland at the
time.
As regards the second part of this Resolution, the necessity for which has also been
referred to by my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Home Affairs, I should explain
that the basis of the average of three years
may in practice be found to work out unfairly in some cases. I think there is only
one payment really affected by this Clause,
and that is in respect of the Clogher Valley
Railway. There are no harbours affected.
The payment to this railway was formerly
governed by the provisions of Section 58 of
the Local Government (Ireland) Act, 1898. It
is now proposed to return to the
basis laid down in the earlier Act
as far as this
particular grant is

original purpose of this grant was to provide

Illegitimate Children (Affiliation
Orders) Bill.
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
CLAUSE I (Power to make Affiliation Order
upon man alleged to be father of illegitimate
child)-
1.-(1) Where a man is alleged by the
mother to be the father of her illegitimate
child, and has been summoned in accordance with the provisions of this Act to
appear before a court of summary jurisdiction acting for the petty sessions district or place in which the mother resides,
or in which the mother or her illegitimate
child is in receipt of relief from the poor
rates of any poor law union, the court shall
have power, after hearing all the circumstances of the case, to adjudge the man to
be the putative father of the child, and to
make an order upon him (in this Act referred to as an Affiliation Order") for
the payment of-
""
(a) a weekly sum of money not exceeding twenty shillings a week in respect
of the maintenance and education of the
child;
(b) the expenses incidental to the birth
of the child;
(c) if the child has died before the
making of the Affiliation Order, the
funeral expenses of such child; and
(d) the costs of obtaining the Affiliation
Order.
(2) For the purposes of this Act the expression "the mother " means any single
woman who is with child or delivered of
an illegitimate child; and, so far as is
necessary to enable a married woman to
take proceedings under this Act against any
man other than her husband in respect of
her illegitimate child, the said expression
includes such married woman, whether or
not she has married after the birth of the
child, or is living with her husband.
(3) The court shall not make an Affiliation Order unless-
(a) the birth of the child has taken
place;
(b) the man alleged to be the father
of the child appears before the court or
it is proved to the court that the summons
was duly served upon him; and
(c) the evidence of the mother is corroborated in some material particular by
other evidence to the satisfaction of the
court.
(4) The court, in deciding whether or not
it shall make an order for the payment of
the expenses incidental to the birth of an
illegitimate child, shall not take into consideration the fact that the mother is entitled to receive maternity benefit under
the enactments relating to National Health
Insurance.
(5) The Bastardy (Ireland) Act, 1863, is
hereby repealed as respects Northern
Ireland.

Mr. ROBB: I beg to move: In Clause 1,
page 1, line 12, after union" (poor-law
union, the court") insert "or in which the
said man is at the date of the service of the
summons residing." If hon Members will
look at this sub-section they will see that it
there provides that the court in which any
of these cases is to be tried is to be a court
in respect of either, first, the place where the
mother of the illegitimate child resides or
the court of the place in which the
mother of the illegitimate child is in receipt
of Poor-Law relief, the Poor-Law Union. That
is a variation from the general rule which
obtains now in all cases that a man shall be
sued where he lives. I cannot see why in this
case, as well as in every other case, jurisdiction should not be given to the home of the
defendant.
I do not quarrel absolutely with the
decision of the Government to have what they
have provided for here, but I do ask that the
ordinary rule shall be followed, and that
there shall be the provision, which I have
inserted in a later Amendment, that where
a man is sued in a place where he does not
reside he shall be paid a viaticum from the
place where he does reside to the place where
the case is to be tried. In order to attain
that object I propose at this point to insert
that the case shall be tried first of all where
the mother resides or where the mother of
the illegitimate offspring shall be in receipt
of relief from the Poor-law Union, or which
would be the ordinary case and the ordinary
rule of law, the place in which the
said man at the date of the service
of the summons is residing. That gives
provision in respect of the ordinary rule
that a
man shall be sued where he lives.
If hon. Members will look further down they
will see that I have an Amendment which is
put down for page 2, line 20, which provides
that where a Court is sitting for a Petty
Sessions district in which at the date of the
service of the summons the man was not
residing, and an order is to be made, it
must be proved that along with the summons
when served there was tendered to the man
reasonable conduct money from the place
where he was then residing to the place where
the court is held. These two Amendments
are for the defendant, and I move this Amendment because I do not think it fair that a
man should not be sued where he resides.
Why should a man who is living in Derry be
brought to Belfast Petty Sessions? The
answer may be that the mother of the child
is living in Belfast. That may not be a sufficient answer. It is certainly not a sufficient
answer to the general case; it may be in a
particular case. It may very well be that
a perfectly innocent man without means has
a summons served on him to appear in Belfast. when he in fact resides in Enniskillen
or in Derry.
Mr. McGUFFIN: What if he is living in
England?
Mr. ROBB: We cannot sue him.
Mr. DONALD: Or the Free State?
Mr. ROBB: He must be within the jurisdiction. My point is this that it is not fair
that the plaintiff should be entitled to select
her home venue contrary to the ordinary rules
of law and should not be compelled to sue the
defendant in his own home which would be the
ordinary rule of law. I should not object
absolutely to giving such power as a right
to bring the case in a district where the man
does not reside, but I suggest that if that
is to be done reasonable conduct money
should be given to the defendant in order
to bring him from where he does reside to
the place where the case is to be tried.
Accordingly I move that at this point, page
1, line 12, these words be inserted.

Mrs. CHICHESTER: I beg to move in
Clause 1, page 1, line 12, after Union'
("of any Poor-law Union ") to insert "the
case shall be heard in camera and."
In moving this Amendment I am trying
to look upon the Clause from two points of
view-first, from the point of view of an
unfortunate girl who has been led astray
and betrayed by an unscrupulous man and
takes an action against him as the father of
her illegitimate child; and, secondly, from
the point of view of a man who might be
wrongfully accused by an unscrupulous
woman for purposes of blackmail of being the
father of her child. Now, in the first case 1
can conceive of the great shame which a
young girl might feel in having to give
evidence before a crowd of so-called friends
and neighbours who, I am afraid, especially
if the case is heard near home, would flock,
just as crows do to the carrion, to the
feast. Then she would have to bear the subsequent and further shame of newspaper
publicity. After all, this unfortunate young
girl whom I have in my mind and am trying
to describe has taken the first downward
step. Is there any need to drive her still
further into the abyss and to make her lose
every remnant of self-respect which she has
left? It seems to me that we want to prevent
her from losing her self-respect, and we
want to try to put her on to the right path
again. The result of these cases being heard´
in an open Court might be that the more
decent of the fallen class-the young girl of
whom I am speaking-might rather than
face the publicity and shame never lay an
information against the father, might prefer
to struggle on and try to maintain the child,
and in the end it is the innocent child who
would be the sufferer. It might even lead to
consequences which we hope this Bill wil.
avoid, consequences which were very graphically dealt with by the hon. Member for the
University (Dr. Morrison) on the Second
Reading of this Bill.
Now I come to the second point of view,
the case of the man who has been wrongfully
accused, who is completely innocent of the
charge brought against him, perhaps a man
of high standing, of honour, of integrity, absolutely, as I say, innocent of the charge,
against whom possibly there may be something which would lend a little colour to the
charge-I mean there might be some circumstance which might be brought forward and
used by an unscrupulous woman to bring him
into this case. I believe, and I am sure, there
are many men such as I have described who
would pay anything rather than face the
publicity of an open Court, because, even if
they are completely cleared and exonerated,
the very fact of their having been connected
with a case of this kind unfortunately leaves,
and must leave, a slur and a shadow upon
them. I know it will be said that publicity
acts as a deterrent. It may do in some cases,
but for all the good it does in one way, I am
perfectly certain it does a great deal of harm
in many other ways, and that it does more
harm than it does good. In addition to the
two points which I have endeavoured to put
as well as I could before the Committee, it
seems to me that publicity also provides the
public with the fare which appeals to their
worst instincts.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Hear, hear.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: On the Second Reading the hon. Gentleman, the Parliamentary
Secretary for Home Affairs (Mr. Megaw), in
reply to my suggestion, said that the hearing
of cases in camera is alien to the system of
justice that has commended itself to the
people of the British Isles, and that cases
heard in camera are certainly regarded with
very great suspicion. It is possible that the
hearing of these cases is alien to the system
of justice that has held sway here hitherto.
I would ask hon. Members: Are we to be
hidebound by tradition all the time? Can we
not strike out for ourselves? Must we always
copy other legislation? Must we always copy
what has been done across the water? It is.
perhaps, something new that I am asking. It
has been, as I believe I said before, tried in
Australia, and I hope that at any rate serious
consideration will be given to what I have
said, because I am convinced that in many
cases a great deal of harm is done by this
scrt of case being heard publicly. I think it
would be worse, and I would press this even

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: It is not an
easy matter to follow the speech that has
been delivered by my hon. Friend (Mrs.
Chichester), who shares with me the representation of the City and County of Derry.
She has made a very good and a very strong
case, and there are very many aspects of it
that make a great appeal to our feelings and
to our sentiments, but I am not quite happy
in my mind that it would be a wise or a
prudent thing for this Parliament to put
into one of its Acts--because this is what is
asked for on this occasion-that all cases of
this kind shall be heard behind closed doors.
I think we must hesitate and ponder very
seriously upon a question of this kind before
putting a Clause of that kind into the Bill.
I quite agree that a strong case can be made
out, and the hon. Member (Mrs. Chichester)
has made out a very strong case for the hearing of cases of this character in private.
But there is another side to this question
that cannot be overlooked. The vast majority
of the people of these countries have a desire
that justice shall be administered openly and
above-board. That is a very healthy sentiment; it is good for justice itself and it
secures in the administration of justice the
confidence and respect of the community.
There are two standpoints that the hon.
Member (Mrs. Chichester) has emphasised,
but I think we have got to look at it from
another standpoint. Unquestionably publicity
does act as a deterrent, but take even the
case of the innocent man who has been mentioned. If he has been cleared by a Court
that sat in secret, and the public have not
been made acquainted with the evidence, will
there not be innumerable whisperings in
regard to what the result was? People
will come to the conclusion that there
was something wrong and it had to be hushed
up, and that the man was guilty all the
same. There is that danger. I have no
objection, if the Government see their way
to accept the suggestion, to leaving it to the
County Court judge and to the resident
magistrates to decide where there are certain
circumstances in connection with a case if
it would not be in the interests of public
decency that it should be heard in camera.
Mr. McGUFFIN: They have that power.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I do not think
they have that power.
Mr. MEGAW: Not magistrates.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Magistrates
have not got that power. The Judge Oi
Assize has in certain cases. I am not an
authority upon these legal matters, but 1
do not think the magistrates' Court have any
right to do anything of the kind. I think
if we gave the resident magistrates that
power it might meet all that is necessary in
connection with this matter. Another criticism levelled against hearing cases of this
description in open Court is that nauseating
details sometimes manage to get into the
public Press. Unfortunately that is so, but
I have read the newspapers of most countries, and I consider that in this respect we
in Great Britain and Ireland have the
cleanest Press that is to be found in any
country in the world. As a rule, except in
very isolated cases, you can trust to the
discretion, sound judgment, and good taste of
any reporter or editor as to what gets into
his columns. On the whole you may take
that as an accepted fact. On the broad principle that it is not wise to insert a Clause
like this in a Bill to exclude the public from
any court of justice I am opposed to this
Amendment, and on the other grounds which
I have indicated, taking everything into consideration, I think there is no alternative for
us but to allow cases to be tried as they
have been tried hitherto, with the exception
that the Government, if it thinks it wise to
do so, may give to the resident magistrate
the right if he thinks the facts of the case
warrant it to try it behind closed doors.
Mr. CRAWFORD: The hon. Member who
has just sat down (Sir Robert Anderson) has
just said that the Press does not publish
unseemly details, and he seems exceedingly
anxious, having regard to the fact that the
people will not see the details in the Press,
that they can hear them in the place where
the case is tried. I would like to say a word

Mr. BEST: I regret very much that the
Government cannot accept the Amendment
which has been so ably proposed by the hon.
Member for Derry City (Mrs. Chichester.)
If anything could induce the Government to
accept the Amendment it would be the splendid speech made by that hon. Member. We
have considered this question very carefully,
and we have come to the conclusion that the
main principle underlying it is that justice
must be done to those who have fallen, and
we consider that the best way of effecting
that is to show up the man who has done the
damage. My hon. and learned Friend, the
Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Megaw), in
speaking on this question on the Second
Reading of this Bill, told the House that it
was a settled principle of our jurisprudence
that all cases should be heard in public.
That is almost the universal rule. There
are one or two exceptions which have been
arrived at in recent years, but the general
rule is that every case should be heard in
public, that any person has the right to come
into a public court, to see how justice is
being administered for the people, and how
it would be administered for himself if he
came in. That is the result of the accumulated experience of centuries, and it is the
one principle more than anything else that
has given the people such confidence in the
administration of the law, because whether
it is the highest judge in the land or the
humblest justice you have the eyes of the
people fixed upon him. They hear his
reasons, they hear his decision, and they
come out and say "That is a wrong decision,
because so-and-so should have happened," or
"That is a right decision, because so-and-sodid happen." I say that is one of the greatest
benefits to the people themselves, to their
belief and their faith in the proper administration of justice.
I am told, of course, that we should not
slavishly follow Great Britain. May I say
this, that the most successful jurisprudence
in the world is the jurisprudence of Great
Britain. Great Britain has given laws to the
English-speaking people; they all follow the
laws of Great Britain with the exception of
Scotland-their law is based upon the Roman
law. Great Britain, as I say, has given a
lead to all the nations of the world in laying
down a proper system of jurisprudence, and I
am not ashamed of following Great Britain
as far as law is concerned, because. I am
following the best example in the world.
But may I say this, when the Criminal Law
(Amendment) Bill of last Session was before
the House, we thought that the hearing of incest cases should be made
public and we had provision to that effect
in the Bill. The Members of the House
pursuaded the Government that it was advisable to keep to the existing law, which
required that those cases should be heard in
camera. I myself, I must confess, was
against that, and I am against it still.
There are other cases that must be heard
in camera. This case of an Affiliation Order
is on quite a different footing to an ordinary
seduction action. Who would suggest that
497 Illegitimate Children Bill-
Committee.

the case of a girl who brings an action for
seduction against the person she states is
the father of her child should be heard in
camera? These cases are not tried in
camera, and it is the experience of most that
publicity is the one thing that enables the
liability to be put on the proper shoulders.
In these cases it is well known in the country
where everybody knows everybody's business
-in 99 cases out of 100-who is the father
of the child in a particular instance. They
know the young man who has been keeping
company with the young girl. They know
he is to blame. I really think-perhaps I
had better not say it, but to a certain extent
it is false modesty to put it forward that
these cases should be heard in camera. I am
firmly convinced that justice will be better
done to the girl who has been wronged by
having these proceedings heard in public, and
after all I think that is the final factor that
should make each of us give a vote one way
or the other. We are agreed it is to do
justice to the girl who has been wronged
and particularly to do justice to the innocent
little child that this Bill has been introduced.

CLASS 1. No. 7.
OLD-AGE PENSIONS.
Motion made and Question proposed:
That a sum not exceeding £817,752 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1925, in respect
of the payment of Old-Age Pensions, for
certain administrative expenses in connection therewith, and for pensions under
the Blind Persons Act, 1920.
as
Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members will find
this estimate on page 62 of the Estimates.
As was the case last year this estimate ranks
third in money value amongst those which
the Committee will be asked to pass. There
is a comparatively slight increase over last
year's figures due partly to an increase in
the administrative expenditure of the Customs and Excise Department acting
our agents, and partly to an increase in
the cost of printing the Post Office Paying
Orders. The provision made in last year's
vote for printing Paying Orders was found
to be quite inadequate. It may be of interest to hon. Members to know that this
printing has during the past been carried
out by the Bank of England, but during the
forthcoming financial year will be placed by
the Post Office with a trade printing contractor. Hon. Members will remember that
in introducing this estimate last year I referred to the saving which had been effected
in the cost of the services performed on our
behalf by the Customs and Excise Department in connection with Old Age Pension
administration. This saving resulted from
a reorganisation of Customs and Excise areas
in Northern Ireland. The saving, however,
was slightly over-estimated last year, and
this explains the slight apparent increase
this year. In other words, the Customs and
Excise Department were over-sanguine as to
the amount by which they expected to
economise in the administration of these
services in preparing the estimates for the
previous year. The expenditure on the
services performed by the Post Office,
namely, the paying of the pension orders,
the cost of the pension books, and the cost
of the paper for the paying orders, shows a
decrease as compared with last year's figures,
due mainly to the fall in the cost of living
bonus payable to the Post Office staff. The
cost of paying an Old Age Pension Order in
1924-25 is estimated at 1059 pence as compared with 1205 pence in the previous year.
The rest of the figures do not call for any
comment, but it will be noted that it has not
been considered necessary to vary the amount
of the estimate of the actual pensions themselves, which remain at £1,050,000, the same
as the previous year, to cover the cost of
pensions paid under the Old Age Pensions
Acts and the Blind Persons Act. The amount
actually paid during the financial year 1923-
24 was approximately £1,040,000. The number of ordinary old age pensioners on 31st
December, 1923, was 41,300.
Mr. McGUFFIN: In the Six Counties?
Mr. BARBOUR: Yes. The number of blind
persons in receipt of pensions under the Blind
Persons Act, 1920, at the same date was 1,000.
The appropriations in aid represent sums refunded by persons who have obtained pensions
without statutory conditions being fulfilled.
The actual amount recovered for the year
1923-24 was £52. That is not a very large
of
sum considering the amount pensions
actually paid. It is evident from the questions
which have from time to time been addressed
to Ministers that hon. Members take a considerable interest in the administration of the
Pension Acts, and it may, therefore, not be
out of place if I refer very briefly to the
manner in which this service is administered.
The service continues to be carried on by the
Commissioners of Customs and Excise acting
as agents, for the Ministry of Finance, and
claims for Old Age Pensions are dealt with
in the first instance by the local Customs and
Excise officers who act as pension officers.
For Excise purposes the country is divided
into a number of districts, each of which is
in charge of an officer responsible to the Collector of Customs and Excise at Belfast, who
thus forms the connecting link between the
local officers and the Board of Customs and
Excise in London. As in pre-transfer days,
hon. Members will understand, the work relating to Old Age Pensions forms only a part
of the duties of the Excise officers. In the
City of Belfast it is necessary to supplement
Committee.

2 APRIL, 1924.
the Excise officers by ten women pensions
officers, who are employed solely on this duty.
I am sure hon. Members will also be glad to
be informed as to the position which has arisen
from the fact that there are now within the
British Isles three Old Age Pension authorities.
The Old Age Pension Acts provide that before
a pension can be granted the claimant must
show that he has, since attaining the age of
50, resided in the United Kingdom for an
aggregate period of not less than 12 years if
he is a natural-born British subject; or if he
is not a natural-born British subject that he
has resided in the United Kingdom for an
aggregate period of 20 years after attaining
the age of 50. The pension rights of a
person removing from Great Britain
to Northern Ireland and vice
versa
are not affected by the change of
residence, there being reciprocal arrangements between the two countries in this
matter; as a matter of fact, the number of
such removals is small. There are no similar
arrangements with the Free State, and
persons crossing the Border from that country into Northern Ireland have to qualify
by the necessary period of residence for
pensions here.
Mr. McGUFFIN: How many years would
that be?
Mr. BARBOUR: As I stated before, after
attaining the age of 50 they would have
to complete a period of residence of twelve
years in Northern Ireland, but hon. Members should remember that prior to the
establishment of the Free State the South
of Ireland was still within the United Kingdom, and so the time they spent in the
South of Ireland prior to the passing of the
Government of Ireland Act, and after they
attained the age of 50, would go towards
this twelve years' residential qualification.
The figures of the Estimates follow very
closely on the lines of last year. I have
already explained the apparent increase in
the Agency charges, but even at this increased figure the cost of administration
represents a saving of nearly £13,000 compared with the cost as it existed, at the
time we took over the administration of
this service. I beg to move.

in view of the fact that the expenditure on
pensions is practically the same for the
coming year as for the current year I have

pensioners is more or less stable and that
there is neither an increase nor a decrease.

Mr. POLLOCK: I think I mentioned to the
Committee or to the House a year ago, or
possibly more, that the old-age pension question required investigation rather from the
point of view of the abuses that exist than the
grievances which have been suggested by some
of my hon. Friends-
Mr. McGUFFIN: Both exist.
Mr. POLLOCK: And also from the point
of view of economy. I did learn from those
who are interested in local Pensions Committees that there were cases that were probably on all fours with some of those
mentioned by my hon. Friend where transfers of property were deliberately made in
order to reduce the income of the persons
concerned and thus to qualify them for the
old age pension. I am satisfied that the old
age pension question is one for close investigation and possible re-arrangement. There
was a very famous statesman who made a
remark at one time that it was very difficult to drive two or three coaches through
Temple Bar at the same time. Our hands
have been so full with a variety of matters
that it has been quite impossible to give
the attention to this question that it deserves. I think I should point out to my hon.
Friends, and particularly to those who are
immediately concerned-and it is a question
that should concern every Member of this
House-that the co-ordination of the various
forms of public relief, whether through the
machinery of old age pensions, national
health insurance, or Poor-law relief, will
probably form the subject of a great inquiry
in Great Britain. In fact I may definitely
make the remark that the whole question
is at present in a state of fluidity, and the
attention of legislators in Great Britain has
been turned for some considerable time past
to the pressing necessity for some reform
in regard to the distribution of public relief.
It is felt particularly that those persons
who have exhibited thrift in the course of
their lives should not be penalised at the
latter end of their careers because they have
practised a virtue that a great many other
thriftless persons did not practise.
However, the whole question is quite too
large to be settled at the end of the sitting and
when we have so few Members, even assuming that it was a matter for general discussion. I do not suppose that anything can
be done, and of course we require our Vote.
Let me, however, finally say that I think
the local Pensions Committees do their best.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) They do good
work. Although the Customs and Excise
act as our agents in the investigation of
matters, it must be remembered that they
are only our agents, and the Court of appeal
is the Home Office. I daresay it does happen
that recommendations made by local Committees, when carried to the Home Office
may have been turned down, because the
Government Department that determines
these cases must necessarily scrutinize them
with meticulous care, and they require to
have definite evidence as to the accuracy of
the material submitted for the purpose of
qualifying for pensions. On the whole, from
the fact that the numbers do not vary in
any material degree from year to year,
think it may be assumed that the grievances
are not so many, and those that do occur
unnecessarily cover the surface and loom
up large, and possibly give colour to the
impression that they are general. I do
not think they are general. At the
same time, it is sometimes very difficult
when a person has got no birth certificate
to give the necessary evidence, and if there
is no corroborative evidence of any kind
that case must necessarily be turned down.

a question. We discussed Amendments here
practically all day and left only about half
an hour for Supply. I want to know does
that count as one day, because if it does I
would like the situation reversed. To-morrow
we are to take Supply, and I would like
Supply to be taken first and the Amendments
afterwards.
Mr. SPEAKER: To-day does not count as
an allotted day for Supply. It is only an
allotted day when Supply is the first Order
of the day. This does not count as one of
the allotted days.
Mr. DONALD: Thank vou.
ILLNESS OF THE PRIME MINISTER.
Mr. McGUFFIN: It is rather a delicate
matter I wish to mention to the House, and
I am very glad that the Leader of the House
(Mr Pollock) is present. We read in the
Press, particularly in the London corresto the
pondence to the papers here, as
condition and progress of the Prime Minister
(Sir James Craig), whose absence from the
House we all so much regret. I think it is
rather strange that we have to borrow our
information or learn it from the Press
instead of having it imparted to us in this
House. I would not for a great deal that
the right hon. Gentleman (Sir James Craig),
with whom in his indisposition we so much
sympathize, should come to the conclusion
that this House is indifferent to his absence,
and it might be so construed if the Ministry
does not take the precaution of making some
intimation to the House, even without a
formal question, as to his progress and the
probable date of his return. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). These are facts which we glean
from the Press.
It was brought more prominently to my
attention to-day when I was travelling
towards the city. I was asked whether the
Prime Minister was in the House or when
he was likely to return. 1 was able to
assure my questioner that the Prime
Minister was not in the House, but as to
when he was likely to return I did not know.
I think the Ministry should at least credit
the House with sufficient sympathy with the
right hon. Gentleman (Sir James Craig) in
his indisposition at the present time to know
that we would be very anxious to learn from
the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock) himself, or from some other member of
the Government, as to how the Prime
Minister is progressing and when we are
likely to see him again in his place. Under
the leadership of the right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Pollock) we have made excellent
progress, and it is a matter for congratulation that in the Prime Minister's absence
we have been able to carry on as we have
done, but we do not want our attitude as a
House to be construed into a suggestion of
indifference as to how the Prime Minister
fares at the moment.
Mr. POLLOCK: I would say, with all
deference, and subject to your ruling, Sir,
that the rules of the House do not offer any
special opportunity—
Mr. SPEAKER: That is quite so. It does
not show any indifference on the part of
the House, I am sure, that this matter has
not been mentioned. It is not exactly what
▲ would call a public matter, but at the same
time I am sure the House appreciates what
the hon. Member (Mr. McGuffin) has said,
and I have no doubt that the Leader of the
House (Mr. Pollock) can perhaps give him
some information on the matter.
Mr. POLLOCK: With your permission, Sir,
I may say that it is very well known that
the Prime Minister's progress has been very
satisfactory.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I have not heard it.
Mr. POLLOCK: And that we hope to see
him in this House taking part in our
deliberations once more after the Easter
Recess. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 3rd April, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
SPEED LIMIT FOR MOTOR VEHICLES.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs if he will consider taking
steps to impose a speed limit for heavy motor
vehicles driven in the cities, towns and
villages of the Six Counties.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The mere fixing of a speed
limit would not of itself be sufficient to
ensure the prevention of accidents, and it is
frequently a matter of difficulty to prove at
what rate a particular vehicle may have been
travelling.
Experience has shown that a much more
effective power is that contained in Section
1 of the Motor Car Act, 1903, under which
it is sufficient to show that the vehicle may
have been driven recklessly or negligently or
at a speed or in a manner dangerous to the
public.
The police have been impressed with the
necessity of enforcing the law and prosecutions have been taken in such cases. The
magistrates can of course assist greatly by
dealing adequately with cases which may
come before them.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
reply, does the right hon. Gentleman not
consider that speed has a great deal to do not
only with the safety of the public, but with
the safety of the clothes of the public as well?
Speed has a great deal to do with mudsplashing.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I quite agree.
Dr. MORRISON: Arising out of that
question, could the Minister give us any
assurance that this important matter will be
dealt with by legislation at an early date.
The whole question of these motor lorries
and heavy traffic?
Mr. DONALD: Before my right hon. Friend
replies, may I ask if it is not a fact that the
police authorities are against the regulation
of the speed? A speed limit would do away
with the whole question of accidents and so
forth.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the police
have ample power to deal with the question.
The whole question is a matter of proof.
Express instructions have been given to the
police to pay particular attention to those
things.
CURFEW AND SUMMER TIME.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will consider withdrawing the Curfew Order when the alteration
of the clocks to "Summer Time" takes place,
on the 12th-13th instant, or whether he will
grant some reasonable extension, such as
three o'clock in the morning, new time, to all
seaside and health resorts in the Six Counties.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The question of
whether the Curfew hours should be modified
in view of the introduction of summer time
will be considered, but it would be premature
to make any statement on the subject at
present.
MANAGEMENT OF ULSTER PAVILION.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he contemplates the appointment of an assistant to the manager of
the Ulster Pavilion at the British Empire Exhibition, and if so, whether he will be an
Ulsterman.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): No definite decision has yet been
reached on this matter, but I can assure the
hon. Member that, whereas it is important
that the best man available should be appointed, the view of the Ministry has always
been that the post is one which, other things.
being equal, should properly be filled by an
Ulsterman.
LOCAL
GOVERNMENT ELECTION
ORDERS.
4. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of Home
Affairs if he has anything to add to his answer
of Thursday, the 13th March, with regard to
Elections Orders in connection with the forthcoming Local Government Elections; whether
he is aware that hundreds of candidates and
their agents and public officials are anxiously
awaiting these orders to enable them to make
preparations for the nominations which, in
some cases, are fixed for the 15th of April,
and whether he can explain the delay in the
issue of these orders.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The delay in issuing
the rules prescribed by the Ministry for the
forthcoming Local Government Elections is
due to delav on the part of the printers. I
assure the hon. Member that the Ministry is
fully cognisant of the necessity of ensuring
that the orders should be in the hands of
officials and persons interested at the earliest
moment, and I am informed that copies will
be ready for issue during the next few days.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Once a year there comes the opportunity to a Minister to justify, or endeavour
to justify, at any rate, his administration of
his Department, and also to take hon.
Members into his confidence and to tell them
something of his policy and what his aims
and hopes are for the future. Personally, I
think that it is an opportunity which should
not be lost, because, when asking the Committee to vote substantial sums for the carrying out of great public services. I think
Members of the Committee are entitled to be
placed in possession of the truth and nothing
but the truth. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I know that it is held in some quarters
that to make a detailed statement in instances
like this is rather inviting criticism. I may
say that I do not take that view, and even if
I did. I do not object to the criticism which
comes from Members in this House, because,
so far as my Department is concerned, I
have always found such criticism to be well
informed, to be reasonable, helpful, and constructive.
I think that the importance of the work
which the Ministry of Labour in Northern
Ireland is doing will be gauged and appreciated by hon. Members when I say that we
are charged with the great responsibility of
looking after and safeguarding the industrial
lives of our working classes from the day that
they enter employment until the day that
they finally leave it. The regulation of wages
in those industries that are liable to sweating, the preservation of industrial peace in
our midst with all that that means to our
workers, our employers, and the general community, the administration of our Truck
Acts, Workmen's Compensation Acts, Health
Insurance, Unemployment Insurance, dealing
with employment problems generally, and
relief works require the services of a competent and able and willing staff; and I am
glad to have this opportunity of expressing
my indebtedness to the staff of the Ministry
of Labour for the very loyal and invaluable
services which they have always so freely
rendered to me and through me to the
Province of Ulster. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
It is true to say that besides these
measures which I have mentioned, the
Ministry of Labour has many important
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Andrews.]
duties to fulfil. In the regulation of the work
Ꮐ the Department we aim at obtaining
the maximum economy consistent with
efficient maintenance of a very important
public Department. The most difficult
problem that we have had to deal with
has been admittedly that of unemployment.
It has given great anxiety to my colleagues
in the Government, to my staff, and to myself,
but I am glad to be able to assure hon. Members
that the dark clouds are gradually passing
away and that a brighter industrial future
lies ahead. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is gratifying to know in this connection
that our rate of progress is even more rapid
than in Great Britain, because while in April.
1922, the difference between the percentage of
unemployment here and in Great Britain was
10.47, the difference to-day is rather under 4.
In the linen trade, in January, 1923, the enormous percentage of 26.37 of insured persons
were unemployed; to-day there are less than
9 per cent. of our insured population in the
linen trade without work. Again the total
figure of unemployment is less than it has
ever been since our Government came into
power, and it is very gratifying to know that
the 43,000 of our people who were on
systematic short time a few years ago are now
fully employed. (Hon Members: Hear.
hear.)
I now turn to the Estimate which hon
Members will find at page 115. Sub-head A
deals with salaries, and it will be observed
that there is a reduction of £6.972. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) That is largely due
to the fact that there has been an automatic
reduction in staff in our Labour Exchanges
owing to the fall of unemployment to which
I have already referred. The reduction
would have been greater but for the
fact that we have changed Our policy
as regards branch Exchanges, and that where
previously we have had men in part time
service who were responsible for providing the
premises and paid the rent and lighting of
same we have now got full time men, the rent
and taxes appearing under another head.
There is a reduction of £1.750 in travelling,
removal and subsistence expenses. This is
principally due to the fact that instead of
having our inspectors all living in
Belfast we have domiciled them over our Six
County area with a saving amounting to the
equivalent of the sum which I have
mentioned.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman are they then only available for
service in those particular districts?
Mr. ANDREWS: They are available to go
wherever the Ministry of Labour tells them.
but as a rule it is natural that we should
decide that they would act within the area
in which they live. The amount under the
head of rent and taxes, fuel, light, water,
cleaning and heating has been increased by
about £2,000. That is due to our change of
policy as regards our branch Exchanges to
which I have already referred. The amount
for furniture and fittings is increased by
£1.307 due to the fact that we are providing
for the furnishing of our new Labour
Exchange in Corporation Street. Under subhead C5, new works, alterations and additions,
there is a reduction apparently of £9,500, but
that is due to the fact that this time last
year we hoped to be able to procure a building which was already in existence and would
be suitable for our requirements. Owing to
certain legal difficulties we were advised not
to take that building, and the result is that
with the approval of the local Employment
Committee who have given a great deal of
thought and attention to this matter, ground
was taken in Corporation Street. The buildings upon it, which were of a very ramshackle
nature, have been demolished, and tenders
and plans are now being prepared to build
there an edifice which I hope will be worthy
of the province and the work we will be
called upon to do.
Printing you will observe shows an increase
of £2.000, but on the other hand there is a
decrease in stationery, books, and office
supplies to the amount of £2.000. This is
really a cross entry owing to the fact that the
Stationery Department have decided, probably quite rightly, that anything that has
any printing upon it shall in future the
placed under the head of printing, and only
those things without any printing upon them
shall come under the head of stationery and
office supplies. The next matter to which I
think I ought to refer is sub-head I.. fees and
expenses of members of Trade Boards. You
will remember that when our Trade Board
Bill was passing through this House a good
deal of anxiety was expressed by hon. Members
as to what the cost of Trade Boards would
be. I said that this year I did not anticipate
that they would cost more than last year, and
I am glad that that prophecy was fulfilled.
At the same time it is only right that I should
point out in this connection that this £1.000
does not cover the whole cost of Trade
Boards. It only covers what it is set out as
covering, namely, the fees and expenses of
members of Trade Boards. Of course, a
certain proportion of headquarters' charges
and a certain proportion of inspectors'
charges could be debited to this head, but it
is more convenient to take them under the
other heads in which they are included. However, the position is as I have explained, and
I hope that hon. Members will feel that there
is no use in passing Acts of Parliament in this
House, unless at the same time we take the
means to see that these Acts are complied
with.

I always feel that these Unemployment

Ballymoney where living 18 presumably
cheaper than in Belfast may mean sweating

I would like to say a word or two as regards
the Estimates put into our hands to-day.
I do not intend to throw any more bouquets
at the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews).
He is apparently going to have a great deal
of bother in carrying them all away. I am
glad he has succeeded in getting a net decrease of £29,000. I think every Member of
this House will congratulate him more because this net decrease on the Estimate is
to a very large extent due to the fact that
unemployment no longer costs so much as it
did. What I am really interested in is the
increase in standing charges that has taken
place. I look down this list of salaries,
wages, and allowances, and I have been perusing with a great deal of interest the officials
established in connection with the Ministry.
The first thing I notice is that in the Industrial Relations Department we have now
got a principal officer with a salary of £900.
Before that we had two superintending officers
with salaries rising up to £700. They have
done away with one of these and given us a
principal officer instead with a salary of £900.
He may be able to make such suggestions of
economy that it will result in a saving, but
I would like the House to note that the
establishment is increased by one principal
officer as against a superintending officer.
Then if we pass on there is an assistant
principal officer with a salary of £500 so
that there is really an addition of £900
altogether. Then if we turn to page 120 we
come to the Claims and Record Office and
here again we have now got two higher
executive officers at £500 in place of one last
year. Opposite that we have done away with
a higher grade clerk with a salary rising to
£400. We have again an increase in the expenses in this branch of the Department.
Then we come to the next Vote, National
Health Insurance, and we have an assistant
accountant, an entirely new officer, with a

be paid to the operatives. I am quite prepared to admit that there was great necessity
for a change in the method of the old
system. It is a branch of industry for the
products of which Americans at that time
and even now would have paid any money
that we in the North of Ireland would have
chosen to charge. To-day they would give
any money and pay even unreasonable
charges, but it cannot be produced, because
the operatives have now passed to other
branches of industry-possibly more remunerative. There is no reason why we should
not have held our grip on that very old,
indeed very ancient handicraft. It is gone.
What we tried to put in its place was
Swiss embroidery, and what is the result today? It was very short lived, simply
because in Switzerland they are working for
very much smaller wages than those fixed by
the Trade Board for Swiss embroidery. Also
in Switzerland they can perform the
operation in their own homes. They are
very small machines-smaller indeed than a
typewriter. Every house in Switzerland has
got these machines. We cannot compete in
the North of Ireland against that industry,
because of the prices fixed by the Trade
Board. I simply want to add that to the matter referred to by ine hon. Member
for the University who spoke first (Dr.
Morrison). I have practical knowledge
of these two trades. 'I ney are gone,
the first almost entirely and the latter
is going very quickly.
With regard to the local Committees, I

I have the honour to be connected with the
employers are better attenders than the employees (hon. Members: Hear, hear)-which
can be borne out by the Secretary to the
Ministry of Labour,
Mr. LAVERY: No; in Newtownards. Our
great difficulty there has been up to the present moment to get the Labour members to
attend. They do not like to come and waste
their time, and they do not like-I can well
understand this to be a party to turning
down some of those who are applying for
what is generally called the dole, because if

many more strikes than we have now. (Hon.

connection alone he has done a work for
which we can never repay him.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
May I try to make the position of the Government in respect of this matter clear?
Government will not accept either of the
Amendments proposed by the hon. and learned
Member (Mr. Hanna). They will not accept
any of those Amendments. They will stand
by the Clause as it is printed, and they ask
the Committee to support them in that. I
am rather astonished at the attitude taken
up by the hon. and learned Member (Mr.
Hanna), because it was obvious to those of
us who are conversant with the law that
there might be a loophole, there might be
means of escape in the unfortunate
event of the mother of an illegitimate child
dying before the proceedings were brought to
fruition. When that was pointed out my hon.
and learned Friend (Mr. Megaw) yesterday
gave an assurance on behalf of the Government that before the Report Stage came on
we would look into the matter and, if possible,
devise a remedy for that omission. Notwithstanding that, the hon and learned Member
(Mr. Hanna) gets up and makes this impassioned attack on the Government because
they will not make a provision to-day which
they have already said they would consider
and provide for on the Report Stage. I do
not think that is quite fair to the Government having regard to the attitude they have
taken up.
Now may I deal with some of the other
points that have been raised? The hon, and
learned Member (Mr. Hanna) asks some one
to say whether this is a civil or a criminal
remedy. It is obvious to the veriest tyro in
the Law that is a civil remedy. It is a civil
remedy which, if the order be disobeyed, may
be enforced by imprisonment, but the remedy
is essentially a civil remedy. Then he went
on to say "Oh what a dreadful thing it would
be if a poor girl came to the workhouse and

over this

The CHAIRMAN: I think I may enlighten

(Laughter).
Mr. HANNA: There was no heat.
Mr. MEGAW: I do not quite understand
how there can be so much rhetorical emotion
on an occasion of this kind, because the
Government are as anxious as the hon. Member is to do the best thing, and I think that
on a little reflection he will see perhaps that
the method adopted by the Government is
not a bad method after all. It is of great
importance in eliciting the truth that the
information should be laid as soon as possible,
and that there should be no time to think with
regard to the person against whom the charge
should be brought. The sooner a charge of this
kind is brought the less likelihood there is
of blackmail or anything of that sort. Besides, it is in accordance with precedent that
has been found useful elsewhere. I think
that the Amendment which the Government
intend to bring in on the Report Stage will be
found to fit in most admirably, and will bring
about the redress that is sought for. I may
state here the idea that the Government have
in regard to the Amendment of the Bill, so
as to enable redress to be had in the case of
the death of the woman between the time of
the information and the hearing of the
application, or in case she dies at childbirth.
The information here is intended to be
the information on which the summons will
be founded. After the information on oath
has been given and the summons has been
issued, the proceedings are started. They can
be brought before the magistrate at any time.
They may be adjourned till after the birth
of the child, but if they are brought before
the birth of the child the lines on which the
Government propose to proceed are that a
deposition should be made or evidence given
before the magistrate, by the mother-aboutto-be, and that the accused person should
have an opportunity of being present and of
cross-examining her just in the same way as a
deposition is made before a magistrate at the
present time. The evidence will be taken
down in writing, and the depositions containing the evidence and cross-examination may
be used in any Court thereafter if the woman
herself is unable through illness or through
death to be present at the final hearing. That
will apply to the hearing not only before the
magistrate but also in the Court of Appeal.
We have a precedent in criminal cases for the
use of depositions in that way. This is not a
criminal case, but we have the same principle
embodied in one of our Emergency Acts, that
the deposition once it is made can be used
at the hearing of the action if the witness is
not available. Where a deposition is taken
in that way, that is, where each party has
an opportunity of being heard, we think that
justice may be done by allowing such evidence
to be given for what it is worth. It never can
have the same effect as oral evidence, but it
is the best that can be done under the
circumstances. Hon. Members will see that
it is absolutely impossible for cases of this
kind to be sustained if the evidence of the
only party who can give direct evidence on
the subject is not available.

8 APRIL, 1924.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 8th April, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
DECLINE OF LOUGH NEAGH
FISHERIES.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can furnish any information regarding the results of the Public
Inquiries into the causes of the decline in
the fisheries of Lough Neagh, held at
Antrim, Toomebridge, Stewartstown, and
Lurgan, by Mr. W. J. M. Menzies, of the
Fishery Board of Scotland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): As the hon. and gallant Member
is doubtless aware, the Public Inquiry relative to the Lough Neagh Fisheries was
not initiated by my Ministry. On inquiry,
however, at the Imperial Secretary's Department I am informed that Mr. Menzies
only concluded his investigations on the 24th
ultimo, and that his report has not yet been
received.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that reply,
may I ask the Minister of Commerce is he
aware of the great interest this inquiry has
created in the country? The people whom
I represent are particularly anxious to
know the result.
Mr. ARCHDALE: This is a reserved service and not in my Department, but I will
try to get the hon. and gallant Member and
his constitutents any information I can.
Colonel WOODS: Thank you.
ISSUE OF INCOME TAX CERTIFICATES
TO SPIRIT GROCERS.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can expedite in any way
the issue of the necessary Income Tax Certificates to Spirit Grocers making compensation claims under the terms of the Intoxicating Liquor Act, 1923.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I need hardly remind the honourable and gallant Member that Income Tax
matters form part of a reserved service outside the jurisdiction of this House. If, as I
presume is the case, the query relates to cases
where applicants for compensation have mislaid or destroyed their notices of assessment,
I shall, if the hon. and gallant Member will
let me have particulars of the cases he has
in mind, make representations to the Imperial Authorities that such applicants should
be facilitated as far as practicable.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer might I ask the right hon. Gentleman
if he could in any way, as I asked in the
question, expedite the delivery of these certificates as I have been told the spirit grocers
cannot get any answers?
Mr. SPEAKER: I think the hon. and
gallant Gentleman is asking over again the
question to which he has had an answer.
Colonel WOODS: Not quite. I merely
wanted to make it clear that these people
cannot get any answer from the Income Tax
Authorities. That means that if their claims
are not in by a certain date they cannot
comply with the order.
Mr. POLLOCK: I take it for granted that
if these claimants have paid their income tax
they will receive from the Surveyor their
necessary certificates. I cannot understand
anything further that is required, and if
there be anything different in the mind of
my hon, and gallant Friend if he would set
it out more clearly and fully I would be glad
to know of it.
Colonel WOODS: It is only a matter of
time.
Mr. SPEAKER: I think notice should be
given of any further questions on this point.
REPORT OF COURTS OF REFEREES.
3. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will issue a report of the
cases and findings of the Courts of Referees
for 1923, under the Unemployment Insurance
Acts.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have considered the suggestion
made by the hon. Member that I should publish a report of the cases and findings of
Courts of Referees established under the Unemployment Insurance Acts, which cases
numbered almost 4,000 in the year 1923, and
have come to the conclusion that the value
of a document of this nature would not
justify the very considerable expense of its
preparation and publication, especially as
their findings turn mainly upon particular
questions of fact. It is the cases which come
before the Umpire that involve points of
general principle and lay down precedents,
and I hope that the publication of his decisions, which I propose to make from time
to time for the information of hon. Members
and the public, will meet with
Friend's approval.
