ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Insurance Bill
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
THE PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): My right hon. Friend the Minister
of Labour gave such a clear statement of the
position of unemployment to the House on
Thursday last, showing the improvement in
the linen industry, and referring to other
industries where there was no improvement
at the moment, that hon. Members will
realise the problem with which the country
is faced. I recognise more than ever that
what our people want is work. They are
passing through a time of anxiety, harassed
through the lack of means of existence, but
bearing their burdens manfully in the hope
that the dark clouds may pass. Both skilled
and unskilled workmen are suffering alike. I
could not use language laudatory enough
of the local authorities for the great
assistance they have given my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) and myself. They
have created relief works of public utility at
a cost of almost £3,000,000 to absorb the unemployed in their various districts, but there
is still a big majority for whom no work can
be found, and they must feel disappointed
and depressed as they face the future. Their
scanty savings are already used up, their
union funds are exhausted, and, perhaps,
their unemployment benefit is exhausted also.
This Bill is introduced to meet the present
situation by extending the benefit period, and
so helping to tide over this difficulty. Our
unemployed cannot be permitted to go without the necessaries of life.
Dr. MORRISON: Hear, hear.
As
Mr. GORDON: We all know the evil that
is caused by prolonged unemployment. The
workman loses his skill, and consequently
through time becomes unemployable.
our industries are interwoven with those of
Great Britain, it is most desirable that there
should be uniformity in Our Insurance
Schemes. This was recognised by the
Shillington Committee, which recommended
that we should continue on the main on
parallel lines with Great Britain. From
the outset the Government has adopted this
recommendation as the basis of its policy,
and this House has frequently confirmed its
action in the passing of the various Unemployment Insurance Acts from time to time.
The object of this Bill is to secure for the
workers in Northern Ireland the same benefit provisions that obtain in the United
Kingdom.
The Bill. first of all, is to give the Ministry of Labour power between now and
October, 1924, which might be looked upon
as the emergency period, to grant an extension of uncovenanted benefit. Existing legislation, both in Northern Ireland and Great
Britain provides for the payment of benefit,
whether covenanted or uncovenanted, up to
aggregate of 26 weeks, which will
terminate on the 17th October, 1924. Those
who have been continuously unemployed
from mid-October, 1923, up to the present
moment, will have exhausted all their rights
to
an
a
covenanted benefit and uncovenanted
benefit, so that the proposal in this Bill is
to meet an emergency between the present
moment and mid-October, 1924. The Ministry is in close touch with the Imperial
authorities on the subject. They have in
contemplation similar Act, and have
already introduced into the Imperial House
two Bills. One is a Bill of considerable
magnitude, which, it is anticipated, will
require some time to pass through the
House of Commons. The other is a
Bill of an urgent nature to continue
the existing rates of benefit for the
period which we are now facing until the
enactment of the larger measure. For the
twelve months following the middle of
October, 1924, to the middle of October, 1925,
no provision has been made in the recent
Act passed through this House for uncovenanted benefit.
Unemployment Insurance Bill-
Second Reading.
8 APRIL, 1924.
Mr. DONALD: 1923-24 instead of 1924-25.
Mr. GORDON: No, 1924-25. We only made
provision in the Bill that passed through the
House here for covenanted benefit up to a
maximum of 26 weeks during the period between the middle of October, 1924 and the
middle of October, 1925. We are asking in
this Bill to give the Ministry of Labour
power to make a further grant of uncovenanted benefit in what is known as the
second benefit year of 26 weeks, or a maximum of both covenanted and uncovenanted
benefit of 26 weeks. Those are the two first
points that I would like to bring before you,
that is to give the Ministry of Labour power
to meet this emergency situation by granting
benefit immediately this Bill comes into force
-granting an extension of benefit right to
the middle of October this year, because all
people have exhausted their benefit.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: May I interrupt the hon. Member? Do I understand
that you are proposing to make any change
in regard to the age limit, or extending anything to any other class more than
we extended up to the present?
Mr. GORDON: No.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: There is no
change.
Mr. GORDON: No. This Bill is merely
to meet an emergency period now
that people have exhausted their right to
covenanted benefit. Many of them would be
without the means of support from now on
to the middle of October, 1924, and my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) desires that
power be given to the Ministry of Labour
that we grant in this emergency period
benefit to those that have exhausted the right
both to covenanted and uncovenanted benefit.
The second point is that we want the same
rate in the second benefit year as we have in
the first benefit year-26 weeks covenanted
benefit and 26 weeks uncovenanted benefit, or
a maximum of 26 weeks over all. The third
point that I desire to draw your attention to
is with reference to special schemes that are
referred to in this Bill. There are what are
known as special schemes of insurance by industry. The only scheme that is in operation
at the moment is the Insurance scheme,
and we want power in this Bill to see that
any schemes of insurance outside the Insurance Act, though closely allied to it, must
pay the same rates of benefit as obtained in
the national scheme.
The final thing that I want to draw the
attention of Members to is that this Bill is
introduced with a desire to do away with the
gap.
Mr. GRANT: Hear, hear.
Mr. GORDON: When uncovenanted benefit was first introduced it was provided that
if a person had received benefit for a certain
number of weeks he had to stand off benefit
for a gap. Now with the prolongation of
unemployment and the depression in trade we
feel that the imposition of these gaps is a
considerable hardship upon the unemployed.
and my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Labour and myself desire the House to give
us power to remove the gap so that those
who require benefit and who have passed
through this long period of unemployment
may not suffer the gap but may have their
benefit paid to them continuously. I do not
think that I need say anything more by way
of recommending this Bill to the Members of
the House. I feel that every Member of the
House will just be as anxious as my right
hon. Friend and myself to see that as the
days advance with little improvement in

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: We have
listened to a very interesting debate on a
very small measure of reform brought in by
a representative of the Ministry of Labour.
It has opened up a lot of very interesting
topics in connection with unemployment and
the economic position of this country, and.
we have also had some interesting statements
from some of the Members of this House.
I was specially interested in the speech of my
hon. Friend, the Member for East Belfast
(Mr. Donald.) It is most refreshing in these
days to find a representative of Labour advocating the complete sweeping away of all
these Government Measures for Unemployment, for Insurance,
Mr. DONALD: And for everything else.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: And for everything else; a complete sweeping away of all
these things and of any interference by the
State, and getting back to the old order of
things when the employer and the worker
together tided over all their difficulties. I
do not think we have many supporters of
Labour who would advocate that sort of
thing. I think we have got to face facts as
we find them. There has been a gradual
evolution of thought in connection with social
questions and whether we like it or not we
have got to face the position to-day that in
regard to these great questions of unemployment and other matters the State, whether
for good or for evil, has got to handle them
and do something for the masses of people
who are out of work. But the State cannot
go on indefinitely doing this sort of thing.
That will not solve the economic problem
that all these things are the result of. Some
of the hon. Members who have spoken this
afternoon seem to think that the State has a
pocket without a bottom, and that they can
go on bringing in measures of unemployment benefit and gradually extending it until
you reach the stage indicated by the hon.
Member for East Belfast, when the State
had either to find work for the people or pay
them a week's wage. If those two things have
got to be done, you are eventually going to
empty the Exchequer entirely and everybody
will march about absolutely independent,
supported by the State until the State's
resources are completely exhausted.

Really we have got to think a little bit deeper,
if I may touch the academic side, on the
question. My hon. Friend, the Member for
North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin) has deplored,
and we all deplore, the departure of skilled
men, skilled engineers and, mechanics of
different kinds who are going away to other
countries and finding employment there.
There was one Statesman in Great Britain
who did put forward what in my judgment
was a really solid remedy for the trouble,
but the masses of the working classes in
Great Britain would not accept the remedy.
That was protection for the home market
and protection for the workers, a policy
that all other countries in the world have
adopted. The hon. Member for North Belfast
must know that the most prosperous country
in the world to-day is the protected country
of the United States of America, and they
are able to absorb all this surplus labour
from Great Britain and Ireland. They are
able to pay those workers a good wage and
they are living there in happiness and comfort. As my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Finance, told us the other day in a very
interesting speech, one person in five in
America is able to provide himself with a
handsome motor car. Whether it is a Ford
or some other type of car I do not know,
but at any rate that is the condition' off
affairs you find in other countries. Therefore, my opinion is that until you have
tackled this question from an economic
standpoint you are going to have these
recurring periods of unemployment to contend
with, and you are not going to solve them
by continually paying doles. You have got
to go deeper, otherwise what is the result?
You are going to destroy the self-reliance of
the workers themselves, and we have got to
face the fact that you are also going to make
a big lot of them a little work-shy. We
know what that means.
You are going to bring up the young life
of the country to feel and to realise that if
work is not plentiful and not easy to find
you are going to be able to pay them a wage
that will support them in moderate comfort.
These are things we all deplore. We see
where we are inevitably leading to, but I
do say that at the moment there is no
alternative but to try to help those who cannot help themselves. Until you better the
economic structure of this country and take
a different attitude to that which the masses
of the people were inclined to take at the
last General Election in Great Britain, I
do not believe you will get to the bottom
of the trouble and be able to find employment for the people. You will not do it
now or in the near future. You will inevitably
have most of our people going out of the
country to find a home in other countries
where they can find good employment and
live in comfortable houses and in pleasant
surroundings.
In connection with this matter some of the
speakers have referred to certain things not
being right in the way of administration. I
am sure the Minister of Labour will deal
with those matters. Unquestionably abuses
do exist at the present moment, and I am
sure that the Department concerned is aware of
a lot of these abuses, and I presume they are
doing their best to remedy them-especially
in those cases where people have received
benefit who are not entitled to it, and in
other cases where people could find work but
are not willing to do so as long as they can
get a small outlay from the State without
having to do a hard day's work. Unfortunately such people do exist to-day, and
it is sometimes lost sight of by those who
pass unmeasured criticism on the representatives of the workers. They seem to infer
that the workers are not doing anything
themselves, and it is well for us to remember
in connection with this question of unemployment that the benefit comes from three
sources. It comes from the State in the first
instance, but the State after all is the
ordinary taxpayer of the country.
Some people seem to think that the State
is a different thing altogether; that it is
something away in the clouds or away in
fairyland where they have nothing to do but
search in some hidden place and any amount
of wealth will be produced. The State is the
ordinary taxpayer of the country. Then the
employer pays another portion, and that goes
to the unemployed. I hope my Labour
Friends will recognise that those of us who
are employers have never grumbled or complained about bearing our share of the burden.
If we happen to continue in business at all
I am sure we shall go on meeting our obligations in this respect.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I take it that the hon.
Member is not in favour of discontinuing
State assistance, as was suggested here this
afternoon?
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I am not even
remotely hinting anything of the kind. I am
quite prepared to put up with it until better
times arrive, recognising that under present
conditions it is inevitable. The third party
are the workers themselves, who, when
employed, are contributing to the relief of
their less lucky brethren who cannot find
employment. Therefore, all three are linked
up in this scheme. I do not think I should
labour the other points that have been
mentioned, except to say that as far as I have
been able to understand this whole question
we as a young State here have been as
generous and as sympathetic to the unfortunate in our midst who are out of

our
employment as have been the wealthier
people in Great Britain. We were told that
we were in debt in connection with this

and that we are likely to continue to do so.
I am glad we have done that, and I hope we
will continue to do it until such time as an

to remedy this problem in this way, and if
we do not do it in a kindly, sympathetic, and
generous manner there are other forces at
work that might take another way of doing
it. I think it would be well for us to think

The Parliamentary Secretary to the
Ministry of Labour has intimated that the
Government are likely to introduce at a later
stage another Bill dealing with this question.
It may be a remarkable Measure, it may be
a revolutionary Measure, although I can say
I have never found the Minister of Labour
a revolutionary in any sense. He may be
slowly developing in that direction, and
eventually he may appear before this House
with a red tie and give utterance to some
very far-reaching and revolutionary schemes
of reform. In this small matter we
are only keeping pace, we are told, with
the Imperial Parliament. That is a doctrine
I subscribe to up to certain point.
It would be extremely interesting to this
House to see how things would eventually
develop if the Government carried out this
principle that they seem to stick to SO
tenaciously. I wonder what would have
happened if a certain measure that has
a

measure on the other side? I shall be a

to happen to my right hon. Friend, the

in a certain direction.
this particular
Mr. McGUFFIN: What direction?
Mr. GORDON: The direction of social reform.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Some develop
upwards, and some develop the other way.
I am sure that my right hon. Friend is big

I do not intend to keep the House any great
length of time over these Amendments, the
object of which is to add two sub-Clauses to
Clause 2. The first is to allow commutation
to take place in any case where a weekly
sum has been made payable by any person
under an Affiliation Order. A man can
apply to have this weekly sum commuted by
the payment of a lump sum subject to the
sanction of the Court as to the amount. The
Court has the right to fix the amount of the
commutation. I think that possibly it would
get away with some difficulties that might
arise upon the Bill as it stands. Take, for
instance, a man against whom an Affiliation Order has been made who might wish
to get married after paying under that
Affiliation Order for five, or six, or seven
years. It would save him from a sort of
enforced celibacy, and perhaps from the uncomfortable position he would be placed in
having regard to the fact that he would have
to pay this weekly Order with the collector
calling at his door and possibly his wife paying this money. No man would care to marry
under such circumstances and we might be
opening a door to more evil if we made it
compulsory in that way. I ask that he should
have a right under this sub-Clause to apply
to the Court to have a lump sum fixed which
would be payable by him into the Court, or
in any other way the Government may think
better, and through that Court it could be
administered by way of weekly payments to
the mother on behalf of the child.
The second Amendment that I move is to
allow, prior even to the Affiliation Order, an
agreement to be entered into by the mother
and the putative father arriving at a lump
sum which would be paid into the Court. I
quite understand that possibly there may be
in Northern Ireland a mother who rather
than face the Court and getting all the publicity would suffer and try to rear her child
without asking any payment. In cases of
this sort where the mother would not wish
to enter the Court and ask for an Affiliation
Order it is quite possible by the addition of
this Amendment to come to an arrangement
for the payment of a lump sum which would
be administered through the Court in any
way the Court may think just and right.
That agreement, I have insisted in the
Amendment, should be witnessed by two
solicitors, one representing each party, or,
if the Court thought right, it could be witnessed by a magistrate, a resident magistrate,
a clerk of petty sessions, or any other person;
but I want to make sure the mother would
be taken at no disadvantage and that the
lump sum which would be settled in payment
for this offence would be a right and proper
sum and not a trivial or insufficient sum.
There are many women in Northern Ireland
who would not like the trouble of going into
the witness box and would prefer that an
agreement would be come to by which a
lump sum would settle the case. It would
enable the woman in question to emigrate, to
leave the country, to leave her child in
the charge of her parents. perhaps, and to
start a new life elsewhere. It would liberate the man from any further responsibility
under the Order and give him a chance of
starting life anew in this or some other land
where he could marry without having these
weekly payments to make.

Dr. MORRISON: I beg to move in Clause
3, page 3, line 43, at end ("by the Court") add
"and the Board of Guardians shall have
power where the collecting officer reports
that a child is being neglected by its mother
to supplement the amount and board the
child in some more suitable position, or
send it to an institution for education."
I think this opens up a very big question,
next indeed in importance to the Bill itself
and it will require all the efforts on the part
of the Government and of the Members of
the Committee to secure the object that this
Amendment is intended to achieve. We
introduced the Bill with a dual object. First,
we intended to help the mother and protect
her in the helpless condition in which she
finds herself, and I think, as the hon. Member for West Belfast pointed out, it is clearly
our duty to do something for the child.
There is nothing in this Bill in the nature
of providing for the child beyond giving some
money to the mother as a weekly contribution
to help her to maintain it. The proposal
that I have put down in this Amendment has
a tendency to meet that defect. I would ask
the Committee to remember that the mother
is responsible in the eyes of the law for the
welfare of her child. If you take the reperts
issued by the Malone Rescue Home you will
find that some of these mothers are 15 years
of age, some of them 16 years of age, the
Illegitimate Children Bill-
Committee.
8 APRIL, 1924.
majority of them under 20, and some of
them at the outside probably not more than
23 years of age, so that these inexperienced
girls are not fit to take the necessary steps
for making correct and ample provision for
their child.
You must remember that the mother when
called upon to provide for her child in this
fashion has been through Gethsemane. She
has been nine months in Gethsemane; further
she has gone in my opinion to Calvary, and
now in the extremity of her helplessness and
the winter of her desolation she is left with
this child in her arms and has got to provide
for it. I told the House of an incident that
came before me as Coroner, where a woman
was going to give her child over to the care
of some other woman to look after it, but
the woman did not turn up and consequently
she committed an act of murder by killing
her child. I would like the Committee to
understand that it is a real grievance with
these girls who find themselves in this
position-those who are not looked after by
the philanthropic ladies in the Malone
Rescue Home but are left stranded without
any help. In the Home they are not only
provided for, but care is taken to find a
suitable home for the child. The danger lies
in the feeding bottle, especially with the child
boarded out. I have found in my experience
the most crucial test of feminine efficiency
is to ask a woman to rear a child on the
feeding bottle. Many of them are unable
to do that-I should say half-and while
benevolent nature recognising the limitations
of the average woman has provided a
substitute that makes provision for this,
unfortunately that substitute is not transferable, and you have the child handed over to
some woman who perhaps knows nothing
about the feeding of a child. The result is
that when the mother goes to service this
child goes wrong, and a large number of them
develop disease gastric afflictions-and die.
As a matter of fact, one half the illegitimate
children in England die at an early datein infancy-and if it is a fact as some people
allege that the value of a worker to the State
is £400, it becomes a serious problem for
us, irrespective of the moral issues involved
in the transaction.
Secondly, you may have the mother or the
foster-mother handing over the child to
some woman in a remote part of the district
where there is no school, and you have no
power to prevent this. This Amendment of
mine suggests you should give the power.
Under the Children Act you have in each
poor-law union an inspector appointed to
look after these boarded-out children. Very
often he is the relieving officer. You have
also this further provision made by the State,
namely, that the inspector of the Society for
the Prevention of Cruelty to Children will
look after these children, and I must say
that this Society does an immense amount of
very valuable work in Ulster and all over
the Empire-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)--
but there are difficulties in the way of
effective interference in many instances. That
is just the problem the Government are helping us to solve. Long before the child has
reached the stage when a criminal prosecution can intervene I maintain that with
sufficient inspection, with an intelligent relieving officer and with a collector who would
take a real interest in the child you would
have discovered that the child was being
neglected, that it was in an unsuitable home,
and if you wanted to save its life it should
be taken away once.
That cannot be done even by the inspector
of the N.S.P.C.C. He is armed with very
large powers, and I think that he has in
the main exercised them very wisely and
very judiciously. He has this power-and
this power only I think-if he finds a child
being deliberately neglected, criminally neglected, he can order its removal for safety
to the workhouse. There are, however, many
of these cases where there is no criminal
neglect but where there is negligence, carelessness, and unsuitable environments that
endanger the child's life and in many cases
produce its death, where perhaps the fostermother or the mother herself is doing her
utmost for the child. It may be necessary to
remove the child from its unsuitable surroundings in the interests of the child's
welfare, and indeed of its life, and it may be
desirable to do that without the prosecution
that according to the present law must follow
any removal on the part of the inspector of
the N.S.P.C.C. If the child were removed,
as I suggest should be done, on the report of
the inspector, I think it would be but right
and proper. Supposing the child for instance
were a deaf mute. The poor-law authorities
have no power to deal with anything but
paupers. This child is not a pauper. It is
in receipt of 5/- a week or 10/- a week, and it
would be illegal for a Board of Guardians to
spend money on it and its mere sustenance.
They could not send it to a home such as the
Deaf and Dumb Institution, or if it were an
imbecile they could not send it to any institution for those so afflicted. Therefore, I think
that they should have power in this case
to add a little, if it were necessary, to the
money that child is in receipt of from its
putative father and board it out in a more
suitable house, that might be selected by
the Guardians after consultation with those
interested. In nearly all workhouses and
Boards of Guardians now there is a committee of ladies who look after these things
for the Guardians and who have done very

CLAUSE 7.-Application of Provisions of

Act. (1) The provisions of the Summary
Jurisdiction (Ireland) Acts shall apply
with respect to the issue and service of any
summons, the hearing of any case, the
making of any order and the taking of any
proceedings by or before a court of summary jurisdiction for the purposes of this
Act, except as otherwise expressly
provided therein.

Summary Jurisdiction (Ireland) Acts, a

appearance of a man who is alleged to be
the father of an illegitimate child may be
served upon him in any part of Northern
Ireland, whether within the county comprising the petty sessions district where

NEW CLAUSE (Recording of Evidence
and Non-Abatement of Proceedings in Certain
Cases)-
(1) As soon as a summons has been issued
for the appearance of, and duly served upon,
the man alleged by the mother to be the
father of her illegitimate child, the Court
may proceed to hear such evidence as may
be adduced on oath and shall record the
same in writing. Such evidence shall be
read over and signed respectively by each
witness who may have been examined, and
shall be signed by the resident magistrat >
hearing the same.
The record of such evidence verified as
aforesaid shall be admissible as evidence in
any proceedings under this Act, where it is
proved that the witness who gave such
evidence is dead or so ill as to be unable
to attend or where his attendance cannot
be procured.
(2) Proceedings under this Act shall not
be determined by the death of either the
mother or the putative father of an illegi
timate child.
In the case of the death of the mother,
the proceedings may be continued by the
person having the custody of the child, or,
if the child is in receipt of relief from the
poor rates of any Poor-law union, by the
Board of Guardians of that Union. In the
case of the death of the putative father,
his personal representative may be made a
party to the proceedings.

is to provide for the case where the mother

This Clause to some extent really introduces
a new principle. It goes rather further than
anything that has been admitted as evidence
before. As hon. Members know, in criminal
cases where depositions are made before
magistrates, and where the accused person
has had an opportunity of being present and
cross-examining when the evidence is given,
that evidence is recorded and may in the case
of the death of the person who has given
evidence be given in evidence in any subsequent proceedings. We have adopted that
principle in this Bill so that in case the mother
dies in childbirth or before the proceedings
can be brought to hearing her evidence can
be made available. The clause goes further
than that. It also enables the evidence of
all witnesses who may have given evidence,
whether corroborative or evidence of any
other kind, to be taken in exactly the same
way. It will be committed to writing, read
over, and signed by the witnesses and the
Resident Magistrate, and the accused person
may have an opportunity of cross-examining
on it. In the case of the death of any of
these parties, that evidence may be read in
any subsequent proceedings, and may be considered by

give his evidence, and that evidence may be
used afterwards. That is the first part of
the new Clause, which deals entirely with
the evidence and with keeping alive the
evidence in the case of the death of the
parties.
The object of the second part of the
Clause is to keep alive the proceedings.
Ordinarily speaking, the proceedings come
to an end on the death of either of the
parties. If the mother dies no proceedings
can be continued for the child. If the father
dies the order cannot be made effective
against him. Under this Clause, in case the
mother dies, the proceedings can be continued by the person who has the custody of
the child, or in the case of a child receiving
outdoor relief the proceedings can be continued by the Guardians. If the putative
father dies and he has any property left, it
can be made available for the support of the
child. They both have an opportunity at an
earlier stage of giving their evidence, and if
the Court is satisfied that he is the father of
the child, it can adjudge that his estate shall
be made liable for the maintenance and education of his child. These are the matters
that are dealt with in this new Clause, and
I think they will commend themselves to the
Committee. It was to try to conform to what
the Government thought was the opinion of
the Committee that this new clause was
brought forward. It goes further than the
English Act. We are not slavishly following the English Act in this case, and we are
taking precautions as far as we can to ensure
that the death of the parties or the absence
of witnesses shall not interfere with the
normal course of the proceedings.

I do want to emphasise one or two points that

is one important point that was never touched
upon, and that is the financial side of the Bill.
That, as much as anything else, was the
reason I rose to criticise the Bill yesterday.
It is quite evident that constructive criticism
is not welcomed in this House, and I want to
say that if the Minister of Labour, or the
Parliamentary Secretary, or the Government
cannot accept useful criticism, then in my
judgment they do not know the meaning of
government. In the first place, I am anxious
in regard to the financial aspect of Unemploy
ment Insurance. In 1922 we were on the
wrong side to the extent of something like
£830,000, and I take it that there was a
similar deficit last year. The Bill now before
the House deals with this very question, and

from the Minister of Labour a statement of
what the position of the Government would
be in the event of a Bill of far more importance being introduced in this House. I feel
that sooner or later we shall arrive at a
stage when some definite steps will have to be
taken by this House to deal with the financial
position of Unemployment Insurance.
raising this question I am acting in the

Sir DAWSON BATES: In submitting this
Estimate for the upkeep of the prison service,
hon. Members will see that we
propose to
effect a considerable saving in the amount
this year-a saving of £47,570. Last year's
Vote was £154,627, and now we are asking for
£107,057. The main cause of the reduction is
due to the more peaceful conditions prevailing in the Province, and that results in a
reduction in the prisoners, and also doing
away with the Argenta. It might interest
hon. Members to know the number of
prisoners that we propose estimating for
as contrasted with the number last year.
In Armagh we are estimating for 85 as
against 100 last year; in Belfast 400 as
against 500 last year, in Derry 100 as against
180 last year, in the Larne internment camp
250 as against 500 last year. That 500, of
course, includes internees on the ship. As
regards convicts in Scotland we are estimating for 65 this year as against 70 last
year, convicts in England 95 as against 116
last year, Borstal inmates in England 24 as
against 40 last year. There happen to be
two Borstal inmates in the Free State at the
present time and we hope soon to get them
away. There were 35 last year. Altogether
in figures we estimate 1,021 as against a total
of 1,542, a very considerable saving. With regard to prisoners, other than internees, I
would like to make one or two observations.
It is the policy of the Government, as I have
stated on previous occasions, to bring back
from England and Scotland all the convict
and Borstal cases, but before this can be
done we must have suitable accommodation
for them here. During the year the Government have taken expert opinion on the subject of how best to provide this accommodation, and there is now a prospect of the
necessary expenditure being found under the
Colwyn Committee Award, which will enable
us to go ahead, and before long I hope we
may be in a position to make a definite statement in regard to this matter. We hope, in
connection with this, to put Belfast Prison
in such a condition as to receive these convicts, but at the present time we are not
including in the estimate any provision with
regard to that until we know exactly how we
stand, but I might point out in connection
with the new prison that we hope to have
works there which will provide the convict
with some technical training which will be of
use to him when he is released and help
him to find employment.
With regard to Sub-head D-materials and
tools for manufacture in and on farms
attached to prisons-this is a new Sub-head
in the Estimates and we ask for a sum of
£5,565. It would appear as if this was an
increase on what we asked last year, but it
is due solely to a better system of accounting
and it really represents the cost of the raw
material that goes to the gaol for the purpose

to other
Government Departments to whom they are
sold. Hon. Members will see that as against
the sum of £2,880 for raw materials for
manufacture, the receipts on this head
amount to the sum of £3,214 There is one
Sub-Head I would likely to draw the special
attention of the House to, namely Sub-Head
"J"-Gratuities to Prisoners." Increased
provision is asked for. The money expended
is for the assistance of prisoners when they
are released. It is desirable that the
money which is provided for prisoners who
are released should be paid through the
Prison Aid Societies, who render very
valuable assistance in helping prisoners after
their release to find employment. At the
present time these Societies are mainly
supported from voluntary sources, and I
think it is only right, having regard to the
valuable work that they do, that they should
get aid from Government funds. As the
result of the action of these Prison Aid
Societies, many a criminal who is released
is helped on in life afterwards, and I hope
hon. Members will approve particularly of
this item. I would like to point out that
there has been a steady improvement in the
prison service and in the discipline in the
prisons themselves. Many of the warders
were new to the work, and I would like to
bear testimony to the very valuable assistance which has been received from the
staffs in the prisons.
I would like to say a word or two in regard
to the question of internees. I am glad
to say that we have got back to more normal
conditions as far as crime is concerned. It
was stated at the time the Law Charges Vote
was presented to this House that the number
of indictable offences for last year was 770 as
contrasted with upwards of 1,600 the previous
year; a reduction of something like 50 per
cent.. but, because we have got back to more
or less normal conditions so far as regards
the amount of crime committed, representations are made by individuals urging, because
this is so, and because life and property are
now safe in Ulster, that the various measures
which had to be taken by the
Government to bring that condition
of affairs about should be removed.
Some of the individuals who make these representations have very short memories. They
seem to forget the chaotic condition in which
Ulster once was, and I do not think they fully
realise the measures the Government took
to bring the present condition of affairs about,
One of the measures taken by the Government, and one which proved most successful,
was internment. Hon. Members will see that
this year we are budgeting for 250 internees
as against 500 last year, and I hope that
later on that number will be found to be
excessive.
I have been struck by the type of petitions
which I sometimes get on behalf of these
internees. I have one in my mind at the
present moment which was sent in on behalf
of one of the most violent Sinn Feiners who
ever occupied the attention of the police. In
that petition it was represented that this man
was a law-abiding citizen, and had only committed one crime in his life. What are the
facts? Within a period of five years that
man had committed twenty-three different
crimes such as house breaking, holding up.
assaults, and so on, and had been convicted
for them. The extraordinary thing about
that petition is that it is signed by very
responsible citizens in Belfast of both creeds.
I must say that it is a very appalling thing to
me that this should happen, and the only
conclusion I can come to is that either the
people who sign this class of petition are
coerced into doing so or else they have not
taken the trouble to find out for themselves
what are the real facts.
Mr. DONALD: Did you release him?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No; I did not.
Captain MULHOLLAND: Who signed the
petition?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would like to
point out that the case I have mentioned is
only one of many. I do not want to weary
the Committee by going into other petitions
of the same kind.
Mr. DONALD: Would you not tell us who
signed it?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not think, perhaps, it would suit the hon. Member (Mr.
Donald) opposite or his friends if I told him.
I would like to point out that all these
internees have the right to have their cases
investigated by the Advisory Committee.
That Advisory Committee consists of a barrister, who was lately Deputy-Recorder of
Belfast, another barrister, who is a Roman
Catholic, and an ex-officer of his Majesty's
Army. In addition, all these cases are very
carefully investigated from time to time
both by the police and by the officials in the
Ministry of Home Affairs. All the circumstances are weighed up so as to prevent any
possibility of any miscarriage of justice
occurring, and I would suggest to the people
who are asked to sign these petitions that,
after all, those in authority and those who
know the facts of the case are perhaps the
best judges of whether or not a man is
wrongly interned. There is a very great
responsibility on the Government in regard
to these internees. The Government are
responsible for the maintenance of law and
order, and I must say I do not think it is too
much that the Government should ask the
law-abiding public at large for their support
in these restrictions. (Hon. Members: Hear.
hear.)

There is no necessity to spend the big sum

Sir DAWSON BATES: Will the hon.
Member explain what positions the Northern
Government are holding over for internees?
Captain MULHOLLAND: The Ministry of
Home Affairs.
Mr. COOTE: If you are to judge by Mr.
Healy, he would very probably handle it as

handled the internees. But that is not the
case to which I refer. I refer to school

Government, do they not? I submit that
there are school teachers interned whose
positions are yet kept open.
The CHAIRMAN: Would the hon. Member
just indicate to me where he gets his reference to that in the estimates?
For any
criticism he founds he must give me the reference. As to the question of policy, there is a
certain measure of latitude there, but to
proceed on this Vote to criticise what really
is a matter for the Ministry of Education
and not for the Ministry of Home Affairs is,
of course, quite a different matter.
Mr. COOTE: If I cannot criticise this
question of the internees I will be glad to
retire. I do not want to do that.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Member must
not endeavour to set me in the wrong. What
he is criticising is the action of the Ministry
responsible for appointing and retaining
the services of school teachers, and he wishes
to do that upon the Prisons Vote. If he
directs his criticisms to the Ministry of
Education, he cannot do it on this Estimate.
This deals purely with the question of internees, which is a different affair.
Mr. COOTE: I said these people were interned at the cost of the taxpayers, and the
Minister challenged me to name any internees
who were in Government positions. I did
name them. Further than that I do not wish
to labour the point; but, with all respect, I
think I am entitled to answer when I am
challenged to do So. Has the time not
arrived when these men ought to be asked to
consider once and for all what their
attitude is going to be to the Northern
Government, and whether they will sign a
form necessary to permit them to go back
to the free life that they can enjoy amongst
us if they will express their peaceable intentions? Hundreds of men have signed
these forms, and I submit that the time has
come when we really ought to ask these
people to sign some declaration of loyalty,
or to take powers to march them over the
Border to the Free State. Let them make
their choice, and let them abide by it; but
it is intolerable that we should keep these
people incarcerated at such cost to the taxpayers of the country. If they will not sign
a declaration that they will behave themselves, if they will not undertake to be good
citizens, the time has come to get rid of
them, and we should relieve ourselves of
this burden as soon as possible.
Mr. POLLOCK: They would come back
again.
Mr. COOTE: They will come back as long
as they have a vacillating Government in
power, a Government that allows ordinary
workers to slip over the Border in order to
get jobs.
The CHAIRMAN: The hon. Member knows
he is now going back to what was part of his

Mr. COOTE: With great respect, I think it
is the Leader of the House that should be
called to order--

Ireland.

vation called in question was, to the particular

Mr. COOTE: I was merely illustrating my
point. To come back to the Estimate, 1
wish to say that I live on the Border and 1
risk my life as much as anybody else. I go

has come when we should recast this whole
thing, and that if these people will not conduct themselves they should be made to go
to another climate where they will have
better terms. If Loyalists in the South of
Ireland objected to take the oath of allegiance
to the Free State we should have no objection
to their being sent over the Border. The Free
State would have the right to deal with them
in that way, and so the people living in the
Northern area have a right to make these
internees submit to the Government. If they
will not do so, it is evident that their hearts
are not right towards the Government, and
it is therefore necessary either to send them
over the Border or to intern them. I wish to
say further how will you keep their positions
open for these men. men who are disloyal
to you, men who will not take the oath of
allegiance? Here in this city you penalise
men because they are loyal; you penalise
Orangemen because they are loyal; but you
do not penalise the Sinn Feiners who will not
take the oath of allegiance-you keep their
jobs for them for a couple of years. No
wonder the Government is losing the confidence of the people; no wonder the people
are losing heart and hope. If we are to make
the Northern Government respected, we must
protect our area and we must protect our
people. This £22,000 is lost money; it is an
insult to us to ask us to pay it. It is wrong,
and I protest against it in the strongest
possible manner.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw): On behalf of the Home Office I wish
to reply to the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Coote)
who has just sat down. He has propounded
a policy that would commit the Government
on a person making a declaration or taking
an oath-how much attention he would pay
to the terms of that oath is another question
-to the step of sending him home. What
was the cause of internment in the first
instance? Internment arose owing to the prevalence of outrage and murder. The police
had information with regard to those who
were responsible for it; they were not able
to produce such evidence as would bring
about a conviction, but still it was wellknown that the people who were interned
were the persons who were responsible. What
are the facts? On the 22nd May, when our
first internments were made, outrage in this
Province had reached its very highest figure.
From the date of the first internments, and
while the internments were takir place,
crime and outrage decreased propo ionately
until it disappeared altogether. The Government claim that by taking the action it did,
and by making the internments it did, it put
a stop to that particular form of crime.
The suggestion that is made by the hon.
Member (Mr. Coote) is this, that the men
who were responsible for that state of affairs
should be let loose on the community
against the advice of the police. We are
taking the advice of our police, who know
the state of the country, and who give us
reports from time to time, reports on whether
these men or any of them might safely be
released or not. Are we in face of those reports to go and open the jail doors, and to
allow those men out if they go through the
form of taking an oath but do not believe
in the substance of it at all? They will take
the oath in order to get out. One after another, men have stated that they were ready
to take the oath, but it was well-known that
that was done only for the purpose of leaving
them free to commit outrages. We hear
from time to time about the reorganisation
and attempted reorganisation of the I.R.A.
Are we, forsooth, to let out the leaders, the
men who were commanders when particular
outrages took place? Are we to let these men
out to assist in the reorganisation of the
I.R.A. throughout our Six Counties?
I should like the Members of this Committee to know that the question of the
internees is considered, and very carefully
considered, from time to time. The number
in the jail and the internment camp is being
reduced from time to time on the reports
that are given by the police. Restrictions,
no doubt, are sometimes required. Now there
are fewer restrictions, and men very often
get out on their own bail. In getting out
in that way they do acknowledge the
existence of the Northern Government, because no man can sign the form without
recognising his responsibility to the Government and to the King. But I wish to emphasise this point, that the time has not
come when every person who says he is ready
to take the oath of allegiance could be safely
permitted to return to the place where he
had been responsible for a great deal of disorder before.
There is just one other point that I wish
to mention. It has been said that we have
power to put these people outside the country
altogether. We have no power to do that.
We have no power to alienate; we have no
power to deport. We do impose restrictions
when necessary under our own Act; but we
have no power under the Act of 1920, the
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Megaw]
Charter of our own Government, to send one
single man outside our own country. We can
prevent him going to certain parts, but we
can go no further than that. I think I have
dealt with all the points that have been raised
by the hon. Member for Fermanagh and
Tyrone (Mr. Coote). He, to some extent,
reflects what has been said from time to
time. I assure this Committee that the Ministry of Home Affairs recognise their responsibility. They are desirous of relieving their
internment camps, but up to the present they
find they cannot do so with safety. When
one looks at the state of affairs before the
internments were made, and how one day
eight or ten fires would occur in one city,
doing perhaps £100,000 of damage, what is
£22,000 to the damage that was done by the
firebugs? We believe we are acting for the
safety of the community by the policy we are
adopting, and, while we are desirous of
relieving ourselves from the liability of supporting these men, we believe it is in the best
interests both of the financial position of our
country and of the law and order of the
country itself. (Hon. Members Hear, hear).
Mrs. CHICHESTER: May I say a few
words in regard to this Estimate, and strike
perhaps rather a different note from my
neighbour, the hon. Member for Tyrone and
Fermanagh (Mr. Coote)? I would like most
heartily to congratulate the Minister of Home
Affairs on the Estimate which he has put
before us. I think when he is subjected to
so much criticism in this House, and certainly
outside this House, that he may be glad to
hear the views of some of the Members within the House who do not wish to criticise but
who wish to congratulate him. I think that
he should be greatly congratulated on the
Estimate, particularly on the condition of
affairs which has led up to the reduction
in the amount asked for. I think that
we have rather short memories, and that we
are very much inclined in the country to forget the conditions which have been recalled to
us by the hon. and learned Gentleman who
has just sat down, the Parliamentary Secretary, the terrible conditions which were
reigning not only in Belfast but throughout
the Six Counties comparatively recently. The
fact that conditions are so different is due
largely--and I want to emphasise this, because I do not think the country realises it
as it should-to the firmness and the courage
which has been displayed by the Minister of
Home Affairs in dealing with these matters,
and, as in an instance which he gave us
to-day, in facing the tremendous pressure
brought upon him by both parties to release
men whom he knew to be a danger to the
community. I think if we congratulate him
on nothing else we should congratulate him
on the firmness and courage which he displayed in that instance and I know in many
others. The Government have exercised a wise
discretion in the past with regard to these
internees, and I should have thought that
we could feel assured we could leave this
question of letting the internees out safely
in their hands.
I cannot understand the attitude adopted
in this instance by the hon. Member for
Tyrone and Fermanagh, because it does not
seem to me to be quite consistent with the
attitude which he adopts outside this House
in his own constituency. I would remind
him that the fact that, as he stated here today, he was able to go about with no other
protection than a blackthorn is largely due,
entirely due I might say, to the efforts of
the Minister whom he takes great pleasure
in, shall I say, criticising. I wish again to
congratulate the Minister of Home Affairs on
the Estimates he has presented.

Really the argument will not hold water. It
is like an argument the Government will
resort to when they want to appear wise.
They say such and such a thing is not in
the Act of 1920 and we are bound by its
provisions. We are administering the law in
our own area and the Government of a State
has a right to do what it likes within that

any oath to be good citizens of the State, the

the Postmaster of Omagh, a rabid Sinn
Feiner. He was such a notorious Sinn
Feiner that he was suspect and his house was
raided. With the British Government you
entered into an agreement whereby that man
was sent into Southern Ireland and a man
from Southern Ireland was sent into your
area and took the oath. Yet you say you
cannot do anything. If you have the
resources and the courage and determination
to do it you
will do it, and the
people will respect you for doing it.
You took this man Sweeney out of the Post
Office at Omagh in agreement with the British
Government and transferred him to Southern
Ireland, and you get a gentleman from

is done within the last couple of years, and

is a lawyer and I am not a lawyer. It is not
common sense, and the law is common sense.
We must have a right to protect our area
and we are protecting it. I submit that there
is nothing in the argument whatever.
That is all I wish to make plain. I wish
to make it absolutely plain that we have the

we shall try to release as many as possible

The whole regime of the prison is entirely

England and Scotland and elsewhere. With

Mr. MEGAW: I think it is necessary, perhaps, that I should reply to some of the
observations made on this question.. The
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Grant) has raised points that certainly
require an answer. The first point that was
made was there were occasions on which internees were released on £10 bail, and on
other occasions some have to give sureties as
well as their own personal bail. Perhaps I
can answer that question and the question
of the other hon. Member for North Belfast
by telling them the system that has been
adopted by the Government in regard to release from internment. First of all no
person could be released who did not come
before the Advisory Committee and get recommended by the Advisory Committee for
release. Latterly it was felt that the condition of affairs enabled the position to be
somewhat relaxed, and we have revised the
procedure from time to time. The police
themselves send us reports as to the various
internees and the conditions on which each
particular internee whom they recommend
for release ought to be released. We in a
great many instances adopt that. It was
felt that the time had come-that was in the
latter part of last year when relaxations
could be made. The state of the country
permittted. The police were consulted--not
only the Royal Ulster Constabulary but the
officers in the county of the Special Constabulary. Each Internee in each county was
considered by himself in the presence of the
County Inspector of the Royal Ulster Constabulary and in the presence of the County
Commandant of the Specials. Every case was
considered, and the report on each of these
men by the intelligence officers who were
also present, was considered, and the cases
that were marked down, in which release
might be safely granted and on what conditions, were there and then determined.
In a number of cases it was felt from these
reports that we might make an experiment
of releasing some persons on their own bail.
That brought about a system by which
some of the less aggravated cases were released on their own bail. That was on the
advice of the Constabulary, not only the
Royal Ulster Constabulary, but the other
Constabulary.
When a statement is made
here about the Constabulary-the position of
the Constabulary here I can assure this
Committee that nothing has been done by
this House or by the Government without
the advice and without the assistance of the
Constabulary in its various branches. Thus
it was thought prisoners might be released
on their own bail. Certain cases were felt
to be more difficult. The police recommended
that certain releases might be made on bail,
perhaps on their own and certain sureties
being given. In these cases security has
been given and sureties have been given.
Each case depends upon its own respective
merits. There is no general system. Each
police report is considered and the man
is released where it is felt he can be
released if he complies with the conditions
laid down.

Gentleman allow me to ask if we are to

to appear before the Advisory Committee

What I do want the House clearly to understand is that there is no general system of
release. Each depends on the particular case
just as the sentences of a Court are not
similar in all cases. You have got to deal
with the particular circumstance of the locality
-whether a man is dangerous in a particular
locality or not, whether he can be trusted,
whether his word can be trusted that he will
behave himself or not, whether his own
bail can be taken, or whether it is
necessary that someone else should be
responsible for his good conduct. My
right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates) in
introducing this Vote mentioned that representations were occasionally made by
petitions for the release of certain persons.
In some of these cases men come forward
and say that such a man might be safely
released. The Minister would occasionally
say "Would you go security for him, would
you go bail for £50?" Oh, no, they would
not do that. They would come forward and
say that this man might be released, but to
go bail-
Mr. McGUFFIN: That is the acid test.
Mr. MEGAW: That is the acid test, and
it is the test that has got to be enforced
when it is advised by the police. We must
for the safety of the Province follow the
recommendations of the police. The hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin)
also asked if men complied with these conditions might they not be released straight
away. Conditions are different for different
prisoners. They all had to comply with the
conditions before they got out, and I am
very happy to say that in the course we have
taken we have been a great deal justified
because in a great number of cases the reports of those who have been released are
very good. The policy has been not to make
a big number of releases at the one time but
from time to time to consider and review
each case in regard to the circumstances, and
if a man can safely be released by complying
with certain conditions it is done. The police
themselves feel it would be dangerous to let
a large number of those belonging to the
same district out at the same time, and, as
I have said, we follow the advice of the police
in regard to that. I find difficulty in replying to what was more or less an attack
on my capacity as a lawyer or my views on
Acts of Parliament. I can hardly find words
with which to try to explain how it is that
we have no power of deportation. A point
was made by the hon. Member for Tyrone
and Fermanagh (Mr. Coote) that because we
could send convicts from here to England and
Mr. COOTE: I said men who would
not become citizens; who refused to become
citizens.
Mr. MEGAW: We cannot help their being
citizens whether they take the oath or not.
Men who are resident here are our citizens
and we have no power to deport them under
the Act of 1920. In fact, we are absolutely
debarred from doing so. We cannot deal
with alienage or matters of that kind. The
Act is absolutely explicit on that point. We
can send convicts from one part of the United
Kingdom to another. We are still part of
the United Kingdom, and we have statutory
power to send convicts to England or Scotland,
but we have no power to take a man by the
neck and throw him out of the country, and
say, "You must not come back here." As
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Best) reminds me,
under the Alienage Act itself a country cannot
deport a citizen unless there has been a
conviction.
Mr. DONALD: The Imperial Government
paid for that.
Mr. MEGAW: They did. We must act
within our powers, and it is really too bad
to be attacked in the Committee on the
grounds that we are not using the powers
we have. We have tried to use the powers
we have. On the one side we are attacked
for using them too strongly; again we are
attacked for not using them at all. I think
the course that has been taken by the right
hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates)
would commend itself not only to the sense
of this House but to the sense of the whole
community, who, if they understood or knew
all that has been taking place during the past
two years, would understand that they owe a
debt that they can never repay to the firmness and courage of the Minister of Home
Affairs.

Mr. MEGAW: I think there has been some
little misconception, for which, no doubt, the
want of clarity in my earlier observations
has been responsible. The hon. Member for
East Belfast (Mr. Duff) has accurately interpreted what I meant to convey. Up to

So far as the question asked by the hon.

is concerned, I cannot say very much more

and a shield for our own safety if we abandoned the policy which we have adopted
with regard to these internments.
Question put and agreed to.
Resolution to be reported to-morrow.
Committee to sit again to-morrow.

10 APRIL, 1924.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 10th April, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
DISCHARGE OF TEMPORARY OFFICIALS
1. Major SHILLINGTON asked the Minister
of Finance if he will state how many temporary officials have been discharged from the
different Government offices during the last
six months; and if it is a fact that all these
officials whose services have been dispensed
with were ex-Service men.
FINAN-
The PARLIAMENTARY AND
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): As with very few
exceptions all temporary appointments in Government Departments are given to ex-Service men, it follows that those temporary
officials whose services have from time to time
to be dispensed with are of necessity almost
all ex-Service men.
The total number of temporary officials
discharged during the last six months is 76
inen and 22 women, of whom 71 men and 1
woman fall within the category of ex-service.
All these employees were engaged either for
seasonal or emergency work or to mest
pressure at the Labour Exchanges where
their services are no longer required owing
to the reduction in unemployment.
COST OF UNEMPLOYMENT FUND.
2. The following question stood on the Paper
in the name of Colonel Woods :
To ask the Minister of Finance whether he
can state the amount chargeable per head of
insurable population in respect of the Unemployment Fund, as at the end of the financial
year.
Colonel WOODS: I beg leave to postpone
question number 2.
CLAIMS UNDER INTOXICATING
LIQUOR ACT.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the
Minister
of Finance whether he is aware that an
order, published in the local Press, by the
authority dealing with compensation claims
under the Intoxicating Liquor Act, states
that all claims must be received on or before
the 14th inst., and if he is aware that it is
necessary for claimants to furnish with
their claims an Income-tax assessment certificate, and if he can assist in any way to
facilitate qualified claimants in obtaining
these certificates within the limit of time
allowed by the administration.
Mr. BARBOUR: The answer to the first
portion of the hon. and gallant Member's
question is in the affirmative. As regards the
latter portion of the question I would refer
the hon. and gallant Member to the reply
to the question addressed by him to my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Finance on the
8th inst.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, is the hon. Gentleman aware that
spirit grocers, who have perhaps been assessed
at £300, have been able to show cause for an
abatement, and therefore, if they have not
been served with notices, and cannot get them
when it is necessary, they are particularly
hard hit in not being able to get a certificate
from the Income-tax people?
Mr. BARBOUR: The first part of the
question raises a
matter referred to an
authority which was constituted by our own
Act-namely, the authority dealing with
compensation claims; and, while it is desirable to proceed as rapidly as possible in the
adjudication of these claims, I am sure the
Committee will only be following the wishes
of this House if they take such measures as
will ensure justice being done. They have
power to extend the period during which
those claims may be put in. Of course, the
notice given in the Rules and Regulations
was published as long ago as 14th March.
So reasonable time has been given. Where
just cause can be shown, I am sure the
Claims Tribunal will take into consideration
such difficulties as my hon. and gallant
Friend's friends have met with.
SUPERANNUATION FOR TEACHERS
IN TECHNICAL SCHOOLS.
4. Mr. DONALD (on behalf of Mr.
MCMULLAN) asked the Minister of Finance
whether he intends to prepare a scheme of
superannuation for teachers in technical
schools, and if so will he produce it at the
same time as that now being considered for
teachers in secondary schools; and whether
he is aware that a complete official register
of the services of such teachers was kept by
the Department of Agriculture and Technical
Instruction, Dublin, from the time of the
inauguration of technical education, in
1899, and latterly by the Ministry of Education for Northern Ireland, and that, in the
case of these servants of the public, complicated questions of private financial interests in their schools do not arise.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Mr. BARBOUR: It is the intention of my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance,
in accordance with Section 70 of the Education Act (Northern Ireland), 1923, to frame
a superannuation scheme, in consultation
with the Ministries of Education and Home
Affairs, in respect to teachers in technical
schools, but he is unable to undertake that
such scheme will appear simultaneously with
that now being considered for teachers in
secondary schools.
The Minister is aware that a register of
the services of technical teachers was kept
by the Department of Agriculture and Technical Instruction for Ireland, and is now
kept by the Ministry of Education; but the
register is by no means complete, as it only
includes whole-time service in technical
schools, and contains no complete details of
educational service that may have been rendered in other directions either in Ireland or
in Great Britain. He recognizes that some
of the complicated considerations which
arise in dealing with secondary teachers are
absent, but it is feared that when the details
in the case of technical teachers have been
fully explored, other difficulties almost
great will emerge before a satisfactory scheme
can be framed.

PARTICULARS AS TO "INTERNEES.”
6. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the names
and home addresses, charges or sentences
against each, and the present whereabouts of
those persons known as internees."

The MINISTER of HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): There are in round numbers
280 persons who have been interned by my
order as suspected of being about to act in a
manner prejudicial to the preservation of the
peace and maintenance of order in Northern
Ireland. The majority of these persons are
confined in Larne internment camp-the
balance being confined in Londonderry and
Belfast Prisons. As the numbers decrease
from day to day owing to the releases which
are being effected, any return of the nature
asked for by the hon. and gallant Member
would be misleading, and in any case I do
not consider it would be expedient in the
public interest to publish any such return.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, would it be possible for anyone calling at the Ministry of Home Affairs to see a
list such as is mentioned in the question?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot add any
thing to the answer already given.
COMPENSATION FOR DEPENDANTS OF
FALLEN SPECIALS.
7. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether compensation has been
paid to the families or dependants of the men
of the Royal Ulster Special Constabulary who
were killed, or to the constables who were injured, at Clones in 1922, and if so, was this
compensation a charge against the Northern
Government, or was it paid by the Free
State Government.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The compensation
assessed by the County Court Judge Green in
respect of the constables killed or wounded at
Clones has been paid in all but three cases.
In two of these the pension granted to the
constable concerned was more valuable than
the amount of compensation fixed by the
judge (Mr. Donald: Hear, hear.)-which was
assessed on the basis that no pension was payable, and in the remaining case the amount
awarded will be paid to the constable as soon
as he reaches the age of 21.

displayed by Constable Francis Morteshed,

Sir DAWSON BATES: Cases where members of the Force display conspicuous bravery
and devotion to duty are dealt with by the
grant to the member of the Force concerned
of a reward in accordance with the Regulations made under sub-Section (5) of Section
4 of the Constabulary Act (Northern Ireland)
1922, or by some other suitable mark of recog
nition.
The case referred to by the hon. and
gallant Member has, however resulted in a
criminal prosecution, which is still sub
judice, and it would, therefore, be improper
and contrary to established practice to consider as yet any award to the member of the
Force referred to, until the criminal proceedings have been finally disposed of in the
Courts.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
The reward is not given, and does not depend

case was pending until this morning when the

MUD-SPLASH GUARDS FOR MOTOR
LORRIES.
9. COLONEL WOODS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he will consider the
advisability of granting permission to local
inventors of mud-splash guards to affix their
inventions to Government motor lorries,
and, if so, will he at the termination of a
two months' wet weather test, call for official
reports upon each device so used?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The proposal
suggested by the hon. Member would not
solve this problem as it would not be a sufficiently comprehensive test.
At the recent tests held by the Royal Automobile Club the appliances submitted for
examination and report were subjected to
all essential tests, including kerb tests,
stability tests, mud-splashing tests, tests
regarding interference with the maintenance
of the vehicle, tests for simplicity, ease of
fitting, first cost, upkeep, amount of projection, noise and appearance.
It would not be possible by the means suggested by the hon. Member to ensure that
the appliances submitted for examination
complied with these various tests, and the
only method by which the test of an effective
mud-splash guard could be ascertained would
be on the lines indicated in the recent, tests
held by the Royal Automobile Club.

ESTIMATES, 1924-25.
CLASS II.-No. 5.
GRANTS TO LOCAL AUTHORITIES.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £291,525 be
granted to his Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during the
year ending on the 31st March, 1925, to
provide for grants to local authorities in
respect of Health, Housing, etc., and in
relief of local rates, including a grant in
aid."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Estimates
submitted to the Committee for the service
of the financial year 1924-1925 under the head
of Grants to Local Authorities have been
prepared on bases which I trust are now
familiar to the Members of the Committee.
They show a net decrease of £122,121, but
that is largely accounted for by the temporary grant in relief of rates on agricultural
land which was passed by the Committee for
the service of the financial year 1923-24 and
which is not included in the present estimates. Accordingly, excluding this item, it
may be stated that the amount which the
Committee is asked to Vote by way of grants
to local authorities under the heading of
Local Government Services approximates to
the amount granted by the Committee for
the financial year 1923-24. At the same
time there are increases on some of the subheads and decreases in others which I will
explain when dealing with the particular
sub-heads. I would also draw attention to
the fact that in preparing the estimates
under this particular class, we have shown
the various housing grants in a group by
themselves. All the remaining grants, including Public Health, Poor Law, and general
grants have been grouped under the head of
Miscellaneous Grants." There is one
special grant included in the current year's
estimates which has not appeared before and
which is of a temporary nature. That is the
grant under sub-head S, which is in aid of
the Belleek Boundary Road and which I will
deal with later.
I will now deal with the two sub-heads A
and B and the sub-divisions of sub-head A
which we have grouped under the heading
of Housing Grants. I think it well to explain
to the Committee that we have in Northern
Ireland three separate sets of financial
arrangements in regard to the building of
Supply-.
Committee
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
houses in urban areas under the Housing of
the Working Classes Acts. The first arrangement was that in connection with houses
built under the Housing of the Working Classes Act, 1908, in connection
with which an Irish Housing Fund
was established by the Imperial
Government, out of which relief was paid
to urban authorities on the basis of their
liability for loan charges. It was
further provided by the Housing Act
passed last year by this House that the
grants to local authorities should be based on
12 per cent. of the loan charges in respect
of the expenses incurred by these local
authorities in providing houses. Then
a new financial arrangement was introduced
by the Housing Act of 1919 under which the
State contribution was fixed on a basis of
deficit not exceeding twenty-five shillings
for every pound of rent collected. Under
this head for the service of last year this
Committee voted the sum of £27,500. This
amount is payable to the Belfast Corporation and four urban authorities which had
adopted the Act in the Six Counties. Hon.
Members will recollect that an agreement
was arrived at between the Government and
the Belfast Corporation with a view to
cutting the very heavy losses which had
been incurred on both sides. Power was
taken in the Housing Act of last year enabling the Ministry of Home Affairs, with
the approval of the Ministry of Finance, to
enter into an agreement with the Belfast
Corporation with a view to cutting these
losses and commuting the subsidy which was
payable to the Belfast Corporation or any
other of the local authorities which had
adopted the Act.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: What amount
is ear-marked for that?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I will deal with
that afterwards. Under that authority the
Ministry arrived at an agreement with the
Belfast Corporation for the payment of a
fixed sum of £27,500, and under that agreement the Government are entirely free from
any future liability.

properly quoted?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon. Member
surely does not accuse me of presenting to
the Committee estimates which are inaccurate? The sum, as I have already
mentioned, is £27,500, which represents the
annual sum the Government is liable to pay
to the Belfast Corporation or to the other
authorities which have adopted the Act.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Pardon me. I misunderstood you.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Under that authority the Ministry entered into an agreement
with the Belfast Corporation for the payment of the sum of £227,500 in order to get
rid of this liability, and consequently, under
sub-head A1, hon. Members will see that that
annual sum in the coming year, instead of
being £27,500, is now reduced to £1,450, which

have adopted the Act. But in order to provide for this sum of £227,500 it was necessary
for the Government to borrow money, and
the annuity which is required to pay off that
sum is estimated at £17,108. Hon. Members
will see that under sub-head A3.

years?

Members will thus see that while there is a

Government have only got to provide an

continued under the Act of 1919. I think
that disposes of items A1, A2, and A3, and I
propose now to turn to items A4 and A5.

were authorised to pay a sum of £60 for

house. These grants are really of a capital

the Act, an item of £1,100, and under subhead A5 they will also find a sum of £5,700,

financial year. The decrease in question is

Sir DAWSON BATES: Up to the present
we have altogether received from local
authorities certificates indicating that 382
houses have been passed as qualifying for the
Government subsidy, and 342 houses are
waiting certificates. In dealing with these
last I refer of course to houses built by both

While the question does not strictly, perhaps, come within the purview of the matter
now before the Committee, I think it well
to make a brief reference to the operations of the urban authorities in regard to the further financial assistance
which they are empowered to make under
the Housing Act of last Session. Of the
thirty Urban District Councils in Northern
Ireland fourteen of them have up to the
present passed formal resolutions undertaking to supplement the Government grant of
£60 by a further grant of £40, or by a loan
free of interest. In the majority of cases
the urban authorities have agreed to give
the full grant of £40. One Urban District
Council has declined to do anything at all.
In the case of the other District Councils
they have still the matter under consideration, and I am very hopeful that many of
them will still come forward and offer some
additional inducement to private owners to
build.
As regards the two Corporations, although
no official information has been received
from the Londonderry Corporation, it is
understood that that body has agreed to
give the full grant or make the additional

reason given for this repudiation is that an
