HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Crawford McCullagh].
position so far as the Corporation is concerned. When the Government passed this
Act they made it retrospective, and I think
they were quite right to do so. I think they
were entitled to take that step, because at
an early date they published a statement in
which they said they would subsidise any
builder who would go on and erect houses.
Consequently, I think they were entitled to
pay the subsidy to any builder who did not
wait until the Bill was passed, but who went
on and took the risk of erecting houses. As
the Act says, the subsidy from the Government applies to those houses, and I take it
that if any local authority passes a resolution
the subsidy will also be available in respect
of any houses it may build. The Corporation had no promise whatever, and I will
explain what they objected to. I know a case
of a builder who had erected four houses.
He sold two of them at a substantial profit,
and he came into the Corporation and said "I
want £40 from you, and £60 from the Government." That was, for the houses already
sold, he wanted £100 each.
Mr. DONALD: They made it a free gift.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: The Corporation take this view-the Government may
do what they like, but the £40 to be paid by
the Corporation, or some part of it, should go to
the party who either rents or buys the house.
That is the policy of the Corporation.
I
quite see the difficulty. After giving the
matter careful consideration, I look upon it
this way-Government subsidies were absolutely necessary as a war measure, but I
think the sooner we get back to the old conditions the better. For the moment, unfortunately, private enterprise cannot provide
the houses that are necessary. I go so far as
to say that if the Government are going to
give £60 the Corporation ought to give
the £40 on the same conditions as the Government are giving the £60. That is to say,
if a man is plucky enough to come forward
and build a house or a number of houses he
is entitled to £100 for each house. That is
my opinion, but let me tell you that even
that will not bring the houses that are
needed. I think the sooner public bodies
stop building houses the better for all concerned, but as private enterprise cannot meet
the demand I think the Act of 1923 ought
to be given a chance. It ought to be supported by the Government and by the local
authorities, and I think the builder ought to
get the £100 without any restrictions.
Here is how it will work out in my opinion.
Assuming that a builder comes forward with
plans for a number of houses, he will get £60
in respect of each house from the Government without any conditions. But the £60,
as I have said, is absolutely no good; it
will not provide you with the houses that
""
are wanted. The additional £40 from the
Corporation will help. If you are going to
say to the builder, When you get these
houses up, you must go to the Corporation.
and they will fix the price at which you may
sell or let them," you will see at once you are
creating difficulties and that no builder will
take that risk. I am sorry that there has
been so much letter-writing between two such
good penmen, if I may so describe them, on
behalf of the Government and the Corporation. The offices of both are not so far
apart that the one official could not walk
round and see the other and settle the matter
in that way. I mentioned that on the last
occasion, and I was told that that was not
the proper way, as the matter had to be put
on record; but I do not think the existing
state of affairs is creditable to either party,
and I think this letter-writing should stop.
If I understood my right hon. Friend aright,

leave it to the Corporation. In my opinion,
the Corporation would be well advised to
pass the resolution giving the £40 subsidy in

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. Member, but I think if he

What is going to happen? The cost of building is too high; but timber is rising; materials are rising; everything required in the

My opinion certainly is that this Act should

Government any more than on the local
authorities or the workers generally, because
these three are involved. That Committee
very wisely went into this whole question.
What have they done? They have made a
unanimous recommendation that a relaxation
of the apprenticeship rule be made and that
apprentices will be allowed to go in, not
based on one to eight journeymen, but on
the quota or the old rating of one to three
journeymen, and that apprentices will be
allowed to go in over the age of 16 and not
exceeding 20 years. Now, that is a solution.
That is a beginning, and the whole thing
amounts to this-my hon. Friend struck the
right note when he said it-lack of confidence.
Is it not lack of confidence between people
throughout the country to-day that is disturbing not only the peace but the whole industrial world? There is no confidence between
workers and employers. The one has no
confidence in the other. We have got into
such a horrible state of things that people
are looking to the Government to regulate
everything. We want rid of all that unfortunate state of things. That is why I made
the suggestion, because I do say that until
people change their minds and begin to think
as in pre-war days, because after all there is
a certain amount of insanity floating in the
minds of the people to-day and a lot of nonsense being discussed-
Mr. DONALD I quite agree with the
suggestion, and there is as much of it in
East Belfast as in any other division.
(Laughter). If my hon. Friend would just
allow me to develop my argument. He has
had his say and I did not interrupt him. I
only want to put it down in my own crude

A very useful suggestion has been made. It
is this co-operation, this bringing together
of those who are going to work the financial

brain and muscle to the building of houses.
That is the co-operation of the workers and
the private builders, because after all I wish

lead to bankruptcy.

THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw) The Minister of Home Affairs has
received SO many compliments during the
debate that he does not quite feel that he
can reply, and he has asked me to do so un
his behalf. The first criticism with regard
to the Vote was that which the hon. Member
for East Belfast (Mr. Duff) made in reference
to the reduction in the Estimate for the
assistance of the blind under the Blind
Persons Act. I am not quite as familiar with

Government and the Ministry of Home Affairs
will, of course, investigate the matters that
are brought before them, but I think there is

was
As I understand it, the point that
raised with regard to the Ministry of Labour
is somewhat of a misconception. The debate
has chiefly turned upon the housing question.
The position of the Government with
regard to that was made very clear
when the Housing Act was before
it. The desire of the Government
was as far as possible to put an end to any
thing in the nature of these restrictions that
have affected building so long, and to encourage the private builder as much as could
be done. In other words, it was to have the
largest number of houses built, and to take
precautions to have as many houses built as
possible. Some criticism was made by the
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin)
that private builders should be let alone, and
he said that if they were let alone the houses
would be produced. The idea of this Measure
was to encourage private builders by giving
them £100 extra. We thought it would be
more likely to produce houses if we gave a
subsidy of £100, partly from the Government,
and partly from the local authority.
Of
course, the underlying idea about all this is
that there is naturally unrest by reason of
so many restrictions and so many conditions
being introduced in the housing question from
time to time. I really think that the Restriction of Rents Act is probably at the bottom
of a great deal of the difficulties that have
arisen.
Builders have no security, or they feel very
doubtful whether they will get a proper return for their money. I think this has
been lost sight of by some who were criticising. As regards houses built now, there
is no restriction under the Act so that,
however much it may cost to build them,
there is freedom as to the rent that may be
charged. Some hon. Members have raised
the point that the rent of houses built ought
to be controlled. That would merely add to
the evil; it would go round in a vicious circle
if a man was encouraged to build and then
care was taken that his rent would not be
what he considered it ought to be.
If a
house is built and produced, we believe that
the real attitude to-day should be that there
be an absolutely free contract, that is, that
a man may sell the house for what he can
get for it or that he may let it at whatever
rent he can, because if there are to be
perpetual restrictions on rent in regard to
new houses there can never be any confidence
on the part of the men who are setting
about building.

thing was not

a question of two authorities coming together
and discussing how they are to evade an Act

by this Vote.

operation between all parties. I wish, and

think the principles that he has enunciated

it is a statutory amount that is given. It

The hon. Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford) as usual brings forward the agricultural

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum, not exceeding £250,000, be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1925, to provide
recoupment to Local Authorities in Northern
Ireland in respect of payments made by them
on foot of Criminal Injury Decrees."
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Estimate needs
very little explanation on my part. Hon.
Members will recollect that as a result of
efforts on the part of the Prime Minister
this Government succeeded in getting a grant
of one and a half millions to cover decrees
that had been obtained for malicious injuries
which had occurred during the period of June,
1920, and January, 1922. Unfortunately the
injuries continued, and as a result of further
representations on the part of the Prime
Minister another half million was obtained
from the Imperial Parliament. This has enabled us to make a grant of 60 per cent. to
the local authorities in respect of the decrees
obtained from June, 1920, to October, 1922.
I beg to move

Oral Answers to Questions
LIMITATION OF PROFITS.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has received copies
of resolutions passed by the County Armagh
Agricultural Committee and other public
bodies, calling for legislation to limit the
exorbitant profits of middlemen traders,
between the producer and the consumer, and
whether he proposes to take any steps in the
matter; and whether he will introduce a Bill
at an early date for the control of prices of
necessities of life.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): I have been asked to reply. My
right hon. Friend has received copies of the
resolutions to which the hon. and gallant
Member refers.
of
I would point out to the hon, and gallant
Member that experience has shown that the
measure which he suggests could only be
made effective by the complete control
foodstuffs, and that even when this has been
attempted the resultant benefit to the consumer has been problematical, and the cost
to the State considerable. The Government
accordingly do not contemplate introducing
legislation of the type proposed by the hon.
and gallant Member at the present stage.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask if the Ministry of Home
Affairs is prepared to follow out the recommendations of the Departmental Committee
which was set up to inquire into the cost of
living?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I can add nothing to the
reply which I have given to the hon. and
gallant Member.

:

indicated.

is required to sign the receipt required in
Regulation 4 to the effect that he has received
the salary corresponding to his place in the
appropriate scale of salary.
ASSESSING OF RATES ON SMALL
PROPERTIES.
4. Major SHILLINGTON asked the Minister of Home Affairs if he has received a
request from the principal Urban Authorities
in Northern Ireland to introduce legislation
which would enable Urban Rating Authorities, if they so desire, to assess all rates on
the owners of property below a certain
valuation, instead of on the occupiers, and
if it is his intention to comply with this
request.
Mr. MEGAW: The answer to the first part
of the hon. and gallant Member's question is
in the affirmative.
The question has carefully been considered
by the Ministry, and I regret that the Ministry are unable to accede to the representations made.
The principle involved by the suggested
change carries with it serious objections on
the ground of policy.
Major SHILLINGTON: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the hon. and learned
Gentleman if it is a fact that Belfast Corporation have power to assess owners of property below a certain valuation instead of
the occupiers?
Mr. GRANT: Arising out of the reply of
the hon. and learned Gentleman, I would like
to know have the Home Office taken into consideration the fact that quite a number of
these occupiers in urban districts are persons
who are unemployed, and whenever this rate
is struck it is not possible for them to find
the amount of money required to be paid in
rates? If it were added, however, to the
weekly rent it would come much easier on
these people. I personally have been asked
by a good many people
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order. The hon.
Member must confine himself to a question.
Dr. MORRISON: Arising out of the answer,
may I ask if it is a fact that the Portadown
Urban Council have lost several hundred
pounds through the absence of this suggested
legislation during the last year in rates?
Mr. DONALD: May I ask the hon. and
learned Gentleman, before he replies, if any
request has come from persons other than the
local authorities in regard to this matter?
Mr. MEGAW: I am not altogether acquainted with the position of the Belfast
Corporation, but I understand that they have
private Acts under which their assessments
can be made on the owners of property. The
Local Government Act, 1898. has adopted a
principle which I think is a good one, namely.
that those who are electors should know what
the rates are for which they are to be
assessed. That is the principle that has been
adopted, and it is felt to be the best principle
that can be adopted.
MIRRORS ON MOTOR VEHICLES.
5. Major SHILLINGTON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs if he is prepared to issue
a regulation compelling all heavy mechanically propelled vehicles using the roads in
Northern Ireland to carry a mirror in such
a position that the driver will be able to
see vehicles coming from behind and desirous
of passing.
Mr. MEGAW: The question of issuing
Regulations requiring heavy motor vehicles
to be fitted with mirrors is at present under
consideration, but having regard to the
growing use on the roads of enclosed light
commercial and private vehicles, the
Ministry require to be satisfied before issuing
any Regulations whether it is justifiable to
promulgate a Regulation applying only to
the heavy vehicles, i.e. the vehicles over two
tons. The matter has been referred again
to the Roads Advisory Committee and the
Ministry await the recommendation of that
Committee before taking definite action in
the matter.
SPEED AND WEIGHT OF MOTOR
LORRIES.
6. Major SHILLINGTON asked the
Minister of Home Affairs if he is contemplating making any change in the speed at
which heavy motor lorries are permitted to
travel, or in the weight of the loads which
they are allowed to carry.
Mr. MEGAW: It is not proposed to make
any change in the Regulations regarding the
speed or the weights of heavy motor vehicles.
In accordance with the undertaking given
by the Minister of Home Affairs recently in
this House, special instructions have been
issued to the Police Authorities in regard
to taking action in cases where it is found
that these heavy vehicles are exceeding the
speed limit on the public roads in Northern
Ireland.
Prime Minister's Statement. 712
The Boundary Question- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The Boundary Question.
STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: Would 1
be in order in asking if the Prime Minister
intends to make a statement on the recent
negotiations which took place when he was
across in London?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
Mr. Speaker, with your permission and with
the leave of the House I would be very glad
to meet my hon. Friend by making a statement in connection with what has happened
during the past week. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). Before I do so, as this is the
first time we have met since the very serious
illness of my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates), I
would like to say-and I am sure I speak
on behalf of all the members present
here how deeply we sympathise with him in
his illness and how we all wish him a speedy
restoration to full health and the strength
which has enabled him to carry on through
such trying times. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
In making the statement-the grave statement-which I propose to do to the House today, I wish to convey to those outside our
walls in the first instance a message of comfort and encouragement-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-because I do not believe that
one's full vigour can be put into any controversial question or one's best be accomplished if you face the difficulty feeling pessimistic and feeling depressed in your own
mind. I am far otherwise. I am, as I said
last Thursday, quite undismayed by this new
attack upon our liberties. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I am not quite certain whether
it was Mr. Lloyd George I believe it was--
who spoke so feelingly on one occasion about
refreshing fruit. Therefore, if I begin my
remarks to-day by quoting one of Mr. Lloyd
George's refreshing letters on this subject
perhaps it will supply adequately the text
for anything I have got to say. Writing on
the 20th July, 1921, to Mr. de Valera, who
was then supposed to be the leader of the
Southern Irish people, he said:
The British Government are actuated by
an earnest desire to end the unhappy divisions between Great Britain and Ireland.
Then follow a page and a half, after which
we come down to the following sentence:
The form in which the settlement is to
take effect must allow for full recognition
of the existing powers and privileges of
the Parliament and Government of
Northern Ireland, which cannot be abrogated except by their own consent.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That is the
beginning of my first few words to-day and
it will be the end. Nothing can be done
without the Government in the first instance,
and the representatives of the people sitting
in this House and in the other House, con-
Parliament
stituting the
of Northern
Ireland.
The question of our Boundary and the
Boundary of Southern Ireland has been
revived again in its intensive form, after
having rested in abeyance for three years, and
as is usual in matters of vast importance
which lie in abeyance for a long time, there
is a sort of scramble, a hurry, a beating up of
everything, and a sudden rush at the end as
though something absolutely necessary must
propel those who have waited and thought so
long into a rash and sudden determination.
I believe that if this matter of the Boundaries
were allowed to peter out, if it were allowed
to remain in the oblivion in which it has
rested for three years, it would be far better
for the people not only of Northern Ireland,
but of Southern Ireland and the Empire as a
whole. The written word, the bond, the
Treaty, the pact, or whatever it may be
called, may possibly tide over a day or two,
and may cause rejoicing; but we have seen
rejoicing turned into sorrow and depression
in a very short time. If you want permanence in the good feeling between the people of
Ireland, then these settlements and pacts and
agreements and Treaties must be entered into
in the heart, and not only by pen upon paper.
I have fought, and fought valiantly, for
a settlement by agreement. What is it that
stands in the way? Clause 12 of the Articles
lays it down that a Boundary Commission is
to be established. It says nothing more. It
has got to be established. But the establishment of a Boundary Commission depends
upon all three-Great Britain, Southern Ireland and ourselves appointing representatives. Southern Ireland appointed theirs
some little time ago. The British Government have announced their intention within
the last few days of appointing a Chairman,
and I have received an official intimation from the Government asking me to
appoint a representative for Northern Ireland. My answer will be in accordance with
the policy of this Government throughout-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-that is, that it
is impossible to accede to any such request.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) What I want
to ask the lawyers especially is this-The
letter of the Treaty having been carried out
what do people mean by the spirit of the
Treaty? I hold that I have placed already
the true and perfect interpretation on the
spirit of the Treaty. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The spirit of the Treaty can only be
carried out in the way I have indicated, and
that is in the hearts of the people, coming
together and agreeing that such and such
shall be the boundary between North and
South. There we stand to-day, and I take
713 The Boundary Question-
Prime Minister's Statement. 714
6 MAY 1924
it from my reception in this Chamber just
now that I have faithfully and justly given
the views as a whole, of hon. Members who
were elected by the free will of the people
to express their views in this House. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
The next point I come to is that between
now and the next stage-the next step taken
by the British Government-there may be
some little flutterings upon the political
horizon. There may be some little ups and
downs. To use an expression that is often
indulged in at Westminster, the Government
stock may go down, or, on the other hand,
it may rise. Whether the bulls or the bears,
about which they talk in this connection,
have spasmodic triumphs from hour to hour,
my answer at the end of it all will be
exactly the same answer as I gave on Thursday (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and I
desire to take this opportunity of saying
a few words to the people outside, once more
simply to reassure them on that important
subject, and to tell them to pay attention
to practically nothing that they see in the
Press, especially from across the water, or
hear from people who are anxious to cause
dissension in our ranks, but loyally to follow
those representatives whom they sent here
and those of the Government who at the
present moment are in charge of this serious
and important matter. If they do that they
will be best serving Ulster and the Empire.
We have sometimes to do things that are
difficult to do with the greater object in view
at the end. I well know that people, not
alone here but across the water, think that
they can offer a solution of this difficulty
off hand. Why, to hear some people talk, you
would think that we were merely selling a
pound of sugar or a pound of tea, and that
the real difference between us was whether
the abatement of fourpence in the pound on
the tea and three halfpence on the sugar
should come into operation to-day or the
day after to-morrow. That is the mentality
of some persons with regard to this critical
question at present looming upon the horizon.
If they would only pause before they send
their suggestions to the papers, and still
better, if they would only keep quiet, instead
of disseminating their false opinions, it
would be easier for the leaders to come to a
proper conclusion. I had occasion the other
day to find very serious fault with Lord
Birkenhead.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Yes, hon. Members can cheer, but they only
cheer, and quite rightly cheer, because he
happens to be a particularly prominent man
who has done this wrong thing; but how
often have others, perhaps not bearing quite
so high a title or name, written and made
suggestions which in every instance gravely
embarrass the Government and those in whose
hands are charged the weighty conduct of
such important affairs? Therefore, shortly,
I pray and beg that people may have patience
and trust and hold themselves in, at all
events, till this great crisis is over.
I think it only right to say that in our
negotiations with the present Labour
Government my colleagues, the Marquess of
Londonderry and the right hon. the Attorney-
General (Mr. Best), as well as myself, have
been treated with the utmost courtesy and
consideration. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is due to the British Government to say
that throughout the whole of this difficult
problem they have spent themselves in
endeavouring to secure an agreement by
consent, and they have shown activity in
every quarter in order to probe to the very
bottom the various channels, the various side
issues, with which the whole question is
surrounded. Of course, it is obvious to all
here that this question, which has engaged
the attention of Mr. Lloyd George's Government, of Mr. Bonar Law's Government, of
Mr. Baldwin's Government, and now of Mr.
Ramsay MacDonald's Government, is one of
first-class Imperial importance. We must
maintain the attitude towards British
Governments that this subject is not a
political subject, but is a matter for the
Empire and a matter of life and death to the
people here in Ulster. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I cannot emphasise sufficiently that
it should be raised from out of the politica!
arena into an arena where only statesmen
should be asked to deal with it.
I would like to go a step further and assure
the House that they need not despair that
the contribution promised by the late
Government towards assisting our Special
Constabulary has been turned down by the
present Government. I still have hopes that
that pledge to us will be amply and properly
fulfilled, and that we need have no hesitation
in saying that the honour of the present Labour Government is as high as
that of any other Government in
carrying out pledges so definitely given. May
I pass to another phase? Whether that
pledge is carried out or not, Ulster will see
that her Special Constabulary are maintained
in the highest state of efficiency, even if we
have to pay every shilling of the cost ourselves. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I
remember very well when our Parliament first
assembled assuring the people that the safety
of the Borderland and peace within the land
itself were the primary objects of the Government. I went pretty far. I think I used the
words that we would become bankrupt rather
than see chaos and murder and disturbance
inside our area. Therefore, we look forward,
it is true with less satisfaction, but at all
events we look forward with absolute confi-
Prime Minister's Statement. 716
The Boundary Question- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister]
dence, to the fact that the people of Ulster
will rise to the occasion and keep that
splendid Force in full power and proper discipline, and in full and complete accord with
its past traditions in order to maintain the
peace, whatever may possibly lie ahead.
In that connection some people have been
heard to say: "You told your audience on
Thursday that the Free State, although
charged as it was in 1920 with the duty of
contributing ten millions a year towards
Great Britain's Imperial services, had not
paid one shilling of that contribution.
Ulster was still paying something between
five millions and six millions a year
towards the maintenance of the Army
and Navy, and other Imperial services,"
and they
do you not
say: "Why
keep that money yourselves; why do you
allow a situation to arise in which you pay
an enormous sum on the one hand and then
beg and implore the Government on the other
to pay you a comparatively small amount to
carry out what, after all. is an Imperial
service the maintenance of law and order
throughout every corner of the British
Empire?" I think in justice to those who
make that statement I ought to make it clear
to the House and to the country that the
obligation to pay the contribution towards the
Imperial services is one in which I gladly
acquiesce, and it is one in which I hope the
people of Ulster will always gladly acquiesce.
For our contribution to Great Britain we
have several privileges which we never could
do without, in my opinion, without going to
the wall, without sinking into the seventh
or eighth class. We never could do without
those services and those compensations. What
are they? Let me run through a small list
of the services for which we pay our contribution.
I would, naturally, put in the forefront the
safety of our Province, because whatever else
is in doubt there is no doubt at all that the
boundary of Ulster is the boundary of the
Empire. (Hon Members: Hear, hear). No
Government at Westminster could stand for
twenty-four hours if it did not protect its
boundary if it was ever in danger. Therefore,
we have a call on his Majesty's Navy if
necessary. Think for a moment what that
means. The whole great British Fleet can be
and must be directed to its defence by the
Imperial Authorities if ever there is a threat
upon the boundary of our beloved Empire,
and that boundary stretches wherever the sea
stretches, and Ulster is part of that boundary
And the Army. The Army has already vindicated the position to which I have just
drawn attention. The Army can be employed
to protect our boundary. Therefore, we have
a call on what is perhaps the finest unit of
fighting men in the whole wide world—you have
that for your contribution. And the Air Force,
the new Force, which with the Army and the
Navy goes to make our fighting Services.
The Air Force is at our disposal certainly if
ever there is a threat from across the Border.
But over and above that there is the representation in the Mother of Parliaments. 1
dare say it is impossible to translate the value
of that into £5 notes. It is the one bond between us and Great Britain that can be seen
by everyone, our members passing freely to
and fro to voice Ulster in that great Parliament, just as those who have been honoured
in past days and present days by elevation to
the Lords can represent Ulster in the Upper
House. It is that representation which is of
invaluable assistance to us when questions of
Imperial importance crop up.
Then, to get down to the financial side
there is the credit of our Province which,
under this arrangement, is exactly the same as
the credit in Lombard Street, which is the
great financial centre in the City of London.
We can, I believe-my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Pollock) will correct me if I am wrong-borrow money here, and business men can contract
business here, on equally favourable terms to
those that obtain in any other part of the
Empire, even in the centre of the City of
London itself.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): Hear, hear.
The PRIME MINISTER: That question is
involved. Then what about the trade of the
world? From the port of Belfast steamers of
gigantic tonnage go to every corner of our
Dominions, to every corner of the world, and
when they get to their destination, colonial or
foreign, they meet the flag that ensures the
trade, they meet at the other end those
Ministers of Great Britain, and they meet the
Consular Service who deal with all that vast
interchange of trade between one country and
another forming the Empire. All that is involved in our contribution to Great Britain,
and I say solemnly here that if, as was at one
time suggested, we should have only to pay
what would be a voluntary contribution, I believe that it would be my duty to stand at this
box and say that the amount should be about
the contribution we now make in order to
maintain the Services and to be able to claim
the beneficent consideration which we receive
as part and parcel of Great Britain-Services
that otherwise would be denied us if we were
a small State on the map by ourselves.
That is the explanation of that point, and
when some thoughtless critics on the other
side try to minimise the efforts that we have
made, may I just say that during the past two
years and four months we have paid to Great
Britain in this connection a gross sum of no
less than £13,524,000? I glory that we were
able to pay that amount. I am delighted to
717 The Boundary Question-

think that my right hon. Friend the Chancellor has been able to give us a balance on the
right side of our Budget since he came into
office, and that at the same time we have been
able to help Great Britain in her difficulties
to the extent of £13,524,000. Long may it continue! The prosperity of Great Britain and
Ulster are so interlocked that we are
bound to insist upon going forward hand in
hand with her, facing her risks and her
difficulties and at the same time enjoying her
prosperity along with our own.
a
Having explained that matter as far as it is
in my power, I would like to come down to
the question of our future here in the realms
of legislation. I think it was my hon. Friend.
the Member for West Belfast-not the one
who is present at the moment (Colonel Woods)
-who one day said in a little petulant manner
that there was far too much legislation going
on. I think that remark pleased the
Government more than anything else
that has ever been said in this House,
although the hon. Member may not have
intended it. Legislation is always
grave anxiety to a Government, and it is
also a grave anxiety to all those who have to
make the necessary preliminary inquiries and
to the staff engaged. Therefore I think
the House will be pleased, and the hon.
Member who voiced those sentiments will be
pleased to hear that the Government propose
to have very little legislation this year. The
reason is that we think it necessary that the
Imperial Members should have an opportunity of being constantly in attendance at
Westminster until this crisis is over. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) it is, of course,
obvious to any one that our case may require
to be stated there at any moment either day
or night, and we can only ensure
that if
allow
we
this House to get
its legislation through quickly, and release
those members to look after our interests on
the floor of the House at Westminster. If we
adjourn this House for a considerable period
we will reserve under the usual custom in
such matters the right to call the House
together again if it is necessary to consult
with regard to the Boundary or any other
serious matter. That course will necessitate
postponing to the autumn the Redistribution
Bill, which we might have had ready at an
earlier date, but as we have still two years
to run there is no need to put it through so
early as we thought, and therefore we propose
to have the Bill cut and dry for presentation
to this House in the autumn.
Before I part from these various topics 1
would like to make an announcement which is
intended to secure the sympathy not only of
the Members here representing other constituencies, but to secure the sympathy of the
people in every quarter of Ulster who may
think that one part of the area is being a
little bit favoured over another part. The
members are aware of the great difficulties
that have arisen owing to the breakdown of that historic bridge in Derry, and
the Cabinet have had a series of meetings-1
think no fewer than four-at which this
subject of the repair of the Carlisle Bridge
has been brought up for discussion. It may
be asked, "How does that matter affect the
Cabinet?" Well, it affects the Cabinet in just
exactly the same way as the Fermanagh
Triangle affects every man, woman, and
child in Ulster, and as our contribution towards the Bridge at Boa Island, interests
them so does this main artery, this important connection, this Bridge across the Foyle,
interests every man and woman throughout
Northern Ireland. It is a link between those
on the Northern sido and those on the
Southern and you must have a bridge of sufficient strength to carry whatever is necessary.
We have therefore determined that as this is
more an 'Ulster matter than a purely local
matter we will ask this House to grant
£100,000 towards assisting them in erecting a
bridge which will meet every necessity of the
case, and I trust that Members will allow this
to go through as a tribute, if I may say so,
from the rest of Ulster to that historic city of
Londonderry which for so many centuries has
maintained its own.
Before I close I would just like to make one
further remark. We have been through very
many troublesome times together, and
although there has been, and continually will
be a difference of opinion between certain
members of thus House, and other members of
the House as well as the Government, I wish
to say in public, as I had an opportunity of
saying earlier in the day in private, that I
do not believe that any other community of
persons situated in exactly the same position
as we have been during these three trying
years, could have conducted themselves in a
more fitting or proper manner than have the
members of the Parliament of Northern
Ireland. I refer to the other Chamber as
well as to this House, and I want the people
in Ulster to understand that their representatives hold that high position not only
in my estimation but in the estimation of
the people on the other side of the Channel.
What have we accomplished here without a
legitimate opposition, and the absence of a
legitimate opposition is always held up as the
greatest danger of a Parliament. They talk
about corrosion and say, "Your institution
will fade away before your eyes, and you will
find it impossible to carry on." That has
not been the case and I can only say
that I have the deepest trust in the good
common sense of the Ulster people.
Ulster people's trusted representatives in the
House have done their duty during these
trying years and have carried us through.
They ought to be proud of themselves as I

Public Libraries Bill (8.)
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. MEGAW: I regret that it becomes my
duty to propose here the Second reading of
this measure, which was introduced in the
Senate by my right hon. Friend the Minister
of Home Affairs. We have all already expressed our sympathy with him, and I assure
the House that his absence from the duties
of the Ministry of Home Affairs has been a
very serious matter, and has placed the
Ministry in very serious difficulties indeed.
The Bill of which I have the honour to
propose the Second reading is not one that
introduces any new principle. The advantages
of reading facilities are generally recognised.
One is not called upon here to discuss the
importance of libraries either from the
education point of view or from the standpoint of providing innocent enjoyment for the
people who favour the lighter side of literature. The principle of providing or assisting
public libraries in Ireland has been recognised for the towns as far back as 1855. By
an Act passed in that year Urban authorities
were empowered to levy a rate of not exceeding 1d in the pound for the purpose
libraries within their district.
of
It was not
supposed that the countryman had need
for like facilities-whether it was thought
that the rustic could provide his
literature, or whether there was
venient
Own
no conmachinery to put libraries in

In 1894 a step forward was taken by an
Amending Act. By the adoption of the
machinery specified in that Act the limitation to the penny rate might be removed, and
two or more authorities might be entitled to
combine their forces for the purpose of more
efficient administration. Now the principle
adopted in that Act was the germ of cooperation, which is the gist of the present
measure, as it is pretty evident that a combined rate of 1d in the £ on two areas will
administratively treble or quadruple the
benefit of the expenditure by a single township. Up to that time the provision of
libraries was still confined to urban areas.
A few years later, in the year 1902, Parliament became alive to the fact that the
countryman might take advantage of the
facilities that had been provided, and that
the use of public libraries might be developed,
and it provided by an Act passed in that year
that the facilities already given to the towns
should be put into operation also in the
country. Of course all these measures were
voluntary. There was nothing mandatorynothing to compel any urban or rural area
to take advantage of the Act. But where the
Act was adopted the Rural District Council
became the Library Authority. That briefly
is how the law stands to-day.
As a matter of fact very few Rural Councils
have put the Act into operation, but I am
glad to say that my own county has set an
example to others in this respect. At least
five rural districts of that county have taken
advantage of the Act. This county, too, has
taken advantage of the Carnegie United
Kingdom Trust, and, despite many difficulties, a very energetic Committee has shown
that there is a recognised want for the circulation of books in the country districts.
of time-not lack of interest-has prevented

The Bill now
before the House is an
endeavour to bring a recognised system up to

Nothing is farther from the fact. The Government desires to utilise the public work of

Rural District are the same, and I should be

In the measure before the House the
isolated endeavour of each of the bodies that
are already administering the existing Acts
can be co-ordinated and they work
harmoniously. So far as I can judge
the Rural will have the preponderating
voice. If Members look at the schedule
of the Bill as introduced they will
see how it is proposed to constitute the
new County Library Committee. Two members of the County Council are in the first
instance compulsorily put on the County
Library Committee. Two members of each
Rural District will be members of the body,
and besides that one member of every Urban
District and a commissioner of every town
will also be joined in the administration of
the provisions of the Measure, while an additional number of members of the County
Council-one for each Urban and Rural District-will form members of the Library Committee. But the effect of that is that the
Rural Council, or members from the Rural
Council, will really have the preponderating
voice. It seems to me that this County
Library Committee is a very representative
body indeed, and I think the form of it,
which was a new provision introduced during the passage of the Measure through the
Senate, will commend itself to those who
approach the subject with an open mind.
I should say before I sit down that there is
nothing mandatory about the provisions of
this Measure. It leaves it to every County
Council to adopt the Measure or not to adopt
it, as it pleases. The Government hope that
the provisions will be largely taken advantage of and that the County Councils will
show themselves alive to the importance of
providing library facilities for the population
of their respective counties. This Measure
preserves all the facilities that exist in the
Acts that are already capable of being put
into operation. I do not think there is anything new in it except the principle of coordination in using the existing facilities,
and perhaps introducing a few improvements
in the administration, but there is
nothing extra in the way of expense included in the Measure. It
preserves all the existing facilities of the
Acts, and enables the Urban Authorities
either to carry on by themselves or to sink
their operations in the county systems. That
again is optional; if they find they were
doing better before they can revert to their
own system after having tried their connection with the county system. I do not think
it is necessary for me to go into the specific
provisions of the Bill. They are really all
that I mentioned in the general terms that
I have used I now have the honour to move
the Second Reading of this Bill.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I do not rise to attempt to
take in any sense of the word what the Prime
Minister called a slash at the Government.
I am in entire sympathy with this Libraries
Bill, but I cannot agree with the hon. and
learned Gentleman opposite (Mr. Megaw),
who is my colleague in the representation of
the County of Antrim, that the Government
have been trying to utilise the existing local
bodies. He said that the rural district
councils would have a preponderating voice
in the management of the library, but my
sole objection to the Bill is that the Government, as they have been doing for some time
past, have been attempting to take away the
power from the rural district councils and
from the representatives of the people of the
rural districts in any capacity and to put
it into the hands of the county councils. I
have only to mention the Reads Act as an
illustration of this thing. Then one has
only to think of the Education Act, which
has absolutely taken away the powers from
the local committees of looking after the
schools, and now this third attempt in the
Libraries Bill suggests, undoubtedly, that
the Government are overlooking those who
have been serving the country well in the
past. The hon, and learned Gentleman spoke
of the County of Antrim, which I have the
honour of representing with him, and he said
that some of the rural district councils-I
think he said five-had undertaken the duties
of the Library Committee; but he omitted
to tell the House a very important thing, that
since the appearance of the schedule, showing the way in which the powers are vested
in the County Council, four of those Rural
District Councils have withdrawn the consent
which they originally gave, Ballymena, Ballymoney, Antrim, and Larne Rural District
Councils have each withdrawn the consent
which they gave when they understood that
this thing would be managed by the Rural
District Councils.
I do not know that I am extraordinarily
good at arithmetic, but, as I look at it, this
schedule provides for the appointment of the
committee in this way: If one Rural District
Council would adopt the Libraries Act there
would be four members of the County Council
on the committee. I know it may be said
that one of those men is a member of the
Rural District Council; being the chairman
of the Rural District Council, he is also a
member of the County Council. But in
reality when he goes to the County Council
he always looks upon himself as a member
of the superior body. There would be four
members of the County Council, one member
of the Rural District Council, and one ad-

I stand here to say that I am exceedingly
desirous that this Bill should be worked well
throughout the country. There is too much
light literature read in the country,
and the people have not the opportunity of getting hold of good literature.
It would be a magnificent thing if the people
could get hold of good literature for their
spare time; but I say it is not a good thing,
if the Government want this measure to
work well, to show even the semblance of
taking away the power from the Rural
District Councils. I think the Government
would be well advised to make it so plain
that anyone can understand that, instead
of taking power from their hands, they are
really anxious to utilise the Rural District
Councils in carrying out this work. I hope
the Government will see their way to alter
this Section in such a way that the Rural
District Councils will be used successfully to
carry out the provisions of this Bill.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: It seems to me that
the chief purpose that this Bill will serve
will be to bring the advantages of the public
libraries system into prominence, to rouse
popular interest in it, to create a demand,
and to encourage the various County Councils
throughout the Northern area to take up the
scheme and work the Bill. But, while you
can bring a horse to the water, you cannot
force him to drink. We have had an example
of this in the fact that throughout the Six
Counties the Rural District Councils, which
by the Act of 1902 could have had public
libraries working in their areas, have, except
in a very few instances, not availed themselves of their powers. I hope very much
that the County Councils also will not
relegate this matter to oblivion, and that, if
they do, public opinion will jog their memory.
Evidently we are prepared to be optimistic
in this matter, and to give credit to the
county councillors for having more public
spirit, more enterprise, it may be more
literary taste, than the rural district councillors. Time, however, will show. I do not
wish in any way to throw cold water upon
the Bill at present before us, because I can
quite see that co-ordination must really be
the best method in this matter. There are
many reasons why it should be so. As has
been stated by the hon. and learned Gentleman opposite, the Parliamentary Secretary
of the Ministry of Home Affairs, the County
Council is the education authority, it is the
rating authority; and so it does seem to me
it is only right that it should be given the
opportunity at any rate of carrying out the
provisions of this Bill. I fear, however, that
it is not realised how very busy the average
County Councillor is, how many committees
are associated with the County Councils, and
that the average County Councillor considers
himself a very hard-worked man; in fact, he
considers himself-many have told me so-to
be much more hardworking than the ordinary
Member of Parliament and he gets nothing
for his labours. In this Bill we are giving
him a new committee, new work, and-this
is a point I wish to make-placing the whole
burden or a great burden on his shoulders.
In this I agree with the hon. Member (Mr.
Crawford) who has just spoken, and, I am
afraid, disagree with the hon. and learned
Gentleman opposite (Mr. Megaw). It seems
to me we are placing that burden on his
shoulders without providing very much outside help, and that sufficient representation
is not being given to the Rural District
Councillors. In the case where the chairman
and a member of each Rural District Council
are to be members of this new committee, I
am not quite sure whether my hon. Friend,
the Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford)
pointed out that the chairman of each Rural
District Council is a County Councillor exofficio, so that that body would have the
power to nominate him. I do consider that it
is a considerable blot on the Bill that
sufficient representation is not given to the
Rural District Councillors, and I would urge
the Government most strongly to amend the
schedule and to give larger representation on
these committees to the Rural District
Councillors.
It also seems to me a great pity that where
an enterprising, public-spirited Rural District
Council, like several which have been mentioned in the County Antrim, has worked
successfully the Act of 1902 it should be
necessary to take away their powers and give
those powers to another body.
I am not
absolutely clear on reading the Bill as to
what will happen if the County Council of a
particular County does not take up these
powers. I am sure I will be reassured on this
point later on. Will the library fall between
two stools, or will the Rural District Council
carry on for that particular area? I hope so.
I am afraid I have to agree with my hon.
Friend (Mr. Crawford) when he referred to
the tendency to discourage Rural District

proposed:
Mr. MEGAW: This is a short Bill, and like
the one I had the honour of proposing a short
time ago it does not introduce anything in
the nature of a new principle. It is a Bill
for simplifying the procedure with regard to
appointments to the Commission of the Peace,
and prescribes the fees that are to be paid by
Justices of the Peace in respect of their
727 728
[Mr. Adjournment.
of the Peace Bill. HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Megaw]
Commissions appointments. The existing practice in
making appointments is very cumbrous and
costly as every time a new magistrate is
appointed for any county it is necessary to
make out a fresh Commission involving a
vast mass of what scems to be rather useless
scrivenery.
The Commission of the Peace
that is now issued for any county recites the
name of every person who already holds the
Commission and to some extent the duties
that are to be discharged by him. The form
in existence is really the survival of centuries.
The office of Justice of the Peace itself is one
of the oldest offices in England. Its history
extends as far back as some 550 years, and I
am not sure whether the method of appointment has changed very much during that
time. In England the procedure for creating
new Magistrates was very largely simplified
by an Act in 1877. That Act has been held
not to apply to Ireland, at least there was
some doubt as to whether that Act, which
was apparently a general Act, applies to
Ireland, and, as a matter of fact, it never has
been put into force in Ireland. Under that
Act rules have been made by which
Commission is issued for every county and a
schedule is attached to the Commission giving
the names of the Justices as they are
appointed from time to time.
one
We found very great difficulty when we
took over the Government here with regard
to the appointment of Justices of the Peace.
It will be remembered that the Clerk of the
Crown and Hanaper used to have control of
the Great Seal and all the Commissions were
issued under the Great Seal. The Clerk of
the Crown and Hanaper had his office in
Dublin, and it was no easy task to get him
moved to have magistrates appointed when it
was thought necessary. A greater difficulty,
however, arose at the time of the burning of
the Four Courts, because in that burning the
Great Seal itself disappeared and it took considerable time to have it replaced. After
that the Treaty Act rather changed the
whole system of Government in Ireland, and
there was also the abolition of the office of
Lord Lieutenant.
Now it is thought right to adopt a system
that is pretty much the same
existence in England, which will only require
as that in
the issue of one Commission on which the
names can be added from time to time as
they are made. It certainly will be very
much more economical, and it will be at
least equally effective to the method of the
past. It will not require the use of the Great
Seal, so that appointments can be made much
more expeditiously, while the question of
fees on appointment will be settled upon a
satisfactory basis, because there is some
doubt as to the legality of the footing upon
which they are at present charged. The form
of the Commission is settled by the Bill itself.
It is set out in the First Schedule and retains generally the wording of the old Commission; but we have shortened the
language; it does not contain all the archaic
forms that were in existence, and the Bill
itself provides that rules will be made for
the proper working out of the methods of
appointment. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.
Bill committeed to a Committee of the
whole House for to-morrow.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Illegitimate Children (Affiliation
Orders) Bill.
As amended, considered.
Mr. SPEAKER: May I point out that the
amendments on the Paper are in the wrong
order, in one respect, namely, that on the
Report Stage of a Bill a new Clause must be
taken first. Therefore, I will call on the hon.
and learned Member in charge of the Bill to
inove his new Clause first. It appears last on
the paper.
NEW CLAUSE.-(COMMUTATION OF
WEEKLY SUMS).
"(1) Any weekly sums payable under an
Affiliation Order may, on the application of
the putative father of an illegitimate child,
be commuted by the Court by which the
Affiliation Order was made for a lump sum,
if that Court is satisfied-
(a) that arrangements have been made for
the proper administration of the lump sum
for the maintenance and education of the
child, and
(b) that the lump sum is sufficient to afford
to the child benefits at least equal to those
which would be afforded by the payment of
weekly sums.
Such lump sum shall be paid to the collecting officer or to such other person or body of
persons as may be designated by the Court,
and shall be invested and applied for the
maintenance and education of the child in
such manner as the Court may direct.
"(2) All sums applicable under this section
for the maintenance and education of an
illegitimate child shall if default is made by
any person in the payment thereof, be recoverable in like manner as sums payable by the
putative father under an Affiliation Order."
Brought up, and read the First time.
THE PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw): I beg to move, "That the Clause
be read a Second time." It was a Clause that
was practically agreed on, I think, in Committee, and we have endeavoured between
the Committee Stage and the present Stage
to put in form the subject matter of that
agreement, which is to enable weekly sums to
be commuted for a lump sum so that in a
case where an Affiliation Order had been made
in which the maintenance was directed to be
paid by the putative father, it might be commuted once and for all by arrangement between the parties. It is arranged on the basis
of what would be the weekly allowance, and
we have endeavoured in the new Clause to
adapt as far as possible the proper administrative methods. I do not think there is
anything in the Clause of a controversial
nature so I will simply move it.

This amendment is to carry out what
seemed to be the mind of the House, that the
proceedings would not be determined by the
death of either of the parties, that is the
putative father or the mother of the child.
This amendment puts that into form and I
think it carries out what was the intention
of the House. It secures that in the case of
the death of the putative father his estate
should be liable for the amount that would
have been decreed against him, and my hon.
Friend, the Member for the University (Mr.
Robb) had an amendment down to that
effect. We have practically adopted that
amendment in the amendment I now move.

"
Marketing of Eggs Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That the Bill be now read a Second time."
THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): The object of this Bill is
to try to help the egg industry, which
is a very large one in this country.
Hon. Members may not know that there
are six and a half million hens in
Ulster, and last year the money brought in
by the export of eggs was about £3,300,000.
That is a very considerable sum to come
into the pockets of people in this country.
We have been trying to help that on in the
Ministry in various ways. We have given
advice in grading and packing, and have sent
instructors into the country, and in other
ways we have been trying to help. The
Charlemont Commission, which sat the other
day, passed a unanimous resolution in favour
of bringing in a Bill of this sort. For about
six or seven months we in the Ministry have
been making ground for the Bill. We have
had meetings with egg merchants, and we
have also had meetings with farmers in the
different districts. The egg merchants are
practically unanimous in favour of a Bill of
this sort. (Hon Members: Hear, hear.)
What we want to do is to concentrate on the
quality of our exports and try to get better
prices. It is very disheartening for anyone
connected with the Ministry to go to England
and find out that the large importers of eggs
from Ireland are giving up using Irish eggs
altogether, because they cannot depend on the
eggs when they open the case being what
they purport to be. Hundreds of times they
have told me they have opened cases supposed
to contain fresh eggs and have found coldstored eggs, in some cases boiled eggs, and in
very many cases dirty eggs and badly packed
eggs. These are things which we hope this
Bill will prevent. We do not intend that the
measure should act viciously on anyone, but
we want, as hon. Members will see on reading
the Bill, to licence all exporters. We have
nothing to do with the retail merchants. We
have only to do with the wholesale merchants.
Under Clause 1 we want to make it recessary for all wholesale egg merchants to take
out a licence, for which they will pay 20s.
That licence will last them until we see reason to recall it, or as long as they continue
to deal properly in eggs. We want to make
regulations from time to time so as to see that
the eggs are properly graded. That is one
thing necessary on the other side. Danish
and New Zealand eggs which come in fetch
the highest prices. All the eggs are of equal
737 Marketing of Eggs Bill-

7 MAY 1924
Second Reading.
size, and are packed together. You grade the
eggs of a certain size in one case, and
the
eggs of a smaller size in another case. We
want to have our eggs packed in that way.
We also want to have them clean. Hens walk
about and dirty the eggs. We do not want
any dirty eggs offered for sale.
Clause 2 provides that all premises where
cold-stored or pickled eggs are preserved shall
be registered with the Ministry. The trade
in cold-stored eggs is perfectly reasonable to
carry on, and it is very necessary, but we
want to register every place where such a
trade is carried on, so that we can examine
the eggs when they come from a certain district. The owners of such premises have to
keep a record, so that it will be easy for our
officials to see what is going on.
eggs
Clause 3 provides that every person dealing
in preserved, cold-stored, or pickled
must have a brand on the box itself in letters
not less than two inches long, so as to make it
clear that the eggs are not fresh eggs, but
cold stored or pickled eggs. In that way they
will not be palmed off on the public as they
were before.
Clause 4 makes it imperative on the market
authority in places where they collect tolls to
have covered places for the packing of eggs.
We find that one of the worst things in
connection with the buying of eggs in our
various country towns. The buyers pack them
out on the streets without any cover. The
rain comes down and makes the straw musty,
and the eggs do not sell as they should at
the proper price in London.
Clause 5 extends the Public Health Acts
Amendment Act and makes it compulsory
on every urban and rural district to carry
out that Act. Up to the present only a
certain proportion of the Urban and Rural
Councils are carrying out the Act. I am
glad to say that Dungannon Urban Council
was the first one to do so. A good many
Councils have now taken it on. Although
the Ballymoney Council had a picture of me
throwing eggs at someone with a cock crowing, I believe that when asked to take this
matter on they did so and found it very
useful.
Clause 6 gives power to any officer of the
Ministry to enter and examine the place
where eggs are kept and being packed to
test them and see that they are what they
are supposed to be.
Clause 7 makes it eligible for us to make
rules and regulations. At first we cannot
say exactly what will be required. We do not
want to make a long Bill with too many
clauses. We want to make it open to us if
we like to make rules for testing and grading
!
so that we can bring our eggs to the market
and have them in the same condition as the
Danish eggs which obtain the higher prices.
Clause 8 deals with the fines. The penalty
for the first offence is a fine not exceeding
£20, for the second offence a fine not
exceeding £50, and for the third
offence a fine not exceeding £100. We
find it is necessary to impose considerable
fines. It is wonderful how many cases there
are of the public being defrauded as regards
I heard the other day of one buyer
getting 200 cases of eggs from a part of
Northern Ireland, and every single one was
condemned by the officer of health in Belfast,
so I think a fine of £50 is not too much for
that kind of thing. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Clause 10 deals only with the title of
the Bill.
eggs.
This Bill is opening new ground so far as
Great Britain is concerned, and I am proud
to think that we in Northern Ireland are the
first to bring in a Bill of this kind to help the
consumer to get eggs of the quality that he
is paying for. We do not intend to carry out
the provisions of this Measure in a hard way.
Hon. Members will remember that the Live
Stock Act also broke new ground in Great
Britain. When that Measure was passed a
large number of people thought they would
be ruined by the refusal of licences for their
bulls; but as a matter of fact we took it so
easily at the start that a great many people
said we were not half severe enough. As time
goes on we intend to become a little tighter
in the application of that Act. We intend to
administer this Bill in a very easy way at
first, and then to become firmer in insisting
on the carrying out of the various provisions.
We know that in order to carry out this Bill
in a proper way we must have the sympathy
of the people of our own country, and we
hope to have the assistance of all the buyers,
small and great. As I said before, practically
all the egg merchants have agreed to the provisions of this Bill. We had several meetings
with them, and we showed them the draft of
the Measure which we proposed to bring in.
I beg to move.
Mr. COOTE: I am sure we have all listened
with a great amount of interest to the
Minister of Agriculture trying to explain this
Bill; but, if I may be allowed to say so, he
has failed to show us how he is going to
eliminate the stale egg, and to deal with the
egg that has arrived at a certain stage.
Nothing in this Bill does that directly, many
things will do it indirectly; but I submit it
is impossible for any Minister or any country
to eliminate the stale egg at once by means
of an Act of Parliament. The industry is so
large and diversified and the commodity
passes through so many hands that it will
require the greatest patience, care, sympathy
and attention to arrive at the stage when you

Mr. ARCHDALE: I said so in my speech.
can say that you are properly directing the

We had experience of Government control

for that matter in any other country. Speaking for our own country, I may say that the
people fear there will be too much fussing

the effect of depreciating the value of the

this Act will resolve itself into a mere official
piece of interference, instead of giving fairplay all round to the producers and the consumers of the eggs, and that officials who
know nothing and care less about the conditions, or at any rate who are not anxious
about them, may do things that are not
above-board. That sort of thing will do great
harm, and will cause an outcry. We wish to

In the first place, I object to the grounds
of the Charlemont Report, on which the Bill
is based. I am sorry I have not the Report
with me, but if you will look at that document you will find in the appendix that only
about half-a-dozen interested people were
summoned as witnesses before the Charlemont Commission. There were some twenty
representative men on the Commission, but
there was very little information given to
them. There were one or two wholesale
people examined, and that was practically
the whole thing; but the people who keep the
fowl, the people who collect the eggs, the
people who live by this means, were not
brought there in order to voice their
difficulties. Something that was pigeon-holed

and that was tried on many a time before,
was brought down and was tried on Ulster.
It was probably thought that we were now
of a more gullible temperament than in the
old days when North and South were together. I hope they are not making a mistake of that sort, because it would be a very
serious thing if they did so.
As to the tone of the Minister in moving
the Second Reading of this Bill, I thought it
was pitched in rather a doleful key. He told
us that Danish eggs fetch the highest price
in the British market. I would like to ask
him does he know the facts? Was it his offi-
Mr. COOTE: Well, it was an unfortunate
thing to say that the trade has practically
gone. It is better to look at the situation in

Province of Ulster. It touches a great number of people who are voters, and we ought

When we have the public behind us we will

(a) the

Some things are disclosed, and others are

There are two things that they intend to do,
but they have not the manliness to say so
here. They intend to exclude the use of boxes
made from native Irish timber, to eliminate
the use of straw, and to bring about the use
of Swedish wood. I believe that is the goal
which they wish to attain-the use of wood
not grown in Ireland, the use of Swedish
timber and wood-wool. Those are two of
the principal factors, but they are not in the
Bill, and they are trying to get a blank
cheque so that they can exercise those powers.
As to wood-wool, this Ministry of Agriculture
is very careful to refrain from the use of anything that might carry Foot and Mouth
Disease. But this wood-wool comes from the
continent, and is dumped down in Liverpool,
one of the areas prescribed under the Foot
and Mouth Diseases Order. They will bring
that wood-wool over to Ireland; it does not
matter if our cattle get Foot and Mouth
disease; not at all. In fact they are insistof wood-wool in the egg
ing on the use
competition at the agricultural show, for

They will not allow straw to be used, but.
they will take material brought from

with the disease.
Take another item in connection with that

You must not take any timber
from your Own doors." That would be

ready to be made into boxes. These are sent
over here in large batches and quantities,
and any novice can nail them, so that the
unemployed in Northern Ireland get no
assistance.

would be simply sending in eggs and the

I apologise to the Minister if I am offending him by making suggestions of this sort.
I only make the suggestions because this is

Then everything will be right. We want to
stand behind the Government for better
markets. We want to eliminate damp and
the necessity for people packing eggs on a

among all that muck and dirt. It is disgraceful. If we eliminate all that we have the
finest district for eggs in the United Kingdom. We have our eggs growing in the
estimation of the British market as you can

Dane; we are beating Europe. Now we should

did not know what he was talking about.
We want a real, practical scheme which will

the most popular schemes it would be possible

mistake one way or another will send
hundreds and thousands of people on the

That is all I have got to say, except that I

plenty of expense

Dr. MORRISON: I must say that I am in
sympathy with every argument put forward
by the hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Coote). I think this is another
illustration of the tendency that economic
causes are producing, causes which have this
affect, that industries-rural industries-are
going to be smothered and killed. In my own
district there are two sawmills, I think, engaged in producing egg boxes. A large
number of people are employed in sending
off these egg boxes to different parts of the
country. And if you give power to this
Ministry to men sitting in armchairs in

perhaps will come to the conclusion that
Swedish timber is better than Irish timberyou may have some restrictions. We have an

You may have these restrictions and these

and I think the House have a right
to guard against them. When we
were discussing the question of local
industries-the shirtmaking industry-the

Dr. MORRISON: Swedish timber is preferred and if it is brought into Belfast in
bulk and cut up by machinery and sent, as
it is, to the creameries you run the risk of
killing this industry in Northern Ireland
which is not only affording employment to
people but is doing the further service of
enabling the farmers of Ulster to dispose of

Ulster, who has not got first-class timber, to

otherwise he would not obtain, because the
timber would only be available for fire-wood.
I do not press that. I am in agreement with
the necessity of preserving the reputation of
the products of Northern Ireland. Forty
years or more ago I went to a Glasgow music

hall. (Laughter.) I acknowledge that even
now I go to the Hippodrome and I think
there is a distinct advance from the
music hall to the Hippodrome. I go there
and I enjoy the performance. One of the
jokes I heard in Glasgow on this occasion has
remained in my mind ever since. A comedy
artist said of something, "It stinks like
Belfast butter." That expression has stuck
in my mind ever since. It expressed a great
truth; that forty years ago, and even more
recently, we did, through neglecting to adopt
scientific methods as applied to agriculture,
export an article that was not satisfactory.
I think the Member for Fermanagh and
Tyrone (Mr. Coote) has shown that judged
by prices our products are now improving.
Notwithstanding that, I think this measure
is a wise and necessary one because there has
been in the past, and there certainly is now,
a considerable amount of abuse in connection
with the marketing of Our produce. I
believe that in some cases, and indeed in
many cases, the consumer has been victimised by what he thought was a sound fresh
article and which was a bad and dishonest
article. Not only does that damage the
consumer but it damages the great body of
honest producers, and as a result of these
frauds prices are lessened. But what I am
chiefly concerned about is another matter,
which I view from the standpoint of Ulster
finance and economy. That is the perpetual
increase of officials who are trapezing
backwards and forwards all over Ulster in
motor cars and by means of railway passes
and thus piling up expense. I am afraid that
if you are to have any effective inspection
of eggs you must have a large staff of
officials, and if you have that you must have
an accompanying increase of taxation which
I very much dread. Therefore I think we
should go carefully and slowly with regard to
this Bill and try to elicit public opinion on
it before we pass it into law.

show that the egg industry has progressed
