I think it is higher now in our Province
than in the whole of Ireland some ten years
ago. That is a great consideration. The right
hon. Gentleman rightly pointed out that if
greater attention could be given to this
matter it would progress considerably more,
probably by one million pounds more in
the export trade. That is a great matter.
The Commission's Report lays it down that
No half measures will enable the Northern
Ireland egg industry to attain the position
which it should occupy. The short-sighted
policy of a comparatively few traders would
largely neutralise the efforts of others to
place the industry in that position.
They go on to say:
We have, consequently, been forced to the
conclusion that a point has been reached
at which, in the interests of the industry
as a whole, the Statethat is this House--
should introduce legislation.
recom-
And they make certain definite
mendations. The memorandum contained in
the Bill is perfectly clear. It says the Bill is
To make provision for the licensing of
wholesale dealers in eggs, the registration
of premises where eggs are preserved, the
better testing, grading and packing of eggs,
and the better prevention of the sale of
eggs unfit for human food; and for other
purposes connected therewith.
There is the whole subject. What has brought
this about? What has helped our Commission to come to that decision? It is due
to complaints from the other side that they
are receiving bad eggs, dirty eggs and so forth.
I wonder are hon. Members aware that
London would be delighted to take the whole
of our eggs if they could get them. I have
experienced the fact when in London that the
people would give a higher price for Irish
eggs than for any other kind, and for Irish
butter too. In fact if a shop displays Irish
Marketing of Eggs Bill-
Second Reading.
7 MAY 1924
eggs they are no time exposed until they are
bought up. That is the very reason we are
attempting to increase the export trade and
build up the industry, even to provide the
London market.
I can well remember in my early life that
butter and eggs were the only means by which
the small farmers could practically raise their
rent. I can also remember when these products were their only means of livelihood.
My right hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale) has so
improved the breeding of poultry that even
where I was brought up the people are going
in for the breeding of fowl and the production
of eggs. They are making a speciality of it.
I know cases where people who were injured
in the war and received some money have set
up poultry farms. That is a splendid idea.
It is work that disabled ex-Servicemen can
do. It is one of the finest things I know.
There are people throughout the country who
could go in for poultry farming. It is light
work. Now these people are going to be encouraged. Eggs will be taken from them
when they supply them fresh and they are
handled and carefully looked after. The
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Archdale) when
introducing the Bill talked about sorting. It
struck me that if this is to be carried out
in the case of the wholesaler why not carry
it out in the case of the retailer? You go
to a shop and you only see on the window
the price of the eggs. If a card is put up
showing the price I think in all fairness to
the consumer he should know what he is
buying. When people go to the retailer they
should know exactly what is the real value
of the egg and whether it is fresh or not.
It struck me that when the right hon. Gentleman was talking about sorting we should
know what we are buying in this country.
This looks a small matter. It is a great
matter, because we are dealing with £3,300,000
which is the value of the eggs exported out
of our country. If the right hon. Gentleman
can increase that in another twelve months
by say half a million pounds I say we will
have done a great service. The Commission
I have referred to has done a great service.
I do not know the man who would say a
harsh word against my right hon. Friend. I
know no Department in the Government
where you are received with greater courtesy
than in the Department of Agriculture. I
wish that could be said about other Departments. I know my right hon. Friend is not
placing restrictions on our people. He only
wants to see that these people are not giving
the public something that they should not
get, and that they should get the real article.
He is setting forth regulations-legitimate
regulations. There is one Clause in the
Report that I wonder if my right hon. Friend
noticed. I refer to the complaint lodged
about the shipping. It seems that the method
of transport in that connection is very bad.
The method of slinging is also bad. We in
this country should be able to find a better
method of exporting eggs and a better
method than slinging. The right hon. Gentleman has only to go into this matter to find
that a simple method could be adopted in
the shipping of eggs from this country. I do
not pretend to know all about this Bill, but
I can see at a glance it is going to do a
splendid thing for Northern Ireland. It is
going to increase our export trade. My right
hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale) has the credit of
introducing the first Measure which comes
before us as a result of the labours of the
Commission on the Natural and Industrial
Resources of Northern Ireland. Let us hope
we will have some other Bills as a result of
the work of that Commission. That is what
they are sitting for, to find out what new
industries they can create in this country.
They are dealing with the coal mines in our
area, but I cannot touch on that subject now.
I say that this Commission deserves great
credit, inasmuch as we are now dealing with
a Bill which has been introduced as a result of their deliberations. I believe this
Commission will render great services to this
country.
Mr. ARCHDALE: My hon. Friend opposite,
the Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr.
Coote), apparently did not notice when I was

We have been taking evidence throughout

important matter. The blocked out scheme
to which my
hon. Friend referred,

regulations on the Table; but we have to

7 MAY 1924
Supply-
Committee.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
There is practically no change from the
Estimate of last year. Our business goes on
from day to day, and from week to week,
on a very level standard, and therefore the
variations are comparatively trifling. There
is only one item of real importance which
will be dropped in this coming year, and that
is the item which is printed in italics at
the bottom, entitled "Special Inquiries,"
£1,000, a non-current charge. That was to
pay for the services of an expert from the
Royal Navy who came over here to launch for
us the new scheme of the Ulster Division
of the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve.
I would like to take this opportunity of
stating to the Committee the deep obligation
we are under to Captain Hartland Mahon
for having carried through what is known
to us as a very difficult operation, and for
having secured for us H.M.S. "Caroline,"
which was present at the battle of Jutland,
and which is at present in the lough, as our
drill ship. I believe that the tenders for
reconditioning and reconstruction are now
in, and, consequently, we trust that within
a short time there will be some work at all
events in the yards making that ship proper
for drill purposes. The Marquess of
Dufferin and Ava has been appointed
Captain of the Division, and when the
vessel is ready recruiting will be begun, and
I have no doubt that the city of Beifast and
our entire district will make the Division
one of the best Divisions in the Royal Naval
Volunteer Reserve.
With the exception of that sum there is
no substantial variation in the Estimate.
Like other departments we are limiting the
expenses as far as we possibly can, so that
there shall be no extravagance if it can be
prevented. If hon. Members care to go back
to the earlier Votes they will observe that
there has been a steady decline in the Estimates put forward. Even on this year, over
and above that £1,000 to which I have referred, there is a saving of £232, and we
hope that next year, if the political waters
are unruffled by any unlooked-for incident,
we may be able to effect further economies.
I beg to move.

the Northern Government. I can only say
that the cost is merely a trifle compared
with the great advantage we will gain in

Naval Volunteer Reserve, which will employ
so many men-I think 500 is the establishment-and which I hope and trust will be
a great success.

Mr. BARBOUR: I am sure hon. Members
will remember the readiness with which

maintaining the dignity of our Six
Counties, in promoting their interests, or
in extending hospitality to those distinguished visitors who from time to time are
good enough to honour us with their presence the expense of adequately discharging those duties should not continue to fall
upon one or two private individuals. The
Committee at that time readily voted the
sum of £3,000 to be set aside to the credit
of this account. All expenditure in connection with this is vouched for by the
Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock) personally, and the Comptroller and Auditor-
General accepts his certificate that the
money has been properly laid out for the
purpose for which it was voted.
During the past year expenses to the extent of about £2,300 were incurred in
Government hospitality. It was stated at
the time this original sum was voted that
any balance remaining at the end of the
financial year would be carried forward to
the credit of this acount in the ensuing
year. Consequently, there remains a sum of
£700 to the credit of this account, and it
is estimated that if the Committee will vote
a further sum of £2,000 it should be adequate to meet the demands that may be

year. It will be seen that we are only
asking for £2,000 this year instead of £3,000

the Committee will consider this sum in no
way excessive. I beg to move.
Dr. MORRISON: I supported this Vote
last year, and I have very much pleasure
in supporting it again this year. I think
it is a very necessary and a very wise provision, and it is the duty of the Committee

valuable thing for us to have distinguished
Members from across the water who can
find the conditions that prevail-conditions

Oral Answer to Question.
NORTHERN IRELAND'S CONTRIBUTION
TO THE IMPERIAL GOVERNMENT.
Mr. DUFF: Might I ask a question of the
Minister of Finance, of which I have given
private notice? It is to ask the Minister of
Finance whether his attention has been
drawn to the reply given in the Imperial
House of Commons by the Financial Secretary to the Treasury on the 6th instant to a
question addressed to him by Mr. Cahir Healy
regarding the amount of contribution paid by
Northern Ireland during the years 1922-23 and
1923-24, and the grants-in-aid voted by the
Imperial Government to Northern Ireland
during those years; whether there is not a
discrepancy between these figures and those
given on the floor of this House; and, if so,
whether he will make a statement on the
matter?
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): On behalf of my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance, I
may say that he is grateful for the opportanity that has been afforded him to make the
following statement on the matter. It has to do
with the reply given by Mr. Graham to Mr.
Cahir Healy. The official report indicates
that the sums of £6,213,700 and £4,500,000 respectively, and not £5,213,700 and £4,500,000, as
stated in the Press, were provisionally deducted from the Northern Irish Residuary
Share of Reserved Taxes in respect of the
two years in question. The total contribution, therefore, for the two years is
£10,713,700, to which may be added the contribution paid in the four months between the
22nd November, 1921, and the 31st March,
1922, amounting to £2,820,800. The gross contribution, therefore, from the date upon
which full financial responsibility rested upon
the Northern Government to the 31st March
last was, as stated by my right honourable
Friend the Prime Minister in his statement
to the House on Tuesday, the sum of
£13,534,500.
With regard to the total grants-in-aid paid
by the Imperial Government in the year
1923-24, I find that there is a discrepancy be
tween the figures published in Mr. Graham's
reply and the accounts of my Department.
This discrepancy-which involves a sum of
£552,534-represents payments for Special
Constabulary and Malicious Injuries voted by
the Imperial Government last year, but
which did not reach the Ministry of Finance
until after 31st March last, and therefore
only appear in our current year's accounts.
The total grants-in-aid paid by the Imperial
Government between the 22nd November,
1921, and the 31st March, 1924, amounted to
£6,780,800, including the sum of £552,534
which came to account in the year 1924-25.
Deducting these grants from the gross amount
of contribution of £13,534,500, a net contribution of £6,753,700 is left.
I have given the net figure for the full
period since the Northern Government was
established. Mr. Graham's net contribution
figure for the years 1922-3 and 1923-4 is
£3,532,840, but in my view the figure should
really be slightly over £4,000,000. I am
investigating this discrepancy, which I
imagine to be largely due to book-keeping
adjustments in the Treasury accounts which
have resulted in an understatement of the
actual position.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer
I think it would be far better that this House
should await the statement of the Minister
of Finance in introducing the Budget before
we take any notice of these questions.

The Education Act will add very considerably to the work of the Ministry-I am sure
hon. Members will readily understand thatboth as regards the new duties imposed by it
on the Department, and the expansion of

think it is perhaps well for me to emphasise

also say that this staff has not all been

of staff as thus set forth is due mainly to the

Even apart from the Act, there has been a

volume of the additional work to be discharged by the Department is such that it
cannot be adequately performed by any lesser
staff. It will be observed that the subhead
has now been classified so as to show the

agree with me that this is a distinct advantage, because at later periods when we wish
to compare it will make that operation much
easier.

National Teachers' Organisation. In the

preceded the signing of the Agreement took
place, the cost of living was rapidly increasing, and, in the month in which the Agreement was signed, it reached its highest point,
176 per cent, above the figure for July, 1914,
the standard month. When it is considered
that the corresponding figure for February
last was 79 per cent., it will be realised how
greatly circumstances have altered since
that Agreement was signed.
The Minister feels that the time has now

it is his intention to appoint at an early date
a Departmental Committee to inquire into
the matter, and advise him whether the
present scales of payment should be revised
from 1st April, 1925, and if so, what revision
is desirable.

Then with regard to building where suitable buildings are not available. I am
interested in one particular case in my own
constituency which I would like to mention
to-day. It is the case of the technical committee in Portstewart. This particular committee and the Urban Council have taken the
greatest interest in technical education. The
local people have done everything in their
power to further technical education since the
inception of the scheme in County Derry,
fifteen years ago. Portstewart was the first
itinerant centre in County Derry in which
instruction was given in domestic economy
and manual subjects. The classes were so
successful that the local people decided to
raise the product of a penny rate by public
subscriptions and the county committee
established a fixed centre there. The work
was carried on in two forms until 1916. After
1916 the town obtained urban powers and one
of the council's first acts was to strike a
penny rate for technical education. Since
1912 they have had a constant struggle
against unsatisfactory accommodation and
the results of their efforts have been very
limited in this respect. They obtained the
Methodist Hall for two sessions and had to
leave. They then got another hall, the old
Presbyterian hall which they have now
received notice to leave. They had to teach
all their subjects in that very unsuitable
accommodation although it was accommodation of a sort. They could not raise
sufficient money to provide better accommodation but rather than see the work close
down the Urban Council unanimously struck
the maximum rate of 2d. realising £44, and
pledged that sum to provide interest and
Sinking Fund on a loan of £600. A free site
has also been offered. I am using this as an
example. No more can be done locally unless
the Ministry come immediately to the aid of
this committee. As far as I can see the work
will have to be closed down and it does seem
terrible that such a step might possibly have
to be taken when we realise the enormous
importance of technical education throughout
all the districts, whether rural or urban, and
the fact that in that particular community
the people are so interested, as they have
proved themselves to be, in the cause of
technical education. That is only one case
which happens to be in my own constituency
where a building grant is urgently required
and where, if it is not given, technical
education will suffer. I know there are very
many other places similarly situated. Banbridge is one and Portadown is another, and
there they are having the same difficulty.
It seems impossible for them to wait for the
Education Act to function properly in the
Counties, and some assistance must be given,

Ministers (Temporary Exercise
of Powers) Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best) :
This Bill, as the title imports, is a Bill to
make provision for the temporary exercise
of the powers of Ministers of Northern
Ireland. Hon. Members are aware of the
emergency which necessitates this legislation.
The Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson
Bates) is unfortunately laid
up with a
serious illness. Certain things can only
be done by the Minister in person.
Accordingly it becomes necessary to make
provision not only for this case but
also in reference to the inability for any
reason of any other Minister to act. The
Bill is made quite general and it gives to
his Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland
power where a Minister is unable to act to
"designate any Parliamentary Secretary of
the Ministry or Department of which such
Minister is the head, or any other Minister
of Northern Ireland, to act for such firstmentioned Minister during such period
as the said Governor may think fit; and,
during the said period, references in any
enactment to such first-mentioned Minister
shall be construed as references to the
Parliamentary Secretary or Minister so
designated to act."
Mr. McGUFFIN: Might I ask the right hon.
and learned Gentleman (Mr. Best) is there a
precedent for this in the Imperial House?
Is it necessary there, and is it observed?
Mr. BEST: In answer to that, it is
generally the Ministry that is specified in
the Acts of the Imperial House and so the
difficulty would not arise.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I see.
Mr. BEST: Take, for example, those regulations under the Civil Authorities (Special
Powers) Act. Take internment orders; all these
things can be done by the Minister and by the
Minister only, and, accordingly, if we wish
to intern a person, or to make a new regu
lation, or anything of that kind, it cannot
be done except by the Minister. The
Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates)
is quite unable to transact business at
present, and, therefore, it is absolutely
necessary that provision of this sort should
be made. I do not know whether there is
a precedent in the Imperial Parliament,
but there is a precedent established by this
Parliament under the office of Attorney-
General Act of 1923. Section 2 of that Act
gave power to appoint a substitute in case
the Attorney-General were unable to act.
Colonel WOODS: No, no.
Mr. BEST: The hon. and gallant Member
says "No, no." I do not exactly know
what the meaning of that observation is. It
seems to have no relevance to any observation I have made, or to any observation
anyone could even think of. There was power
taken to nominate a deputy to the Attorney-
General, because in his case there are many
things which can be done only by him. There
are many statutory obligations which he has
to carry out, and if power had not been
taken to enable a substitute to be appointed
then, if the Attorney-General for the time
being were suddenly to be ill, or for some
reason he had to be absent, that particular
work could not be done. Accordingly, Clause
2 of the Office of Attorney-General Act, 1923,
provided for the nomination of a substitute.
This does precisely the same thing for any
Minister who for any reason may be unable
to act.
Mr. McGUFFIN This Bill seems quite
innocent. It hardly challenges criticism, and

point.

Mr. POLLOCK: My hon, Friend who has
just spoken is under
a grave misapprehension with regard to this matter. This

authority for that signature. There is an unwritten law in Great Britain of a similar

immemorial.
It requires a Statute here to
bring into operation the same condition,
that is to say in the absence of a Minister
where a signature has to be made some other
person shall be endowed with the necessary
authority.
Mr. DONALD: That is exactly the information I wanted from my right hon. Friend.
This only refers to cases where a signature
is required. I am perfectly satisfied.

strikes me as a person who thinks that he is

Oral Answers to Questions,
R.U.C. GUARD FOR ULSTER PAVILION
AT WEMBLEY.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has now decided to
furnish a guard from the Royal Ulster Constabulary for the Ulster Pavilion, British
Empire Exhibition, at Wembley.
:
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw) This matter has been carefully considered, and it has been ascertained that
before members of the Ulster Constabulary
could exercise the powers of police officers at
the British Empire Exhibition they would
have to be sworn in as special constables in
London. Apparently Canada is the only Colonial Government which has sent a detachment of police to the Exhibition.
In all the circumstances of the case, the
Northern Government does not consider it
would be justified in incurring the heavy expense which sending a party of the Ulster
Constabulary to the Exhibition would entail.
MANAGEMENT OF THE ULSTER
PAVILION AT WEMBLEY.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can now state if an
assistant manager has been appointed for the
Ulster Pavilion, British Empire Exhibition,
at Wembley.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
McKeown): I am replying for my right honourable Friend. The reply is in the negative.
I should add, for the information of the hon.
and gallant Member, that it is not intended
to make the appointment to which he refers.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask if it is possible for the
Ulster Pavilion to be properly carried on
without a manager?
Mr. McKEOWN: We have an official of the
Ministry of Commerce there, and he is able
to deal with any matters that arise.
ADMINISTRATION AND DISCIPLINE OF
THE C1 SPECIALS.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will consider the
adoption of certain sections of the Army Act
to apply to the administration and discipline
of the C1 Force, Royal Ulster Special Constabulary, or whether he will lay down definite
regulations for the guidance of the administrators and commanders of that Force.
Mr. MEGAW: The question of supplementing the disciplinary powers for this branch
of the Constabulary is under consideration.
Such disciplinary powers must be framed
with regard to statutes and regulations
governing the Police Forces in Northern Ireland.
PRIVATE WORK BY GOVERNMENT
ARCHITECTS.
4. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Finance whether any of the whole-ti'ne
architects employed and paid by the Northern
Government are allowed to do, or are doing,
private work outside their official duties.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I have no information concerning
the manner in which members of the
Northern Civil Service occupy their time
outside official hours, and it would be improper for me to institute any inquiry on
the subject.
The general principle governing questions
of this nature is that a Civil Servant must
not accept any employment which is likely to
interfere with the proper discharge of his
official duties. The conditions obtaining in
the Imperial Civil Service, which have been
adopted as far as possible for the Civil Service
of Northern Ireland, are generally defined in
the Order in Council of 10th January, 1910.

RECOMMENDATIONS OF COST OF
LIVING COMMITTEE.
5. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he was prepared to
follow the recommendations of the Departmental Committee on the cost of living.
:
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr. Andrews) I have been asked by my right honourable Friend to reply to this question, as the
matter is one with which my Department is
primarily concerned.
In so far as the recommendations of the
Cost of Living Committee are matters clearly
within the scope of my Department, I
arranged, on receipt of the Report, to put
them all into operation with one exception;
namely, the publication of figures for the
retail prices of coal in selected towns in
Northern Ireland and in Great Britain. I
have discussed this recommendation with the
Imperial Minister of Labour, and we ar3
agreed that there is great difficulty in giving
effect to it in each area, owing to the varying
qualities of coal and the different costs of
transport, etc., making it impossible to obtain
reliable comparative figures. The remaining
recommendations which concern matters
within the sphere of other Departments were
duly communicated to them by me.
THE CURFEW ORDER.
6. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he is now prepared to
consider the withdrawal or modification of
the Curfew Order, in view of the inconvenience caused to tourists and others.
Mr. MEGAW: The Government has this
matter constantly under consideration, but,
in their opinion, the present moment is not
opportune for further relaxing the Curfew
restrictions.
WAGES IN THE BUILDING TRADE.
7. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance whether he will state the wages
paid to skilled and unskilled workers on the
various housing schemes, including houses
under the Land Trust Powers Scheme;
whether the contractors are carrying out
Mr. POLLOCK: There are now engaged on
the various housing schemes many classes of
workmen, and the expenditure involved in
the preparation of a detailed schedule of rates
of remuneration paid would be out of proportion to the information afforded, especially
having regard to the fact that the Fair Wages
Clause forms an integral part of every
housing contract entered into by my Ministry.
So far as I am aware, contractors are carefully observing the Fair Wages Clause. Two
complaints as to the non-observance of the
clause have, in the course of the past year,
been notified to my Ministry, but both of
these have been satisfactorily disposed of.
The position in regard to the provision of
ex-Servicemen's houses is that when the Land
Trust was established on 1st January last,
221 houses were in course of construction. Of
these, nine houses have since been completed.
Invitations to tender for a further 43 houses
have been issued, and invitations for 47 more
houses will be issued shortly. Negotiations
for the acquisition of sites for the balance of
the number of cottages allotted to Northern
Ireland are still proceeding.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that reply,
may I ask is my right hon. Friend aware that
great inconvenience is caused by the Trust
sitting in London; if it is a fact that even
the applications have to be sent there to be
decided upon; and if he knows that these
matters are causing great inconvenience to
the ex-Servicemen here? Therefore, I am
sorry the Trust was set up at all, because we
have been-
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order.
Mr. POLLOCK: I must remind my hon.
Friend that the location selected by the Trust
-that is, London, as my hon. Friend has
observed is entirely a matter within the
jurisdiction of the Trust itself, over which
we have no control whatever. It is purely
an Imperial Service, the money is provided
out of Imperial sources, and is expended by
the Trust which the Imperial Authorities
have set up. My Ministry and the Ministry
of Home Affairs merely act as agents in
carrying out the mandates of the Trust.
Mr. DONALD: Is not my right hon. Friend
aware that in Great Britain there is no such
nonsense, and that they can get at the Department right away without having any trouble
such as we have in going from Belfast to
London with every application, and thereby
spending money unnecessarily?
Mr. POLLOCK: We cannot control them.

8. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour what the directions are by the
Imperial Government to Local Employment
Committees under the heading (Unemployed
Persons Seeking Work) contained in appendix
II. to pamphlet L.E.C. 82/2, and whether a
copy of the same will be placed in the
Library of the House.
Mr. ANDREWS: The document to which
my hon. Friend refers was not issued in
Northern Ireland, and does not form part of
my Department's directions to Local Employment Committees. A similar pamphlet for
the use of Local Employment Committees in

UNOCCUPIED COASTGUARD COTTAGES.
9. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he will state the number of
houses at present unoccupied at the various
coastguard stations in Northern Ireland, and
what is the policy of the Government with
respect to these houses.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have taken this question
in the regrettable absence of my right hon.
Friend. As the hon. Member is aware, the
Coastguard Service is an Imperial one, and
therefore not within the jurisdiction of this
House. The Ministry of Finance acts as
agent for the Imperial Government in respect
of the letting of coastguard cottages, and I am
therefore enabled to acquaint the hon. Member that the number of houses at present
unoccupied at the various coastguard stations
in Northern Ireland is twenty-of which nine
are available for letting. Unfortunately, in
the case of these nine no applications have
been received, due, doubtless to their isolated
position. The remaining eleven are
undergoing certain structural alterations,
upon the completion of which the cottages will
be occupied by members of the Coastguard
Service.
now
Mr. DONALD: May I ask my right hon.
Friend if he is aware that people will now
know, as the result of his answer, who can
really let the houses? I thank my right hon.
Friend for his reply.

REPORT OF THE REFORMATORIES
COMMITTEE.
11. Mr. McGUFFIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has considered the
Report of the Committee appointed to inquire
into the working of Reformatories and Industrial Schools in Northern Ireland, and if
so whether he proposes to give legislative
effect to certain of his proposals, and, if so,
when he proposes to introduce such legislation.
Mr. MEGAW: With regard to the proposals of the Committee appointed to inquire
into the working of Reformatories and Industrial Schools in Northern Ireland, which
involve an increased financial burden on the
Government and on the Local Authorities
it is considered desirable before arriving at
any final conclusion to consult the local
Authorities concerned, and with this end in
view it is proposed at an early date to invite
representatives of the Local Authorities to
discuss the whole question. Meanwhile it
would be premature to say how far it may
be found possible to give effect to these
recommendations of the Committee.
The other recommendations of the Committee are being very carefully considered.
Action has been taken on some of them,
but in some instances there are difficulties,
mainly financial, in the way of carrying these

PROMOTION IN THE ROYAL ULSTER
CONSTABULARY.
12. Mr. McGUFFIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether he can state what
procedure is followed in the promotion of
members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary;
whether it is on the basis of educational
qualification; whether examinations have
been or are to be held for this purpose, and,
if not, what system of promotion is to be
observed.
laid
Mr. MEGAW: So far as practicable promotions have been carried out in accordance
with the system in force in the Royal Irish
Constabulary, but it will be realised that a
strict adherence to the procedure as
down in R.I.C. Code (which as a matter of
fact had fallen into disuse for a considerable
time prior to the establishment of the
Northern Government) was not feasible in
the early stages of the formation of the new
Force. Adherence, for example, to the requirement of 7 years' service prior to promotion would have debarred from promotion
any member of the Special Constabulary who
had joined the Force.
Educational qualifications are taken into
consideration in selecting men for promotion.
The whole question of the system of promotion is at present under consideration in
connection with the revision of the R.I.C.
Code, and it is proposed to issue in advance
that portion of the new Code dealing with
this matter. The passing of an Educational
Examination will be one of the qualifications
required by candidates for promotion.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the hon. and learned
Gentleman whether promotions have been
made irrespective of educational qualifications,
and whether up to the moment any examinations have been held with a view to
ascertaining the qualifications of those who
have been promoted?
Mr. MEGAW: I cannot say at the moment,
but if my hon. Friend would give notice of
the question, I would be pleased to answer it.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I also ask the hon.
and learned Gentleman if he is aware that a
great deal of dissatisfaction exists amongst
the men in regard to this matter, and that
the present state of affairs stultifies the ambition and aspirations of certain young men
who would like to qualify for promotion, but
who have not had the opportunity of qualifying up till the moment?
Mr. MEGAW: I have not heard of that.
BROADCASTING STATION FOR THE
SIX COUNTIES.
13. Mr. McGUFFIN asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can state what agreement has been entered into between the
Northern Government and the British
Broadcasting Company for the erection of a
station for the Six Counties, and when it is
likely to be completed and ready for
operation.
In
Mr. McKEOWN: I am replying for my
right honourable Friend. Under an agreement entered into between the Postmaster-
General and the British Broadcasting Company, the latter secured the sole right of
establishing wireless broadcasting stations in
Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
December last the Postmaster-General informed the Ministry of Commerce that he had
received an application from the company for
permission to establish a broadcasting station
in Belfast, and inquired whether the Government of Northern Ireland would desire to
impose on such permission any special conditions. After consultation with the Ministry
of Home Affairs, the Ministry of Commerce
replied specifying certain conditions which,
in the opinion of the Government of Northern
Ireland, should be attached to the Postmaster-
General's permission. It is understood that
the company has been able to proceed with
the erection of the station subject to those
conditions, and, while I am unable to make
any definite pronouncement on the point, I
am informed that it is expected that the
station will be completed and ready for
operation by the middle of July next.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the hon. Gentleman if he
can state what the conditions are? That is
the point of the question. He only refers to
the fact that a certain agreement has been
entered into, without stating the conditions.
Is he prepared to submit the conditions themselves?
Mr. McKEOWN: One of the conditionsand a very important one-is the right to stop
the transmission, at any time that such a
course is considered necessary or desirable in
the public interest. That right is reserved
to the Northern Government.

MINISTRY OF LABOUR.
CLASS III. No. 2.
NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
'That a sum, not exceeding £110,100, be
granted to His Majesty, to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st day of March, 1925, in
respect of the contributions and grants in aid
of the cost of benefits and expenses of administration under the National Health
Insurance Acts, 1911-1922."-(Note-£35,000
has been voted on account.)
Mr. ANDREWS: The figures shown in this
Estimate are few, and by themselves require
little explanation. They disclose a decrease.
as compared with 1923-24, of £4.175. which I
think the Committee will consider satisfactory, especially having regard to the fact that
the Estimate is made on the advice of Sir
Alfred Watson. who probably is the chief
authority in the United Kingdom on such
matters. Sub-head A (£145,000) provides for
grants in aid of benefits. That is the State
share of two-ninths of all benefits paid by
approved societies. The reduction of £1,100
is partly due to closer estimating, and partly
due to a reduction in administration allowances to approved societies, from 4s 10d to
4s 5d per insured person per annum.
Under
Sub-head B a sum of £100 only is provided,
the same as last year, to meet belated claims
relating to the period prior to the 1st April,
1922, when the cost of medical certification
was paid for by the State. The Estimate for
expenses of members of Insured Committees
will in future be charged in the ordinary
administration fund of these committees.
I may say that since the Ministry of Labour
took over control of National Health
Insurance we have been able to introduce a
considerable number of economies. In the
first place, there were in Dublin-and I think
are still-three Commissioners. We have
been able to get on without any Commissioner
here. In addition, there are three medical
advisers, and, for so far, any little work of
that kind we have required to be done has
been done for us by the Home Office, at a very
moderate cost. Then, again, there is in
Dublin, I understand, a legal adviser, with his
staff. So far, we have not required to seek
advice of that kind. We have also been able
to introduce savings by means of having a
combined Health Insurance inspector. All
these savings, it is estimated, have amounted
to about £16,000.
Approved societies, the Committee will be
interested to know, have distributed during the
past financial year in sickness benefit £196,150;
disablement benefit, which I would prefer to
call, for the sake of clearness, continuous
sickness benefit, £113,750; maternity benefit,
£44,700; sanatorium benefit, £21,000, or in all
£376,000. It is gratifying to know that in
benefits paid directly to our sick
workers more than the total amount
collected in contributions from Our employers and workers has been paid,
and that the cost of administration and
creating these large reserves, which it is estimated by those who are responsible is
necessary in order to keep the fund solvent
through future years, has been paid out of
the State contribution of two-ninths of the
benefits actually paid. It is estimated that
about 40,000 persons drew sick benefit and
disablement benefit in Northern Ireland during the past year. This works out at an
average of sixteen weeks per person claiming
benefit or an average of slightly over two
weeks for all our insured persons per annum.
I quote these figures because it is often
held, I think by people who do not
fully understand the position, that of all the
contributions actually paid a large sum does
not go into the pockets of the insured
sick persons. I think the figures I have
quoted show that that is not really so, because when you remember that 40,000 of our
people have actually drawn benefit during the
year it shows the splendid work which is
being done by means of this fund. And it is
especially gratifying to me to know that this
fund is in a sound financial position. I wish
I could say exactly the same in connection
with the other insurance fund, for administering which my Department is responsible,
namely, Unemployment Insurance. (Hon.
Members: "Hear, hear.") However, I am
not dismayed as regards that fund either,
because, although we have passed through
very trying times, which have been a very
serious drain upon the fund, I think there is
reason to assume that the worst is over, and
that the drain upon it in future will be
nothing like what it has been since we took
over our part.
The Free State, as hon. Members no doubt
know, went in for a clean cut with Great
Britain in conformity with their policy of
cutting the last link with that country. That
threw some little work upon my Department,
and gave some little inconvenience to insured
persons, because 53,000 of our people who were
insured persons were insured in Southern
Ireland societies, and they had to be provided
for in our societies here owing to the action
of the Free State, but I am glad that through
Supply-
Committee.
13 MAY 1924
the perseverance and patience of my officials,
who were chiefly responsible for the matter,
it has been done without any inconvenience or
loss to the insured persons.
Now, I am afraid the hon. Member for the
University (Dr. Morrison) and I have on
occasions had what to us no doubt were very
interesting discussions in connection with
this matter, and I am glad to feel that in the
main, at any rate, we are in agreement.
Dr. MORRISON: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: We agree that a health
insurance scheme on a contributory basis is
absolutely necessary-
Dr. MORRISON: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: And it is only on the
question of administration, I think, that we
now differ. I would point out, however, that
I do not hold that everything in connection
with our health insurance scheme is on the
most approved basis. I do not think probably
we have arrived yet at the last word in connection with health insurance. I freely yield
that to my hon. Friend (Dr. Morrison), but
what I have held, and still hold, is-and I
think he will agree-that it would be very
foolish of us at this stage to make radical
departures from the scheme in operation in
Great Britain, because if we do we would,
whether we liked it or not, be driven into
the position of having a clean cut here. By
being members of the national scheme of
health insurance we derive very considerable
benefits which I think it would be a great
pity for us to sacrifice, apart altogether from
political considerations. For instance, of our
307,000 insured persons in Northern Ireland
12,300 are actually insured in British societies.
Now, this is a great advantage, because it
spreads the risk, and in a small area like ours
that is particularly desirable.
Again, there is a central fund which has
been built up through the years that have
gone of about £2,000,000. That fund is available for meeting the liabilities of societies
that may temporarily get into a somewhat
embarrassing position. In other words, that
central fund is available for the whole of the
United Kingdom, and it can be claimed upon
just as readily by approved societies working
in Northern Ireland as by approved societies
working in either England or Scotland.
There are other funds that we share in common with Great Britain; but, as I have
already said, I do not personally feel that this
is the last word upon health insurance, and
the Committee will, I am sure, be interested
to know that the Ministry of Health in Great
Britain have decided to appoint a Royal Commission to go into the whole question of
health insurance upon a very wide and ex-
ļ
tended basis, and I have had the privilege of
discussing this matter with the present Minister of Health. I have put before him the
claim that Northern Ireland should be represented upon that Commission, and that Northern Ireland people or societies who may desire
to give evidence before that Commission shall
have the opportunity of doing so. I am very
hopeful that our wishes in this matter will be
agreed to by the Minister of Health, and if
so it will allow our problem here to be investigated along with the problem in Great Britain, which, after all, is very similar, and I
hope there will be good results. At the same
time, I feel confident that in the meantime
nothing is really being lost, as our working
classes are undoubtedly receiving tremendous
help from this fund, and they would be in a
very hard position without it.
I have heard it said that some of Our
approved societies are not as generous in paying claims as they ought to be, and sometimes
delays occur which are regrettable, and held
by some to be unnecessary. I really do think,
as regards straight cases, payment is made
almost immediately. There are, of course,
involved cases which require a great deal of
investigation; but where a doctor certifies
that his patient is not in a position to work,
the insured person may feel reasonably satisfied that in a very short time he will get the
benefit to which by statute he is entitled.
Personally speaking, I do not think the medical profession can be accused of harshness.
On the contrary, I think I can say from personal experience I have always found them
to be overflowing with the milk of human
kindness. They are not likely to refuse a certificate to any insured person on other than
proper grounds. In fact, I have heard it
said that on occasions they are so sympathetic
that they are inclined to stretch a point to
meet the insured person beyond which the
approved societies think is fair to them.
However that may be, I do not know exactly
myself, but I do feel, as I have already said,
that this is a great social benefit to cur
people, and I have the greatest pleasure in
moving.
Dr. MORRISON: I wish to criticise this
Vote a little in a friendly way. I quite
appreciate the complimentary reference the
Minister has made to me, and I reciprocate
his feeling. I may say that so far as I know
I am in agreement with everything he has
said and done in his public life in Northern
Ireland, and no man has a higher respect for
him and for the great family from which he
is descended than I have. I may say in the
first place that in the matter of administration he has done what I think is a wise and
prudent thing. In this controversy over the
payments of benefits where there was some
friction between the societies and the

HOUSE OF COMMONS

Committee to a case which I have already
brought before the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) a case that happened in this city
of Belfast. This girl, who is now employed
in a Government office in Belfast, was insured
on the 23rd January, 1917, and she paid her
contributions from 1917 till the 21st January,
1920. She was out of work through illness
from December, 1920, down to the 31st of
October, 1921. She was ten months out of
work, and her contribution from the
society in that time was £4 11s. She continued under treatment and got her certificate
from her doctor-a recognised medical man in
Belfast-and she says that, on the calculation
of her father, the society owes her thirteen
months' benefit, which they decline to pay.
What happened was this-and it is an example
of the technicalities that surround this question-she got a notice from the society that
she should go and be examined by the doctor
of the society. She was ill in bed and unable
to go, and did not go. She had no information
and did not know anything except that after
that her benefit stopped. She did not know
that she should write and say that she was
unable to go. I maintain that it was the
duty of the society to find out whether the
girl was able to go to be examined or not.
At any rate she did not go, and because she
did not go she was struck off, and for her
ten months' sickness the total contribution she
got from this beneficent Act was £4 11s 6d.
Mr. GORDON: Did she continue to send
her weekly certificate?
Dr. MORRISON: She did, but it had not
the effect of getting her any money. The
laws of the Medes and Persians are nothing
compared to the administration of these
friendly societies. Worse than all, she was
not then considered to be in receipt of
benefit. When you are sick you are not expected to contribute, but they did not hold
that she was free from contribution. Again
she got treatment, and they then had a big
pile of arrears against her about which the
poor girl knew nothing at all. In the administration of a great Act like this instruction and direction should be clear and distinct,
so that even the most illiterate person would
be able to read them and to know what to
do, while the names of the different inspectors,
whose duty it is to look after these things,
should be shown in the Post Offices or on the
backs of the cards, so that people may
know that they can go to these persons for
advice in any difficulty. I have known people
to do that, and the society at once cleared
the matter up. Very often the difficulty
arises from a little technicality. Many of
these people cannot write. What I urge upon
the Committee is that they should insist that
something is done to simplify the administration, and that something is done also to give
these people an easy Court of Appeal, instead
of this useless thing which they have at present, and which is like the protection afforded
to the unmarried woman in the past. They
should have some protection from the law
which is supposed to be of such advantage to
them. Even the poorest and humblest in our
community should have this protection.
I have dealt at some length with this

CLASS V. No. 2.
AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed :
That a sum not exceeding £51.029 be
granted to his Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during the
year ending on the 31st March, 1925, in
respect of the expenses of the Ministry of
Agriculture in respect of Agricultural
Institutions, Improvement of Live Stock,
Agricultural Research and Development,
Agricultural Statistics and Sundry Grantsin-Aid. (Note-£24,900 has been voted on
Account).
Mr. POLLOCK: I feel sure that every
Member of the Committee deplores as deeply
as I do the circumstances under which it
is my duty to submit this Estimate for the
Agricultural Services. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I feel that our hearts go out
to our Colleague (Mr. Archdale) in the very
dark cloud that has overshadowed his life.
In submitting this Estimate I would call
the attention of the Committee to the fact
that there is an increase of £10,419. This is
accounted for by the fact that it arises from
a special grant made under somewhat unusual circumstances in the interest of
agriculture last year. The objects for which
the grant was made are shortly those of
agricultural education, of milk-recording
associations, the development of the poultry
industry, and the improvement in the
character and standard of mountain sheep.
I think it would be convenient if I spoke
of the incidence of that grant as the items
arising out of it appear from time to time
in subheads, and it may be, therefore, informative to hon. members if I recall the
fact that it arose out of a special grant
that was made to agriculture, following the
Report of a Committee which I appointed
and of which Viscount Pirrie, it will be
remembered, was the Chairman. A grant
of £128,000 was made in relief of rates on the
recommendations of that Committee. I do.
not say I was quite in agreement with that
recommendation because I felt that if that
very large sum of money had been devoted
to reproductive purposes-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear) it would have accomplished
very much more valuable results than the
comparatively small advantage that accrued
from the reduction that was made in the rates
of agricultural holdings. But the Committee
made a very important recommendation in
deferring to the wishes of the agricultural
community in which they urged upon the
Government the propriety of adopting the
considerations that were submitted by the
Secretary to the Ministry of Agriculture.
The result of that was that the Government
felt it was imposed upon them as an obligation that some grant should be made
that would be applied to matters of a reproductive character in the Province. The
result of that decision was that it was agreed
that a sum of £54,000, spread over four
years, should be devoted to the purposes
I have indicated, and a part of that sum
amounting to £14,925 will be spent during
the coming year and will be devoted to these
purposes.
I now come to the first sub-head, that is,
agricultural research. This Estimate shows
a decrease of £2,236, which is explained by a
reduction in the provision for initial capital
expenditure on new buildings and equipment.
The equipment of the Plant Breeding and
Poultry Divisions has been now practically
completed. You will see from the sheet on
page 49 we are asking for a re-vote of a
sum of £500 in respect of the former Division
being approximately the balance still due
to the contractors at the close of last
financial year for work almost completed.
There is also on the same sheet a more important sum of £3,500, intended for the
adaptation and equipment of buildings at
Stormont for the purpose of an Animal
Diseases Division. Some provision was
made for this Service last year, but it was
not found practicable in that period to set
the work in motion. The necessary buildings, however, are now being put in hand
and, we hope, will be completed at an early

date. I should like to make it clear that the

£400,000 should be devoted to the object

The decrease in the total provision for

of our research organisation. Provision
has been made for a second assistant to the

of this officer will be in connection with
matters relating to animal nutrition, that
is "baby" beef experiments, which hon.
Members may have noticed took place some
time ago, and the feeding of ensilage to milch
cows instead of roots. It is interesting to
notice that during 1922 and 1923 of the recorded cows, about 50 to 60 samples of milk
a week were tested. At present the number
is 550 per week, showing, of course, a very
remarkable advance in the development of
this side of the Division.
In regard to research work I should like
to refer particularly to one small item of
£150 concerned with zoology. Hon. Members
must not assume that this is the initiation
of a zoological gardens scheme. It is intended for experimentation in respect of the
suppression of insects and those pests which
are so destructive to crops of all descriptions.
It should be of interest to the Committee
to know, for example, that the ravages of
the warble fly alone are estimated to reduce
by no less a sum than £1,000,000 annually
the value of the hides of animals slaughtered
in Ireland. There are other pests-parasites
in poultry, worms in pigs, gapes in fowl.
and so
on. and there are also pests which
do much damage to fruit. These will all
be dealt with, at any rate initial arrangements will be made by this small grant of
£150 to proceed with the work of discovering
whether it will be possible to eliminate these
pestiferous insects. It may be of interesti
to the Committee to know that the seedtesting station work is being largely availed
of. Last year the samples of seeds received
for testing were 250, this year they amount
to 1,700, which is an indication of the extent

capital provision of £5,100 has been inserted

The next sub-head -Grants to County Committees is a much more pretentious item.
It follows what has been the custom for
many years in the past, and the amount is
practically the same as last year with the
exception of a very important item of £5,400
for agricultural development, which
devoted to providing increased facilities for
agricultural education generally. The County
Committees are provided with this money
because it is felt that it is a great advantage
to decentralise the work and to place most
of these duties upon the County Committess
rather than upon the Ministry itself. There
were only eight instructors and one agricultural overseer at work in Northern
Ireland in the past, and, in view of the fact
that there are 130,000 farms scattered over the
Six Counties, it will be understood that it
would be quite impossible for these officers
to cover the whole of that area and to keep
in constant touch with all farmers, more
especially those in far away or backward
districts which it was more difficult to get
at. The Ministry is, therefore, arranging
that, in addition to the instructors at present
employed, ten overseers and two instructors
will be provided. The ten overseers will be
placed in backward districts to which in the
past the instructors have not been able to
give adequate attention. The cost of this
additional work for the current year is
estimated at £4,200.
The next item concerns the improvement
of pastures. In reply to the question which
was put some little time ago by the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin),
scholarships to the value of £100 each are
provided, and this is expected to defray the
cost of these students to whom reference was
made earlier. Then we come to Grants to
Agricultural Societies. Following the grant
which was made by the Department in
Dublin to the Irish Agricultural Organisation Society, last year the Committee passed
an Estimate for £1,000 as Northern Ireland's
share of what had been done in the past It
was found, however, in operation that the
grant was not made use of to the extent
which was contemplated, and, therefore, this
year it is decided to discontinue that grant
of £1,000 to this society for the organisation
of co-operative societies. There are many
arguments that I might use in relation to
that, but I think probably the main argument
that weighed with the Ministry was that in
the North of Ireland there are sufficient
co-operative societies at the present time
for the conversion of milk into butter, and
any increase in the number might possibly
embarrass the existing societies. In order
to counter-balance this to some extent, and
to assist the educational work of the Ulster
Farmer's Union amongst the farmers, it is
suggested that a grant of £1,000 be made to
that body, and the Ministry are prepared
to justify that from the great assistance
they have had from the Farmer's Union in
carrying on the agricultural development of
the Province. The Ministry also believe that
until the machinery necessary to deal with
the maketing of agricultural produce, that
is eggs, has been developed, it would be unwise to undertake the organisation of other
forms of co-operative societies for the
disposal of agricultural produce.

Mr. MARK: The hon. Member has not
heard what I was going to say. The Ministry
has been in close touch with the Farmers'
Union. When the Department, in former days

Department first started. The Farmers'
Union does not exist for the purpose
of exploiting other people, as my good friend

Union for the benefit of the farmers generally, and I for one think that this sum of

that it is not larger.

whose absence to-day and the cause of it we
all regret, could tell of the immense benefit

Union. The Farmers' Union exists in every

have heard some of the lectures and know

Mr. GRANT: I join with other hon. Members in regretting the circumstances which
prevent the Minister of Agriculture (Mr.
Archdale) from presenting his own estimates
this afternoon. I want to join with the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin) in
protesting against this grant of £1,000 to the
Ulster Farmers' Union. The hon. Member
for Derry (Mr. Mark) states that we should
not call them a Union. It does not really
matter what we call these people. In the
eyes of the public they should be called "the
Ulster Farmers' ring "--because it is used as
a ring for fixing prices-and, after all, that
is as bad as calling them a Union. They are
a trading Union for the farmers and protect
the farmers' interests. Very often in this
House we hear Members of the Ulster
Farmers' Union congratulating the Minister
of Agriculture. I belong to a Union, though
they do not call it a Union-they call it an
association, just as the hon. Member for
Derry (Mr. Mark) would call his Union-and
if we got a subsidy of a thousand pounds
from the Minister of Agriculture we would
congratulate him too, and have every right
to do so.
The hon. Member (Mr. Mark) points out
the educational advantages they get for this
money. That is not paying very much of a
tribute to the other educational departments
of the Ministry of Agriculture. There is
another side to the Ulster Farmers' Union.
They are a trading Union just as well as
being a farmers' protective union, and I do
not think that the Government should subsidise the Union to which I belong any more
than they should the Ulster Farmers' Union.
It seems very absurd that the consumers or
ordinary individuals in the community
should have to contribute their share of this
£1,000 for the very purpose of giving this
Union an opportunity of charging whatever
prices they like for whatever commodities
they grow.
On behalf of the consumers of
Northern Ireland I strongly protest against
this £1,000 being given to the Ulster Farmers'
Union.

business in another room in the House. I do
hope that no hon. Member of this Committee
will seriously object to this miserable grant

people in the Six Counties. They are the
only producers. They are the only people
who sell their produce at the cheapest end,
and buy all their produce at the dearest.

of this matter, which the Committee will
have to consider very seriously, and that is
that, if something more is not done for
agriculture than was done in the past, the
young people will go away out of the country
and leave us very much the poorer. The
other day I was in the farmstead where I was
brought up. Within a very small area round
that house there used to be twelve or thirteen
houses with families in them. Now there is
not a single person in any of those houses.
The country is getting depopulated because

listen to anyone who says that this sum of

There were various points raised by different hon. Members with regard to the triparty conference that was held, and which
imposed no financial obligation whatever on
the Government. It was simply a friendly
conference for the purpose of discovering to
what extent the development of the flax area
for this reason could be improved with
advantage to the community, and to
that extent it seems to have succeeded.
The Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone
(Mr. Coote) criticised the action of
the Government in not allocating grants
for the testing of flax seed of a special
description. He must not overlook the fact
that the Government has subsidised the Research Department for the production of
special seed.
The Lambeg Institution has
largely been maintained by the Government.
The Imperial Government gave a grant in
one year of £5,000 on condition that the
Northern Government did likewise, and the
Northern Government did so in order to
secure the Imperial grant of £5,000 and at
the same time to have the advantage
of improved research work in regard
to the development of a flax seed which
it was understood could be developed
and would yield increased production. During
the present year the research work has
been developed on a large scale in Somersetshire out of seed provided by the Research
Department at Lambeg. This is a very important subject and I thought it worth while
detaining the Committee a few minutes while
I shortly explained what had been done.
My hon. Friend (Mr. Coote) decried the
value of forestry. One of the largest and
most important landowners in Northern Ireland informed me that on all the large areas
of land he owned forestry gave
a better
return than if he had attempted to cultivate
the land, so that even on the ground of
practical monetary results forestry on certain
coarse mountain land is a paying proposition. It is for that reason the Government
have thought it right to acquire such large
areas of land, not in one patch, but in various
parts of the country, so far distant as Newcastle in the south to the northern part of
Tyrone in the north, where these trees have
been planted for the use of coming generations.
The Faculty of Agriculture was also
criticised by the Member for Fermanagh and
Tyrone (Mr. Coote), who complained that the
education provided for the students simply
fitted them for going elsewhere to take up
positions. I would remind the hon. Member
that when we require technical lecturers for
the purpose of imparting agricultural information we have got to go to Great Britain
to obtain them, and it is because we feel it is
necessary to develop our own talent and
employ our own people for this work that
assistance is given to this Department. Hon.
Members should not also overlook the fact
that it was on the ground of such necessity
that we were able to claim through the Colwyn
Committee money that would represent the
work done by the Royal College of Science
in Dublin. If it had not been for that we
would not have received the money we now
propose to devote to the University.
With regard to the destruction of weeds,
does my hon. Friend realise that a policeman's education on weeds is necessarily very
limited, and that it requires a
man who
knows something about weeds to endeavour
to deal with that very trying and very difficult problem. It is a matter involving very
material loss to the Province of Northern
Ireland. I have had put into my hands the
different species of weeds, and their
peculiarities, which a policeman would require to know, and they include ragwort,
charlock, docks, etc.
Mr. DONALD : He would require some
training.
Mr. POLLOCK: Exactly. Therefore, I do
not think the training of a policeman is
exactly suitable for the prosecution of
farmers for allowing the development of a
Supply—
Committee.
13 MAY 1924
particular type of weed.
A question was
asked about inspectors in connection with the
flax and potato industry. There are, I think,
eight instructors in the methods of growing
flax, and 17 supervisors are engaged in endeavouring to restrict and eliminate this
awful black scab. I need not impress on hon.
Members the importance of that work, because until we can establish absolute
freedom from the spread of that horrible
scourge our position as exporters of potatoes
to Great Britain is very much prejudiced,
and our potatoes do not realise the prices
they should do there because of the existence
of that blight. The hon. Member for Derry
(Mr. Mark) spoke of the value of lectures and
the interest now taken in them by the
younger members of the farming community.
The results of these lectures have been seen
in every department of agriculture down to
the laying of hens' eggs. I think I have
travelled over most of the ground my hon.
Friends have dealt with, and in view of the
fact that I have no special technical knowledge of the work of this Department, I am
sure they will recognise that I have tried to
do my best.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I be permitted to
say one or two words as to the way the
objections that I raised to this Vote have been
received in the Committee?
re-
The CHAIRMAN: As the hon. Member
knows, I have no right or desire to stop him,
but I think he will appreciate that he has
made his case very fully, and it has been
replied to by the Minister, and to
embark on the discussion might mean the
re-opening of the Estimate. I think I have
allowed him a very wide latitude, and I
would remind him and the Committee that we
have still two Votes to get through.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I will not detain the
Committee long, but I think my attitude has
been misinterpreted. I recognised that the
farming industry was a very important one,
and I emphasised the fact that it was well
provided for. The Educational Department
is well provided for, and I pointed out that
in respect of two heads the claims of education had been dealt with, and that in connection with this particular organisation a
special sum was devoted to education. I cannot see the propriety of that, and the only
interpretation I can put upon it is that it is
done for organisation purposes. Of course,
the right hon. Gentleman has made the plea
that the same thing is done for Trade Unions.
I disagree with that, because what you are
doing in that direction you are doing on
behalf of the community, and not through
the Trade Unions themselves. It is the
community that receives the benefit
but I question whether the
munity will benefit in the case I am referring
to. I must demur to the statement made by
comthe Member for Derry (Mr. Mark), who
seemed to imply that I am antagonistic to
the farmers of the country. I am nothing
of the sort; but he made out a bad case for
them when he pointed out that there was a
time when they did work against the interests of the State by certain nefarious
operations. I hope it did not take £1,000 to
buy their loyalty, as seems to be suggested.
What I have said I have said on the ground
that if it is justifiable to make a grant of
this kind in this case it is equally justifiable
in the case mentioned by the hon. Member for
North Belfast, where the money might be
devoted to educational purposes.
Question put, and agreed to.
The CHAIRMAN: I would remind the
Committee again that we have still two Votes,
and that we have a very short period of time
in which to get them through. I would not
dream of interfering with the discussion in
the slightest, but possibly the next two Votes
may not require such a large amount of

Public Libraries Bill (S.)
Considered in Committee.
I
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
CLAUSES 1 (Power of County Councils to
adopt the Public Libraries Acts), and 2
(Arrangements between certain existing
library authorities and County Councils), ordered to stand part of the Bill.
CLAUSE 3 (New Clause) (Expenses of
County Councils and limit on rate.)
(1) The expenses of a County Council
under the Public Libraries Acts shall be defrayed out of the county fund, and the
amount required shall be raised by means
of the poor rate equally over so much of
the county as comprises the county districts
and towns as respects which the County
Council is for the time being carrying the
Public Libraries Acts into execution.
(2) The amount to be raised as aforesaid
for defraying any such expenses shall not
exceed in any one local financial year a sum
equal to a rate of one penny in the pound
on the rateable value, at the beginning of
that year, of the county districts and towns
Public Libraries Bill-
13 MAY 1924
as respects which the County Council is for
the time being carrying the Public Libraries Acts into execution:
Provided that in an urban district or
town, as respects which the Public Libraries
Acts are being carried into execution by a
County Council, the said limit may, with
the consent of the Ministry, be exceeded to
an extent not exceeding two pence in the
pound.
Brought up and read the First time.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
the Clause be now read a Second time."
Mr. MEGAW: The necessity for any reference to this arises partly from a question of
procedure. The Bill was introduced in
arother place and included originally this

to deal with a Bill that imposes rating, and
the Clause was struck out. Consequently,
though it is placed in the Bill here, still it
has been underlined to show that it was not

It is a Clause that fixes the expenses of
County Councils and the limit on rates. Hon.
Members have had it before them since the
Bill was introduced on its Second reading,
and as it speaks for itself I need not take up

CLAUSES 4 (Transfer of property, rights
