SCHEDULE.
Constitution of County Library Committee.
The County Library Committee shall consist of the following persons :-
-
(a) The chairman and vice-chairman of
the County Council:
(b) Two members of the council (of
whom the chairman shall be one) of each
rural district, as respects which the
County Council are carrying the Public
Libraries Acts into execution;
(c) One member of the council of each
urban district and one commissioner of
each town the council or commissioners of
which have relinquished their powers and
duties under the Public Libraries Acts in
favour of the County Council;
(d) An additional number of members
of the County Council equal to the number of rural and urban districts and
towns as respects which the County Council are carrying the Public Libraries
Acts into execution.
The County Library Committee may
choose in addition to the aforesaid members
further members (not being members of
any local authority in the county), not exceeding in number one for each rural and
urban district and town as respects which
the County Council is carrying the Public
Libraries Acts into execution.
"
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I beg to move in the
Schedule, paragraph (b), to leave out two
("Two members of the council") and insert
"three."
I put down this amendment because I was
of opinion, as I stated on the Second Reading,
that there are not sufficient numbers given
to the rural district councils in the constitution of the County Library Committees according to this Bill. The figures, it seems to
me, have been to a certain extent doubled,
and although the rural district councils have
been given a representation of two members,
in reality they have only been given a representation of one, because it is laid down that
the chairman of the Rural District Council
should be one of those members, and the
chairman of the Rural District Council is, by
virtue of his office a member of the County
Council. Consequently, he could have been
nominated by the County Council on this
committee, quite apart from the fact that it
is suggested or laid down that he should be
nominated by the Rural District Council. It
would appear that the rural district councils
should have a say in this matter of the Library Committee in, at any rate, equal numbers with the County Council; if not, and
this is a debatable question, in preponderating numbers, because a very important duty,
quite apart from the ordinary functions of
the Library Committee lies with those original county councillors and rural district
councillors who form that committee, and
that is the selection of the outside members
provided for in the last Clause of the Schedule. My suggestion that three members
should be selected from the Rural District
Council is, I think, a right and proper one.
Rural district councils, as I pointed out, on
the Second Reading, have been somewhat
overlooked, at least, they have the impression
that they have been overlooked, not only in
this Bill. but in other Measures which have
been before the House. I do not in any way
suggest there should be any mistrust of the
county councils or the county councillors, but
I do think, and I make this suggestion to the
Public Libraries Bill-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mrs. Chichester]
Government, that the rural district councils
should be considered in this matter, that their
wishes and their views should be met, and
that it should be, perhaps, shall I say, a matter of courtesy? without going any deeper
into the question. They are feeling very hurt
and they are very sore, certainly in some districts. I know they feel in County Antrim,
where five out of eight rural district councils
have been working the public libraries, and
have been doing it satisfactorily, that their
powers are being taken from them,
they think somewhat arbitrarily, and are
being transferred to another body. In the
case of the County Council of Antrim it has
shown itself very interested in this particular subject, and has given every
facility for the Carnegie Library scheme.
But the same thing does not apply to the
other County Councils, and those who
sympathise with the Rural District Councils,
and are, like myself, Rural District Councillors, are not quite sure that the
County Councils throughout the Six
Counties will take up the attitude
adopted by the County Councils of
Antrim and Derry. I suggest that we ought
to show to the Rural District Councils, which
feel themselves somewhat aggrieved by this
Bill, some little consideration. We ought to
meet them half-way at any rate. They do
not think they are being given enough representation. I had a letter from the Antrim
Rural District Council enclosing a resolution,
which, I fancy, has been handed in in manuscript, and perhaps may be discussed later on.
They make use of a few sentences here which
I think I might read to the Committee. They
say:-
"It is the considered opinion of the Association that the County Council is already
an overloaded machine, the members having
manifold duties to perform, and they do not
believe the management of the scheme will
be satisfactory unless local interests are
predominantly represented."
I do not wish to say very much more on this
question, but before I sit down I want once
more to put as strongly as I can before the
Government the fact that these District
Councils must be considered more than they
have been in the past. They, perhaps, have
a feeling that they are the House of Commons
and that the County Council is the House of
Lords, and they feel a little jealous and
resent this donation of their privileges to
another body-privileges which they have had
in the past. I suggest that that resentment
can be wiped away and their feelings soothed
over if they are given larger representation on
the County Library Committee. For that
reason I move that three members of the
Rural District Councils should be nominated
instead of two.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Might I just say a word
or two in support of the Amendment proposed by the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester)? The idea is not in any way to
wreck this Bill. We are entirely at one with
the idea of the Bill. We want simply to see
an arrangement made so that it will be carried out smoothly throughout the county.
This would be a very small concession to make
to the Rural District Councils. The Committee cannot close its eyes to the fact that
since the way in which it was intended to
constitute the Committee was made known
no fewer than five Rural District Councils in
Antrim have said that they would withdraw
from the scheme. It is not that they do not
want the library scheme. They do want it,
and are prepared to carry it out, but they
think that the way the Committee is constituted is a slight upon them.
If this Committee passes legislation in such
a way it will not be kindly received in the
country, and in doing so they would be acting, in my opinion, in a very foolish way.
By making a concession such as is proposed
here you would smooth the feelings of the
people, as the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester) has said, and let them see that
you are not trying to slight them in any way.
By adopting this Amendment you would be
doing good work. Remember that these Rural
District Councillors are unpaid men put in
that position and trying to do their best for
the country. They have considerable influence in their different localities, and if they
go round saying that the whole library scheme
is a concoction of the Government, that they
are trying to take the power out of the hands
of the people in every way possible, that it
is for Belfast and Belfast alone, and that the
representatives of Belfast want to have all
the power in their hands it will do the scheme
a great deal of harm. The Parliamentary
Secretary (Mr. Megaw) shakes his head as if
I were talking nonsense. I know what the
Parliamentary Secretary means, but I am
living in the country and I know what the
people are thinking and saying, and I know
what the result will be if you do not yield
something in this respect. It is a mistake
to appoint the Committee in this way, and
I strongly support the Amendment that has
been proposed by the Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester.) If you read the Press you will
see that resolutions are being passed by Rural
District Councils outside County Antrim, and
the burden of their complaint is that the
Government is taking away power from the
Rural District Councils We do not want
that. We want to take the people with us,
and if there is any way we can do that let us
do it and not turn the people against legislation passed in this House. I hope the Government will yield in this small and comparatively unimportant matter. It may be
sentiment, but sentiment has a good deal to
do with the dour Ulsterman, and even if it is
sentiment I think you ought to yield to it.

Mr. McGUFFIN: I intervene only to say
that I still continue my opposition to the
application of this Measure to all the Ministries. I can quite recognize the necessity
of it in this particular case, where a Minister
has been laid aside through serious illness,
and may not be in this House or in attendance at his Ministry for a considerable time.
I recognize that provision of that sort is
necessary under the circumstances, but to
think of applying the Bill to every Ministry,
and to say that where a Minister happens
to be indisposed for a short time his Parliamentary Secretary shall take his position is
oreating a precedent that, I think, will prove
very awkward for us. I recognize the
necessity for the Bill in this particular
instance, but really I think it is absurd to
apply it to all the Ministries, and to say that
where a Minister is absent his Parliamentary
Secretary is to function on his behalf. That
is the only protest I have to make. Otherwise the Bill is acceptable to me.

The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): The details of this
Vote will be found on pages 52 to 58 in the
book of Estimates. Hon. Members will recollect that on the occasion of introducing
the Supplementary Estimates in March last I
drew attention to certain changes in the
form of the Estimates which it has been
desirable to make, so I do not consider it
necessary to refer at any great length to the
changes in form which were made at that
time or the reasons which led to their adoption. It would be sufficient, I think, to
remind hon. Members that the changes we
made in dividing the form of the Estimate
into three sections were in order to show
clearly those expenses which are repayable
by the United Kingdom to the Northern
Ireland Exchequer as compared with those
expenses which are either recoverable or
non-recoverable from public departments in
Northern Ireland, the totals of each of
which are to be found at the foot of the
different sections to which I have referred.
Section 2 deals with those items of expenditure which do not fall either under
those which are recoverable from the United
Kingdom or from those which are chargeable
against Northern Ireland Departments. It
will be seen that on this occasion they
amount to the comparatively small sum of
£1,227.
As regards Section No. 1, hon. Members
will notice that this is expenditure in respect of which the Imperial Government puts us in funds, and the
increase of approximately £65,000 is
due almost entirely to the inclusion
of the large item of £100,000 which is the
estimated amount which will be actually
expended in connection with the new buildings at Stormont during the present
financial year. Hon. Members will regret
that the progress in connection with these
buildings has not been more rapid than it
has been, but there were difficulties in regard to the manner in which the preliminary
work was carried out by the firm of contractors. and the contract has been
cancelled by His Majesty's Office of Works
in London. The work has now been entrusted to a Belfast firm, and I am glad to
say that fairly satisfactory progress is being
made. Under Section 2 hon. Members will
notice that the principal item is dropped
out of the sum which was voted last year-
£26,000-which was principally in connection
with the approach road to Stormont. This
was completed some time ago, and is now in
regular use. There is a small item of £250
under sub-head E, which is a contribution
towards the cost of the electric installation
necessary in connection with the buildings
on
the Stormont property. The Belfast
Corporation is laying a large main out in
that direction, and it was considered in the
interests of economy that we should take
advantage of that in order to equip certain
buildings there with electric light. This
sum of £250 has been fixed as our share
towards the cost of the electric main now
being provided.
Section 3 calls for rather more detailed explanation, and in particular regarding the progress which it is hoped to
make on the various works provided for. 1
have already pointed out in connection with
former Works Estimates that we are
engaged in an abnormal amount of building
construction and renovation work, not only
concerning services for which we are
directly responsible, but also on behalf of
the Imperial Government in the carrying
out of their liabilities under the Government of Ireland Act. The comparatively
large staff which it has been necessary to
recruit for the carrying on of this service
are not provided for on this Estimate, but
are included in the Estimate for the staff of
the Ministry of Finance, which Vote we
propose to take to-morrow.
The main expenditure will be found
under sub-head K-the tabular statements
on page 57 of the Estimates-and it will be
seen that the new works, alterations and
additions amount in the aggregate to a sum
of £138,750. Column 6 of this tabular statement shows the corresponding provision
which was made last year. In the first
place under this heading we have to provide
for a very large programme of work
to meet the requirements of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. In connection with
Barracks for the permanent force a large
scheme is in course of preparation in the
Drawing Office, involving the erection of
new Barracks to replace unsuitable rented
buildings and the renovation on a large
scale of existing Barracks, for which a total
expenditure of not less than £400,000 is
eventually involved. I think it is intended
to proceed almost at once with the erection
of forty new barracks in order to bring
them up to the standard of equipment and
comfort that obtains in England, and when
that is done the payment for this will be
by money advanced from our Consolidated
Fund and repaid by means of a sinking fund.
The first instalment of it is provided for on
page 113 of the Estimates in connection with
the Estimate for the Royal Ulster Constabulary. It will take an annual sum of
£6,215 to extinguish this outlay, and for the
half year, that is the remaining half of this
year, the sum of £3,100 is provided in the
Constabulary Estimate. My reason for referring to it at the present time is to give

attention of the Ministry to one or two

hear that some alteration is going to be
made in regard to improving our police

would draw the attention of the Ministry to
one or two in my own constituency. I want

cannot they have a place for drill, an outlet
at the back of these new buildings-if they
are going to construct them-where the men
can drill at their own convenience. The old
barracks are simply out of date. On the
Antrim Road an improvement has been made
in that direction. The barracks there were
in a most unsanitary state. They have purchased new buildings, and they are most
comfortable. They are more up-to-date.
Another matter is with regard to the new
Labour Exchanges. I want my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Labour also to take
note of the vast increase in the numbers of
unemployed. I would like his attention
drawn to the state of the Y.M.C.A. Branch in
the Mountpottinger district. Over 4,000 people
are signing there and you enter by the back.
There is only a very narrow stairway with
no exit. The building when you get in is
quite suitable, but until we get our new
Exchanges I hope my right hon. Friend will
see to it that there is a better method of
getting into the Y.M.C.A. Exchange even
temporarily. My attention was drawn to
that. I say it is most inconvenient for the
public when such large numbers of people
are going there to sign. There is only a
little narrow stairway into it and no exit.
That is against the regulations. I hope his
attention will be drawn to that matter. With
regard to the new Exchange is it a fact that
they cannot find a foundation where they
have purchased?
Mr. McGUFFIN: I would not be surprised.

Mr. DONALD: It seems an amusing item,
but if we are to be involved in a double expenditure before a suitable foundation is
found-like what has taken place-then this

can remember perfectly well what our new

want the Government to speed up our new

-men being sent from this district to other

hands somewhere. Those who are interested

be a most useful centre for the unemployed
when it is properly constructed.
I deplore the fact that the unemployed list
is increasing, more especially of our ablebodied men. During the last month it has
gone up by 2,000. I am going to stop at that.
It does not come under this Vote. I deplore
that fact. I was going to remind the Government of the fact that they should speed up
even alterations in order to give these people
some employment on these alterations. Even
in our relief schemes there have been a large

I would impress upon the Government the

Another matter arising out of this Vote is
with regard to our new schools. My attention
was drawn to the fact-and I hope my hon.
Friend the Parliamentary Secretary will take
note; I am sorry the Chairman of the Local
Education Committee is not present-that we
have row got our director appointed and the
attention of the Local Education Committee is
naturally directed towards where to place our
new schools. My attention was drawn to
what is practically a new school which was
built not very many years ago, and could
be easily altered to suit the requirements. It
is not in the centre of the City; it is in one
of the districts. What is happening? There
was half an acre of land right behind the
school which could have been extended into
beautiful playgrounds and the school brought
up to our requirements. The land has been
taken quite recently. Now, the foundations of
working-class houses have been cut, and houses
are being built right up behind the school. I
think these are matters worthy of attention,
because there was land that could have been
acquired and saved our Education Authorities
from building an entirely new school in a
district that is growing tremendously. Over
500 houses are under construction right round
this school, and this school is full up. Now it
does appear to me that our Education Authorities should centre their minds on a matter of
that description That school could be enlarged
without building another school in that area.
And here the ground has been taken up quite
recently. I only noticed this week that the
foundations for these houses were being cut.
I refer to Glandore Avenue, a beautiful site
and a healthy district. I know of no better
in the City of Belfast. My attention was
drawn to it. What are the Education Authorities doing? Here is a school that with
little money could be extended to meet the
requirements of the new regulations, and you
find foundations being cut for houses to be
built right up against the school. That is a
matter if it cannot be remedied in that district
is surely worth looking into in some other
district's. I thought it only right to put
these matters before the Government.

Committee.

Under the Government of Ireland Act the
position of those officers who were transferred
to the Northern Ministries was safeguarded by
the Imperial Parliament to the extent that
the Imperial Parliament made itself responsible for the payment of their gratuities,
retiring allowances, and pensions. The
Imperial Parliament recoups itself by deducting the amount required from our residuary share. That arrangement still continues
in force so far as the officers transferred
under the 1920 Act are concerned, but we have
to make provision in our own Estimates for
any retiring gratuities or pensions that may
be payable to those specially appointed
officers, that is to say those members of the
Civil Service whom we have selected and appointed to the different posts which they hold,
or to our newly-recruited staff. Of course,
having regard to their recent appointment,
it is not likely that many of them will be
retiring for some years to come, but still,
should any, by sickness or other cause, retire
or wish to become qualified for pension it is
necessary that we should have a certain sum
of money on hand to meet such gratuity
should it become due.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask the hon.
Gentleman is any limitation observed with
regard to age at the time of selection?
Mr. BARBOUR: I may almost answer that
in the negative-No. We certainly did have
their
ages before us, but in the case of
specially appointed officers who are already
members of the Civil Service they had acquired very considerable pensionable rights
in the Imperial Civil Service. If such men
were appointed in our service and they eventually came to retire the Imperial Government would recognize its liability and responsibility in respect of the pensionable rights
earned while in the Imperial Government
service, and we would only be entitled to pay
such proportion of the pension as was earned
during service in our employment. In the
case of any specially appointed officer who
is appointed by us late in life, hon. Members
will always remember that a new entrant to
the Civil Service has to serve ten years before
he becomes qualified for pension. The existing rules safeguard us pretty well in that
respect. I just wish to remind hon. Members
that the displacement that will take place in
future will mean that this sum for which we
shall have to come to the House will decrease

Mr. POLLOCK: We pay five years, and the
Imperial Government the remainder.

Mr. MEGAW: So far as the Estimate now
before the House is concerned there is little
or nothing which calls for any comment. The
total is slightly less than that for 1923-24, and
this decrease is entirely due to the reduction
in the number of youthful offenders and children for whose maintenance in Reformatory
and Industrial Schools provision is made.
The figures are based to a large extent on the
actual expenditure during 1923-24, which was
as a matter of fact considerably lower than
the amount estimated, owing to the fact that
the numbers of children committed were less
than estimated and did not counterbalance
the number discharged. The decrease in the
number of committals might be regarded
from one point of view as a matter for congratulation, but there is unfortunately ground
for believing that this decrease is due rather
to a natural, though mistaken, leniency on
the part of magistrates than to any decrease
in the number of cases suitable for committal.
As a result there is ground for apprehending
that children who, if they had been
placed in time in a reformatory or
industrial school and subjected to the
excellent discipline and training afforded
in such schools, would probably have made
good in life and become useful citizens,
may turn out quite otherwise. But
very often the magistrates seem to think
that it does harm to give children what is
called the taint of the reformatory. It is
always unpleasant to any person to have
the taint of the reformatory, but it is very
much more important that he should have
the opportunity of undergoing the discipline
that is not always given him at home. The
result has been that the Ministry of Home
Affairs has issued a circular to magistrates
in regard to this very matter, as it is clearly
most desirable in the interests of the children

of the child, and the magistrates have only
two options open to them. One is to punish

school, then the only other option the magistrates have is to send that child to the

a factor that would not tend to lower the
number of children sent to Industrial
Schools. Previously when a child was
brought before the magistrates for nonattendance at school every excuse was taken

fine the parent if the parent is responsible,

if the child is responsible for the nonattendance. I would like to know if that
factor has been taken into consideration by

We are very fond of following English precedents here, and if we would only adopt
the regulations in force across the water in
respect of this matter the financial difficulty
would be easily solved by halving the expense
connected with these institutions between the
Government and the Local Authority. I may
quote this from the Report of the Departmental Committee:
Broadly speaking these regulations provide that each school shall furnish an
estimate of its income from all sources and
of its expenditure. From these estimates
the average cost of maintenance per week
per child is calculated for all the voluntary
schools in England (or Scotland as the case
may be). Half this average cost is paid by
the local authority and the remainder of
the amount required to cover the estimated
approved expenditure on maintenance is
provided from Government funds.
I think that solution could be adopted, and it
would not require conference and discussion
in regard to it. I think it is an obligation
on the Government to make provision under
these circumstances, and I would go so far as

likely to reduce the Prisons Estimate that is

financial difficulty.

ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS.
The Education Act, 1923.
EXPENSES OF EDUCATION AUTHORI-
TIES IN BELFAST AND LONDONDERRY.
1. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the approximate amount of money respectively allocated,
or applied for, by the Education Committees
of Belfast and Londonderry up to date, for
expenses incurred in connection with the
Education Act.
:
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown) The actual expenses incurred by
the Education Authority for the County
Borough of Belfast under the operation of
the Education Act (Northern Ireland), 1923,
in the financial year ended 31st March, 1924,
amounted to £528 6s 11d, towards which the
Ministry has made a payment on account of
£300.
The estimated expenditure of this
Education Authority under the operation of
the Education Act in the current financial
year is £55,700; the Ministry of Education
has undertaken to provide two-thirds of
this amount, or of such smaller sum as may
be properly incurred and disbursed within
that year, but no actual payment has yet
been made by the Ministry in respect of the
current year's expenditure.
The Education Authority for the County
Borough of Londonderry has not yet completed its scheme for carrying out the
provisions of the Education Act within the
area under its control, and no payment has
been made by the Ministry to this Authority
up to the present.
NEW SCHOOLS FOR BELFAST AND
LONDONDERRY.
2. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education, whether he can state the approximate estimated cost in respect of new schools
required for Belfast and Londonderry.
Mr. McKEOWN : With regard to new
school buildings and enlargements and
structural improvement of existing school
buildings as required in case of the Belfast
County Borough, the Education Authority
estimate the total capital expenditure on
this work as not likely to be less than
£500,000, and as possibly reaching as large
a sum as £750,000. These figures must,
however, be taken merely as approximations.
There are not sufficient data available at
present to enable an estimate to be prepared
which could be relied upon to show the
probable expenditure with any close approach
to accuracy.
No estimates have yet been submitted to
the Ministry of Education in regard to the
estimated cost of providing w school
houses which may be required in the Loudonderry County Borough.
SELECTION OF SITES FOR NEW
SCHOOLS.
3. Dr.
MORRISON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can give any assurance
that the boards of management and teachers
in existing schools will not be penalized by
unreasonable selection of sites and attractions offered to children by provided schools.
Mr. McKEOWN: Under Section 8 of the Act
the Education Authority is empowered to provide such schools as may be determined by the
Ministry to be necessary for the education
of all the children residing within the
education area for whose elementary
education sufficient and suitable provision
is not otherwise made. The selection of
suitable sites for the erection of new schools
is, accordingly, a matter for the Education
Authority in the first instance, and the Act
further provides that the Education Authority shall take into account the accommodation available in existing schools.
If by "attractions" the hon. Member
refers to meals, books and scholarships, he
will find that under the Act there is no
discrimination in favour of children attending provided or transferred schools.

The Ministry will endeavour to secure, with
I am sure, the full co-operation of the
Education Authority that possible hardship
to individual managers and teachers shall be
obviated as far as possible.

Mr. MCKEOWN: Certainly.
MEALS FOR NECESSITOUS CHILDREN.
4. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether the cost of meals for
necessitous children is met from the school
rate or from a grant by the Ministry.
Mr. McKEOWN: Expenditure incurred by
an Education Authority under Sections 49
to 52 of the Education Act, 1923, in providing
meals for necessitous school children will
form part of the general expenses of the
Education Authority, which will be defrayed
by the Authority out of the funds available
for that purpose, as specified in Section 73
of the Act.
Under Section 76 of the Act, the Ministry
may make a grant in aid of such expenditure
if it has been properly incurred in accordance
with a scheme previously approved by the
Ministry.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask my hon. Friend
if any money was expended for this purpose
during the past year?
Mr. McKEOWN: We are not aware of any
money having been spent up to the present
time.
SALARIES OF TECHNICAL TEACHERS.
5. Mr. McGUFFIN asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether, in view of the repeated
promises for a speedy announcement of the
scales under which Technical Teachers are
to be paid, and of the fact that this body of
teachers is still kept in suspense upon this
matter, he can now name a date at which this
information will be available.
Mr. McKEOWN: I regret that the Ministry
is not yet in a position to name a definite
date upon which information with regard to
the proposed scales of salaries for Technical
Teachers will be available.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask is the hon.
Gentleman aware that serious discontent
exists amongst the teachers in respect of this
matter, and does he not think it would be
eminently expedient to make some effort to
allay their suspicion and discontent?
Mr MCKEOWN: I am well aware of the
fact, and no one regrets it more than I do.
the
6. Mr. McGUFFIN asked the Parliato
mentary Secretary
Ministry of
Education whether it is a fact that the
scales proposed by the Ministry of Education
for salaries of Technical Teachers have been
materially reduced by the Ministry of Finance, and if so, can he state the amount of

Mr. MCKEOWN : The Ministries of

Mr. McKEOWN: I am not aware of that.
RENT RESTRICTION COMMITTEE
REPORT.
7. Mr. GRANT asked the Minister of Home
Affairs whether he has considered the Report
of the Rent Restriction Committee, and if so
whether he proposes to give legislative effect
to certain of its proposals, and if so, when
he proposes to introduce such legislation.
9. The following question stood on the
Order Paper in the name of Mr. DONALD :
To ask the Minister of Home Affairs whether
he will state the intentions of the Government with regard to the Rent Restrictions
Act; whether it is proposed to introduce a
Bill, as promised, this Session, and if so,
at what date.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw) I propose to answer questions No.
7 and 9, which are about the same matter,
together.
The Report of the Rent Restriction Committee has been carefully considered, and the
preparation of the Bill is well in hands.
Some important points in the draft Bill still
remain to be settled, and it is hoped to
introduce the Bill in the Autumn Session.

GALLANT CONDUCT OF CONSTABLE
F. MORTESHED.
8. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will now consider
the recognition of the services rendered to
the State by Constable Francis Morteshed,
Royal Ulster Constabulary.
Mr. MEGAW: This matter was brought
under notice in the ordinary course on the
conclusion of the criminal proceedings involved, and it has afforded me much pleasure
to approve of the recommendation of the
R.U.C. Reward Board that Constable Francis
Morteshed should be awarded a First Class

referred to.
THE FAIR WAGES CLAUSE.
10. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the Government have
instructed local authorities to continue to
carry out the "Fair Wages Clause" when
placing contracts, and whether the members
of a local authority can be surcharged if
they place contracts with the lowest tender
who may refuse to carry out the "Fair Wages
Clause."
Mr. MEGAW: The instructions issued by
the Local Government Board on the 29th
November, 1911, in regard to the inclusion
of
entered into by local authorities are still in
operation, and, SO far as the Ministry
is aware, these instructions are generally
complied with.
The power of surcharge is of course confined
to payments which have already been made
by a local authority, and does not extend to
directing a local authority to make payments
in the future.
Mr. DONALD: I would like to ask my hon.
Friend if he is aware that the Home Office
was applied to for instructions, and that the
answer given was most indefinite? That is
why I put the question. The answer given
to me to-day is definite.

15 MAY 1924
PRICES OF CLOTHING, &c.
12. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will state the present
prices of clothing, fuel, light, rent, and miscellaneous items, as compared with 1914, in
Northern Ireland.
Mr. GORDON: This matter was considered
by the Departmental Committee on the Cost
of Living of which my hon. Friend was a
member. That Committee reported that the
Imperial Ministry of Labour did not, for the
purpose of the Cost of Living Index Number,
collect in 1914 in Northern Ireland statistics
regarding the average retail prices of clothing, light, fuel, rent and rates, and miscellaneous items; and, owing to the difficulty
of collecting at the present date reliable comparable data for these items in 1914, the Committee was of the opinion, with which I
agree, that it is not possible to supply the
information requested. In accordance with
another recommendation of the Committee,
statistics are at present being collected regarding these items, and a statement will be
published in due course showing the percentage increase or decrease in price over a given
quarterly period.
"CASTLE GUARD" AT HILLSBOROUGH.
13. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether the Government will consider the retention and reorganization of the
historical "Castle Guard" at Hillsborough,
Co. Down.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): So far as I am aware, the Castle
Guard referred to by the hon. and Gallant
Member is a body privately organized and
equipped by the Marquess of Downshire.
There is no intention on the part of the
Government to adopt the course suggested
by the hon. and Gallant Member.
a statement to the House on the question
of the discontinuance of the grant to the
Ulster Agricultural Organization Society.
During the past year the Ministry of Agriculture was in close touch with that organization, and has always been and still is in
entire sympathy with its objects.
The grant of £1,200 which was voted by
this House last year was discontinued, as the
work of the organization of Co-operative
Societies did not appear to require any
further assistance from Government funds.
It was felt, therefore, that the work of supervising the existing Co-operative Societies
should be carried on at the expense of the
Societies themselves.

The FINANCIAL SECRETARY
THE MINISTRY OF FINANCE (Mr.
Barbour): The details of this Estimate will
be found on page 38 and following pages of
the Estimates which hon. Members have in
their hands. It will be observed that for
the first time this Estimate, Sub-head A,
which refers particularly to salaries, wages
and allowances, has been divided up so as
to show the numbers and cost of the staff employed in each of the various divisions and
branches of the Ministry. If hon. Members
will refer to the first paragraph at the head
of this Estimate they will be reminded once
again of the very varied duties carried on
under the heading of the Ministry of
Finance, and the object of dividing the
salaries in the manner I have referred to
is to enable the House to form a better
opinion than could be obtained previously
of the cost involved in administering the
different services carried out by the Department.
Hon. Members will, of course, understand
that an absolutely accurate allocation of
cost cannot be shown having regard to the
fact that none of the branches work in completely watertight compartments, while in
several of them, notably the Establishment
Division, and the Accounts Division, the
staff are engaged to a greater or lesser extent in duties essential to the
functioning of all the other branches. However,
by showing the distribution of the staff in
branches, the Estimate for the current year
is possibly of a more informative nature
than those submitted in previous years. In
proper
glancing roughly over the abstract as shown
on page 38 hon. Members will see that the
estimated cost of salaries, wages and allowances for the present year exceeds the
amount of last year's estimate by £13,520,
of which about £9,000, or two-thirds of the
excess is absorbed by the Works Division
and attributable to Public Works services.
In introducing the Supplementary Estimates
for the Ministry on the 19th March last,
I referred in some detail to the numbers and
cost of the Works Division staff, and explained that a very large proportion of their
activities is devoted to agency work for the
Imperial Government and to the considerable amount of new constructional work in
connection particularly with police, educational and agricultural services, which,
having accumulated through a long period
into a formidable arrear, had to be put in hand
at the earliest possible moment.
The various projects I referred to at that
time are all in progress and involved as 1
say a considerable addition to our staff, and
even work which was undertaken subsequently has involved a very slight increase,
but as will be seen when I come to deal with
the item Appropriations-in-aid the extra
amount to be recovered from the Imperial
Government in respect of the services
rendered by our various officers has increased
over the previous year by £3,159. The other
division in which a fair increase has arisen
is the Accounts Division. Where there is
more work being carried on necessarily
there is more supervision and checking required by the Accounts Division. The
increases in the cost of other divisions, as
will be seen, are all comparatively small
amounts and are mainly due to the ordinary
incremental increases in salary, the establishment of temporary clerks in permanent
posts, and a few minor staff adjustments.
Generally speaking the staffing arrangements of the various divisions have recently
been the subject of close personal investigation, and I am satisfied that the provision
made for the work is no more than is absolutely necessary. The staff, I regret to say,
many directions continue to work
under conditions of undue pressure, and
a considerable amount of attendance
in excess of the normal hours is being cheerfully given without extra remuneration.

Then I come to a new service which will
be found at the head of page 47. It is called
the Statute Law Committee. I am not sure
but the question has already been asked as
to what progress was being made in the
editing of the legislation which has been
passed by this House. On the 10th March
last, by warrant of his Grace the Governor,
this Statute Law Committee was established.
It follows the lines of the Imperial Statute
Law Committee. The members consist of
representatives of the Judicature, of officers
of both Houses of Parliament, of the
Parliamentary Counsel Office and His Majesty's
Stationery Office. The Committee is called
upon to superintend the work of publishing
the Northern Ireland Statutes in annual
volumes and the editing of the Statutory
Rules and Orders in Northern Ireland. It
is hoped that the Statutes for 1921-22 will be
ready very shortly, and the preparation of
the volume of Statutes for 1923 is well in
hand.
I now come to agency services (page 47).
This relates to work that the Departments of
the Imperial Government carry on for us.
The nature of the services which they render

for the collection of entertainment duty,

cost of running the Stationery Office
£16,680. This represents a slight reduction

There is one other matter to which I would
like to refer arising out of a comment that was
made yesterday afternoon in connection with
the agency service which the Ministry of
Finance renders in connection with the
sailors' and soldiers' houses. It was stated
that this work was not being carried out as
expeditiously as it had been, and, further,
allusion was made to the very great difficulty
in obtaining information on this subject.
The question of these sailors' and soldiers'
houses has been alluded to with such
frequency in this House that I should have
thought that hon. Members would thoroughly
understand the position, but, on the other
hand, I can quite understand that this is a
subject in which several of our hon. Members
are so keenly interested that they wish to be
constantly informed up-to-date as to what
progress is being made and what the exact
position is. Therefore, I think it would assist
the Committee if I were to give a little
statement telling exactly what the position
is at the present moment. In the first place,
I would remind the Committee once again
that the sailors' and soldiers' housing is an
Imperial service, and that the officers of our
different Ministries merely act as agents in
carrying out the administration of the
general policy which is laid down by the
Irish Sailors' and Soldiers' Land Trust which
has recently been appointed. This Land
Trust consists of five members, of whom
three were to be appointed by a Secretary of
State, one by the President of the Executive
Council of the Irish Free State, and one by
the Prime Minister of Northern Ireland.
This Trust has been duly established and
came into existence four months ago.
In Northern Ireland the Ministries of
Finance and Home Affairs act as agents for
the Trust in obtaining sites, building the
cottages, collecting rents, etc., but questions
of policy are dealt with by the Land Trust,
whose local representatives are in close
touch with the agent Ministries. The prescribed number of houses allocated
Northern Ireland is 1,046. Of this number
417 have actually been completed, while 248
are now in course of construction. Of these
248, 146 are at Cregagh, Belfast, 57 at Londonderry, 36 at Whiteabbey, 4 at Tandragee, 2
at Downpatrick, 2 at Dungannon and 1 at
Lisnaskea.

Loans Guarantees are a matter of interest

CLASS II. No. 7.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Motion Made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £598,041 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during the
year ending on the 31st March, 1925, in
respect of the Salaries and Expenses of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary, including
Police Women and Temporary Inspectors
of Weights and Measures."-(Note-
£215,000 has been voted on account).
Mr. MEGAW: In introducing the Royal
Ulster Constabulary Estimates for 1924-25,
I would like first of all to bring to the notice
of Members of this House the work done
by the Royal Ulster Constabulary in conjunction with the other sections of the Constabulary in Northern Ireland. I should
like, first of all, to draw the attention of
hon. Members to the very harmonious way
in which the different sections of our Constabulary Forces are working together. When
we took over control of the police things
were not in so satisfactory a condition.
There was then really a great lack of harmony and co-operation between the regular
police and the Special Constabulary. All
this has changed and I am glad to say that
when the Inspector-General, who was then
in command of the Special Constabulary,
took over control of the R.I.C., he brought
about a completely different spirit. The
Royal Ulster Constabulary is largely
recruited from the Special Constabulary.
The figures of recruitment in
Royal Ulster Constabulary are very
eloquent in this respect. The members of the
old R.I.C. and the members of the Special
Constabulary who have been recruited to
the Force are approximately equal, the
advantage being with the members of the
Special Constabulary. The actual figures
are, 1,378 members of the Special Constabulary are now in the Royal Ulster Constabulary, 1,362 members of the old Royal Irish
Constabulary. That has brought about the
happiest results, for just as the R.U.C. and
the Special Constabulary now work together
so has their efficiency increased, and the
rivalry between the various branches of our
police is now a healthy rivalry.
the
Attention has lately been drawn to the
magnificently courageous act of a constable
of the R.U.C.-indeed, it formed the subject
of a Question in the House to-day-in the
arrest of an armed murderer. It was a fine
act and was worthy of all the commendation
received, but I should like to
say
that I think the same courage
that was displayed in a case which has come
it

so largely before the notice of the public
actually exists and is shown by many other

although these acts may not come to such
prominent notice. It has been that courage
and the discipline that exists in the Force
that have brought about the present state of

There is no fundamental difference between the Estimate for the forthcoming year
and that for the last financial year. It has
been found possible to effect some reduction,
and Parliament is only being asked to vote
the sum of £813,041 for this financial year as
against £822,243 in 1923-24. Before going into
the different sub-heads in which the Vote
is taken, it would be well to point out the
substantial reduction which has taken place
in the number of outrages reported and
other branches of crime. This is due to a
large extent to the magnificent manner in
which the Royal Ulster Constabulary have
carried out their duties.
In the year 1922, there were 4,502 outrages
reported in Northern Ireland, and this figure
decreased in the year 1923 to 1,330.
Indictable Offences.-In 1922 there
5,103, and last year approximately 1,412.
were
than
In
Firearms Prosecutions.-Firearms prosecutions really indicate perhaps more
anything else the state of the country.
1922 there were 352 prosecutions, 247 convictions, and 105 dismissals, in 1923 the
number of prosecutions sank to 159, and there
were 123 convictions and only 36 dismissals.
Civil Authorities Cases.-In civil authorities cases, exclusive of curfew cases, in 1922,
there were 73 prosecutions, 35 convictions
and 38 dismissals. Last year there were
only 16 prosecutions, with 15 convictions and
1 dismissal.
Malicious Injury Cases.-In 1922 in the
City of Belfast, there were 1,152 malicious
injuries and last year 84. In the counties
in 1922 there were 393 and last year 104.
With regard to persons receiving protection, in 1922 there were 54 persons receiving
constant police protection, and 27 persons
receiving protection by patrols. Last year
there were 17 of each. These figures show
the great change that has taken place in the
state of the country, and it will be seen there
is practically a return to normal times.

With regard to recruiting for the police,
the total numbers of the Royal Ulster Constabulary are now in their last hundred,
that is they are over 2,900 out of a normal
force of 3,000. Recruiting has gone on
steadily, and at the present day there
are 2,907 men in the force.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask the hon and
learned Gentleman if the arrangement for
their segregation according to religion has
been observed in the proportions laid down?
Mr. MEGAW: I am not sure that I can go
into that at the moment. There was a report made by the Committee, I know, about
the segregation of the Force according to
religion. Of course we have endeavoured to
carry out that recommendation as far as
possible, but it was impossible to do so
entirely by reason of the lack of recruits
from one section. As I have said, the number
that is in the Force is very largely made up
of recruits from the old Royal Irish Constabulary, of whom we have over 1,300, and
from the Special Constabulary, who number
a few more. The training of the new recruits
goes on in the Newtownards Camp and is
very successful indeed. The quality of the
recruits is very good, their training is very
fine, and I think anyone who pays a visit
to that camp will see that a very great state
of efficiency is reached before the recruit
is sent out to do ordinary duty. Of course
at the beginning we had to use the police
without the same training as they are getting
now. When the Royal Irish Constabulary
were dissolved we just had to improvise a
Force and use the best material we could get.
It proved very good indeed, but it had not
perhaps the same training in actual police
duties as one naturally would have desired.
With regard to the pay of the Police Force,
that is still at the rates laid down in the
Constabulary Act of Northern Ireland and
the R.U.C. Pay Order dated November 6,
1922. In our present Estimates we have
estimated for the full strength of the Force
-that is 3,000--and it is hoped that within
a few months the Force will be up to that
strength. The increase in the amount shown
here is mainly due to the ordinary increments, and partially to the increase in the
number of sergeants. Fifteen sergeants are
used in connection with the Customs patrols
along the Border. During the past year the
Customs duties that are levied on the
Border required continuous patrols, and
fifteen sergeants are employed on that duty.
Our Government receives a refund in respect
of the services of those fifteen sergeants,

Some changes have been brought in with

Allowances Order dated November 6, 1922.
Hon. Members will notice that a sum of
only £500 has been inserted for Separation
Allowance for officers and men during the
present financial year. This is due to a reversion to the old system, whereby men who
may be transferred by order of their authori
ties may receive separation allowance for a
period of two months, but no longer. During
the past two years while the Force was in
formation and changes were frequent, it was
not considered desirable or safe for men
stationed in certain districts to have their
families in the vicinity, and it was thought
proper that they should, personally, live in
barracks and not with their families. Hence
it was necessary to pay the allowance for a
prolonged period. However, the time has
now come when we can revert to normal,
as I have just stated. Under sub-head C
hon. Members will find the Subsistence
Allowances. The amount inserted under
this sub-head last year was found inadequate,
and it is anticipated that the sum now
estimated will be nearer the amount required.
Sub-head E deals with clothing. Aproximately we have 100 men still to be equipped
on joining the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
We are now contemplating the establishment.
of a clothing store, and it will be necessary

ensuing year. This results in rather a larger
estimate than should ordinarily fall upon
one year, but the establishment requires that

and the report has been received. The condition of the barracks is very largely a heritage from the Imperial Government, but the

responsible, and careful investigation has now
been made of every R.U.C. barracks through-

That is, the free quota for the
out the Six Counties. As a result of that
investigation the Government have decided to
abolish twenty-three existing barracks
being totally unfit for habitation or unnecessary, to build eighteen new barracks, in lieu,
in areas where barracks had not previously
existed, to replace seventy-three existing barracks by new barracks, and to reconstruct or
renovate a further 103 existing barracks.
The cost of this scheme was estimated by our
technical adviser at £400,000, and as the
Government could not see their way to secure
this large sum from current revenue, it is
their intention to raise the money by a system of short period loans. The amount which
it was proposed to expend annually is in the
neighbourhood of £100,000. We hope to get
the work done as quickly as possible, because
it is of great importance to such a fine body
of police that they should be suitably housed.
The scheme has a twofold advantage, in that
it provides for the better accommodation of
the police, a very necessary and desirable
achievement, and also will have the result, it
is hoped, of affording considerable relief to
existing unemployment. For the current
financial year it is proposed to deal with forty
barracks-that is, the reconstruction of
twenty and the initial building of twenty.
These include the Border areas. I may add
that in case of undue difficulty being encountered in securing sites for the twenty
new barracks, the Government may find it
necessary to ask the House for compulsory
powers to acquire such sites as may be considered necessary and suitable by the police
authorities.

a special patrol was put on in order to secure

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig) :
I came down to the House this afternoon
without any knowledge that this question
would crop up, because I had hoped that the
Nixon incident was closed. However, in response to the appeal of the hon. Member (Mr.
McGuffin), whom I see returning to his seat,
and the hon. Member (Mr. Grant), who has
just sat down, I am quite prepared to give
the Committee and those outside who are so
actively interesting themselves in this matter
my opinion of the whole subject, and also to
give the final and concluding decision on the
part of my colleagues and myself with regard
to it. First of all, may I say that I think
my two hon. Friends have put the case very
calmly and very clearly, and I admire them
for the way they have stuck up for their
friend who is in difficulties. I think it is the
Ulster character that causes one to help a
friend who has, either on his own initiative
or through bad advice and ill-advised friends,
got himself into a position of great difficulty.
They have carried out their duty very well
this afternoon, and I hope it will be possible
for me to respond to them with equal calmness and to review the position as I see it.
Now, first of all I do hope that hon. Members will acquit any of us of having the
slightest feeling of vindictiveness towards Mr.
Nixon. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Why,
to whose interests is it to have in the R.U.C.
men of integrity, men who can be relied on,
and men who have a sense of obedience to the
orders that come from the Government? To
whose interest is it? First of all, does not
the Inspector-General of our fine Force want
to get the very best, most loyal, and responsible men around him in order to carry out
his arduous duties? Secondly, is it not the
duty of the Home Office to have in our splendid Force the very best that Ulster can produce? And thirdly, the Government and
myself look in all directions expecting to get
the best men in order to uphold the honour
of our new R.U.C. To suggest, therefore, for
a moment that any one of us is actuated by
feelings of a vindictive character towards any
officer in the Force is perfectly ridiculous.
Our whole and sole idea is that the Force
which costs the people of Ulster £813,000 a
year-a very costly item-should be the best
that can be obtained for the money-permeated from top to bottom with that discipline
which is absolutely essential to make any
Therefore, we must get the best for our
money. I can easily picture the Committee
assembling on an occasion of this sort and
finding fault with the Government from the
highest to the lowest because of some unfortunate happening in the Force at a later date
-for instance, that discipline had got lax and
things had become careless. I can picture a
debate in this Committee, in which my
friends and myself are pilloried for allowing
discipline in its Police Force to get low down,
for allowing people to get into the Force who
are not the proper custodians of the honour
of the Force and of the great responsibilities
which Ulster placed upon its shoulders.
Therefore with us as a Government, so long
as we are a Government, this holds true. We
must from start to finish, from top to bottom,
rely upon a Force which will not only equal
but surpass the traditions of the old R.I.C.
When discussing this question, do let us, if
we can, dissociate ourselves from personality,
let us even dissociate ourselves from friendship, because it should not arise where either
a military or constabulary force is concerned.
My hon. Friend (Mr. McGuffin) tried to
draw an analogy between some teachers and
the case in point. It is impossible to get an
analogy to a Force like this. What do we get
down to? First of all, a great deal of this
trouble has arisen from the fact that Mr.
Nixon was an Orangeman. Many of us in
this Committee are Orangemen, and we treasure the reputation of that loyal Institution
as much as anyone outside this Committee
What a splendid thing it was for us as a
Government to be able to say to those who
belong to the R.U.C.-" You need not any
longer stay outside the ranks of the Lyal
Orange Institution. You can come in. You
can have your own lodges." But when you
give a great privilege like that, it is up to
every man to honour it, and to see that no
discredit falls upon it, because it is always
the case that the majority suffer for the indiscretions of the minority. You find, however,
that privilege after privilege is taken advantage of by ill-advised persons, with the result
that the privilege has to be withdrawn. The
Ulster Government do not desire to withdraw
from either the members of the R.U.C. or the
Specials the privilege of being Orangemen
and having their own Orange Lodges, but it
can only be done if there is strict adhesion
to the orders issued from the Inspector-General's Department, and it can only be done by
each and all those members, like ourselves,
obeying the laws and ordinances of the Institution on the one hand, and of the R.U.C. on
the other hand.

[The Prime Minister]
And may I say how very unfortunate it is
that this has taken place at a time when we
are particularly anxious that we should have
no friction and no difficulties?
How very
unfortunate it also is that the case has
occurred with a member of the old R.I.C. and
our own R.U.C., an old member who knows
the old Regulations from A to Z. If he did
not, he could not have risen to the position
which he attained. He must have known of
the existence of this Rule, which is one of
the guiding rules of the old R.I.C. No. 6 of
the Code reads:-
"As the character and efficiency of the
Royal Irish Constabulary would be seriously injured even by a suspicion of
partizanship, the expression or manifestation of political or sectarian opinions on
the part of any member of the Force is
strictly forbidden."
That is a very old and a very proper Rule
in the Code, and superimposed upon that was
the direct order which was issued not as some
people think by the Inspector-General alone,
but after, I think, it was considered and
thought out by the Home Office and by the
Government itself-an order to prevent a
disaster of this kind occurring, and it was
disobeyed within a very few days. What are
we to expect if these specific orders are immediately disobyed? Why, at a critical
moment, we might find that the morale of
the Force had gone down, and that some
other instructions that were issued had been
equally disobeyed. You would say, "You
passed that one over, why not pass over this
one? Gradually, our Force instead of being
the magnificent Force it is, would become of
no value.
""

There is the Grand Master of County Down

says "yes" there is an acknowledgment that
he had been drinking. If he says "no," it
implies he is still drinking. It was not a fair
explanation if it was absolutely necessary to
say "yes" or "no," and Mr. Nixon was not
allowed to make an ordinary explanation.
I would like to draw the Prime Minister's
attention to that, before he absolutely decides
that there is no case for Mr. Nixon at all,
because I take it, it was the fault of the
Government. There are three faults against
the Government and one indiscretion against
Mr. Nixon. That he allowed the publication
of his speech is accounted for by the fact that
he was not in Belfast and knew nothing about
the publication of the speech and the photograph until he returned too late to stop it.
So I am told.
Question put, "That Sub-head A, Item 1.
be reduced by £500."

Colonel WOODS: If I am in order now, 1
want to draw attention to compare the Headquarters' Staff of the R.U.C. with the Headquarters' Staff of the old R.I.C. in Dublin
Castle. Dublin Castle Headquarters' Staff
consisted of five officers, who administered
11.000 men, over 32 counties. The R.U.C.
Headquarters' Staff consists of 10 officers, who
administer less than 3,000 men
six counties. I do not know whether there
is an increase of efficiency equal to the
proportion shown by the figures. I hope so.
Taking the Force as a whole, it works out
roughly that every policeman on the street
costs the taxpayer £300. He is pretty costly,
ornamental but very expensive. Of
that is not what the men get. They get little
more than half, less than two-thirds, in their
pay. The rest goes in administration, which
is excessive. We have nine County Inspectors, and really they only administer five
counties, because I understand County Derry
has not got a County Inspector at all. The
Commissioner of Londonderry receives an
extra allowance for doing the job of the
County Inspector.

manders of the R.U.C. are not getting
chance. They are being interfered with by

to carry on and get the best out of the Force.
If you turn the Police Force into a political

point of disobedience.
to the
Another point that I wish to bring forward
is that this expensive Force has not added
much to the joy of life of the Ulster people,
especially after Curfew. The Curfew restrictions have now been in force for four years.
We are told how peaceful things are. We are
told of the decrease in crime, and the reduction in the number of police cases. A few
days ago in Portadown we had a prosecution
against people who were holding a prayermeeting and were curfewed. I think the hon.
Member for Portadown was not there; I am
not sure. If he had I am sure he would have
got them home peacefully. People in this
Committee and officials know they can always
get a permit that will enable them to get
home. If they have not got a permit it is
their own fault, it is due to their own laziness, but the people cannot do that. I went
down one night to the headquarters in
Chichester Street, and at twenty minutes to
twelve I asked for a permit to enable a friend
of mine to get home to Bangor in his car.
There was no officer there, or I am sure I
would have had no difficulty. The sergeant
in charge said "No." and he said it in such
a way that it was almost insulting. After
some trouble I did get it-I got it from a
head-constable-but it was only because I was
a Member of Parliament that I was able to
get it. I do not think that is fair. I know
that a few minutes after I had gone another
gentleman went into the office to get a permit. His son had been injured and had been
taken to the Royal Victoria Hospital. This
gentleman asked for a permit to enable him
to go to the hospital and to get home again
after twelve o'clock, but his request was not
complied with. That is an undue annoyance
and is hardly fair to the law-abiding citizens
of Belfast who are subscribing £300 per man
to keep up a sort of Prussian guard.
I would ask the Home Office to take into
consideration the feelings of the ordinary
people who cannot get permits. I think
there should be more men employed on
night duty. They have plenty of men to
do it. They have more men than they had
in the old R.I.C. There was a statement
made about the clothing by the hon. and
learned Gentleman (Mr. Megaw). I believe
that this clothing is not produced under
trade union rates, and that it emanates
from one of the industrial homes. You will
find that is the case if you make a few
inquiries. I think that is how it happens.
I appeal to the Minister of Home Affairs
to have Curfew removed before the country
is ruined. The tourist season is now on.
Who is coming to Belfast and the seaside
towns in Ulster when they hear Curfew is
on? They do not want to see policemen in
the streets with revolvers. They will say:
"What kind of a country have we come to?
You will get shot, or if you are not shot
you will be arrested after twelve o'clock."

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

to ventilate it. I give our new Constabulary
Force every credit for doing their duty faithfully and well. I had occasion to draw the
attention of the Inspector-General to the
actions of some of our young, inexperienced
constables who want to overstep their duty
and, unfortunately, in doing so they are making
enemies of their best friends. One has only
to take a walk up the Newtownards Road.
On two occasions my attention was drawn to
them by a deputation. Two men were standing
at the head of Dee Street waiting on a friend
to go to a football match. They were on the
footpath and a constable came up and used
language which was certainly not becoming.
Somehow or other some of the younger men
have not got a right idea of what their real
duties are. It would be a pleasure to some
of them if they would just take a trip to
London and walk round casually and speak to
the London policemen. They are civil and
courteous-the London policemen above all
others--and will go out of their way to help
the public in every respect. I would like to
see our men carry out their duties in a more
diplomatic manner. A third man came up, a
very respectable citizen, a man who worked
with me for years, and when he came up the
two other men were arguing the point with the
constable as to their right to stand on the
footpath. The constable used some language
not becoming to a member of the Force. The
third man very wisely took the two other men
by the shoulders and he said, "Let us go on
to the match. We will see more about this."
They reported the thing to me. It may be a
little thing, but it is a great matter that our
officers should carefully instruct these young
men in the exercise of their duty. I will tell
you why. Let any man take a walk up some
of the main thoroughfares when some of the
people have got a little intoxicated. In a
very busy thoroughfare it takes a man to be
very wise to handle people who are not
altogether too---

own men in training to put into this particular
service. I am afraid something that has
transpired since, makes it very likely that a
larger number will be required, because the
Board of Trade regulations are very strict
and not very easy to be applied, and it is
difficult to get our men into a state of training that will enable them to obtain the
certificate necessary for their operations as
inspectors of weights and measures.
With regard to barracks, the barracks that
we propose to have refitted or reconstituted
are situated throughout the country, because
those returned to us as being the worst cases
are being treated first. There is also some
difficulty in places where a site can be obtained.
There is difficulty in obtaining a site at a
reasonable figure. There is no particular part
of the country that is being preferred to any
other part. The matter is really being determined by the condition of the barracks in
different parts.
Mr. DUFF Might I rise to a point of

Mr. DONALD: We can talk in the dark.

Oral Answers to Questions
EX-SOLDIERS' COTTAGES--LISBELLAW
AND BALLINAMALLARD.
1. Mr. DUFF (for Mr. COOPER) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs if he is aware that
no ex-soldiers' cottages have been built in
either Lisbellaw or Ballinamallard, Co. Fermanagh, although there are many applicants
from both villages, and whether he can see
his way to allocate a few of these cottages to
each village.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw): The question of the allocation of
cottages to localities is a matter for the Irish
Land Trust. I understand that the Northern
Ireland share of the cottages to be erected
has practically been allocated, and the question of the allocation of the few remaining is
at present under the consideration of the
Trust.
I will see that the hon. Member's representations are placed before the Trust.
TULLYVAGHY NATIONAL SCHOOL.
COUNTY FERMANAGH,
2. Mr. DUFF (for Mr. COOPER) asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education if he is aware that there are no
pupils from Northern Ireland attending
Tullyvaghy National School, in the Pettigo-
Belleek area, and if the Northern Government pays the teacher of this school, which is
maintained altogether for the use of Free
State children, and whether he proposes to
abolish this school.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): Tullyvagey National School,
County Fermanagh, is situated in the territory of Northern Ireland, less than 100 yards
from the boundary, and there are at present.
so far as is known to the Ministry, no pupils
in attendance who reside in Northern Ireland.
The average attendance has recently declined,
and is now less than 10 pupils.
The question of withdrawing grants from
the school has been considered from time to
time, and is now being discussed with the
manager.

I understand that an appreciable number of
children whose parents reside in Northern
Ireland continue to attend the schools in the

SPEED LIMIT FOR MOTOR VEHICLES.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether there is now imposed
in the Six Counties a speed limit for motor
vehicles, and, if so, will he give reasonable
publication of such regulations?
Mr. MEGAW-The limits of speed fixed by
law will be found in Sections 1 and 9 of the
Motor Car Act, 1903, and as regards heavy
motor cars in the Motor Car (Ireland) Order,
1905.
I have no reason to believe that motorists
generally are not aware of these speed limits,
or that further publication is required.
Major SHILLINGTON: May I ask the
hon. and learned Gentleman if he is aware
that during the past few weeks large numbers
of prosecutions have been instituted against
motorists who were travelling at a rate of
20 or 23 miles in country districts in which
there is practically no traffic?
Colonel WOODS: Is the Parliamentary
Secretary aware that there are police traps
laid just outside the city, and that the police
have been successful in prosecuting a number of trade motorists who are trying to show
their cars, and must of necessity travel at
the rate of over 20 miles an hour?
Mr. MEGAW: I am not aware of these
matters personally, but of course if the
persons concerned transgress the law I do not
see that the Ministry of Home Affairs can
interfere
THE PRISON SHIP ARGENTA.
4. Colonel WOODS asked the Prime
Minister whether he could state the decision
now taken by the Government as to the disposal of the prison ship Argenta?
Mr. MEGAW: The s.s. Argenta is at
present berthed at Belfast in charge of a
watchman. The Government have under
consideration the question of her ultimate
disposal, but they consider it would be prenature to make any statement on the subject
at present.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask is the Cabinet
going to use it during the summer?
Mr. DUFF: Would it not be possible to fit

LETTING OF CONSTABULARY DRILL
HALLS.
5. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will consider the
advisability of letting or hiring the Constabulary Drill Halls to Badminton Clubs, when
these halls are not required for drill purposes, and thus reducing expense.
Mr. MEGAW: The suggestion made by the
hon, and gallant Member has been considered,
but it would not be practicable or desirable
to make any arrangement of the nature indicated.
EQUIPMENT WORN BY POLICE
CONSTABLES.
6. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will consider the
modification of the equipment worn by police
constables on duty, which is at present about
14lbs. weight, and is without adequate support.
Mr. MEGAW: The weight of the usual
articles of equipment worn at the belt is 3lbs.
12ozs. (baton, baton case, handcuffs, and handcuff case). If revolver, holster, ammunition
pouch, and ammunition be added the total
weight is 8lbs. 12ozs.
The belt is supported by hooks and the
equipment is identical with that of the Royal
Irish Constabulary.
This equipment has proved quite satisfactory, and no complaints in regard to it
have been received from members of the Force.
It is not considered necessary or advisable
to make any alteration in the existing arrangements in this respect.
Colonel WOODS: Is the hon. and learned
Gentleman aware that the total weight is a
great deal more than 8 lbs., taking the
revolver, the pouch containing ammunition,
the belt and handcuffs? Is he aware that I
have had many complaints about the drag on
the two hooks which are only sewn on to the
tunic, with the result that the men
rendered very uncomfortable on a warm day?
The men should get some consideration.
