THE BOUNDARY QUESTION.
Statement by Prime Minister.
Motion made, and Question proposed: "That
this House do now adjourn." (Mr. Burn.)
The PRIME MINISTER (who was received
with general cheers): Parliament meets once
again faced with a grave crisis, brought about
as was the case in India, in Egypt, and in
1205 The Boundary Question-
Prime Minister's Statement. 1206
7 OCTOBER 1924
the
Southern Ireland by, in the first instance,
the adoption of a policy of surrender. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) And I would like
to ask are the peoples of those two great
countries, India and Egypt, and are
people in Southern Ireland better governed,
happier, more content or more prosperous
than in the good old times before the first
step towards surrender was taken? But
people may say that we are not faced with
a great crisis; that Mr. Lloyd George settled
the Irish question when he entered into that
midnight Treaty with the representatives of
Southern Ireland in 1921. At that time caps
were in the air, the church bells were ringing, there were cheers throughout the whole
country, and the telegraph wires were
blocked with messages of congratulation upon
the settlement of the Irish question for all
time. We here in Ulster were loth to participate in those ebullitions and displays of
rejoicing and our feelings at that time have
been fully justified. I say solemnly that as
dangerous a condition of affairs now confronts
us as at any time in the whole history of
our country.
I have no desire to weary the House by
going back over the various stages that have
brought us to the present situation, but I
would like to point out that the Treaty with
Southern Ireland was carried out not only
without the consent of Ulster, but against the
distinct, written promise of Mr. Lloyd George
that it would not be done. That is my first
point. Secondly, Treaties are both unconstitutional and undemocratic when they are
carried out between two parties affecting a
third without the consent, authority, or
knowledge of the third party. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Parliament being the
supreme authority, it is, in my opinion,
absolutely unconstitutional to enter into a
Treaty of that kind and then to go to the
House of Commons and hold a pistol at its
head and say, "Unless you pass this Treaty,
unless you pass it without altering one word,
one line, one comma, the whole Treaty
must go by the board, and it cannot be
carried out." The present British Government, in face of the storm that arose over
the Treaty of 1921, took steps to bring in
a new Treaty once more against the wishes
of the inhabitants of Ulster, and without
our knowledge or consent. If this is to
continue there will be no safety for Ulster
in the future. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
If the Boundary Commission were to sit,
and if when it sits it were to grant to the
Free State less territory than it hoped for
and expected, what is to prevent the Free
State applying the screw once more on the
British Government, or any British Government by entering such protests that
it might be forced into another Treaty
and take away from Ulster so much of her
territory that the Northern Government
would find it impossible to carry on, and
the Northern Parliament would be nothing
but a laughing stock. We might waken up
some morning to find that once more the
British Parliament had a pistol at its head,
and had entered into a fresh Treaty which
must go through without the alteration of
a line, a word, or a comma.
manner of dealing with the
Ulster we say Stop."
Hear, hear.) We say emphatically that it
must stop, and it must stop now. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)

Against this
territory of
(Hon. Members:
Your recollection in this House will be
that your Government refused to appoint a
Commissoner in the first instance. The
firm belief held by us was that by
so acting Article XII of the Treaty could
not become operative, and in that belief we
were abundantly supported by the decision
given by the Judicial Committee of the
Privy Council. When debating Article XII,
the then British Government said that not a
word, not a line, not a comma could be altered
without breaking the whole Treaty. The
present Government have adopted the very
plan that was so, unfortunately, carried out
by their predecessors, but by doing so, in
my opinion, they have actually broken the
original Treaty, around which they wrapped
so much honour in favour of the Free State.
When they decided to introduce a new Bill
it was open to them to meet the wishes of
Ulster by defining the functions of the Commission in accordance with the desires, the
wishes, and the expressed intentions of the.
British signatories of the Treaty, but they
had not done so.
Now an entirely new situation has arisen.
I can scarcely emphasise that sufficiently.
An entirely new situation has arisen. Protest meetings have been held throughout
Ulster culminating in that magnificent demonstration in the Ulster Hall presided over
by our esteemed Lord Mayor. Our Imperial
Members of Parliament fought our battles in
the House of Commons at Westminster with
skill, with valour, and with effectiveness.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I have myself
over and over again impressed upon those in
the highest places the grave danger of proceeding with a compulsory Commission. All
this has been in vain.
Well then, to meet the situation, a Government faced as we are with such an issue is
bound to have a fixed and determined policy
for the people, and that policy should represent the wishes and the desires of the
people, and should be carried out to its
logical conclusion. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I am sure the House will accept my
apology for reading out important matters.
so much depends upon every word that is
said. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) If this
new compulsory Boundary Commission is
persisted in and the finding is such that it
is acceptable to the Parliament of Northern
1207 The Boundary Question--
Prime Minister's Statement. 1208
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister]
Ireland as representing the people then I
say, "Well and good." On the other hand,
no matter whom the British Government
may nominate as the third member, if the
decision is such as cannot be accepted by the
Parliament of Northern Ireland I for my
part will not hesitate for a moment, if no
other honourable way out is open, to decline
to be responsible for carrying on the Government. I would then resign and place myself
at the disposal of the people, no longer as
Prime Minister but as their chosen leader,
to defend any territory which we may consider has been unfairly transferred from
under Ulster, Great Britain, and the flag of
our Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
That will be my duty, and that duty will
be faithfully performed (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear)--and that is the policy of a
unanimous Cabinet. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
-
It is frequently urged upon me that our
difficulties in this, as in all other matters,
would be entirely removed if I were to make
a gesture. Too many people in the South of
Ireland would expect that gesture to be the
hauling down of the Union Jack and the
hoisting of the white flag. To that sort of
gesture I refuse to be any party (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear)-and I refuse
further to be any party to a hypocritical gesture of any kind which might
possibly convey to the British Government
and to Southern Ireland that there was a
prospect of Ulster going in under a Dublin
Parliament. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I wish to be honest in my gestures, and
certainly never so long as I hold the position
that I do will I hold out-and I gravely
doubt whether in my lifetime it will be
possible to do so-the slightest hope that
Ulster will ever change her ideas about
passing under a Free State Government in
Dublin. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) But
that does not mean that if the South will
settle down Ulster will withhold from her
every good wish and desire that she should
be prosperous, happy, and contented. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) By no means. Peace
to the South is just as essential as peace to
the North in order to get over the aftermath of the Great War and the internal
troubles affecting the country.
So far what I have said in the main may
be taken and understood as somewhat uncompromising. I intend that it should be
so. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Do those
who are urging upon us the surrender of
further territory realize all that is implied?
Can they visualize the effect in the Colonies
of any other policy than that which I have
suggested? Can they picture
the agony
through which we have passed ourselves,
our efforts, fortunately crowned with such
+
success that we now have a compact area,
peaceful, contented, and certainly as prosperous as any other part of the great
Empire? Do they for a moment contemplate
where this coercive Measure may lead? Who
is at the bottom of it all? I have asked it
before. I ask it again. Who is at the
bottom of it all? Who would wantonly
throw us back to 1914 or 1922 and disturb
to their depths the passions of the people,
who rightly resent this abrogation of their
privileges under the Act of 1920? May I
ask have we failed in our duties that we deserve to be dismembered, degraded, and
punished? Have we or have we not faithfully kept the solemn charge of His Majesty
at the opening of our new Parliament when
he used these words:-
"I am confident that the important
matters entrusted to the control and
guidance of the Northern Parliament will
be managed with wisdom and with moderation, with fairness and due regard to
every faith and interest, and with no
abatement of that patriotic devotion to the
Empire which you proved so gallantly in
the Great War. . . . . I feel no misgiving
as to the spirit in which you who stand
hero to-day will carry out the all-important functions entrusted to your care."
If we had been false to the trust so
graciously placed in us by misgoverning our
area then I could understand the desire of
even moderate men, reasonable people, to readjust the situation. But it is a monstrous
proposition that territory deliberately
handed over to our jurisdiction should be
filched away at the bidding of those who
have repudiated the Act of 1920 and who
appear to me to be drifting farther and
farther away from the ideals which are the
foundation of our faith and the faith of
those of our forefathers who helped to build
the British Empire. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
In this hour of our trial I earnestly
appeal to all good citizens from this day
forth to maintain peace, to stand fast by
one another, to rally round the Government
of Northern Ireland as by law established,
to give it no unstinted support, but to
throw all the power and weight that each
individual possesses into strengthening its
hands so that we may lead you and them
through one of the most anxious and critical moments in the history of our distracted
country. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Sir ROBERT LYNN: I simply rise to say
in a few words how thoroughly I agree, as
I am sure the whole House agree, with the
statement that has just been made by the
Prime Minister. He ended his statement
with an eloquent appeal which I am sure
will be responded to as wholeheartedly by

serious consequences for the country.
the people of Ulster as other appeals made
so eloquently by him, because whatever
minor differences we may have in this House
or in this Province, in this crisis in which
we find ourselves to-day there are no
differences whatever. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Ulster stands more firmly indeed
than she ever stood. The Prime Minister

I was glad to hear him refer to gestures.

Mr. COOTE: I should like to contribute
something to this discussion, lest there
should be any misunderstanding on the part
of any person as to the attitude every section
of this House is taking up on this most important question of the liberties of Ulster.
I want to congratulate the Prime Minister
upon the calm, dignified, and earnest
statement which he has given to us. Of
course it is not the time for any gesture of
any sort. It is the time for stating the
facts in the old Ulster fashion, and sticking
to the truth as you believe it, and being
ready to die for it. That is the position of
Ulster to-day, and it is the position of the
most important man in the whole economic
life of Ulster to-day-the Prime Minister.
I want to assure the Prime Minister, if I
may, that every man in Ulster, and every
woman in Ulster, everyone who loves civil
and religious freedom, and everyone who
wishes well to Ireland-North and Southis behind him in the strong, manly statement he has made to-day; and, please God,
we will do all we can to see him through in
the policy he has laid down.
But there are some points which it is
probably well that we should review, and
the first is that the Ulster people are insulted by this series of log-rolling and of
trickery which is being carried on by various
sections of British politicians. We have
been insulted by the Conservative Party, we
have been insulted by the Liberal Party,
and now we are being insulted by the
Socialist Party, who are attempting to coerce the most democratic community of the
whole United Kingdom, the Six Counties of
Ulster. You may search through every
ramification of the Empire and you cannot
find a more democratic people than those
here in Ulster, a people who wish to play
the game,
a people who accepted these
counties very reluctantly, a people who had
to give over about 300,000 Loyalists in the
three Provinces-in the Twenty-six Counties
--and about 35,000 Loyalists in the three
counties of Ulster. We did so
very reluctantly, in order that we should have
some place where we might cease from this
turmoil of eternal hate, of eternal bickering, and eternal war, where we might settle
down with our families and work out something like peace, and liberty, and settled
government. We have settled this under a
tremendous strain, and we have honoured
the Act of 1920-we have honoured its
financial resolutions, we have met the
British Treasury, we have contributed cur
quota to the expenses of the war and to the
upkeep of the nation. Side by side with
this there are the Twenty-six Counties which
are being "coddled" by successive Ministries. They are rebels practically every
one, men who have not paid a penny to
Britain, men who would be delighted to see
Great Britain go down, men who did
not implement Article 5 of the
Treaty. Successive Governments have insulted us by suggesting that we should give
way to those people every time they get up an
agitation to save their faces. That is most
horrible and offends the good feeling of the
British people to-day. In my judgment a
matter which the electorate of Great Britain
ought to take up and consider for themselves
is whether they will allow their kith and
kin to be always trampled upon and insulted, and that by rebels. When British
Governments cease statesmanship and adopt
politics it is time the British electorate
should cry "halt" to the politician and see
that some better and more righteous method
may be introduced into British politics and
that they will stand by the friends of Britain
who are standing by them in their hour of
need.
There is another matter. The Prime
Minister has very truly said that we were no
party to this Treaty. We were not permitted
to be a party to this Treaty, and if this
Treaty has been adopted behind our backs,
are we now to allow any Government by an
act of coercion to set up a Boundary Commission, two parties on which will be representing Great Britain and one representing Southern Ireland, to say what is going
to happen to a little community of people
who at great cost and great stress and strain
have made law and order respected, have
made it possible for the King's writ to run,
and have restored peace? Are we to allow
those people to come in and harry and harass
us still further in the most unpardonable
manner? The Prime Minister in the grave
statement which he made has not visualised
the situation too seriously when he adopted
this very strong language. That is the
principle which is beating in the heart of
every Ulsterman and every Ulster woman
to-day. It is this in short: "You British
people may fool as you like and try to fool
the Ulster people, you may set up your
Boundary Commission, you may bring in

your finding, but you cannot put it
into force. Whatever is the result of
your Boundary Commission it will be
another matter to put it into practice.
It will not be a matter of talk and
playing with words and denying letters,
it will be a matter of coming and taking our
territory and bringing it over to the other
side, and people who come to do this must
come prepared for the worst." The Ulster
people, in the language of the Prime Minister,
have made up their minds that they will
stand no more nonsense about this, and that,
for them, the chapter is entirely closed.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The British
people should know what is going to happen.
We will fight to the bitterest end to maintain
the rights and liberties of Ulster-rights we
have gone sponsors for. Every Member of
Parliament is a sponser for the liberty of
Ulster. We have taken a solemn trust under
the Act of 1920. When our Gracious King
came over he committed a solemn trust to
us. We have tried to keep that trust, and
to respect that trust, and, please God, we
will maintain that trust at whatever cost.
I would like, also, to remind the British
electorate and the British statesmen that we
belong to a stock of people who do not believe
in bluster or brag. We have very strong
personal traits in our character. We have
the blood of the old Scottish Covenanters, the
blood of the French Huguenots, and very
largely the blood of the English Cromwellians, and these three great forces have
made a very tremendous impress upon the
manhood of the people of Ulster. We do not
believe in bluster, or brag, or threatening,
but we devoutly believe in defending rights
given to us to hand on to our children afterwards. We are not down and out, we are
not downhearted in this matter. We are
not standing alone. We will have the best
of the British people with us, the best of the
Colonies with us, and the best of the Army
and Navy with us. The people who when
this country was at war tried to destroy its
liberties and life will never be assisted by
the Forces who were shot in the back in the
South and West of Ireland at a time of great
stress in Great Britain.
Lastly, let me again assure the Prime
Minister that Ulster is absolutely serious in
this matter. He mentioned the question of
a policy. I suggest, if I may, to the Prime
Minister that the policy of the Ulster people
is a very simple article, very easily drawn
up. They are a race who are very direct
and they do not beat about the bush, or
dodge or prevaricate; they do not take after
that great juggler of Treaties, Mr. Lloyd
George, in the least. They have a most
horrible contempt for a trickster of that
kind. We are a direct people and we are a
plain people, and our policy is that we want
to play the game with Great Britain. We
are loyal to Great Britain and we want to
maintain, and shall maintain, our British
citizenship. We have carried the burden of
Empire and we must also carry the
privileges of Empire. Because there is a
threatened upheaval in the South of Ireland
and Republicanism is going to gain the
whole sway there in a few years the British
politician thinks that by giving a sop to the
South of Ireland he will stave off the evil
day of Republicanism. He may try it on his
own but not on the people of Ulster. We
are sick of all this dodging to placate rebellion, and the day is not far distant when
the British people will be very thankful
that we stood where we do and that in this
outpost of Empire there was a section of
loyal people who took such measures as we
taking to ensure that there shall
be no Republicanism in this part of Great
Britain and that there shall be liberty
throughout every part of the Six Counties.
are
We believe Republicanism is coming. We
know it is coming and we are sorry to see
it is coming. We believe the financial strain
in the South of Ireland will be dreadful to
contemplate, because if Republicanism comes
and they start their own currency they will
reduce the value of their currency by fifty
per cent. They will be in the depths of
despair the moment they start Republicanism, and it is our business to see that we
are no part and parcel of that Republicanism
but that we are still members of the British
Empire and that loyalty to the old flag
beats as true in our hearts to-day as it did
in the days gone by. This being so we want
plainly to tell the British Parliament that
we want no part of our territory interfered
with. At the same time, as the Prime
Minister has so often said, he is willing to
barter with them on mere boundary lines
for the adjustment of territory, but that
ought to be done in a friendly and neighbourly manner. We are willing to do this
but further than this we will not go. If a
coercion Government by a coercion Act think
they can overawe us and subjugate us and
take away the liberties that were handed
down to us and which we hold dear they
will find they cannot do it. They will be
very much undeceived if they try to exploit
us in the days to come.

ORDERS OF THE DAY,
Unemployment Fund (Money).
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
Motion made and Question proposed:
a
That it is expedient to authorise
charge upon the Consolidated Fund in respect of any further sums required to be
advanced by the Ministry of Finance, not
exceeding in the whole Seven Hundred
and Fifty Thousand pounds, under
powers to be conferred by an Act of this

of Northern Ireland.
Mr. POLLOCK: By arrangement with my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Labour, I
propose to take this Resolution. The Committee will see from the reading of the
Resolution its principal object, but it is
necessary that I should explain some of the
details in order that the Committee may
realise the object of the Bill which I propose
to introduce to-morrow, and of which this
Resolution is simply the usual preliminary
step. The Resolution is something in the
nature of an emergency. It is intended to
confer additional borrowing powers upon the
Unemployment Insurance Fund. On 30th
May last year Parliament authorised borrowings to the maximum of £2,000,000 by this
Fund. It was calculated, and it was
hoped, that that maximum would have been
sufficient to carry the Fund over probably
until our next Session of Parliament, but
matters supervened which upset these calculations and it was found late in the
month of September that the powers of the
Unemployment Insurance Fund had expired
and it was necessary, being a matter of
emergency, to take the necessary steps to
finance the Fund pending the action of
Parliament giving the necessary authority
for new borrowing powers.
The Committee will see that the sum
asked for by the Ministry of Finance is
£750,000. How long that will carry the
Fund it is impossible for me to say because
it is dependent on SO many contingencies,
and the rise and fall of unemployment
naturally affect the amounts which weekly
have to be provided in order that the
benefits accruing to the unemployed shall be
secured. The position of this Fund is one
that has given me personally, and has given
the Government, a great deal of concern. At
the time that the financial relations of
Northern Ireland to Great Britain were determined no account Was taken in the
Treasury White Papers that were furnished
of this very important service, the result of
which was that it was thrown entirely upon
the Northern Government to bear the
burden of whatever unemployment should
accrue in the forthcoming years. We have
resented from that time to this the action
of the Imperial Parliament, because there
was obviously a burden contemplated and
that burden should have been explained and
the necessary provision should have been
made for it. That, however, was not done,
and we have been recently pressing, and are
still continuing to press, upon the Imperial
Government the necessity of rearranging the
position of this Fund as between Great
Britain and Northern Ireland.
Our claim in fact is that the fund should
be a single fund, for various reasons-I may
mention one or two. The benefits are reciprocal, that is to say, they are paid equally
in Northern Ireland and in Great Britain,
apart altogether from where the contributions have been made. The bulk of the
unemployed in our area are members of
British trade unions-(Mr. McGuffin: Hear,.
Unemployment Fund-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
hear) and perhaps the most important
argument of all is that the cutting off of a
small area such as ours from the large area
covered by the Imperial fund was an unfair
arrangement. The whole principle of insurance, as hon. Members will realise, is that
the extent of the area, the largeness of the
area, if I may say so, is the only security
that any insurance scheme can have. Therefore, it has been found by examination, and,
indeed, by results and by experience, that
our area is too small to bear comfortably a
burden of this kind.
Of course the conditions have been exceptional, and we must not lose sight of that.
Industrial conditions in Belfast cannot be
regarded as having been satisfactory during
the past year or two. The present position
of shipbuilding is something that is giving
us all very serious concern, and it is in that
very important department of industry that
the most serious unemployment exists at the
present time. How long these conditions
will obtain it is impossible to say, but on
the assumption that sooner or later normal
conditions will result in the Province, it has
been hoped that the position of this Unemployment Insurance Fund would become
normal, and, therefore, that the large amount
of money which the fund at present owes to
the Government would be liquidated. It is
merely speculation on my part to offer any
opinion as to when that is likely to take
place, but it is perfectly obvious at the present moment that the burden of this unemployment insurance is something that will
before very long require the close attention
of the Government, and it is just conceivable
that some rearrangement will have to be
made in order that the fund itself should
be put into something like a proper, normal,
and solvent condition. I do not know that
it is necessary for me to go into any question
of the percentages of unemployment, because
it is perhaps hardly relevant to the submission of a Resolution such as I am now
bringing before the Committee, and, when
the Bill itself is submitted, if any matters
develop in the meantime out of the Bill,
which hon. Members will have in their
hands, either I or my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Andrews) who sits beside me will be in a
position to give that information in regard
to the general position of the fund and the
relative position as between Great Britain
and Northern Ireland. Therefore, as this is
an emergency matter, and as I shall have
to ask Parliament to get through the necessary stages of the Bill to-morrow in order
that the Unemployment Fund may be in a
position to borrow sufficient to carry it on,
I will reserve any further details that may
be required until the Second Reading of the
Bill itself. I beg to move.
Mr. COOTE: I hope I am in order, but if
I am not I apologise in advance. I speak

to inform us as to the facts in relation to

there should be no loss to the fund. I would
like to know if we have reached the datum
line of the necessary employed people to

but have we come to the time that we
can breathe freely and feel that we are out

should like an answer to to-day, or if it can

We simply want the information. We want
to know where we are in regard to this fund,
faced as
we are with the comforting fact
that unemployment is slowly disappearing,
and that we are getting stronger and into
more stable conditions in Northern Ireland.
That is all I should like to raise in regard
to the fund at the present time. We want

he can do it more explicitly then.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James
Craig): Perhaps it would suit the convenience of the Committee if I reply, as

opposite, so that when we come to discuss

the Minister of Labour and the Minister of
Finance, and myself have been gravely concerned about this Unemployment Insurance
Fund, and we took the view that with a
Labour Government in power this was the
time to put the real facts of the case before

them, because the question affects the great

up for ever this
anomaly, this wrong that was done us in

My right hon. Friends and I have held
from the beginning that it would be much
fairer to treat the Unemployment Insurance Fund on the same basis as Health
Insurance. The Health Insurance covers
Great Britain and Northern Ireland, one
large fund spread over the whole of the
country, and we are endeavouring with all
the power that we possess to get the Government to use the same system with regard
to Unemployment Insurance, that is to say,
to have the one pool for the whole
of Great Britain and Northern Ireland,
and in that way to spread the risk over
the whole country. When there is depression in special businesses, in special
trades like shipbuilding and linen-and we
have gone through very acute distress in
both those great industries in Ulster-it is
made up by prosperity in a thousand and
one other trades throughout Great Britain
on which we cannot depend here, because
with agriculture, shipbuilding and the linen
industry we have exhausted as it were our
greatest industries in Northern Ireland.
We had really some hope when we were unable to convince the Coalition Government
and the Government that succeeded it as to
the justice of our case, that with a Labour
Government in power we might be able to
establish the principle, and I have not
given up that hope. A great many of His
Majesty's Ministers have most sympathetically treated my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews), and my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance
(Mr. Pollock), and I believe if we had more
time to go on and bring pressure to bear on
this matter, it might be possible to incorporate it in the whole big scheme, so
that in our time of prosperity we would be
contributing to Great Britain in their time
of poverty, and thus helping to sustain
their multitude of industries. We shall

going and help in the discussion which may
take place on the Bill to-morrow.

Mr. McGUFFIN: I do not think I would
have intervened in this discussion were it
not for the fact that in a very large degree
I was responsible for the transfer of labour
interests to the Northern Parliament.
think those of us who were in the Imperial
Parliament can recollect that it was originally intended that labour interests should
be retained or made a reserved service in
the Imperial Parliament. But I pictured
to myself what would be the nature of a
Government in which the proletariat or
democracy of this area would have no
interest? You could not ask the people,
for instance, at the time of the election to

own particular interests to be overlooked
and neglected. They would have had no

Upon that ground I suggested that it would
be well that Labour interests should be
transferred to the control of this House.
I do not regret that I took that course, and
there is no use in any hon. Member of this
House saying that he knew what would be
the effect of that, for that is not the case.
It was never presumed for a moment that we
would become insolvent. That was not one
of the difficulties that were put up when we
as private Members were considering the
advisability of having this Department transferred to the Northern Government. it
was never for a moment entertained, and
there is no reason to suppose that we
would be in the almost insolvent position in
which we are at the moment. That is due
to circumstances over which we had no control, and circumstances, moreover, which are
affecting the industrial classes and the
Government in Great Britain just as much
as they are here.
There is an obligation devolving upon us
in respect of the industrial classes and we

them. I am not opposed to the suggestion

be some arrangement made by which

I think it should be done, but we need not

Government here. That is not implied at
all, and, even if the right hon. Gentleman
(Sir James Craig) does not succeed in effecting such an arrangement across the water. I
am not as hopeless in respect of this fund
as some people are. It often has been predicted, and I myself have thought, that in
the near future, the fund would become

solvent through a reduction in the number of

I suppose this Vote amounting to £750,000

Industrial Assurance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): The Bill to which we are asking
the House to give a Second Reading this
afternoon is one of great moment to a
considerable number of persons. Hon.
Members are acquainted with the type of
insurance referred to as industrial insurance, which I may in passing explain as
being the insurance of comparatively
small sums, about £10
upon an average,
which shows that the persons concerned are
in relatively humble circumstances, in return for premiums collected at weekly or
monthly intervals. In 1921 it was estimated
that £37,000,000 was collected in premiums
in the United Kingdom, and as the average
premium was estimated at about 24d. per
week the very large number of persons
directly interested in this form of insurance
can be readily calculated. The collection is
usually a door to door one conducted by
agents who get a commission on the insurance, and naturally the more glib of tongue
they are and the more they impress people
the more commission they get. Industrial assurance is carried on by Assurance Companies incorporated under the Companies'
Acts and also by Collecting Societies which
are registered as Friendly Societies. A
typical example of a company carrying on
industrial assurance business is the Prudential, and the Royal Liver Friendly
is a very good example of a Friendly
Society.
SO
Side by side with the honest business which
has grown up it is unfortunately true that
a number of abuses have sprung up,
much so that in 1919 the Imperial Government set up a Departmental Committee
under the chairmanship of Lord Parmoor.
This Committee issued in 1920 a unanimous
Report as a result of which a remedial
Assurance Act,
measure, The Industrial
was passed by the Imperial Parliament
last year. I will not explain in detail the
lengthy indictment of the system which the
report of the Parmoor Committee embodied,
but among other things they found that far
too heavy working expenses were connected
with the insurance. The result was that
out of every 1/- paid in premiums only 7d.
went to the benefit of the insured person.
Lord Parmoor's Committee also found
that in the case of one Company during a
period of 10 years 9,300,000 policies were
issued, of which 6,400,000 lapsed, and also
in 10 of the concerns nearly 5,000,000 policies
lapsed in the year 1913 of which nearly
4,000,000 policies had been effected in the
years 1912 or 1913. There is no doubt,
therefore, that the House will see the need
for a protective Measure to try to remedy
those abuses. So far as the Insurance
Companies are concerned there was some
protection against persons without resources
forming companies because, under the provisions of the Assurance Companies Act,
1909, a deposit of £20,000 had to be made
before a Life Assurance Company could be
registered or carry on business. There was,
however, no such protection in the case of
Friendly Societies and any seven persons
could get together and register as a Society,
without paying any deposit at all. Moreover, as a general rule industrial assurance
policies carried no right to a surrender
value or to a free paid-up policy. Another
weakness pointed out by the Committee was
that there was no effective valuation of the
assets and liabilities of the Societies and no
proper control of the auđit.
The Measure now before this House
follows closely the Imperial Measure of last
year in order to eliminate these abuses.
In Northern Ireland there is at the present
time only one collecting Society registered
while there are no Northern Ireland Industrial Assurance Companies. All the
business of that description done in Northern
Ireland is carried on by Companies and
Societies incorporated or registered in
London or in the Irish Free State. So far
as British Companies and Societies operating
in Northern Ireland are concerned they are,
of course, subject to the control of the
Industrial Assurance Commissioner in
London, and Northern Ireland will
derive a good deal of benefit from his
administration. The British Companies are
not, however, under any compulsion to extend the benefits of the English Act to
members and policy holders in Northern
Ireland until the Measure now before this
House has been passed into law by us.
Following on the precedent of the Imperial
Act our Bill proposes that all foreign
or Dominion concerns shall be precluded

The whole Measure as it stands is designed
for the protection and benefit of the industrious poor in Northern Ireland. I beg
to move.

I exonerated the Minister at the time, and

I am afraid now that he has some sympathy

industry which in these days of unemployment has a right to be protected. It does
much to keep up the price and value of
native timber for the farmers and landlords,
and it is an asset we cannot think lightly
about. The box-making trade of Northern
Ireland makes it worth while conserving the
timber and planting new supplies. These egg
boxes are very largely made out of beechwood. which is much heavier than
Swedish timber. The home-grown timber has
the misfortune not to be grown in Sweden,
but it is a much better timber for the purposes of the egg trade than Swedish timber.
I challenge the Minister of Agriculture to
deny that the home-grown timber is a better,
a cleaner, and a nicer timber than the
Swedish timber, and that it will make up
much better from the carpenter's point of
view.
Mr. McGUFFIN: What is the difference
in the cost?
Mr. COOTE: I will come to that. It is
much cheaper. It can still keep out the
Swedish trade, but that is not to happen
because there are certain interested people
in Belfast, importers of Swedish timber, who
wish to destroy the box-making industry of
Northern Ireland. They found they could
not do it on the merits of the wood because
the boxmaker can turn out a neater and a
cleaner egg box from home-grown timber

box that will be more appreciated across the
water. They cannot get at the boxmakers

was not his business to interfere with the

If you cannot destroy their trade by fair

miles away there is another mill going.
Right up the valley the mills are going, producing timber purchased from the landlords

for the relief of unemployment and the development of the country, and yet the Minister

seasoned and dry. If you make egg boxes
out of fresh wood, as the hon. Member wants
to do, the wood is heavy. Fresh wood wets
the straw that the eggs are packed in. I
myself have been shown hundreds and
hundreds of boxes with the eggs tainted
owing to the wood that the hon. Member
(Mr. Coote) wants the boxes made of.
Mr. COOTE: I would like to know have
you asked for sample boxes?
The CHAIRMAN: I think the Minister
must be allowed to proceed unless he wishes
to give way. The hon. Member (Mr. Coote)
has had a very full fling indeed. It is
preferable that the right hon. Gentleman
should be allowed to develop his argument
without interruption.
Mr. ARCHDALE: The hon. Member cannot have it all his own way. As I was remarking, I have seen in Belfast hundreds of
boxes of eggs that were unfit for sale in
England because of the damp unseasoned
•
As regards the farmers in the country
growling about the inspectors coming round,
I thought the hon. Member (Mr. Coote)
yesterday was urging that more inspectors
be appointed. He said that the £128,000 for
the relief of the rates was doing no good to

spend Government money without having
someone to oversee the spending of it. I do
not exactly see how the hon. Member's remarks come in. I only hope that no man
will be turned off in the mills in his neighbourhood, but that all saw millers will season
the wood out of which they are going to make
the egg boxes. If they will not we will certainly see that our regulations, when drawn
up, are carried out regardless of any person.
Dr. MORRISON: I thought this question

when it was last before the House, and that
the utmost care would be taken not to injure
this growing industry in Ulster. That certainly was my impression. I desire to associate myself with what the hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. Hanna) has said with regard
to this business. If I could eliminate some
of the harsh remarks of my hon. Friend (Mr.
Coote) I would be glad to associate myself

regulations have been issued with regard

Ulster. From the time I leave my house

Mr. COOTE: Hear, hear.
Dr. MORRISON: Those industries were the

£3,000,000 a year to the workers of rural

go out of employment and come to Belfast.
You have unemployment, you have the

It starts a vicious circle that is ruining industries and destroying the prosperity of
rural Ulster. I hope that there will be an
opportunity of taking the opinion of the
House on this matter, and certainly if it.
comes to a division, I will go into the Lobby
against the Government.
Mr. DONALD: I really had no intention

between 17lbs. and 22 or 24 lbs.--what it
would mean in transportation?
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Mr. DONALD: I read in the report of the
Industrial Commission on roads, that the
upkeep here, as regards transportation was
33 per cent. above Great Britain. Look at
the state of our roads. The weight of the
box is an important thing. You have got
to pay largely by weight. If we adopt the
suggestion of my hon. and learned Friend
(Mr. Hanna), it means that we are going to
increase the weight by one third. There has
been a great deal of nonsensical talk about
the weight. I sat on a committee at which
evidence was given that 100 per cent. of the
wood used in building our houses is imported.
Ninety-eight per cent. of the wood that goes
to build our ships is imported. Why? It
is because we cannot grow suitable wood in
this country. The wood grown in this country would not be suitable for box-making at
all, and it is owing to the weight. People
talk about making boxes from pitch pine.
Supposing I make a tool box of pitch pine,
which I have to carry from morning to night,
and another one made of yellow pine, which
is imported, what would be the result? I
wish my hon. and learned Friend would come
along and carry the pitch pine box for a day
and he would see the difference there is in
carrying one made of imported wood. The
same thing applies to boxes for carrying eggs.
With regard to this question about which
we have heard so much, I could not help
thinking that here is a whole discussion
about £10, and yet scarcely a word was said
on a Vote for £2,000,000 that was introduced
here to-day. What is the difference between
the two? One goes to help the farmers by
purchasing seed, oats, and potatoes for distribution to necessitous farmers at reduced
prices. The Vote for £2,000,000 is to be
given to people on loan, and you do not
know when you are going to get the money
back-that is the unemployment insurance.
Let us be consistent. Is not the farmer, if
he is in difficulties, entitled to be supported
equally with other people. We are really
only giving the money on loan, because, as
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale) has
said, we are going to get that money back.
A whole lot has been said about the
Government taking this step. The seasons
will not wait for the farmer. The farmer
has got to purchase his seed at a certain
time, and the Government comes to his
aid. I am surprised at my hon. Friend
(Mr. Coote) coming, as he does, from an
agricultural area. If this criticism had
come from some hon. Member such as myself there would have been some excuse.
Even to the furthest inland district in Ireland you can import your timber and make
your boxes more cheaply than you can make
them with Irish wood. Any one will tell
you that.
With regard to the money for
the farmer. I think it is a shame for any
hon. Member to say he will go to a Division
over this question when a Vote for £2,000,000
was passed, and hon. Members did not know
that they were passing it for practically a
similar purpose. It is ridiculous.

CLOSING OF ALBERT BRIDGE SCHOOL.
3. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education,
whether he has received a request from a
public meeting of past pupils and parents of
children educated at Albert Bridge Public
Elementary School, protesting against "cruel
and harsh treatment of Mr. Samuel
McCambley, the Principal Teacher, and also
against closing the school, and requesting
the Minister to hold an investigation; and
if so, what course the Ministry proposes tó
adopt?
""
The following Question stood on the Paper
in the name of Mr. DONALD:~
5. To ask the Parliamentary Secretary to
the Ministry of Education, if he will state
the circumstances regarding the closing
down of the Albert Bridge School and the
dismissal of the principal of the school;
whether it is the intention of the Govern
ment to take steps to have this school reopened, in view of the shortage of school
accommodation, and the principal reinstated.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am empowered, in the absence
of my hon. Friend (Mr. McKeown) who represents Education in this House, to take
this question.
There is another question on the Paper
in regard to this matter in the name of the
hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr. Donald),
and with his permission, I will reply to both
questions at the same time..
When the Ministry of Education took over
control of National Schools in Northern Ireland, on 1st February, 1922, the persistent
neglect of the Principal Teacher of Albert
Bridge School to give effect to the orders
of the Commissioners of National Education,
and the highly improper tone of a communication received from him, had led to a
position of considerable difficulty. The
Ministry, however, decided to investigate the
whole case de novo, with a desire to obtain
an unprejudiced view of the facts and to
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
9 OCTOBER 1924
create a more friendly atmosphere, and on
28th February, 1922, the Chief Inspector was
instructed to confer with the Manager and
Principal Teacher, and with the Senior and
Section Inspectors, with a view to furnishing a full report on the needs of the school,
as they then existed.
Following upon the Chief Inspector's report
the Ministry laid down certain requirements,
as to the maximum number of pupils who
might be enrolled in the school, and also
made certain stipulations as to the re-organisation of the whole work on lines designed
to improve the education of the pupils.
Mr. McCambley, however, has persistently disregarded the instructions of the
Ministry, particularly those relating to the
exclusion from the school of children in excess
of the number which could be accommodated
therein, with due regard to the conditions
of health and efficient school work.
Since the month of October, 1922, repeated
efforts have been made to induce Mr.
McCambley to comply with official instructions in regard to the conduct of his school,
but without effect. Finally, in May, 1924,
the Ministry was reluctantly compelled to
suspend payment of salary, and as this
measure even then failed to secure compliance with its instructions, the Ministry
had no alternative other than to withdraw
recognition from this teacher,, who is 59
years of age and eligible for pension under
the ordinary regulations. This decision was
notified to the school manager on 1st August,
1924, and he was informed that Mr.
McCambley's recognition as teacher would
cease not later than the 30th September,
1924. The manager thereupon informed the
Ministry that the school, which was held in
a non-vested building over which the
Ministry has no control, would not be available for school purposes after the date of
withdrawal of recognition from Mr.
McCambley.
The Ministry duly received a copy of resolutions purporting to have been passed at a
public meeting held on 18th September, 1924,
relative to the compulsory retirement of the
teacher on pension and the closing of the
school. It does not, however, see any
necessity for holding any further investigation into the facts, nor does it propose to
restore salary to Mr. McCambley, who will
be permitted to retire on pension.
In reference to the question of the reopening of this school, it is pointed out that
the duty of providing school accommodation
in Belfast rests with the local Education
Authority, which has already made arrangements for the education of the children
formerly attending Albert Bridge School in
a suitable building in the neighbourhood.
The Ministry does not propose in any circumstances to recognise Mr. McCambley again
as a teacher.
It will further be noted that the school was
not closed by the Ministry, nor were grants
withdrawn from it until the Ministry had
been notified that the premises would no
longer be available for school purposes.
I am authorised to add that the action
which has been taken in regard to this matter
has throughout the proceedings not only
been approved, but also directed by the

was improved and heating apparatus and

the teacher was informed that this concession

EXAMINATION RESULTS IN
SECONDARY SCHOOLS.
4. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education
if he is aware of the serious inconvenience
caused to the secondary schools of Northern
Ireland by the delay in publishing the examination results; and whether he can explain
the cause of such delay, and guarantee that
it will not occur in the future.
Mr. POLLOCK: The delay in issuing the
results of the Intermediate Examinations in
the present year was due to the fact that the
printing of them was not so expeditiously
performed as is usual in connection with
these results. The Ministry regrets the inconvenience caused by the delay. When it
became evident early in September that the
results would not appear in due time the
schools were informed at once as to all the
pupils who had passed the examination. In
every case in which application was made
to the Ministry the fullest possible information was given to University authorities
as to the results obtained by candidates for
matriculation and to County Councils and
other educational authorities with regard to
candidates for scholarships. I may add that
new arrangements have been made whereby
the publication of the results in future will
be subject to no avoidable delay.
Hon. MEMBERS: Hear, hear.

NEW SCHOOL BUILDINGS IN BELFAST.
6. Mr. DONALD asked the Parliamentary
Secretary to the Ministry of Education if
he will state what progress has been made, or
is being made, with regard to new school
buildings, enlargements, and structural improvements in Belfast; and whether steps
have yet been taken to provide meals for
children under Sections 49 and 52 of the
Education Act, 1923.
Mr. POLLOCK: The duty of providing new
schools where such schools are needed in
Belfast now devolves on the Belfast Education Authority set up under the Education
Act (N.I.), 1923, for the County Borough of
Belfast. The Education Authority has already
submitted to the Ministry of Education proposals for the erection of five new schools,
providing accommodation in all for about
4,000 children. In two of these cases the
plans have been approved by the Ministry,
and the Education Authority is taking steps
to obtain tenders with a view to starting
work at an early date. In one case the
general approval of the Ministry to the proposed erection of the new house has been
given, and plans in connection therewith are
in preparation. The remaining two cases
are at present under consideration by the
Ministry, as regards the need for the proposed
new schoolhouses, suitability of site, etc.
The Belfast Education Authority is responsible for the enlargement and structural
improvement of all existing Public Elementary Schools within the County Borough
transferred to it under Section 14 of the.
Act. Proposals for the enlargement of two
such schools have been received. In one of
these cases, in which the preliminary arrangements for the transfer of the school have
been made, the final plans of the proposed
enlargement are under consideration by the
Technical Officers of the Ministry of Finance,
and in the other case the consideration of
the proposal to enlarge the school awaits the
settlement of the arrangements for
transfer of the school premises.
the
It is to be added that the Belfast Education Authority has rented the buildings of
the McQuiston Institute for temporary use
for the purposes of a Public Elementary
School. A school was opened in this building,
which affords accommodation for over 500
pupils, on 1st instant.
It has been notified to the Ministry that
the Belfast Education Authority is at present
organising a system for feeding necessitous
school children, and hopes to have the system
initiated at an early date.

SAILORS' AND SOLDIERS' LAND TRUST
АСТ.
8. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the present
position of the Trust set up by the Sailors'
and Soldiers' Land Trust Act, and whether
any new contracts have been made recently
for the building of ex-Service men's houses
under the Act?
Mr. POLLOCK: The hon. and gallant
Member no doubt refers to the Trust set up
under Section 3 of the Irish Free State
(Consequential Provisions) Act, 1922. The
Trust has been functioning since 1st January
last, and although no formal agreement has
yet been made, the Ministry of Finance is
acting as its agent in the building of houses
and receiving applications from prospective
tenants. The functions of the Ministry are
necessarily circumscribed, firstly, because
the number of houses to be built in Northern
Ireland has been fixed by the Treasury at
1,046, and, secondly, because the Trust, acting either as a body or through its local
Trustees in Northern Ireland, controls the
selection of localities, the price at which
houses are to be built, the selection of
tenants, and the fixing of rents. Certain
administrative difficulties which arose have
to a large extent been settled as the result
of meetings which took place recently in
Belfast between the Trust and Members of
this Government. The last contract for
houses placed was on 29th July, 1924, and it
is anticipated that others will shortly
follow.

right hon. Friend a question. The last time
I raised this question I was informed that
this was a matter for the Imperial Government, and should be raised there.

Our contention is that an Insurance Fund
of this character, operating in such a comparatively restricted area, should not have
been transferred to us without sufficient provision being made in order that whatever
liability accrued from it should be provided
for by the authority which made the
transfer as it is perfectly clear that no
similar small area in the United Kingdom
could be cut off from the general scheme
without results accruing similar to those
which we have experienced in the North
of Ireland. If I may take a typical case,
let us assume that in the Clyde district an
area of similar size to that of the Six
Counties were placed under similar conditions to those in which we find ourselves
to-day. It would be discovered that the results would be exactly the same as if not
perhaps worse than, those which obtain
with us in Northern Ireland. As I
mentioned yesterday, and as the Prime
Minister confirmed, we have been making
every exertion to bring home to the
Imperial authority the unfairness of the
treatment which has been meted out to us
in respect of this matter. Local autonomy
was not intended to imply that our status
in regard to schemes or measures of social
reform should not be equal to that of
England, Scotland or Wales. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) We have unfortunately, however, been the victims of the many political
changes which have taken place in Great
Britain. One Government refuses to implement the obligations of its predecessors, and
although I cannot say that we have any
undertakings from any of those Governments in respect of the matter which I am
now discussing, still I think there can
hardly be any doubt that our claims have

These are generalisations which I submit on

is probably the most important of all the

Province. The Government of Ireland Act

quite obvious that the object of this provision was that in that period sufficient
experience would be reached to enable those

here with the Government of this Province

their determination that we should pass away

In regard to this particular fund, on the
31st May of last year, as I mentioned yesterday, the deficit was £1,500,000, and it was
necessary at that date to ask Parliament
for authority to borrow an additional £500,000,
making a total of £2,000,000, for which the
fund would be liable. Towards the end of
September, that is the September that has
just passed, the last grant was exhausted,
thus bringing the deficit of the Insurance
Fund up to a sum of £2,000,000. As our
Parliament was not sitting at that time, it
was necessary to adopt expedients for the
purpose of financing the fund during the
hiatus or interim between the exhausted
period and the meeting of our Parliament, in
order that the beneficiaries of the fund might
not be deprived of the benefits which in the
ordinary course of matters accrued to them
pending the authority of this Parliament.
It is the authority of this Parliament that
I am asking to-day in presenting this Measure
for power to borrow a further sum of
£750,000. If this sum is exhausted, or when
it is exhausted, it will bring the liability
up to a total sum of £2,750,000. Reference
to the Bill, which I assume is in the hands
of hon. Members, will show that the sum
mentioned there is £2,250,000. That is
because no account was taken of a sum of
£500,000, which was authorised by an Order
in Council before the machinery was set up,
and our Ministry of Labour, who had control over it, began to function.
Possibly it would be of interest to hon.
Members if I gave a few figures in connection with this fund, just to give an idea
as to the position in which it stands. The
approximate number of insurable workers
in the Six Counties is 255,000. The approximate number of unemployed is at present
close upon 42,000. The present percentage
figure of unemployment may therefore be
taken at almost 17 per cent. The estimates
for this year were based upon a 13 per cent.
basis as against the present 17 per cent.,
and that will to some extent explain the
necessity for the present Measure. The
additional liability has resulted from two
causes, as was touched upon yesterday in
submitting the Money Resolution-in the
first place, the deplorable conditions of one
of our important staple industries-the most
important-and, secondly, the recent Act of
the Imperial Parliament, which was passed
in the month of August. That Act increased
the benefits to men and women by 3s., and
it also doubled the benefits to dependantsto children. It may be of some information
to the House, therefore,. if I say that the
present income from benefits of an average
family, say a man, wife, and three children,
is about 29s. per week. There also arise
other little matters to which I need not
refer, and which have contributed to the additional drain upon the Fund. Perhaps my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Andrews) in following me will explain these matters in more
detail if Members are anxious for further
explanation. It was calculated by the
British Ministers that the additional benefits
which in the month of August were provided
by the Measure to which I have referred
could be secured to the members of the
British fund, without impairing the solvency
of that fund, and it was expected that in the
year 1926 the deficit of that fund, which is
to-day in the region of about £6,000,000, would
be repaid. I am afraid that we cannot reckon
upon any such good fortune in respect of

our own fund, and it is because of this that

I would remind the House also that a
special burden is laid upon me as Minister
of Finance in regard to this matter. It is
the Minister of Finance who is responsible
for the condition of the fund, and who is
required by statute of the Imperial Parliament as well as by our own legislative
authority to take whatever steps are necessary to obviate any danger of insolvency. We
have always been hoping that industrial
conditions would improve. but I cannot see
that any other policy at present can be pursued than to continue to exercise all the
pressure which we have been and are bringing to bear upon the Imperial Government
to merge our fund into the general Unemployment
Insurance scheme presently
existing in Britain and covering the whole
country.
I would remind the House also, that when
prosperity returns, as no doubt it will some
day, in such a case where our Fund is merged
in the general scheme, that general scheme
will enjoy the advantage of the contributions
which we make, but in the meantime, by
the acceptance of the claim which we make,
we shall be temporarily helped to bear the
burden during a period of unexampled industrial and commercial depression. I think
I have given sufficient information to warrant
me in asking the House to pass this Measure. It is a Measure of emergency, and it is
desirable that it should be completed to-day,
in order that the Minister may assume his
functions in regard to advances of this
money. I beg to move.

SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES, 1924-25.
CLASS 1. No. 5.
PUBLIC WORKS AND BUILDINGS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That a supplementary sum not exceeding £12,889 be granted to His Majesty to
complete the sum necessary to defray the
charge which will come in course of payment during the year ending on 31st
March, 1925, in respect of Public Works
and Buildings, including Sundry Grants
in Aid.
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY OF THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): In moving
this Supplementary Estimate I would remind hon. Members at the start that this
falls within what is called Section 2 of the
Public Works Estimate which was submitted earlier in the year. The feature of
Section 2 is that it is a charge that remains
on the Public Works Estimate. It is not
recoverable either from the Imperial Parliament or from our Departmental Estimates.
It represents in the first place, as hon.
Members will see on page 5, the final
payment to the Belfast Corporation of
£1,900 in respect of the work which
they undertook to do for us in the
construction of the Killeen Road, or, as it
is now known, Massey Avenue, which will
form the new approach to our Parlia
mentary buildings at Stormont. There is
another small item of £170 which is required to complete the provision of
hutments on the Stormont Estate, a previous sum of £1,000 having been voted by
this House. Hon. Members, of course, will
remember the kind offer of the Prime
Minister to place at the disposal of the Boy
Scouts and similar organizations spare land
at Stormont that it might be available for
camping purposes, and this sum of £170 was
required to complete the hutments in order
to provide that accommodation
The next item is one of £7,819. The
major part. to the extent of £7,750, is a revote of a sum passed during our last
financial year. It was hoped that payment
would have been made and included in the
accounts for last year, but delays were met
with and so the payment was made during
the present financial year. We have, therefore, to come and ask your sanction to revote this sum. The small difference is
made up of interest. The third item is
£3,000 in respect of insurance of the interest
that we have in the buildings we occupy.
Hon. Members, I dare say, will be quite
familiar with the practice of the Imperial
Government of carrying their own insurance,
but they will also appreciate that for
stability in insurance matters risks must
be made wide and be very well spread. We
have not that large insurable risk, and so
after giving the matter careful consideration
it was decided that the much more prudent
policy on our part would be to insure our
buildings with the ordinary insurance companies. It may interest hon. Members to
know that the amount of property covered
by insurance is very nearly one and threequarter millions. We cover not only those
buildings which we actually own but we
also cover the insurance risks of those buildings which are provided as temporary
premises for us by the Imperial Government. We also thought it prudent to insure those other buildings which are carried
on by the Reserved Services and are looked
after by the Imperial Parliament, such as
Post Offices. I should explain that our
reason for doing so is that if a Post Office
were burned the Imperial Government
would replace it, but then they would
charge the cost of replacing it against our
residuary share, so the cost of it would fall
on us. Therefore, it is just as important
for us to cover by insurance risks of that
character as other risks in which we are
more directly concerned.
Mr.
McGUFFIN: May I ask if this
£3,000 may be regarded as the total
premiums paid in connection with this insurance? Is that the total premium paid?
Mr. BARBOUR: I think it is rather
more than the total annual cost because
there is a certain amount of arrears which
are included in this sum. The schedules
setting forth the different properties and
values are not yet complete, but the
work is being pushed on, and it is estimated that this sum will be sufficient to
cover the cost of insurance this year and also
such arrears as were not settled in time for
payment during the past year. I beg to
move.
Question put, and agreed to.

The class of man employed on the Mourne

otherwise people who really are not deserving cases, but they have some land. That is
one instance of a scheme in which there is
a very large sum of money involved, and
yet practically nothing has been done to
relieve our people.
It is only right that our Government, in
view of the approaching winter, should tell
us if they have anything more to offer to
our people, because I am informed on very
good authority that, in spite of the orders
that are in the shipyards to-day, the shipyards have been cut down to such an
economic figure in competition with the
other shipyards of the world that they
cannot go through the same form or procedure in building a ship that they did in
pre-war days. They have been restricted.
They are compelled to carry on at one ship,
complete her, and then when she is gone the
staff is removed to another ship. That does
not relieve unemployment, unfortunately,
but that is the system they are compelled
to adopt as a result of the economic conditions that exist in the country. We have
12,000 or 13,000 people who are dependent
upon that industry for a livelihood, and these
people naturally will want to know are the
Government thinking of them. Undoubtedly
they are getting the increased benefits, which
were discussed here. I do not want any
misunderstanding to arise or the suggestion
to go out that anything I have said is
against the people, because we all know perfectly well, and they have said it to us,
that they would rather have employment a
thousand times over than be going to draw
this money.
You have thousands of men
who hate the very thought of going to draw
the dole, but they cannot get employment
and, therefore, we have to give them some
little assistance. But how far does that
assistance go when you take into consideration the increase in the cost of living that
has taken place from the first of this month?
Milk has gone up.
Look at the price of
potatoes. Look at the prices people have to
pay at the present time in addition to high
rents. When all those things are taken into
consideration, after all, these people are not
getting any additional benefit from the extra
few shillings they are receiving.
It struck me that the present would be
an opportune time to borrow money and
bring our railways up-to-date. Even in the

have only to look at Bloomfield to see that

and that things would be much better, but
he has been disappointed in that respect. He
these

matters. It was only a prediction on his

to introduce a great amount of criticism in
this matter, or to insist that the Government

That will require grave consideration. What
the Government has pledged itself to do is

Government's privilege to instigate the
public authorities to do it. Public authorities
have to undertake it, and if the Ministry
think it advisable they contribute to and
support the carrying out of any scheme.
Therefore, they are not to blame in respect
of the matter. I have no hesitation whatever in supporting the Vote that is asked
in this case.

CLASS IV. No. 2.
EDUCATIONAL SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding
Ten Pounds be granted to His Majesty to
complete the sum necessary to defray the
charge which will come in course of payment
during the year ending on the 31st March,
1925, to provide for Educational Services,
including Grants in Aid of the Teachers'
Pension Fund, Northern Ireland, and of the
British Empire Exhibition Educational Fund
and Grants."
Mr. BARBOUR: In the absence of the
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education, I beg to move this Vote. It is
one that I am sure will attract the interest,
sympathy, and hearty support of all the
Members of the Committee. Just as our
last Session was drawing to a close here, the
attention of the Minister of Education was
drawn to the fact that steps were being
taken by various local education authorities
throughout the United Kingdom to raise
funds whereby school children might be enabled to go up and see the wonders of the
Wembley Exhibition. It was too late at that
time to bring any Vote before this Parliament to enable steps to be taken here. Our
own local education authorities, with the exception of the City of Belfast, and the City
of Derry, were not yet in motion, and so
the Minister of Education felt that it
rested with him to take the necessary steps
to enable children in our Six Counties to enadvantages
joy the same
as were being
extended to the young people in England
and Scotland. He approached the Minister
of Finance, who felt that the largest sum
which he could authorise to be voted out of
our public funds was the sum of £1,000. It
is estimated that there will be a saving on
the elementary education services of an
amount of £990, so we come to the Committee with what is called a token vote of
£10, merely to draw the attention of this
Committee to the nature of the expenditure
and to solicit their approval. The right
hon. Gentleman, the Minister of Education,
also enlisted the services of the Press by
whose efforts a further sum of £990 was
raised. In addition to that, local efforts were
made, and in this connection I think it
only right to mention the very gratifying
response that was made by the people of
Omagh,
who recently showed in just as
emphatic a way their great appreciation of
their position in the Empire. They raised a
very satisfactory sum, making with what
was raised by other bodies a sum of £400.
The Minister of Education himself headed
the list of subscriptions for which he
appealed to the public by the very generous
personal donation of £500. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.)
Steps were then taken to ensure that the
fullest advantage might be taken of their
opportunities by the school children who
went over to Wembley. Leaflets
were distributed amongst the public elementary schools
setting forth the foundation, geography, development, and immense natural resources of
the various constituent parts of the Empire,
and an examination was held at which
1,600 students presented themselves. It is
very gratifying to know that the answering
was satisfactory in the extreme, and in
some cases brilliant. Of the 1,600, it was only
possible to send 900 forward to the ENhibition. It Was found that the most
economical way in which they could be sent
was to divide them into detachments of 100.
The ages of the children, being between 13
and 16 years, required that they should be
suitably escorted. Consequently a
nurse, one head conductor, and six other
conductors took charge of each batch of 100
children. They were taken over to Wembley,
and were split up into smaller parties.
They were taken round and encouraged to

important matters, and some excellent essays
have been written. I myself would be disposed to give a prize, although I have not
very much money, to give the boys an opportunity of putting their impressions on paper
in the form of a short essay. Then the
House could judge of what the effect had
been. The teachers, who are the examiners,
would be the best judges of what had been
done. It is not a mere matter of composition
I want to test, but rather if the children
got an intelligent impression of the places
they were brought to visit, and if they
were under instruction which gave them at
least an idea of the importance of the great
Empire of which they are subjects, of its
widespread power, its commerce, and So
forth. I would suggest, if I am permitted,
that the Education Department should be
the means or instrument of instituting a
competition of this description. Of the 900
children who attended, at least a proportion
would be able to show that excellence of
intelligence and acquisition which has been
the result of their visit to Wembley. I leave
the suggestion at that, but I think that
without this we would not be assured of
the success we were entitled to expect from
the visit of these children to London.

SALE OF FIREWORKS TO CHILDREN.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Mr. Burn.)
Mr. GRANT: There is one matter to
which I would like to draw the attention of
the right hon. the Minister of Home Affairs.
Within the past few weeks there have been
in the local police courts a considerable
number of prosecutions of children for
throwing fireworks, and squibs and crackers
in picture palaces and on the public streets.
I recognise that owing to the trouble we
had in the city a few years ago these things
are an absolute nuisance and cause great disturbance in the minds of people, but on the
other hand it seems to me rather unfair
that the parents of children of tender years
should be fined in sums of 20s and 40s and
costs when the people who sell them are
allowed to do so without interference. I
recognise that the police are doing their
duty in bringing up these cases, and I recognise also that the magistrates are doing
all they can to put a stop to it by inflicting
these heavy penalties, but it certainly is a
hardship to a man who has been unemployed
for a considerable time to have to pay such
a heavy penalty if the children are summoned for using these particular crackers.
I was on the Bench this morning and I was
asked by some of the magistrates to bring
this matter forward as Hallowe'en is coming
on and there will be a considerable amount
of these fireworks used. I would like to know
from the right hon. Gentleman if it is not
possible for the Home Office to bring into
effect immediately some Order prohibiting
the sale of these crackers and fireworks. I
think it is very necessary that something
should be done.
Mr. LAVERY: I would like to support
the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Grant), who has
just sat down, in this connection. I was on
the Bench this forenoon also in my town,
and there were four cases brought forward
of a similar kind, the children being from
seven to ten years of age. We could not
see or feel that we would be justified as
magistrates in fining the parents of these
children. We simply let them off with costs
of court, believing that those who sell should
be punished. I hope that the Minister of
Home Affairs will see if it is possible that
this sale of fireworks should be stopped
immediately.
Sir DAWSON BATES: May I suggest to
my hon. Friends that there really must be
a limit in the State controlling the movements of children? I do not see that the
State should relieve the parent of the responsibility of looking after his child. The
suggestion is that the sale of fireworks should
be prohibited. Under the Explosives Act all
these shops have to be registered with the
local authority, and it is an offence for a
shopkeeper to sell any explosives, fireworks,
or things of that sort to any child under
the age of thirteen, and I think it is not
fair to impose further restrictions in peaceful times on shopkeepers. I would like to
emphasise again that there is far too much
tendency to grandmotherly legislation. The
whole tendency among a certain class of
parents appears to be to throw the entire
responsibility upon the Government.
I hope these prosecutions that have recently taken place will have the effect of
putting an end to a most objectionable
practice. Children must realise that they
cannot behave in the way some of them did
in the past. I heard a case not very long
ago of a child throwing a lighted squib on
a lady's dress, where it exploded. If anyone
looks at the Press he will see constant complaints. I think the Government are doing
the right thing in strictly enforcing the
law. I am only sorry that the Member for
Down (Mr. Lavery) has taken the attitude
he has. I would commend my hon. Friend
who sits opposite me (Mr. Grant) for sitting
on the Bench and having the courage to
enforce the law.
Mr. GRANT: I must say I am exceedingly
disappointed at the reply of the right hon.
Gentleman——
Mr. SPEAKER: I thought the hon. Gentleman was rising to ask a question.
I may
point out that on the adjournment he can
only make one speech.

nursing certificates conferred in the Free

Sir DAWSON BATES: The governing
body in connection with the medical profession in Great Britain and Northern Ireland
is the General Medical Council established
by the Medical Act of 1858. In that body
is vested the duty of registration of members
of the medical profession and of general
control and supervision of the profession.
Arrangements have recently been entered
into between the General Medical Council
and the Irish Free State Government under
which the Council will continue for a year to
register holders of medical degrees conferred
in the Free State on the same terms and conditions as obtained prior to the establishment
of the new regime in Southern Ireland.
As regards the question of nurses:
Negotiations are still pending between the
Nursing Council of Northern Ireland and
the Irish Free State Nursing Council with
a view to the establishment of reciprocal
arrangements between the two Councils
under which nurses registered by one Council
would be recognised as eligible for registration by the other Council and vice versa.
The arrangements have not yet been formally completed.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman, if, in the meantime, nothing can
be done for nurses who have taken out
certificates in the Free State and wish to
register in Northern Ireland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid not.

SUBSIDY.

Home Affairs whether the subsidy of £40
promised by the Belfast Corporation to
builders of new houses in the City is now

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The Belfast Corporation
have not, up to the present, passed a resolution in the general terms indicated in the

subsidy of £40, to builders of houses coming
within the scope of that Act.

and seaside districts in Northern Ireland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Every Rural and

is a Sanitary Authority and employ for the
purpose of supervision of Public Health
