POLICE OCCUPATION OF
CO-OPERATIVE HALL.
4. Mr. McGUFFIN asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he is in a position to state
when the premises known as the Co-operative Hall, Frederick Street, Belfast, commandeered for police occupation in 9th
January, 1922, are likely to be handed back
to the Co-operative Society; whether he is
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. McGuffin]
aware of the serious inconvenience and loss
occasioned to this important organization by
the long continued occupation of these premises, and whether, in justice to this Society
he will take measures to have them restored
at the earliest possible date, seeing that
peace and order are restored and the need
for their retention has ceased?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Every effort has
been made to obtain alternative accommodation for the Constabulary at present
in occupation of the Co-operative Hall,
Frederick Street, but I regret no suitable
alternative building is available. I need
scarcely point out that the locality was a
very troublesome one during the period of
recent outrages in the city. The presence
of a platoon in Frederick Street Hall has
done much to bring about the present
peaceable state of affairs. It is, however,
regarded as imperative to maintain a platoon
in the area so as to preserve this satisfactory
condition of affairs.
Efforts are still being made to obtain
other premises at reasonable cost for adaptation, etc., but many difficulties have been
experienced.
As soon as Frederick Street Hall can be
vacated, either by securing alternative
accommodation, or by withdrawal of the
platoon, if conditions permit of it, steps
will be taken accordingly.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Arising out of the
answer by the right hon. Gentleman, can
he say if there is any other trading organisation in the city which has been subject to
the same treatment as the Belfast Cooperative Society, seeing that you have had
their premises in occupation for the last two
and a half years?

Friend replies, may I ask what is the

large hall at the Grove not suit the convenience of the police? We are now in
times of peace, and it should not be
necessary to commandeer private property.
Mr. GRANT: Arising out of the right hon.

and he promised then-
Mr. SPEAKER: Will the hon. Gentleman
put his remarks in the form of a question.

others to visit these premises? I happened

Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard to
the supplementary question put by my hon.
Friend, the Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Grant) it is perfectly true that I received
a deputation, and I promised them, as indicated in my answer to-day, that if suitable
accommodation for the purpose is available
we shall only be too glad to vacate this
place. It is costing the Government a lot.
Mr. McGUFFIN: It is costing the Cooperative Society a great deal more.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I can assure the

OFFENCES AGAINST LICENSING LAWS.
5. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister
of Home Affairs, if he can state the number
of offences against the Licensing Laws and
the number of cases of drunkenness in Belfast and each of the Six Counties of Northern
Ireland during the first six months of 1923
or 1924 respectively; also the number of
offences and cases of drunkenness on Sundays
in the same districts and for the same
periods?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It would be difficult, within the compass of an oral answer,
to give in detail the particulars asked for
by the hon. Member, but the totals are as
follows:-
Offences against the Licensing Laws by
Publicans and Spirit Grocers during the
first six months of 1923 and the corresponding period of 1924 were 436 and 121
respectively.
Cases of Drunkenness during the same
two periods were 3,650 and 3,177 respectively.
Offences on Sunday by Publicans and
Spirit Grocers during these periods were
164 and 73 respectively.
Cases of Drunkenness on Sunday during
the same periods were 234 and 59 respectively.
I am circulating with the official report a
Return giving the full details asked for by
the hon. Member.

Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the House doth agree with the Committee in the said Resolution."
Mr. DONALD: When this Vote was before the House I asked a question with
regard to it, but I got very little enlightenment. The matter, in fact, arose out of a
question put by my hon. Friend, the Member
for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin), as to the
allocation or expenditure of £2,400 odd for
fees, and the answer was that it was to
cover the fees of the Attorney-General (Mr.
Best), Sir Douglas Hogg, and others. I want
to be clear about this matter. We are quite
satisfied that certain evidence was given before the Judicial Committee on the various
points; first, can the Commission be set up
or be operative? second, can the Crown instruct the Governor-General of Northern
Ireland to appoint a Commissioner? third,
failing this may the Crown make the
appointment? and fourth, is there any constitutional way of setting up the Commission?
When our representatives came to No. 4,
which is a very important point, and is the
one I take exception to, a suggestion was
made by Sir Douglas Hogg. He says the
means are simple. Passing on to consider
the fourth question, as to whether or not
there was any constitutional means of
overcoming the difficulty, and of bringing the
Commission into existence, he said, that in
his opinion, there was a very simple means
and that was by passing an Act of Parlia
ment. Parliament, he said, was the body
which passed the statute to constitute the
Commission, and, if, for any reason, it
turned out to be impracticable to carry out
that particular scheme, Parliament was the
only body that could remedy the difficulty,
by passing through legislation. When I
read that in July I was very much disturbed;
in fact, I wrote to a friend of mine in
London, and do you know what he told me?
He said the Bill was practically based on
the suggestions of Sir Douglas Hogg. That
is the Coercion Bill that we have heard so
much about. I am, as I say, disturbed about
this matter, and I want to know why we
are paying other people who do not represent Ireland. As my hon. and learned
Friend (Mr. Robb) said we had very capable
men in Northern Ireland, men who could
have represented us as well as Sir Douglas
Hogg. I fail to understand how he could
go and introduce other means whereby
the Government could bring in a Bill with
regard to this matter. If I do not get a
clear explanation I am going to divide the
House as a matter of protest.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
This matter has been rather sprung upon
me, but I will endeavour to the best of my
ability to meet the arguments of my hon.
Friend. First of all, it would be an ungracious thing to divide the House on a Vote
to pay the fees of Counsel, who was engaged
by the Government to put up their case
before the Judicial Committee of the Privy
Council, in view of the fact that the findings
of the Judicial Committee were all in favour
of Ulster, that is to say, they confirmed the
opinion upon which I stood from the very
beginning with regard to the Commission
and supported all through, as I was, by a
unanimous Cabinet, and this House. Sir
Douglas Hogg's duties there were to defend
Ulster's case, and our own Attorney-General
was associated with him, also junior counsel
and solicitors who were acting in London
under instructions from our Attorney-
General. Having won his case Sir Douglas
Hogg's remarks may possibly be read in two
ways. I myself understood what he meant
by the remarks to which the hon. Member
(Mr. Donald) refers, to be that legislation
in the British House of Commons could be
introduced, defining the duties of the Commission under Article XII of the Treaty;
and both in the House of Commons and in
the House of Lords on the other side, an
attempt was made so to define the duties of
the Commission, that it would have been
possible for us to consider favourably the
appointment of a Commissioner. But the
energies of our friends in both Houses unfortunately, were not rewarded with success.
Consequently we are faced with the position
in which we now find ourselves. I certainly
think that whatever learned cousel, in
a case of this sort, may say or do, so long as
he wins his case it would be very inappropriate for us to cast any aspersions upon him
for language he may use in what he considers the best way of conducting his case.
Mr. COOTE: Is this not a matter in which
silence is golden? We submitted our case to
this very eminent lawyer supported by our
own Attorney-General. He fought our
battle, and, from his point of view, fought
it successfully. If we take the very language a man may use in bringing his case
into court and hold him responsible for every
word he utters, I am afraid we would have

some trouble. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
If we give a brief to any eminent lawyerand the more eminent he is the more independent he will be-he will not like to take
the brief if we hold him responsible for every
word he utters. If we look at the objects—
were the objects attained? (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) We won our case.
We are
just where we were on the whole question.
Sir Douglas did not impress us in the least
in anything he said. It is a matter for Sir
Douglas Hogg himself as to the line of
action he takes in defending us. I think
the more we talk upon this we are creating
a bad case. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
If we just let the matter drop we will be
doing a greater service to Ulster.
To
Sir ROBERT LYNN: In fairness to Sir
Douglas Hogg, a colleague of mine in the
other House, I ought to point out as one who
went through all the negotiations and all
that happened, that my hon. Friend the
Member for East Belfast (Mr. Donald) is
quite wrong in saying the Bill was drafted

lawyer knew that there was no hope whatever of their carrying through their case.
They actually had their Bill drafted before
ever the Privy Council Committee sat.
blame Sir Douglas Hogg for his suggestion
is I think most unfair. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I think this House and the
Loyalists of Ulster are under a deep debt of

Attorney-General and the law officers for
the way they fought that case. They fought
it magnificently, and instead of saying anything derogatory I personally would rather
see the House passing a vote of thanks for
the way he presented the case. There never
was a case handled with greater success or

Mr. McGUFFIN: I hope the hon. Member
for East Belfast (Mr. Donald) will not press
the House in this matter. I would point
out that the money is being paid for what
was done inside. He fulfilled his duties well
there. He upheld our case very successfully.
I do not think it would be right to found
any suspicion with respect to the learned
gentleman upon a remark. Some people felt
rather acutely over the fact that the
Northern Bar had not had more representatives in the counsel before the Judicial Committee. That is another matter entirely.
Our own Attorney-General performed his
duties, I understand, adequately, and we
had the best legal talent available in the
person of Sir Douglas Hogg. Now, as he
performed his duties well, I think it would
be rather ungrateful on our part to be lacking in appreciation.

CIAL SECRETARY OF THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): This resolution is the forerunner of a Bill which, if it
secures a First Reading to-day, will be available for distribution in the Vote Office. The
main principles of the Bill are administrative, and the objects are to give
effect to the finance proposals brought be
fore the House by my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance when making his budget
statement earlier in the year.
One of the principal provisions is to give
some relief to taxpayers in respect of motor
taxation. It would confer a surrender value
upon motor licences, and it also reduces the
amount of surcharge on the motor licences
granted for shorter periods than one year.

Economic Conditions in Rural Ulster.
Dr. MORRISON: I beg to move:
That this House views with grave concern
the Economic Conditions existing in rural
Ulster, especially as regards the farmers
and agricultural labourers, which are deplorable, and not to be remedied by Grants
in Aid of Local Rates; and calls upon the
Government to formulate a policy which
will give both farmers and workers a fair
opportunity to develop the resources of the
greatest industry in Ulster, thereby relieving the pressure of congestion and unemployment in urban centres.
The immediate cause of the Motion, which
is on the Order Paper, and which hon.
Members can see for themselves, is the little
discussion we had the other day with regard
to the egg industry. But I would have raised
this question, and indeed I have raised it,
on many occasions since I came into this
House. Some people, I believe, ask what
business it is of mine to interfere with duties
that belong to ordinary Members and farmers
generally. My excuse is that I have for
thirty years lived amongst a population of
farmers and labourers, and have attended to
them medically-5,000 people. I know their
wants and I know their difficulties.
Perhaps I
do many
and it is
know them better than
Members of this House,
simply because I respect
and admire their independence and pluck
under most distressing circumstances, and
sympathise with them for the hard and
distressing conditions under which many of
them carry on their work, that I support
them in every claim that is just and fair. I
think I also have the right to speak for them,
considering that I represent the University,
and that in every parish in Northern
Ireland there are four or five graduates from
that University, who are directly or indirectly
affected by the prosperity of the farming
community. Therefore, I think it is my duty
to interfere in everything that has a tendency
to promote the welfare of the community,
and consequently the welfare of those people.
I hope, and I believe that everybody in
this House is as sympathetic on this matter
as I am. I regret to say that on one occasion,
and on one occasion only, I have noticed
that the Labour Members of the House were
inclined to criticise the grant the Agricultural Department gave to the Farmers'
Union. I know these Labour Members well,
and I consider them fair, reasonable, moderate men.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Dr. MORRISON: If they knew the conditions under which the agricultural labourer
carries on his work, and the distressing
conditions that have governed agriculture
for the last three years, I think that instead
of cavilling and raising objections they would
give every assistance they could.
I confess at once that the Cabinet has done
everything it could. I have no fault to find
with anything the Cabinet has done or with
what it has not done. Many of the conditions
to which I have referred are legacies handed
over to this Government from the British
Parliament, and reforms cannot be effected
in a day. To the Prime Minister especially
I would pay a tribute for what he has done.
I quite understand that the Minister of
Finance and the different heads of the
Departments here are friendly, but for the
special grant we got to relieve the distress
of secondary teachers, the grant to the Derry
Bridge, and the grant of £128,000, which we
have got for two years, I think that, while
everybody else deserves credit, the Prime
Minister is the man to whom it is really due.
1305 Conditions in Rural Ulster
Conditions in Rural Ulster 1306
14 OCTOBER 1924
I want to stress this policy the Prime
Minister has adopted. I want also to point
out that so far as I can judge we as a Government should go further. As many of the
Members of this House know, the present
year is the worst within living memory for
the agricultural community. People talk
about the labourers in Belfast, but I can
tell you for a fact that the majority of the
farm labourers, and many of the farmers,
were on three days out of six all through
this summer wet to the skin, when they were
at their work. They went into the house,
but there was no turf brought home from
the bog, and how they managed to dry their
clothes and carry on their work under the
conditions that prevailed would be a puzzle
to the town dweller.
I propose to deal with what I call the
injustice done to the agricultural industry
in the incidence of rates and taxes, and when
I speak of the agricultural industry I mean
farmers and labourers and the people who
carry on industry in rural Ulster. To my
mind the interests of the farmer and the
labourer are closely allied, and what affects
the prosperity of the farmer affects the prosperity of the labourer, and vice versa. Going
down from the House last Thursday I came
across a gentleman who is perhaps one of the
most experienced local government administrators in the Six Counties. I refer to
Senator Long. He is the chairman of the
Londonderry Asylum Board, chairman of the
Londonderry County Council, and he has
been for thirty years chairman of the Limavady Rural District Council. We were
talking about these conditions, and Senator
Long said:
"The questions you raised have been very
prominently before us in connection with
the Asylum, and I can get you figures to
show how the legislation presses unduly
on the ratepayers. I will call with the
clerk and ask him to send them to you."
I have the figures here, supplied by the
clerk of the Londonderry Asylum, and they
bear out what I say is the injustice done
in the administration of the finances of the
Asylum by British legislation. But what I
want to deal with is something in addition
to that, namely the whole administration of
Local Government affairs in Ulster in
addition to the asylums-the whole administration, not a part such as is covered by
the asylums. The asylums were established
in 1821. At first all the expense of running
the asylums fell on the local rates raised
by the Grand Jury Acts. In 1874 the
Treasury paid their first contribution, and
that first contribution was half the cost of
maintenance or four shillings a week,
whichever was tho lesser.
This continued until the passing of the
Local Government Act of 1898 when a
special grant was made by the Treasury to
uneet past moral liabilities, and the year
1897 was fixed as the standard year for
their contribution. All further additions
to the expenditure were in future to come
wholly from local sources. This also
applied to the Medical Charities Act and
all Local Government Board administration
except in one little respect, and that was
the payment of salaries for the Medical
Officers of the Unions. The medical profession, the Poor Law officers scattered
over Ireland could not get holidays. The
position was that, owing to existing arrangeof
ments, the whole
the cost of the
holidays came off the ratepayers. Representations were made to the Treasury with
the object of their paying half of that.
The Treasury consented, with the result that
all Beards of Guardians in Ireland and in
Ulster gave the doctors a four-weeks holiday;
but that was a special case. How did this
system work out, and how did it affect the
local ratepayers-that is in the main the
farmers? The grant in aid in 1874 paid half
the cost of the eight shillings a week, but
long before 1898 it had ceased to do so. An
asylum that has to provide new accommodation suffers in the Capitation Grant. Inspectors and public opinion demand considerate treatment and every facility for the
care of these lunatics. Londonderry Asylum,
as well as all other bodies in Ulster.
approved of special consideration being given
to these afflicted people, and consequently an
auxiliary asylum has been built at Gransha
costing £51,381. The original Londonderry
Asylum was built to accommodate 120
patients, and was to serve the counties of
Tyrone and Donegal. The cost was £27,500.
Additions were made to accommodate
337 patients at a cost of
Tyrone and Donegal got an asylum each of
their own and the patients were transferred
in 1853 and in 1866. Notwithstanding this
relief of the congestion the auxiliary asylum
had to be built at Gransha to accommodate
64 patients. There is a total deficiency in the
grant in aid of maintenance since 1910, that
is taking the year 1897 as the standard year
--from 1910 up to the present time there is
a total loss, which comes on the ratepayers,
of £7,950. This has to be made good from
local taxation, which, as I maintain, comes
in the main from the agricultural industry.
£29,000.
What I would like to know is when is this
to stop? We have been demanding increased
care and increased comfort for everybody
who is distressed, and rightly demanding it,
and if this thing goes on I can see that the
burden of taxation will grow indefinitely.
The grant in aid for the last four years represented 16 per cent. instead of 50 per cent.
of the capitation grant. The total amount of
rates raised in County Derry-and this illu-
1307 Conditions in Rural Ulster
Conditions in Rural Ulster 1308
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Dr. Morrison]
strates what happens all over the county in
connection with different Local Government
bodies, such as the rural councils and the
urban councils; and County Derry, as I have
said before, is fairly representative of the
other counties in Ulster-has risen steadily
from 1897. In 1905 the rate amounted to
£40,000. In 1918 it amounted to £56,000. In
1920 it was £77,000, that is an increase of
£37,000 as compared with 1905. Now I take
1920 with its £30.000 of an increase as a fair
sample. We had some troubles afterwards
which probably increased the rate, but they
should not be counted. At any rate in 1923
the amount raised by rates in the county
was £100,000, and in 1924 it was £110,000.
This obviously affects every farmer and
labourer in the county. The average man
who occupies a district council cottage pays
his rates. It has been decided as a policy
by the farmers in many cases where they
let houses to ask the tenant to be liable for
the rates. Previous to twenty or thirty years
ago the rates were a negligible quantity. No
farmer bothered about paying them. If he
got the rent the thing was all right. Now
the bargain is always made for the working
man to pay the rates. I had a woman in
my house yesterday morning doing some
work. She lives in a district council cottage,
and that woman tells me that her rates when
she first got the cottage were less than 10s
a year. Two years ago, she says, they were
close on 30s. For the last two years
they have been reduced, but these reductions
are due not to the system under which she
lives so much as to the special grant given
by this House.
We would like to see if something could
be done to meet the difficulties. Work,
such as is carried on in an asylum for the
treatment of lunatics, medical treatment for
the poor, the prevention of disease, I maintain, are matters of national moment as well
as local matters, and the Government have
recognised that fact by paying this grant.
That being so, I think we should demand
that we should get the half of all the expenditure that is incurred in regard to these
matters. In olden days, in my young days,
the question of the rent was the serious
thing. To-day it is the question of taxation.
The labourers pay their share of indirect
taxation. They pay taxes on whisky and
tobacco and other dutiable articles, and they
can surely in justice claim relief from direct
taxation when it is a matter of promoting
the national well-being.
In connection with the question of National
Health Insurance, I would like to say--
and I do it freely-that, of all the
Ministers with whom I have had to deal,
the most friendly, if I can make a distinction
at all, is the Minister of Labour. He meets
me if it is at all possible, and I think he
has got some ideas from me that have been
helpful to him. I think that with my assistance he will be able to straighten things out.
Everybody knows that this matter of health
insurance causes a heavy tax on the farmer
and on the labourer. I have pressed again
and again to find out how this money has
been spent. I have pointed out to my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Labour, that
the contribution has been doubled, and that
we have no means of telling whether the insured get the benefit of this doubled contribution. I take the Presbyterian report, the
report of my own church, which I have here.
It is managed by men who give the best
service that they can for the help of the poor
and the administration of this fund on a
wide and proper basis. I maintain that
from any of these reports you can gather
no information as to what is done with this
large sum of money. I will read this from
the report:-
The total amount paid in cash benefit
to members since the inception of the Act,
up to the 31st December, 1922, exceeded
£172,000.
That is a very large sum, but I would like
to know how much this Society got in by
contributions from the poor people in Ireland, and then we could tell whether it is
quite as big a sum as we would be inclined
to think from looking at it here. It is an
extraordinary thing, and it has always
caused amazement in my mind, that while
we here pay 8d per member, and
only get disability benefit and maternity benefit, in England, for 2d
more, every insured person gets full
medical benefits. He gets the full attendance of a medical man of his own choosing,
no matter how long he may be sick. Here
he gives 8d., and he gets no medical attendance
at all.
There is another point that I want to press,
and this is a thing that affects the farmer
and the labourer. The Minister has inspectors placed in different parts of Ulster. It
is the duty of these men to see that the
farmer and the labourer contribute and put
the stamps on the paper. I have again and
again urged on him that, in the matter of
seeing justice done to the poor and to the
helpless, who cannot defend themselves, he
should instruct these inspectors to place
themselves at the service of any person who
has a complaint to make, and who is being
refused his or her benefit, possibly on some
technicality. I recognise that the Minister
has done a great deal, but I think that in
some cases he is up against forces that he
does not want to tackle just for a little time
until he gets more firmly established. I would
like to see him dealing with this question-
I put that to the House-in the interests of

the poor. The average working man in rural
Ulster is as loyal and as ready to stand by,
fight for, and defend the interests of Ulster
as any man in Belfast or any place over the
Six Counties.
I want to take the question of education,
and to show you how that injuriously affects
local taxation. I lay aside altogether what President Kruger called moral and intellectual damages. We differ in our estimates of that. I lay
that aside, and I just touch on the financial
question. I take from the Lynn Report a
statement that practically all the schools in
Ulster are voluntary schools. For 150 or 200
years-long before the British Government
passed the Irish National Education Actprimary education of a sort and what was
called classical education was going on. I
have in my district two schools with which I
am associated, and those schools were there
since at any rate the time of Oliver Cromwell.
They have been built and rebuilt, and 1
maintain that if that was done, as it was
done, by the Christian Churches, without
the aid of a penny from the Government
until the Education Act was passed, probably seventy or eighty years ago, it is
unfair in the case of these two schools where
the whole expense except the teaching is
paid by the people, that where good moderate buildings are provided the people should
be penalised if they do not transfer their
schools, and at the same time be compelled
to build other schools and to pay a rate in
support of other schools. That is the
position in the country in that respect. I
had in my district a national school inspector. He was a very clever, capable man.
I said to him-"in that district which you
rule how many schools are unnecessary?"
and he told me that there were 18 schools
that were clearly unnecessary, and that 10
more could easily be dispensed with-28
schools. I figured that that, at a cost of
£300, is a loss to the State of £11,400 a year
in that district alone. If you look at the
Estimates you will find, I think, that we
have 15 inspectors, so you can calculate the
total loss. This House has appointed a committee to inquire into the salaries of primary
teachers. You propose to reduce them, but

the Government will not consider me as

am not going-I have no right-to say anything as to what that Commission are doing
until they bring in their report. I believe
if that Commission go on and it looks as if

very top. If they go on in that spirit I

question is a big question. The biggest
question we have is agriculture. There are
tremendous capabilities in it. Instead of
looking at the flooding of land, crops destroyed, people wringing their hands, suffering in a morose mood, feeling that everything
is bad-I do not see these things at all. I
see drained land, well tilled fields.
smiling farmsteads, industrious little people,
children of poor people getting employment.
Now everybody seems to be crouching round
the fire, keeping in the villages, hiding
round the corner, nothing doing. It is a
hopeless state to see and one that is a disgrace to Ulster. I hope the Minister of
Agriculture will try to bring about a change.
I submit he can. I want to show why he
can. Our climate is depressing, Heaven
knows, but I think it can be compared with
the climate of Norway. Yet the Norwegians
live by agriculture. They do not live by
I see
fishing alone. Denmark has an extraordinary climate, and geographically it is
the same size as Ulster. The Danes are as
well educated, as civilised, and as Christian
as the Ulster people, and they are as refined
as the people of Ulster. The Dane is a
credit to his country, and industrially he is
far ahead of us. His land is no better than,
if it is as good as, the land of Ulster, and
I question if, on the whole, he has a better
climate. What do we find in Denmark in these
decadent days? We find that Denmark is the
first of all the foreign countries sending
bacon, hams, and other foodstuffs into the
British Market. In that comparison I include Ireland, to Our own condemnation.
Denmark is ahead of all other countries as
an importer of foodstuffs into Great Britain,
and here we are, with all our Ministries of
Agriculture, Ministries of Commerce, Committees here and Committees there, and
£1,000 here and £1,000 there. But we have
got the men who should be tilling the farms
and draining the land sitting by the fire
reading the newspapers and saying, "Coote
is a fool and should be out of politics." You
have the men who are willing to do the work
if you encourage them, and it is the duty
of the Ministry of Agriculture to lead and
encourage the people. Denmark is killing
from 50,000 to 60,000 hogs per week, and here
is Ulster, with the same area and with
sturdy people second to none, only killing
from 5,000 to 6,000 hogs in the same period.
5,000 to 6,000 in Ulster and 50,000 to 60,000 in
Denmark. Ulster shipped £1,500,000 worth of
bacon last year, but she ought to treble it.
She did ship £2,202,132 worth of eggs, but
she ought to increase that by 50 per cent.
She would be more contented and there
would be far less irritation and ill-will in
the Province. Last year we warned the
Ministry of Agriculture that there would be

try to give some inducement to the farmer
to grow more flax. Now we are face to face

the works. Flax has paid as no other crop
has paid this year. Although it has been a
wet season flax has grown well and is scutching heavily in the mills. There is a high percentage of fibre and the flax is selling at a
guinea a stone. We are losing the benefit of

farmer to increase his output. We were
laughed at and it was said we were talking
through our hats, but the country sees
where we are now. In addition to our other
difficulties unemployment stares us in the
face.

a matter which should not be dealt with

haphazard. Merely because a certain river

There are millions of acres of good land
going to loss and the crops are being destroyed. There are so many small holdings
and there is such a hunger for land that in
the spring time the people will till their
low-lying land because it is in their blood to
do so.
Then the Autumn comes with its
floods and destroys it all. The Minister
ought to take this question into serious consideration. I am sure that in his heart he
says he will, but he must take the rock out
of the road and he must give the people the

an easy matter to place the power in the

Do something on a well-considered scale instead of answering questions here to-day
about £128,000. That is a mere bagatelle.

us
to as high a state of perfection as Denmark or

The PRIME MINISTER: Before I make
a few remarks, I was going to ask my hon.
Friends who have moved and seconded this
Resolution whether they would be willing
to drop out everything after the word
deplorable," the effect of which, I think,
would be to enable all hon. Members in the
House to support my hon. Friends in their
Resolution. It would be impossible for the
Government to join in supporting the hon.
Members if this question of the grants in
aid of local rates were not cut out, because
we are pledged to that, and, therefore, it
would be impossible for us to vote for the
Resolution as it stands. We are quite prepared, however, to vote for it down to the
word "deplorable," which I hope will satisfy
my two hon. Friends.

in with the views of the Prime Minister
and ask leave to amend the Resolution on
the lines he has suggested.

on this very point?
The PRIME MINISTER: I think, all the
same, my hon. Friend (Mr. Crawford) will
see the great difficulty in asking the Government to vote for the Question here. The

to vote for the Resolution as it stands.

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I only want to intervene in this debate for a few moments, because sometimes I think a feeling gets
abroad that we in Belfast take no interest
in the rural districts. I do not think there
is an hon. Member of this House, whether
he represents, as I do, an industrial seat or
a rural seat, who is not keenly interested
in our premier industry. After all agriculture is the premier industry in this
country-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and
are grateful to the two hon. Members
who in very moderate and very wise language have brought this matter before the
House to-day. Agriculture is passing
through a very terrible time. For some
years to come it will want the fostering
care of a sympathetic Government, and I,
as representing an industrial seat, would
appeal most sincerely and most heartily to
the Members of the Government to help
agriculture at this time, and in helping
agriculture they are going to help the whole
of Ulster, because if the agricultural industry is prosperous it will keep a great
many people on the land who would otherwise leave it. Believe me there is nothing
in which we hon. Members of this House
could take part that would do greater good
to our country than in keeping the people
on the land. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We hear a great deal of talk about "Back
to the land." It is a very difficult thing to
get people back to the land once they have
left it, and, therefore, our business ought to
be to concentrate on keeping them there.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).

[Sir Robert Lynn]
I agree with the hon. Member for the
University (Dr. Morrison) and the hon.
Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr.
Coote) that the burden of taxation does fall
with undue weight upon the agricultural
districts, and I think the Government might
consider the whole question of the incidence
of taxation. We could have no better man
to go into that subject than my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr.
Pollock). We know his sympathy as well as
his ability and his all-round knowledge of
the conditions that prevail in Ulster. I do
agree with my hon. Friend, the Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison) that the time
has come when the whole cost of local
government services should be gone into and
revised. Parliament for the last twenty
years has been imposing enormous burdens
on local councils, without ever thinking for
a moment of how the money is going to be
raised. It is all very well for members of
Parliament to shout vote for things, and
then leave other people to pay for them. I
am in the position that I have always
preached economy, and I hope I shall continue to do so. I think we have got to go
into the whole of the services of Northern
Ireland, not with the object of seeing how
much more we can spend, but with the
object of seeing how much we can really
save. I think our whole local government
system-roads and quite a number of other
things that I am not going to deal with now
-might be remodelled on lines that would
take a very heavy burden off the shoulders
of the unfortunate ratepayers.
There is just one other point that I should
like to stress, so far as the Minister of
Agriculture is concerned, and that is in
regard to afforestation. I really think there
is no part of the United Kingdom that calls
out more for afforestation than Ulster does.
Those of us who know Ulster well know that
you can grow trees in every part of the
Province, and grow them successfully. Unfortunately, it is one of the things that you
find difficulty in getting the smaller people
to engage in, though, I think that the
Minister of Agriculture might do a great deal
in that regard through schools, and also by
placing grants of young trees at the disposal of farmers for nothing, or, if that is
not possible, at a very small cost indeed. I
think that a very excellent scheme of afforestation might be introduced in this Province.
I do not say that it is going to bring its reward immediately, but as my hon. Friend
for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Coote) says
we ought to take a long view in these matters, and we ought to think of the benefit
it would be to the whole community.
Then another thing is, can we do anything
to get cheap power? I was greatly interested
in the last Session of Parliament when I
thought there was going to be cheap power

-because if we could get cheap power in

We are trying not to do away with the sawmilling industry. As I said the other day

Mr. COOTE: Would you question it if I

Mr. ARCHDALE: We met them on several

egg industry, a far greater industry than

As regards Education, the Ulster Dairy
School is full, the Greenmount Agricultural
School is full, the North-West School at
Strabane is full, and the Agricultural
Scholarships at Queen's University are
taken up. We are doubling the accommodation at Greenmount School, and I think that
when we have done that there will be no
occasion for anyone to say our people are
not as well educated as they possibly can be
to take up Agriculture in this country.
Agriculture and research must go together.
There is no doubt about that in these times.
The notion is long dead that the fool of the
family goes into agriculture. In my opinion
it takes the cleverest man in the family for
agriculture and there is no doubt that our
farmers are as shrewd and clever as they
are in any other country. Anyone who
comes to this country and sees the farmers

We do not know of anything that can be
done to further that state of things, but
anything that can be done, and anything
that anybody can suggest should be done
we will do.
With regard to the interest taken in farming, so many people wish to visit the Ulster
Dairy School that we have had to put a stop
to it. There have been nineteen visits this

very keen interest in the work done there.
There were about forty different parties of
farmers and their wives who wished to visit

THE CURFEW ORDER.

Home Affairs whether he will now consider
the withdrawal of the Curfew Order in view
of the peaceful conditions now prevailing in
Northern Ireland.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir

Member to the reply to his question of 13th

Expiring Laws Continuance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed :
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
This Bill continues temporarily certain
enactments whether of the Parliament of the
United Kingdom or of this Parliament which
may be regarded as still being experimental
or liable to revision. A certain date is fixed
for their continuance, namely, 31st December,
1925. The Bill has been framed so as to fit
in with the corresponding Imperial Bill of
the present year. That Bill applies to
Northern Ireland. The Expiring Laws Continuance Bill of Great Britain or of the
United Kingdom applies to Northern Ireland
in so far as it deals with any enactments relating to a subject with respect to which the
Parliament of Northern Ireland has not the
power to make laws, and the present Bill
supplements this provision by dealing with
enactments in respect of which we have
power to make laws. The two measures,
therefore, taken together deal with all temporary laws applicable to Northern Ireland
according as they come within the one
category or the other.

years only, but as will be seen from part

Continuance Act, as long as the Housing conditions in Rural Districts remain what they

This Section which is being continued for

The next measure to which I would direct
the attention of hon. Members is the Inspectors of Weights and Measures Act
(Northern Ireland), 1923. I think it would be
desirable to recall to the memory of hon.
Members the circumstances under which it
became necessary to introduce the Weights
and Measures Act of 1923, which is included
in the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill now
before the House. The Constabulary Act
(Northern Ireland), 1922, establishing the
R.U.C. provided for the continuance of the
system formerly in operation in Ireland,
under which the duty of inspection of
Weights and Measures was imposed upon
members of the police force in possession of
a certificate of qualification from the Board
of Trade as prescribed by Statute. It was
subsequently found that the number of R.I.C.
possessing this prescribed certificate of
qualification who joined the R.U.C., was entirely inadequate for the efficient discharge
of this important duty and it, therefore, became necessary to obtain statutory authority
to enable the work to be carried out by
persons other than members of the Force.
The Weights and Measures Act, 1923, gave
the Government the required authority to
avail ourselves of the services of ex-members
of the R.I.C. who possessed the Board of
Trade Certificate and who were qualified to
undertake the work.
This arrangement as hon. Members are
aware, was regarded as a temporary expedient only, and the House will remember
that last year the mover of this Bill-I think
it was myself-expressed the hope that it
would not be necessary to continue this Act
further as it was expected that a sufficient
number of members of the R.U.C. would
obtain the necessary Board of Trade Certificate to do away with the necessity of
employing persons who are not members of
that Force as Inspectors of Weights and
Measures. I regret to say that these expectations have not been realised and at the
examinations held in April last none of the
candidates belonging to the R.U.C. was
successful. I am informed that the standard
required from the candidates is now so high
that it is very difficult for a man who has
police duties to perform to reach it. The
question of whether we should arrange to
release a number of police from their
ordinary duties so that they can prepare
themselves for the next examination, or
whether we should ask the local authorities
to undertake the work is now under consideration, but in the meantime the work of
examining weights and measures must be
carried on, and, therefore, we must continue
last year's Act for another period so that
we may not be left without any Inspectors
whatsoever. I have no further observations
to make on this Measure, and I, therefore,
beg to move.
Mr. COOTE: I wish to make a few observations on some of the measures which have
been brought to the notice of the House by
the learned Attorney-General, and particularly on that one to which he alluded
just before he sat down, namely the Inspectors of Weights and Measures Act. This
is the third time that authority is asked
from this House as a result of the dilatory
conduct of the police, or those in charge of
the police, or the Home Office, in not having
measures complete for the inspection of
weights and measures. You would imagine
that the object was to carry out a survey of
some of our colonies or something equally
important in its functions, whereas it is
just a simple inspection of weights and
measures such as we have been accustomed
to all our lives, where an ordinary sergeant
of police comes round with his standard
weights and measures. He simply has the
necessary adjustments made by an ordinary
smith, a white smith. In the past they
simply came along and stamped these
weights and measures, and they did the
whole thing as a matter of course.
Now, simply because this thing has been
overlooked and shelved year after year the
Attorney-General builds a case, from the information given to him of course, that there
is such a tremendous inspection and such a
tremendous examination that the men cannot undertake it if they have to do ordinary
police work. Why you could go into any
barracks and get half a dozen men who could
carry out these very elementary duties. It
is only a matter of time, and why there
should be a Board of Trade examination of
such an intricate pattern would beat the

I should like to ask further, in connection
with the Civil Authorities (Special Powers)
Act-I am speaking from memory and cannot recall the circumstances under which
that Act was passed-am I right in being

in fact-does not the Minister consult the

is taken depriving the citizens of their right

and I am sure the Ministry of Home Affairs

There
may be certain circumstances in which the
Minister of Home Affairs must act in this
way, but does he do so in concert with the

My next point is in regard to Summer
Time. Well, I do not believe in being in
the humiliating position of saying ditto to
every Act that the British House of Commons
passes. I think it is a great misfortune
that we will not act until the British
authority acts, and then say that they have
set us the example. I hold that the time
has come when we ought to realise that we
control an area of our own, and I think
we ought to take steps to do the best thing
in the interests of that area in the circumstances peculiar to it, and in the many
matters that come up affecting it. Sometimes this Parliament is asked to wait until
it sees what is done across the water. We
are a community by ourselves, self-supporting, and, I hope, self-developing. Certainly
we will have to develop ourselves if we are
to develop at all. We must look after the
citizens in our area according to the requirements of the local situation. I want to say
that I object to the application of Summer
Time on behalf of the great farming community who form the largest industry and
probably half the electorate of this Province.
I object for very cogent reasons. The farmers
cannot carry on their industry properly
because of the conditions of this Act. They
have difficulty in the ingathering of their
crops if you impose upon them a day which
brings them out at an hour in the morning
when the dew is on the crops. They must
attend to other things or walk about until
the sun rises in the heavens. I hold that
you are taking one-eighth of the time of
the husbandman, and that is a very
serious thing in the economic conditions
that prevail in Northern Ireland. I object
for other reasons. I hold that there is something unfortunate in the whole of this
Summer Time business. I hold that it is wrong
from the medical point of view. It is doing
an injustice to childhood. It is disorganising
home life; it is making the children restless
and nervous. You know that children will
not go to sleep contentedly while there is
daylight. All these things are unfortunate
for the child life of the country, and
latterly, whatever the reason, be it divine
or otherwise, while you have tried to improve
the hand of the clock and the circle of
the sun there has been no blessing to agriculture or any other industry either in
Ireland or in Great Britain. You want to
be wiser than your Maker. For these
practical reasons I object to Summer Time.
I know that Ministers may say "Why cannot farmers change their hours for
commencing and ending their work?" You
cannot ask a lot of labouring men employed

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I have to admit that I am somewhat involved in the question affecting weights and
measures. The House will recollect that on
two former occasions objection was taken by
many Members to the manner in which the
Government had to deal with this affair,
and I promised that I would personally see
that every step was taken to qualify
members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
to take up the duties of inspectors of
weights and measures. I have constantly
inquired into the progress of those who
were preparing for these examinations,
and, like the rest of my colleagues, I
was hoping that it would be possible for
a sufficient number of the selected men of
the Royal Ulster Constabulary to qualify,
and, therefore, to enable us as a Government
to appoint them in place of ex-constables
who were carrying on, as we thought temporarily, this very delicate work. However,
to our great surprise, and also of course to
our great disappointment, the result of the
examinations was that they were not successful. The men tried and they failed. I then
made careful inquiry, and I discovered that
the examination was a very exhaustive one
and a very difficult one for them to pass. I
know that my hon. Friend opposite (Mr.
Coote) has a ready remedy for all these
things. He says we ought to improvise in
some way and make our own regulations.
and that it does not matter very much. A
man can go in and examine scales and go
out again, and that is all there is in it.
That may be. By the Act of 1920, Section 4,
taken with sub-section 1 and sub-section 7,
it will be seen that
Subject to the provisions of this Act
the Parliament of Northern Ireland shall
have power to make laws
with the
following limitations . . . The protection of traders of Northern Ireland from
fraud.
And the consequence is that it is very doubtful whether it is possible for us to lower
the standard of the examinations in any
way. We are faced with the problem as
to how to continue in future, and my hon.
Friend thinks, of course, that we can institute here a standard lower than that of the
rest of Great Britain. I am very doubtful
about that, because of this Act and the
necessity of assuring the traders throughout
the country that their interests are safeguarded. And remember when we are
fighting this particular point, it is in the
interests of the great consuming public and
of the poor of the country to see that they
are justly treated in all these shops where
the weights and measures have to be constantly examined. As to the very high
standard that is set by the Board of Trade,
that is a matter that I will have to go into.
Now that we are faced with the new situation
-we cannot get our men to pass the examination-I will take up the further point as
to whether it is possible to lower the
standard in any way, and whether it is
possible to arrange for some different method
of carrying out this work or not. But in
the meantime, pending these inquiries, and
seeing that we are not able to get at the
object in one way, we will have to ask the
House to continue the Bill whilst we probe
the possibilities of this delicate matter.
I can assure the House that all we desire
is to have a proper standard, and that there
shall be no fraud, because if there is one
fraud in one shop it may cause the whole
countryside to go wrong. It is apparently
a technical matter to discover whether
scales and weights and measures are of the
high standard they ought to be.
I then pass on to what my hon. Friend
said about the question of certain of our
legislation following too closely the pattern
of legislation on the other side. I have upon
other occasions indicated to the House the
great importance of travelling as far as
possible along the lines adopted by Great
Britain until our financial arrangements are
absolutely stabilised. My right hon. Friend,
the Minister of Finance, is much more
acquainted with the question and able to
deal with the subject than I am, but it is
obvious to everyone here that whilst the
future contribution of Northern Ireland to
Imperial Services is still under discussion by
the Colwyn Committee it is inadvisable for
us in carrying on the Services in this part
of Great Britain to depart too far from the
system carried out in the other parts of
Great Britain for fear that they might be
called new Services and not the same Services
as across the water. If they are the same
Services they will carry with them an equivalent grant to help Ulster to go along the
same lines of social standards in operation
in the other parts of Great Britain. I hope
I have made that clear to the House-the

Mr. McGUFFIN: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman if the Colwyn Committee is

The PRIME MINISTER: My hon. Friend
is quite right in his interjection. I understand that the Colwyn Committee has
practically finished its labours and we are
anxiously awaiting the result. The result, we
hope, will be such that the formula my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Finance, has put
before them will be accepted. The gh
idea at the back of that formula is that for
every Service initiated in the British Parliament, Services which go towards assisting
any particular social class, whatever it may
be, the same quota, the same portion, should
accrue to the Ulster area without any
special application from the Northern
Government; that it should flow from the
Treasury in the ordinary course, because we
as part of Great Britain are entitled to that
part of the taxation which we contribute
to the rest of Great Britain. As my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance says,

I now pass on to the hon. Member's remarks about the continuance of Summer
Time. I know quite well that the Government has to stand up against harsh criticism
from time to time, but we have faced this
problem on many former occasions. I can
only say for my own part that I believe
that the creation of Summer Time has been
of enormous benefit to the people as a whole,
and I think that if a plebescite was taken
throughout the length of England, Scotland,
Wales, and Northern Ireland it would be
predominantly in favour of getting as much
sunshine as possible during the summer
months, especially for the sake of the
children. The idea of the Government is to
introduce a short Bill, and to say that whatever time is fixed by the Imperial authority,
either by Act of Parliament or Order in
Council, our clocks in Ulster should synchronise with British time. The difficulty
and the trouble that would result from
having times different here and across the
water are such that it makes it impossible
to think of going back to the difference of
27 or 25 minutes-I have forgotten the
exact figure-in the old days. Therefore, it
is proposed to bring in a Bill enacting that
whatever time is fixed by the Imperial
Parliament shall automatically be observed
here. At the same time we shall exercise an
influence in coming to a decision, because

PARLIAMENTARY
SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw): I think a considerable amount
of confusion has arisen during the course
of the debate with regard to the Weights
and Measures Act, and there have been what
I regard as some rather serious misstatements and reflections which should not have
been made. How does the matter stand?
Previous to any legislation on our part the
only persons who could act as inspectors of
weights and measures were the Royal Irish
Constabulary. Prior to 1904 I do not know
that there was anything specially required
of these particular men, but in 1904 an Act
of the Imperial Parliament was passed
which is in force at this date. It says that
"The Board of Trade shall provide for the
holding of examinations for the purpose of
ascertaining whether applicants for the post
of inspector. . . England and Ireland both required that the person who is
appointed as inspector shall qualify by a
Board of Trade examination.
That is the position that met us when we
took over office here. There was only one
set of persons required to be inspectors, that
is members of the Royal Irish Constabulary
who had the certificate of the Board of Trade.
Then when the Royal Ulster Constabulary
was formed there was not a sufficient number
in that force who held those certificates. My
recollection is that there were only five who
were qualified to act as inspectors of weights
and measures. Then we passed our Act. I
was entrusted with the duty of proposing the
Second reading of that Act, and there was a
very considerable debate during its progress.
I pointed out, either in Committee Stage or
on the Second reading, that this examination
was not of the trival character that the hon.
Member for North Belfast seemed to think
it was. There seemed to be an idea in the
House that any man in the street who knew
anything about trade-say by going into a
grocer's shop and buying something-could
adjust weights and measures. Weights and
measures like very many other scientific instruments have been greatly changed during
the last number of years. They are very
different as you can see going about the
world. It is not the ordinary balance that
very often has to be adjusted. There are
other manipulations required in instruments
that are of a very delicate character, at any
rate the Board of Trade has so decided. We
have got to deal in commerce with England
and other parts of the world, and it is of
the highest importance that our weights and
measures should be of a proper standard—
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and that our
traders should not be accused of fraud
when they are not guilty of that offence,
but when perhaps the mistake arises from
imperfect instruments.

[Mr. Megaw]
We realised all that. We found it was
absolutely necessary that we should have
inspectors of weights and measures appointed
because during war time that service like
many others was neglected. Hardly any
attention was paid to it during war time.
It became necessary, therefore, to appoint a
proper number of inspectors of weights and
measures through the various counties, and
we took what we considered was the easiest
way. We had men who had the Board of
Trade certificates-men in the R.I.C. They
were the only available men who were qualified prior to the Ulster examination. I do
not think it was an expensive service. Inspectors of weights and measures are paid
at the rate of £150 a year. They are only
able to do the work at that salary because
they have got their pensions. At any rate,
we had no choice. We had to take one or
the other. We had either to abandon the
service altogether or to take the men who
were qualified. The Prime Minister has
already pointed out that we cannot make
any legislation that will infringe on this
question. We have got to take the Board of
Trade Certificate to-day and there is no getting out of it.
What was done was this. We endeavoured
as far as possible in the R.U.C. to have men
trained in the inspecting class who would
get that examination and qualify. Reflections have been made on that school.
When a sufficient number of members of the
R.U.C. did not come forward what did the
Inspector-General do? He invited volunteers
who wished to get into that service to come
forward. All who were thought to have
a chance were given a training in that
school. I am not at all sure that the best
men in the R.U.C., who had better prospects
opening for them in the way of promotion
to Head-constableship and District-Inspectorship, volunteered for that service. Once
men get into the weights and measures
department they seem to get side-tracked
there, and there is little chance of their
doing other work. They are specialised in
that work, and will probably confine themselves to it all their lives. The training was
instituted in Newtownards. I cannot say
of course, whether it was as good a training
as might have been given, at any rate it
was given, and it was the best that could
be instituted by the Inspector-General. Men
went in for the examination, and you have
heard the result.
Reflections have been cast on the men.
Reflections have been cast on the teachers
by those who know little about it, except
that the men did not come up to the
standard. It is easy to make reflections of
that kind. I think if you consider the circumstances you will come to the conclusion
that the Government have done their
best. They have carried out the pledges
they gave. They did their best to see that
men connected with the R.U.C. would be
appointed to these posts. Now it has turned
out unfortunately, and no one is more disappointed than the Minister of Home Affairs
or the Inspector-General that it should be
so, but at any rate there it is. The situation
now is: Is there to be any inspectorate of
weights and measures at all? So far as
the thing stands there is none at present
except that provided for by legislation. The
Prime Minister has mentioned what is to be
done for the future. He has said that as
the Royal Ulster Constabulary evidently are
not able to carry on that service another
way will be provided. I do not think the
House can have any objection to the method
that has been suggested. Let it be open for
public examination. Let all classes of the
community be eligible for that Board of
Trade examination. Let proper men be
appointed, and then the service should be
efficiently conducted. But that cannot be
done at present without legislation. We
have legislation at present with regard to
who may be inspectors. We have only one
class of men who are qualified to be inspectors, and if this objection is to be upheld
nothing can be done except to abandon the
proper inspection of weights and measures
until a new Measure has been introduced.

measures should be a man of high character,
and I think we have as great an assurance
of that if we know that the man belongs to
the Royal Ulster Constabulary as we could
possibly have. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I would be very sorry if you open the door
to all people-people from the universities
and everyone else. Let me ask the House if
a man can come across the Border and enter
for this examination. Do you intend that?
Can a man from England or Scotland enter
for this examination when our fellows are
so terribly stupid that they cannot pass it
themselves? Is the House going to determine that for the future there are no members of the Royal Ulster Constabulary who,
if they had a little further training, will
be able to pass this examination?
I have particular confidence that there are
men in the Royal Ulster Constabulary who,
if they were properly tutored, would give
proper attention to their work, and who,
having passed their examination, would
make ideal inspectors. It would save us a
considerable amount of money, because, as
has been pointed out by the hon. Member
for the University, you would save a great
portion of the salary you are already paying.
I do hope that this will be kept a confined
service to the members of our own Royal
Ulster Constabulary. Then, again, there
are many members of the Special Constabulary who cannot hope to remain constables
for much longer. Why not open it to
them? At any rate I implore the House not
to have this examination whereby any person, of whom we may know nothing, not
even his name, may become an inspector.
Confine it to the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
Encourage the Royal Ulster Constabulary to
be a force of which we may be rightly proud.
Do not side-track a man because he may
show special efficiency in a skilled job. Encourage them all. I do implore the Prime
Minister to go on, as he has been doing,
making every provision for this important
service, in spite of the setbacks the Government has had. I ask him to confine it to
men of the Royal Ulster Constabulary.

Mr. DONALD: I am delighted to hear

house as far back as 1920, and they are not

I only wish there had never been this restriction. It is part of the legacy left
by that Welsh Wizard, Lloyd George, He
brought in restriction of rent at a time when
everybody was profiteering. Even the poorest
man was earning big wages. You restricted
the small property owner from receiving anything at a time when he was duly entitled
to it, and then you continue to restrict after

and you are afraid to remove it because you

that keeps peoples' minds disturbed from

whether the House sits or not, this thing
will go on. I do not like this continuance
of expiring legislation.

Deceased Brother's Widow's
Marriage Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed,
That the Bill be now read a Second Time."
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
We now turn from this interesting question
of weights and measures and various matters
that have been discussed, and come to a
more human matter, that is, to discuss this
Bill which is to remove doubts as to the
application of the Deceased Brothers Widows
Marriage Act, 1921, to Northern Ireland.
The Bill is necessary in order to place the
law relating to marriage with a deceased
brother's widow in the same position as it
has been in Great Britain since 28th July,
1921. On that day the Royal Assent was
given to the Deceased Brother's Widow's
Marriage Act, 1921, and that statute contains
no express words applying it to Northern Ireland. That statute, however, was passed
after the 3rd of May, 1921, which was the
appointed day for the transfer of legislative
power to the Parliament of Northern Ireland, and it relates to a matter in respect
of which the Parliament of Northern
Ireland had at the time of its passing power
to legislate. The Imperial Act, therefore,
has no force in Northern Ireland. It is of
very great importance indeed that the Act
should be declared to be applicable in
Northern Ireland, and to be so applicable
not only from the present date but from
the date of the passing of the Imperial Act--
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-that is, the
28th July, 1921.
In the course of the administration of
the Office of Registrar-General, which is
by
carried on under the direction of my right
hou. Friend, the Minister of Finance, and
his Ministry, evidence has become available
to show that at least one marriage has taken
place in Northern Ireland between a man
and his deceased brother's widow, in the
belief that such marriage was valid
reason of the Act of 1921. Information has
also been received of a case in which it is
desired that a marriage should take place
between parties in Northern Ireland who are
in the same degree of affinity. There is also
good ground for the presumption that a
number of such marriages have been consummated, and that conditions have been
established whose validity should not now
be allowed to be questioned.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Was the officiating
clergyman aware at the time the marriage
was performed?
Mr. BEST: I say not, and of course the
parties were not aware either. As a matter
of fact the Registrar-General for Ireland
issued a circular to registrars of marriages
throughout Ireland. That circular was issued in August, 1921, and it indicated that
marriages could take place under the
authority of the Deceased Brother's Widow's
Marriage Act of 1921. We came to the conclusion, however, that the law was not correctly stated. It is quite clear therefore that
it is necessary to pass legislation to remove
these anomalies, and it is considered best,
in view of any existing cases which may be
affected, to pass such legislation in a declaratory form, so as to give the fullest possible retrospective force at the cost of the
least possible disturbance of present conditions.
Accordingly if hon. Members will look at
Clause 1 of the Bill, they will see that it
declares that the Act of 1921 applies to
Northern Ireland.
It is hereby declared that the Deceased
Brother's Widow's Marriage Act, 1921,
applies to Northern Ireland, and the said
Act shall be deemed to have applied to
Northern Ireland as from the passing
thereof:
The Act of 1921--I have got it here- is itself retrospective. It purports to amend
the Act of 1907, which first legalised marriage
with a deceased wife's sister. As I say the
Act of 1921 is retrospective as from the date
of its own passing, and it achieves this effect
by providing for the insertion of certain
words into the Deceased Wife's Sister
Marriage Act of 1907. The effect of the main
provisions of that Act of 1907 taken in conjunction with the Act of 1921 may be stated
as follows:
"No marriage heretofore or hereafter
contracted between a man and his deceased
1381 Brother's Widow's Marriage Bill- 15
OCTOBER 1924
Second Reading. 1382
wife's sister, or between a man and his deceased brother's widow. within the realm
or without, shall be deemed to have been
or shall be void or voidable, as a civil
contract, by reason only of such affinity."
The words "heretofore" and "hereafter "
of course refer as regards cases within the
1921 Act to points of time before and after
the 28th July, 1921, but the two Acts, taken
together afford protection to persons who,
having contracted marriage within the prohibited degree of affinity either had it annulled-that is, had it annulled when they
learned of its irregularity-or disregarded
it as unlawful and made a further lawful
marriage. The Acts provide that if before
the passing of the Act of 1921-I am talking
now of the two Great Britain Acts-a
marriage between a man and his deceased
brother's widow had been annulled-that is,
annulled by going to a court of law or either
party thereto after the marriage and during
the life of the other had lawfully married
another by ignoring that previous marriage.
the former marriage, that is, the marriage
with the deceased brother's widow is to be
deemed to have become, and to be void upon
and after the date of its annulment or upon
the date on which either party made a further marriage, which was lawful according
to the law as it stood before the passing of
the Act of 1921. This proviso was the inevitable accompaniment of the retrospective
legislation of the two Acts. It has been
thought to be equally necessary that a proviso in analogous terms should accompany
the present Bill, because it deals not only
with the period prior to the passing of the
Act of 1921, but also with the further period
intervening between the passing of the 1921
Act and the date of the passing of the present Bill. The proviso to Clause 1, therefore, enacts a saving for marriages which
may have taken place during this later
period in disregard of previous marriages
which were lawful as the law then stood.
This is the period which is referred to in
the proviso as "on and after the 28th day
of July, 1921, and before the passing of this
Act." If it should be that some persons
have contracted marriages of this description and if the House passes the Bill in its
present form these marriages would be
legalised, not only from the present time, but from the date
on which they
were consummated.
so that relief would be given to such persons, if there be any, who have contracted
such marriages; and in addition to that it
will be open in future for a man if he so
desires to marry his deceased's brother's
widow. I beg to move.
Mr. GRANT: I do not rise to oppose this

Mr. ARCHDALE: This Bill, as the headings say, is
"to amend and remove doubts as to
certain provisions of the Assurance
Companies Act, 1909, as they apply in
Northern Ireland."
an
It is mainly administrative. It is
amending Bill, and it is brought in to remove doubts that have arisen as to people
insured in Northern Ireland under these
Acts. The Bill now under consideration
deals with Assurance matters in general,
while the Industrial Assurance Bill, which we
have already had before the House this afternoon, as its name implies, is confined to a
special class of life assurance. As hon. Members are aware Assurance Companies are required by the Act of 1909 to make a deposit
of £20,000 upon the warrant of the Board
of Trade in respect of certain classes of
business undertaken, such as Fire, Life,
Accident and Employers' Liability Assurance, either in London or in Belfast. The
Order in Council which adapted the provisions of the Assurance Companies' Act of
1909 to Northern Ireland relieved existing
companies which had already made a deposit from any obligation to make in
Northern Ireland a second deposit in respect
of the same class or classes of business,
and, conversely, the one Northern Ireland
company which had made a deposit was relieved of the obligation to make a second
deposit in London.
The Order in Council did not, however,
cover the case of companies which after
the establishment of the Government of
Northern Ireland might be formed to carry
on operations in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland, and as the law stands at
present any such company would be under
the necessity of paying a deposit of £20,000
in Belfast as well as in London. After carefully considering this question my Ministry
and I have come to the conclusion that such
a requirement is not altogether necessary
or advisable, and accordingly Clause 1 of
the Measure now before the House provides
that we in Northern Ireland will recognise
deposits made in London and relieve from
the necessity of making a further deposit
in Northern Ireland any company which
proposes to commence operations in
Northern Ireland and which has made or
makes such a deposit in London. I
should also mention that the concession we
now make would apply to any Dominion
company which makes a deposit in London.
Clause 2 is designed to facilitate
administrative arrangements, and provides
that the Ministry of Commerce may accept
from an Assurance Company copies of its
accounts and other documents as deposited
with and accepted by the Board of Trade.
As hon. Members are aware, practically all
Assurance Companies carrying on business
in Northern Ireland also operate in Great
Britain. The Board of Trade and the
Government Actuary's Department at Westminster subject the accounts and valuations
of these companies to close scrutiny, and,
accordingly, there is much to be said for
the proposal that copies of these examined
accounts should be accepted in Northern
Ireland, where only a very small portion of
the company's business may actually be
carried on. I beg to move.

Mr. HANNA: By the courtesy of
all those concerned, and especially by
the courtesy of my hon. and learned
Friend and colleague in the representation of Antrim (Mr. Megaw), I
desire to take advantage of the Motion for
Adjournment to-night to raise only one
point in connection with matters arising
out of the Intoxicating Liquor Act, 1923.
This matter is one of very considerable
importance. There can be no gainsaying
that, because no matter what paper you
take up nowadays you will find reference
to a Resolution one way or to a counter
Resolution the other way in regard to this
matter of the right of the general public to
The Prime Minister himself, in reply to
representations made by the Association of
Northern Ireland Chambers of Commerce
on the subject of licensed yards being open
to farmers for stabling purposes before
10 a.m on week-days, has said that-
"There is nothing in the provisions of
the
Act rendering it impossible for
farmers to secure accommodation for
their horses and carts in licensed premises before 10 a.m, and that the Minister
of Home Affairs is of opinion that there
is no offence committed under the Intoxicating Liquor (Northern Ireland)
Act, 1923, in opening or keeping open a
yard for the purpose of permitting horses
to be stabled before 10 a.m., provided
there is no sale, exposure for sale, opening,
or keeping open for sale."
With that opinion on the law I do not find
much fault; it is good as far as it goes, but
it rather does suggest that licensed people
themselves are to blame where they have
refused admittance to members of the
general public during prohibited hours. I
want to make it perfectly clear that I am
absolutely desirous in this matter that
every member of the general public should
have the fullest stabling accommodation on
licensed premises if he wants it, and I am
sure so are the publicans. But is that the
law that there is to be no impediment, that
any person can as formerly just go out and
in as he did before? The whole thing, the
Minister says, is not an offence. What does
the Act say? If the House will bear with
me a moment I will read Clause B of
Section 6 of the Second Schedule, Part I of
the Act:-
The following provisions shall have
effect with respect to offences in connection with premises licensed for the
sale of intoxicating liquor by retail:-
If, in any prosecution of a licensed
person for an offence under any enactment relating to the sale of intoxicating
liquor by retail, it is alleged by the
prosecutor that any person was on the
licensed premises of such licensed
person in contravention of that enactment, any person whose presence on the
licensed premises is alleged to have
been in contravention of that enactment, and who is proved to have been

there is the possibility of a man being apprehended at any time under the circumstances.
I do not think it is proper on behalf of the
Government to say there was ambiguity at
the outset. It should not have been there
at all, and if it exists now it should be
cleared away.
A very fine case has been
put up, and I hope the Government will
address itself to the difficulty, and see the
Trade is properly protected, and that there
will be no injustice visited on the head of
any individual who happens to have recourse
to the yards.
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: I was very interested to hear the hon. and learned Gentleman's reply, and I think he sympathises and
sees where the weakness is, but he has, in
my opinion, not met one of the dangerous
points in the whole thing. It is a matter
simply for the police. He has his finger on
the police. I am no lawyer, but I understand
that any member of the public can take
action in this matter. I am afraid occasions
might arise when some personal spite might
prompt a man to take an action against a
publican for a contravention of the law. The
publican is hauled before the magistrate, and
the magistrate has to carry out the law, with
the result that the man is convicted. I do
not know how the thing could be remedied,
but I think the Government ought to take
steps to make the law right, and not leave
it in the hands of individual Members of
the Government to say whether the law
should be enforced or not. They ought to
bear that in mind, whatever they do in the
matter.

Minister thinks it desirable to state clearly

or exposing for sale or opening or keeping

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 16th October, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.

Ministry of Education.-Regulations for
