Oral Answers to Questions.
HIRING OF POLICE MOTORS.
1. Mr. COOTE (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs, if he will state
who is responsible for the hiring of motor
cars for the use of the police at Lisnaskea,
Co. Fermanagh; why the work has been
taken from the man who did it in troublesome times; whether he received any notice
of the transfer, and who has the work now,
and on what terms?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As a rule the police
use their own transport, and do not hire
cars, but when the necessity arises for such
hiring the District-Inspector is the officer
responsible for making the arrangements.
No contract is entered into, but in the
ordinary course the man who is most convenient is employed, provided his charge is
within the authorised maximum rate, viz.:
10d per mile-within the last two years
three persons have been employed in this
way at various times at Lisnaskea, and I
am not aware that there is any foundation
for the allegation that the work has been
taken away from any individual.
COTTAGES FOR EX-SOLDIERS IN
FERMANAGH.
2. Mr. COOTE (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs, if he can now
say whether any cottages for ex-soldiers are
to be built at Lisbellaw and Ballinamallard,
County Fermanagh, and if he can give the
reason why none of the cottages have been
so far allocated to these very loyal villages
in County Fermanagh, seeing that a large
number of applications have been made by
ex-soldiers in both villages?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This is a matter which comes
under the survey of my Ministry, and
therefore I reply to my hon. Friend.
I would refer him to the reply given to
his question on the 20th May last. Owing
to the restricted number of cottages which
are to be erected in Northern Ireland it is
unfortunately inevitable that cottages
cannot be built in every locality from
been
which applications have
received
from ex-Service men.
REAR LIGHTS ON BICYCLES.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether he intends to follow
the recommendation of the Roads Advisory
Committee in regard to rear lights on
bicycles, in the interests of the safety of
cyclists and motorists.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have carefully
considered the recommendation of the Roads
Advisory Committee, and also of the Special
Committee appointed by the Imperial
Government on the subject of rear lights on
pedal cycles.
While there is much to be said for the
proposal that these cycles should be fitted
with rear lights, it is also bound up with
all
the larger question of rear lights on
horse drawn vehicles.
The matter, as the hon. and gallant
Member no doubt realises, affects a very
considerable section of the community at
large, and is, accordingly, not one for hasty
or ill-considered legislation. I am carefully
considering the whole question in all its
bearings, and will be prepared to deal with
it as soon as a suitable opportunity arises.
MARRIED SPECIALS' SEPARATION
ALLOWANCE.
4. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether married members of
the Special Constabulary stationed at Newry
have had their separation allowance of 2/-
per diem deducted from their pay.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The only cases in
Newry in which payment of separation
allowance to married members of the Special
Constabulary has been discontinued, are
those in which the families of the men concerned have accommodation in the town, and
permission has been given to the men to
reside with their families. In such circumstances separation allowance is not payable.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
reply, are there no cases where married
constables are compelled to sleep in the
barracks?

Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Where there are
cases of a constable being ordered to sleep
in the barracks of course he is entitled to
separation allowance.
Colonel WOODS: That is the point.
THE BELFAST-LISBURN ROAD.
5. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether his attention has
been drawn to the condition of the road
surface on the Belfast-Lisburn Road, and
whether he intends to take any action in
the matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Antrim County
Council are at present engaged on work of
reconstruction on the Belfast-Lisburn Road,
partly in concrete and partly in asphaltic
cement. These works form part of a general
scheme for the reconstruction of the Class 1
roads in the county, for which a loan of
£115,000 has been sanctioned, and for which
the Ministry of Home Affairs have accepted
financial responsibility up to the extent of
60 per cent. Naturally during the progress
of these important works it is necessary to
close to traffic certain specified portions of
the road-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-but
every effort is made to reduce
as far
as possible inconvenience to the travelling
public. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
MOTOR TAXATION INQUIRY.
6. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether any report had been
received from the Commission appointed by
the Northern Government to work in conjunction with the Commission set up by the
Imperial Government to inquire into the
system of Motor Taxation.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon, and gallant
Member appears to be under a misapprehension regarding the appointment of a
Commission by the Government of Northern
Ireland to inquire into the system of motor
taxation. The situation is as follows:-
In view of the desirability of keeping in
close touch with the Imperial Government
on questions of taxation of motor vehicles,
arrangements were made by permission of
the Ministry of Transport, Whitehall,
whereby three representatives of the Government of Northern Ireland were enabled to
attend the meetings of the Imperial Government's Departmental Committee on Motor
Taxation, with a view to their being in
a position to assist and advise the Government of Northern Ireland in the event of
the question of the introduction of new
legislation dealing with the Taxation of
Motor Vehicles being considered.
The Departmental Committee submitted
their Report to the Imperial Government
recently, and the recommendations may be
said briefly to fall under three heads:-
In the first place they recommended that
immediate legislation should be enacted, remedying existing defects in the system of
Motor Taxation in relation to the surrender
of licences and to the surcharge payable on
quarterly licences.
These recommendations have been accepted
by the Imperial Government, and also, on
the recommendation of the representatives
referred to above, by the Government of
Northern Ireland, and it will be found that
the proposals in question are embodied in
the Finance Bill, which comes before this
House for Second Reading to-day.
The second and main recommendation was
to the effect that a tax on petrol is not at
present practicable, and consequent on that
was the third recommendation that the question of the revision of the present Treasury
Horse Power Rating of Motor Vehicles
should be referred to a special Technical
Committee.
The Government of Northern Ireland are
keeping in close touch with developments in
this connection, but pending the findings of
that Technical Committee consideration of
the whole question must be necessarily deferred.
OBSTRUCTIONS IN THE SILLIES RIVER.
7. Mr. COOTE (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Prime Minister if he is aware that the
Ministry of Labour agreed to give the Fermanagh County Council £1,000 towards the
cost of removing shoals and obstructions in
the Sillies river, on condition that such sum
would be 60 per cent. of the cost of labour
spent on such work, but that the County
Council were unable to proceed with the
work owing to the absence of statutory
power to raise the remaining 40 per cent.
in any manner whatever, and whether the
Government is prepared to introduce a short
Bill to enable the County Council to carry
out this work, and if he can now state the
intentions of the Government regarding the
general question of drainage, which has become more acute owing to the recent very
wet seasons.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am taking this question
on behalf of the Prime Minister.
I am
As regards the first part of the question,
aware that a scheme of the nature
suggested by the hon. Member was approved
at a total estimated cost of £1,000, but that
it could not be proceeded with owing to the
statutory difficulty. I may perhaps correct

the hon. Member's figures. The amount of
the unemployment relief grant sanctioned
was not £1,000, but 60 per cent. of the labour

As regards the latter part of the question,
the Government have had the the whole

of the existing law relating to Drainage

been the subject of no fewer than nineteen

Mr. COOTE: Arising out of that answer,
and in view of all the discussion that has
taken place in regard to this matter, is the
Government not yet prepared to propound a
policy to aid the development of agriculture
by a drainage scheme, or are they still
merely theorising in the matter? What is
their policy? That is the question the
country is asking, and will the Minister not
soon be able to give an answer?
Mr. POLLOCK: The Government is not
theorising. It is taking advantage of all the

NEW SCHOOL FOR LISBELLAW.
8. Mr. COOTE (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education, if a new Protestant school is
urgently required at Lisbellaw, Co. Fermanagh; how long the people have been
agitating for the work to be carried out;
what is the cause of the delay, and if he will
undertake to have matters put right.
Mr. POLLOCK: The premises at present
used for the Lisbellaw Public Elementary
School have been reported by the inspectors
to be old and generally unsuitable for school
purposes, and an application for a grant
towards the erection of a new building under
the management of the Reverend Canon
McTighe, LL.D., rector of Lisbellaw, was
under consideration by the Commissioners of
National Education prior to the war. In
view, however, of the total suspension of
grants during the war and the restrictions
placed by the Imperial Treasury on such
grants in the years that followed, the Commissioners were unable to proceed with the
case.
When the Ministry of Education took over
control of the Educational Services for
Northern Ireland, in February, 1922, the
consideration of the case was re-opened, and
in November, 1923, the Ministry sanctioned
grants towards the erection of the new house
to accommodate boys and girls only. Following the sanction of this grant, the manager
suggested the erection of a larger house than
that which the Ministry was empowered
under the regulations to allow, and as a
result of the manager's proposal the Ministry had the case further investigated by the
senior inspector in charge of the district.
As the result of this investigation the
Ministry decided that the proper course in
the educational interests of the district was
to provide accommodation in the new house
for the pupils of the infant school as well as
of the senior school, especially as the principal of the infant school is due to retire at
an early date. The manager has agreed to
this course, and plans of the new house on
this basis are in preparation. It is hoped
that these plans will be ready in a few days.
The Ministry of Education is endeavouring
to expedite the case as much as possible.
PUNCH HEMSTITCHING PIECE RATES.
9. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Labour, whether he can state the result of
the recent investigation into the yield of
the piece rates as fixed by the Trade Board
on punch hemstitching, as the result of a
strike which took place in Lurgan during
May of this year.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): At the request of the Linen and
Cotton Handkerchief Trade Board, my Department carried out the investigation to
which the honourable and gallant Member
refers. The inquiry consisted of inspections
in a number of firms selected by the Trade
Board, and the resulting particulars were
furnished to the Board in accordance with
their request. On the 7th August the Board
informed me that "having regard to the
returns so submitted and to all the circumstances of the case, the Board are of opinion
that no sufficient cause has been shown for
an alteration in the present general minimum piece rates for punch hemstitching,
which the Board are satisfied yield to a
worker of ordinary skill and experience in
the trade the existing piecework basis time
rate of 7d. per hour."
Colonel WOODS: As this is rather an important matter, I give notice that I will
bring it up on the Motion for Adjournment.

A GOVERNMENT OFFICIAL'S PENSION.
10. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he will state the
amount of pension now paid to Mr. Crowe,
late of the Ministry of Agriculture, and
whether Mr. Crowe retired by reason of the
age qualification.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am taking this question
for the Minister of Agriculture, who is absent because of duties elsewhere. The reply
is-Mr. Crowe's retirement was not on
grounds of age, but was voluntary in pursuance of the privilege accorded by the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, to transferred Irish officers of retiring on special
terms. His superannuation allowances were
fixed by the Civil Service Committee, and
consist of a non-variable pension of £143
15s 0d, a supplemental pension of £52 18s 0d,
variable quarterly in accordance with the
fluctuation of the official increased cost of
living figure, and a lump sum additional
allowance of £498 18s 4d.

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Unemployment Insurance (No. 3) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Mr. ANDREWS: In connection with the
debates which we had last week on the Unemployment Fund Bill, and also on the
Relief Grants Estimate for £100,000, I purposely took a very minor part, because I felt
that a more favourable opportunity would be
given to me to-day to deal with the problem
of unemployment in a general way. It will
be in the recollection of hon. Members that
before our House rose in May last we passed
what was called the Unemployment Insurance (Temporary Provisions) Act. At that
time legislation dealing with Unemployment
Insurance was passing through the Imperial
Parliament, and we were anxious that the
same things should be done for our people
as were being done for their brothers and
sisters in Great Britain in this connection;
and by means of our Unemployment
Insurance (Temporary Provisions) Act our
Governor in Council was authorised to
bring into force here the provisions
of the Imperial Measure. That Bill,.
as its name indicates, was only temporary
in character, and it was clearly defined
that it should only apply either as
regards the Act itself or Orders in Council
made under the Act until December of this
year. And this Bill which I have the honour
to ask the House to give a Second Reading
to to-day is brought in to regularise the
position and to ensure that the provisions
which the temporary Act brought into force
here shall be continued.
1405 Unemployment Insurance Bill- 16 OCTOBER 1924

Second Reading.
I was astonished to find a few days ago
that I have been Minister of Labour in
Northern Ireland for a longer period than
any other Minister of Labour has ever
acted in Great Britain-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear) and I think, therefore, it may
meet with the approval of the House if I
were to take advantage of this opportunity
to give hon. Members some views that I have
formed during these years in connection
with this all-important, most distressing,
and, probably, most difficult social problem
with which we are called upon to deal. I
am encouraged to take this course because
hon. Members opposite said last week that
they were particularly desirous that the
problem of unemployment should be discussed here at an early date from every
standpoint. An hon. Member also said that
something must be done and I would like
to tell the House with the permission of hon.
Members something of what the Government has done in this connection since it
came into existence.
In the first place through our relief
schemes, promoted by our local authorities
and subsidised by the Government, work has
been found involving an expenditure of two
and three-quarter millions, on which 15,500
persons who would otherwise have had no
work to do, have through
Labour
Exchanges been placed in employment for
various periods. Through
Loans
Guarantee Act, which is most carefully
administered by my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Finance, three ships have
already been completed in our Belfast yards.

our

Mr. ANDREWS: I am quite satisfied to

which is the only purpose for which the
fund can be applied. But there are those
who may say,
Why not find employment
for everyone?" I would like to tell the
House that to find employment for our menfolk who are unemployed would cost the
substantial sum
of about £8,000,000 per
annum, and even then we would be left with
our women and young persons unprovided
for except through the means of our Unemployment Insurance Acts. I am frequently
being told, in fact, I am tired of being told,
to end this dole. I am told that it is demoralising our people. I do not think so.
Mr. McGUFFIN: No.
Mr. GRANT: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: If our people are being
demoralised it is because they cannot find
work to do. It is work that we want for
them; but if we cannot guarantee the right
to work, at any rate through our unemployment insurance we have the right to
give maintenance. Various parties in England, in fact I think all parties, when in
opposition, have professed to have cures for
the unemployment problem, and yet successive Governments, when they have come into
power, have not been able to carry out their
intentions. Well, I have never been in
opposition yet, and, therefore, I have no embarrassing pledges of the kind to give effect
to, or to be accused of not giving effect to.
I say here advisedly that the reason why all
Governments have failed to end unemployment completely is because there is no short
cut. The only way in which it can be done
is by getting the wheels of industry going
afresh, and by private enterprise being left
in security and peace to develop along economic lines. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

But I do feel and I say it in no party

I know that there is a feeling, too general,

further from the truth. (Hon. Members:

The next fence over which our friend has
got to get is this: an inquiry is sent to his

his unemployment is occasioned by a trade
dispute or by his own misconduct; and, in

were inflicted. Fifty-four cases only were
dismissed, and the remainder were disposed
of, in the great majority of cases, by the
disallowance of benefit wrongly obtained and
its subsequent recovery from the claimant to
benefit.

Now, I would like to impress upon the
House that these precautions are taken
because my Department feel that we
really the trustees of this fund, and that
we have two duties to perform. The first
is to see that everybody who, according to
Statute, is entitled to benefit gets it as
expeditiously as possible, and the second is
to see that none get it who are not entitled
to it. I know that it is frequently said
that such and such a person, who is working,
or who is not entitled to get if for some
reason, is drawing benefit. I generally find
that when these claims come up to be investigated on the facts they crumple up,
and I think it will gratify hon. Members to
know that of the 15,500 persons who have
obtained work on our relief schemes not one
half per cent. of those who have been offered
work have refused it. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I think that that shows clearly
that our people are playing the game, that
what they want is work above everything
else; but when I say that I wonder do these
foolish, thoughtless people, who suggest that
this unemployment benefit should cease, ever
consider what the effect would be if 40,000
of our brothers and sisters were left without
the means not only of earning their daily
bread but actually living? They would not
starve. Why should they?

to give benefit in the form of charity it was
felt that this name should for ever be wiped
off the slate.

[Mr. Andrews]
Two new classes of dependants are now
brought within the scope of the insurance
scheme. The first is the dependent widowed
mother of an insured claimant, and the
second is the housekeeper in charge of the
dependent children of a widow
or unmarried woman claimant. When a woman
is working she is obliged in many instances
to get someone to look after her children,
and when she gets out of employment it was
felt to be a hardship, especially when the unemployment might be for only a few weeks,
that she would be obliged to discharge the
person who was looking after her children.
Therefore, to prevent that hardship, not
only will the insured widow worker be
allowed to claim benefit on her own account,
but she will be placed in the same position
as a man as regards her household.
Another important clause in this Bill is
one which deals with Trade Disputes. Under
the Act of 1920 a worker who went on strike
was of course deprived of benefit whilst
was not on strike
another worker who
himself, but who worked in the same concern
and who was not financially contributing to
the strike, had no statutory right to obtain
benefit. Take the case of the moulders.
During the moulders' strike the moulders'
labourers who had no part in the strike,
and had nothing to gain from the strike,
and were contributing nothing to it, were
deprived of a great deal of benefit which
under the new Act they will be entitled to.
The next provision that I wish to refer
to is that which deals with contributions.
I need not go through all the changes that
it is ultimately intended to make in this
respect, because no changes will be made
until after the deficiency period, and, unfortunately, that is not in sight yet, I fear.
After the deficiency period, however, the
contribution which is paid by the employer
for his male worker will be reduced from
10d. to 6d. The amount which the worker
himself pays will be reduced from 9d. to 6d.,
and the amount, 63d., which the State pays,
will be reduced to 6d. It will appear to hon.
Members that the proportion which
State pays will then be increased. At the
present time the State pays something over
one-third of the total contributions of the
employers and the workers. After the
deficiency period the State will pay exactly
one-half.
the
The next Clause that I desire to refer to is
that governing refunds. As hon. Members
no doubt know, up to the present the
worker who was fortunate and remained in
steady employment could at the age of 60
draw from the fund all the unexhausted
contributions which he himself had paid
into the fund, plus compound interest. I
know that this matter can be argued from
two points of view. One way of looking at
it is that it is contrary to the principle of
insurance that a man should pay premiums
and then if the worst does not happen that
he should be entitled to a refund of those
premiums; while, on the other hand, he
ought to be thankful to God that the
misfortune which he had insured against
did not come about. At the same
time I cannot help but say that there was
something about this refund at 60 which
rather appealed to one, because it was an
incentive to thrift. It was an incentive to
men and women to remain in employment,
so that when they came to 60 they would
have this nest egg to fall back upon. However, as we have decided in these matters
to maintain our social standards on parallel
lines with Great Britain, we cannot
obviously go to the British Bill and take
all the best out of it and leave the worst.
Besides I think that there is one strong
argument for the giving up of these refunds,
and that is that it puts a contingent, increasing, unascertainable liability on the fund,
which might be of very serious importance,
when we are not responsible for affairs in
Northern Ireland. That is the argument
which convinces me that there is no course
open for us, in my opinion, but to accept
the inevitable in this connection.
As regards the waiting period, in the past
an insured person claiming benefit had to
wait for one week before he was entitled
to obtain any. That period is considered
to have been too long. It possibly put the
worker into debt right at the beginning
of his period of unemployment, whether it
was short or long. Therefore this Bill proposes to reduce the waiting period from six
to three days.
Now, the House is entitled to be
told what this Bill is going to cost.
So far as the waiting period and the change
in the rules of continuity are concerned it
will cost £130,000 per annum, and the increased benefit rates, it is estimated, will
cost about £170,000 per annum, or £300,000
in all. At the same time it is right that I
should say that there are provisions in this
Bill which, if strictly enforced, would put
a good many persons out of benefit. In
Great Britain these provisions have not up
to the present been very literally applied, and
we here have not decided exactly what course
we propose to take. However, it is interesting to notice that a decrease of one per cent.
in the percentage of unemployment means
a saving of £110,000 per annum. So that
if we could get our percentage of unemployment in Northern Ireland down from 17
per cent. to 14 per cent. the liability under
this Bill would be entirely liquidated.
I have put a tax upon the patience of the
House beyond what I am entitled to do-

The PRIME MINISTER: I apologise for not
being in the House the whole time. I was
called away to an important consultation. I
want to emphasise to the House the endeavours
that we are making to have this fund absorbed
in the whole fund of unemployment insurance
throughout Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
That is the solution of our difficulties, and
I have not given up the hope that it will
be possible whatever Government is returned
on the other side to show them the justice
of our claim the discharge of which is
beyond yea or nay, because there is no question whatever that in the preparation of the
White Paper on which the finances of
Northern Ireland are based in the first instance this mistake of the Treasury was made
through no fault of ours, because we had no
Government in possession here at the time,
nor had we a Chancellor of the Exchequer or
any other person who could argue with the
Treasury on the other side regarding the
grave error in arriving at the actuarial figures
when they divided the funds between Great
Britain and Northern Ireland.
Now it is a very simple proposition in my
opinion. I would not stand here for one
moment if I thought in the Act of 1920 the
citizens inside Northern Ireland had to live
compulsorily under worse conditions than
1429 Unemployment Insurance Bill 16 OCTOBER 1924
Second Reading.

those who are across the Channel. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) We only accepted
the Act of 1920 with the gravest reluctance
on all grounds, but certainly one point has
always been before the minds of my colleagues
and myself, and that is this: We will lay
down the reins of office if the fact of the
1921 Act means that the working man, no
matter how humble he is, has to bear a
heavier burden for less results in the end,
or if he pays the same contribution as those
across the water he does not get the same
benefits as those across the water. That
does not refer only to the subject of unemployment insurance, but refers generally to
the social well-being of the people.
The division of Ireland is a matter in which
we had no part, and the acceptance of the
responsibility for the Government of Northern Ireland carried with it the duty on those
who conferred self-government on Northern
Ireland to see that her citizens did not suffer
by accepting the grave responsibility of selfgovernment. Therefore, I think my hon.
and learned Friend will understand that as
long as we are here there must be no law
for those across the Channel that differs from
the law that governs us here in Ulster,
broadly speaking, with regard to benefits
derived from the Insurance Acts or contributions to be made by the people.
Just imagine for one moment what state
we would be in and what complications would
arise if a man working on the Clyde came
over here. I think my right hon. Friend
will correct me if I am wrong in saying that
the essence of labour is that it should be
very liquid and should be mobile. If there
is a shortage of varnishers in the yards on
the Clyde there is no reason why our men
should not go over there automatically and
find work there, carry on their trade, or if
they fail to get work or go out of employment the benefits they receive upon the Clyde
or in Belfast shipyards should be exactly the
same. And vice versa, if there is a shortage
of some particular artisans here in the Belfast
yards, well, it is open to the Clyde, Tyneside or other great shipping centres as to
the men over here; and when they arrive
here they can carry on the job under the
same conditions as on the other side.
We in Northern Ireland recognise no boundaries whatever between ourselves and Great
Britain—(hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and
so long as there are no boundaries then, in
my opinion, there is only one policy for this
House to adopt, and that is to carry on along
parallel lines in the meantime, until we get
thoroughly stabilised financially. If we do
that we are on safe ground. If we depart
from that there is no way of knowing how
far that departure may go.

on this question and the representatives of

are matters for grave consideration and I
would suggest to my right hon. Friend that

to bring to his notice is with regard to the
Refund, and he knows I am interested in
this important Clause. Why am I interested? Because it is the very foundation
of the Act. It is the only remnant left of
the principle that established Unemployment Insurance. When the Trade Unions
administered Unemployment Insurance for
the benefit of their members they established
the principle that when a member who was
fortunate enough to be in employment all
his life reached the age of sixty he should
receive a refund and thus have something
to fall back upon in his old age. The
Minister said we were drifting, and I am
afraid we are unconsciously drifting into a
period when we are going to nationalise
people. The tendency is that the more
people you bring under Unemployment
Insurance the greater is the unemployment.
That has proved to be the case from the
very inception of the Act in 1911, and I fail
to see any solution of the problem. The
late Government were apparently inclined
to encourage a greater number of people to
be brought under the Act, and I am afraid
that will tend to further increase the
number of unemployed.

There is no cure. I have referred to this

and assure that benefit would be given to

and that principle was established by men

sorry to say that to-day there is no co-operation between these two. It is quite evident
from the way we are drifting that the old
friendly feeling that I can remember well
as existing between employers and their employees has gone, because the State has
stepped in and, gradually, year after year,
unconsciously, I do not care what Government is in power, we are coming to the stage
when they are nationalising the people
which is the next thing to pauperising them.
There will have to be another method
adopted, and I do not think the old plan
was a bad one.
I know perfectly well that in the old days
there were many workmen who would not
have been unemployed, because that feeling
existed between their employers and themselves. But to-day the employer has no
interest in his employees, for the simple
reason that the Government have taken over
control of the workers, and the employer
knows they will not go to the workhouse.
What are they attempting to-day? I heard

going to bring in domestic servants. Will a

I believe we are going the wrong way towards solving the unemployment problem.
Having said so much you ask me what is
the cure. I will tell you what is the cure.
Unfortunately the people to which I belong,

game any more than the capitalists.
cure is increased production. Increase your
export and import trade. And the most likely

nation steadily before it.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 21st October, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
PAPER PRESENTED TO PARLIAMENT.
Ministry of Finance. Northern Ireland
Secondary and Preparatory Teachers'
Superannuation Scheme.
Oral Answers to Questions.
SECONDARY TEACHERS' PENSIONS,
1. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of Education,
whether his attention has been drawn to the
following resolutions unanimously passed by
the Irish Union of Assistant Mistresses of
Secondary Schools in Northern Ireland :-
(1) That a system of pensions based on the
principle of "three years for one" is highly
unsatisfactory;
(2) That all contributions towards pension,
plus compound interest at the rate of 3 per
cent. should be refunded to all teachers who
voluntarily retire before pensionable age;
(3) That teachers may retire at sixty, and
that women teachers may retire after thirtyfive years' service;
and whether he can assure the House that
these reasonable requests will receive the
consideration to which they are obviously
entitled.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): As the preparation of a Pension
Scheme is a matter for the Ministry under
my charge, I have arranged with my hon.
Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary to the
Ministry of Education, whom we are glad to
see here to-day after a short absence, to
reply.
The three Resolutions referred to by the
hon. Member have been brought to my notice.
The terms of the first are misleading. If
Members will refer to the clauses of the
Scheme which have been presented to the
House to-day they will see that, as a special
concession, the Ministry is prepared to allow
ne-third of the service given before the
Scheme comes into operation to count for
pension. All service after that counts in
full. The concession in regard to past service
is the atmost to which I am prepared to go.
As regards the second, the matter has been
carefully considered and it is regretted that
the proposal to add interest to contribution
repayments in the case of voluntary withdrawal from the Scheme is one that cannot
be accepted. In regard to the third Resolution, the Scheme provides for retirement at
60, but after consultation with the Ministry
of Education I can see no valid grounds,
educational or other, for allowing women
teachers to retire before that age, even though
they have had 35 years' service.
COLERAINE AND PORTRUSH POLICE
DISTRICTS.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether he can state the
number of police prosecutions for offences
against the law that have been brought in
the Coleraine and Portrush police districts
during the first six months of this year, and
can he state the number of convictions and
dismissals in those cases.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): During the first six
months of the present year, there were 241
police prosecutions in the Coleraine Police
District. Convictions were obtained in 220
cases, 12 cases were dismissed and 9 cases
withdrawn.
In the Portrush Police District during the
same period, the corresponding figures
were:-60 prosecutions, 52 convictions and 8
cases dismissed.

There is a second fallacy that I should

have heard again and again from Members

and that we might dispense with our meetings altogether and use the rubber stamp,
instead of discussing and passing legislation.
These flights of fancy and metaphors are in
my opinion absolutely uncalled for, and this
Bill itself shows it. You have here a Bill
dealing with great and widespread abuses
that exist in every industrial centre, that
exist in Belfast, and that exist, as I know,
in rural Ulster. You have helpless people
who are being systematically defrauded of
their money, and we have never had a word
in this House with regard to those
abuses. Yet in England, where the question
is more urgent, they have taken time to
appoint a Commission which was presided

have heard evidence on the matter. They
have introduced a Bill to meet those gross
abuses, and now we are adopting it here. I
say that instead of finding fault with the

Industrial Assurance Bill
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Dr. Morrison]
House without discussion. It went through
the committee stage without discussion. I
was interested in a statement made by the
Minister of Commerce, who introduced the
Bill. There were three official amendments
from the Government, which, I think, did
not materially affect the Bill, which is now
up for Third reading, and the first criticism
has come from my hon. Friend the Member
for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin). I have
had a good deal of experience of the working of this system in rural Ulster, but I
had no idea that the disease was so widespread and so general as was indicated by
the Minister, when he pointed out that one
company in ten years had issued 9,300,000
policies and that 4,000,000 of those had lapsed
inside the ten years.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): 6,400,000.
Dr. MORRISON: I took the figures from
Hansard. I would ask the House to tell me
what that means. These people who were
insured for small sums, such as £10, £15,
and £20, are the most helpless portion of
the community. They have been robbed, in
my opinion, during those ten years of
£4,000,000, probably £8,000,000, and I would
like to tell the House how it is done, because
I have seen how it is done. When I began
my professional work there were four or five
insurance societies that dealt with large
sums. Industrial assurance was then a mere
bagatelle and was only acting on a very small
scale. But since then societies that I knew
started in a humble way in my district have
grown into vast corporations which control
a huge number of policies and deal with a
huge number of insured. In every district in
Ulster, and in every district in Belfast, you
have, according to the system now, an area
mapped out, you have an inspector for a
definite area, and you have a staff of canvassers working all through the district not
for one society alone but for other societies.
Every society has its agent. These people
are coaxing and persuading, and, I am sorry
to say, misleading poor helpless people. They
come round and offer a policy of insurance
and say--I am speaking of what I know-
"Your age does not matter, sign your name
here at the bottom of the application form
or make your mark" It is usually the
father or the mother who is being insured
and provision is being made for the burial
expenses. These people will say to the insurance agent, "But, sir, my father is a very
old man, and my mother is a very old woman,
and the expenses will be great." The insurance agent then says, "Oh, it does not matter,
put down your name. I will fill in the form
and I will see the thing through." The
applicant signs his or her name or makes
his or her mark, but when the policy
matures and when these old people die the
question of age is raised, and the probabilities are that instead of getting 100 per cent.
of the sum insured these people get five, ten,
or fifteen per cent.
As I said before they are the most helpless
class in the community. They do not belong
to the trade union classes, who are organised
and able to protect themselves. These people
are living and struggling. They have perhaps
a delicate son or a delicate daughter, or an
aged father or aged mother, and they do
this with the object of securing enough
money to enable them to bury their relatives
in decency. Again and again as a Registrar
of the deaths of these people I have been
asked to alter the age. The Registrar has to
put down when registering the death the age
of the deceased, and people will come to me
saying, "I want to register my father's
death," and when I come to the column
where you have to put in the age they will
say, "Put it down at 50 or 56 years of age."
The age of the man may be 60 or perhaps
80 years of age. The registration form is
completed on proper, straight lines, and
then objection is taken to the policy. When
these people make a complaint it is pointed
out to them, "You have signed the application, here is the name at the foot of the
form; you cannot get beyond that." That
has happened again and again; in fact, it
is the ruling system. I knew one man who
was too old to be insured, and the representative of one company, when he refused
to state his age, would not insure him. In
a dispensary district such as I was in I
could tell generally what an individual's
age was. This agent refused to insure the
man, but another agent came round and put
him down twenty years below what the
really was, and then his daughter
went on paying the premiums for ten years.
An objection was raised to a false declaration when the policy matured, and the person got no money whatever.

years who is alive to-day. They forged the
doctor's name, they took out a policy on the
woman's life, and they insured this woman
who is alive to-day. I do not know how many
cases they were successful in, but this case
was detected, and the doctor whose name

You have good agents and bad agents, and
you have good companies and bad companies.
but my experience is that you want specially
to protect the poor from these agents and to
see that justice is done to them. I do not.
know what the cure is, but there are two
things that I think should be in this Bill
which we are going to pass. You should
protect poor people who take out a policy
and pay perhaps for ten years, and then
they find when they are not able to carry
on the payments the policy lapses.
I think the Minister of Commerce should
put in a provision in this Bill that if a
policy does lapse the person who paid the
premiums should be refunded at least one
half what he has paid. In the second case.
I think you should have the state of health
that is entered in the policy accepted and
the question barred from being raised at any
subsequent date. Say you are insuring a person for ten years for £10. An agent is able
roughly to say whether a person is healthy or
unhealthy, and he is able to tell the age also
by a look. If the company is not satisfied
with that they should ascertain the ground
on which there could be no controversy about
it. It is easy finding the age of a person. It
is easy asking for a doctor's certificate and
paying for it, but to raise the question of
health after the policy has been taken out
and to refuse to fulfil the conditions of that
policy when the patient dies on the ground
that something was withheld and that the
application form was false is unfair. I think
an amendment should be introduced that
would bind the company to accept the
age as put in and debar them from
raising it when the policy matures and
when they are called upon to pay.
I
make these three suggestions to the Minister,
and I think he would be wise to accept them,
because so far as I can see it is the only

Unless the existing Government could reconcile the wishes of the North and the wishes
of the South, they excluded Ireland from

great problems, and bring them before the
House, and try and get them established in
Northern Ireland.

Mr. GRANT: I am sorry I missed Clause
1, but I would just like to crave your indulgence for a moment if I am out of order.
I would like to get some information from
the Attorney-General about a particular
question in connection with this Bill. The
point is this: A woman was married to a
man who was serving at the Front. He was
killed in the year 1917. His brother was also
at the Front with him, and he came home
and told the woman the exact circumstances
of the death of her husband. About a year
later this brother married the widow.
This was in 1918. The War Pensions people
were paying a pension to the widow for the
death of her husband and also in respect of
her children. Their officials came along and
told the woman that she was not legally
married to this man, and, of course, the man
had to go. They carried on the pension
right up to the passing of the Act of 1921,
and then her pension stopped, and at the
moment she has neither husband nor pension.
I would just like a reply from the right hon.
and learned Gentleman to see exactly what
position the woman is in. Is she entitled to
a pension, or is she entitled to have the man
back as her husband? I would like some
information about it.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
I think in answering that question I am
in the position of a friend of mine who at
one time was arguing a case before a
learned judge. The learned judge said:
"Now, Mr. So-and-So, what do you say to
a question such as this?" and proceeded to
propound a question. The learned counsel
replied: "My lord, before I answer that
question, I should like to have a case submitted to me and a proper fee sent to me."
Now, it is not a question of having a
proper case submitted to me or a proper
fee sent to me in this case-that is out of
the question-but this is a very complicated
question, and if my hon. Friend (Mr.
Grant) will come and see me and put the
facts fully before me, I will give him the
best opinion I can. But I will say that the
officials in saying that the woman was not
legally married prior to 1921 were perfectly
right, and it was for the purpose of provid
ing for a case of that kind that the Act of
1921 was passed and the Royal Assent given
to it in July of that year. We are now
trying to do the same for marriages that
have taken place since 1921. We are now
doing a similar thing in reference to
marriages here that may have taken place
since 1921. The Bill will legalise those
marriages when it becomes law.
Mr. GRANT: I fully appreciate the
courtesy of the right hon and learned
Gentleman (Mr. Best), but my point is that
in our Bill we are going back to 1921, and I
want to know if it goes back any further
than 1921. I have been looking at a whole
lot of law-books in the library, but they are
of no use to me as I cannot interpret them.
This is really a hard case, and, of course,
if I cannot get an answer in the Committee
--and I appreciate the difficulty-I
will have great pleasure in putting the case
before the right hon. and learned Gentleman.
Mr. ROBB: May I say that, for what my
opinion is worth, I have looked into this
particular matter and, as far as I can read
the Statute, such a marriage as the hon.
Member (Mr. Grant) refers to would be
legal when this Bill passes. The Act is
framed in a curious way, but it legalises
marriages that had taken place before the
passing of the Act of 1921, unless they had
been by some Court declared null. This
particular marriage, as I understand, had
not been declared null, and consequently
when it passes this Bill will have a retrospective effect, and that marriage will be
legalised.

The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): It is hardly
necessary for me in moving the Second
Reading of the Finance Bill to explain in
detail the limited nature of our powers of
taxation. The Finance Bill recently passed
at Westminster effected certain important
changes in the taxes collected by the Imperial Government in Northern Ireland,
and a note to this effect was scheduled in
the printed statement which was circulated
by my right hon. Friend, the Minister of
Finance, at the time he made his Budget
statement in May last. It now remains for
us to decide whether any alterations similar
to those made in what I may term the local
English taxes are to be made in the corresponding Northern Ireland taxes over which
we have complete control.
that
Hon. Members are already aware
allusion has been made many times in the
last few days to the very important inquiry
that is being carried on under the name
of the Colwyn Committee. Its sittings are
drawing to a close, but we have not yet
been informed in any way as to the nature
of what their findings may be. There are,
in addition, two matters which have been
submitted to the Colwyn Committee, matters
of the greatest importance, which have been
under discussion with representatives of the
Imperial Treasury in London. Until those
vital matters are decided we have to confess
that we are very much in the dark as to
the state of our own finances, whether it
will be possible to conclude the present year
with an assured surplus or
whether
an actual deficit may arise. Therefore,
under circumstances such as these I think
hon. Members will agree that it would not
be prudent-in fact, it would hardly be
justifiable-to make any important reductions in those taxes which it is within
our province now to consider. As a
consequence of this, my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance, informed the House in May last that
he could not see his
way to give a
corresponding reduction in what we know
as the Entertainment Taxes, in respect of
lower-priced charges for admission to certain
entertainments. A corresponding reduction
here to that made in England and Scotland
would affect our revenue to the extent of
£45,000, and that was a reduction he did
not feel justified in facing under these
circumstances
As regards the Bill itself, I do not think
that hon. Members will find it complicated
or difficult to follow. Most of the provisions
are purely of an administrative character,
and have been suggested as the result of
our experience in working the existing
law.
The first three Clauses relate to the Entertainments Duty. Members of the agricultural
community will be gratified to learn that
we have redrafted the provisions exempting
agricultural shows from the Entertainments
Duty, and so we hope that for the future
agricultural and other societies promoting
shows for the advancement of industry or
the fine arts will have no doubt as to the
exact terms under which exemption from Entertainments Duty may be obtained.
As a
matter of fact, the reduction in our revenue
arising from this concession will be a small
one. I think the great difficulty our friends
who are interested in agricultural shows had
to face was the uncertainty of what could
properly be included in the programme
without forfeiting the right to exemption
from duty. This applied particularly to the
question of musical items, and I understand
that a number of shows have been held
without the attraction of a band. We have
been able to meet them in this respect without any anticipated cost to our revenue.
Another point is that we are following the
British Government in adopting the suggestion of a Committee which was appointed
to inquire into the incidence of taxation on
motor cars or mechanically - propelled
vehicles, and, as I mentioned in introducing
the Money Resolution a day or two ago, it
has now been decided to grant the surrender
value to motor licences; that is to say, if
a motor licence is given up before its whole
term has expired the licensee can receive,
on payment of a small fee, a proportionate
refund in respect of each full month that
the licence has yet to run. In addition to

that, the surcharge on quarterly licences has
been reduced from 20 per cent. to 10 per
cent. I may say here again that this concession is being made without reducing our
revenue. It is met at the expense of the
motor taxes, which go to the Road Fund,
and will be an easement to the licence

Clause 5 has been introduced as a result
of the abolition by the Imperial Parliament
of the duties on cider, perry, and other
table waters. Dealers in these commodities
were hitherto required to take out a licence
costing 10s per annum, and it was felt that
the duty these commodities having
been abolished almost as a corollary to that
the duty on the licences to deal in these
commodities should also be relinquished.
This affects us only to a very slight extent
in Northern Ireland, and I do not believe
we shall lose in revenue in this respect to
the extent of more than £50 per annum.
Another matter which is a convenience to
a few is the result of representations made
to us by persons who move backwards and
forwards between Northern Ireland and
England and Scotland and who have been in
the habit in the past of taking out game
licences. After the transfer of this tax to
us a game licence issued in Northern Ireland
was only valid within our Six Counties, and,
similarly, licences issued in England and
Scotland were only valid there and would
not be accepted in the Six Counties. Now,
as the result of negotiations
between
Northern Ireland and the Imperial Treasury
it has been mutually agreed that licences
issued in Northern Ireland should be valid
not only here but also in England and
Scotland, and vice versa.
Part II of the Bill deals with a matter
which I also touched on in moving the Money
Resolution and that is the 2d. receipt stamp
on payments of wages or salaries.
It was
felt that in the case of the small wage earner
or salary earner whose wages might only be
just in excess of £2 a week the payment of
the 2d. receipt stamp constituted a disproportionate charge on this class of taxpayer,
and so it has been decided that in respect of
wages or salaries no receipt shall be
necessary irrespective of whether these are
paid weekly, monthly, or at longer intervals.
The loss accruing to our Exchequer in respect of this is estimated at between £1,000
and £2,000 per annum.
There is another Clause which possibly may
have aroused the curiosity of hon. Members,
and that is a reference in the Bill to the
Treaty with Turkey. I do not expect that
this will affect us to any extent at all, but in
embodying it in our Bill we are keeping
faith with the Imperial Parliament who had
Then we come to Part III. Section 9 is a
provision with which all the Members of this
Committee will be most heartily in agreement, that is the exemption from Estate
Duty in the case of sailors or soldiers who
have lost their lives while fighting for the
Government irrespective of the exact nature
of the warfare in which they may have lost
their lives. It is extending a provision which
already exists, but it is necessary that we
should pass legislation on this subject, because the Act was passed by the Imperial
Government whereas Estate Duty is one of
the transferred taxes and is now under control of the Government in Northern Ireland.
At the time the Bill was passed in the
Imperial Parliament "Civil Servants"
necessarily meant members of the Imperial
Civil Service and they were granted the same
concession, namely, that if they lost their
lives in a state of warfare or in conditions
similar to those of warfare they were exempted under certain conditions from Estate
Duty.
We are now granting the same
privilege to members of the Civil Service of
Northern Ireland should such a case arise.
These are all the points to which I need
draw attention as the matter was very carefully gone into by the Minister of Finance in
making his Budget statement earlier in the
year. The present Bill merely seeks to give
statutory conformation to the proposals
which he laid before the House at that time
and with which, I think, the House expressed itself as being in thorough agreement. I beg to move.

impression, that we would be safeguarded by

I submit that this tax is not in any sense a
popular one. It is most unpopular in view
of the fact that it affects the great majority
of the industrial classes of this city. Therefore, if you put it to a plebiscite you would
find that an overwhelming majority would
decide against this tax. Moreover, I think
the tax should be equitable, and really
it is not equitable, for the conditions
under which it was imposed have changed
and very seriously changed with regard
to the industrial classes. This is not
have
the first or the second time that I
voiced my opinion of this matter in the House,
and, as I have said before, the workers are
earning only about 50 per cent. of the amount
that they received when this tax was first
introduced. They did not feel the pinch of
it then-it really did not amount to a hardship-but to-day the wages have been so reduced that in many instances people who
attend an entertainment have to deprive
themselves of something else. It is inequitable, and as it relates only to the lower payments for entrance to entertainments it becomes invidious, and in my opinion should
not be continued. It is recognised by the
right hon. Gentleman that the people who
will suffer under this Bill are those who are
in most need of entertainment. They are
immured within the walls of mills or
factories for, perhaps, eight or nine hours a
day. It is most important that they should
get away from the drudgery of every-day
life, and in order to get away from it they
seek entertainment in the picture houses,
the Hippodrome, or the Theatre as the case
may be. But before they can enter those
places you lay your hand very heavily on
their shoulder and you tell them "You must
pay me the tax." I do not think it is at all democratic that that should be the case, and
that it should be applied, above all others,
to those who can least afford to pay it. I
would not mind, for instance, if you increased
the taxation in respect of others who could
afford to pay for the higher seats at these
entertainments, so long as you remit it in the
case of those who are least able to pay it,
and I think it would be only equitable if you
did so.
The hon. Gentleman who presented the
case (Mr. Barbour) reminded us of a matter
that the Minister of Finance disclosed in his
Budget statement, that the remission of this
tax would involve a sum of £45,000. Well,
even if it did involve a loss of £45,000 we have
ventured as much as that before now. We
have done a great deal more than that, and
I hope the right hon. Gentleman is not going
to be so apprehensive in regard to the
establishing of a National Debt in connection
with this Parliament. I think the sooner
we do it the better. At the present time the
Imperial Parliament is carrying a
National Debt of between £7,000,000,000 and
£8,000,000,000, and its credit has not been
shaken. If we make this concession, even
though it may amount to a sort of disability
with regard to the financial resources of the
Government, it is one of those things that
we are entitled to undertake, and I think in
view of the classes that it affects the right
hon. Gentleman should consider the matter
and make what concession he can. The tax
is most unpopular. There is an outcry
against it from all quarters, and he must be
aware of it. I saw in the Press that several
deputations had approached him upon the
matter. I do not know what the right hon.
Gentleman said to them, but I know what
some of them said to me. (Laughter.) That
is of another character. I do not think he
promised them anything very material. I
think there was nothing that they could base
their hopes on, but in face of a special appeal
from the Members of this House perhaps the
right hon. Gentleman will consider the
matter and see what he can do under the
circumstances. There is just one question I
would like to ask with regard to the statement made by the hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Barbour.) You are relieving agricultural
shows of the tax, I suppose on the ground
that they are educative.

In respect of game licences, to which my
hon. Friend behind me (Mr. Lloyd Campbell)
referred, it should be widely known now to
those who are interested, and they are very
few in number, that game licences issued in
Great Britain or Northern Ireland as the
case may be are reciprocal in their rights.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That is to say,
a game licence taken out and paid for in
Northern Ireland will run equally in Great
Britain, and conversely the conditions in
Great Britain will obtain in Northern
Ireland.
Those are the points raised, and I make
an appeal to my hon. Friends generally with
regard to the effect of the entertainment
tax. In the meantime Northern Ireland requires money, and requires it very badly.
The House understands fully the object for

at an early stage of the Session. (Hon.

Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That for the purpose of any Act of the present Session to amend the Unemployment
Insurance Acts (Northern Ireland), 1920 to
1924, it is expedient to authorise the payment out of moneys provided by Parliament
as from the date prescribed by the Ministry
of Labour under sub-section 2 of Section four
of the Unemployment Insurance Act (Northern
Ireland), 1923, as the date on which the reduced rates of contributions by employers
and workmen are to come into force, of a
contribution towards unemployment benefit,
Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members will
observe that Clause 5 of the Bill, which
they will find at the foot of page 7 and which
appears in italics, proposes that the Exchequer contribution shall, after the end of
the Deficiency period, be increased to onehalf of the combined contributions of employers and employed, that is to say, the
Government will contribute one-third of the
total sum paid into the Fund. At the present time the Exchequer contribution is
6 d. as against 10d. by the employer and 9d.
by the employee, that is to say, only about
one-fourth of the whole, and under Clause 4
of the Unemployment Insurance (Northern
Ireland) Act of 1923, in addition to a provision
for reduced rates on contribution after the
end of the Deficiency period, it was also provided that the Exchequer contribution was
to become one-fourth not of the whole but
of the combined contributions of employers
and employed. The present proposal, therefore, constitutes an amendment of that
particular Act, and this amendment contemplates at some future date throwing a
larger relative contribution upon the State
than either at present is the case or would be
the case under the 1923 Act when the Section
came to operate.
In view of this possible and extra burden
in respect of the Exchequer contribution it
is necessary, therefore, to ask the Committee
to pass this resolution. I may inform hon.
Members that it is impossible to estimate
or give any idea of what the effect of this
concession will be in terms of cash, as
Members are aware that the Exchequer contribution varies with the change in the
unemployment situation, and in any case as
it cannot operate until the Ministry of
Finance is in a position to certify that
the Unemployment Fund is solvent, the
question of the financial implications involved is largely an academic one. This
arises from the fact, which may appear
strange to hon. Members, that the
greater the unemployment the less will be
contributed from the Exchequer, as the
Exchequer only contributes to the fund in
respect of the number of persons actually
employed. Therefore, the more persons employed the larger the Exchequer contribution, and it is due to that variable condition
we are unable to make any estimate as to
what extra charge or burden on the Exchequer may be caused by the Unemployment
Bill to come before the House. I beg to
move.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I am very much
obliged to the hon. Member (Dr. Morrison)
for allowing me to intervene at this stage.
I would like shortly to explain the position
which the Government take in regard to
this matter, and I think such a course will
shorten the discussion. If I may say so,
I think a great deal of unnecessary heat
was shown on the Second reading debate.
That partly arose from an entire misapprehension in the minds of a great many hon.
Members, and I also fear that one or two
hon. Members had an idea that the Government were not bona-fide in their desire to
retain the administration of weights and
measures in the hands of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary. I would like to assure hon.
Members that, so far from this being the
case, the Government are only too anxious
to retain this service in the hands of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary if that is at all
possible. The fact that when we introduced
the Constabulary Bill we gave the service
to the Royal Ulster Constabulary by that
Measure ought to show hon. Members that,
so far as the Government are concerned,
they are really anxious that this particular
service should be retained so far as is possible in the hands of the Royal Ulster
Constabulary.
The Government have up to the present
done their best to obtain men from the ranks
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary to qualify
for this Board of Trade certificate. Hon.
Members have suggested that there are
certain reasons why up to the present we
have failed to obtain these men. One reason
suggested was that the teaching has not
been altogether what it might be. All I can
do is to assure hon. Members that I will
undertake to go very closely into this matter
and secure the best possible teachers for the
men, so that it cannot possibly be put up
as an excuse again. Then again, another
reason suggested was that the course in
which the men were trained was not sufficiently long. There also I intend to go into
the matter. I have already discussed it with
the Inspector-General, and we are prepared
to give the men as long a course as is
necessary. In the first place we intend to
have a tentative examination thrown open
to all the men of the R.U.C. If they pass
that preliminary examination, and show that
it is worth while giving them further instruction, they will get a long course under
the best possible teachers, and during that
time we propose to relieve them of ordinary
police duties. Up to the present there has
been a certain amount of difficulty in doing
that, having regard to the condition of affairs
in the country, but I think I can promise
that during their course of instruction the
men will be relieved of any other police
duties.
Another reason suggested by hon. Members
was that the examination was unnecessarily
severe. I can assure hon. Members that the
Government of Northern Ireland are not responsible for those examination papers.
Under the law as it stands at present the
examination is set by the Board of Trade
and no one can have any connection with
weights and measures in Northern Ireland
unless he passes that examination.
Members suggested that the examination was
too severe. I have looked at the papers and
I must confess that I think very few Members of this Committee could pass that examination unless after a long course of instruction of course I except the hon. Members for the University. I intend to take

Dr. MORRISON: I should like to say a

I got a Bachelor of Science with four or

Mr. McGUFFIN: There was a difficulty
raised yesterday with respect to the scope
of this Bill-not exactly its scope, perhaps, but its application, and the House, I
think, is not satisfied with regard to it, at
least I was not. There is no use in re-stating
the case. I see that it has been spoken of
in the papers as a tangle. Perhaps even the
right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Best) would
admit that there is a tangle in connection
with it. He said, at any rate, that a layman
is not supposed to be able to unravel it, but
I think the House is entitled to hear from
the right hon. Gentleman how the Bill
applies to the particular case that was submitted by the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. Grant). Before we adopt a Bill of
this description, it is necessary that we
should be satisfied with regard to this matter. Though this is not a very important
Bill I always take up the position in this
House that no Member is entitled to allow
a Bill to pass through the House that contains any point puzzling to the comprehension of the Minister in charge and perhaps more puzzling to his own. Therefore,
I submit that it would be but right that the
Minister should take this opportunity of
explaining publicly in the House, the thing
he promised to do in camera to a private
Member.
The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps my hon.
Friend would be more specific, and ask the
Government exactly on what point he requires elucidation?
Mr. McGUFFIN: Well it is on the question submitted here yesterday. I cannot
quote the question now, but my hon. Friend
the Member for North Belfast (Mr. Grant)
submitted it here. He asked was a certain
thing covered by the scope of the Bill, and
1487 Brother's Widow's Marriage Bill.

HOUSE OF COMMONS Third Reading.
[Mr. McGuffin]
the right hon. Gentleman has to reply to
that specific question. That is not a difficult matter, is it? Perhaps the right hon.
Gentleman was not present in the House
when the discussion took place.
The PRIME MINISTER: Yes, I was present, but I thought the point had been cleared up. I thought my hon. Friend had some
further question to be elucidated, and if so,
we will be glad to give any information we
can.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Not at all. It is with
regard to a matter that was under discussion
and that the Attorney-General is quite cognisant of. It is in connection with a question submitted by the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Grant). If he wishes to
withhold the information I do not care.
Mr. GRANT: I would just like to say a
word as one who was responsible for creating the tangle. It was not done intentionally, because I put the question in all good
faith. The right hon. Gentleman in his
reply, stated that if I would see him privately and put the case up to him, he would
try to give a satisfactory answer. I want
to say in all fairness to the Attorney-General
that I have seen him, but I think the tangle
has increased a little since I saw him in
connection with this matter. I am quite
satisfied, at any rate, with the explanation
he has given me. Of course, I cannot say
whether the House should know exactly
what the answer is. However, as far as I
am concerned, I am satisfied with the explanation, though I cannot say that I am
very much wiser in connection with it.
Colonel WOODS: I think that the House is
entitled to know just as much as a private
Member what the answer of the Attorney-
General is. When the Attorney-General
looks on anyone who criticises what he says
as a fool and himself as an angel, he upsets
all my preconceived ideas of what an angel
may look like, except of course that variety
that we do not wish to associate with.
Mr. BEST: I have not the slightest objection to give any information at my disposal,
not only to my hon. Friend (Mr. Grant)
who raised this matter yesterday, but also
to hon. Members in general. The matter
arose in this way, in Committee on this Bill
yesterday. My hon. Friend the Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Grant) raised a point as
to what would happen under certain
circumstances; if I understand the circumstances, they were these. The hon.
Member said he has not been enlightened
very much by what I told him. I think I
tried to answer every question he put to me,
and I tried to discuss the thing from every
aspect. Possibly it may be my fault, or it
may be the fault of the hon. Member, that
I have not thrown as much light on the
subject as he wished.
Mr. GRANT: It is my fault.
Mr. BEST: I do not say whose fault it is.
The question was this: A man and woman
were married, I think he said, in the year
1917. They had children-
Mr. McGUFFIN: In 1918.
Mr. BEST: There was a family as a result
of that marriage. The man was killed in
the war, and his brother married the widow.
Up to the time of the second marriage the
widow and her children had been receiving
a certain amount of pension. The amount
is not material. I do not know because I
do not know the number of children or other
details. But the question was then raised
that as she had married she was no longer
entitled to the pension. My hon. Friend
then put the question to me: Was that a legal
marriage? My answer then and my answer
now is that it was not a legal marriage
according to the law as it then stood, because at that time, a marriage with a
deceased brother's widow was not lawful.
Accordingly these people were not married,
and I think I am right in saying that the
widow would still be entitled to the pension
for herself and also for her children, at least
assuming that all other conditions were fulfilled. The mere fact that she had married
her brother-in-law would not have deprived
her and her children of pension rights. I
understand that some pension officer took
it upon him to disallow the pension and the
pension was disallowed. I may be wrong in
that, but if that were so, in my opinion it
was not a correct method of procedure. It
was not fair to the widow and her children.
Now, I understand the question propounded to me, and which I am expected to
answer, and to which I intend to give an
answer is this-Will this Bill of ours when
it becomes law legalise that marriage?
Mr. McGUFFIN: Yes, that is the point.
Mr. BEST: My answer is simple and I
will make it plain to the dullest if there be
any dull people in this House. If that socalled marriage-the second marriage-had
been annulled by a Court of course there is
an end to it, or if the man who had
married, or the woman who had married
in the belief that the marriage was then
lawful-if either went off and contracted a
legal marriage then that legal marriage will
be validated by our Act, and the previous
marriage would have been wiped out. I cannot go any further because I do not know
what the facts are. When I was discussing
the matter with my hon. Friend he was unable to tell me all the facts, but assuming that
either of these people got married and
assuming their so-called marriage was not
dissolved by court of law then the Bill which
we are now passing when it becomes an Act
will, in my opinion, validate that marriage.

GRANTS UNDER HOUSING ACT
(NORTHERN IRELAND), 1923.
1. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, if he will state the total
amount paid by the Government towards
Housing, under the Housing Act (Northern
Ireland), 1923; and how many houses have
been erected, or are in course of erection,
in Belfast and elsewhere in Northern Ireland?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The total amount paid
to private builders up to the present under
the Act of 1923 is £16,850.
The total number of houses erected or in
course of erection by private builders is
1,390, of which 639 are in Belfast.
In addition, schemes providing for the
erection of 440 houses by local authorities
have been sanctioned by the Ministry, of
which 250 are in Belfast.
OFFENCES BY "B" SPECIALS.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether he can state the
number of men of the "B" Class, Special
Constabulary, Ligoniel district, who, during
the first nine months of this year, have
been fined for various offences under the
Police Code, including absence from patrol
on the 12th July; the average amount of
these fines, and the total amount derived
from all fines, and if he will state to what
purpose this money is applied?
Sir DAWSON BATES: During the first
nine months of the year no members of "B"
Class Special Constabulary, Ligoniel District, were fined for disciplinary offences
under the Police Code.
Such fines are paid to the credit of the
Special Constabulary Reward Fund under
the provisions of the Special Constabulary
Reward Fund Regulations dated 17th
October, 1922.
Deductions were made in the case of 13
men for absence from patrols and drills,
including 3 men who were absent from
patrol on 12th July.
The total amount of such deductions in
the period from 1st April last is £4 2s 6d.
The following is the provision in the
Conditions of Service under which these
deductions are made:-
"If without due and sufficient reason
in the opinion of the County Commandant any man shall fail to perform
the number of patrols or drills laid
down for each quarter a deduction of 5s
for each patrol and 2s 6d for each drill
not performed will be made from his
quarterly bonus."
It will be seen that these deductions are
in no sense fines. They are simply nonpayments of an allowance resulting from
the non-performance of the duty for which
the allowance is payable, and constitute a
reduction in the expenditure under the
appropriate sub-head of the Vote.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Arising out of that question might I ask the right hon. Gentleman
if he has had any complaints from any particular section of the community with
respect to this matter, and whether at the
present time there is known to him any
reason that would make this question de
sirable in this House?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, Sir.

IRELAND.
4. Mr. DONALD asked the Parliamentary

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION
(Mr. McKeown): It is presumed that the
first portion of the hon. Member's question
relates to the sums voted by the Imperial
Parliament for education in Ireland.
The total amounts specifically voted by
the Imperial Parliament towards the cost
of Elementary Education in Ireland in
1919-20, 1920-21, and 1921-22 were respectively
£3,172,636, £4,444,261, and £4,738,239. The
provision for payments to the teaching staff
included in these total amounts was
£2,868,480 in 1919-20; £4,130,590 in 1920-21,
and £4,378,950 in 1921-22.
The total amounts voted towards the cost
of Intermediate Education in Ireland in
1919-20, 1920-21, and 1921-22, were, respectively, £90,000, £140,000, and £140,000.
It is not possible to say how much of each
of these sums related to teachers' salaries.
The total amounts voted as Grants to
Irish Universities and Colleges, and for the
higher education of ex-officers, etc., were-
£317,675 in 1919-20; £176,000 in 1920-21; and
£242,546 in 1921-22.
The sums specifically voted for schools of
Science and Art in the three years were-
1919-20, £124,100; 1920-21, £129,540; 1921-22,
£128,950. In addition, considerable sums
were voted each year towards the expenses
of local Statutory Committees of Agriculture and Technical Instruction, but the
printed Estimates do not show what portion
of the sums so voted related to Technical
Instruction.
The above figures do not include sums
voted in respect of buildings, maintenance,
and repairs, fuel and light, rates, stationery,
postage, etc., nor do they include the sums
expended in these years out of the Endowment Funds of the Intermediate Education
Board and the Department of Agriculture
and Technical Instruction for Ireland
respectively.
The total net amounts voted by the Parliament of Northern Ireland towards the cost
of education in the years 1922-23 and 1923-
24 were, respectively, £1,799,283 and
£1,914,465. The amounts voted for salaries
and other administrative expenses of
Ministry (including stationery and printing,
postage, fuel and light, etc.) were, 1922-23
£71,661; 1923-24, £68,660.
ance,
The amounts voted for Elementary

The amounts voted for Higher Education

The expenditure on Intermediate Education and Technical Instruction, which was
formerly met from the Endowment Funds
of the Intermediate Education Board and

Motion made and Question proposed:
