PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A message was delivered by the Gentleman
Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:-
Mr. Speaker, his Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland commands this
Honourable House to attend immediately
in the Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the Clerk's
place at the Table): I have to acquaint the
House that the House has this day been to
the Senate, where his Grace the Governor
delivered his Speech to both Houses of
Parliament as follows:-
KING'S SPEECH.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.

I have to congratulate you upon the
legislative measures passed this session,
which mark steady progress in the promotion of the general welfare of the people.
I am glad to learn that there are hopeful
signs of a recovery from the acute period
of depression generally experienced, although
I regret that it is less rapid than we all so
earnestly desire. The weather, which has
proved so unfortunate to agriculture-our
greatest industry-and the continued slackness in the Shipyards, have prejudicially
affected conditions in Northern Ireland, but
prices for agricultural produce are showing
an upward tendency which will mitigate
the losses sustained by farmers. I also note
with pleasure that an improvement has
taken place in shipbuilding, where the prospects are now somewhat brighter It is
still necessary to create work specially designed for the relief of unemployment, and
in this regard it is satisfactory to know
that the Government continues to receive
the cordial co-operation of Local Authorities
in whose districts unemployment is serious.
An Act has been passed this session which
has conferred increased rates of benefit for
those who are unemployed, in conformity
with similar legislation by the Imperial
Parliament.
The King's Speech.
Prorogation.
7 NOVEMBER 1924
In other directions by means of the Loans
Guarantee Act, you have promoted the development of private industrial undertakings calculated to relieve unemployment. A
sum of £5,000,000 has been made available
for this purpose and guarantees have already been given of over £4,500,000. A
satisfactory sign in this period of trade depression is the continued popularity of
Ulster Savings Certificates, in which nearly
£1,500,000 has now been invested.
It is with great pleasure that I am able
to state that the maintenance of law and
order has been so satisfactorily continued
and to record the thanks of our people to
officers and men of the Royal Ulster and
Special Constabulary. Their vigilance, tact
and devotion to duty has enabled the whole
community to settle down to a life of
confidence and security.
I am gratified to know that the development of the new system of Educational
Administration under the Act of last
session is proceeding smoothly and rapidly.
Statutory rules and orders have been laid
before Parliament. Negotiations are in progress with the County Councils for the
establishment of the Local Educational
Authorities in the Counties, the 1st day of
October 1924 having been appointed by Order
in Council for the bringing into operation
of those provisions of the Act under which
these Bodies are required to be set up.
Your Housing Act extends the provisions
of last year's measure with a view to affording a further opportunity to private
builders and to local authorities to erect
houses with Government assistance.
The Exchequer and Financial Provisions
Act which was passed early in the Session,
has provided for the disposal of the sum of
£400,000 granted by the Imperial Government in final satisfaction of the claim for
the provision of buildings in accordance
with the Government of Ireland Act 1920,
excluding Parliamentary Buildings, new Law
Courts and administrative offices. This sum
will be utilised in connection with a Training College and Hostel for School Teachers,
a depôt for the Royal Ulster Constabulary,
a Convict Prison, a Borstal Institution and
Criminal Lunatic Asylum, and Institutions
for agricultural instruction and research.
Members of the House of Commons.
I thank you for the provision of supplies
for the public services.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
Various Commissions which have been set
up are still engaged upon work of farreaching importance and the members are
deserving every praise for the industry
and care with which they are prosecuting
their inquiries.
I am satisfied with the success of the
Ulster Pavilion at the British Empire
Exhibition, which provided a useful link
in connecting Northern Ireland with other
parts of His Majesty's Dominions. Upwards
of 900 children, mainly from elementary
schools, visited the Exhibition, and it is
believed that the effect will be to foster and
encourage Imperial ideals.
Many representatives of the Dominions
and Colonies have visited our shores this
year and will I hope take away with them
recollections of the loyalty of our people
towards the Empire of which they and we
are so proud to form a part.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty God
may rest upon your labours.
After which the Proclamation proroguing
Parliament was read as follows:-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
Proroguing the Present Parliament of
Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by Section
Eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
the Irish Free State (Consequential Provisions) Act, 1922, that the Governor of
Northern Ireland shall, in His Majesty's
name, Summon, Prorogue and Dissolve the
Parliament of Northern Ireland.
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that this
. present Parliament of Northern Ireland
should be Prorogued to the Tenth day of
March, One Thousand Nine Hundred and
Twenty-five.
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, Governor of
Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do
publish and declare His Majesty's Pleasure
that the said Parliament be, as from the
reading of this Proclamation in the Parliament of Northern Ireland, Prorogued to
Tuesday, the Tenth day of March, One
Thousand Nine Hundred and Twenty-five.
AND I Do Hereby Further Declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall, on the said
Tenth day of March, One Thousand Nine
Hundred and Twenty-five, assemble and be
holden for the despatch of divers urgent
and important affairs, and the Senators and
Members of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland are hereby required to
give their attendance accordingly.
Prorogation.
End of Session.
HOUSE OF COMMONS
Given at Belfast, this Sixth day of
November, One Thousand Nine Hundred and
Twenty-four.
Signed by his own hand,
End of the Fourth Session (opened

Tuesday,
11th March, 1924) of the First Parliament
of Northern Ireland, in the Fifteenth year
of the Reign of His Majesty King George
the Fifth.
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.

BUUN TU 08452

Tuesday, 11th March, 1924.
The Fourth Session of the First Parliament
of Northern Ireland, appointed to meet 11th
March, 1924, in the fourteenth year in the
Reign of King George V, was opened by the
Governor (His Grace the Duke of Abercorn,
K.P.) in person.
The House met at Ten Minutes before
Twelve of the Clock. Mr. Speaker (Right
Hon. Hugh O'Neill, D.L., M.P.) in the Chair.
The Gentleman Usher of the Black Rod
(Major T. D. H. Hackett, D.S.O.) was
announced.
Addressing Mr. Speaker, the Gentleman
Usher said; His Grace the Governor of
Northern Ireland commands this Honourable
House to attend immediately in the Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
The Sitting was suspended until Three of
the Clock, and then resumed.
LOCAL BILLS.
Mr. SPEAKER laid upon the Table Report
from the Examiner of Petitions for Local
Bills, that he has certified that the Standing
Orders have been complied with in the
following cases:
Belfast Corporation,
Londonderry Corporation,
Belfast Water,

SESSIONAL ORDERS.
ELECTIONS.
Ordered, That all Members, who are returned for two or more places in any part of
Northern Ireland do make their Election for
which of the places they will serve, within
one week after it shall appear that there is
no question upon the Return for that place;
and if anything shall come in question
touching the Return or Election of any
Member, he is to withdraw during the time
the matter is in debate; and that all Members returned upon double Returns do withdraw till the Returns are determined.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been elected or returned a Member of this House or endeavoured so to be,
by Bribery, or any other corrupt practices,
this House will proceed with the utmost
severity against all such persons as shall
have been wilfully concerned in such Bribery
or other corrupt practices.
WITNESSES.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that any
person hath been tampering with any
Witness in respect of his evidence to be
given to this House, or any Committee
thereof, or directly or indirectly hath endeavoured to deter or hinder any person
from appearing or giving evidence, the same
is declared to be a high crime or misdemeanour; and this House will proceed
with the utmost severity against such
offender.
Resolved: That if it shall appear that
any person hath given false evidence in any
case before this House, or any Committee
thereof, this House will proceed with the
utmost severity against such offender.
ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Ordered: That the Commissioner of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary do take care that,
during the Session of Parliament, the passages through the streets leading to this
House be kept free and open, and that no
obstruction be permitted to hinder the passage of Members to and from this House,
and that no disorder be allowed in the precincts of or in the passages leading to this
House, during the Sitting of Parliament,
and that there be no annoyance therein, or
thereabouts; and that the Serjeant at Arms
attending this House do communicate this
Order to the Commissioner of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary aforesaid.
VOTES, PROCEEDINGS, AND RECORDS.
Ordered: That the Votes, Proceedings and
Records of this House be printed, being first
perused by Mr. Speaker; and that he do
appoint the printing thereof; and that no
person but such as he shall appoint do presume to print the same.
PRIVILEGES.
Ordered: That a Committee of Privileges
be appointed.

House that the House has this day attended
in the Senate to hear his Grace's Speech,
on behalf of the Crown, to both Houses of
Parliament; of which I have for greater accuracy obtained a copy. The Speech is as
follows :
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
When a year ago I first had the privilege
of addressing this House as Governor of
Northern Ireland I expressed the hope that
respect for the law would prevail and that
the good order which had recently been
established in the Province might continue,
King's Speech.

I am glad to be able to state that this
expectation has been most happily realized
by the experience of the past twelve
months.
This
Shortly after their assumption of office
I received and transmitted a suggestion
from the new Imperial Government that
there should be a Conference to consider
the Boundary question and certain other
matters outstanding between Northern
Ireland and the Irish Free State.
suggestion was accepted and the Government was represented at a Conference
which took place with three Members of the
Imperial Government and three Members
of the Free State Government by the Prime
Minister of Northern Ireland, the Minister
of Education and the Attorney-General.
After two preliminary meetings the Conference was postponed for a month, but
owing to the ill-health of the Prime
Minister, which I am sure we all greatly
deplore, a further postponement has been
requested.
There are indications of a revival in
trade, and in the Linen Industry an improvement has already occurred which has
exceeded general expectation. This is likely
to have a salutary effect on other
Industries. In other directions, however,
I fear that the position is still abnormal
and exceptional measures are still required
for relieving the graver cases of distress
among our people. I am happy to note that
the Local Authorities have realized the
continued seriousness of the situation and
are doing their utmost, with the assistance
of the Government, to promote most useful
work to meet the difficulties created by
unemployment. The success of the Loans
Guarantee Act has been of such a character
as to render it very desirable that further
steps should be taken in this direction.
Accordingly, your assent will be invited to
proposals seeking for authority to issue
guarantees over and above the existing
limit in respect of loans to be applied
towards the carrying out of capital undertakings calculated to create employment in
Northern Ireland. Legislation dealing with
Unemployment Insurance will be introduced to make the necessary provision a
regards unemployment benefit for the latter
part of the current year.
I take this opportunity of endorsing the
appeal which has recently been made by
the Government on behalf of unemployed
disabled ex-Service men, and I trust that
every employer who has not yet enrolled
on the King's National Roll of Honour will
take immediate steps to qualify for enrolment by employing the requisite number of
ex-Service men.
I would also appeal to every firm to do
all it can to provide work for the large
number of persons, both men and women,
whose return to their normal employment
is so essential.
I am glad that the relations of employers
and employed in Northern Ireland continue on such harmonious lines, and it is
my earnest hope that this satisfactory state
of affairs may be maintained in order that
there may be no injury to the reviving
industry of the Province.
The Commission
on Development, to
which I referred last year, has been actively at work and has already presented
Reports on which the Government intends
to take action during the present session.
The reports of the Reformatory and Industrial Schools Committee, and of the
Committee which investigated the Jury
system have been received and are receiing careful consideration
I am glad to learn that it is intended

inquire into the suitability and cost of the
existing local administrative machinery in
connection with Local Government, Public
Health, Poor Law and the allied Services.
Steps have been taken to put into operation the Education Act which was passed
last session. An Order in Council was

on which the whole of the Act should take

The absence of facilities in Northern

has for some time been a source of anxiety

University of Belfast, acting in conjunction with the Ministry of Agriculture, have
now decided to establish a Faculty of Agriculture within the University, so that
henceforth in the matter of agricultural

handicapped by lack of suitable buildings
and equipment, but provision is being
made in the estimates of the Ministry of
Agriculture for a contribution towards the

Debate on the Address.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I beg to move:
"That an humble Address be presented
to His Grace the Governor of Northern
Ireland, as followeth :
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal
subjects the Commons of Northern Ireland,
in Parliament assembled, beg leave to offer
our humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed
to both Houses of Parliament."
Before touching upon the matters of public
interest and public welfare which have been
embodied in the King's Speech I would like
to express my appreciation and my realisation of the honour which has been conferred upon me to-day in asking me to move
this Address. I fully realise that it is not
a personal honour, but that it is, first of
all, a compliment to the city and county of
which I am one of the representatives, and
also that it is a tribute-if I may take it
as such-to the sex to which I belong. (Hon.
Members Hear, hear.) I believe I am
correct in saying that I am the first woman,
at any rate in the British Empire, who has
had this privilege-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) and I take it as a recognition of the
altered position of our sex in the councils
of the Empire-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) and also, coming nearer home, as a
recognition, perhaps, of the work which has
been accomplished by the women of Northern Ireland. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
As such I need not say that I value it most
highly.
At the commencement of the Session of
1923 two Bills of great magnitude were
foreshadowed, Bills which dealt with two
of the most vital problems affecting our
community. To-day both these Bills are on
the Statute Book, but as reference has
been made to one of them-the Education
Act-in his Grace's Speech to-day may I be
permitted to say that I rejoice to see that
the extension of the application of that Act
to the Counties later on in the year is under
consideration? I firmly believe this
Act will prove to be a boon to the
whole community, that it will ensure a good
education to every future citizen, no matter
how humble and how poor he may be, an
education, primary and technical, which he
can claim as his right. If that is the case,
then the sooner those in the country as well
as in the cities have this privilege conferred
upon them the better. I am also sure we are
glad to see in this connection that rules and
regulations under the provisions of this Act
will be shortly laid before us. Misunderstandings have arisen, and I hope that all

anxiety in the minds of those who are natur-

I feel sure that all Members of the House will

made at the end of last Session that he would

I know I will be voicing the sentiments of
every hon. Member of this House when I say
that every one of us, whether directly representing labour, as certain hon. Members do,
or indirectly representing Labour, as I hope
we all do-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-is
most anxious to assist the authorities by
every possible means to alleviate the intolerable burden
of unemployment-the
aftermath of the war-which has been cast
upon this land, a burden which is undermining the courage, sapping the resistance,
and lowering the self-respect of those who,
if less fortunate than ourselves, we cannot
forget are equal citizens with ourselves of
this State. Feeling like that we naturally
welcome the statement in his Grace's Speech
with regard to further relief and to an extension of the Loans Guarantee Act. In
stating this we also place on record our realisation of the great efforts already made in
this direction by the Government. I cannot
leave this subject, which I know will be
dealt with far more adequately by the hon.
Member (Mr. Grant) following me, without
referring to the next paragraph in his
Grace's Speech with regard to the unemployed ex-Servicemen. Words are of little
avail, but if our hearts soften towards the
unemployed men and women who have a
right to live and a right to work, and who
cannot get work, and who can hardly live,
how much more do our hearts soften, do our
hearts bleed for the unemployed ex-Serviceman who fought for us, who served his
country, who suffered for us, and who is now
walking the streets of our cities looking for
the work which we cannot extend to him?
An appeal. I know, has already been inade
by the Government to the employers. This
appeal has been endorsed to-day in his
Grace's Speech, and I know that it will now
be further endorsed by this House. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).
There are very few interests that seem to
have been overlooked in the somewhat extensive programme before us. I know we
are all glad that a Commission will shortly
be set up to inquire into Local Government
matters. All of us know how badly reform
and co-ordination are needed, and if we did
not realise this the debate which took place
last Session on the Local Government Bill
would have lifted, for a little at any rate,
the veil and given us a glimpse of the scenes
behind. I do not think I would be uttering
a heresy, and I believe my hon. Friend
opposite (Sir Robert Lynn) will agree with
me, if I say that this Commission will deal
with matters which affect the community
even more vitally than the Education Act.
Believing this may I say that I hope their
labours may be blessed and that they will
prepare the foundation for another and even
greater monument to Ulster's progress?
The House will, I am sure, eagerly await
the report of the Commision on Development
and the Government action thereon, and we
venture to hope that a new era of commercial
prosperity and consequent absorption of unemployed workers is dawning on our horizon,
and that it will be found that Ulster's soil,
Ulster's native resources, and Ulster's riches
may be exploited for the benefit of Ulster's
sons and daughters. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
As I have said, very few matters have been
overlooked, and agriculture finds its place
among the outlined proposals. May I say
that I wish it had been possible to outline
something more definite (hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-in the way of asistance to our
premier industry, which cannot benefit as
other industries do under the Loans Guarantee Act? I venture to hope that the Government may, perhaps, sce their way later on
to go a little further in this direction.
It would be impossible for me to omit a
reference to the suggestion that after the
5th of June it is possible that certain proposals may be laid before us with reference
to our distribution of Members in the
counties and the general reorganisation of
our registration. All I would like to say in
this connection is that it is obvious, to me
at any rate, that the unwieldy size of the pre-

In conclusion, may I say I note that there
is one feeling which we all share, one thought
in every mind, and that is that we all miss

on these occasions. We here can ill spare
our Prime Minister-(Hon. Members: Hear,
hear) just as the country can ill spare him,
the country for which he has not spared

detriment of his own health, the country
which perhaps does not realise as we here
realise the debt which it owes to him and
perhaps will not realise the debt until it
is out of its power to foot the bill. I believe
it was Burke who said that good government depends not upon laws but upon
individuals. We have an example here
when we realise how much that applies to
those who govern as well as to those who are
governed, for we have in our Prime Minister
a man whom we are proud to follow, who
has gained the affection and confidence of
all who are anxious and willing to work.
We wish him a speedy recovery, and hope
that he may soon come back to us fit and
well, able to once more take up the heavy
burdens laid upon his shoulders. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) I beg to move.
Mr. GRANT (in morning dress): I truly
appreciate the encouragement I have received from hon. Members of this House
because no person at the present moment
requires it more. I feel greatly honoured
at having been asked to second this motion
so ably and gracefully proposed by the hon.
Member for County Derry, and I take it as
a recognition on the part of the Government
of the legitimate claims of labour. May I
at the outset join in the expression of regret
at the absence of the Prime Minister. We
all know the arduous time through which the
Prime Minister has passed lately, and it is
not surprising that the heavy responsibility
and constant strain together with the worry
and annoyance to which he has been
subjected have told upon his health
and strength. We gladly give him
a respite from active duty, and
hope that with the rest cure will come a
speedy recovery. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). I believe it was the Dean of St.
Paul's who said that "in our generation
there are no great men." Well, the Dean
may be right as regards London, but had he
lived in Ulster, especially during the past
four or five years he might not be such a
pessimist. He might have found that we
have great and distinguished men who are
whole-heartedly and courageously devoting
themselves to the service of their country,
and one of the greatest and most distinguished of these is the Prime Minister.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
After the remarks of the Member for
County Derry I do not intend to dwell at
length on the several matters alluded
to in the King's Speech. That Speech deals
with a variety of subjects, and I fancy it
is sufficiently comprehensive to please even
the most exacting critic. Of course the role
of critic is very easy. I have sometimes
adopted that role myself. It is hard,however,
for the critic to estimate the difficulty with
which this Government, and indeed, all
Governments, have been struggling during
the past few years. Apart from anything
else a great deal of adaptability is necessary.
For a long period we had to strain every
nerve towards putting down crime and outrage. We succeeded, and a serious
handicap to industry was thus removed.
Public confidence has been restored, and it
is now recognised throughout the world that
trade can be carried on with Ulster with
the same trust and uniformity as with the
rest of the United Kingdom. We are now
bending every effort towards reconstruction
and building up, and it can hardly be
doubted that we are winning through, slowly
but surely, to stability and prosperity. Law
and order prevail within our borders and
the people realise and appreciate the advantages of firm and impartial government.
I am glad to see the reference in the King's
Speech to the Boundary between Northern
and Southern Ireland. This is a matter
that has attracted widespread attention, and
we commend the Prime Minister for so readily responding to the suggestion from the Imperial Government that he should take part
in a conference in London. Of course that
is a very different thing from participating
in a Commission such as that referred to
in the Irish Treaty. The attitude of our
Government has all along been clear and
distinct. We are prepared at any time to
consider in a friendly spirit the Boundary
question with the Free State Government.
We recognise that the frontier needs slight
adjustment here and there, and it would be
well for both parties if an understanding
could be arrived at. But under no circumstances will we allow any portion of the
territory granted to us under the 1920 Act to
be filched from us. That is why we have declined to have anything to do with the
Commission arranged for behind our backs,
and we hold that no such Commission can be
set up without our consent. The attitude
we have taken up is reasonable and logical,
and is well known to the Imperial Government. To put it in a sentence it is-Agree-

I am sure that Members have noticed with

regards linen. I wish this revival was
general, but I am afraid that many of our

The Government, however, deserve great
praise for the measures adopted by them to
create employment. In June, 1921, the
number of persons totally unemployed in
the Insured Trades in Ulster was over
63,000 while about 45,000 persons were
short time. At present the number of persons totally unemployed is 37,000 of whom
27,000 are men, while the number of persons

or very large
have been put into operation. In
Belfast alone the total cost of the
Works which have been sanctioned is over
£2,200,000, while outside Belfast, Relief
Works involving an expenditure of £300,000
have been put in hands. I hold that relief
works of permanent utility are the proper
way to relieve distress. Our people do not
want unemployment benefit if work can be
provided. The Local Authorities are doing
all they can to help, and it is up to our
employers of labour to do their fair share.
If they do, the responsibilities of the
Government will be lightened, and the
unemployed given work.
The Loans Guarantee Act passed last year
has been a big success. The capital cost
of the works put in hand under this Act
amounts to over £3,000,000, and I am glad
to note that this House will be invited to
give authority to issue further loans. The
work consists largely of shipbuilding construction. I suppose that most of the Hon.
Members know that shipbuilding has not
been very prosperous since the War, and
the workers in the yards have lower rates
of wages that those in many other industries.
They have, however, given no trouble. They
have been loyal. They have not gone out
on strike or threatened to strike. They
are, therefore, deserving of sympathetic
Consideration, and I hope that additional
work will be found for them by means of
these Guarantee Loans.
In order to provide for those who are
still unfortunately unemployed the provisions
of the Unemployment Insurance Acts have
been applied to Northern Ireland on precisely the same terms as in Great Britain.
Since the 1st January, 1922, a sum of about
£3,100,000 has been paid in Unemployment
Benefit. For the week ended 22nd February
last the sum paid amounted to £28,675.
Those are large figures, and indicate how
the Government is endeavouring to cope
with the problem. I may say that the
administration of this Unemployment Benefit
has been greatly improved by the association
with each Employment Exchange of a Local
Employment Committee, consisting of representatives of employers, workers, and the
general public ín each area. Benefit is now
paid only to those who are entitled to it.
I would like to join in the appeal on behalf
of the unemployed disabled ex-Servicemen,
and I hope that employers throughout our
area will qualify for enrolment on the
King's National Roll of Honour. It is their
duty to do so, and I trust they will not
confine themselves to the necessary
percentage.
As the House knows, the Government has
appointed a strong representative Commission consisting of employers, workers and
experts to inquire into the natural and
industrial resources of the Province with a
view to creating new industries and taking
further measures for removing unemployment. This Committee is hard at work, and
there is no doubt that its activities will
have an important bearing on the industrial
future of Ulster. They have already presented reports in regard to special subjects,
and upon these the Government intends to
take action during the present Session.
The Government has striven to preserve
industrial peace, and it can truthfully be
asserted that as a result of the reasonableness of both employers and workers, and a
sympathetic understanding of each other's
points of view, Ulster has been singularly
free from industrial troubles. Long may
that happy state of affairs continue.
It is the intention of the Government to
appoint very shortly a Commission to inquire into the suitability and cost of the
existing local administrative machinery in
connection with Local Government, Public
Health, Poor Law and the Allied Services.
I think such a Commission is absolutely
necessary, and I trust that the outcome of
its labours will be more efficient administration and greater economy. I do not
think I need add to the reference in the

We are to have a Bill dealing with rent

presentation has been postponed until the
Measure about to be introduced into the

I do not altogether approve of that. Hon.

appointed by this Government considered

quickly enough. The Bill introduced into

found satisfactory, and the Labour Member

I cannot agree with this procrastination.
I sincerely hope that when the Bill is introduced into this House the tenants will receive
sympathetic treatment, and that they will be

I am pleased to see that steps are to be

barracks. There should be no delay in regard to that work. The buildings of various
Societies throughout the country have been
commandeered for use as temporary
barracks, and the owners have been put to
considerable inconvenience. The sooner these
premises are handed back and the police provided with their own barracks the better.
Among other matters that will engage the
attention of the House will be Bills to amend
the existing Pharmacy Laws, and to
strengthen the safeguards against the illegal
traffic in dangerous drugs. I
Measures of this description will meet with

am sure
Lastly, allusion is made to the recently
published report of the Colwyn Committee.
This Committee, as you know, was set up
to deal with the financial relations between
the Imperial Government, and the Government of Northern Ireland. I do not feel
competent to criticise such a complicated
document at present, but it is not difficult
to see that in some respects we have been
unfairly treated. Take for instance our
claim to 40 per cent of the Irish Grant,
under the Provision for Soldiers and Sailors
Act, 1919. This was a War relief measure.
Under Lord French's recruiting scheme
and as an additional inducement to men
to join up, plots of land and houses were
to be provided for ex-servicemen. Twenty
eight per cent of these plots and houses
have been allotted to Ulster apparently on
the ground that this represents the ratio
of population in the six counties to the rest
of Ireland, but it should not be forgotten
that the recruits from Northern Ireland
were at least 50 per cent of the whole. If
the allocation is not to be on the basis of
recruiting, then what other basis is there
that can have the least regard to fairplay?
Yet our claim to 40 per cent is disallowed.
The Committee has cut down by £200,000
the £500,000 unemployment relief grant.
That is also an injustice, but I am
pleased that our Northern Government has
decided to provide the £200,000 so that the
original amount of £500,000 will remain.
The claim to £1,000,000 contribution towards
malicious injuries since January, 1922, the
date when administration powers were
transferred, has been reduced to £500,000.
As a matter of equity and justice the Imperial Treasury ought to meet all the
malicious injuries awards up to the restoration of law and order by the Northern
Government, because the Imperial Government was alone responsible as a Government
for the destruction of life and property in
Northern Ireland. I shall not further
discuss the report as it will take some time
to digest it, but I am sure that the Minister
of Finance, who revels in figures, will enlighten us upon all these statistical matters.
I am afraid I have wearied you with a
somewhat uninteresting speech, and I shall
conclude with the hope that we may have
a useful and fruitful Session.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: We have been

speech she has just delivered. Those of us
who have been acquainted with the hon.

has excelled herself, and not only done honour, if I may be permitted to say so, to this
House and to the sex she represents, but to
the constituency she happens to represent,
the County and the City of Londonderry.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I am quite
free to say that in making this history this

evening the hon. Member has set up a

It is not an easy matter in a speech of

the King's Speech is to take the things of

with them on an occasion of this character.
Before doing so may I say what I am sure
every hon. Member is in agreement with,
and that is that we regret the absence of
the Prime Minister? (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). We deeply regret that absence because of the reason of it. We know the

was
Now the first thing in connection with
this King's Speech that strikes me is the reference to law and order. It is only right
that an ordinary Member of this House on
such an occasion as this should offer oongratulations to the Minister of Home Affairs
and. to those associated with him on the
work they have rendered since this Parliament last met in keeping Ulster in the splendid position which she occupies to-day with
order restored, with law respected and with
peace prevailing on every hand. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). I trust that that
happy state of affairs will long continue; that
there will be not only the co-operation and
assistance of every Member of this House
with the Minister and those acting with him
but that all classes of the community
throughout the Six Counties will try to
create the healthiest possible feeling and do
everything within their power to make this
Province of ours a peaceful, law-abiding community, for without peace there can be no
progress or advancement.
The next outstanding thing in connection
with the Speech is the question of unemployment. I am not going to deal with any
figures. These have been presented, and presented most effectively, by the hon. Member
who has just spoken (Mr. Grant). We are
all glad that there are signs of improvement
in many directions, but the sky is not as
bright as we would like it to be just at the
moment. We are all glad that the Minister
of Labour has been doing his share in trying
to remedy the unemployment which meets
us at every point and which is one of the
greatest difficulties with which the Ministry
have at the moment to contend. Much has
been done, much remains to be done, and
much, I am sure, is going yet to be done.
In this connection I want to put a question
to the Government Originally there was a
grant of £500,000 from the Imperial
Exchequer to help the unemployed in the
city of Belfast, preference being given, of
course, to ex-servicemen. According to the
report and findings of the Colwyn Committee other aspects of this report I shall
deal with at a later stage-we are now to be
deprived of the unexpired portion of that
grant, something like £200,000. The hon.
Member who has just sat down (Mr. Grant)
has stated that we as a Government are
going to implement that £200,000 out of our
resources. I hope we are going to have confirmation of that, but I would like to say if
it is going to be done by the Minister of
Finance that I should claim as far as I am
personally concerned that no restrictive
Clause will exist-that if the £200,000 is
going to be conceded it is not going to be
confined to any part of the Six Counties,
but that it is going to be available not only
for the city of Belfast but for every town and
district throughout the entire Six Counties.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I am sure no
other intention exists, but that this money
which will come from the Exchequer of
Northern Ireland, will be devoted to the
relief of the unemployed throughout every
part of the Province, and, of course, in
that case if Belfast happens to be the
neediest portion, then it will get the largest
share.
The next point in connection with the
Speech that I wish to touch upon is one in
regard to which I want to put a question
to the Minister of Home Affairs. In the
last Session of this Parliament we passed
an Act dealing with Housing and we had a
good deal of argument and debate over it.
Some were hopeful of a great deal of good
and some were not quite so hopeful. I
should like to know from the Minister of
Home Affairs what is the position to-day.
How many of the local authorities have
sent in schemes and what are the numbers
of houses contemplated by those local
authorities? I think it is well for us to
know what is the position in regard to those
houses, because it lies, to my mind, at the
root of a good deal of the unrest that exists
at the present moment. Whether the scheme
which was passed by this Parliament at its
last Session is going to accomplish, and

accomplish effectively, what has been contemplated I am not in a position to say, but

In this connection of necessity the Rent
Restrictions Act is bound to occur to one's
mind. I am very glad to find myself in
agreement with the hon. Member who has
just sat down (Mr. Grant) in regard to this
matter. May I be permitted to say that for
a considerable time I have been of the
opinion that there has been a desire shown
by the Government too slavishly to follow
every movement of the British legislature?
(Mr. McGuffin: Hear, hear.) I know there
are many questions and many measures in
which it is absolutely essential that we
should have similarity and uniformity, but
I am surprised that it has been suggested
that this matter should be postponed. And
postponed for what reason? We appointed
a Committee to inquire into the whole
matter, and a report has been made to the
Department concerned. I take leave to say
that they have got all the information that
can be possibly given to them, and the time
has come for the Government to legislate on
their own account. Are they really serious
in thinking that in the coming days they
are going to adopt all the measures that
any Government that may be in power at
Westminster is going to pass? Are they
serious in suggesting that on questions of
Housing and Rent Restriction, and other
matters, we must wait to see what the
Government in power there is going to do,
and then that we are going to say "ditto"
to their measures? I protest against the
principle involved here, and I sincerely hope
that the Government will immediately
proceed to implement the report that was
presented to them by their own Committee,
and allow the House to come to its own
conclusions in regard to this Rent Restriction measure.
There are two other matters that I should
like to refer to before I sit down. Probably
they are the most important matters that
could be referred to, and they are subjects
that the people we represent are thinking
about constantly. First of all there is the
question of the Boundary. I am not going
to argue that particular subject-it has been
done by the hon. Member (Mr. Grant) who
has just sat down-but I would like to make
one or two observations upon it. Sometimes
we find a good deal of criticism, a good of
scepticism, is expressed by people outside in
regard to this whole subject. I think that
this matter can be safely left with those who
have handled the question, and handled it so
successfully, up to the present moment.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). I think that
the House will have the utmost confidence in
those who are representing them and that
the people of the Six Counties may rest
assured that the Prime Minister, and those
that are working with him, will see that
the interests of this Parliament and the Six
Counties will be protected to the fullest
possible extent. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
I come now to a familiar subject, the
importance of which I think every member
of this House will recognise. I hope that
all the Members have studied the report
presented by the Colwyn Committee. There
is plenty of material there for consideration
in their quiet moments, and I think the
conclusions that the Committee have arrived
at on many subjects lie at the very root and
foundation of the efficiency of this Parliament. I hope we recognise that. I
have no intention of going into detailmatters of detail can be dealt with when we
come to the Estimates-but there are a few
questions I wish to put to the Minister of
Finance upon this subject. Most of you will
recollect that when the Act of 1920 was
passing through the British House of Commons we were assured by British Ministers
that Ulster would probably have a surplus
of close on £2,000,000 to play with. Has
that promise been fulfilled? As far as I
can read the report, nothing of the kind has
been accepted. If I am wrong in the
opinions I have formed from this report, the
Minister of Finance can correct me.
The Committee have laid down the principle
--and I assume the British Treasury will act
upon it in the coming years-that the contribution from Ulster for Imperial purposes
-and we know what those Imperial purposes are shall be the balance remaining
over after we have paid our way. I think
that is roughly the principle laid down.
They have laid down the further principle
that we as a Government will receive what
might be considered to be our normal expenditure, and I think I am right in
assuming, too, that they are not going to
give us credit for any new Services or
improvements in existing Services.
No one in this House will say for a
moment that the condition of this Province,
when we took over the administration of
affairs, was such as any progressive community-and I hope we are considered a progressive community-could possibly be satisfied with. But what had the Colwyn
Committee done? They have laid
down this principle that all these
increased charges for improving the Services
in Northern Ireland must in future be
borne by the Ulster taxpayer himself. I
consider that that is neither reasonable nor
fair treatment to give us.

However, they have done one thing which

do that with will be the £600,000 of land

naturally enough, has a bearing upon the

I think in the last Budget statement he

We are going to have a margin there, but

There is also another sort of prefatory

Before I touch upon the matters raised by
the hon. Member (Sir Robert Anderson) who
preceded me I should like to refer to a
variety of matters which naturally emerge
from the Gracious Speech to which we have
listened to-day. The first matter which was
touched upon was a congratulatory reference
to the restoration of peace and order in our
community. Under normal conditions, of
course, such e. reference would be unnecessary, and perhaps really unnatural.
but, although the Government has succeeded
in eradicating the turbulent element which
disturbed our Province so greatly in the
past, and in reinstating respect for law
and order, there is no disguising the fact
that if we are to enjoy a full and permanent
measure of that peace and security to which
we are entitled the mentality of many of our
neighbours in Southern Ireland must
undergo a radical change, and there must
be something of a human consciousness that
there are other people in the world who have
equal rights with themselves and who are
equally determined to maintain those rights.
Therefore, I should say now, almost at the
outset of my remarks, that watchfulness on
the part of the Govenment is just as necessary
now as it has ever been, and I think it is
hardly necessary that I should give the
assurance, which has been iterated and reiterated, that there can be no betrayal of
the trust which has been laid upon the
Government in that respect.

and they would regard it as a betrayal of

certain that the intentions of the Southern
Government are entirely pacific and that Mr.
Cosgrave and his colleagues do not entertain
any schemes of positive aggression against

there are strong contingents of intransigent
elements in the South of Ireland which even

additionally necessary that we should adopt

Now, I leave these purely political matters,
if I may so describe them, which weigh very
heavily indeed at the present time upon the
Government, and I come to touch upon those
grave economic and social problems which
so greatly affect our national welfare. The
depression in trade, which has hung like a
pall for such a time over the kingdom, has
not yet been entirely relieved. The outward
and visible manifestation of the condition
of trade is really the condition of employment. Indeed I may say that the rise or
fall of unemployment provides a sort of
barometrical index of the prosperity of the
country. In Great Britain generally, and
even to some extent in our own Province,
the glimmerings of the dawn of healthier
business conditions are apparent, but it will
require the sun to rise to a much higher
altitude, I am afraid, before we can consider
that we have returned to anything like
healthy or normal conditions. The first
signs of local trade revival, as has been referred to to-day by the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. Grant), is in the linen
trade. If only a full and adequate supply
of raw material-and I wish to impress this
upan hon. Members from the country-could
be provided at the present time, it may be
stated that every mill and factory in
Northern Ireland would be going on full
time. This is a matter of considerable
interest to the farming elements of the
country. If the farmers of Ulster could only
realise how greatly their own welfare is
bound up with the welfare of the staple industry of the country, we should have a
much larger sowing of flax than we have had
in recent years. Certainly the outlook for
flax growing was never more promising than
it is at the present moment, and I am sure
my right hon. Friend (Mr. Archdale) beside
me here has taken full cognisance of that
fact, and will endeavour, if it is possible,
greatly to increase the acreage under raw
material for our staple trade in the season
on which we have just entered.

Now, if I am not transgressing too long
upon the time of the House I come to a subject that has been a matter of considerable
attention, namely, education, and I propose
for a moment to touch upon it, because I
think it is necessary that the Government
should make its position clear. It is not unnatural, perhaps, that the magnum opus of our
last Parliamentary Session should continue to
form a subject of animated debate and discussion. It is quite obvious that a scheme
of education transforming a century-old
centralised State system to the direct control
of the people themselves, could hardly be
carried out without criticism of some of its
features. And what, part was likely to be
more vulnerable to difference of opinion than
that of religion? Has there been a period in
the world's history when religious differences
have not provided material for quarrels,
great and small, for colossal wars, as well as
family jars? And so it has proved in the
case of our small but ambitious education
scheme. I do not wish to say a word to
increase the feeling aroused in connection
with the discussion on the religious clauses of
this Act, but it is my duty, as well as my
anxiety, to defend the position of the Government in its provision of a scheme of popular
education, which has met, in my judgment
and within my knowledge, with more general
approval than any similar effort that, at any
rate, I am familiar with. Clergymen of the
different Protestant denominations have
declared their intention of refusing to take
full advantage of the Act unless a different
method of providing religious instruction is
set up. I have especial and personal reasons
for feeling regret at this decision. When the
Clause dealing with this subject was
originally drafted exception was taken to its
wording by the heads of the Protestant

Churches. With a view of meeting their

66 He ventured to think that that provision was wider, more generous, and more

Some
defects and shortcomings might be de
veloped in this Act when it was put into
operation, but it would be churlish and

This is the spirit which we had hoped
would have animated the Churches. No one
that I know of wishes to divorce the Bible
from the schools. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Even on lower or secular grounds, the
Bible as one of the great classics of the
world's literature must find its natural place
in the education of the children. But from
the higher or ethical point of view, it is
essential that every boy and girl should be
familiarised with the Bible story. It is the
only hope for the regeneration of the world.
Therefore, we say, in Dr. Semple's wise
words "Don't strangle the child in its
cradle." Give it a chance for life, and if it
should develop any vicious tendency this
Parliament which brought it into being can
provide the necessary remedy to be applied.
That is the view this Government takes of
this Measure, and I think that if the
Regulations are properly framed all this
dissatisfaction will probably disappear, and
the value of the Act will be fully realised.

generally of the results attained by the Government and Parliament in the year that has
just passed, I may say that sometimes I think
our people do not fully realise all the advantages that have accrued from the transfer of
local government to the province. Nor do
they seem to show much appreciation of the
results of the legislation which has been
passed by the labours of this Parliament, as
well as by the administrative work that has
been carried out. Reforms long overdue have
been effected by the earnest labours of this
Parliament from which not only this generation but also the generation that follows us
will reap considerable benefit. Much public
money has been well used by grants to local,
authorities, and it is estimated that through
the assistance thus provided, a sum of at
least £2,500,000 has been spent on relief works.
This matter was referred to by my hon.
Friend who seconded the Address (Mr.
Grant), and it is of some interest to know
that it was through the action of this Government that that enormous sum of money has
been spent in the province. I would like to
know if any other part of the Kingdom could
show greater sympathy with suffering and
distress, or give more practical evidence of its
interest in the welfare of its people than this.
I should again remind the House that the decentralisation of the Government departments
from Dublin and their establishment in Belfast has been the means of circulating during
the past two or three years a vast sum of
money hitherto spent elsewhere. With all
these advantages then, do not let us dissipate
our strength by internal dissensions on small
and relatively trivial matters. We may need
all our strength. Let us bear in mind that
the safety of States does not necessarily depend on the justice or righteousness of their
cause. All history, indeed, gives complete
evidence of this. But let me say this, I do
not believe there is any danger to our
national safety so long as we remain true
and loyal to ourselves, as we have always
done when danger threatened us in days gone
by. (Hon. Members: "Hear, hear.")

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
is
Your Grace,
We, His Majesty's most dutiful and loyal
subjects, the Commons of Northern Ireland,
in Parliament assembled, beg leave to offer
our humble thanks to your Grace for the
Speech which your Grace has addressed to
both Houses of Parliament."-(Mrs. Chichester.)
Question again proposed.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: According to ancient
custom in rising to speak on the Address the
first word that one has to utter is a word of
congratulation to the mover and seconder of
the Address. Sometimes it is a mere
formality, simply an act of courtesy, but in
this case I can say most sincerely that I have
listened to the moving and seconding of
the Address with the greatest possible
pleasure. The mover of the Address (Mrs.
Chichester) was making history, I think, yesterday, because, as she rightly pointed out,
she is the first lady Member of any Parliament in the British Empire, and possibly in
the world, who has had the privilege of
moving an Address such as she moved yesterday; and I am sure I carry the House with
me when I say she lived up to the occasion.
The speech was logical, it was forcible, it was
eloquent. But the hon. Member for Derry
her
(Mrs. Chichester) has already won
Parliamentary spurs, and it was only the sort
of speech we would expect from her. The
same remark might be made with regard to
the seconder of the Address (Mr. Grant), who,
in his own outspoken way always says what
he thinks, and even when seconding the
Address he was not at all averse from using
some criticism of the Government that he is
commending to the House. I think this
House has every right to be proud of the
fact that the moving and the seconding of
the Address yesterday were so well done.
The only other point on which I would like
to say a word is with regard to the length
of the Speech. I have seen many Speeches
from the Throne in my time, but I have
never come across one in which so many
words were used to say so little, and I would
commend to the consideration of the Government the advisability of curtailing these
Addresses very considerably. If I were a
member of the Government I would curtail
them for the very selfish reason that the
broader the target the more chance there is
for one to get a shot at it..
I am sure every hon, Member of the House
regrets the absence of the Prime Minister,
and we all sincerely hope that he will soon be
restored to health again, and take his
accustomed place in this House. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
I followed with great interest the speech of
the Minister of Finance a very interesting
speech, if I may say so. At the very beginning of it he emphasised how much has been
done by way of restoring law and order in
this Province. I think people are apt to
forget how much the Government and how
much this Parliament have had to do in the
way of bringing order out of chaos during
the last two years. These things are easily
forgotten, and we have not forgotten, and we
ought not to forget, that the conditions very
near to our own border are not so settled at
the present time that we can afford to go to
sleep. We wish well to our neighbours in the
South, but we realise the difficult conditions
under which they are living, and at any
moment, it appears to me, such conditions
may arise that the Government in the South,
with the best will in the world, may not be
able to control their own people. Therefore,
it is the business of our Government to be
watchful, and to be prepared for any and
every emergency that may arise. In that
connection I would join with the Minister of
Finance in expressing the hope that the
Imperial Prime Minister will carry out the
pledge that has been given with regard to
the Special Constabulary. A million is a
large sum for a small Province like this to
have to raise, and I think we can rightly
contend that we are carrying out Imperial
work with the Special Constabulary in
Northern Ireland at the present time, and
that, therefore, we are justly entitled to the
money that has been promised to us.
The Minister of Finance asked us to use
restraint with regard to the Boundary
question. I cordially agree with him. There
is very little that we can say here that can
have any effect on it; and we might rashly
say something that would hamper the hands
of the Government. Our attitude as a House
and as a people is well known from the beginning. From that attitude we have not
departed in the slightest, and we have no
intention of departing. Beyond that I do not
intend to say anything more on the Boundary
question.
It is pleasant to hear the Minister of
Finance saying that trade is in
a much
healthier condition. We are all delighted to
know that it is. But there is one point that
he made yesterday which I am afraid is not
generally known, and that is that if there was
more raw material-that is, flax-in the
Province every mill and factory in the city
could be running full time. I join most
heartily with the Minister of Finance in the
appeal that he has made to the farmers of
Northern Ireland to grow more flax this year.
It is essential that there should be a large
supply of flax in their own interest and in
our interest as an industrial community as
well, because the two are absolutely linked
together, and we should look not at what is
going to benefit the farmer only, or what is

12 MARCH 1924.
going to benefit the manufacturer, or what is
going to benefit the worker in Belfast, but
what is going to benefit the whole community,
and it is in the interest of the community
that we should have plenty of raw material.
I believe that the Minister of Finance has
said that it will pay our farmers to provide
raw material, and in that way provide more
employment. In that connection I would
like to congratulate the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Archdale) on the fact that he is
going to establish a Faculty of Agriculture in
Northern Ireland. That is something that
has been long overdue. I am sure it will be
of the greatest benefit in Northern Ireland.
We wish it all success, and we hope that
there will be no red tape to stand in the way
of carrying out the establishment of this
Faculty of Agriculture.
With regard to unemployment-and I am
sorry the Minister of Labour (Mr.Andrews) is
not here it is interesting to know that if we
could get the number of unemployed reduced
by 10,000 we would be able to make ends meet.
We have spent very large sums on unemployment, and sometimes I ask myself wliether
we have spent most of this money wisely or
not-(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-because
we have spent so much, and yet what have we
to show for it? It is necessary, of course, that
our people should not be allowed to starve. I
think the seconder of the Address (Mr. Grant)
said yesterday, and said rightly, what the
people in Northern Ireland want is not the
insurance dole, but work. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) If we could provide them with
I work it would be a great deal better than
simply providing a small dole. I suggested
in this House on several occasions last year
that we ought to go in for a large scheme of
road improvement and road development in
Northern Ireland. (Hon Members: Hear,
hear.)
No one who knows this province
of ours has
any doubt with regard
to the bad condition of our roads.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Why
ought we not to utilise, at the
present time, when there are so many people
out of employment, these men for improving
the roads? When trade improves, as it is
improving and as we hope it will improve,
and we get back to something like normal
conditions, that will not be the time to take
men for the purpose of improving roads. We
ought to do it with the men unemployed,
who might be utilised for that purpose. I
throw out the suggestion again, and I hope
the Minister of Finance will give it his earnest attention.
With regard to his reference to the Colwyn
Report, there, again, he has asked for restraint, and, as one who knows a good deal
of what is going on behind the scenes at
Westminster, I would emphasise what the
Minister of Finance has said on this point.
We might easily do a great deal of harm, but
to those Members who do not know all that
has been going on, I would say that the cause
of Ulster could not be in better hands from
a financial point of view than in the hands
of the Minister of Finance. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Those of us who know the
battles he has fought with the Treasury in
London, and who know how successful he has
been, are anxious that not a single word
should be said that would hamper him in
that work he is carrying on.
Now, with regard to education, that is
question I am only going to touch on briefly,
because it has been dealt with pretty fully by
the Minister of Finance and in another place
yesterday. There has been a good deal of
misunderstanding, and a good deal of unnecessary heat which always arises from misunderstanding, with regard to this education question. I think it might be taken that the
whole differences on the education question
narrow themselves down to two points, simple
Bible teaching in the school, and Protestant
teachers for Protestant children. With
regard to the simple Bible teaching if anyone
will take the trouble to read the Regulations
issued yesterday he can see that that point is
met. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I will
just read one sentence from the explanatory
Memorandum, Paragraph 2, which lays down
that
Religious instruction (including Bible
reading) must have a definite place in the
school time-table.
That read in connection with the Regulations
that have been issued make it clear to my
mind that there can be no doubt in the future
with regard to the place of simple Bible
teaching.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Is that consistent with
the present Act?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Quite consistent with
the present Act, and it makes what was only
a matter of courtesy, so to speak, in the past
a statutory matter, so that there can be no
doubt in future with regard to Bible
teaching in the school. I agree with
the Minister of Finance that both from
a
literary and from a religious point
of view Bible teaching must be carried
on in our schools, because, as I said in this
House on the First Reading of the Education
Bill, any system of education that is not
based on religion is bound to wither and
decay. I think there is no doubt in the mind
of the Government-and I am sure there is
no doubt in the mind of any Member of this
House that Bible teaching is to be carried
on in the school as it has been carried on in
the past. I think with a little goodwillall

the questions that have been agitating us for
the last few months will disappear, and we
will find that the Education Act will be an

Reference was also made in the Address to
the Rents Restriction Act, and I agree with
those Members who say that we should not
wait on what the Imperial Parliament is
going to do. Remember this, the Imperial
Parliament is overburdened with work at the
present moment, and if we wait until the
Imperial Parliament, as constituted at the
moment, settle anything you may have to
wait for a long time, and I would not advise
the House to wait until the Imperial Parliament has settled the question on the other
side. Surely we can settle these questions for
ourselves. I would like in this connection to
say this, that the housing problem is not
going to be solved by the Rents Restriction Act.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) If the housing
problem is ever going to be solved it is going
to be solved by building cheap houses. (Họn.
Members: Hear, hear.) That is the thing
that we have got to aim at. In that connection I would like the attention of the Home
Secretary just for a moment. I would like
to ask the Home Secretary what progress has
been made under the Act that was passed last
year? If the House will remember, that Act
gave a grant of £60 per house, and it allowed
public bodies to contribute another £40 per
house.
The MINISTER of FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): That is the Housing Act?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Yes, the Housing Act.
It allowed public bodies to contribute another
£40. I would like to ask my right hon.
Friend (Sir Dawson Bates) how many local
authorities have agreed to give this £40.
There are rumours afloat-I do not know
whether they are true or not, but my right
hon. Friend will be able to satisfy me on the
point-that the Belfast Corporation, which
represents a body that controls one-third of
the population of Northern Ireland, has not
agreed to this grant of £40. I would like to
ask my right hon. Friend (Sir Dawson Bates)
whether he has approached the Corporation
on this point, whether there is any correspondence, and whether if there is a correspondence with regard to this point he will
lay it on the Table of the House so that the
public may see exactly what is happening.
I think it is not an unreasonable attitude
to take up, because if we have a large Corporation that is pursuing a policy like this and
is trying to prevent private enterprise from
developing in this city, then there is no hope
whatever of settling the housing problem.
Why, the Belfast Corporation aided and
abetted by the Northern Government has
undoubtedly demoralised the building trade
in this city of ours. Yes, my right hon.
Friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock)
looks all amazement. I think it has demoralised the building trade, and I am going
to prove it. Not so long ago you gave a
very large sum for houses, too large a sum I
think, and probably the Chancellor of the
Exchequer will sympathise with me on this
point. Houses were put up at a cost of from
£1,000 to £1,300 that a private builder would
have put up for one-third of the money. At
the present time my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Labour (Mr. Andrews) is providof
ing 60 per cent. the cost of building
houses-houses that are being built by the
Corporation.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr. Gordon): Workmen's houses.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Quite so; I am dealing with those houses. Those are the houses
largely necessary. I am dealing with them.
They are providing 60 per cent., but mark
this point, whereas the Corporation is only
able to get 300 bricks a day laid, private
builders are laying 800 and 1,000, and I know
of one case 1,200 a day. As my right hon.
Friend knows, across the water, even in
Liverpool, the Corporation is getting twice
the number of bricks laid a day that are laid
for the Corporation of Belfast. If you give
the 60 per cent. to a private builder instead
of to the Corporation, for every house you
build you get three built, and, therefore, 1
say that the Corporation, aided by the Northern Government, is demoralising the building trade in this city. If this condition of
affairs goes on there is no hope of getting
back to the normal conditions that ought to
be existing. I would suggest to the Minister
of Finance that he might take a big, broad
view of this housing question. There is no
other problem, at least so far as this city is
concerned, that approaches in importance the
housing problem. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) It has got to be settled in some way.
You can never settle it except by restoring
private enterprise to its old position, and I
would suggest to my right hon. Friend,
whether under the Trades Facilities Act or
some other way-I am not bound to any
scheme-he could not encourage private
enterprise to come along, set the machine
working, and get a large number of people
employed.
On the other side of the water I believe
the building trade has agreed to a dilution
of labour. (Hon. Members: No, no). Yes,
the thing is practically settled. I have some
knowledge on the point. The thing is
practically settled, and you will discover in
a short time that on the other side of the

Channel there has been a large dilution of
labour in the building industry. Why
cannot the men who were able to fight for us
during the War be utilised for building
houses for themselves? (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). We want 10,000 houses in the
city of Belfast to bring us up to normal.
Why should we not get to work on these
houses as quickly as possible instead of
fencing with the subject as we are doing?
I am sure my right hon. Friend the Minister
of Finance (Mr. Pollock) will give this matter
very serious consideration and do what he
can to get private enterprise started once
more, because as I have said already until
we get private enterprise at work in the
building trade we can never provide the
people with plenty of cheap houses.
My right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) in an
eloquent passage winding up his speech
asked us to get rid of internal dissensions
and to hold together. There is great necessity for preventing anything in the form of
internal dissension. I do not think for a
moment that any Government will please
everybody, and there are very few Governments that ever please any body outside the
Government; but we have got not to look on
individuals, not to look at small things, but
at the big principles for which Governments
stand, and, therefore, I for one join heartily
with my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock) in urging that there
should be unity in Northern Ireland. We
are bound to have our differences of opinion
on most questions-independent people
always will-but do not let us magnify the
small points; let us get rid of those things
that really do cause friction. That brings
me to the last point I wish to make, and it
really has a bearing on this subject of keeping internal dissension out of our ranks. An
incident happened quite recently which has
caused a good deal of feeling and friction in
my constituency at any rate. I mean the
dismissal of Mr. Nixon.
Mr. McGUFFIN: On a point of order, you
will be aware, Sir, by looking at the Notice
Paper that there is a question down for tomorrow plying the Minister of Home Affairs
(Sir Dawson Bates) with a series of queries
with respect to this matter, and I want your
ruling as to whether intervention in the
debate at this particular point would prevent
the Minister dealing in detail with that
question on the Paper.
Mr. SPEAKER: I am inclined to think
without considering that the fact that the
question is on the Paper will preclude our
discussing it to-day, because that would be
what is called an infringement against the
rule of anticipation. If a Motion is down on
the Paper in the name of one hon. Member
other hon. Members are not entitled to
raise it in advance. But, quite apart from
that point, I was going to draw the attention
of the hon. Member for West Belfast (Sir
Robert Lynn) to the fact that I think the
discussion of this particular question, which
is really one of administration which has
recently arisen, should be raised by way of
an amendment to the Address. The matters
he has discussed hitherto have been questions
dealt with either in the King's Speech or
very closely allied to it, just as housing is
allied to rent restriction or loans guarantee,
but I think this particular question should be
raised either on the adjournment, as I understood was the original intention, or as a
distinct amendment to the Address. In view
of the question by the hon. Member for
North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin) on the Paper
for to-morrow I do not think the matter can
be raised to-day.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: With all respect this
is the first time I ever heard that the putting
down of a question precluded the discussion
of a particular subject. I know the putting
down of a Motion would prevent the discussion of a subject, but I never heard that
the putting down of a question did so. If
that were so then I could guarantee that I
could prevent any discussion taking place on
any subject in this House.
Mr. SPEAKER: I have not the Paper be
fore me, but I understood that what the
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
McGuffin) had put down was a Motion calling attention to this question for discussion
in the House. Is that not so?
Mr. McGUFFIN: By way of explanation I
want to say that this was simply a question
put down, but it was to be answered to
inorrow.
Mr. SPEAKER: An ordinary question?
Mr. McGUFFIN: An ordinary question.
Mr. SPEAKER: Then I think the hon.
Member for West Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn)
is right. If it is an ordinary question I do
not think the general rule of anticipation
would apply. At the same time I think this
question should be raised by way of an
amendment to the Address.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I further inquire
what will happen with regard to this question when I present it to-morrow? How will
I stand with regard to that? Will I put it
afresh?
Mr. SPEAKER: Answers to questions do
vary according to things that have taken
place beforehand. I do not see how
this question can come on to-day, unless by
general consent the general discussion is
allowed to lapse, and a particular amendment
is taken dealing with it. I think this is au
important question that raised a good deal

Mr. COOTE: Have not we the right to raise
this question in reply to the first paragraph
of the Speech of his Grace the Governor where
he says:
I expressed the hope that respect for
the law would prevail, and that the good
order which had recently been established
in the Province might continue?"
We are all anxious that good order should
prevail. We realise that there are circumstances which tend to the disruption of the
good order that is prevailing, and have not
we, as custodians of the public safety and representatives of the people, the right to raise
this question now?
Mr. SPEAKER: Certainly; but the hon.
Member (Mr. Coote) must know that where
it is a question of attacking the policy of the
Government, as this is, it is always done by
way of an amendment to the Address. The
discussion on the Address itself expresses more
or less agreement with the policy of; the
Government, and the proper way of attacking
the policy of the Government is to move an
amendment to the Address. It was on an
amendment to the Address that the Unionist
Government was defeated in London recently.
That is the proper way to do it. Of course if
it is not desired to attack the policy of the
Government the matter may be raised on the
adjournment.
Sir. ROBERT LYNN: In view of what
you have said I will not refer further to the
question, but I give notice that on the
Motion for Adjournment to-night I will raise
the question.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I quite agree with the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Sir Robert
Lynn) that we have had submitted to us a
King's Speech which is, perhaps, one of the
longest that is possible for one to imagine
in connection with a Government that controls such a small area. I have not myself
any recollection of having read a Speech of
such a lengthy description and of such a detailed character. However, I pass away
from that simply to say that up to the
present I think that the matters contained
in the Speech have been dealt with fairly
faithfully and I do not propose at the
moment to serve up a re-hash of what has
been said in the course of the debate. I
rather propose to address myself to a different aspect of the case from any I have
heard submitted here this afternoon, or, for
that matter, yesterday afternoon. What I
want to bring before the House is that, while
we exist as a Parliament, and have a perfect
right to legislate with regard to any matter
that comes within our purview or within our
powers, up to the present moment we have
failed to take that
which as a
course,
Government we are entitled to take.
we
There has been a lack of what I might call
Government initiative. Emulation is one
thing, but imitation is a very different thing.
If we
were emulating the British Government with regard to certain measures that
they had already passed then I for one would
encourage the Government to do so, but, if
it is going to be the policy of this Government to act slavishly with regard to all
their measures and to await their introduction and passage through the other House
before they are introduced here, then I say it
stultifies us as a Parliament and creates a
very bad impression abroad. In so doing
have practically renounced our independence in respect of legislative
matters. It means, as it were, that we have
not the confidence, the wisdom, the experience to discuss these matters, and we must
await the lead of the Imperial Parliament
before we are in a position to express our own
political opinions. This has given, amongst
the public at any rate, a very mean impression of this House and its powers. Only the
other day when a letter appeared in the
papers calling upon the Government to
hasten certain legislation with regard to unemployment the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) wrote through the Press in reply
to say that if the question is introduced in
the Imperial House of Commons undoubtedly it will be introduced here.
What
Minister
a slavish attitude for a
to take up, to say that we must first
of all wait to know what the Parliament across the water is going to do
before we take the initiative to provide for
certain circumstances that have arisen here!
It commits hon. Members, moreover, to
opinions from which I dissent absolutely. It
simply means that if the Imperial Government decides a certain thing we are prepledged, and when it comes up here we are
expected to support it. I ask any hon.
Member who has any independence of mind
or thought at all if he acquiesces in this
policy I for my part do not.
What does it mean when we take up that
attitude? Let me recall to the memory of
the House the fact that we have existed under
three different administrations and have
borrowed from each of them. We
have existed as a Parliament under
a Coalition, and we have borrowed
from them. We have existed as a
Parliament under a Conservative Government, and we have borrowed from them.
Now we are existing under a Socialist Government, and the probability is that we are

going to borrow from them, too. Is that exactly the attitude to which this House should
commit itself? This is a very serious question, and whether the House realises it
or not it is doing more to disparage this Government, which we all wish well, than anything I know at the moment. We have a

What is going to happen now? Supposing
that the Government at present in power

would be calculated to undermine the
