There is one thing that the House should
not forget, and I am sure it is present in the
mind of my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance (Mr. Pollock), and it is that in all
these agitations and measures across the
water this House here will incur, in all probability, grave expenditure. It is quite within our knowledge it only happened quite
recently-that an announcement was made
in the Imperial House to the effect that there
will be an amendment with regard to what
is called Unemployment Insurance. It will
reduce the age from sixteen to fourteen for
insurance purposes, and it will protect men
whose interests are vitally affected by a strike
with which they have no direct connection.
Is this going to increase the expenditure in
connection with the administration of these
matters under this Northern Parliament, and
are we obliged in every case to follow this?
Though I for my part as an industrial representative would be willing to assent to it,
it is rather the principle I am discussing at
the moment, whether we are to wait to see
what the Imperial Parliament does, or
whether we would not ourselves, in proportion to our financial power discuss these
things ourselves and do on our own initiative
what hitherto we have been doing through
imitation.
Then take the question of Old Age Pensions.
What is proposed in connection with that?
Remember it is a Socialist Government you
have in power at the moment, and I speak
with all respect of it as such. Up to the
moment they have been severely Constitutional, but it is by reason of the fact that
they are dependent for their existence upon
the support of the Constitutional parties in
the House. What would be the effect if, for
instance, they reduced the age from seventy
to sixty-five? What would it be if they removed what is called the income limitation,
Now I say it is a very important matter
that we in these circumstances should have
the initiative ourselves and control our own
Parliament-if you like, in emulation of the
Imperial Parliament, but by no means in
imitation of it in
every particular. I
would have the House remember-I am sorry
that the Labour Minister is not here and
that the House is growing gradually thinner
-but I see the Parliamentary Secretary is
here and would impress upon them that
Mr. Shaw, the Labour Minister, made a
statement in the Imperial House the other
night. To what effect? He said the man
who is unemployed is entitled to be
supported. That is a big proposition even
for the Imperial Parliament. It means
something coming from a Minister. Now if
an ordinary Member had made a statement
like that it would have been jeered at. Are
we prepared to follow it here? If provision
is made for that are we equal in our finances
to meet the obligation?
Then coming to the question of rent restriction the Government is not involved in
any financial responsibility whatever. But
it delays legislation. Why? I would like to
know. Has the Government not the courage
of its convictions? Is it afraid of defeat?
Is it afraid of having a divided House? I
would commend the Government to have
some courage in the matter. They set up a
Committee and they have had a report in regard to the matter. They
are not likely to have further information even when the other Act
is passed across the water. Why not
take the initiative now? Why not take it
up this Session and deal with the question
as an urgent problem at once? I heartily
support nearly all that has been said by the
hon. Member for West Belfast (Sir Robert
Lynn) as to how this question is connected
with what is called house building. Now I

I am
more than ever convinced that we
will be rather disappointed. It will
Debate on the Address.
HOUSE OF COMMONS. Debate on the Address.
[Mr. McGuffin]
certainly not conduce to giving us more
houses, which was the purpose of it. I am
not at all disposed to believe that in that
respect it will succeed.
Now I am coming to a very serious
matter. Perhaps I will be charged with a
degree of impertinence, or putting it in the
more modern way, undue temerity. But if
there is no other person in the House to
do it I will do it. (An hon. Member: Hear,
hear). I want to know what the policy of
the Government is. Or has it a policy at all?
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Are we not as
a House entitled to be taken into consideration? Are we not entitled to have submitted to us for our opinion and discussion
certain important matters that have become
the subject of a conference across the water,
regarding which we know not one scintilla?
Are we to assume that the things under
discussion there are of no importance to us
as a House? (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
Are we to exercise such unlimited faith in
the honesty and the ability of the representatives at that Commission that it will not
be necessary for them to report here in this
House? Now there has been a conference
held at which our Government was represented by the right hon. Gentleman the
Prime Minister, by the most hon. the
Marquess of Londonderry, and by the right
hon. the Attorney-General, and not one
solitary word is mentioned with respect to
that matter. The Finance Minister appealed
to us to defer criticism. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-to say nothing about it, just
to trust and that in doing so we would not
be disappointed. Well I have just as much
faith in the Prime Minister and in the
Government as perhaps any other hon.
Member of this House. But the House has
also rights that it cannot ignore and
Members have duties which they cannot
shirk. Our duty in this case is to press the
Minister. I am sorry it devolves upon him
(Mr. Pollock) in the absence of the Prime
Minister. I sympathise with him in the
attitude he has adopted. He has discharged
his duty magnificently, with a patience and
almost unlimited courtesy that have seldom
been experienced from any other Minister
in this House. But now we are asked to say
that the thing is all right. What is all
right? What was the conference about? Are
we not entitled to know what it was about?
We have had it stated here and reiterated
that we were not going to budge one solitary
inch with regard to the Six Counties. Is
this Commission that has been sitting to inquire whether it would be possible to do so,
because the suggestion of that contingency,
of that possibility, naturally awakens the
public mind to the fact that after all
something will have to be done, that something inevitably will be done. You say we
should have confidence in the Ministry, and
I have confidence. But is it not true that
the Free Staters have a certain degree of confidence too as to what is going on and what
will eventuate from the conference? They
are quite as confident as we are ourselves
at the moment. (An hon. Member: No, no).
Well it may be that they are not, but there
are those who, from time to time, in their
speeches, have encouraged their supporters
to believe that they will see this thing
through. They say "We have bargained for
and we will never desist until we have a
united Ireland. We have a right to govern
it in its entirety and not on any principles
of partition." Then this conference was
adjourned and it was rumoured at the time-
I do not know whether I am right or not.
I have seen the statement-that the purpose
was to enable our representatives to come
home and put the matter before the people to
know what their opinion would be with respect to certain proposals. If that was not
the purpose I would like to know what it
was. I am very glad the right hon. Gentlethe Attorney-General, has returned to the House, because it is most
important that he should have heard these
remarks as he was a member of the Commission that had this matter under consideration. I want to know how is it that
these conferences always take place when the
House is out of session. The House is never
in session when these things take place.
The conferences take place during an
adjournment and when the House meets it
has forgotten all about it. The issues are
none the less important.

I did not wish to

They want all sorts of instructions which, if

in a school. The necessary instructors are
not there. For that matter you have no

goes to show that the only real solution of
the education question is the secular system.
In saying that I do not by any means want
to drive the child from religious institutions

spiritual influence. Quite the opposite. I
have always maintained that the school is

intend to criticise or dwell at any length
on the matters contained in the Gracious
Speech. We have had some excellent

Belfast (Sir Robert Lynn) has made some
statements which I am sure he believes are
correct-
Sir ROBERT LYNN: They are quite
correct.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: But they
are so wide of the facts that I feel it my
duty to put him right. It is a pity that a
man of the eminence of my hon. Friend did
not provide himself with the true facts
before he made his speech. He came here
and gave figures which I dare say will
appear in the Press to-morrow and which
will be very misleading and not to the credit
of this House or the Belfast Corporation.
One statement he made was that the Government and the Corporation had demoralised
the building trade in the city of Belfast.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Quite correct.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: Another
statement he made was that the Corporation
houses cost £1,000 to £1,300 when a private
builder could and would have built them for
a third of that cost.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Hear, hear.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: He went

its wisdom-and I think it was very generous

these houses.

Government had contributed 60 per cent of
the wages, not of the cost.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: I am
sorry, but I took you as saying 60 per cent
of the cost of the houses. The Government
gave and are giving 80 per cent of the wages,
which is 30 per cent of the cost. They are
giving 80 per cent not 60 per cent.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: That makes it all the
worse.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: As far as
the Rent Restrictions Act is concerned, it
must be considered in conjunction with the
greater and wider question of the building
of houses, and if you sum up the complaint
of the hon. Member for West Belfast, it
simply means that the Belfast Corporation
or any other corporation cannot be entrusted
with the building of houses. You must get
the building done by private enterprise.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Hear, hear.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: I want to
tell the House to-day-and I know what I
am talking about-that under present conditions private enterprise will not do it. It
cannot be done. Why? There are two very
important factors. One is the want of
security. That is bound up with the Rent
Restrictions Act, and until you bring private
enterprise back you will never solve the
housing question in this or in any other
country. It is not the duty of this Govei n
ment or of the Belfast Corporation to build
houses.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Hear, hear.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: It is only
their duty to bridge over the difficulty unlil
such time as private enterprise can provide
for houses. No man will to-day on any large
scale invest his money in building houses for
people to live in, for no sooner does an individual get into a house than it virtually
becomes his own. Owing to the restrictions
the man who builds the house cannot interfere with it, and he does not know what this
or any other Government will do. He does
not know his real position.
Even assuming for one moment that you
draft a Bill that will bring back security,
then you are met with the difficulty of the
cost of building. When the Minister of Home
Affairs introduced his Housing Bill I spoke

Would this House approve of a man who has
built houses and sold them at a profit going
to the Corporation after he has sold them
and asking for the £40 subsidy from the
Corporation and the £60 from the Government? The Corporation are anxious that
the money they are spending should go to the
individual who is living in the house.
Another point is in regard to the cost.
The subsidy that the Government and the
Corporation offers would not bring the price
of the house down to the price of a similar
house across the water. Assuming that the
difficulties of the Rent Restrictions Act were
overcome, the private builder cannot possibly
build houses at a price at which he can
economically let them. Why? Because of
the small output, and on this question I join

I would like to see a larger output, and until

these houses were built by the Corporation
at a cost of £1,000 and £1,300 when they could
be built at a third of the cost by private

Corporation were able to build by direct

as against possibly £300 across the water.

Would dilution solve it?
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: Cheaper
houses will solve it. Bring down the price
of houses. The Corporation endeavoured to
build concrete houses. The concrete house is
the coming house; it is a good one. You can
utilise semi-skilled labour in the erection of
concrete houses. We started to build concrete houses in the Woodvale Road, but when
we put them up by means of unskilled labour
the bricklayers refused to lay the bricks of
the chimneys, and the carpenters refused to
put in the doors and other woodwork. The
result is that if you attempt to erect houses
with unskilled labour the skilled men will
walk off the job. We had to stop it. Then
we said we would build houses with concrete
blocks. There are beautiful houses built of
concrete blocks in several districts of the
city; there is nothing to equal them anywhere. The idea of building houses with
concrete blocks was to get the price down. A
block represents six bricks. We were informed that across the water the men were
able to lay 2,000 bricks. We said: "That is
the very thing for us; that will bring down
our prices; we will get 2,000 bricks laid
instead of 300, 320, or 350 as the case
may be." The Corporation got the
machinery and put down the plant.
The Government gave us a free hand; they
said "go on," and they paid 80 per cent.

of the wages. What happened?

question, at the present time rural Ireland

farmers of Northern Ireland. The farmers
pay £600,000, in addition to their ordinary

they are to pay such a large sum into the

One of the things farmers have been appealing for for a long time is to get better
drainage in County Fermanagh. We have a
river called the Sillies River. Every now and
again it overflows its banks, and this year it
has ruined large numbers of the most loyal
supporters of this Government. They have
appealed to every Government for sonie
remedy. It would take very little money
indeed to clear out the shoals and to deepen
the river in one or two places so as to let
all this water away into Lough Erne. These
people want some legislation. They want the
County Council to get some power to improve
these rivers, and to take away the floods.
They want a grant from this Government of £25,000 or £30,000, and they
are entitled to get it, for it is
their Own money.
The farmers in
the rural districts, as I said, are giving you
£600,000 a year out of their farms. In addition to that, I would like to say that none of
the rural districts receive one penny from

people in the city of Belfast, and why should

"Hear,
hear.") Many of the old houses are falling.
In the country the houses are very bad. You

Mr. DONALD: There are
Belfast.
no slums in
Mr. COOPER: No slums in Belfast!
There is one other point, and one only, to
which I wish to refer. All round the Border
there are persons who suffered considerable
loss during the recent troublous times. People
came in from the Free State; they took away
their goods; they took away their motor-cars,
and they took away their property. Those
people have never received from this Government, or from the County Court or anywhere
else, one penny of compensation. When they
went to the Courts they were told that these
articles had been stolen, and that the
ordinary criminal injury law did not apply,
while people two yards over the Border whose
cars were stolen and whose goods were stolen
all received compensation from the Free State
Government. The only people who have been
left without any remedy and without any
compensation are the loyalists of Northern
Ireland living along the Border. I think
that it is up to this Government to compensate these people for the losses they have
sustained. In Belleek, where the people were
left entirely without police, the Republicans
came and took possession, and as soon as the
police went there the Republicans carried
away all the goods.
I do not want to say anything against the
Home Office; I am one of the very few
persons who would not say anything against
it. But I would like to say that the Belleek
affair is the only black spot against the Home
Office in the County Fermanagh. Ever since
that occurred we have received protection
from police. Everything that could be done
for us has been done, and we are most grateful for what has been done. We thank the
Home Office for what it did; but, having done
so well, we would just ask them to do one
thing-to wipe out the one black spot, and to
compensate these people for their losses.

early in the debate to-day I want to raise,
and raise calmly and without any feeling,
the question of the dismissal of District-
Inspector Nixon. I want at the outset to
say that so far as I am concerned in taking
this step I am not influenced in the slightest
degree by anything that has taken place recently at public meetings in my own constituency or elsewhere. As a matter of
fact, a week ago I had intimated

Minister of Home Affairs that I would raise

I am doing so now. First of all an Orange
Lodge was set up with the approval of the
Ministry of Home Affairs of which members
of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
eligible to become members. I know there
are differences of opinion with regard to
whether the police should be allowed to be

of Home Affairs, and it appears that District-
Inspector Nixon was Master of that Lodge.
In the month of January, I think the 28th
or 29th January, I forget which-
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The 29th.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: On 29th January
District-Inspector Nixon attended an Orange
meeting at which he made a brief speech
in reference to the boundary question, which
was then being discussed in public and
in the public Press. He is alleged
to have made some reference to conditions
that prevailed in the Free State on the
border of Ulster: As a result of that speech,
which appeared in the newspapers, District-
Inspector Nixon was summoned before a disciplinary court. This court sat, and I understand that the charges made against him
were the charges that appeared in the newspapers, but if my information is correct no
evidence whatever was produced to show
that the statements in the newspapers were
correct. After the court had sat for some
days it was suddenly abolished. Afterwards
District-Inspector Nixon was brought before
his superior officers and questions were put
to him which he naturally refused to answer
as they were questions that would incriminate himself. The result was that some days
afterwards the Minister of Home Affairs
dismissed the District-Inspector. I think I
have put the main facts of the case fairly-
Mr. POLLOCK: The Governor dismissed
him.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: It is the Governor,
of course, acting on the advice of his regular
Ministers. That we take for granted.
I am not standing here to justify anything
in the form of indiscipline. In a police
force or any other force you have got to have
discipline and to enforce discipline. There
can be no two opinions on that point; but
the question which I want to ask the Government is this: Was the punishment not too
great for the crime, supposing there was a
crime? First of all, why was not
the District-Inspector dealt with by this
Court? If the Court had given its
decision then the public and this
House would have been in a different
position to the position they are in now.
They would have had some information.
The Court would have told us why they had
recommended the dismissal of the officer or
any other punishment that you like. I
would like to know from the Minister of
Home Affairs, firstly, why the Court was not
allowed to proceed and secondly, why after
the court had ceased to function the Government recommended the extreme course that
was taken. There is a feeling undoubtedly
amongst the public that the Government have
treated this officer. harshly—
Mr. POLLOCK: What public?
Sir ROBERT LYNN: The general public.
I am only giving you the impressions that
have reached me. There is a feeling that
this officer has been treated harshly. So far
as this House is concerned, I am sure that
what they want to do is to see that justice
is done to the humblest man in the service of
this House. The Minister of Home Affairs
may have information that I have not got.
It may be that there is no justification for
the feeling that is abroad, but undoubtedly
there is the feeling that this officer has been
harshly dealt with. If he had been indiscreet
-surely dismissal is a very severe punishment for indiscretion? If everyone of us
was dismissed because we were indiscreet, I
am afraid a great many of us would be dismissed often. I would ask the Government,
because, after all, it is not a sign of weakness in a Government if they think they have
done something that ought to be rectified,
to look into this whole question in a sympathetic frame of mind, not to be influenced
by people who try to terrorise, or people who
try to cajole, but to ask themselves plainly end
squarely: "Have we done the right thing?
Are we justified in the course we have taken?
Can we justify our action before Parliament
and before the country, and prove that we
have done the right thing?" If the Government have a shade of a shadow of doubt that
they have taken a more extreme course than
they ought to have taken, then it is not a
sign of weakness to retrace their steps. On
the contrary, it is a sign of greatness. If
people find they have made a mistake they
can go back on it and rectify that mistake.
I do ask the Government to go into this
whole question in a sympathetic manner.

force, of which Mr. Nixon was fully aware,

structions, made another political speech in

Mr. COOTE: Question.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There are very
few people in this House and very few people
in the city of Belfast, who have not read
that speech, and a great many people outside
Ulster have read it. I think what attracted
a good deal of attention to it was not that

think the vast majority of readers can come
to no other conclusion than that a more
mischievous and misleading statement could
not have been made by anyone who had the

Inspector-General then proceeded to exercise
the right that he had as Commanding Officer
of the Force. He framed a charge against
Mr. Nixon, and formed a Court of Inquiry.
The charges were disobedience of orders, and
infringing the Code. Following on that
the Inspector-General suspended Mr. Nixon
from duty.
On the eve of the first sitting of the Court
of Inquiry, a demonstration took place in
the heart of Mr. Nixon's own district, with
banners and bands and placards. These
placards contained demands for the instant
dismissal of the Inspector-General, the
instant dismissal of the Commissioner of
Belfast, my own dismissal, and, incidentally,
the reinstatement of Mr. Nixon. That demonstration was organised and took place in
the heart of Mr. Nixon's district, and I do
not think anyone in this House will disagree
with me when I say that without Mr.
Nixon's active approval and support that
demonstration could not have taken place.
But worse followed-a campaign of intimidation-intimidation in its worst form.
Persons connected with the Inquiry and
Members of the Government received letters
threatening their lives, and when that did
not avail to stop the Inquiry, the intimidation was then directed against the witnesses
necessary to prove the specific charges made
against Mr. Nixon.

The Government was faced with this

I think this affair has taken an altogether

thing that is involved is the case that a
police officer misconceived what police duty
was. He thought at the same time that he
could act as a policeman and as a politician.
Now, that is a thing that cannot be admitted
for one moment, because a policeman's duty
is entirely different from that of a politician.
What is all right in a politician is not what
is required in a policeman at all. However,
the matter gets an importance from another
point of view-that is, that the policeman
had courted the populace to intimidate the
Government, and the question became one
whether the Government would yield to
popular clamour that was largely fostered
in the interests of the policeman himself?
If such a thing could be tolerated it would
be an end to government. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) As our system of government
is constituted we cannot have members of
our Judiciary as politicians. If a member
of our Judiciary were to make a political
speech it is entirely contrary to his position.
In the same way a policeman may not interfere and may not take part in politics,
especially in cases where a precise instruction has been given against it. While
government is by the people, through the
people, and for the people, it is not the

members. Until the voice of the populace

I
A good deal has been said about Mr. Nixon
not having an opportunity to defend himself.
That is one of the gravest charges that could
be made against us.
When he was called up
by the Inspector-General, as he was by the
direction of the Government, as they were
entitled to, to have certain specific questions
put to him why could not he have taken the
opportunity, as any honourable man would
have done, and say, "I did not say that.
did not mean that," and if he had any explanation to offer let him offer it? At no time
has he ever made any statement. If Mr.
Nixon at the time had said he had made a
mistake, had expressed his contrition, and had
said that the matter would not occur again
the case would have borne a different aspect
altogether. But, so far from that being the
case, he does nothing of the kind. When
those questions are put to him he practically
declines to answer, and we can only draw our
own conclusions.
As I have said, the whole accusation was met
with two voices. One was that he did not
make the speech at all, and the other glories
in the speech and regards it as the utterance
of a patriot. These two are entirely inconsistent, but we still have the tenour of them
running through all the speeches from the
opposite side of the House this afternoon.
At one stage they say he has been wrongly
convicted that he did not make the speech,
and then on the other hand they say that he
did make the speech but that the punishment
is too hard. No other course was open to
the Government in the situation that arose,
because, instead of having submitted himself
to discipline in the ordinary way, or expressed
any contrition for his breach of discipline, he
gloried in the speech, has done so openly, and
has not, as I have said, made one expression
of regret for what has occurred. The policeman who is to uphold the law and carry out
orders appeals from his superior to all sorts
of irregular assemblages and attempts to
throw the machinery of Government and of
administration out of gear. if the Government were to yield to that it would mean an
end of government altogether.
Was there ever outside Mexico such a
meeting as took place before the Court of
Inquiry? We had speakers at that meeting
who desired to remain anonymous, and who
directed the Press that if they knew the
names of the speakers they were not to
publish them. The House will recollect that
in the Press the next day there appeared the
statement that the speakers desired to remain
anonymous and not one name of a speaker
was given. We had also threatening letters
conveyed to members of the Government aud
to others. This made the position absolutely
plain. It is absolutely impossible to yield to
popular clamour, and now here in this House
we have dragged in that fine body of men the
Orange Order. Why was the Orange Order
introduced here? What have we to do
with it here. We have to do with the conduct of a policeman. Who is to judge the
conduct of a policeman ? Is it his superior
officer or is it the mob of people outside? We
say that, so long as we are a Government,
policemen must be subject to discipline and
to their superior officers, and we decline to
be overawed by any of these Soviet assemblages that take place and have taken place
in regard to this case.

TEACHERS' RELIGIOUS CONVICTIONS.
1. Mr. MILLER asked the Prime Minister
whether it is the intention of the Government to introduce and pass an Act making
it a capital offence for any member of a
Regional Committee under the Education
Act to ask a candidate for the position of
a teacher under the jurisdiction his religious
convictions; if not, can he advise any other
method of carrying out the same object; or
whether in the event of no means being devised by which members of Regional Committees could be prevented from inquiring,
receiving information, verbally or by letter,
as to the religious convictions of candidates,
he will see that Section 66, Clause 3, of the
Education Act is repealed.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The answer to the first part
of the question is in the
negative.
In reply to the second part of the
question, the Act provides that appointments by Regional Committees shall
not be made dependent upon religious belief. It would obviously be impossible to
prevent members of these Committees from
becoming acquainted with the religious
faith of candidates for these appointments.
Mr. MILLER: Why cannot they be
prevented?
Mr. POLLOCK: The record of the teachers
and their training are very well known to
the authorities, so it is not conceivable that
should
any candidate
present himself as
an applicant for the position of teacher
without the fact of the denomination to
which he belongs being made known.

Sir DAWSON BATES: As the admini
stration of the Act referred to by the hon.
Member is one reserved by the Imperial
Government, all questions regarding it
should be raised in the Imperial Parliament.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask my right hon.
Friend does he not misunderstand
me?
Question No. 10? It is as to the building of

Mr. SPEAKER: I understand it is a

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Trust is formed under the Imperial Government and the
Imperial Government is responsible for that
Trust. I cannot undertake to hold myself

suggest to my hon. Friend that he should

The attention of the Ministry of Education
has been drawn to the case referred to by the
hon. Member.
Under the Rules of the Commissioners of
National Education, which are still in force,
married women teachers appointed for the
first time subsequent to 30th June, 1911, are
required to absent themselves from their
schools for two months continuously during
the period preceding and succeeding childbirth and to provide substitutes at their
own expense, but there is no rule governing
the dismissal of a teacher in the circumstances in question. The appointment
and dismissal of teachers in public elementary schools has always rested with the
managers, and the terms on which teachers
hold their positions are set forth in the agreements entered into between the parties concerned.
The Ministry has fully considered all the
circumstances of this case and has decided
not to interfere with the discretion of the
manager.
I cannot within the limits of Question and
Answer deal with the large question of the
employment of married women teachers.
That is a question on which the views of
educational authorities are much at variance.
The absence of general agreement amongst
perfectly fair-minded persons on this subject
seems to the Ministry to constitute a strong
reason for declining to lay down any hard
and fast rule in regard to it.
Under Section 68 of the new Educational
Act teachers are protected against unreasonable dismissal, but the Ministry is not prepared to hold that that section of the Act
should be applied so as to restrict the discretion of managers in cases of this kind.
I may add that the Government do not
propose to introduce further legislation on
this subject.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Arising out of this
answer, may I inquire is the action of the
Ministry in this matter not calculated to
prejudice the interests of the teachers concerned? If it is established as a general
principle are we to take it that the Ministry
will in future decide as they have done in
this matter in respect of other cases that
may crop up?
Mr. POLLOCK: My hon. Friend raises in
his inquiry, if I may say so, the general
question which is and always has been a
very debatable one, and I could not pretend
in reply to a question to enter into all the
arguments either for or against the pursuance of any particular policy in regard to
the matter. I did say in the formal reply
I gave that the Ministry objected, seeing that
there was strong reason for it, to lay down
any hard and fast rule in regard to it, the
presumption being that the managers of
schools, those who are responsible for their
organisation, should have some discretion in
matters of this kind, because I think it must
be clear to hon. Members that circumstances
often vary in different cases, and they love,
therefore, to be treated by different methods.
For that reason the Ministry has come to
the conclusion that it would not be wise to
lay down any definite ruling in regard to how
matters should be conducted in these circumstances.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I further inquire,
is the action of this manager not absolutely
without precedent? It appears to be not
only cruel but autocratic. Is the Government going to sanction a course taken
with
respect to a teacher which has
never been adopted in connection with any
other case?

Iwill have to be done.
Dr. MORRISON: I would like to know if

Sir DAWSON BATES: The Court of
Inquiry set up to investigate the charges
preferred against Inspector Nixon was dissolved under circumstances which
matters of common knowledge. It was not
by reason of the fact that the Court made
no finding that the Inspector was dismissed.
Mr. Nixon had every opportunity of making
his defence before his superior officers, of
which he did not elect to avail himself. He
was dismissed from the Force on the recommendation of the Government, who satisfied
themselves that his disobedience of orders
rendered his continued employment a menace
to peace and good order amongst the general
community.
The reasons which led to Inspector Nixon's
dismissal have been published in the Press,
the accuracy of which is not denied.
Under the circumstances of the case the
Government is not prepared to reconsider
its decision.
I may add that the Inspector is now in
enjoyment of the full pension to which he
would have been entitled had he completed
his service in the Royal Ulster Constabulary.

LOANS GUARANTEE ACT.
13. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can state the amounts
of money
advanced under the Loans Guarantee Act to the firm of Harland and Wolff,
Limited, and how many extra men were
employed in consequence of the subsidy.
Mr. POLLOCK: The hon. Member would
appear to be under a misapprehension regarding the facilities provided by the Loans
Guarantee Acts. No advances or grants are
made by the Government under the terms
of this legislation, but guarantees are given
and nothing more. No immediate charge on
public funds is involved and it is hoped
that no ultimate charge will result. Firms
taking advantage of these facilities must
raise the money in the ordinary way in the
open market, and in so doing they are assisted by Government credit. Up to the
present date Messrs. Harland and Wolff
have received guarantees in respect of
capital undertakings up to an amount of
£248,000, and, in addition, guarantees of
£2,190,000 have been given to various
large shipowning Companies in connection
with the construction of ships in the Yards
of Messrs. Harland and Wolff, Ltd., Belfast,
making in all a total of £2,438,000.
I may add that returns have already been
laid upon the Table of the House showing
the guarantees which the Government have
undertaken to give up to the end of September, 1923, and a further return for the six
months ending the 31st instant will be presented to Parliament after the close of the
present financial year.
In reply to the latter part of the question,
the average number of men employed in connection with the construction of these.
vessels during February, 1924, was 5,500.
Mr. DONALD: Hear, hear.

Mr. DONALD: The first question to which
reference is made to His Grace's Speech
is with regard to the boundary, and
like my hon. Friend, the Member for North
Belfast (Mr. McGuffin), I can say there are
certain suspicions abroad in regard to this
very complex question. To some extent these
suspicions are aroused in view of the fact
that this matter is being brought continually
before the Imperial House. I noticed in the
paper yesterday that a question will be
asked there with reference to this conference.
That, to some extent, arouses suspicion in.
the minds of our people here. There is
something to be said with regard to what
my hon. Friend said yesterday that we at
least should know something from time to
time as to what takes place at these conferences in order to allay these suspicions.
When I say that I cannot help thinking
about a reference that was given by the
Noble Marquess, Lord Londonderry, at the
Reform Club the other night. He said that
we should be loyal to the Government. I
could not help wondering was the Government loyal to itself, and that is why I am
referring to this matter. Very often
suspicions are aroused through misunderstandings, but the people should at least
know something of what is going on.
Secondly, the Noble Marquess referred to
hon. Members, and said they should devote
a great deal of time in their constituencies
talking to their people. That is exactly the
thing that I feel a great difficulty about.
When I go into my constituency, I am
approached about this very thing, and I
cannot tell any of my people what is going
on. I merely mention that to show that we
should be told something from time to time
as to what is going on at this conference.
Personally, I am satisfied with the statement made by the Prime Minister at the close
of the last Session, and I am going to refer
to the very able speech which he made on

question. I, for one, am satisfied that there
has been no change as regards our position,
and I have every confidence in our Prime
Minister and those who with him represent
us at that conference. The Prime Minister
said with regard to the boundary question:-
The whole thing is that if Mr.
Cosgrave and his representatives claim the
whole of Fermanagh and Tyrone, and if I

The next matter is with regard to education and the establishment of a building for
the teaching of agriculture, that is the

industry in our country, and why we have
departed from the teaching of this in our

This will be a splendid thing, but all these
people will have to come to Belfast in order

next important question in the Speech is
with regard to rent restrictions. I think the
Government are well advised to postpone
this matter, although I am not in agreement
with other hon. Members. We could have
taken this question up, but a difficulty might
have arisen by our deciding one thing and
the Imperial Government deciding another.
It is a most difficult question. Yesterday it
developed into rents with houses. These two
are linked together, and, in my judgment,
the whole trouble arose through the Imperial
Government having restricted rents at all.
That was where the mischief was first
created. They restricted rents at a time
when the people were really able to pay a
fair increase on a sliding scale, in keeping
with their income at that time. But a most
unnatural thing is taking place to-day.
Rents are high and wages are low. The
people are not in a position to pay the rents.
That is the position we are confronted with
at the present time, due, I say, to Government interference. There is too much
Government interference (hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-not only with rents but with
housing. I want to see the private builder
getting in, for until the private builder gets
in we are not going to get houses.
Members: Hear, hear.)
(Hon.
That is apparent, because somehow or other
I have a feeling, because I have learned

I could not help taking note of a speech I

ill-health. I refer to Sir Auckland Geddes.
Sir Auckland Geddes dealing with this
question referred first to prices. He said the
rise was due to the fall in the value of gold
and the unavoidable paper inflation which
accounted for 20 per cent. to 25 per cent. of
the increase; scarcity values; the diminished
utilisation of capital, the result in the main
of labour readjustment. Thank God we
have no labour readjustment in this part of
the country! Also to the diminished use of
shipping. We regret that also. My right
hon. Friend has given us an idea that freights
are going up. We trust they will go up; that
they will result in a revival in trade and
help the shipbuilding industry. He also said
it was due to unreasonable individual profitmaking. I say there is still unreasonable
individual profit-making in house building,
and that these "rings" that are holding up
cement, timber, and other materials that go
to the building of houses should be broken up
by some means. The right hon. Gentleman
said the cure for all this was increased production, increased export and import. I
agree with him.

I have taken out here an exact copy of the
amount it costs a farmer to produce fourteen
pecks of flax, that is, a bag sown on two
statute acres of land. I have the figures
here, and if it will not weary the House I
will give them, as I think they will be very
instructive. If you take for taxes, rent, and

would not be at all an adequate amount; if
you take for ploughing the fields the sum of
£2 for two statute acres, and it would not
pay it if a man had to hire horses and

ready, and it takes an immense amount of
work to make the ground ready for flax after
it is ploughed; if you allow £5 to buy a bag of
seed-it will cost from sixty to sixty-five shillings now-and the artificial manure which is
necessary to grow flax; if you hire a man to
sow it in a scientific manner it will cost 10s;
if you allow £2 for harrowing the field and
rolling it afterwards; if you allow 10s
weeding, £5 for pulling the flax after it is
grown, and £2 for carting it up a steep laneway to be steeped in the dams, and it would
not do it at all; if you allow £1 for putting
it into the dams, putting stones upon it,
examining it every day according to the
temperature of the weather, and trying to
discover if the flax is getting steeped
properly; if you allow £1 for throwing it out,
and I have seen it thrown out. I have seen
a relative of my own in the water almost to
his waist throwing flax out when he could
not get a man to do it, and he has pointed
to a man a short distance away, and asked me
did I know what that man was doing, and
when I said I did not he has told me that he
was watching lest a drop of water from his
dam should escape into a burn and kill a
trout. It is a fact. A man was buried
some time ago. He could not get seven pecks
of flax thrown out of the dam unless he paid
35s for it, so he went into the water and
threw it out himself. He was a pretty
elderly man, and he contracted a cold which
resulted in his death. I know another man
who has three daughters, who help sometimes
to work on the farm as well as in the house,
and he was asked such an extravagant price
for the throwing of his flax out of the dam
that those girls said to their own father, "We
will never pay it," and they got up at three
o'clock in the morning, those three women,
and one of them went in to the flax dam up
to her waist and threw out the flax while her
sisters pulled it along the ground across the
field. I am only putting £1 down here, and
I would not take £50 and throw out a dam of
flax at three o'clock in the morning. For
carrying the flax from the dams to the field
allow £2; for spreading, a filthy job, allow
£2, for lifting it when it is dry allow £1, for
putting it into stooks, hovels, or stacks allow
£8, and it would not do it; for carting it to
C
the mill, perhaps four or five miles along a
country road, allow £2, for taking it to the
market £2, and for scutching it allow £8 8s.
When I total that up I find it comes to
£46 8s for fifty-six stones of flax. He sold it
in the open market for 12s 6d a stone, and
got £35 into his pocket for it, and at the
miserable prices I have quoted here it cost

to the most eminent judge of agriculture in

less than a shilling per pound at the average
of fourteen shillings per stone, which is a
high average.
I was sitting the other day on a Board
which was accepting contracts for a large
institution in County Antrim, and I was
greatly struck by the fact that the prices
quoted for linen-thread was 16s, I think, per
pound. I am speaking from memory and
cannot say exactly whether it was 15s or 16s,
but I would point out to the House that the
farmer, who produces the flax and sells it in
the market at less than one shilling per
pound, loses a matter of £11, and that every
other person who touches the flax from the
time the farmer sells it until it reaches the
consumer is paid, as he ought to be, a decent
wage. The directors and shareholders of the
mills and factories can make a good profit,
pay a good dividend, and build up a reserve
fund, while the poor farmer who produces
the flax does it at a loss, and the Government ask him now to continue doing it and
to produce more. I blame no manufacturer,
I blame no worker. They all have the right

I see that a good deal of money is to be
spent in the construction and renovation of
police barracks throughout the country, and
I want to draw the attention of the Government to one portion of the country that the
police were removed from some time ago.
There are eighty square miles of the County
of Antrim in which there are no policemen
at all. It is immensely creditable to the
people of the Templepatrick district that
they are so peaceful and law-abiding.
remember reading in Holy Writ of a district
that was so peaceable that there was neither
magistrate in the land nor bar nor bolt in
the doors. The peace and prosperity of that
part of the country attracted a band of people
who were looking for booty, and they came
and took advantage of the peace and prosperity of the place, ousted the inhabitants,
and took possession of their crops and stocks.
I do not want that to occur in the peaceful
district of Templepatrick, and I ask the
Government is eighty square miles of country
not too large an area to be left without a
police barracks? I will tell you of something that happened in the case of a respectable clergyman. A gang in a motor-car came
to his door and demanded to be put up for
the night. He was compelled to let them
take refuge in a loft, and he afterwards discovered that one of the men, who was
wanted for a serious crime, escaped to
America. I say the Government is not doing
its duty when it allows eighty square miles

Templepatrick and Parkgate will have a

now, in the Speech from the Throne we are
told that we have to wait on England. Why
should we wait on England? (Hon. Members:
"Hear, hear.") Is this House to be committed definitely to the policy of always waiting until the House of Commons in London
passes an Act? And, if we are to wait, is
this House to be bound slavishly to follow
every such Act? Our conditions are not, or
at any rate may not be, the same as in England. We have here the material and the
machinery for making our own laws upon
this subject, and I cannot understand at all
why it is necessary, when our conditions are
not the same, to wait for the passing of an
Act in London for Great Britain. Surely we
can do these things for ourselves.

agree

of Finance, Home Affairs, and Labour.
sympathise a good deal with the picture that

men, I think representing spinning, in the

But I did not get up to speak on this
matter. I wanted to say a few things with
regard to the Speech from the Throne. It
covers very many points. There is one point
of which I think notice should be taken. It
has already been referred to by my colleague
from the University. That is, the friendly
attitude that the Labour Government have
shown to Ulster. I think that many of us
had doubts in our mind as to how we would
be treated if a Labour, or even a Liberal,
Government got into office. It should be a
great satisfaction to all of us that they have
approached this question not from a party
standpoint but from the great, broad
principle that Ulster is a loyal, prosperous,
and industrious unit in the Empire, and deserves the support of all parties irrespective
of politics. In connection with that I think
there is a corresponding obligation on us.
In my opinion it would be a wise course if we
as a party remained neutral in party controversies across the water, and we did not interfere in English elections. I can imagine
that if our Prime Minister went to the
Prime Minister of a Labour Government,
and the Prime Minister of the Labour
Government found that at the General
Election we had been sending over very
intellectual and capable people to try to injure the Prime Minister of that Government,
he would think it was very unfair. I merely
make that suggestion.
What I wish to speak specially about is
this Illegitimacy Bill, which is mentioned in
the King's Speech. In connection with that
I would like to congratulate the Minister of
Home Affairs and his Deputy, and I think I
should include in my congratulations the
very able official who looks after Local
Government Board work in the Home Office,

on the Ministry of Home Affairs. Some of

great deal of it is undeserved. I think that
by and by, when these controversies have
subsided and disappeared, it will be found
when the history of Ulster is written, that
the Minister of Home Affairs has immortalised himself by placing a Bill of this nature
on the Statute Book of Northern Ireland.
It removes a stain that unfortunately has
lain upon this Province for a long time. It
is inconceivable to the average mind that for
fifty years the girls in Ireland have been
without the protection that their sisters in
England have. For those fifty years these
girls have been outside the law, but now the
question is viewed by us and by every reasonable man from a new standpoint.
Wo believe that the ideal of womanhood
lies neither in the fair saint nor fair sinner.
The female type of character is neither worse
nor better than the male, only weaker. Women
are meant to be neither men's guides nor
their play things, but their comrades, their
fellows, and their equals so far as nature
puts no bar to that equality. In potential
motherhood nature has put a bar, and seeing
that this is her lot she is found to be fearfully weighted in the race of life. It is, therefore, the duty of men to see that not one
ounce is put upon that load beyond what

Hon. Members are perhaps feeling rather

If only a full and adequate supply of raw

That is a very wide statement, and if it is

Friend (Mr. Pollock) that either he or my

(Mr. Archdale) should go a good deal further
into this matter. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). After all you cannot tell farmers or

advise a man to grow mustard and cress in
his garden
As my hon. Friend the Member
for Antrim (Mr. Crawford) has pointed out
it is a speculative crop, and unless you have
very strong indications that the price of
flax will be remunerative to farmers
you will not get them to grow flax
throughout the Six Counties. It is difficult to offer suggestions as to how farmers
would have an adequate price, but it is
possible that the other gentlemen interested
in the trade might get together and buy flax
in advance or else give guarantees that the
farmers would get a reasonable price.
What I would like the Minister of Agriculture to tell us is the various indications of
prosperity in the agricultural industry. I
would like to get some information about the
potato trade this year. It is within the
recollection of hon. Members that last year
potatoes could not be sold, and some farmers
were giving them away in order to get the
land clear. I would like the Ministry of
Agriculture to give some information as to
the varieties of potato that have been grown
in the past year, and as to whether they are
considered suitable for the Bristol Channel
ports. I would also like to know whether
the restricted areas have been extended or
decreased, and how the black scab disease
has been progressing. As everybody knows,
the millennium of the potato farming
industry in this country is that the whole of
the Six Counties should grow immune
varieties, and as to how far that has progressed the Ministry of Agriculture might be
able to inform us later on. Another point of
great importance is the milk recording stations,
and also the registration of bulls. I would
like to know how far the scheme has progressed, and whether it has proved a success.
Hon. Members will agree that it costs as
much to feed a cow producing 300 gallons of
milk as it costs to feed a cow that produces
900 gallons. It is almost staggering to the
imagination to realise that if we could only
raise the average in the Six Counties up to
600 or 700 gallons per cow the output would
be so enormous that it would bring a great
deal of employment to our population.

It is not everyone who knows that from the
Cockerel descends three-fourths of the producing qualities of the egg. It is not everyone
who knows that the egg-laying propensities

if attention was paid to that point, and that

will find that the average number of eggs

I can assure you that the eight million
pounds worth of eggs imported into the

There is a great future for the egg-laying

to the Ministry of Agriculture.

the Ministry of Agriculture are fully alive to

Mr. MARK: I would like to add a few remarks to those of the hon. Member (Captain
Mulholland) on the question of agriculture.
The hon Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford)
has given very interesting figures, which I
had the opportunity of seeing just before I
entered this House, and I can assure hon.
Members that he is really within the price
when he quotes the figures he has given with
regard to the production of flax. No farmer
to-day, at the present rate of wages in the
country, could grow one acre of flax, or two
acres or ten acres, to pay for the cost of
production. But that is nothing very strange
in the agricultural world to-day, because I
do not believe for a moment that a farmer
can grow any crop now which would pay for
the cost of production. Last year, undoubtedly we had potatoes going to waste. One farmer told me he had 100 tons of potatoes that
went to waste. He bought cattle to eat them.
They managed that part all right, but
when the slump in the prices of cattle came
he only got the cost price of the cattle. He
lost £8 per head on the cattle. This year no
farmer has any potatoes to sell. I saw a man,
whom I knew to be a summons server, going
round a country district the other dav carrying a huge bag. I saw him serving a summons on an individual. I asked him, “What
are you doing? Are you giving him something?" He said he was. He was burdened
with summonses for the payment of rates by
the agriculturists of Northern Ireland.
Where that state of affairs exists it will, I
am sure, be evident to hon. Members that
agriculture has reached a very low ebb.
I came across one particular case recently.
where a man bought a small farm for £700.
He had a small overdraft at the bank. His
wife got a little money left her by a friend
who died, and they sold out the shares and
paid off the overdraft. Notwithstanding
very frugal management the farmer got into
debt again; and only a few weeks ago they
had to sell out. They sold in time to pay
their debts, and now they are left without a
penny. That state of affairs will be brought
more to our attention during the next two
years. We heard in reply to a question that
this Government is going to follow in the

I would like the Government to do something
that would encourage the farmers in this
connection. They could undoubtedly give a
subsidy of so much an acre if they want flax
grown in the country. If trade opens on the
Continent and cotton gets cheap in price
flax will be at a low ebb again. The

way as to be lasting. Undoubtedly, it has
been experiencing good times within the
last two months and I hope that will continue. I know the spinner has been paying
a price to the farmer which has not paid him
for what he got for the yarns. He is
now trying to make up for the rainy day
he has come through. I am not saying that
he did anything wrong in trying to buy flax
in the cheapest and best way he could, but I

in the linen industry we must have some

should be adopted by the Ministry of Agriculture. In regard to eggs I am told we are

we can stand. I think we will have to have a

this House before we see that Bill right
through, and I hope when it does come
before the House it will be a credit to us.
When in Glasgow I inquired into this

in view.

the cases?

Mr. McBRIDE: I would just like to add a
word in support of what the hon. Member for
Antrim (Mr. Crawford) and the able speech
he made as regards agriculture. Now everbody understands, of course, that the

was sufficient flax grown in the country all
our mills would be on full time. Now
everybody knows that the linen industry is
what is called the staple industry of the
country, and I say that supposing that that
flax is not grown and supposing the Continental and Russian supply fails then
where is our industry to come from? (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). At the same time I
was wondering what inducement the farmer
had for launching upon a scheme of growing
flax without some guarantee of a fair price
for the labour that he put upon it. Now our
Minister of Labour, I am thankful to say,
has grappled with a great many trade disputes in this, our Province, since the Government started. He has brought employer and
employee together and settled these disputes
without any trouble. I was wondering to
myself could the Government, through the
able Minister of Agriculture, in some shape
or form bring the spinners and the Farmers'
Union together and in some way give them
a guarantee of a fair price in order that
they might be enabled to grow flax,
with the understanding that when it
would come to the market they would receive something adequate for the labour they
had bestowed upon it. I am only rising to
throw out the suggestion in order that when
the Minister of Agriculture gets upon the
floor of the House-as I hope he will very
soon be restored to his former health-he
may be able to work out some scheme which
will be for the benefit of our Province and
for the welfare of our people.
Everybody knows that there has been a
great cry" Back to the land". If we could
get the people back to the land it would do
away with the congestion in the towns and
cities. There is no way of getting back to
the land except by getting the people into
the agricultural system, and I think the
Government would be well advised to put
themselves in the position that I suggest
through the Minister of Agriculture, backed
up by the Cabinet, and try to get some
arrangement whereby the farmer will have
a guaranteed return for his labour and the
country will have a supply of flax which will
enable our mills to be kept going for the
time to come. With these remarks I leave
it to the Government.

But what was the actual condition in
which we took over? We were suffering
from a world-racking war which had shaken
every civilised community and taxed every
resource of men and governments, taxed the
patience of every population and every
country in the world, wearied them at times
to a feeling of exasperation at the wholesale
disturbance of commerce, business, and industry, and then the sudden throwing back
into the ordinary course of commerce of a large
number of men who had been called out to
the defence of their country.
Apart from
these general conditions which prevailed over
the world, we in Ireland had added to it a
condition practically of rebellion. At all
times there was a feeling of dissension between
the two parties of our country, and unfortunately to the two parties who had
always existed in Ireland, there was added
a third party at that time. I refer to the
Republican Party, who seemed absolutely
opposed to any form of recognised government, and opposed to any sense of loyalty or
attachment to England which even might
exist in the Southern part of this island.
13 MARCH 1924.
Debate on the Address.

Debate on the Address.
A number of the matters which have been
Idealt with in the course of this Debate on
the Address are matters necessarily which
might possibly have been more fruitfully
dealt with had they been raised at Westminster. They were the actions of the Parliament at Westminster in some respects
which have been most severely criticised.
For instance, there is that sum of £500,000,
which is so familiar to us all. We must
remember that that was in the nature of a
free gift to this part of the country, more
or less without counterpart in any expenditure of the United Kingdom. It was made
to us at a time when we were struggling
with difficulties over here. It was volunteered by the Imperial Parliament, or by
the Government of the time, and at the time
it was given conditions were attached to it.
I think our Prime Minister and our Minister
of Labour, instead of being criticised for the
way in which we were bound to administer
this fund once it was given to us, deserve
our thanks. The sense of gratitude seems
to have vanished. We owe a great deal to
those two right hon. Gentlemen for getting
that money and making it available in this
part of the world; but, whatever we may
feel, everyone of us must entertain a sense
of disappointment. Although I do not like
to dwell upon the sense of injustice to Ireland, this affords an instance of treatment
to which really one is almost justified in
giving that name. We certainly were le
to expect that we would get this £500,000.
It was handed over to our Minister of
Labour, and he very properly wished to see
that that money, although it was given for
the relief of unemployment, was spent upon
some justifiable, some useful object. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) It has been said
here that our working people do not want
money if they possibly can help it.
Then again there was this condition of unemployment. I really think sufficient stress
has not been laid upon the peculiar conditions
which attached to our Province here. I do
not say unfortunately. I think every one of
us regard it as a fortunate thing that the
great productions of our industries here
were matters of vital importance in the conduct of the war. There is no doubt that in
our shipyards and in our linen industries we
had two absolutely indispensable factors in
carrying on and in the preservation of our
country. This had different results. One
was that it caused these businesses to be more
subject to Government interference and
Government regulations than industries of a
less essential character. It had also the effect
of drawing into this part of the world a very
large additional number of working poeple to
those who were in the ordinary habit of
living about here. A large number of loyal
men went out to the front, and not only
were the places of these men filled by men
who had not felt called to the defence of
their country as strongly as ours had, but our
shipbuilding yards during those few years of
the war added to their capacity nearly as
much as was the accumulated growth of their
previous existence. Such an expansion in our
industry really could hardly have been conceived. Those in our industry, for the
ordinary products of which we enjoyed
world-wide reputation, were practically prohibited from manufacturing them. The
work of the spinners and weavers had to be
concentrated upon aeroplane cloth. We
were controlled in every department of our
business-every detail of it, and then, just as
nearly every productive spindle had been
concentrated upon these articles to the exclusion of domestic articles and articles for
export, the war suddenly came to a close.
Our men came back from the war to Belfast,
and consequently our unemployment fund was
burdened, not only with those who came
back and for whom the Government had the
entire support of the Province in their
readiness to help them in every way they
could, but we have also on our unemployment
fund those men who had been drawn in from
other parts of Ireland and who, had the war
not taken place, would not have been located
here and would not have been, except for
that on
our unemployment fund.
Conseqently I think that if ever a special
appeal were justified for special consideration in respect of our Unemployment Fund it
ought to be entertained in connection with
these two industries, which were of such
vital importance during the war, and whose
ordinary course was so tremendously interfered with by the regulations which were
instituted during that period.

On the matter of education I would like
hon. Members to listen to me more in my
individual capacity, but still as one who is
keenly interested in education. It struck
me that this House had unanimously accepted the principle that our Education Act
should be of a non-sectarian character. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). We realised that
we have in this Province people holding
very conflicting views, and so it was the
attitude of this House that, in dealing with
an Act which affected every family throughout the Six Counties, we should try to make
it sufficiently elastic that it would be
possible in one way or another for every
member of all the communities in the Six
Counties to take advantage of the facilities
which existed and yet not to do violence to
his religious or conscientious scruples. I
think the Act accomplishes this. If there
is any reluctance to transfer schools there
certainly is no object in transferring them
at the present time, and I would not call
any man disloyal, or say that he was in
any way attempting to thwart the proper
working of this Act, if he did delay in
transferring a school in order to see how
the Act is going to work out. We must
remember that it is possible to retain control of your Own school, to
carry on
practically under the old conditions and yet
receive 95 or 96 per cent. of the cost of
conducting your school from the Government under this Act. Therefore, whatever
party, or body, or individual, who retains
what he sets such store on, namely the
appointment of teachers and the manage
ment of his schools, is able to do that at
a cost of, say, three or four per cent. of
the total cost of running the school. That, I
think, is very generous support.
Another thing which has been repeatedly
affirmed in this House-I daresay some are
more enthusiastic in their support than
others-is that this is a democratic age, and
we want to try to get control of all public
activities more and more under democratic
lines. The object of the Education Act is
to decentralise, to make the control of a
more and more popular character, and in
this, again, I believe that if people, instead
of showing ruffled feelings where, perhaps,
their old rights have been encroached upon
in some way, if they have the real interests
of education at heart, approach this by
saying Well, here is this Act, which places
more money at our disposal than ever before;
let us see if we cannot improve on it, and take
hold of it with the determination to make it
as efficient as possible," we will have a better
system of education than ever before. It is
not so long to wait, so I would appeal to
everybody, both in this House and outside, to
give the Act a fair trial and try to make it
the success we would like to see it.

stantly realise the importance of the country

Another matter which is of vital importance to the farmer is the completion of
land purchase. That is another thing in
which we must have a certain amount of
sympathy for this House. In these matters,
where the Imperial Parliament is concerned,
it must be remembered that this Government
has had to deal with no less than three
Governments over there during our short life.
The question of land purchase had been
brought up to the point when it was practically ready for submission to the Imperial
House, when unfortunately the Government
under Mr. Baldwin was defeated. In the
course of negotiations which have taken place
the new Government have informed us-and
we must accept their word-that they will
honour any commitments into which their
predecessors entered. That is the present state
of the negotiations.
Mr. POLLOCK: If non-controversial.
Mr. BARBOUR: If non-controversial. So
I think we can count with a fair measure of
confidence on that Bill being passed through
Westminster if we agree, and if the farmers
and landowners in the Six Counties accept
the Bill as provisionally drawn up. I believe
that every Member of this House will do the
farmers throughout the Six Counties a good
service if he will do his very best to persuade
them to accept the Bill which has been drawn
up to try to do justice between the parties,
and thus to ensure that it will be passed.
Otherwise it will be thrown back, and I am

Reference has been made in the Governor's
Gracious Speech to another thing which is of
considerable importance to the country districts, that is the improvement of the police
barracks. It is intended, as soon as this work
can be taken up, to spend between £400,000
and £500,000 in the remodelling of the police
barracks throughout the Six Counties. This
will be financed by means of a sinking fund
extending over a period of 20 years, so that,
while we hope to derive immediate benefit in
the shape of employment and better accommodation for our Constabulary, the burden
will not be too oppressive at the start.

TO THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS

always approaches matters in the most

Home Affairs with regard to that matter is
this they have prepared and published regulations under which the amounts voted will be
given, and it has been fully explained to
the various Councils concerned how they
may take advantage of the provisions of this
measure. Under the Act it is necessary for
the various local authorities to pass resolutions putting the scheme into operation, so
that the amount of the free loan may be
made available for them. I am glad to say
that resolutions have been already passed by
upwards of thirteen urban district councils
and one rural district council. These have
indicated their desire to make grants
corresponding to the £60 given in respect of
each house by this Government. Twentyfour other authorities have the matter under
their consideration. It has not fructified yet,
but the Ministry of Home Affairs hopes that
before very long these bodies will also have
passed resolutions making the scheme available for themselves. While the Ministry regrets that certain bodies are holding back,
it feels, all the same, that they are likely to
come in, and that the undoubted advantages
given by the Act passed last year will be
taken advantage of. It is evident, on the
face of it, how much this would be to the
advantage of the local authorities themselves.
Take a case where a scheme for 100 houses is
passed. £40 advanced by the local authoritv
in respect of each house would mean they
would be liable for a sum of £4,000. According to the scheme available, that amount
would be repayable over forty years, and on
the terms on which they could get money it
would involve in respect of each house that
a payment of £2 6s 0d a year would have to
be made by the local authority. When one
takes into consideration the amount of rates
and taxes that would be payable, as well as
the great advantage that is given to the
community, it is absolutely clear that it
would be of very great advantage to those
bodies themselves to put into force the provisions of the Act.

A few other questions were touched upon

remember that when we were discussing the institution of the police force, he insisted that it

Motion made and Question proposed: "That

I hope that the discussion will not be on

that even
from the Government benches,
as well as from other parts of the House,
there was too much feeling introduced into
the matter. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
I want to say at the outset that I do not agree
personally with everything that has been
said regarding the Nixon case in this House.
I do want to tell the members of the Government that there is a strong feeling outside
the House that this man has not been fairly
dealt with, and I want to approach the
matter rather with the object of holding out
the olive branch, to see if something cannot
be done to settle matters. I want to remind
the members of the Government that in the
South of Ireland a number of officers of
high position perpetrated a worse crime
than that-
Mr. DONALD: On a point of order, it is
rather unfortunate that during this discussion
there is not present a representative of the
Home Office.
Mr. SPEAKER: Yes, one is here.
THE PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw) rose.
Mr. DONALD: I beg your pardon.
Mr. GRANT: In the South of Ireland a
number of very high officers of the Free State

Hear, hear)-and that Mr. Nixon

of making
victim of any
a
man, and
there is a feeling that Mr. Nixon has been

mentioned by the hon. Member

Colonel WOODS: I wish to repeat what I

in regard to the matter. Mr Nixon made
his first speech on the 4th January, I believe,
and after that an instruction was issued by
the Inspector-General that no political
speeches were to be made. I have seen that
circular, and a very reasonable one it is.
But I hold that it was a private speech made
in an Orange Lodge, and that Mr. Nixon did
not know that it would be published. Therefore, so far as that circular was concerned,
it was not a political speech in the ordinary
sense of the word. A misunderstanding exists
in that respect. If the Government can
prove that Mr. Nixon knew it was to be made
public, then I hold there is no excuse for Mr.
Nixon, and the Government is perfectly
justified in its action; but if he did not
know the speech was to be published, then
I hold it was a misunderstanding and a
mistake upon the part of the Government.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 18th March, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
OLD AGE PENSIONS AND WORKHOUSE
INMATES.
1 Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether old age pensioners who,
through sickness enter a Union Hospital,
have their pensions cancelled; if so, on what
conditions; and whether, after being discharged from hospital, a fresh claim has to
be made for their old age pensions?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): Under Section 3 (1) of
the Old Age Pension Act of 1919 a person who
has become an inmate of any workhouse or
other Poor-Law institution for the purpose of
obtaining medical or surgical treatment is
not disqualified for receiving or continuing to
receive an old age pension during a period of
three months from the date on which he or
she enters the workhouse or institution as
long as such medical or surgical treatment is
required. If the person remain in the institution for a longer period than three months,
then, under the provisions of the Section, he
or she would become disqualified, and would
have to make a fresh claim for pension on
leaving the institution.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman
if he does not consider that the old age pensioners have a grievance inasmuch as they
would have to re-apply for the pension? They
find it very difficult at any time to make the
claim, and I suppose they would find it even
more difficult to ask that it should be renewed.
Could the right hon. Gentleman, therefore,
not abolish, this procedure?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not think there
would be any great difficulty, because the
facts would already be before the Old Age
Pension Committee, and they could deal with
a case very rapidly.
Mr. DONALD: My object in putting the
question was to ascertain the existing law on
the matter, and I am quite satisfied with my
right hon. Friend's answer.
DEPARTMENTAL COMMITTEE ON
VALUATION.
2. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance whether the Departmental Committee on Valuation have concluded their
labours; if so, whether a final report will be
issued, and whether it is proposed to introduce legislation dealing with this matter?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am informed that the investigations of the Departmental Committee on
Valuation have been completed and that the
Committee now have under discussion the
terms of their final report.
Before the issue of that report it would be
premature to anticipate whether or not
legislation might be necessary or desirable.
EX-SERVICE MEN'S HOUSES IN
CLEEMISH ISLAND.
3. Mr. MILLER (for Mr. Cooper) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs if he is aware
that a very good scheme for ex-soldiers has
been carried out on Cleemish Island, County
Fermanagh, over a dozen houses having been
built and good farms acquired, but that no
means have been provided to enable these
men to get to their homes; and if he can
state what is the difficulty about providing
a right-of-way and a bridge to the island,
or how it is proposed to remedy this great
drawback to an otherwise excellent scheme.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The question of the
provision of holdings for ex-Servicemen
under Sections 1 to 3 of the Irish Land (Provision for Sailors and Soldiers) Act, 1919, is
one entirely for the Imperial Government,
and all such schemes under the Act are administered by the Land Purchase Commission (Northern Ireland).
It is understood, however, that that Department, which is an Imperial Department,
has already made provision for the establishment of a ferry to provide communication
between the Island and the mainland.
