ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Payment of Members of the Senate.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That in the opinion of this House, as and
from the beginning of the current Financial
Year, provision shall be made for the payment at the rate of £2 2s 0d per diem to
cach Member of the Senate who has subscribed to the necessary Oath and taken his
seat, in respect of incidental expenses and
expenses incurred in travelling from the
country to Belfast for attendance at meetings of the Senate or Committees, excluding
any Member who is for the time being in
receipt of a salary as an officer of the Senate
or a member of the Government; provided
that the total of such payments of £2 2s Od
per diem made to any Member of the Senate
shall not exceed the sum of eighty guineas
in any one year.
Mr. BARBOUR: I feel that it is not necessary for me to say very much to hon. Members of this House concerning this Resolution
Hon. Members will, of course, be aware that
those Members who have fulfilled the necessary conditions are entitled to receive in
respect of their expenses in the discharge or
their Parliamentary duties during the present
financial year the sum of £200, and it has
been considered only right that similar
arrangements should be made in the case of
Members in another place. The scheme of
payment, however, is not quite on the same
lines as is provided in the case of hon. Members of this House. Speaking generally, the
length of Sessions in the Senate is very much
shorter. Last year the actual days of sitting
in the Senate only numbered 33. And so it
has been considered that a daily rate, rather
than an annual sum, would better meet the
conditions obtaining in the case of Members of
that House. It has consequently been proposed to fix a payment of two guineas per day
in respect of incidental expenses, subject, however, to a maximum sum of eighty guineas
being paid to any Member in any one year;
and, in addition thereto, first-class railway
fare should be allowed in the case of Members
living outside Belfast who have not permanent
businesses or other offices in Belfast. The
Resolution also proposes to make this retrospective to the 1st April, 1923.
I would like to draw your attention to the
word
""
and ("and expenses incurred in

for "and" may be read "together with," so as

guineas does not include the expenses of
travelling to Belfast. The additional charge
which is expected to fall on public funds as a
result of this Resolution is estimated in one
year to amount to about £500. The expenditure in question is of a somewhat special
character, and so it has been deemed a more
appropriate way to bring this matter forward
by means of a Resolution rather than that it
should appear for the first time in the Estimates. I beg to move.

Mr. McGUFFIN: The principle underlying this resolution is, in my opinion, very
much similar to that which governed a

The proposal is, in my opinion, a democratic
measure. That may sound strange. It is
a democratic measure in so far as it would
be impossible for what we call democracythe working classes-to have representation
in the House without the financial support
contained in a similar proposal. There was
a time when it was not of much importance
what Member represented a constituency.
The only qualification that seemed necessary
at the time was that he had sufficient money,
and it did not matter what intellect or
integrity he had in connection with his
purpose as a Member of Parliament. But,
as the Franchise became extended, it became
inevitable that something of this sort would
have to be done. There was a time when
there was no Labour representation in the
House. It is not so long ago-about twentyfive years ago.
Up to 1832, when the great Enfranchisement Bill was introduced, there was no representation of the industrial classes, nor was
there any likelihood of there being any; but
when the franchise was extended it made a
way for Labour representation in the House,
with the almost inevitable consequence that
provision would have to be made for them.
I know there are many people in the community who would demur to the Government
supporting representation of that description,
but if there is no other means
by which Labour can be represented
than through the financial support
of this House I do not think it should
be a deterrent on this House to provide the
necessary money. The workers require representation, and if they have not the representation they are inclined to favour they
may be driven to other extremes, and to
adopt other shibboleths and other creeds
they have not hitherto accepted. As to the
need of a Second Chamber and its claim for
financial support, that is a very different
matter; but, after all, a Second Chamber
is absolutely necessary, because if I remember aright, when the Education Bill passed
through this House and was committed to
the Senate for revision, it came back a very
different Bill. I remember sitting beside my
right hon. Friend the Chairman of Committees (Mr. Moles), and we were just interchanging opinions as to the number of emendations and revisions that took place in connection with that Bill. If the Senate is
not necessary as a check upon extravagant
expenditure in this House, it is certainly
necessary as a means of revision of the indiscretions and mistakes that we frequently
make in this House. I do not know how far
those are chargeable upon the Law Officers
who are responsible for the Bills presented
here, but certainly it does not reflect much
credit on us as a House if we allow a Bill
to pass in such a shambling way that it has
to be returned to the House, and we scarcely
know it because of the number of emendations made.

Resolution reported:
"That it is expedient to amend the Loans
175 Loans Guarantee (Money)- HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Report.
Guarantee Acts, Northern Ireland, 1922 and
1923-
(i) by increasing from £3,500,000 to
£5,000,000 the limit on the aggregate capital
amount of the loans, the principal or interest of which may be guaranteed by the
Ministry of Finance thereunder; and
(ii) by extending to the 31st day of March,
1925, the period within which guarantees
may be given under the Loans Guarantee
Act, Northern Ireland, 1922;
and to charge on the Consolidated Fund of
Northern Ireland any moneys required for
fulfilling any such guarantees."
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That the House do agree with the Committee in the said resolution."
Mr. BARBOUR: When this Resolution
was originally brought before the House, it
was at a late hour, and I said I would be
happy to afford hon. Members some additional information, which. I thought they
would like to have, before the final voting
of this Resolution. The position at the
present time is that, under the Acts already
passed, the sum guaranteed amounts to
£3,340,500, and the balance available in
respect of guarantees under these Acts
at the present time is £159,500. The object of
this Resolution, which will form the basis
of a Bill to be brought in, would be to extend the limit on the aggregate capital
amount of the loans by the sum
of one and a half millions-(Mr. Donald :
"Hear, hear.")-making an aggregate amount
of £5,000,000. The second part of the
Resolution deals with the period during
which guarantees may be given. It is felt
very desirable to keep a close check on these
facilities, and to restrict the period of them
to the ensuing financial year. So it is proposed to make the period during which such
guarantees may be given terminate on 31st
March, 1925.
I should like also to explain, if I may, to
hon. Members the way in which these guarantees are given. It is not quite fully understood, I think, by members of the outside
public, however fully hon. Members may
understand it, that it is not the function of
the Government under this Act to advance
any money or even to arrange loans. It is
entirely the duty of whatever firm or group
of persons wishing to take advantage of this
Act to make their own arrangements with
their bankers or whatever business houses they
may be able to arrange with for the actual
advance to be made. All that the Government does under this Act is that when that
arrangement is made, if the Committee
appointed to deal with these guarantees
consider the security offered is ample, and
that the terms of the loan are reasonable,
they then give their guarantee both as to
principal and interest to the banker or other
financial house that actually makes the loan.
These facilities cannot be regarded in any
sense of the word as a grant or subsidy: they
are merely lending the State credit to the
trader or firm who is able to arrange his
own loan. Seeing that this Committee are
dealing with the credit of the community,
they see that the security offered is of such
a character that it is only by a very remote
chance that any burden may ultimately fall
upon the Exchequer; in fact, some hon.
Members or members of the outside public
might possibly think that the conditions
which this Committee imposed are of too
onerous a character, or are conditions such
as might possibly restrict the extent to which
advantage might be taken of the facilities
offered under this Act; but, of course, the
reply to that is, that in spite of those conditions and in spite of the ample security
demanded, we have come to the House the
second time, and we have now come to the
House the third time, to have the amount
of the sum which we may guarantee increased. Therefore, it is undoubtedly proving
of very great advantage to those firms who
take advantage of it; and in reply to a
Question in the House the other day information was given as to the number of men who
have been employed directly in consequence
of the facilities given under the previous
Acts. I beg to move.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I rise merely to ask a
question. Are these guarantees given only
in connection with what is called capital
expenditure?
Mr. POLLOCK: Yes.
Mr. McGUFFIN: As expendable upon new
work Would reconditioning a ship come
within this?
Mr. DONALD: Yes.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Would reconditioning a
ship come within it the same as if a ship
was being built?
Mr. POLLOCK: The reconditioning of a
ship might or might not employ capital expenditure. If a ship were cut in two and a
hundred feet put into her length the presumption is that that. would be capital expenditure, but if it was simply putting her
into her original condition I would say that
that was not capital expenditure but reinstatement.
Mr. McGUFFIN: That was the point upon
which I wished to have some enlightenment.
There is a point also as to how the Government proceeds with regard to the allocation
of these guarantees. Are they advised in
respect of them? Is there an Advisory Committee in connection with this? We have

t

never heard their names mentioned in this
House. To what extent are the Government
advised by them? This matter should be
mentioned to give us at least sufficient confidence in the procedure of the Government
to know that it is being gone about in a
businesslike way. I rather, regret the limitations that are adopted in regard to these
guarantees. There is a sense in which probably it will conduce to greater employment,
particularly in shipbuilding, but there are
other industries which, I think, might be

Mr. POLLOCK: Hear, hear.
Mr. McGUFFIN: The only difficulty is in
securing the necessary guarantee as to the
nature of the thing and being able to place
before the Government sufficient assets to

should be expanded in such a way as to
encourage operations in other sections of industry. That is all I have got to say regarding the matter. I think that up to the
moment good has attended the scheme, and
that shipbuilding might be in a more depressed condition just now if it were not for
the aid that has been given through the
Government. I only hope it will be possible
for the Government to extend this so as to
enable other industries to come in and take
advantage of this rather novel departure.
Mr. DONALD: It is not often, at least
not always, I find myself in agreement with
the Government; but in this case I congratulate them in extending this loans guarantee
money. My hon. Friend (Mr. McGuffin) referred to reconditioning. The word "reconditioning" has another meaning, and applied
to where a ship was used during the war for
a different purpose from that originally intended was put back into her former shape
and form. This money could not be
expended for that purpose; but, as my
right hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) said, if
a ship was to be cut in two and
extended this money could then be expended.
I can remember when this matter was first
discussed in this House, that I tried to
approach it from different angles. Some
people thought I was stupid or silly or something, or that I was advocating the subsidising of industries. There was nothing further
from my mind. All I was wanting was that
this House should adopt the attitude that
has been adopted for a very long time by the
Imperial authorities. Under the Trades Facilities Act very large sums of money were
granted for the extension of works. Take
for instance London. Lord Pirrie borrowed
a very large sum of money under this Imperial Act and extended his works. Therefore
I was anxious that this money should apply
sooner than it did to the extension and development of our industries here, as far as
possible, to relieve unemployment.
I agree
with this sum-it is not very large in comparison with the amount under the extension
of the Act in the Imperial House. Even the
present Government is going further than
the old Government under Mr. Baldwin.
What is the idea at the back of the minds
of the Government, no matter who they may
be, in taking this better way of relieving
unemployment? Is it not that the people
who get the employment may produce something for the money spent? That is really
the object or principle underlying this Guarantee Loan. That is the principle I advocated and have advocated for many years.
There is nothing so demoralising to any man
as to have to go and get money for nothing.
I wish that our Government could develop
within their own scope some scheme of public utility on which money could be spent
and that a larger number of our people
would get into employment.
I regret to see in the papers that we are
likely to have trouble in the shipbuilding
industry. That will not tend to help the
question If anybody has a grievance in the
country, it is the people who work in the
shipyards with regard to the amount of wages
they receive. They have a just grievance.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) Men who
served for seven, six, or five years are working for a pound a week less than men who
never served an hour. That is a most unfair
stato of affairs in this country as well as in
Great Britain. I would like to ask my right
hon. Friend has the money in hand all been
taken out under this loan? He need not
reply just now. I would ask him to take a
note of it-how much we have in hands, and
what hope does he hold out for the expending
of this money. I hope he will be able to give
us some idea, and our congratulations should
go out to the different Departments who are
in charge of this money. They are doing a
very useful work. The Chairman gave me
an idea that the Government hoped to get
more money in hands. I would like to know
how much they have in hands, and what hope
they hold out of these captains of industry
or shipowners taking out this money.
I am especially interested in the shipbuilding industry. There is nothing that will
relieve the situation more than the building
of ships. So far as I know in this country
there is nothing will take a greater number
of people off the streets. And may
just appeal on behalf of those
the streets. The largest number
of people on the streets are people from the
shipbuilding industry. They are all highlyskilled men, and they are feeling it very hard.
If my right hon. Friend could give any hope
I
on
179 Loans Guarantee (Money)—

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Report.
[Mr. Donald]
that in the near future, as a result of this
money going through the House, more money
would be taken out by the shipowner and
shipbuilder, then there will be more hope
for these men on the streets, who are at
present living on a few shillings a week, far
below the amount the unemployed have received in Great Britain. We regret that.
It is not the fault of the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews). I have even thought
that he overstepped his duty; but he has
such a large heart, that he has stretched the
law to the very last in order to meet the
cost, seeing that other people would not come
along and do their duty. These people have
at their disposal a mere few shillings. The
maximum that can be paid-I have said it
before in this House-to a married man
with four or five children is 25 shillings a
week. It may be said that that does not
come under this, but it does in this way,
that we are doing great service to our
people if we are going to get this large
sum of money whereby these employers and
others may extend their works and also that
new works may be taken in hand to give
employment to our people. I congratulate
the Government.
Mr. POLLOCK: I thought that I had made
it very clear in my statement on the Address
in reply to His Majesty's Gracious Speech
that the Loans Guarantee was not limited to
shipbuilding, and while we have made every
effort to induce shipowners to take advantage
of it we had hoped that it would have been
utilised to a larger extent. May I repeat
what I said?
As I have said, we have offered every
inducement, through the machinery of the
Loans Guarantee Act, to attract shipowners
to Belfast. Up to the present we have
found this a very potent influence in procuring work for our yards, and but for its
operations, I should think that our shipyards at the present moment would be
almost idle. I am glad to say that there
is some hope at the present moment that
several orders for large steamers may
shortly find their way to Belfast. This
will, I hope, help to relieve some of the
unemployment which at present exists.
But I wish to make it abundantly clear
to the House, and particularly to the
country, that our Loans Guarantee Act is
not limited to shipbuilding. It has been
found to apply in a large measure to the
shipbuilding industry simply for the reason
that a greater measure of unemployment
existed in shipbuilding, but there is no
reason why in a matter of capital expenditure every other industry. or any industry,
in the country may not make use of it, and
I am sure the Government will be prepared
to encourage it, assuming, of course, that
the claims are legitimate and the security
definite.
I had hoped, by giving publicity to that,
that possibly those who had contemplated
capital expenditure might be led to enlarge
their views by the encouragement given
through the machinery of the Loans Guarantee. I think my hon. Friend behind me (Mr.
Barbour) informed the House just now that
the amounts actually guaranteed up to the
present were £3,350,000, leaving a balance, if
this resolution is passed, of £1,650,000 to be
utilised in further guarantee schemes that
may arise, and we hope will arise. All these
questions come before an Advisory Committee.
It is merely an advisory body. The ultimate
responsibility rests with me as Minister of
Finance, and I cannot divorce myself from
that responsibility. It is the duty of the
Advisory Committee to investigate thoroughly
the whole character of the enterprise which
is submitted to them in connection with the
guarantee. The names of these gentlemen,
who are well known, are Mr. H. L. Garrett,
head of Dunville & Co., Mr. Hardy, manager
of the Provincial Bank, who approaches this
subject from the point of view of the banker.
and Mr. J. H. Stirling, a director of the York
Street Spinning Company. They advise the
Ministry of Finance with regard to the security that is offered in connection with each
individual submission.
I would repeat, before I sit down, that I
hope it will be more widely known that there
is no limitation in regard to the character of
the industry coming under the head of the
Loans Guarantee Act. It is purely a matter
of the security offered, and that security must
be reasonable. Subject to that, the operation
of the Act can be extended ad infinitum.

There is a matter I should like to explain

31st December, 1922. The grant to the Council
of Law Reporting has already been before

Reporting that the grant shall be payable
half-yearly in advance and represents payment in respect of the six months ending
the 30th June, 1924. So that while the

it so happens that by reason of the half

Mr. McGUFFIN: There is just one question

The CHAIRMAN: I think the hon. Gentleman will see that he is travelling from the
exact purpose and the specific motion before
the Committee, which is that a given sum

Mr. BARBOUR: Possibly the word used
does not convey to hon. Members the exact
nature of the services rendered under this
Vote. We have to go back prior to the 1920
Act when there was a Council of Law Reporting established in Dublin. The reporting
actually has to be done by a Barrister with
considerable legal knowledge. It is not
merely to provide a verbatim report of
ordinary cases that come before the Courts.
As hon. Members of this Committee will
realise, a great deal of our administration
of justice is founded on what we call Case
Law. I speak before hon. Members who are
more familiar with that than I am, but it is
essential in any case which creates a precedent, or in any case of great public importance, that a proper record of that case should
be prepared and preserved. It is the duty of
this Council of Law Reporting to see that
such a record is made and prepared. The
records are then printed and bound and are
available for Members of the legal profession
and for our own officials here who require to
make reference to them from time to time.
It is an absolutely necessary work in the
interests of the conduct of justice.

CLASS II, No. 8.
CRIMINAL INJURIES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£10 be granted to His Majesty to defray
the charges which will come in course of
payment during the year ending 31st March,
1924, to provide recoupment to Local
Authorities in Northern Ireland in respect
of payments made by them on foot of
Criminal Injury Decrees.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Hon. Members will
recollect that as a result of the Prime
Minister's efforts a grant was obtained from
the Imperial
Government of £1,500,000
towards the relief of Local Authorities
in respect of malicious injuries which
had been committeed between June,
1920, and January, 1922. Unfortunately,
these malicious injuries did not cease
after that date, and a great many
injuries took place subsequent to January,
1922, with the result that further representations were made by the Prime
Minister to the Imperial Government. As a
result a further grant of £500,000 has been
obtained towards injuries which had been
incurred between June, 1922, and October,
1922, making in all a total sum of Two Million
pounds. Relief has been granted to Local
Authorities to the extent of 60 per cent. of
the amounts paid by them in respect of
these injuries up to January, 1922, and the
Government asked the authority of this House
to make a similar grant of 60 per cent. to
the Local Authorities in respect of injuries
occurring between January, 1923, and October,
1922, and utilise the balance which has been
left over, amounting to £460,000, in payment
of the 60 per cent. paid for the injuries incurred prior to January, 1922. I beg to move.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I would just like to say
that the Government deserve the heartiest
congratulations for the way in which they
managed to relieve the ratepayers in regard
to matters that would otherwise have gone
against them. I want to offer my hearty
congratulations to the Government for the
successful way in which they dealt with the
matter.
Mr. GRANT: I should like to ask a

CLASS III. No. 4.
UNEMPLOYMENT GRANTS.
Motion made, and Question proposed:-
That a supplementary sum not exceeding
£125,000 be granted to His Majesty to defray the charge which will come in course of
payment during the year ending 31st March,
1924, for grants to Local Authorities. &c.,
in Northern Ireland for assistance in
carrying out approved schemes to relieve
unemployment.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): It will be within the recollection of the House that on the 30th March,
1922, through the influence of the Prime
Minister of Northern Ireland, we obtained a
promise of £500,000 from the Imperial Government for relief works in the city of Belfast
and neighbourhood. This sum, however, is
not to mature. The Colwyn Committee
considered the matter, and, for some reason
or other, which I have never been able to
fully understand, they reduced the amount
to £300,000. My right hon. Friend the
Leader of this House (Mr. Pollock) has
counselled that in our criticisms of this
particular act of the Colwyn Committee we
should be moderate, and, as I always appreciate his wisdom and desire to follow his
advice, all that I will say in this connection
is that because faith has been broken with
us I see no reason why we should go back
on those to whom we have made definite
promises. Believing that the whole £500,000
would be available we entered into arrangements with our local authorities and public
bodies that we would give grants in connection with approved schemes in order to provide
employment for as many of our people as
possible up to the full total of £500,000.

The amount which you are asked to vote
now is £125,000, and I am glad to be able
to say that £44,000 of that will be returned
to our Treasury by the Imperial Government before the end of the present financial
year. My hon. Friend the Member for Derry
City and County (Sir Robert Anderson) said
that he hoped that in the future some vote
would be available for the whole Six County
area, and that no part of the Six County area
would be left out. As a country Member
myself I naturally hold the same views, and
in the future any sum voted will be voted
and applied for the relief of unemployment
right over the Six Counties. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). But as regards this particular
Vote that is not possible, because it is all
required, as I think I have already said, to
discharge the liabilities which face us at the
moment. There was one other point raised
by my hon. Friend the Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Donald) to which in this connection I would like to refer. He does not seem
to be altogether satisfied with regard to the
recruitment of labour for these relief schemes
within the city of Belfast, and I understood
him to say something to the effect that he
would like the green card system done away
with altogether.
Mr. DONALD: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: Or in other words that
there should be a free market for labour.
Well, if a free market-
Mr. DONALD: Will my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Andrews) excuse me for a moment?
My reason for making that statement was in

"In view of the special conditions consequent on the political situation in
Belfast and neighbourhood, the British

Other conditions were laid down. It was
to be expended upon certain people, and at
the very beginning I took exception to that
as a trade unionist, because all members are
free and should not be bound to any agreement by any people, no matter how great
their authority. They should be free agents
to seek employment anywhere. That is the
situation that exists to-day. My right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) or his Government,
even in these most distressing times, cannot
prevent any man from coming across from
Scotland or England and obtaining employment. Why? Because we laid it down
distinctly in our rules that any member is

That is why I took exception to any Government or Governments, and there are three
involved in this transaction. When it was

What is in the green card? My right hon.
Friend knows perfectly well the trouble that

People came to me and said: "You only want

I understand that the grant of £500,000

existed, and the conditions that then existed

We had a good claim to the money, but that
is no reflection on the administration of the
Department of the right hon. Gentleman
opposite (Mr. Andrews). I would be the
last to listen to that, and for no other reason
than this. As the Member for East Belfast
(Mr. Donald) remarked, we have a higher
proportion of unemployed here than they
have across the water, so that the problem
here was all the greater on that account.
But in addition to that the Minister of Labour
was working under circumstances that had
never obtained in Great Britain. The hon.
Member for East Belfast objects to the apportionment of this money on a religious basis.
We all dislike that very much. Anyone who
has ever heard me speak on the matter knows
how strongly I object to the principle of
sectarianism in any department, but, after
all, we might have had worse results if we
had not resorted to this method, because we
have a community here that is divided in
religion in such a way that it would probably
have aroused suspicion if the money had not
been allocated in this way. When it was
definitely laid down that one-third of the
money should go to one section, and twothirds to the other section, it opened up a
course on which the Minister of Labour could
proceed without being suspect, and I believe
he would feel immensely relieved of responsibility on that account.
With regard to the green cards, I have
the impression that they were absolutely
necessary in order to secure justice. The
green card provided that the man who
was longest out of work should have the first
claim, or that the man who had the largest
family should have a prior claim to a man
who had a smaller family, and the justice
of that cannot be challenged. In so far as
the green cards have operated to bring
about that result I think they have done
great service. The unfortunate thing is that
the Ministry of Labour is under suspicion
in regard to that matter, but the right hon.
Gentleman's Department is not alone in that.
All Departments are subject to suspicion in
connection with their administration, but
I have always had the pleasure of being able
to explain any alleged mal-administration in
the Ministry of Labour. If I had known
before that I was going to speak on this
subject I could have brought several letters,
including two received this morning, saying
the way this particular Department had been
administered was a crying shame, and that
men who had been out of work for two
years and two and a half years had not
been able to get a job, while other men had
got work inside six weeks. Of course, that
would have to be substantiated, and if 1
was brought face to face with these individuals I have not yet, but I probably will
be I would ask them for their proof, and
when it was given to me I would send it
to the right hon. Gentleman (Mr. Andrews).
My own impression is that it is the ordinary
clap-trap that is going about in order to
discredit the Government and this department in particular.
I have not found that there is any injustice
in the administration of the Ministry of
Labour. My view is that what could be
done has been done and is being done, and
I admire the attitude of the Government in
determining to make good the deficiency
occasioned by the withholding of part of
the grant by the Colwyn Committee. They
were afraid to pay in advance but now they
are fulfilling their obligations and we hope
that in the near future the need for such
grants will disappear. I am glad to learn
of the improvement in the Textile industry
and that workers are being absorbed who
have been unemployed for very many weeks,
and that others are in full employment who
have for a long time been on short time.
That is very encouraging and all to the good,
but so far as the male element of the unemployed is concerned I am afraid the situation has not very much improved. However,
with the aid of the loan facilities that have
been under discussion to-day, I think better
times are in store. It has been suggested
that in the near future our shipbuilding
yards will in all probability be working at
greater speed. If that could be brought
about perhaps the time will come when unemployment will be reduced to such a state
that the income and the expenditure will
balance. When that comes about we will
have every reason to congratulate ourselves
However that may be, there is one thing

under the guidance and direction of the

that has placed him above suspicion in
regard to his motives and intentions. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).

Mr. ANDREWS: There are just one
two misunderstandings that I would like to
clear out of the way. My hon. Friend, the
Member for North Belfast (Mr. Grant) has
asked me how much of the £500,000 has

will have been spent on the 31st March next.
I think my hon. Friend, the Member for
East Belfast (Mr. Donald)-I am sorry he is
not in the House-is under a misapprehension.
In the first instance, when the £500,000 was
given, no time limit was specified. No time
limit was fixed during the first year, but
during the second year a letter was received
by our Ministry of Finance to the effect that
the money might not be re-voted after the
end of the then current year, which is the
present current year. That was the first
intimation that this Government got that
the money would not be available at any time
that it was required. When I heard that I
naturally endeavoured to impress upon the
local authorities and public bodies, more
forcibly even than I had done up till then,
the necessity of absorbing as much of the
£500,000 as possible during the present
financial year. The reason I said and repeat
that the decision of the Colwyn Committee
was unfair is that we will not receive the
amount actually spent in the current financial
year. In other words, if the Treasury letter
had been acted on, we would have received
about £400,000, while under the award we
will receive only £300,000, so that I feel I
was justified in saying all that I said in this
connection. I did not want to speak more
strongly, because the Colwyn Committee are
still sitting, and we are not without hope
that what we have lost in the merry-gorounds we may pick up in the swing-boats.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
There is one other 'matter to which I
would like to refer. Hon. Members have
alluded to the fact that this grant was given
on the distinct understanding that one-third
of it would be devoted to the employment of
Catholics, and that two-thirds would be devoted to the employment of Protestants.
That has been objected to, but no one has
ever said that it was not a fair proportion,
and if hon. Members will carry their minds
back to the conditions that existed then I
believe they will come to the conclusion that
no other scheme would have been workable,
or could possibly have been carried out.

direction of making the issuing of them more

charge which will come in course of payment

Mr. ARCHDALE: This token Vote of £10
is for the purpose of putting up erections and
fitting up buildings in the Six Counties
corresponding to those of Southern Ireland.
The House has already agreed to these sums
on the Works Estimate for the year. The
House agreed to the new works, alterations
and additions in connection with the Plant
Breeding and Poultry Research, in the Greenmount Agricultural College at Antrim, and
in the North-West Institute at Strabane.
Since then the Colwyn Committee has estimated that £400,000 is the amount that we
should receive against the sums claimed for.
The object of the Vote now before the House
is to place this on the Agricultural Vote and
to take it off the Works Vote. We will recoup it from the £400,000 which has been
granted to us, and carry out the work already
agreed upon. The Plant Breeding Division
gets £4,000, and the Poultry Research
Division £2,450. We have got to increase
that a little, because we have found there is
a good deal more to do at Stormont in connection with our Poultry Research Station
than we anticipated. It is only the estimated
amount that we have put down for this
financial year. In regard to the North-West
Institute at Strabane, very little can be done
this year, and we have only put down the
sum of £400 opposite it. So far as the Greenmount Agricultural College is concerned, we
are pressing on as hard as we can, because
we have candidates ready and pupils applying
for the scholarships available in that place.
I beg to move,

I would like to bring before the House. During

factor in this matter, and I trust the right
hon. Gentleman will soon be able to give us
a statement reassuring farmers especially in
the matter of flax growing. (Hon. Members:

Mr. ARCHDALE: I might say something
on the subject now, because there seems to
be a misapprehension amongst hon. Members
and the public that the Ministry of Agriculture was not taking into account anything
about flax. The papers have printed a number
of letters on the subject which seem to indicate that nothing was being done. In the
autumn of last year we were very much
perplexed about the whole matter. We did
not believe that farmers, owing to the price
they got for flax during the past year, were
inclined to sow as much as they could or
should sow. We got together a conference
of the leading farmers, flax growers and linen
merchants. We had also representatives of
the spinners at the conference, which was
held in the Ministry. The result of that was
rather negative, I am afraid, because the
farmers would not consent to grow flax unless
they could get a fixed price from the spinners.
The latter would not give that. Trade was
very bad at the time, and the whole thing
practically fell through. We still bore it in
mind, and when trade began to revive we
thought it would be a good thing to have
another meeting. This very afternoon there
is a meeting being held in the Ministry of

I noticed the other day that other gentlemen in the papers, and also hon. Members.
in the House were abusing the Northern
Government for not looking ahead a
bit and saying we never acted on
our own initiative. As a matter of
fact the Ministry of Agriculture has
brought in Bills on its own initiative.
There is the Licensing of Bulls Bill, and also
the Scutch Mills Bill, for which there was
a craving for a number of years. The
English authorities have been writing to us
to know if we can help them in any way to
get such a Bill passed in England. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear). The Scotch farmers
have been trying to do the same. The
Southern Government intend bringing in
such a Bill, and they have also heard that
we are going to bring in a Bill for the
better preparation and sale of eggs for the
English markets. They are writing to us to
know what we have done on the subject, and
asking will we help them to bring in such
a Bill of their own. I am glad to say we
have, as I have said before, a very sympathetic Finance Minister. We have got
from him a contribution this year of £14,900
to spend. We hope to do so by helping on
agricultural education, more for reproductive
purposes, as the hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. McGuffin) suggested. There are
129,000 farms, most of them small, in
Northern Ireland, and at present there is
only one instructor in each county. We are
appointing a number of other instructors to
help on the work, and attention has been
called to what we propose to do.
I do not wish to occupy the House too
long, but I might just run quickly through
what we intend to do. We intend to encourage cow-testing. There are 300,000 cows in
Northern Ireland. In 1921 there were only
six cow-testing associations. In 1923 there
were seventeen, and we hope that in a short
time there will be a great number more, and
we propose to do everything we can to help
towards that end. At present each member
pays 3/- a cow. We are reducing the price.
The number of cows required for a COWtesting association was 200; we are reducing
that number to 150. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) We are also giving £40 a year towards
the salary of a supervisor, because you
must have a competent supervisor in each
cow-testing association so that the records may
be kept correctly. The amount which would
be brought to the country if the produce
of the cows were increased from about 400,
which it is at present, to about 600 or 700
gallons a year each would be over £3,000,000.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That is one
thing which I think ought to be encouraged to the fullest extent.
We also are providing prizes for dairy
COWS. We are buying 30 dairy-bred bulls for
small farmers, and are going to re-sell them
to the dairy associations at about one-third
of their price. Then we are providing eight
pure-bred dairy shorthorns for pedigree
breeders, so that the supply of bulls for the
pure-bred people can be bred from the dairybred bulls to increase the marketing power
of their animals. Harking back for a
minute to the question of bull-licensing I
may say that there was a great deal of talk
when that Bill was passed to the effect that
people would not send their bulls in to be
registered. As a matter of fact we have
10,000 bulls registered in Northern Ireland.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) We tried,
through the police in the Six Counties, to
find what owners were holding bulls that had
not been licensed. There are less than thirty
in the whole Six Counties. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) Therefore, the predictions of
those men, who made such a tremendous fuss,
and claimed that we were only working for
the benefit of officials, are rather upset.

perity of the linen trade in this city and in

House will agree with me that my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Archdale) is very much to be

I understand, with reference to the growing

afternoon, and, of course, we are unable to

right hon. Friend at the very first opportunity

SUPPLEMENTARY ESTIMATES, 1923-1924.
CLASS I, No. 1.
HOUSES OF PARLIAMENT.
Motion made and Question proposed:

That a supplementary sum not exceeding Ten Pounds be granted to his Majesty
to defray the charge which will come in
course of payment during the year ending
on the 31st of March, 1924, for the salaries
and expenses of the Senate and the House
of Commons."
THE PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): It is not necessary for me to do anything but briefly to remind hon. Members of the discussion which
took place yesterday on the Resolution dealing
with this same matter. It authorises the
payment to members of the Senate, other
than members who are for the time being in
receipt of salaries as officers of the Senate or
members of the Government, in respect of
incidental expenses at the rate of two guineas
per day for each attendance at meetings of
the Senate or Committees, and in addition,
the expenses incurred in travelling from the
country to Belfast for such attendance, subject to a maximum of eighty guineas in any
one year in respect of such payments of two
guineas per day. It is necessary now by
means of this Supplementary Estimate to
provide the necessary funds to enable these
payments to be made, and the total amount
involved, viz., £500, is made up of £400 for
incidental expenses and £100 for travelling
expenses. This Estimate has been based on
the claims which have been submitted by
members of the Senate in respect of the current year. I beg to move.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I suppose there is no use
in protesting against this Vote as it is set
forth here, but I wish to reiterate my protest against travelling expenses being paid in
respect of this matter. The Resolution, I
admit, was accepted by the House yesterday, but we refrained from a division on the
matter not because we had changed our
minds with respect to it, but rather because
we felt that we were quite unequal to a division and that we would appear a very paltry
vote in the Division Lobby. The principle is
of a vicious nature, because when salaries
were fixed for hon. Members of this House it
was on the understanding that the £200 was
to cover the cost of travelling and other incidentals; but here you are establishing the
principle, apart entirely from the amount of
money you are voting with respect to attendance at the House, of covering travelling expenses. In my mind it is anomalous and
should not be persisted in. I do not say I
will divide the Committee now, but I wish to
reiterate my protest against travelling expenses being paid to Senators. I would have
preferred that they should be paid a lump
sum. I see no reason why hon. Members of
this House, who have to journey from Londonderry and other remote districts of the Six
County area, should not be reimbursed in a
similar way. I enter my protest against it,
and with that I am satisfied.
Question put, and agreed to.
CLASS I. No. 3.
MINISTRY OF FINANCE.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a supplementary sum not exceeding Ten Pounds be granted to his Majesty
to defray the charge which will come in
course of payment during the year ending
on the 31st of March, 1924, for the Salaries
and Expenses of the Ministry of Finance,
including Revenue Services, Valuation,
Registration, Loan Services, Public Works,
Charity Funds, Stationery Office, Teachers'
Pensions, Civil Service Commission, Ulster
Savings, Loans Guarantee Act (N.I.), 1922,
and Collection of Land Purchase Annuities,
and Tithe Rent Charges..
Mr. BARBOUR: Hon. Members will observe that the gross total of this Supplementary Vote amounts to £8,960, and of this
sum approximately £8,000 represents expenditure incurred in connection with the
additional staff which it has been found
necessary to recruit during the current year.

Mr. BARBOUR: I would call attention, in

I can best illustrate the abnormal works
services by referring to some of the more
important schemes in detail. In the first
place, the Housing Schemes under the provisions of the Irish Land (Provision for
Sailors and Soldiers) Act, 1919, which are
undertaken on behalf of the Irish Land
Trust, and necessitate the employment of a
large number of technical officers, are now
being vigorously pushed forward. A sum of
£5,500 is included as a receipt from the
Imperial Government in respect of the
administration of this service. Again, a
considerable volume of work has arisen in the
course of the current year in consequence of
our taking over the maintenance and repair
of coastguard stations, the setting up of
Customs posts on the Border, the search for
and fitting up of new accommodation for
Government Offices both Imperial and
Northern Ireland-all carried out as an
agency service for the Imperial Office of
Works.
Other services which do not fall within
the category of agency services are the large
undertaking at Stranmillis, where a Training
College and Hostel is in course of construction for the accommodation of teachers in
training. I should like to say in connection
with this that the first instalment was
opened about ten days ago, and about ninety
lady teachers are in the course of training
there. If hon. Members who have time would
walk down there they would be greatly ininterested in and much gratified by the appropriate and comfortable quarters which have
A considerable amount of preliminary work

In the current year considerable progress
has been made in connection with building
construction at various Institutions of
the Ministry of Agriculture-viz.:
Plant Breeding Station and Poultry Station
at Stormont have been completed, while
considerable progress has been made in
connection with the adaptation of Greenmount Agricultural College, work which will
be completed in the course of the coming
year. The plans have been prepared for the
erection of labourers' cottages and farm
buildings, &c., at the North-West Institute,
Strabane, work which also will be completed
in the forthcoming year.
A site has been procured and the necessary
demolition work carried out in connection
with the erection of a Central Labour Exchange in Belfast, and the building construction is about to be commenced.
Then further work has arisen in connection
with the proposed reconstruction of the new
Constabulary Barracks accommodation; and,
as I mentioned to hon. Members a couple of
days ago, it is proposed to expend a very
considerable sum of money during the coming
year in connection with the improvement of
existing barracks and construction of new
barracks. All this work, which I hope will
be completed before very long, is of a temporary character, and so to deal with it a
temporary staff has been engaged in order to
carry out this important work.
Then the continuance of the Special
Constabulary force also imposes a considerable amount of work upon the Works
Branch. This actual construction work is
reflected in directions cther than mere
technical staff. It has necessitated not only
the strengthening of the administrative side
of the Works Department, but also the
administrative and executive branches of
the Ministry such as the Accounts Branch,
the Establishment Branch, and, in particular, the Typing Branch. Thus it has
been found necessary to place the Works
Branch of the Ministry under an officer
of principal grade, which explains the
substitution of a post of principal
for one of superintending officer. A
slight increase has also been necessary in the
staff of the Legal Branch occasioned by the
development of the legal work of the Department to cope with Income Tax appeals,

estimates are submitted to the House we have
no opportunity of testing the necessities of
the case. I read the other day, and was
somewhat amazed to read it, that, in connection with the estimates submitted to the Imperial House of Commons for the last 25

been indulged in, and all the criticism, they

Twenty-five years' criticism never resulted in

pound. I do not know that we are better cir
cumstanced here. It is certainly no reflection
on us at any rate if we do not succeed in an

All I can say is that the hon. Gentlemen
who used to insist on economy on the part of
this House are not at present here. I was
not too insistent on that matter. I never
gave them very much trouble: I trusted
them that they would not exceed the limitations that were necessary. I have heard marvellous eloquence indulged in here in this

being observed in this matter

Section 34 of the Government of Ireland Act.
The incidence of this charge falls finally on
the United Kingdom Consolidated Fund, and
the terms of the Act necessitate the voting
of the money by the Parliament of Northern
Ireland. The money, being placed in the
Northern Exchequer by the Imperial
Treasury, must be voted out of the Northern
Exchequer before the London Office of Works
or the Ministry itself-that is our Own
Ministry-acting for that Office, can
be placed in funds for the purpose
carrying out the service. Not only must this
accounting procedure be followed in the case
of moneys required for the actual materials:
etc., used in the building operations, but also
the staff and other administrative expenses of both the London Office of Works and the
Ministry of Finance, acting on their behalf,
have similarly to be made available by the
same procedure. I do not think we need
spend too much time criticising the procedure. We may focus our attention on its
effect on our own Exchequer, but, first of all,
the amount of expenditure has to be proved.
As soon as that is done the Imperial Government pays the money into our Northern

CLASS 1. No. 13.
REFUGEES' COMPENSATION.
Motion made and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £18,036 be
granted to his Majesty to defray the charges
that will come in course of payment during
the year ending 31st March, 1924, to refund
certain expenditure incurred by the Imperial
Government in connection with the payment
of compensation to refugees."
Mr. BARBOUR: The details furnished in
this estimate are self explanatory and will
hardly require further elucidation on my
part. But their ramifications may interest
hon. Members and so I propose to explain
the situation to them. As hon. Members are
doubtless aware, the Imperial Government
set up in London an Irish Grants Relief
Committee in order that temporary assistance by way of grant or loan could be made
to Southern loyalists who had been driven
from their homes or who had lost their entire belongings as a result of the disturbances
of recent years. They came to an arrangement with the Free State under which that
Government would repay to the Imperial
Government any moneys so granted or advanced. At the same time it was found that
a very small number of persons who had
hitherto been resident in Northern Ireland
had also sought refugee in England as a
result of the disturbed conditions prevailing
here. The amount of money expended in
order to grant the necessary assistance to
those from Northern Ireland was £385, and
for this the Government, subject to the
decision of this House, agreed to accept
liability.
That more or less established a principle
that the responsible Government of an area
from which people had to fly were liable for
the necessary assistance that had to be given
to these people when they sought refuge elsewhere. At the same time that this request
for repayment of this sum was made by the
British Government they coupled with it a
request that Northern Ireland should refund
to the Imperial Exchequer a further sum of
£17,651, which had been expended by the
Free State in the relief of residents of
Northern Ireland who at the time of the disturbances here sought refuge in the Free State.
These payments were all made, the vouchers
for them were duly submitted to the Imperial Government, and a statement prepared.
The Imperial Government checked it carefully, and they came to the conclusion that
this request of the Irish Free State to be
reimbursed to this extent was a reasonable
request. The Imperial Government,
believe, made payment of it and proposed
that it should be deducted from our residuary share, and so it is right, if this Committee approves, that this amount should
be voted out of our funds.

At the same time, hon. Members will be
aware, a Relief Committee was set up in
Northern Ireland to deal with cases which
were somewhat similar, the only difference
being that in England and in the Free
State the relief was granted to refugees from
a territory outside the Free State or outside England. The greatest amount of distress in Belfast was caused by people being
displaced, but still remaining within the
area of Northern Ireland. Still relief had
to be granted in Northern Ireland to the
people who sought refuge there coming from
the Free State, and so a counter-claim will
be prepared, and it will be submitted to the
Free State or to the Imperial Government,
for the amount of money expended by our
Relief Grants Committee which was set up
in Northern Ireland. Unfortunately details
are not ready to be submitted to the Government within the present financial year, and
so I am not able to inform the Committee as
to what the amount of that claim may
possibly be, but the preparation of it is being
pressed on, and as soon as it is ready it will
be submitted in due course.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Will that claim be made
through the Imperial Government on our behalf, or will we have to deal directly with
the Free State in this matter?
Mr. BARBOUR: The question of whether
we should present our claim to the Imperial
Government and ask them to collect it from
the Free State is really a matter for a higher
authority than myself, but I think we might
be guided by the fact that the Free State
claim on us was presented through the
Imperial Government. I beg to move.
Mr. DONALD: I only wish to offer a few
observations with regard to this matter. I
have the greatest sympathy with the object
for which this money is required, but I
think we are entitled to a little more explanation. What assurance have we that this
money really was spent? Further, dealing
with the first part before I come to the
counter-claim, at the time the Relief Grants
Committee was set up by the Imperial authorities I took very strong exception to Ulster
Supply-
Committee
•
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Donald]
being excluded. I thought we had a better
case than the Free State, and here let me pay
a tribute to the right hon. Gentleman the
Chief Whip (Captain Dixon). (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). Lord Carson and others took
up this question, but we were never able to
impress the Imperial authorities far enough
to include us. Why should not we have been
included in the participation in these grants?
I was a member of the Committee, and I
felt that we were really ignored, that we
were doing work voluntarily for the people
who had to fly and who were being exterminated from the Free State. They came in
at our different railways here, and the
Committee appointed people to meet them to
see that they got decent treatment when they
came to a more peaceful country. I think we
were most unjustly treated with regard to this
money, and I am sorry my right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) had not in his counter-claim
then. It is only a question of balancing
accounts. His account will probably come
to the same figure-I hope more, because
really from my own knowledge we have done
far more with regard to refugees than they
have done in the Free State.
The Relief Grants Committee treated us
very shabbily indeed by not giving us a
grant equivalent to the money that was being
expended on other parts of Ireland. However,
I see my right hon. Friend (Captain Dixon)
in his place and in all probability he will
tell us something more. He knows more
about these cases than I do. I do not know
what the expense has been
or in what
position we are at the moment, but I do
say that it was heartrending many a time
to meet these people at the railways. In
many cases the husband had to fly and did
not know what position his wife and children
were in, and then in a month's time the wife
and children had to fly also. We had to
provide for these people. We had to get
our people to take them in for there was no
housing accommodation. The people here were
good enough, and here is where I want to
make an appeal. I think these people are
entitled to some thanks from us. There
were a large number of people in Northern
Ireland who took in refugees and did not
charge a farthing. I think that is to the
credit of the people of Northern Ireland.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). Had we been
keeping the expenditure it would have gone
up to a very large sum. The greatest credit is
due to our people who rose to the occasion,
took these refugees in and did not charge very
much. When they found that my right hon.
Friend (Captain Dixon) had established a
fund then rightly they were entitled to be
reimbursed for the expenditure incurred in
housing people who had to fly and whose
only crime was that they were good citizens.
I am quite certain that when my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Pollock) does make his claim
there will be no criticism, but I would like
to know what guarantee we have that this
money was spent in the Free State.
Mr. GRANT: I was rather surprised at one
remark made by the hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Barbour) who spoke on behalf of the Ministry

no supervision over this amount. I understand that claims as refugees were made by a

Mr. POLLOCK: In relation to the discussion
on the Unemployment Grant, I rise to crave
the indulgence of the House to make a
statement regarding a matter which has
considerably exercised not only myself
but also the House, and to which
reference was made in a prominent
issue of the local Press this morning.
I refer to the award of the Colwyn Committee
which reduces the £500,000 Unemployment
Relief Grant to £300,000.
Members will recall that in replying to the
debate on the Address I suggested that in
view of the delicate matters which were still
under discussion before the committee we
should refrain from indulging in criticism or
comments on the interim findings of that
body, in whose fairness and impartiality we
have the most perfect confidence. As I have
already pointed out, the Colwyn Committee is
an arbitration board set up mutually by the
Imperial Government and the Northern
Government to hear, and decide, upon outstanding financial questions, over which there
was considerable difference of opinion between
the two Treasuries. I would beg of the House
not to make my work more difficult at the
moment. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear).
When the committee has finally reported 1
will take the earliest opportunity to make a
full statement of the effect of the decisions
upon our. finances.
With regard to the question of the £500,000
grant, I should like to read the salient clause
of the agreement which was entered into on
the 31st March, 1922, between the Government
of Northern Ireland and the Provisional
Government countersigned by the British
Government:-
"In view of the special conditions consequent on the political situation in Belfast
and neighbourhood, the British Government
will submit to Parliament a vote not exceeding £500,000 for the Ministry of Labour
of Northern Ireland, to be expended exclusively in relief work-one-third for the
benefit of Roman Catholics and two-thirds
for the benefit of Protestants. The Northern signatories agree to use every effort to
secure the restoration of the expelled
workers, and wherever this proves impracticable at the moment owing to trade depression they will be afforded employment
on the relief works referred to in this
article so far as the one-third limit will
allow. Protestant ex-Servicemen to be
given first preference in respect to the twothirds of the said fund."
My right hon. Friend the Minister of
Labour (Mr. Andrews) immediately sanctioned the inception by local and
public authorities of various schemes
for works of improvement and with
the approval of the Government,
concentrated upon works of permanent public
utility taking a considerable time to complete, rather than ephemeral relief schemes
which could be rapidly executed. The result
of this arrangement was that in 1922-23 we
only spent approximately £56,000, and had to
ask the Treasury to re-vote the balance of the
£500,000. The Treasury stated that they were
prepared to consider a re-vote in the current
year of so much of the balance as would be required, but for the first time since the original grant was given the question of a time
limit was raised.
I quote from the Treasury letter:

Having regard to the fact that the
grant was given in March, 1922. in the exceptional circumstances then prevailing as
regards "expelled workers" My Lords do not
think they would be justified in asking Parliament to provide money for expenditure
later than the 31st March, 1924."
In view of the fact that this stipulation
definitely introduced into the administration
of the grant an element of time not found in
the original agreement between the Northern
Supply-

Government and the Provisional Government, we took the view that this was a matter
which should properly be referred to the

Treasuries.

intended to deal with the exceptional political

I may add that all these matters developed

I think the House should be informed of

Mr. DONALD: I do not rise to apologise in
any sense. I am prepared to stand over any
utterances I have made in this House. I have
not seen the Press, but my hon. Friend who
has spoken last surprised me. My right hon.
Friend has made two points; he has made a
very good case for our Government. First,
he admits that an agreement was entered into
and signed-an undertaking that we were to
get £500,000. We have rever broken that
agreement. He has enlightened us to-day of a
fact of which we were not aware that
this money was to be expended within
a given period. Had my right
hon. Friend known that he was given
£500,000 on the distinct understanding that
it must be spent within a given period he
would have spent it inside that time and far
more quickly. That coincides with what the
hon. Member for East Belfast (Mr. Duff) suggested; and of course with what I am saying now-that our Government were labouring under a misunderstanding. That is what
the Colwyn Committee attribute their de
cision to. They say: "You are only entitled
to sufficient money to tide you over the period
of disturbance." That is the interpretation
I take from the right hon. Gentleman. They
say "Our finding is this: "The disturbance is
ended after you spent £300,000.'" But for
the life of me I never understood why this
question was ever put before the Colwyn
Committee at all. I cannot get away from
the one fact that an agreement was entered
into, and that a sum of money was voted and
signed. I read a copy of it to the House
yesterday. It is signed. The signatories are
the representatives of the three Governments.
I take it this is in our arrangement, that we
were to get £500,000, and for any committee
to come along when we have committed ourselves, as my right hon. Friend says, to a
sum not exceeding £500,000. We have been
committed to even a larger sum than that.
Well, I sympathise with this Government in
treatment like that. My right hon. Friend
says we have been treated well; we have received just consideration and all that kind of
thing from the Imperial authorities. I do
not dispute it; but it leaves a suspicion in
my mind if an undertaking, binding such as
this is, is put in black and white, and signed
by three Governments, and then a committee
comes along after a certain period and breaks
that agreement and tells us that we must
raise £200,000 as the balance. They have reduced it to £300,000.
Question (That this House doth agree with
the Committee in said resolution) put, and

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
This Bill comes before the House for Second
Reading. The main object of the Bill is to
increase the facilities for dealing with the
illicit drug traffic; and Clauses 1, 2, and 3
make provision accordingly. Clause 4 varies
in case of registered medical practitioners,
dentists, and veterinary surgeons certain
regulations required by the Poisons (Ireland)
Act, 1870, to be observed in the sale of
poisons. Clause 5 provides that the labels
placed upon poisons in accordance with the
Act of 1870 must contain certain particulars
The
additional to those already required.
provisions of the Bill follow the provisions
contained in the Dangerous Drugs and
Poisons (Amending) Act, 1923, passed last
year by the Imperial Parliament. That Act
applies to Northern Ireland only to a limited
extent, namely, it amends the law in relation
to matters in respect to which this Parliament has no power to pass legislation. So
far as the subject matter of the Amending
Act of 1923 was within the powers of the
Parliament of Northern Ireland we are left
free to deal with it, that is, we are left free
to make similar provision if it is considered
desirable that this illicit traffic in drugs is
to be dealt with in Northern Ireland in the
same way as it is dealt with in Great Britain.
There is, however, one important set of
provisions that has not been inserted in the
Act of 1923, so far as Northern Ireland is concerned, and which we ourselves cannot deal
with. and these are provisions dealing with
persons committing acts which would in a
foreign country be offences against laws
passed in that country, in fulfilment of the
International Opium Convention of 1912.
However representations are being made by
the Minister of Home Affairs to the British
Government with a view to having this provision of the Act of 1923 extended to Northern
Ireland at the earliest possible opportunity.
As I say they have not been already extended
to Northern Ireland by the Act of 1923,
having regard to the fact that under Section
1, sub-Section 1, paragraph 4 of the Government of Ireland Act, 1920, we have not power
to deal with these matters. But as I say my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Home
Affairs will if possible get the necessary
Clause inserted.
I will make a few observations on the various clauses Clause 1 of the Act seeks to
increase the powers of search. There are
already powers of searching places, and the
idea underlying this Clause 1 is to extend
these powers of searching.
Clause 2 increases the penalties that can be
imposed under the Act of 1923, which were
found to be totally inadequate for the purpose for which they were inserted. They
were found to be no deterrent to illegal
trafficking in these drugs. And I may observe
in this connection that France has already
the
pointed out the way, and
Nations has recommended
ments to follow suit.
League of
other Govern-
Sub-clause (2) a provides that no person shall
be proceeded against by indictment without
the consent of the Attorney-General. Persons,
of course, can be proceeded against either by
summary jurisdiction or by indictment.
Naturally, in an indictment, the case would
be a more serious one, and it is felt that some
protection should be afforded against bringing
frivolous charges. Accordingly, an indictment
cannot be preferred except with the consent
of the Attorney-General.
Clause 3 makes it clear that nothing in the
Bill shall be construed as affecting the particular section of the 1920 Act relating to
import and export of drugs, which, of course,
is outside the powers of this House. We have
no power to deal with the question of import
or export. We want to have it made explicitly clear we do not purport to deal with
matters of that description.
Clause 4 enables medical
practitioners,
dentists, and veterinary surgeons to get
certain drugs without having to apply personally. They will be allowed to get these
drugs on presenting certain orders prescribed in the case. The concession is
safeguarded by provisions which will prevent
the drugs being obtained by unauthorised
persons.
Clause 5 deals with the proper labelling of
preparations containing poisons. As I said
before certain additional particulars will
have to be put upon those labels.
I sincerely hope the House will allow the
Bill to pass the Second Reading. I think it
is our duty in Northern Ireland to associate
ourselves with the people not only in Great
Britain but in other parts of the world who
are trying to repress, and stamp out if
possible, this nefarious traffic in drugs.
These drugs, we know, are detrimental not
only mentally but also physically and
morally to great numbers of people; they are
Dangerous Drugs Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS
Second Reading
[Mr. Best]
detrimental not only to people of the present
generation but, remembering the well-known
statement in Holy Writ that "the sins of the
fathers are visited upon the children unto the
third and fourth generation," we feel that
harm will be done to those people who are
to come after us. I, therefore, would appeal
to the House to give the Bill a Second Reading
so that it may be debated fully when it goes
into Committee. I beg to move.

Dr. MORRISON: Before saying one or two
words with regard to this Measure I would like
to note the fact that this is the third Bill
that we have amongst the batch that comes
from the Ministry of Home Affairs, which
shows that they are alive to the necessity of
keeping things moving and keeping this
Northern State of ours in such a position
that it will compare favourably with any
part of the Empire. Not only this Bill but
one of the others, the Illegitimate Children
Bill, is in my opinion a first-class Measure.
The introduction that has been given by the
learned Attorney-General puts the House in
possession of all the facts that they require
to know. We want in this matter
come up to the English standard.
think that in some respects we are behind
the English standard, and it is a very praiseworthy thing to find the Government so alive.
to the necessity of attaining to the English
mark. In regard to the Illegitimacy Bill,
as I pointed out a few days ago, we are fifty
years behind them. We are correcting that,
and every defect like that that prevents us
from holding our place as a progressive,
intelligent, well-conducted State will, I am
sure, receive the attention of the Government
and remedies will be devised. The aim of
this Government-which should also be the
aim of all other Governments-is to make it
easy for the people to do right and hard for
them to do wrong. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear). If we allow evils and abuses to grow
up we are creating vested interests, and when
you come to deal with the problem those
people who have a vested interest in an abuse
or something that is vicious and bad raise a
hullabaloo about the principle of the liberty
of the subject that is sometimes disconcerting
and sometimes deceives the public. So, if we
take this measure and adopt it before any
evil of an extensive nature has been developed
in our State we shall prevent that charge
being brought against us.
The drug habit is a very serious one.
Every medical man is aware of the danger
that a person is exposed to who is tampering
with drugs and especially drugs of a certain
nature. Everybody who has read the newspapers is familiar with the terrible tragedies
and the terrible evils that the abuse of
cocaine, and morphia, and glyco-heroin, and
other drugs have produced in many parts of
the world. Fortunately in this State of ours
the drug habit is not at all prevalent, and we
are giving power to the Government to take
the necessary steps to prevent its ever developing in our State. I think it is a wise thing that
we should do that before the evil has arrived
upon us as it has done in America, and in
England, and on some parts of the Continent.
The drug habit is very insidious in its growth;
it is most deadly in its results, worse than
any other abuse that I can think of or contemplate. It destroys absolutely the mental
and physical properties of any being who indulges in it, and it has been the means of
destroying some of the most brilliant people
who have ever been created. Indeed, it is
so dangerous that it frequently happens that
doctors may incautiously by the prescription
of medicines for the relief of pain perhaps
bring about a desire for the drug habit. The
House will understand the seriousness of this
danger when I tell them of a couple of
experiences that I had myself. I remember
a patient of mine who suffered very severe
pain. She was a poor girl and suffered from
a stone in her kidney, which brought on very
severe attacks of pain. She was not able to
pay me and I brought her to my house-she
was an old acquaintance-and she ultimately
got better and stayed in my house for 25 years
and nursed my children. But she had these
terrible attacks of pain. That lasted for
twenty years and I naturally feeling dis
tressed to see her suffering prescribed for her
a dose of morphia. I gave her a little bit of
morphia in solution and she took that any
time the pain came on, but at last I said to
her, This thing cannot go on. You are
acquiring a habit of this thing, or you will
acquire a habit, and it must be stopped." She
made no complaint and stopped it, but ten
years later she told me that if she had known
where she could buy that medicine she would
have bought it. If she had been able to buy
it she would have acquired the morphia habit
and it would have ruined and destroyed her
mentally and physically.

There is another drug which is called glycoheroin. It is an excellent thing for the
relief of a cough, but it contains a large
portion of morphia. Anyone can go into a
druggist's shop and buy that stuff. One time
a friend of mine suffered from a bad cold and
I gave him a little glyco-heroin. And what
did I find? He went to a druggist's shop and
got it for himself and for his family when they
were suffering from a cough or cold-a
dangerous drug sold over the counter as you
would sell any ordinary drug and handed into
family use without an ordinary prescription
or other medical directions. That shows you
how dangerous it is and how under the present law it is possible to get proprietary
remedies such as glyco-heroin and preparations of cocaine. They can be bought,

and I can easily understand how it might be
possible for a druggist or a person of the

be produced with the dangerous results that
would follow to the community. This Bill
will enable the Government in case an

It will prevent the indiscriminate selling of
those drugs to people without a proper
medical prescription, and is a good and
wholesome and necessary thing for the State.
I am sure the House will readily pass the
Second Reading.

Explosives Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read the Second time."
Its
Sir DAWSON BATES: This is a short Bill
to amend certain provisions of the Explosives
Act, 1875, so far as that Act applies to
Northern Ireland. It follows the Act which
was passed last year by the Imperial House
and which did not apply to this area.
object is to provide greater security in the
keeping of explosives and to afford increased
protection to young persons engaged in
explosives factories. Under the existing Act
of 1875 the occupier of premises used as an
explosives factory is required to take
precautions to prevent accidents taking place
and to prevent unauthorised persons getting
access to those places. In the Act there is no
power given to the authorities to prescribe
what these precautions should be, and the
result was that the only method of enforcing
that particular provision was to bring
proceedings for the purpose of determining
whether or not an individual had taken
precautions. In Clause 1 of the present Bill
the Ministry of Home Affairs is empowered to
direct what special care is to be taken in the
event of the necessity arising, and it also
provides and if these measures that are
prescribed are not taken by the individual
the Ministry can intervene and take the
necessary steps to have these measures
carried into effect.
Clause 2 deals with the employment of
young persons in these factories. Under the
existing Act persons under sixteen years of
age are not allowed to be employed in these
factories unless under the supervision of
some grown-up person. In England it
was found that this was not a sufficient
protection for these young persons and in
the result frequent accidents occurred.
This Clause proposes to raise the age
to eighteen, and provides that no young person under the age of eighteen is allowed to
work in these factories unless under the
supervision of a person of the age of 21 years
or upwards, and it also provides that in no
case is any young person under the age of
sixteen to work in these factories except at
certain non-dangerous processes, and these
non-dangerous processes are to be prescribed
by the Ministry of Home Affairs.
Clause 3 provides for increasing the penalty
for keeping explosives in unauthorised places.
At the present time the penalty is 2/- for each
pound of explosives that is so kept, and now
it is proposed to increase the penalty to
£100 or 2/- per lb., whichever is the greater.
I beg to move.
Question: "That the Bill be now read the
Second time" put, and agreed to.
Bill committed to a Committee of the whole
House for to-morrow.
