HOUSE OF COMMONS
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 27th March, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions
REVISION OF OLD AGE PENSIONS.
1. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs if he has received a resolution
from the General Purposes Committee of the
Belfast City Council regarding a revision or
amendment of the Old Age Pensions Act,
and whether the Government propose introducing legislation dealing with this
matter.
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I am replying to this question
addressed to my right hon. Friend the
Minister of Home Affairs.
The answer to the first part of the
question is in the affirmative. It will be
within the knowledge of the House that the
Imperial Government are investigating the
subject of the revision or amendment of the
means limit in the case of applicants for
Old Age Pensions, and while the policy to
be pursued by the Government of Northern
Ireland might be materially influenced by
any legislative action taken in the Imperial
Parliament, it must be borne in mind that
any amendment or revision in the manner
indicated would involve the Government of
Northern Ireland in additional expenditure
which it might not have the means to meet.
What Northern Ireland's ultimate resources
may be for the expansion of social or other
services must, as Members are aware, largely
depend on the findings of the Colwyn Committee, and it would, therefore, be unwise for
me at the present time to make any definite statement on the point raised by my
hon. Friend.
SECONDARY TEACHERS' PENSION
SCHEME.
2. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Finance if he can state when the details of
the Pension Scheme for Secondary Teachers
will be issued.
Mr. POLLOCK: I propose to take this
question relating to the pensions of secondary teachers as it comes entirely within the
purview of the Ministry of Finance.
The framing of the Pension Scheme for
Secondary Teachers has been entrusted to a
Departmental Committee representing the
Ministry of Finance and the Ministry of
Education.
The financial considerations involved have
been fully explored actuarially and the results, together with the various administrative points arising therefrom have been
considered in detail by the Committee. 1
anticipate that the Committee will be in a
position to report to me within the next
month, and therefore it should be possible to
lay the scheme on the Table of the House
on some date not long after the Easter recess.
INTERMEDIATE EXAMINATION RULES.
3. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education
if he can state when the Rules and Regulations for the Intermediate Examinations
(1924-25) will be issuel by the Ministry.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION: (Mr.
McKeown): The Ministry has under consideration the regulations and programme
for the Examinations for Intermediate and
Secondary Schools to be held in 1925, and it
hopes to be able to issue these at
early date.

an

Mr. McKEOWN: The Ministry is giving

RENTS OF LABOURERS' COTTAGES.
4. Mr. HANNA asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether it is a fact that he
has given authority to the Lisburn Rural
District Council to increase the rents of
Labourers' Cottages in their area; if so, what
is the extent of the increase so permitted, and
for what reasons was the permission given.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): The Lisburn Rural
District Council applied some months ago
to the Ministry for approval to certain
increases of rents in their labourers' cottages.
They pointed out that the existing rents
were very low, ranging from 1s. a week in
some cases to 2s. 6d. a week, and that the
yearly loss on the rates involved by these
very low rents was £1,944.
The proposals of the council were that the
scale of rents should range from 2s. to 5s.
according to the nature of the cottage, size
A
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
27 MARCH, 1924.
of the holding, and the general amenities of
the district in which the cottages were
situated. They also urged that some regard
should be had to the individual circumstances of the tenants.
Following representations made by the
tenants protesting against these increases, the
Ministry ordered a local Inquiry to be held by
their Inspector.
a
This Inquiry was of a most comprehensive
character and extended over a period of two
days. The Inspector had before him
number of the tenants and also made a careful examination of the circumstances of the
tenants generally. As a result of his recommendations and after careful examination of
the proposal in all its aspects, the Ministry
decided that they could not approve of increasing the rent to 5s., or even 4s., as proposed
by the rural district council, but have given
their provisional approval to a scale of rents
which involve 73 cottages being let at 2s. a
week, 197 at 2s. 6. a week, and 31 cottages
at 3s. a week.
With regard to the cottages which are to be
let at 3s. a week, it may be pointed out that
the majority of these are situated in the
neighbourhood of urban or industrial centres.
It should be pointed out that even with the
revised scales provisionally approved, the
yearly loss to the ratepayers on the scheme
will amount to upwards of £1,000.
The Inquiry brought to light the fact that
many of the tenants of the labourers' cottages
were in comparatively affluent circumstances.
It was even reported in one case a tenant was
the owner of a motor car, while many of
them were in possession of horses and cattle.
It would appear to the Ministry that, either
through inadvertent letting on the part of
the rural district council, or through changing circumstances of the tenants, a considerable number of the cottages are inhabited by
persons who do not strictly come within the
definition of agricultural labourers, and the
Ministry have impressed on the council the
necessity for restricting the lettings to those
classes for whom the cottages were originally
intended.
Mr. HANNA: I beg to give notice that
I will continue this speech on the Motion

CONDITIONS FOR PAYMENT OF
UNCOVENANTED BENEFIT.
7. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister
of Labour if
he will state the conditions imposed by Statute for claimants
uncovenanted benefit under the Unemployment Insurance Act, 1923, and
the nature of these conditions, now that the
gap week has been abolished; and whether
uncovenanted benefit will be paid irrespective of age or family income.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Every applicant for uncovenanted
benefit must satisfy three special statutory
conditions which are shortly as follows:
(1) that he is normally employed in an insurable occupation.
Oral Answers
Oral Answers
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Mr. Andrews]
(2) that he is genuinely seeking but unable
to obtain whole time employment; and
(3) that 20 contributions have at some time
been paid in respect of him or he has at any
rate been employed for a reasonable number
of weeks in some insurable occupation since
the 31st December, 1919.
The abolition of the "gap" week has made
no difference to the necessity for the observance of these conditions, but hitherto it has
been the rule in Northern Ireland as in Great
Britain that an applicant for uncovenanted
benefit should in addition satisfy the Local
Employment Committee that his circumstances were such that the withholding of a
grant would involve hardship. In view,
however, of the prolongation of unemployment due to the continued trade depression,
it has been decided that, provided the three
special conditions that I have mentioned are
satisfied, no consideration of the age or family
income of an applicant shall affect his claim
to uncovenanted benefit either in Northern
Ireland or Great Britain.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
may I ask the right hon. Gentleman from
what date these conditions will be made
operative?
Mr. ANDREWS: From the same date as in
Great Britain.
Mr. DONALD: Thank you.

by the Postal Authorities. The technical

Sir DAWSON BATES: As to the point
raised by hon. Members with regard to the
complaints of injury caused by mud-splashing, I think everybody will agree when I say
that it may be prevented in two ways,
first of all by better roads, and secondly by
the use of some sort of guard to prevent mudsplashing. With regard to the first of these
points, one would really think that the
Corporation were the proper people to reply
to the attack made on the Home Office.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I quite agree,
however, that the streets in Belfast might be
improved. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
There is one aspect of the question that has
been overlooked, and that is that for the last
six months a great deal of the surface of the
streets has been opened up for the purpose
of relaying tramways and giving employment
to those who want work. I think hon.
Members are sometimes too particular as to
their own convenience when it comes to a
question of finding work for the unemployed. So far as the Ministry is concerned
we allot money from time to time out of the
Road Fund to the different authorities, and
I think hon. Members who have gone through
the Six Counties-after all we are not speaking about Belfast alone-will agree that
generally speaking the surface of the roads
has very much improved.
Sir ROBERT LYNN: Where?
I find
Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard to the
second point, namely the question of efficient
protection from mud-splashing, this problem
is not confined to this part of the world. In
England and Scotland they have had the
same difficulty, and the Ministry of Transport
have been looking for an efficient guard for
this road splashing. Last year I think, the
Royal Automobile Association offered very
valuable prizes to anybody who could produce
an efficient mud-spiash protector.
from a report here that something like 36
different appliances were sent in and were
tested by the Royal Automobile Association. I
do not know whether my hon. Friend (Mr.
Donald) brought his patent out at that particular time. Perhaps his patent may overcome some of the difficulties that were met
with at this important test, but the judges
in the final paragraph of their report-I will
be glad to let hon. Members see this report
because it is very enlightening-say:
The judges after careful consideration do
not recommend any award in either class.
They have come to this decision because in
their opinion the device has failed in the
first essential of a mud-splash guard; that
is to say, no device would reduce the
amount of mud-splashing to a negligible
quantity.
In England and Scotland the Ministry of
Transport realised the injustice that would be
imposed upon motor owners in forcing them
to put a guard on to their vehicles which
would not be efficient for the purpose, for
this reason that even if they did put on the
guard and people were splashed, it would not
prevent the owners of vehicles from being
prosecuted if an order wa's put in force.
After consulting, our own Advisory Committee, of which the hon. Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Donald) is a member, they
arrived at the same conclusion, and that is
if an efficient mud-splash guard cannot be
provided it would be a very unfair thing to
impose on motor owners the responsibility of
putting on a guard which would not be
sufficient for the purpose and would not prevent them being prosecuted in the event of
mud-splashing.

There is another matter I wish to bring before
the Minister. May I humbly ask him to consider in his schemes the question of agricultural
education? I understand there is a Faculty of
Agriculture to be created in the University,
research laboratory and all the rest
of it. That is a good thing. I submit that
is very little use to the people of Ulster if
there is not something more done. I hold
that the place where agricultural teaching
should be carried on is first in the primary
schools of the country. I have one or two
instances in mind of men who graduated in
the national school. I travelled with a
gentleman from Liverpool to London, and I
learned more about agriculture in that time
than I got from most people in twelve
months. That man graduated in his primary
school, where he had a teacher who had
great knowledge of agriculture and who imparted that knowledge very consistently to
his scholars.
I submit that the young people of our
country should be initiated into chemistry
and the various other things in research
work, in connection with the average farm.
That is where we lose hold of our young men.
They are not taken in time, not interested in
time. That particular time passes, and they
have no appetite for the education which
comes too late. Research may be all right.
It is quite commendable in the University,
but there ought to be a link between teaching in the University and the opening up of
the child's mind in agricultural research in
the primary school. I do not go further in
this matter. I leave it to the Minister if he
will care to think about this part of agricultural work, which I think, is of primary
importance.
The reason I rose here to-day was in regard to another matter connected with agriculture. The Leader of the House (Mr.
Pollock), in his opening statement, made a

these markets are of no use if you have not

to use the fibre at home.

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I have no
intention of travelling over a variety of
subjects here this afternoon, but before making the few observations that I intend to
make may I say, what I know is the feeling
of the House, how gratified we are to see
the hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh
(Mr. Coote) able to make such a vigorous
speech, which clearly indicates that in a
short time he will be as energetic as ever.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear). He has raised
in his speech one or two very interesting
matters. I intend to deal with one only,
and that is the question of flax production.
He has told us what the remedy is, if we
want an increased supply, and in doing so he
has raised a very important question, and
one that any Government must consider very
seriously before adopting. The moment you
begin to give a subsidy to one particular
branch of industry, where is it going to end?
It is a very dangerous principle, and can only
be adopted, I think, in the case of some
extreme emergency. I cannot say whether
that position of affairs has arisen in this
case or not. I do not know whether I am
right in my history or not, but I think the linen
industry in Ulster was originally established
through a bounty. I think I am right in that.
If the linen industry was brought here and
encouraged and made into the industry that
it has become in the last few generations,
it might be worth considering whether under
existing conditions some financial assistance
could not be given in the way indicated by
the hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh
(Mr. Coote). It is for the Government to say
whether their financial resources are equal
to the occasion, and whether they are prepared to start out on the granting of
subsidies.
Another observation I want to make is in
regard to the question of motor vehicles going
through the country. Some of the hon.
Members who have spoken seem to think that
the local authorities can do everything.
Parliament for the last ten or twelve years
has been consistently handing over things to
the local authorities involving a large expenditure of the money of the ratepayers, and
I am satisfied of this, you cannot expect the
county councils or the local authorities to
spend the huge sums needed to keep the roads
in proper condition for this traffic unless the
money comes from the State. It cannot come
from the local ratepayers because they are
overburdened at the moment, and as I say
Parliament is contemplating already placing
further responsibilities upon them, involving
taxation upon the local councils. They have

The real thing that brought me to my feet
this afternoon was this. I did not happen
to be in the House when my hon. Friend, the
Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr.
Cooper), who sits opposite, raised a very important question which has not been dealt
with by the Government in the manner that
I believe the people outside expected them
to deal with it. We are all familiar with
what happened in the extreme end of County
Fermanagh a couple of years ago. I mean the
trouble that arose at the Border between Fermanagh and Donegal at a place which is now
famous, Belleek, where a force from the
Twenty-six Counties invaded the Six Counties
and left their mark behind them to the detriment and injury of a great many of the
citizens of that particular district. Those
people suffered seriously, and they have
suffered up to the present without the
slightest thing being done for them. What
happened to them? Their shops were raided
and their goods were stoien, and when they
sought redress in the law courts they were
met by the answer that their goods were
stolen, and that the law was such that no
redress could be given them. That, I presume, has been the answer of the Government up to the present, but surely the exceptional circumstances in connection with
this case demand a different answer from
them. (An hon Member: Hear, hear.) Suppose by any chance that raid had taken place
in another district and a huge quantity of
goods had been taken away and a lot of injury done the question would have become
of serious importance. I am sure this House
will support the Government if they make
the suggestion here that they are prepared
to consider these cases. Bring in a Bill if it
is necessary and see that justice and
fair play is done to those people who
do not ask for anything but what I
believe they are entitled to from the
State of which they are citizens. When
they are raided and invaded by
outside foe the Government under which they
live should see that right is done by them.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The amount
involved would not be very great, and if the
Government took this matter up, and placed
the facts before the House, they would find
an
that they would be acting not only in harmony with the wishes of the House but in
harmony with the wishes of the whole community of the Six Counties. Those of us who
live in security in some places-those who
have not had to put up with what these unfortunate people have had to put up withwould be prepared, I am sure, to say that
they ought to receive kindly and generous
consideration.

people are just as well entitled to consideration as the unemployed. Some of them as a

As regards education, which the hon. Member (Mr. Coote) talked about. we are going

Mr. ANDREWS: There is just one matter
to which I would like to refer, as the others
have been dealt with, or will be dealt with

trouble, because the strange thing is that
the workers of both unions-the Ulster
Workers' Union and the General Transport
Workers' Union, are working together in this
firm on perfectly friendly terms. The trouble,
however, exists because certain members of the
General Transport Workers' Union, at the

to force the members of the Ulster
Workers' Union who are employed in this particular firm to join their union, and in order to

with the directors of this firm. I have had a
conference with them, and they are perfectly
satisfied with the action which I have taken in

healing the trouble. I have also been in touch
with the representatives of both unions affected.
The Ulster Workers' Union are in my opinion
in no way to blame. I have found that the
leaders of the other union in Great Britain
are anxious that this trouble should end, and
they also expressed the desire that this embargo should be removed. The local leaders

their principals across the Channel, and so the
dispute drags on in a most regrettable fashion.

with the parties affected, I am hopeful that

The duties of this Committee which is composed of the Lord Chief Justice as Chairman,

Sir Ernest Clark, and the Comptroller of the
Imperial Stationery Office, are to edit the
Northern Ireland Statutes and also the Statutory Rules and Orders, and also to bring out a

is a similar body in existence in Great Britain

Estimates. The whole of the work which

Editor who is a King's Counsel. lt
is proposed that he should be paid £250
for his services. I am sure my hon. and
learned Friend (Mr. Robb), who is a professional man himself, will appreciate the
onerous duties that will naturally arise from
work of this kind.

The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): I move
this Vote for the Public Record
Office which hon. Members will find
on page 70 of the Estimates. This Office was
established, in accordance with an Act of the
Parliament of Northern Ireland, in 1923,
Its creation was necessitated by the destruction of the Record Office in Dublin and
the dissociation of Northern Ireland from
the Irish Free State. In the Estimates for
1923, provision of £2,500 was made for initial
expenses. However, as the Department was
not in a position to operate until January
last, the whole of this sum has not
been expended. Temporary suitable fireproof premises have been obtained and
records to the number of several
thousands have already been deposited; these
relate in the main to the transfer of property
on death-Probate papers would, I think,
convey a more familiar meaning to most of
us-and also to the proceedings of Assize and
County Courts during the period 1900-1903.
I may remind hon. Members that papers are
supposed to be kept for a period of nearly
twenty years and it is only when they become older that they are transferred from
the various courts to the Public Record
Office. As several years have elapsed since
the last transfer of records to Dublin, there
is a heavy accumulation of documents
awaiting accommodation. This department
will eventually be accommodated in the new
law Courts buildings when they are erected
and ready to receive them
I am sure it will also interest hon.
Members to know that the information in
the possession of the Government as to the
fate of Northern Ireland records formerly
preserved in the Dublin Record Office shows
that these have been, almost without exception, destroyed; the main repository was
completely ruined and only a few documents
which happened to be in use on the day of
the occupation were preserved. The Northern
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Barbour]
Record Office has taken as its first task
the replacement of these destroyed documents
to such extent as is possible. In some cases
copies were preserved in public custody and
search has been made through official papers
with encouraging results. It is estimated
that from 6,000 to 10,000 copies of destroyed
documents relating to Northern Ireland will
be found scattered through the papers of
various public departments, and if the necessary arrangements can be made for their
concentration in the Record Office here, as
records available to the public at large, a
considerable step will have been taken towards the re-construction of the Four Courts'
collections.
will involve
Many copies of the destroyed Dublin
records are also in private custody, for example, in the possession of solicitors, rent
agents, etc. It is hoped that some scheme
may be devised whereby, with the COoperation of the possessors of these documents, they too may be made available as
public records. This course
comparatively little individual sacrifice, and
it is of great importance to the community
at large, and to the legal profession in particular, that the replacement of destroyed
documents should be as complete as is possible in the difficult circumstances. Probably
there are at least 10,000 copies of destroyed
public documents in private custody at present
available only to the owners. If there is
united effort directed towards re-construction
of records, the effect of the disaster of the
Four Courts may, for Northern Ireland, be
considerably mitigated.
Besides providing for the reception of
recent legal or official records and copies of
destroyed documents, it is intended to
establish a depository of documents of all
kinds bearing on the history of the Province.
In this respect the Government would make
an appeal to all public-spirited people in
Northern Ireland who have old records, old
papers and old maps that are really of
historic interest to the Province to hand
them over to the Public Record Office for
deposit and safeguard, where they will
be indexed and preserved. They will thereby be accessible to the public and be of
great historic interest to the six counties. 1
am glad to say that some documents of this
class-some interesting old maps-have
already been deposited by private individuals, and it is expected that others will follow.
It will be noted that the total whole-time
Staff at present employed is three persons,
which is no more than is required to arrange,
catalogue and index the records as they
arrive. In the future, when these have
been duly catalogued and indexed, fees will
be charged for access to the documents and
for copies and so a revenue will be derived
which will to a great extent off-set the cost
of running the Department. However, it
will be understood that very little revenue
will be derived for some time to come. 1
beg to move.

Mr. MEGAW: As I said, the Attorney-
General when he was proposing this Vote
last year, expressed the hope that the condition of things would soon become normal
again, and the hope that he then expressed has
fructified. For a considerable time there has
been an almost complete disappearance of
abnormal crime, but it would hardly be prudent to assume that that state of things was
absolutely permanent. Considering the uncertain condition that exists in other parts
of Ireland, we must be on our guard and
keep the services in their ordinary condition.
We have very great cause for thankfulness
at the improvement that has existed in the
condition of the country, and satisfaction
has been expressed by the Judges of Assize
in almost all the counties. The figures that
I will give will to some extent give good
grounds for our feelings of satisfaction, and
will indicate, I think, that the impartial
administration of the law that has existed
throughout the year has been of very good
effect. Hon. Members, of course, know that
the conditions that existed some years
ago required special legislation,
and
emergency legislation was passed in the
measure that was known as the Civil
Authorities Aet. That Act was of the most
valuable assistance to the Government in
coping with the situation that had arisen
in regard to crime in Northern Ireland, and
it still to some extent becomes necessary in
its operation. The Government do not intend
in the meantime to do anything to abrogate
the provisions of that very valuable measure.
Hon. Members will be interested to know
the statistics referring to the particular
crime with which that Act was intended to
deal, namely, firearms. The number of firearms cases during the last twelve monthsthat is firearms cases of all kinds-is 120 as
compared with 650 that unfortunately
occurred in the year before. In regard to
an exceptional remedy that was introduced
by the Civil Authorities Act, the punishment
of flogging, it is fortunately the case that
during the last year in only one instance
was corporal punishment resorted to. During
the previous year it had been ordered in something like 46 cases. In the same way the
number of indictable cases has very largely
fallen; it is only 50 per cent. of what it was in
the previous year. Hon. Members will, I
think, agree that these indications show a
very considerable improvement in the state
of the country, and we have every reason to
congratulate ourselves on the result. The
improvement does not so much affect this
bit Estimate as
it does some of the others,
that is, the Prisons Estimate and the Home
で
Office Estimate, because the better condition
has resulted in a considerable falling off in the
amount that is being required for the services
during the forthcoming year. The Vote we
are now interested in is the ordinary Vote
for the law charges that exist in normal
times.

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: That is not the

It is the increase of 100 per
cent. on the standard rent originally fixed.
An increase of 25 per cent. was allowed by the
Imperial Parliament on the rent paid by the

"The economic rent.") Will my right hon.
Friend say it was ever the intention to charge

rent. To my mind there is a strong justification for a moderate increase of rent to balance
the increased cost of upkeep, and I would say
that the District Council would be lacking in

to compensate it for the increased cost of the
necessary upkeep. They are bound to do that,
but in this case I would like to know if these
houses were neglected for a long number of
years and that in consequence a huge bill then
came in for repairs. It might be a bit of
impertinence on my part if I offered any advice
to the Ministry of Home Affairs as to what
rents they should charge, but if from this time

connection with farm work are decreasing and
not increasing, they are going to heap up for
themselves a great deal of trouble, while at
the same time I do not think they are dealing
fairly with a class of the community who are
in receipt of the smallest wage of any labouring
class. (An hon. Member: What about the
ratepayer" ?) The members of the Rural
District Council were ratepayers when they

from
men
that class at

The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As I have already stated
it is not intended to make any reductions in

answer, may I ask if during the past fortnight
a circular was issued giving the changed

Sir DAWSON BATES: A circular was
issued setting forth the conditions of service
of the "B" Constabulary, but as to when
those will take effect that is a matter for the
Government; but there will be no alteration
at the present time.

Gentleman (Sir Dawson Bates) if it a fact
that a circular has been sent broadcast
amongst the Specials to the effect that there
will be both a reduction in the number of

Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not know
whether the hon. Member (Mr. McGuffin)
has seen the circular in question.

morning.
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is a pretty long
circular. It sets out the different provisions, and proposes at a later date to
divide the "B" Constabulary into different
categories according to the conditions of
peace in the districts. As I have already
stated, it is not proposed to put these conditions into force at the present time.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
may I. ask the right hon. Gentleman, now
that there has been a rumour of demobilisation, whether there is to be any reduction

course,
Sir DAWSON BATES: No, there is no reduction in the bonus. I think hon. Members
entirely forget the circumstances and terms
of service in the "B" Constabulary. At
the present time the terms of service are
roughly these: Every man has to do one
night in ten, and for that he receives an
allowance-not bonus-towards clothing and
other things. It is proposed at a later date,
if circumstances permit-and. of
that depends upon the conditions of peace in
the Six Counties--to ask those men not to
do so much work, that is to say they will do
one night in twenty, and for that they will
receive £7 instead of £10. In some
districts it may be unnecessary to have
them even doing that one night in twenty,
and then they will be put into the reserve,
and for that they will receive £3 for attending drills. As I have already informed the
House, it is not proposed to make any change
at the present time.
Mr. DONALD: Either in demobilisation or
allowance?
Sir DAWSON BATES: That is so.
Mr. DONALD: Thank you.

The
TO THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
McKeown): I am pleased to be able to point
out to hon. Members that the Estimates for
Harbour and Commercial Services 1924-25,
administered by the Ministry of Commerce
show a net decrease of some £12,000 as compared with 1923-24, and contain no feature
which has not already been considered by
the House. Under Sub-heads A and Al-
Royal Harbours, we have a sum of £1,215
as against £1,270 in 1923-24. In order to
show the cost of the Works' Services at the
harbours as distinct from the cost of salaries
and wages, the sub-head for Royal Harbours
has been divided into these two Sections.
The decrease of some £250 for the maintenance, etc. of the harbours is due to the
fact that the removal of a rock shelf from
the berthage at Ardglass Harbour has been
practically completed, and consequently only
a nominal sum of £60 has been inserted for
new works.
Sub-head B-Grants-in-Aid of Harbour
Works-shows a decrease of £5,500 consequent upon the disappearance of the £2,500
grant to assist the construction of new lock
gates at Newry, and a further disappearance
of £3,000 of the £9,000 granted from Government Funds towards provision of special repairs at Kilkeel Harbour. The new lock
gates at Newry are now in position and constitute a most valuable asset to the harbour
'works at that port. I think the Committee
has a right to congratulate itself on the fact
that this work has been so expeditiously and
so efficiently carried out. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) The Committee will recollect
that the sum of £9,000 was granted from
Government Funds to meet part of the cost
of special repairs at Kilkeel Harbour on the
basis of a pound for a pound payment by the
Down County Council. It is anticipated,
however, that only £3,000 of this sum will
be spent in 1923/24, and it is necessary,
accordingly, to revote the balance of £6,000
for 1924/25.
Sub-head C.-Weights and Measures.-The
verification of the local standards and scale
beams in Northern Ireland has been undertaken by the Board of Trade under an agency
arrangement with the Ministry of Commerce.
The work has been proceeding smoothly, and
I am happy to inform the Committee that, as
a result of the Ministry's efforts, the weights
and measures in Northern Ireland are now

Sub-head D.-Collection of Trade Statistics.
-The provision made for this Service is
identical with that of 1923-24. The returns
rendered have proved most valuable, and indeed essential to the compilation of
various groups of the trade statistics of
Northern Ireland.
Sub-head E.-Reconstruction of Companies
Records I have only to recall the attention
of hon. Members to the fact that a Bill passed
through this House to enable us to have these
reconstituted. The work of reconstructing
the files of the Joint Stock Companies in
Northern Ireland, whose records were destroyed in the Dublin Custom House fire in
1921, is now proceeding, and it is anticipated
that the total reconstitution will be effected
before the end of 1924. The sum of £1,000 was
voted for this service by the Supplementary
Estimate of October last, but, owing to the
complicated nature of the work involved, it
is anticipated that only £500 of this sum will
be expended in 1923-24. Accordingly, it is
proposed to revote £500 for 1924-25, together
with an additional sum of £250, thus making
the total cost for this Service £1.250.
Sub-head
F.-Exhibitions.-The Foreign
Samples Exhibition, which was organized by
the Ministry in December last, was well
attended by representatives of the commercial community, and proved to be of very
considerable value. Provision is, therefore,
made to enable further Exhibitions to be held
as and when advisable. I am sure quite a
number of hon. Members attended this
Exhibition which was held in the Ulster
Minor Hall, The Ministry received afterwards quite a number of letters from commercial houses pointing out the advantages
that they had obtained owing to the Exhibition. Experience has shown us that we can
perhaps assist the Board of Trade in getting
samples from Northern Ireland which will
be, if anything, more beneficial to the industries of the Province. We are taking
steps, in conjunction with the Board of Trade,
to make this Exhibition and the samples
provided at it such as will enhance the prosperity of the industries throughout the whole
of the Six Counties. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
Now we come to the grant for the British
Empire Exhibition. Hon. Members are aware
The Committee will observe from the daily
Press that a considerable amount of doubt
exists as to whether the Exhibition

has been given for the supplementing of this
sum by such revenue as will be received from
sub-letting of space in the Pavilion to various
Northern Ireland firms and industries.
£11.000 was voted by the Supplementary Estimate of October last, but it is now estimated

in 1923-24, and it is, accordingly, proposed to
re-vote this £4,000 in 1924-25, together with the
balance of £1,000 new money, thus completing
the total Government grant of £12,000. It is
very satisfactory to know that the Ulster
Pavilion will in every detail be ready for the
official opening. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)

Local Government (Financial
Provisions) Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read the Second time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Bill now before
the House is of a very short nature, and I do
not think it contains any features of a controversial character. It contains two Clauses.
The first relates to borrowing by County
Councils, and the second relates to grants payable to local authorities.
As regards the first Clause, which relates
to the limitation of borrowing powers of
County Councils, under the existing law the
borrowing powers of County Councils are restricted to an amount equal to one-tenth of
the annual rateable value of the rateable property in the county.
I would remind hon. Members that last
year, under an Act passed by this House, the
County Councils in Northern Ireland were
handed over the entire responsibility of maintaining first-class and second-class roads in
each county, and I think I am correct in saying that since that time there has been on
the whole a steady improvement in the condition of the roads.
In the old days, when roads were used
mainly for horse traffic, the expense of maintaining these roads was as a rule met out
of income. Modern conditions, and the birth
of the motor-car, have changed all that, and
County Councils have been forced for some
time past to have recourse to borrowing for
the purpose of carrying out the necessary improvements in roads. At the present time
there are several schemes before the Ministry,
put up by the various County Councils, which
involve the borrowing of considerable sums
to carry out road works-sums which are in
excess of the existing borrowing powers of
County Councils, and the object of Clause 1
of the Bill is to exclude sums borrowed by
the County Councils for the purpose of road
works from the limitation
posed by the existing law.
at present im-
So far as I can see there can be no objection
to this course. It is not a new principle, as
it has been already embodied in the Criminal
Injuries Act of 1920, when County Councils
were forced to borrow large sums of money
to pay off criminal injury decrees, in order
to spread over for a period of years the
liability of the ratepayers.
The present proposal will not necesarily impose any large burden on the ratepayers. On
the contrary it is hoped that it will ultimately
mean a saving to the ratepayers. It is hoped
that as a result of the carrying out of these
various large schemes by the County Councils,
which in many cases will mean a re-construction of roads, there will ultimately be a
cost
saving in the annual
of road maintenance. These works will also rank for recoupment out of the Road Fund, and where
these works involve re-construction they will
also qualify for an increased grant from the
Road Fund on the basis of one-fifth over and
above the normal scale.
Now, with regard to the second Clause,
which deals with grants to local authorities,
hon. Members will recollect that under the

Local Government Act passed last year,
special provision was made for the continuance of the payment by the Government
to local authorities, which was formerly made

As I pointed out when that Bill was introduced, the Local Taxation Account became
inoperative. Accordingly we devised a
scheme which was embodied in the Local Government Act of last year under which local
authorities would receive from the Government grants on the basis of the average
amounts which had been made to these local
authorities for the years 1918, 1919, and 1920.
But when it came to the practical working of
the Act, we found that owing to the fact that
these years were not normal years owing to
circumstances which are only too apparent to
Members of this House, in many cases payments which had accrued to these local authorities during these years had not been paid
to them, and were not paid until some time
after the close of these particular financial

འ
In all the circumstances we thought it
would be more equitable in calculating the
amount that should be payable to these local
authorities to proceed on the basis of the
average amount which had accrued to the
local authorities, rather than the amount that
had been paid to them, and Clause 2, Sub-
Clause (1) gives effect to this principle.
Hon. Members, I think, will agree with me
that it would be a hardship that local authorities should be penalised owing to circumstances over which they had no control, and
especially having regard to the principle
which has been laid down in this House on.
several occasions that local authorities should
not be placed in a worse position in regard
to grants, as a result of the passing of the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920.
Sub-Clause (2) of Clause 2 involves the same
principle. It relates to grants made to local
authorities in respect of railway and harbour
guarantees. If the Government were to pay
these grants to the local authorities on the
principle of the average sum they received,
rather than the average sum they should have
received, it would work out very unfairly
for them, and, consequently, in regard to this
particular grant, which is of a very insignificant character, we propose to revert to the
principle laid down under the Act of 1898 and
pay in the future 90 per cent. of half the
excess over the 6d rate. I beg to move.

Char-a-Banc Regulation Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Mation made and Question proposed :
"That the Bill now be read a Second time."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The object of the
Bill now before the House is to confer upon
urban authorities in Northern Ireland power
in regard to the licensing and control of
motor chars-a-banc. Some time ago the
Government received memorials from practically every urban district in Ulster pointing
out the necessity of conferring upon them the
same measure of control over motor chars-abanc which they had in regard to hackney
vehicles under the Towns Improvement Act,
1854. I might point out that the motor charsa-banc, while they are hackney vehicles for
the purpose of motor taxation, do not come
within the meaning of hackney vehicles "
as defined by the Towns Improvement Act,
1854. As a result up to the present time these
local authorities have had absolutely no control over these motor chars-a-banc.

The matter was referred to the Roads
Advisory Committee by the Government..
That Roads Advisory Committee is a body
which is responsible for advising the Government in regard to roads and the control of
traffic. That Committee went into the whole
problem, and before making the representations which are now embodied in this Bill
they took the opportunity of having a conference with representatives of the Urban
District Councils, and also the char-a-banc
proprietors. They met in conference, and I'
think it is safe to say that the recommendations of the Roads Advisory Committee,
which are embodied in this Bill, are acceptable both to the Urban District authorities
and to the proprietors of the motor chars-abanc
The powers which I ask this House to
confer upon Urban District authorities are by
no means novel in Northern Ireland. The
Belfast Corporation and the Londonderry
Corporation have ample powers to deal with
the char-a-banc problem; and also the
Bangor Urban District Council in 1905
obtained a private Act which conferred
similar powers upon them to those which I
now ask this House to confer generally upon
Urban District Councils.
The objects of the Bill really come under
two heads-those regulating the powers of
urban district councils in regard to motor
vehicles domiciled inside their area, and also
their powers in regard to vehicles coming
from outside their area into their particular
districts. The general effect is to empower
urban authorities to make by-laws determining where char-a-bancs and such vehicles may
depart, where they should stand for hire, and
the place where vehicles can park while waiting to pick up passengers for the journey.
Personally I do not think it is necessary to
dwell upon the great necessity of this
measure. It cannot be denied that in our

With regard to the Clauses themselves,
Clause 1 simply applies to chars-a-banc, the
now affecting hackney
general law
vehicles. Sub-Clause (1) of Clause 1 limits the
power of the authority to fix fares to the area
inside the jurisdiction of the local authority,
which extends to a four-mile radius from the
post office in that town.
Sub-Clause (2) defines what is a char-a-banc
and excludes from the operation of the Act
railway omnibuses and tramcars.
Clause 2, Sub-Clause (1) provides dates in
which proprietors can apply for licences
Sub-Clause (2) of Clause 2 gives the owner
the right of appeal in the event of the
authority refusing to issue a licence.
Clause (3) enables an offence to be dealt with
by the magistrates of the district where
Subthe owner resides, or where the offence was
committed, or where the hiring commenced.
It was felt that this wider power would be
of material advantage in administering
the Act.
Clause 3, Sub-Clause (1) sets out the various
purposes for which by-laws may be made by
the authorities, and Sub-Clause (3) excludes
a railway yard from the operation of the Act.
Clause (4) has for its object the prevention
of over-crowding of chars-a-banc on the
public roads, and the prevention of
disorderly conduct on such chars-a-banc in
areas outside the control of these various
urban authorities. It proposes to apply
Section 11 of the Summary Jurisdiction
(Ireland) Act, 1851, which, at the present
time, only applies to stage coaches, to charsa-banc as defined in this Bill, and also to
omnibuses.
Clause (5) is necessary in order to bring
the Bill into harmony with the present local
legislation in Northern Ireland. As I have
already pointed out, the Bangor Urban
District Council have already got powers.
We do not propose to take away these powers,
but to give them the additional powers
contained in this Bill, with the small
exception that the present area of seven
miles is reduced to the area of four miles.
I beg to move.

Mr. JOHNSTONE: I would like to support

One other point I would like to emphasise
is the question of the speed not only of
char-a-bancs but of motor lorries. I know,
and every other driver in Northern Ireland
knows, that the average speed of the heaviest
of these vehicles is usually between twenty
and twenty-five miles per hour. We all know
how much money is being spent on the roads
at the present time. There is not much use
in spending money on the roads if you are
going to allow these vehicles to drive along
at what is an absolutely absurd speed for

proving offences against the drivers of

Something also should be done either by

way to encourage the use of lighter
char-a-banas. There are a number of quite
light char-a-bancs which do nothing like the
same amount of damage to the roads and I
do not see why the use of those should not
be encouraged. There is one point about

I am sorry that my motion should interfere
with such an interesting discussion, but
according to the laws of the House I suppose
it is unavoidable. The Motion I have put
down on the Order Paper relates to a
matter that I have been very seriously
considering for twelve months. If the House
will remember I had an Amendment to the
Address, which in a measure covered the
matter I am now about to bring before the
House, but the discussion on that Amendment
to the Address was prolonged to such an extent that I thought it better to withdraw it.
However, I have the Motion down there, and
I may tell the House before going into it
that I have had consultations with several
of the leading members of the medical profession, and many others familiar with the
questions with which it deals, and they agree
with me that this matter should be brought
before the House. When I put down the
Amendment to the Address a Member of
the Government said to me, "Are you going
to put the Government out?" I said I had no
intention of doing anything so very serious
and that my whole efforts were directed to
keep the Government in. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I do not know if the Government
understand how stiff a proposition that may
become. No matter how stiff it is unless
their conduct is worse that it has been in the
past, they can depend on me to help them.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
In beginning this question I want to begin
with facts, as facts are stubborn things, and
the curious thing about it is that they are not
more often brought before the House. I have
in my hand some figures that I got almost a
year ago on the 11th April, 1923-showing
the number of deaths from cancer in the year
1922. There were 363 cases of death from
cancer in Belfast and 854 in the Six Counties.
That is a total of 1,217. The question I would
like to ask is this: Can we do anything to
help to reduce this mortality? Can
the Government do anything? I maintain that they can. I have had
a long experience as a professional
man, and in the districts where I reside, with
the object of helping people who perhaps
had little chance of receiving surgical
assistance, we erected a cottage hospital, and
one of the things we did was to do operations
for cancer and other diseases. If the operation
was a mild one or within the capacity of the
local practitioner we did it ourselves, and
if it was a serious one we brought some of
our friends from Belfast who helped us in
our difficulty. I may tell the House that
these men who came from Belfast came very
often at very serious inconvenience, and they
charged such a fee, or no fee, as the local
doctors instructed them. (Hon. Members :
Hear, hear.) One thing that struck me and
impressed itself upon me forcibly all through
my professional career was this, that while
in some cases you appear to have good results
from operations, yet in the long run and as
time passed they proved disappointing. The
tendency of all malignant diseases is to recur
if the patient lives long enough. Our
experience was very disappointing, and I
think it is the experience of all surgeons and
medical men.
In the beginning of this year I was across
the water doing some medical work, and it
was my duty to see in the list of patients I
had to attend, three patients who had been
and were suffering from cancer. Two of them
had serious disease in a part that is difficult
to remove, namely, the rectum. Another had
it in her stomach. They were all young
people. Many people think that cancer is a
disease of degenerating organs, and that it is
only old people who suffer from it. These
three people were all young, fresh people who
had twenty or thirty years of life under
normal conditions, and here they were. They
had been operated on in their county or city
infirmary. They had all the advantages that
special knowledge and skill could give, and
here were the results of the cases as I am
about to tell you. The two men who had
cancer in the rectum had a recurrence of the
growth, and it closed the passage. An artificial opening had to be made, and there they
were lingering on in agony waiting for death
for which they were longing. In the case of
the woman a piece of her stomach had been
cut away, and the disease recurred. In that
case also the passage was stopped and everything she had was vomited. While cancer
operations and secondary operations sometimes give great relief, yet in the majority of
cases all these malignant diseases end in
death, death which is death by inches, and
often the agony is unspeakable.
We live in a scientific age. 1 do not know
that it is wholly an advantage. I think
sometimes we suffer from our scientific discoveries. I think it was the poet Tennyson
who said:
"An infant crying in the night,
And with no language but a cry."
I think he expressed a great truth there, but
notwithstanding that, and be that as it may,
the results of science in medicine have been
amazing and wholly advantageous and beneficial to the human race. In no field of scientific research have there been better results.
The discovery of the bacterial origin of
disease and its treatment by sera and vaccines, together with antiseptic surgery, has
opened a wide field for surgical and medical
efforts which have been most beneficent and
helpful to the human race. You have in this
great city a number of magnificent hospitals
doing brilliant work, and I glad

have
to see that the working classes
supported these hospitals, and that at the
annual meeting quite recently it was announced with pride that they had contributed £20,000 to the Royal Victoria Hospital.
Belfast is a city practically of mushroom
growth, the result of a century and a half
of labour and industry on the part of its
citizens, and it suffers, I think, in comparison with many of the older cities such as
Dublin, London, Edinburgh and Glasgow, in
the fact that the medical staff of Belfast and
the philanthropic people of Belfast have been
taxed to meet a great want that has suddenly sprung up and which has more or less
overwhelmed them. It is the same with
regard to the churches. Nevertheless the
task has been done, and done well, but
Belfast is more or less handicapped by these
conditions.
When you come to the immediate subject of
my resolution, and that is the recent discoveries of the beneficial influence of X-ray,
I would draw your attention to several points.
Superficial X-Ray has been in force for quite
a long time, and it has done wonderful
things for superficial cancer, that is cancer
on the outside of the body and the skin, but
it is not so far as we know able to deal with
cancer that is deep seated, and in the development of X-Ray scientific men have views that
by intensifying the power of the ray, multiplying it enormously, they have been able to
deal with tumours deeply seated in the body
that otherwise were beyond their reach. Let
ine give an example of what I know was the
experience of a friend. A concrete case sometimes brings home a matter like this with
more force than a whole argument. This
friend is a very intellectual man, a man of
wide influence and of wide popularity. He
got ill six years ago. The disease was obscure. He developed dropsy in his abdomen.
He was tapped six times, and after the sixth
time he was brought to Belfast and operated
on.
up
When his abdomen was opened it was
found that the condition was such that no
advantage could be gained by further surgical
interference. The wound was stitched
and he was sent to London for treatment by
radium. The radium treatment helped him,
and he came home much benefited and improved for two years. But a year ago
the disease returned, and that man seeing that all other agencies were useless was
recommended to try this modern plan of deep
or intensified X-Ray therapy. He was sent
to a hospital in Dublin, and I saw him shortly
after he came back. He said that it would
take months before the beneficial result of
that treatment developed, but he was quite
sanguine as to the result. I met him last
week walking about Belfast. He can walk
more quickly than I can. He seems a better
man physically than I am, and I hope and
believe, as he hopes and believes, that he is
finally cured of his disease. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear).
Now, I tell this House, and any medical
man will tell you, that that man by all past
experience was certain to die if this intense
X-Ray had not been applied, and if it had
not had the results of which I have now informed you.
I told the House about three
months ago that I travelled from this House
one morning with one of the most distinguished surgeons in Belfast. We talked
over diseases and the efforts the medical profession were making to combat them. He
spoke of cancer and the results of intense
X-Ray treatment. He told me of two cases
that he had been called upon to deal with,
one of them cancer of the rectum and the
other cancer of the womb. He said according
to his knowledge these were not expected
to live, and he sent them to London.
They were treated by deep X-ray therapy,
and he tells me that apparently both are
cured. I brought that before the House, and
I suggested it was a matter that should be
taken into consideration by this House with
the object of developing that treatment here
in the North of Ireland. There has been
published in Dublin a "Cancer Journal,"
and I find in that "Cancer Journal" that
have been sent by leading surgeons
from Belfast to the Cancer Hospital in
Dublin. At least two cases have been sent
there from Belfast, and there have also been
cases sent from Ballycastle, Coleraine and
Derry. They say plainly in their report
that it is too early to speak of the permanent results of the treatment, and it is
undoubtedly true that the profession may be
disappointed in these cases as they have been
in the past, and that given a sufficient time
the disease will reappear. But whether that
is so or not, with the knowledge that I have
of these cases, I say that so far as I can
judge the results are extraordinarily satisfactory, and that in my opinion we are on
our way to solving the problem of this
terrible scourge that has afflicted the human

cases
race.
With regard to the cost of treatment, that
becomes an important thing in connection
with what I propose to do. The cost of
treatment, I am told-and I speak with
hesitation, because I know it only approximately and the fees may vary according to the
special conditions of the case-is £50 in
Dublin, and £100 in London. As to the cost
of the apparatus, I wrote to the Secretary of
the Cancer Hospital in Dublin, and I have
his reply here, dated 17th November, 1922.
He says:-
I am in receipt of your letter of the 14th
inst., and in reply I beg to state that if
the apparatus referred to is intended for

It is obvious that no poor person can pay
£50 for treatment, and in this matter I speak
only for the poor. The rich are able to
provide for themselves, and do not need our
help. They can go to Dublin or London or
Vienna; our poor people cannot.
I go
further and I say that it is the first duty
of this House, as it is the first duty of every
Government, to provide for the poor, and to
help them.
Now I come to the second point of my
resolution, and that is the treatment by insulin. In 1922 there were 142 people in the
Six Counties who died of diabetes. A new
discovery has taken place with regard to
that malady, a discovery that, if it does
not make a cure certain, goes so far as this,
that a man or a woman who is doomed to a
life of invalidism is enabled by this treatment to resume his or her ordinary work and
to discharge his or her ordinary avocation
for an indefinite time. But in order that it
may be effective a central institution is required in Belfast for both these diseases.
Regarding insulin, work is already being
carried out in this respect in the Royal
Victoria Hospital, and the young surgeon
who is carrying it out tells me that in his
Hoy opinion there should be a central clinic in
the city for dealing with this matter of insulin. You want to train the patients to
test the sugar in their blood and in their
urine. You want to show them how to use
insulin, so that they can go home with a
hypodermic syringe, graduate the test, and
keep in a condition of health. He tells me
what I think is an appalling state of things
to announce in this civilised community of
Northern Ireland, that two of the patients
that he had under treatment, and whom he
had taught how to treat themselves, died
since owing to the fact that they had no
means of getting the necessary insulin with
which to cure themselves.

Mr. POLLOCK: How recently?
Dr. MORRISON: He mentioned that to me
a month ago. I do not know how long ago
it is, but the fact remains that two people
died through their inability to get the insulin that was necessary for their health.
What I want to point out to this House is
that in the meantime the whole field is clear
in the Six Counties. By and by some hospital
-Ballyniena, Coleraine or Larne will be
establishing a system of deep X-Ray therapy,
and perhaps it will be building a wing for
the purpose. I think it would be far better
for the Government to come to the aid of
the people of Ulster, and especially of the
poor of Ulster, by taking this matter into
their own hands and building or fitting up
in the centre of Belfast a hospital that would
meet this want and would provide for this
intense X-ray treatment for those who unfortunately suffer from cancer, and insulin
for the many people in the Six Counties who
suffer from diabetes. Clearly in the meantime Boards of Guardians cannot do this; for
them to send patients to Belfast and to
Dublin, and to pay these fees, is impossible.
Therefore, I think, seeing that that is the
position of affairs, and that the field is comparatively limited for the Government, it is
clearly the duty of this House to pass the
Motion that I have the honour to put before
them, and to ask the Government to make
provision to meet this want and to provide
for these unfortunate people.
I feel that to allow this matter to linger,
and not to bring it before the House for twelve
months, puts a responsibility more or less
upon me. I had hesitation in bringing it
forward-hesitation that, as you know, has
'only been really overcome now. I knew that
this thing was possible, but I was waiting
for developments and to see if some provision would not be made to meet this want.
But now that I have put these facts before
the House the responsibility for the matter
rests on the Members of this House, and it
rests on the Government of this State of
ours. If we are animated by the principles
which I am sure animate every Member of
this House and animate the whole body of
the Government, something will be done to
meet this case. I have talked over the matter
with the Minister of Finance. He has a
clear head, he has a sympathetic heart, he
is open to any argument that you can bring
forward. He and I discussed this thing, and
he received my advances in a very favourable manner. The difficulty was finance. 1
think, when you look at the amount of money
that we expend, the sum of £10,000 can be
easily provided. When you look at the
enormous amount of suffering that this thing
involves, owing to the impossibility of bringing relief to these poor suffering creatures
unless something like this is done, I think
you will see that this is a matter for Government action, and I hope you will support
me by passing this Motion. Then it becomes
not a Departmental matter; it becomes a
matter for the Government, and I am sure
that if you pass this Motion the Government
will consider it as favourably as they can
and see that something is done to meet this
urgent need and to bring about this very
necessary reform. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)

This question is a rather interesting
little sidelight on international politics
and the reason why deep X-Ray
therapy has been boomed to such an
extent is because it is a German invention.
A good many years ago now a very able
French woman, a genius practically, Madame
Curie, discovered radium. Radium is an
instrument which has been used very widely
in the treatment of cancer with results very
comparable with those obtained by deep
X-Ray therapy. I have seen a case myself
where a patient had been condemned three
years before as being an inoperable case of
cancer. She received the radium treatment.
and was still alive, her condition being very
little the worse to all appearance than at
the commencement of the three years. As
far as we know deep X-Ray therapy cannot
do very much more than that. But it was
discovered, of course, that radium produced
this effect by very highly-penetrative gamma

who were always

as they boomed Koch as against

Now it is suggested that the only way to

not such a tremendous matter that it cannot

The question has been repeatedly con-.
sidered as to whether deep X-Ray plant

so far as to say that we should make it
compulsory. This Bill does not go far
enough. I would like to see it extended to
the rate of speed and also to the people who
drive these vehicles, while I further think
that the driver of a vehicle carrying passengers should not be allowed to take drink.
We read very often about people under the
influence of drink being at the wheels of
these vehicles.

Mr. DONALD: I hope I will not be disturbed again. I will not be very long till
I finish. While this Bill that is before the
House at the moment may not interest hon.
Members, in my judgment it is most important. I would like to see a little notice,
such as is on tramcars, placed beside
the drivers of these vehicles to the
effect that
"Your speed is so-and-so,
whether a car wants to pass you or not." Today we find a motor car capable of travelling
at fifty miles an hour kept blowing to get
past, while the other fellow increases his
speed to the danger of his passengers in one
of these big cars. We have had cases where
they have been fined time and again for
excessive speed. The speed of these vehicles
is a very important matter, especially where
the lives of such a large number of people
are involved.
Another thing I would like to see-and my
attention was drawn to it going from Portrush to Portstewart round those narrow
bends-is the driver of a char-a-banc
separated entirely from the passengers.
Very often the passengers get into conversation with the driver, and he forgets for the
moment that he is on a narrow bend, another
car comes round, and we know what happens.
I would like to see some regulation introduced so that the driver of one of these
vehicles would be in a separate place so that
the passengers cannot distract his attention
from anything coming in an opposite
direction.
Another matter to which I would like to
direct attention for a moment is in connection with Clause 2. It was clearly pointed
out by the right hon. Gentleman (Sir Dawson
Bates) that this Clause gives the Local
Authorities power to fix dates for the granting of these licences. But sub-Clause (2) says
that
"Where, upon application for a licence
in respect of a char-a-banc, the Local
Authority either refuses to grant a licence
or grants a licence subject to conditions, in
every case the applicant shall have a right
of appeal to the Ministry of Home Affairs
for Northern Ireland.
That appeal is final. I think that is the
interpretation of the Clause, that if the
Minister decides that the applicant cannot
get a licence that ends it. He has no right
of appeal to any other court. I question
very much if that is elastic enough.
Supposing the members of a Local Authority
are interested in a fleet of cars, they may
say, "We will not grant another fellow a
licence." Supposing also that they could
bring influence to bear on the Government
not to grant the licence, a syndicate could be
set up to keep other individuals from trading
in that particular area. I am simply pointing out that that in my judgment is not just and fair to everyone seeking these licences. I do not
wish to criticise this Bill further,
but before very long I would like to see a
Bill of a more comprehesive character
dealing with all vehicles that use the roads
and embodying greater precautions against
reckless driving, as well as laying down a
speed limit not only for char-a-bancs but for
motor lorries. The latter class of vehicle
should not be allowed to increase speed when

Oral Answer to Question.
SALARIES OF TECHNICAL TEACHERS.
1. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he is now in a position
to make a pronouncement with regard to
the revision of the salaries of principals
and teachers engaged by Technical Instruction Committees in Northern Ireland, as
promised in this House on November 6th,
1923.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown) : A Departmental Committee
has been considering the question of
the salaries of teachers in Technical
Schools and has recently made a report containing their recommendations
to the Minister. These recommendations are
now being examined by the Ministry of
Education and the Ministry of Finance, and
I hope it will be possible to make a definite
pronouncement at an early date.

As regards the second part of this Resolution, the necessity for which has also been

Illegitimate Children (Affiliation
Orders) Bill.
Considered in Committee.
Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
CLAUSE I (Power to make Affiliation Order
upon man alleged to be father of illegitimate
child)-
1.-(1) Where a man is alleged by the
mother to be the father of her illegitimate
child, and has been summoned in accordance with the provisions of this Act to
appear before a court of summary jurisdiction acting for the petty sessions district or place in which the mother resides,
or in which the mother or her illegitimate
child is in receipt of relief from the poor
rates of any poor law union, the court shall
have power, after hearing all the circumstances of the case, to adjudge the man to
be the putative father of the child, and to
make an order upon him (in this Act referred to as an "Affiliation Order ") for
the payment of-
(a) a weekly sum of money not exceeding twenty shillings a week in respect
of the maintenance and education of the
child;
(b) the expenses incidental to the birth
of the child;
(c) if the child has died before the
making of the Affiliation Order, the
funeral expenses of such child; and
(d) the costs of obtaining the Affiliation
Order.
(2) For the purposes of this Act the expression "the mother " means any single
woman who is with child or delivered of
an illegitimate child; and, so far as is
necessary to enable a married woman to
take proceedings under this Act against any
man other than her husband in respect of
her illegitimate child, the said expression
includes such married woman, whether or
not she has married after the birth of the
child, or is living with her husband.
(3) The court shall not make an Affiliation Order unless-
(a) the birth of the child has taken
place;
(b) the man alleged to be the father
of the child appears before the court or
it is proved to the court that the summons
was duly served upon him; and
(c) the evidence of the mother is corroborated in some material particular by
other evidence to the satisfaction of the
court.
(4) The court, in deciding whether or not
it shall make an order for the payment of
the expenses incidental to the birth of an
illegitimate child, shall not take into consideration the fact that the mother is entitled to receive maternity benefit
the enactments relating to National Health
Insurance.

for Antrim (Mr. Hanna) has touched upon.
I fear that in his suggestion there would be
great delay in these cases. Of course, I will
raise it later on on another Amendment, but
if I am in order now I would appeal to the
hon. and learned Member (Mr. Hanna) not
to press his Amendment but to help me in
pressing the Government to bring in an
Amendment later on, say on the Report stage,
that two Resident Magistrates. as in
licensing cases, sit on these cases in the
different districts with an appeal later, on,
if necessary, to the County Court Judge
sitting alone.
I think this whole question is a very
delicate one, and I do not want to labour
the point very much, but I do not think
that the atmosphere of a Petty Sessions
Court is the one in which these cases should
be tried (hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and
so in that respect I certainly am with the
hon. and learned Member for Antrim (Mr.
Hanna) in hoping it may be possible to come
to the agreement which he suggests with regard to the resident magistrates.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: The one question that weighs with me in considering the
aspect of this case that has been presented by
the hon. Member (Mrs. Chichester) is this-
What Court is the most likely to do justice
and fair play to both parties concerned?
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I am satisfied
in my own mind that if we have cases of this
character dealt with by local justices we will
be making a great mistake. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) And I will tell you the reason
why. If cases of this character are to be
dealt with at Petty Sessions it is inevitable
that one thing will happen. We cannot close
our eyes to what we know happens in other
cases. Both parties will be canvassing the
local magistrates in regard to the whole
subject, and very often the two parties concerned

Mr. MARK: As one who has had
experience of appearing before benches of
magistrates in Northern Ireland, I would be
inclined to support the Government in this
case. With one resident magistrate I think
we could trust our magistrates to do justice
throughout the Six Counties. I do not like
to hear this continual finding fault with the
magistrates. In all cases in which I have
been interested I have found the magistrates
to be eminently fair, and I have had
experience of magistrates trying all classes of
cases. Undoubtedly in some parts of Northern
Ireland in regard to the liquor laws changes
were desirable, having regard to the fact that
gentlemen interested in that business appeared on the Bench occasionally when these
cases came before the Court. I do not for
one moment favour two resident magistrates
to try these cases. It would be absolutely
unnecessary. One resident magistraté with
the ordinary Bench of magistrates would be
absolutely fair, with an appeal to the County
Court Judge sitting alone. I do not see why
any miscarriage of justice should take place
under such circumstances.
Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard to the
Court of first instance, the Government feel
that if the Committee considers that the
Court should consist of one resident magistrate sitting by himself they are perfectly
willing to leave it to the Committee. Now
with regard to the Court of second instance,
the hon. and learned Member for Antrim
(Mr. Hanna) suggests that the Court of first
instance should be the Court of Quarter
Sessions with an appeal to the Judge of
Assize. The whole question really turns upon
two points. The first is the question of convenience and the second is the question of
cost. With regard to convenience, the Quarter
Sessions, as the hon. and learned Member
(Mr. Hanna) knows, only meets four times in
the year, and I do not think that even he
would suggest for one moment that you could
bring cases more cheaply before Quarter
Sessions than you could before Petty Sessions.
If he turns to an amendment which he himself proposes to move later on he will find
that he suggests that the legal charge should
not exceed five pounds. I suggest that it is
quite possible to have a case tried at Petty
Sessions for a guinea or two.
Wth regard to the question of cost surely
the hon. and learned Member (Mr. Hanna)
does not suggest for one moment that an
appeal could be undertaken to the Judge of
Assize for the matter of two or three guineas.
All I can say is that my experience of Assize
work has been that when the bill of costs
came in it was more in the nature of twentyfive pounds. It really would be putting an
obstacle in the way of a poor woman getting
redress in a case of this sort. As I have said
there are only four Courts of Quarter Sessions
in the year, and if the Quarter Sessions meets
in or about July, or say, in September, the
next Court may possibly be in March, convenient to the Assize Court, which would
mean that the wretched woman would be
held up for about nine months before having
her case finally decided. Hon. Members will
agree that, with the County Court judges we
have in Northern Ireland, justice would be
done to both man and woman. For these
reasons the Government cannot accept the
amendment.

Mr. ROBB: I beg to move: In Clause 1,
page 1, line 12, after union (poor-law
union, the court") insert "or in which the
said man is at the date of the service of the
summons residing." If hon Members will
look at this sub-section they will see that it

the court of the place in which the
mother of the illegitimate child is in receipt
of Poor-Law relief, the Poor-Law Union. That
is a variation from the general rule which
obtains now in all cases that a man shall be
sued where he lives. I cannot see why in this
case, as well as in every other case, jurisdiction should not be given to the home of the
defendant.
I do not quarrel absolutely with the
decision of the Government to have what they
have provided for here, but I do ask that the
ordinary rule shall be followed, and that
there shall be the provision, which I have
inserted in a later Amendment, that where
a man is sued in a place where he does not
reside he shall be paid a viaticum from the
place where he does reside to the place where
the case is to be tried. In order to attain
that object I propose at this point to insert
that the case shall be tried first of all where
the mother resides or where the mother of
the illegitimate offspring shall be in receipt
of relief from the Poor-law Union, or which
would be the ordinary case and the ordinary
rule of law, the place in which the
said man at the date of the service
of the summons is residing. That gives
provision in respect of the ordinary rule
that a man shall be sued where he lives.
If hon. Members will look further down they
will see that I have an Amendment which is

that where a Court is sitting for a Petty
Sessions district in which at the date of the
service of the summons the man
was rot
residing, and an order is to be made, it

reasonable conduct money from the place

are for the defendant, and I move this Amendment because I do not think it fair that a
man should not be sued where he resides.
Why should a man who is living in Derry be
brought to Belfast Petty Sessions? The

is living in Belfast. That may not be a suffi
cient answer. It is certainly not a sufficient

a perfectly innocent man without means has
a summons served on him to appear in Belfast. when he in fact resides in Enniskillen
or in Derry.

England?

Mr. ROBB: He must be within the jurisdiction. My point is this that it is not fair
that the plaintiff should be entitled to select
her home venue contrary to the ordinary rules

Accordingly I move that at this point, page
