Mrs. CHICHESTER: I beg to move in
Clause 1, page 1, line 12, after "Union
("of any Poor-law Union ") to insert " the
case shall be heard in camera and."
In moving this Amendment I am trying
to look upon the Clause from two points of
view-first, from the point of view of an
unfortunate girl who has been led astray
and betrayed by an unscrupulous man and
takes an action against him as the father of
her illegitimate child; and, secondly, from
the point of view of a man who might be
wrongfully accused by an unscrupulous
woman for purposes of blackmail of being the
father of her child. Now, in the first case 1
can conceive of the great shame which a
young girl might feel in having to give
evidence before a crowd of so-called friends
and neighbours who, I am afraid, especially
if the case is heard near home, would flock,
just as
crows do to the carrion, to the
feast. Then she would have to bear the subsequent and further shame of newspaper
publicity. After all, this unfortunate young
girl whom I have in my mind and am trying
to describe has taken the first downward
step. Is there any need to drive her still
further into the abyss and to make her lose
every remnant of self-respect which she has
left? It seems to me that we want to prevent
her from losing her self-respect, and we
want to try to put her on to the right path
again. The result of these cases being heard
in an open Court might be that the more
decent of the fallen class-the young girl of
whom I am speaking-might rather than
face the publicity and shame never lay an
information against the father, might prefer
to struggle on and try to maintain the child,
and in the end it is the innocent child who
would be the sufferer. It might even lead to
consequences which we hope this Bill wil.
avoid, consequences which were very graphically dealt with by the hon. Member for the
University (Dr. Morrison) on the Second
Reading of this Bill.
Now I come to the second point of view,
the case of the man who has been wrongfully
accused, who is completely innocent of the
charge brought against him, perhaps a man
of high standing, of honour, of integrity, absolutely, as I say, innocent of the charge,
against whom possibly there may be something which would lend a little colour to the
charge-I mean there might be some circumstance which might be brought forward and
used by an unscrupulous woman to bring him
into this case. I believe, and I am sure, there
are many men such as I have described who
would pay anything rather than face the
publicity of an open Court, because, even if
they are completely cleared and exonerated,
the very fact of their having been connected
with a case of this kind unfortunately leaves,
and must leave, a slur and a shadow upon
them. I know it will be said that publicity
acts as a deterrent. It may do in some cases,
but for all the good it does in one way, I am
perfectly certain it does a great deal of harm
in many other ways, and that it does more
harm than it does good. In addition to the
two points which I have endeavoured to put
as well as I could before the Committee, it
seems to me that publicity also provides the

Mrs. CHICHESTER: On the Second Reading the hon. Gentleman, the Parliamentary
Secretary for Home Affairs (Mr. Megaw), in

of justice that has held sway here hitherto.
I would ask hon. Members: Are we to be

more strongly, if the case is going to be heard

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: It is not an
easy matter to follow the speech that has
been delivered by my hon. Friend (Mrs.
Chichester), who shares with me the representation of the City and County of Derry.
She has made a very good and a very strong
case, and there are very many aspects of it
that make a great appeal to our feelings and
to our sentiments,' but I am not quite happy
in my mind that it would be a wise or a
prudent thing for this Parliament to put
into one of its Acts-because this is what is
asked for on this occasion-that all cases of
this kind shall be heard behind closed doors.
I think we must hesitate and ponder very
seriously upon a question of this kind before
putting a Clause of that kind into the Bill.
I quite agree that a strong case can be made
out, and the hon. Member (Mrs. Chichester)
has made out a very strong case for the hearing of cases of this character in private.
But there is another side to this question
that cannot be overlooked. The vast majority
of the people of these countries have a desire
that justice shall be administered openly and
above-board. That is a very healthy sentiment; it is good for justice itself and it
secures in the administration of justice the
confidence and respect of the community.
There are two standpoints that the hon.
Member (Mrs. Chichester) has emphasised,
but I think we have got to look at it from
another standpoint. Unquestionably publicity
does act as a deterrent, but take even the
case of the innocent man who has been mentioned. If he has been cleared by a Court
that sat in secret, and the public have not
been made acquainted with the evidence, will
there not be innumerable whisperings in
regard to what the result was? People
will come to the conclusion that there
was something wrong and it had to be hushed
up, and that the man was guilty all the
same. There is that danger. I have no
objection, if the Government see their way
to accept the suggestion, to leaving it to the
County Court judge and to the resident
magistrates to decide where there are certain
circumstances in connection with a case if
it would not be in the interests of public
decency that it should be heard in camera.
Mr. McGUFFIN: They have that power.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I do not think
they have that power.
Mr. MEGAW: Not magistrates.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Magistrates
have not got that power. The Judge 01
Assize has in certain cases. I am not an
authority upon these legal matters, but 1
do not think the magistrates' Court have any
right to do anything of the kind. I think
if we gave the resident magistrates that
power it might meet all that is necessary in
connection with this matter. Another criti
cism levelled against hearing cases of this
description in open Court is that nauseating
details sometimes manage to get into the
public Press. Unfortunately that is so, but
I have read the newspapers of most countries, and I consider that in this respect we
in Great Britain and Ireland have the
cleanest Press that is to be found in any
country in the world. As a rule, except in
very isolated cases, you can trust to the
discretion, sound judgment, and good taste of
any reporter or editor as to what gets into
his columns. On the whole you may take
that as an accepted fact. On the broad principle that it is not wise to insert a Clause
like this in a Bill to exclude the public from
any court of justice I am opposed to this
Amendment, and on the other grounds which
I have indicated, taking everything into consideration, I think there is no alternative for
us but to allow cases to be tried
as they
have been tried hitherto, with the exception
that the Government, if it thinks it wise to
do so, may give to the resident magistrate
the right if he thinks the facts of the case
warrant it to try it behind closed doors.

the man whom she accused of being the
father of some child that she bore while she
was actually living with her husband. That
is not and was not the intention of the
Government when this Bill was drafted.
What was intended to be provided for was
what was taken up by some hon. Men bers
in the course of the Second Reading, namely
that, where a man found himself married to
a single woman who was in the family way,
and where he was not the father of the child
she was bearing at the time, that woman
might make the putative father, or the person she alleged to be the father of her child,
liable under this Bill. Accordingly, the
course that the Government have taken is
to propose this Amendment that I am now
bringing before the Committee, that is after
the word "against" in line 6 to delete the
words as they follow in the section as it
stands and to insert these other words, so
that the section, if the Amendment is
accepted, will read in this way:-
"(2) For the purposes of this Act the
expression "the mother" means any single
woman who is with child or delivered of
an illegitimate child; and, so far as is
necessary to enable a married woman to
take proceedings under this Act against
the putative father of her illegitimate
child, the said expression includes a
married woman who, at the time of her
marriage, is with child of, or has been
delivered of, an illegitimate child."
I think that carries out the actual
proposals and makes this only applicable to
a case such as I described a moment ago.

is that there is a too rigid scrutiny of the

can almost tell by the appearance of a
claimant whether she is 70 years of age or
not, and such a case is the one I am referring to now. If you are maintaining the
numbers on a uniform basis upon the mere
policy of reducing the claims-(hon. Members:
No, no)-I think it is very undesirable.
This is probably the Vote above all others
that will have the sympathy of this House.
I am sure I speak the mind of the House when
I say that we do not grudge the money we
pay to these poor old people. It has been
earned, if not in signal service to the State,
in the ordinary drudge service of citizens.
They have atttained old age, and we should
not be too rigid in scrutinising their claims.
I rather regret that this service is not under
our own immediate control. I do not see why
it should not be, and I wonder if there is any
hope that it will come under our administration. I am not objecting to the cost of the
service, because I think that on the whole it
is moderate, but I think this is one of the
services we should have under our own control.
We are providing the money for it, and instead
of using an agency we should administer the
service ourselves. I believe we could do it as
effectively, and we could certainly do it as
honestly, as it is being done at present.
The only point I would put before the Committee is whether there could not be some kind
of relaxation in the scrutiny of these claims,
so that claimants who are in appearance over
70 years of age may receive the pension,
although they may not have a birth certificate.
I do not know whether the Minister of Finance
and the Parliamentary Secretary have the
same experience as other Members of the Committee in having brought before them claims
which have been refused. We take this, the
only opportunity we have in the year, of
making this appeal on their behalf, and asking
if there could not be some relaxation in the
scrutiny of claims in order that justice may
be done in cases where an applicant may not
possess a birth certificate, but is obviously of
the qualifying age.

what the hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.

Mr. POLLOCK: I think I mentioned to the
Committee or to the House a year ago, or
possibly more, that the old-age pension question required investigation rather from the
point of view of the abuses that exist than the
grievances which have been suggested by some

Mr. McGUFFIN: Both exist.
Mr. POLLOCK: And also from the point
of view of economy. I did learn from those

mentioned by my hon. Friend where transfers of property were deliberately made in
order to reduce the income of the persons
concerned and thus to qualify them for the

age pension question is one for close investigation and possible re-arrangement. There
was a very famous statesman who made a
remark at one time that it was very difficult to drive two or three coaches through
Temple Bar at the same time. Our hands
have been so full with a variety of matters
that it has been quite impossible to give
the attention to this question that it deserves. I think I should point out to my hon.
Friends, and particularly to those who are
immediately concerned-and it is a question
that should concern every Member of this
House that the co-ordination of the various
forms of public relief, whether through the
machinery of old age pensions, national
health insurance, or Poor-law relief, will
probably form the subject of a great inquiry
in Great Britain. In fact I may definitely
make the remark that the whole question
is at present in a state of fluidity, and the
attention of legislators in Great Britain has
been turned for some considerable time past
to the pressing necessity for some reform
in regard to the distribution of public relief.
It is felt particularly that those persons
who have exhibited thrift in the course of
their lives should not be penalised at the

However, the whole question is quite too
large to be settled at the end of the sitting and
when we have so few Members, even assuming that it was a matter for general discussion. I do not suppose that anything can
be done, and of course we require our Vote.
Let me, however, finally say that I think
the local Pensions Committees do their best.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) They do good
work. Although the Customs and Excise
act as our agents in the investigation of

Government Department that determines

think it may be assumed that the grievances

unnecessarily cover the surface and loom

impression that they are general. I do
not think they are general. At the
same time, it is sometimes very difficult
when a person has got no birth certificate
to give the necessary evidence, and if there
is no corroborative evidence of any kind
that case must necessarily be turned down.
It is a very large question

that count as one day, because if it does I
would like the situation reversed. To-morrow'
we are to take Supply, and I would like

ILLNESS OF THE PRIME MINISTER.
Mr. McGUFFIN: It is rather a delicate
matter I wish to mention to the House, and
I am very glad that the Leader of the House
(Mr Pollock) is present. We read in the
Press, particularly in the London correspondence to the papers here, as to the
condition and progress of the Prime Minister
(Sir James Craig), whose absence fron' the
House we all so much regret. I think it is
rather strange that we have to borrow our
information or learn it from the Press
instead of having it imparted to us in this
House. I would not for a great deal that
the right hon. Gentleman (Sir James Craig),
with whom in his indisposition we so much
sympathize, should come to the conclusion
that this House is indifferent to his absence,
and it might be so construed if the Ministry
does not take the precaution of making some™
intimation to the House, even without a
formal question, as to his progress and the
probable date of his return. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). These are facts which we glean
from the Press.
It was brought more prominently to my
attention to-day when I was travellingtowards the city. I was asked whether the
Prime Minister was in the House or when
he was likely to return. I was able to
assure my questioner that the Prime
Minister was not in the House, but as to
when he was likely to return I did not know.
I think the Ministry should at least credit
the House with sufficient sympathy with the
right hon. Gentleman (Sir James Craig) in
his indisposition at the present time to know
that we would be very anxious to learn from
the Minister of Finance (Mr. Pollock) himself, ΟΙ from some other member of
the Government, as to how the Prime
Minister is progressing and when we are
likely to see him again in his place. Under
the leadership of the right hon. Gentleman
(Mr. Pollock) We have made excellent
progress, and it is a matter for congratulation that in the Prime Minister's absence
we have been able to carry on as we have
done, but we do not want our attitude as a
House to be construed into a suggestion of
indifference as to how the Prime Minister
fares at the moment.
Mr. POLLOCK: I would say, with all
deference, and subject to your ruling, Sir,
that the rules of the House do not offer any
special opportunity-
Mr. SPEAKER: That is quite so. It does
not show any indifference on the part of
the House, I am sure, that this matter has
not been mentioned. It is not exactly what
I would call a public matter, but at the same
time I am sure the House appreciates what
the hon. Member (Mr. McGuffin) has said,
and I have no doubt that the Leader of the
House (Mr. Pollock) can perhaps give him
some information on the matter.
Mr. POLLOCK: With your permission, Sir,
I may say that it is very well known that
the Prime Minister's progress has been very
satisfactory.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I have not heard it.
Mr. POLLOCK: And that we hope to see
him in this House taking part in our
deliberations once more after the Easter
Recess. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear). .

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 3rd April, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
SPEED LIMIT FOR MOTOR VEHICLES.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs if he will consider taking
steps to impose a speed limit for heavy motor
vehicles driven in the cities, towns and
villages of the Six Counties.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): The mere fixing of a speed
limit would not of itself be sufficient to
ensure the prevention of accidents, and it is
frequently a matter of difficulty to prove at
what rate a particular vehicle may have been
travelling.
Experience has shown that a much more
effective power is that contained in Section
1 of the Motor Car Act, 1903, under which
it is sufficient to show that the vehicle may
have been driven recklessly or negligently or
at a speed or in a manner dangerous to the
public.
The police have been impressed with the
necessity of enforcing the law and prosecutions have been taken in such cases. The
magistrates can of course assist greatly by
dealing adequately with cases which may
come before them.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
reply, does the right hon. Gentleman not
consider that speed has a great deal to do not
only with the safety of the public, but with
the safety of the clothes of the public as well?
Speed has a great deal to do with mudsplashing.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I quite agree.
Dr. MORRISON: Arising out of that
question, could the Minister give us any
assurance that this important matter will be
dealt with by legislation at an early date.
The whole question of these motor lorries
and heavy traffic?
Mr. DONALD: Before my right hon. Friend
replies, may I ask if it is not a fact that the
police authorities are against the regulation
of the speed? A speed limit would do away
with the whole question of accidents and so
forth.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think the police
have ample power to deal with the question.
The whole question is a matter of proof.
Express instructions have been given to the
police to pay particular attention to these
things.
CURFEW AND SUMMER TIME.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will consider withdrawing the Curfew Order when the alteration
of the clocks to "Summer Time" takes place,
on the 12th-13th instant, or whether he will
grant some reasonable extension, such as
three o'clock in the morning, new time, to all
seaside and health resorts in the Six Counties.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The question of
whether the Curfew hours should be modified
in view of the introduction of summer time
will be considered, but it would be premature
to make any statement on the subject at
present.
MANAGEMENT OF ULSTER PAVILION.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he contemplates the appointment of an assistant to the manager of
the Ulster Pavilion at the British Empire Exhibition, and if so, whether he will be an
Ulsterman.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): No definite decision has yet been
reached on this matter, but I can assure the
hon. Member that, whereas it is important
that the best man available should be appointed, the view of the Ministry has always
been that the post is one which, other things
being equal, should properly be filled by an
Ulsterman.
LOCAL GOVERNMENT ELECTION
ORDERS.
4. Mr. MILLER asked the Minister of Home
Affairs if he has anything to add to his answer
of Thursday, the 13th March, with regard to
Elections Orders in connection with the forthcoming Local Government Elections; whether
he is aware that hundreds of candidates and
their agents and public officials are anxiously
awaiting these orders to enable them to make
preparations for the nominations which, in
some cases, are fixed for the 15th of April.
and whether he can explain the delay in the
issue of these orders.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The delay in issuing
the rules prescribed by the Ministry for the
forthcoming Local Government Elections is
due to delav on the part of the printers. I
assure the hon. Member that the Ministry is
fully cognisant of the necessity of ensuring
that the orders should be in the hands of
officials and persons interested at the earliest
moment, and I am informed that copies will
be ready for issue during the next few days.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Once a year, there comes the opportunity to a Minister to justify, or endeavour
to justify, at any rate, his administration of
his Department, and also to take hon.
Members into his confidence and to tell them
something of his policy and what his aims
and hopes are for the future. Personally, 1
think that it is an opportunity which should
not be lost, because, when asking the Committee to vote substantial sums for the carrying out of great public services, I think
Members of the Committee are entitled to be
placed in possession of the truth and nothing
but the truth. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
I know that it is held in some quarters
that to make a detailed statement in instances
like this is rather inviting criticism. I may
say that I do not take that view, and even if
I did. I do not object to the criticism which
comes from Members in this House, because,
so far as my Department is concerned, I
have always found such criticism to be well
informed, to be reasonable, helpful, and constructive.
I think that the importance of the work
which the Ministry of Labour in Northern
Ireland is doing will be gauged and appreciated by hon. Members when I say that we
are charged with the great responsibility of
looking after and safeguarding the industrial
lives of our working classes from the day that
they enter employment until the day that
they finally leave it. The regulation of wages
in those industries that are liable to sweating, the preservation of industrial peace in
our midst with all that that means to our
workers, our employers, and the general community, the administration of our Truck
Acts, Workmen's Compensation Acts, Health
Insurance, Unemployment Insurance, dealing
with employment problems generally, and
relief works require the services of a competent and able and willing staff; and I am
glad to have this opportunity of expressing
my indebtedness to the staff of the Ministry
of Labour for the very loyal and invaluable
services which they have always so freely
rendered to me and through me to the
Province of Ulster. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
It is true to say that besides these
measures which I have mentioned, the
Ministry of Labour has many important
Supply-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

[Mr. Andrews.]
duties to fulfil. In the regulation of the work
of the Department we aim at obtaining
tho maximum economy consistent with
efficient maintenance of a very important
public Department. The most difficult
problem that we have had to deal with
has been adinittedly that of unemployment.
It has given great anxiety to my colleagues
in the Government, to my staff, and to myself,
but I am glad to be able to assure hon. Members
that the dark clouds are gradually passing
away and that a brighter industrial future
lies ahead. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is gratifying to know in this connection
that our rate of progress is even more rapid
than in Great Britain, because while in April.
1922, the difference between the percentage of
unemployment here and in Great Britain was
10.47, the difference to-day is rather under 4.
In the linen trade, in January, 1923, the enormous percentage of 26.37 of insured persons
were unemployed; to-day there are less than
9 per cent. of our insured population in the
linen trade without work. Again the total
figure of unemployment is less than it has
ever been since our Government came into
power, and it is very gratifying to know that
the 43,000 of our people who were on
systematic short time a few years ago are now
fully employed. (Hon Members: Hear,
hear.)
I now turn to the Estimate which hon.
Members will find at page 115. Sub-head A
deals with salaries, and it will be observed
that there is a reduction of £6.972. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) That is largely due
to the fact that there has been an automatic
reduction in staff in our Labour Exchanges
owing to the fall of unemployment to which
I have already referred. The reduction
would have been greater but for the
fact that we have changed our policy
as regards branch Exchanges, and that where
previously we have had men in part time,
service who were responsible for providing the
premises and paid the rent and lighting of
same we have now got full time men, the rent
and taxes appearing under another head.
There is a reduction of £1,750 in travelling.
removal and subsistence expenses. This is
principally due to the fact that instead of
having Our inspectors all living in
Belfast we have domiciled them over our Six
County area with a saving amounting to the
equivalent of the sum which I have
mentioned.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman are they then only available for
service in those particular districts?
Mr. ANDREWS: They are available to go
wherever the Ministry of Labour tells them.
but as a rule it is natural that we should
decide that they would act within the area
in which they live. The amount under the
head of rent and taxes, fuel, light, water,
cleaning and heating has been increased by
about £2,000. That is due to our change of
policy as regards our branch Exchanges to
which I have already referred. The amount
for furniture and fittings is increased by
£1,307 due to the fact that we are providing
for the furnishing of our new Labour
Exchange in Corporation Street. Under subhead C5, new works, alterations and additions,
there is a reduction apparently of £9,500, but
that is due to the fact that this time last
year we hoped to be able to procure a building which was already in existence and would
be suitable for our requirements. Owing to
certain legal difficulties we were advised not
to take that building, and the result is that
with the approval of the local Employment
Committee who have given a great deal of
thought and attention to this matter, ground
was taken in Corporation Street. The buildings upon it, which were of a very ramshackle
nature. have been demolished, and tenders
and plans are now being prepared to build
there an edifice which I hope will be worthy
of the province and the work we will be
called upon to do.

will remember that when our Trade Board

At the same time it is only right that I should

other heads in which they are included. Howthe position is as I have explained, and
I hope that hon. Members will feel that there
is no use in passing Acts of Parliament in this
House, unless at the same time we take the
means to see that these. Aots are complied
with.

Unemployment Fund. Owing to the fact that

very much in the same way as I look upon
the annual balance in connection with a
business firm. It is a time to look back and
recognize the mistakes that have been made,
and to endeavour to see that they are not
made in the future. It is a time to take
stock of the entire position and to look forward to the future with confidence and hope,
and as, regards the work of the Ministry of

creeds in this loyal Province of ours. I beg
to move.

was pointed out that this Act affected very

country were handicapped by the policy that
was adopted in the towns as to the standard
rate of wages. I pointed out that the shirtmaking industry, which meant £2,000,000 to
rural Ulster and the out-workers, had been
killed by this Act and these Trade Boards.
I want to give a concrete example. The
Prime Minister told me that rural Ulster
would be looked after and its interests carefully guarded. I want to read a letter which
I had from a businessman who is a member
of one of these Trade Boards, with regard
to an industry that was started in Ballymoney. That industry was killed by the conditions under which it existed in competing
with prices in Belfast. Here is the letter:-
Referring to our conversation about Trade
Boards, I have had a conversation with Mr.
Pettigrew, who was the secretary of this
industry, and he tells me that Messrs.
Douglas & Green, Donegall Street, say they
cannot open their factory in Ballymoney as
they cannot afford to pay the Trade Board
wages, which are the same in Ballymoney as
in Belfast. I understand they are most
anxions to do that, but the carriage to and
from Belfast and the present rate of wages
make it impossible.
Now, there is an industry in a prosperous
little town that has been smothered according
to that evidence by these Trade Boards fixing
wages that are unreasonable. This gentleman also tells me, and I would like the Committee to grasp this fact, that he does a large
amount of tailoring, he is a draper spending
a large amount of money in employing a large
number of hands in making up clothes, that
the rate of wages imposed upon him by these
Trade Boards will result in the tailoring
trade going out of these little provincial towns
and all being concentrated in Belfast to the
detriment of rural Ulster. I would put it to
the Labour Members who are present in this
House that if vou kill a local industry and
compel everybody to come to Belfast to buy
a suit of clothes and have it made up, you will
compel the Ulster people to fall back on
readymades. Readymade clothes will be produced in bulk in England and sent over here,
and even Belfast will not profit by this unfair
system that prevails. Seeing I am shut out
from the other question, that is all I have
to say. I promise the Minister of Labour
that I will give him some facts to consider
when we come to deal with National Health
Insurance, and I will not bring it on the Committee without giving him proper notice.

"inclusive" is mentioned bonus is implied
8 I was just wondering if the bonus is added

With reference to the question mentioned

of view, which has no interest, of course, in

cake and eat it. I would like an answer

mistress of the suit, and it should be at her
discretion whether an action is brought at

Or if one has been dismissed

The CHAIRMAN: I think I may enlighten
the hon. and learned Gentleman. He must
not mistake mere rhetorical emotion for heat.
(Laughter).
Mr. HANNA: There was no heat.
Mr. MEGAW: I do not quite understand
how there can be so much rhetorical emotion
on an occasion of this kind, because the
Government are as anxious as the hon. Member is to do the best thing, and I think that
on a little reflection he will see perhaps that
the method adopted by the Government is
not a bad method after all. It is of great
importance in eliciting the truth that the
information should be laid as soon as possible,
and that there should be no time to think with
regard to the person against whom the charge
should be brought. The sooner a charge of this
kind is brought the less likelihood there is
of blackmail or anything of that sort. Besides, it is in accordance with precedent that
has been found useful elsewhere. I think
that the Amendment which the Government
intend to bring in on the Report Stage will be
found to fit in most admirably, and will bring
about the redress that is sought for. I may
state here the idea that the Government have
in regard to the Amendment of the Bill, so
as to enable redress to be had in the case of
the death of the woman between the time of
the information and the hearing of the
application, or in case she dies at childbirth.
The information here is intended to be
the information on which the summons will
be founded. After the information on oath
has been given and the summons has been
issued, the proceedings are started. They can
be brought before the magistrate at any time.
They may be adjourned till after the birth
of the child, but if they are brought before
the birth of the child the lines on which the
Government propose to proceed are that a
deposition should be made or evidence given
before the magistrate, by the mother-aboutto-be, and that the accused person should
have an opportunity of being present and of
cross-examining her just in the same way as a
deposition is made before a magistrate at the
present time. The evidence will be taken
down in writing, and the depositions containing the evidence and cross-examination may
be used in any Court thereafter if the woman
herself is unable through illness or through
death to be present at the final hearing. That
will apply to the hearing not only before the
magistrate but also in the Court of Appeal.
We have a precedent in criminal cases for the
use of depositions in that way. This is not a
criminal case, but we have the same principle
embodied in one of our Emergency Acts, that
the deposition once it is made can be used
at the hearing of the action if the witness is
not available. Where a deposition is taken
in that way, that is, where each party has
an opportunity of being heard, we think that
justice may be done by allowing such evidence
to be given for what it is worth. It never can
have the same effect as oral evidence, but it
is the best that can be done under the
circumstances. Hon. Members will see that
it is absolutely impossible for cases of this
kind to be sustained if the evidence of the
only party who can give direct evidence on
the subject is not available.

Oral Answers to Questions.
DECLINE OF LOUGH NEAGH
FISHERIES.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can furnish any information regarding the results of the Public
Inquiries into the causes of the decline in
the fisheries of Lough Neagh, held at
Antrim, Toomebridge, Stewartstown, and
Lurgan, by Mr. W. J. M. Menzies, of the
Fishery Board of Scotland.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): As the hon. and gallant Member
is doubtless aware, the Public Inquiry relative to the Lough Neagh Fisheries was
not initiated by my Ministry. On inquiry,
however, at tho Imperial Secretary's De
partment I am informed that Mr. Menzies
only concluded his investigations on the 24th
ultimo, and that his report has not yet been
received.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that reply,
may I ask the Minister of Commerce is he
aware of the great interest this inquiry has
created in the country? The people whom
I represent are particularly anxious to
know the result.
Mr. ARCHDALE: This is a reserved service and not in my Department, but I will
try to get the hon. and gallant Member and
his constitutents any information I can.
Colonel WOODS: Thank you.
ISSUE OF INCOME TAX CERTIFICATES
TO SPIRIT GROCERS.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he can expedite in any way
the issue of the necessary Income Tax Certificates to Spirit Grocers making compensation claims under the terms of the Intoxicating Liquor Act, 1923.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): I need hardly remind the honourable and gallant Member that Income Tax
matters form part of a reserved service outside the jurisdiction of this House. If, as I
presume is the case, the query relates to cases
where applicants for compensation have mislaid or destroyed their notices of assessment,
I shall, if the hon. and gallant Member will
let me have particulars of the cases he has
in mind, make representations to the Imperial Authorities that such applicants should
be facilitated as far as practicable.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer might I ask the right hon. Gentleman
if he could in any way, as I asked in the
question, expedite the delivery of these certificates as I have been told the spirit grocers
cannot get any answers?
Mr. SPEAKER: I think the hon. and
gallant Gentleman is asking over again the
question to which he has had an answer.
Colonel WOODS: Not quite. I merely
wanted to make it clear that these people
cannot get any answer from the Income Tax
Authorities. That means that if their claims
are not in by a certain date they cannot
comply with the order.
Mr. POLLOCK: I take it for granted that
if these claimants have paid their income tax
they will receive from the Surveyor their
necessary certificates. I cannot understand
anything further that is required, and if
there be anything different in the mind of
my hon, and gallant Friend if he would set
it out more clearly and fully I would be glad
to know of it.
Colonel WOODS: It is only a matter of
time.
Mr. SPEAKER: I think notice should be
given of any further questions on this point.

3. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will issue a report of the
cases and findings of the Courts of Referees
for 1923, under the Unemployment Insurance
Acts.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): I have considered the suggestion
made by the hon. Member that I should publish a report of the cases and findings of
Courts of Referees established under the Unemployment Insurance Acts, which cases
numbered almost 4,000 in the year 1923, and
have come to the conclusion that the value
of a document of this nature would not
justify the very considerable expense of its
preparation and publication, especially as
their findings turn mainly upon particular
questions of fact. It is the cases which come
before the Umpire that involve points of
general principle and lay down precedents,
and I hope that the publication of his decisions, which I propose to make from time
to time for the information of hon. Members
and the public, will meet with
my hon.
Friend's approval.

SECRETARY
on
THE PARLIAMENTARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): My right hon. Friend the Minister
of Labour gave such a clear statement of the
position of unemployment to the House
Thursday last, showing the improvement in
the linen industry, and referring to other
industries where there was no improvement
at
will
the moment, that hon. Members
realise the problem with which the country
is faced. I recognise more than ever that
what our people want is work. They are
passing through a time of anxiety, harassed
through the lack of means of existence, but
bearing their burdens manfully in the hope
that the dark clouds may pass. Both skilled
and unskilled workmen are suffering alike. I
could not use language laudatory enough
of the local authorities for the great
assistance they have given my right hon.
Friend (Mr. Andrews) and myself. They
have created relief works of public utility at
a cost of almost £3,000,000 to absorb the unemployed in their various districts, but there
is still a big majority for whom no work can
be found, and they must feel disappointed
and depressed as they face the future. Their
scanty savings are already used up, their
union funds are exhausted, and, perhaps,
their unemployment benefit is exhausted also.
This Bill is introduced to meet the present
situation by extending the benefit period, and
so helping to tide over this difficulty.
Our
unemployed cannot be permitted to go without the necessaries of life.
Dr. MORRISON: Hear, hear.
Mr. GORDON: We all know the evil that
is caused by prolonged unemployment. The
workman loses his skill, and consequently
through time becomes unemployable. As
our industries are interwoven with those of
Great Britain, it is most desirable that there
should be uniformity in our Insurance
Schemes. This was recognised by the
Shillington Committee, which recommended
that we should continue on the main on
parallel lines with Great Britain. From
the outset the Government has adopted this
recommendation as the basis of its policy,
and this House has frequently confirmed its
action in the passing of the various Unemployment Insurance Acts from time to time.
The object of this Bill is to secure for the
workers in Northern Ireland the same benefit provisions that obtain in the United
Kingdom.
an
The Bill, first of all, is to give the Ministry of Labour power between now and
October, 1924, which might be looked upon
as the emergency period, to grant an extension of uncovenanted benefit. Existing legislation, both in Northern Ireland and Great
Britain provides for the payment of benefit,
whether covenanted or uncovenanted, up to
aggregate of 26 weeks, which will
terminate on the 17th October, 1924. Those
who have been continuously unemployed
from mid-October, 1923, up to the present
moment, will have exhausted all their rights
to covenanted benefit and uncovenanted
benefit, so that the proposal in this Bill is
to meet an emergency between the present
moment and mid-October, 1924. The Ministry is in close touch with the Imperial
authorities on the subject." They have in
contemplation a similar Act, and have
already introduced into the Imperial House
two Bills. One is a Bill of considerable
magnitude, which, it is anticipated, will
require some time to pass through the
House of Commons. The other is a
Bill of an urgent nature to continue
the existing rates of benefit for the
period which we are now facing until the
enactment of the larger measure. For the
twelve months following the middle of
October, 1924, to the middle of October, 1925,
no provision has been made in the recent
Act passed through this House for uncovenanted benefit.

The second point is that we want the same
rate in the second benefit year as we have in
the first benefit year-26 weeks covenanted
benefit and 26 weeks uncovenanted benefit, or
a maximum of 26 weeks over all. The third
point that I desire to draw your attention to
is with reference to special schemes that are
referred to in this Bill. There are what are
known as special schemes of insurance by industry. The only scheme that is in operation
at the moment is the Insurance scheme,
and we want power in this Bill to see that
any schemes of insurance outside the Insurance Act, though closely allied to it, must
pay the same rates of benefit as obtained in
the national scheme.
The final thing that I want to draw the
attention of Members to is that this Bill is
introduced with a desire to do away with the
gap.
Mr. GRANT: Hear, hear.
Mr. GORDON: When uncovenanted benefit was first introduced it was provided that
if a person had received benefit for a certain
number of weeks he had to stand off benefit
for a gap. Now with the prolongation of
unemployment and the depression in trade we
feel that the imposition of these gaps is a
considerable hardship upon the unemployed,
and my right hon. Friend the Minister of
Labour and myself desire the House to give
us power to remove the gap so that those
who require benefit and who have passed
through this long period of unemployment
may not suffer the gap but may have their
benefit paid to them continuously. I do not
think that I need say anything more by way
of recommending this Bill to the Members of
the House. I feel that every Member of the
House will just be as anxious as my right
hon. Friend and myself to see that as the
days advance with little improvement in
trade at least we will endeavour to make the
lot of the unemployed less hard than it is
at the present moment. I beg to move. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear).

employed, but as that is not the case at

I welcome the Bill that has been introduced.
I am glad that the hon. Gentleman (Mr.

But are we putting that into action? Are
we protecting our people and making proper
provision for them? Come with me to the
quays at Londonderry. Is it not a fact that
there are Sinn Fein and Nationalist stevedores there, employing men working at these
quays, who have adopted the system of
bringing in a certain number of men from
Donegal ? They employ them in three
batches in the week. They employ a man,
say, for two days' work and four days'
unemployment, and then another batch comes
along, so that there are three batches of
men finding employment in the Northern
area, and each receiving four days' unemployment benefit paid by the ratepayers of this
country. The Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) will know whether that is correct
or not. I fancy he has heard of it before
now. Indeed I have heard it said that there
is no remedy for it. If there is no remedy
we ought to close down. If we cannot find
a remedy in this area to keep the Sinn
Feiners from coming over the Border and
finding employment here, dodging the Executive, it is time something was done
for the protection of the bona fide unemployed who are walking the streets of our
cities and who are getting a mere pittance
of fifteen shillings a week.
Take another case. I am told that in the
Silent Valley-I was told this by a gentleman in this city, a man of position, a man
who ought to know, and whose authority 1
would be very sorry to question,
and he is referring to very recent times-that
120 men are coming over the Border and finding employment in the Silent Valley, County
Down. Is this true or not? If it be true is
the Minister of Labour, is this House, and are
we doing our duty if we allow these people
to come in just as they wish while our own
people cannot find employment? We are
allowing the risk later on of these people
being thrown on the labour market here in
the Northern area, and we will have to find
the Unemployment Fund to provide for them.
I say the thing is unfair; it is time it was
exposed; it is time something was done
in order to stop this thing which is prevailing all around our Border. Take Enniskillen
and various other smaller places around.
There is a continuous dropping over the
Border. They are coming in and they come
before the Union and ask for benefit and outdoor relief. They and their friends come
begging around. They are coming from the
Free State. They are a certain amount of
tax directly and indirectly on our various
resources. They have got to be kept alive,
and many of them were shooting down loyalpeople a year ago or two years ago. They are
now being provided for by the people
privately or from local funds.
I say the
Ministry of Labour ought to wake up in this
matter. If they want powers; if they want
their position strengthened; if they want
legislation they will get it. Have they been
refused legislation by this House? They have
only to come and present their case, because
it is an honest one, and I am sure we will
support them. There must be no preference
given to people coming over the Border with
all sorts of subterfuges and lies trying to
make believe that they are residents here and
coming for employment which is denied to
our own people.
To my mind it is the administration that
is wrong. You talk now of giving unemployment relief from the age of fourteen in the
next Bill. You may carry on as you wish.
but if you will not put down your foot and
administer well what you have you are going
to make a serious mistake if you think the
taxpayer will be relieved by anything you are
doing here. The taxpayer does not object in
the least to helping his own people who have
been sympathising with him in his trouble
and now in their trouble look for sympathy
from the taxpayer in the Province.
ought all to stand together-stand or fall

Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: We have
listened to a very interesting debate on a
very small measure of reform brought in by
a representative of the Ministry of Labour.
It has opened up a lot of very interesting
topics in connection with unemployment and
the economic position of this country, and
we have also had some interesting statements
from some of the Members of this House.
I was specially interested in the speech of my
hon. Friend, the Member for East Belfast
(Mr. Donald.) It is most refreshing in these
days to find a représentative of Labour advocating the complete sweeping away of all
these Government Measures for Unemployment, for Insurance,
Mr. DONALD: And for everything else.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: And for every.
thing else; a complete sweeping away of all
these things and of any interference by the
State, and getting back to the old order of
things when the employer and the worker
together tided over all their difficulties. 1
do not think we have many supporters of
Labour who would advocate that sort of
thing. I think we have got to face facts as
we find them. There has been a gradual
evolution of thought in connection with social
questions and whether we like it or not we
have got to face the position to-day that in
regard to these great questions of unemploy
ment and other matters the State, whether
for good or for evil, has got to handle them
and do something for the masses of people
who are out of work. But the State cannot
go on indefinitely doing this sort of thing.
That will not solve the economic problem
that all these things are the result of. Some
of the hon. Members who have spoken this
afternoon seem to think that the State has a
pocket without a bottom, and that they can
go on bringing in measures of unemployment benefit and gradually extending it until
you reach the stage indicated by the hon.
Member for East Belfast, when the State
had either to find work for the people or pay
them a week's wage. If those two things have
got to be done, you are eventually going to
empty the Exchequer entirely and everybody
will march about absolutely independent,
supported by the State until the State's
resources are completely exhausted.

Really we have got to think a little bit deeper,
if I may touch the academic side, on the
question. My hon. Friend, the Member for
North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin) has deplored,
and we all deplore, the departure of skilled
men, skilled engineers and mechanics of
different kinds who are going away to other
countries and finding employment there.
There was one Statesman in Great Britain
who did put forward what in my judgment
was a really solid remedy for the trouble,
but the masses of the working classes in
Great Britain would not accept the remedy.
That was protection for the home market
and protection for the workers, a policy
that all other countries in the world have
adopted. The hon. Member for North Belfast
must know that the most prosperous country
in the world to-day is the protected country
of the United States of America, and they
are able to absorb all this surplus labour
from Great Britain and Ireland. They are
E able to pay those workers a good wage and
they are living there in happiness and comfort. As my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Finance, told us the other day in a very
[ interesting speech, one person in five in
America is able to provide himself with a
handsome motor car. Whether it is a Ford
th or some other type of car I do not know,
but at any rate that is the condition' of
affairs you find in other countries. Therefore, my opinion is that until you have
tackled this question from an economic
old standpoint you are going to have these
the recurring periods of unemployment to contend
with, and you are not going to solve them
by continually paying doles. You have got
go deeper, otherwise what is the result?

In connection with this matter some of the
speakers have referred to certain things not
being right in the way of administration. I
am sure the Minister of Labour will deal
with those matters. Unquestionably abuses
do exist at the present moment, and I am
sure that the Department concerned is aware of
a lot of these abuses, and I presume they are
doing their best to remedy them-especially
in those cases where people have received
benefit who are not entitled to it, and in
other cases where people could find work but
are not willing to do so as long as they can
get a small outlay from the State without
having to do a hard day's work. Unfortunately such people do exist to-day, and
it is sometimes lost sight of by those who
pass unmeasured criticism on the representatives of the workers. They seem to infer
that the workers are not doing anything
themselves, and it is well for us to remember
in connection with this question of unemployment that the benefit comes from three
sources. It comes from the State in the first
instance, but the State after all is the
ordinary taxpayer of the country.
Some people seem to think that the State
is a different thing altogether; that it is
something away in the clouds or away in
fairyland where they have nothing to do but
search in some hidden place and any amount
of wealth will be produced. The State is the
ordinary taxpayer of the country. Then the
employer pays another portion, and that goes
to the unemployed. I hope my Labour
Friends will recognise that those of us who
are employers have never grumbled or complained about bearing our share of the burden.
If we happen to continue in business at all
I am sure we shall go on meeting our obligations in this respect.

I do not intend to keep the House any great
length of time over these Amendments, the
object of which is to add two sub-Clauses to
Clause 2. The first is to allow commutation
to take place in any case where a weekly
sum has been made payable by any person
under an Affiliation Order. A man can
apply to have this weekly sum commuted by
the payment of a lump sum subject to the
sanction of the Court as to the amount. The
Court has the right to fix the amount of the
commutation. I think that possibly it would
get away with some difficulties that might
arise upon the Bill as it stands. Take, for
instance, man against whom an Affiliation Order has been made who might wish
to get married after paying under that
Affiliation Order for five, or six, or seven
years. It would save him from a sort of
enforced celibacy, and perhaps from the uncomfortable position he would be placed in
having regard to the fact that he would have
to pay this weekly Order with the collector
calling at his door and possibly his wife paying this money. No man would care to marry
under such circumstances and we might be
opening a door to more evil if we made it
compulsory in that way. I ask that he should
have a right under this sub-Clause to apply
to the Court to have a lump sum fixed which
would be payable by him into the Court, or
in any other way the Government may think
better, and through that Court it could be
administered by way of weekly payments to
the mother on behalf of the child.
The second Amendment that I move is to
allow, prior even to the Affiliation Order, an
agreement to be entered into by the mother
and the putative father arriving at a lump
sum which would be paid into the Court. 1
quite understand that possibly there may be
in Northern Ireland a mother who rather
i
than face the Court, and getting all the publicity would suffer and try to rear her child
without asking any payment. In cases of

Order it is quite possible by the addition of

for the payment of a lump sum which would
be administered through the Court in any
way the Court may think just and right.
That agreement, I have insisted in the
Amendment, should be witnessed by two
solicitors, one representing each party, or,
if the Court thought right, it could be witnessed by a magistrate, a resident magistrate,
a clerk of petty sessions, or any other person;
but I want to make sure the mother would
be taken at no disadvantage and that the
lump sum which would be settled in payment

sum and not a trivial or insufficient sum.
There are many women in Northern Ireland
who would not like the trouble of going into
the witness box and would prefer that an

enable the woman in question to emigrate, to

under the Order and give him a chance of

where he could marry without having these

a real grievance with

of the average

Secondly, you may have the mother or the
foster-mother handing over the child to
some woman in a remote part of the district
where there is no school, and you have no
power to prevent this. This Amendment of
mine suggests you should give the power.
Under the Children Act you have in each
poor-law union an inspector appointed to
look after these boarded-out children. Very
often he is the relieving officer. You have
also this further provision made by the State,
namely, that the inspector of the Society for
the Prevention of Cruelty to Children will
look after these children, and I must say
that this Society does an immense amount of
very valuable work in Ulster and all over
the Empire (hon. Members: Hear, hear)—
but there are difficulties in the way of
effective interference in many instances. That
is just the problem the Government are helping us to solve. Long before the child has
reached the stage when a criminal prosecution can intervene I maintain that with
sufficient inspection, with an intelligent relieving officer and with a collector who would
take a real interest in the child you would
have discovered that the child was being
neglected, that it was in an unsuitable home,
and if you wanted to save its life it should
be taken away once.
That cannot be done even by the inspector
of the N.S.P.C.C. He is armed with very
large powers, and I think that he has in
the main exercised them very wisely and
very judiciously. He has this power-and
this power only I think-if he finds a child
being deliberately neglected, criminally neglected, he can order its removal for safety
to the workhouse. There are, however, many
of these cases where there is no criminal
neglect but where there is negligence, carelessness, and unsuitable environments that
endanger the child's life and in many cases
produce its death, where perhaps the fostermother or the mother herself is doing her
utmost for the child. It may be necessary to
remove the child from its unsuitable surroundings in the interests
of
the child's
welfare, and indeed of its life, and it may be
desirable to do that without the prosecution
that according to the present law must follow
any removal on the part of the inspector of
the N.S.P.C.C. If the child were removed.
as I suggest should be done, on the report of
the inspector, I think it would be but right
and proper. Supposing the child for instance
were a deaf mute. The poor-law authorities
have no power to deal with anything but
paupers. This child is not a pauper. It is
in receipt of 5/- a week or 10/- a week, and it
would be illegal for a Board of Guardians to
spend money on it and its mere sustenance.
They could not send it to a home such as the
Deaf and Dumb Institution, or if it were an
imbecile they could not send it to any institution for those so afflicted. Therefore, I think
that they should have power in this case
to add a little, if it were necessary, to the
money that child is in receipt of from its
putative father and board it out in a more
suitable house, that might be selected by
the Guardians after consultation with those
interested. In nearly all workhouses and
Boards of Guardians now there is a committee of ladies who look after these things
for the Guardians and who have done very

The hon. Member has referred to the law
of seduction, but in all other cases in connection with these sexual matters the law
always requires corroboration, however slight.
It does not necessarily mean another witness.
My right hon. Friend the Attorney-General,
when the point was being argued in the
earlier section referred to what might be
taken as corroboration-if the girl had been
seen walking with the man, if there were
letters of any kind, if there had been an
admission of any kind. It certainly stands
to common sense that the law that has been
generally accepted by those who have had considerable experience, even more experience
than the hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Cooper) should be maintained.
Is it to be laid aside and are we now to go
back to the principle that this is a case in
which corroboration shall not be necessary?

As a matter of fact, in the English affiliation
orders-but perhaps it is, heresy to speak of
what has been accepted law in England-and

certainly should ask the House to pause

If the introduction of this qualifying clause

soon be

NEW CLAUSE (Recording of Evidence
and Non-Abatement of Proceedings in Certain
Cases)-
(1) As soon as a summons has been issued
for the appearance of, and duly served upon,
the man alleged by the mother to be the
father of her illegitimate child, the Court
may proceed to hear such evidence as may
be adduced on oath and shall record the
same in writing. Such evidence shall be
read over and signed respectively by each
witness who may have been examined, and
shall be signed by the resident magistrate
hearing the same.
The record of such evidence verified as
aforesaid shall be admissible as evidence in
any proceedings under this Act, where it is
proved that the witness who gave such
evidence is dead or so ill as to be unable
to attend or where his attendance cannot
be procured.
(2) Proceedings under this Act shall not
be determined by the death of either the
mother or the putative father of an illegi
timate child.
In the case of the death of the mother,
the proceedings may be continued by the
person having the custody of the child, or,
if the child is in receipt of relief from the
poor rates of any Poor-law union, by the
Board of Guardians of that Union. In the
case of the death of the putative father,
his personal representative may be made a
party to the proceedings.
Brought up and read the First time.
Mr. MEGAW: I beg to move: "That the
Clause be now read the Second time." This
new Clause is being introduced in accordance
with a promise given by the Government when
this Measure was last before the House. It
is to provide for the case where the mother
dies during the course of the illness. As the
Bill stood, if the mother had died, her
evidence could not have been made available.
This Clause to some extent really introduces
a new principle. It goes rather further than
anything that has been admitted as evidence
before. As hon. Members know, in criminal
cases where depositions are made before
magistrates, and where the accused person
has had an opportunity of being present and
cross-examining when the evidence is given,
that evidence is recorded and may in the case
of the death of the person who has given
evidence be given in evidence in any subsequent proceedings. We have adopted that
principle in this Bill so that in case the mother
dies in childbirth or before the proceedings
can be brought to hearing her evidence can
be made available. The clause goes further
than that. It also enables the evidence of
all witnesses who may have given evidence,
whether corroborative or evidence of any
other kind, to be taken in exactly the same
way. It will be committed to writing, read
over, and signed by the witnesses and the
Resident Magistrate, and the accused person
may have an opportunity of cross-examining
on it. In the case of the death of any of
these parties, that evidence may be read in
any subsequent proceedings, and may be considered by the magistrate. The same
principle has been applied to the putative
father. He also has had his opportunity of
coming before the magistrates, and he may

that we are in. An hon. Member here has
charged servants of ours with fraud and with
collusion with our enemies. He has stated
here, on the floor of the House, that he is in
a position to prove these charges. I would
like, as a private Member of this House, to
know from you what can be done in this
matter. We have heard from the Attorney-
General his point of view, and we are entitled
to know, even as a matter of edification, what
can be done, or what privileges a Member of
this House has to make such charges.
Mr. SPEAKER: The privilege of a Member
of this House is to say practically anything
he likes, provided he does not overstep the
bounds of Parliamentary language in criticism
of the Government or of individuals responsible to the Government. That, I think, is
elementary. Of course, if he makes a statement regarding a particular individual, and
repeats it outside the House, the privilege no
longer applies, and an action for libel or
slander can be taken.
Mr. DONALD: On a point of order. Does
that not place a private Member of this House
in a peculiar position if he receives a letter?
I have received a letter, with a name signed
to it, from Derry, stating that this thing did
occur, and the same letter, 1 understand, was
sent to the Minister. Therefore the thing
did happen; there is no doubt about it.
Mr. SPEAKER: I think we all know that
everything that appears in a letter is Lot
necessarily true, and, of course, there again
this question of entering the courts of law
comes up. I am sure the Minister will be
always glad to have information.
Mr. DONALD: I understand the Minister
did take action to prevent this thing from
occurring again.
Mr. COOTE: He tried to take action.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Would I be in order in
suggesting to the right hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Andrews), in view of the case that has been
presented by the hon. Member for Tyrone and
Fermanagh (Mr. Coote) that he would see his
way to set up a Committee of Inquiry into this
matter to preserve the dignity and honour
and honesty of his own Department, and, in
a degree, in a similar way the dignity of the
Government? I think it is an occasion that
calls for such a Committee, and if he sets up
a Committee of that sort I think it would
meet the situation to some extent.
Mr. ANDREWS: I am not prepared to
take the course suggested in respect of unsupported statements of this kind, which, in
my opinion, do not warrant an inquiry. I
want to say here and now absolutely definitely
that no case of fraud of any kind has been
brought before my notice in which the wrong.
doers, no matter who they are, have not been
prosecuted, and it has been left to the Courts
to decide what sentence it was proper to mete
out to them. A Court of Law is the proper
place for such cases, if such cases exist, to be
decided, and I think it would be wrong of me
to agree to set up.any Court of Inquiry where
I find there is no need for it.

himself not admit, as an honourable man.
that he heard and knew of this thing going on
in Derry and tried to stop it?
Mr ANDREWS: I would like to ask the
hon. Member what thing.

Sir DAWSON BATES: In submitting this
Estimate for the upkeep of the prison service,
hon. Members will see that we
propose to
effect a considerable saving in the amount
this year-a saving of £47,570. Last year's
Vote was £154,627, and now we are asking for
£107,057. The main cause of the reduction is
due to the more peaceful conditions prevailing in the Province, and that results in a
reduction in the prisoners, and also doing
away with the Argenta. It might interest
hon. Members to know the number of
prisoners that we propose estimating for
as contrasted with the number last year.
In Armagh we are estimating for 85 as
against 100 last year; in Belfast 400 as
against 500 last year, in Derry 100 as against
180 last year, in the Larne internment camp
250 as against 500 last year. That 500, of
course, includes internees on the ship. As
regards convicts in Scotland we are estimating for 65 this year as against 70 last
year, convicts in England 95 as against 116
last year, Borstal inmates in England 24 as
against 40 last year. There happen to be
two Borstal inmates in the Free State at the
present time and we hope soon to get them
away. There were 35 last year. Altogether
in figures we estimate 1,021 as against a total
of 1,542, a very considerable saving. With regard to prisoners, other than internees, I
would like to make one or two observations.
It is the policy of the Government, as I have
stated on previous occasions, to bring back
from England and Scotland all the convict
and Borstal cases, but before this can be
done we must have suitable accommodation
for them here. During the year the Government have taken expert opinion on the subject of how best to provide this accommodation, and there is now a prospect of the
necessary expenditure being found under the
Colwyn Committee Award, which will enable
us to go ahead, and before long I hope we
may be in a position to make a definite statement in regard to this matter. We hope, in
connection with this, to put Belfast Prison
in such a condition as to receive these convicts, but at the present time we are not
including in the estimate any provision with
regard to that until we know exactly how we
stand, but I might point out in connection
with tho new prison that we hope to have
works there which will provide the convict
with some technical training which will be of
use to him when he is released and help
him to find employment.
With regard to Sub-head D-materials and
tools for manufacture in and on farms
attached to prisons-this is a new Sub-head
in the Estimates and we ask for a sum of
£5,565. It would appear as if this was an
increase on what we asked last year, but it
is due solely to a better system of accounting
and it really represents the cost of the raw
material that goes to the gaol for the purpose
•

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Sir Dawson Bates]
either of manufacture of articles for use in
the gaol, or for articles to other
Government Departments to whom they are
sold. Hon. Members will see that as against
the sum of £2,880 for raw materials for
manufacture, the receipts on this head
amount to the sum of £3,214 There is one
Sub-Head I would likely to draw the special
attention of the House to, namely Sub-Head
"J"-Gratuities to Prisoners." Increased
provision is asked for. The money expended
is for the assistance of prisoners when they
are released. It is desirable that the
money which is provided for prisoners who
are released should be paid through the
Prison Aid Societies, who render very
valuable assistance in helping prisoners after
their release to find employment. At the
present time these Societies are mainly
supported from voluntary sources. and I
think it is only right, having regard to the
valuable work that they do, that they should
get aid from Government funds. As the
result of the action of these Prison Aid
Societies, many a criminal who is released
is helped on in life afterwards, and I hope
hon. Members will approve particularly of
this item. I would like to point out that
there has been a steady improvement in the
prison service and in the discipline in the
prisons themselves. Many of the warders
were new to the work, and I would like to
bear testimony to the very valuable assistance which has been received from the
staffs in the prisons.
I would like to say a word or two in regard
to the question of internees. I am glad
to say that we have got back to more normal
conditions as far as crime is concerned. It
was stated at the time the Law Charges Vote
was presented to this House that the number
of indictable offences for last year was 770 as
contrasted with upwards of 1,600 the previous
year; a reduction of something like 50 per
cent.. but, because we have got back to more
or less normal conditions so far as regards
the amount of crime committed, representations are made by individuals urging, because
this is so, and because life and property are
now safe in Ulster, that the various measures
which had to be taken by the
Government to bring that condition
of affairs about should be
removed.
Some of the individuals who make these representations have very short memories. They
seem to forget the chaotic condition in which
Ulster once was, and I do not think they fully
realise the measures the Government took
to bring the present condition of affairs about.
One of the measures taken by the Government, and one which proved most successful,
was internment. Hon. Members will see that
this year we are budgeting for 250 internees
as against 500 last year, and I hope that
later on that number will be found to be
excessive.
I have been struck by the type of petitions
which I sometimes get on behalf of these
internees. I have one in my mind at the
present moment which was sent in on behalf
of one of the most violent Sinn Feiners who
ever occupied the attention of the police. In
that petition it was represented that this man
was a law-abiding citizen, and had only committed one crime in his life. What are the
facts? Within a period of five years that
man had committed twenty-three different
crimes such as house breaking, holding up.
assaults, and so on, and had been convicted
for them. The extraordinary thing about
that petition is that it is signed by very
responsible citizens in Belfast of both creeds.
I must say that it is a very appalling thing to
me that this should happen, and the only
conclusion I can come to is that either the
people who sign this class of petition are
coerced into doing so or else they have not
taken the trouble to find out for themselves
what are the real facts.
Mr. DONALD: Did you release him?
Sir DAWSON BATES: No; I did not.
Captain MULHOLLAND: Who signed the
petition?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I would like to
point out that the case I have mentioned is
only one of many. I do not want to weary
the Committee by going into other petitions
of the same kind.
Mr. DONALD: Would you not tell us who
signed it?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I do not think, perhaps, it would suit the hon. Member (Mr.
Donald) opposite or his friends if I told him.
I would like to point out that all these
internees have the right to have their cases
investigated by the Advisory Committee.
That Advisory Committee consists of a barrister, who was lately Deputy-Recorder of
Belfast, another barrister, who is a Roman
Catholic, and an ex-officer of his Majesty's
Army. In addition, all these cases are very
carefully investigated from time to time
both by the police and by the officials in the
Ministry of Home Affairs. All the circum.
stances are weighed up so as to prevent any
possibility of any miscarriage of justice
occurring, and I would suggest to the people
who are asked to sign these petitions that,
after all, those in authority and those who
know the facts of the case are perhaps the
best judges of whether or not a man is
wrongly interned. There is a very great
responsibility on the Government in regard
to these internees. The Government are
responsible for the maintenance of law and
order, and I must say I do not think it is too
much that the Government should ask the
law-abiding public at large for their support
in these restrictions. (Hon, Members: Hear.
hear.)

of them have been removed from time to
E time, and I hope that in the course of time

not think any of the other items call for particular explanation on my part. Most of
them are self-explanatory, but I shall be only
too happy to try to elucidate them further

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw): On behalf of the Home Office I wish
to reply to the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Coote)
3 who has just sat down. He has propounded
a policy that would commit the Government
on a person making a declaration or taking
an oath-how much attention he would pay
to the terms of that oath is another question
-to the step of sending him home. What
was the cause of internment in the first
instance? Internment arose owing to the prevalence of outrage and murder. The police
had information with regard to those who
were responsible for it; they were not able
to produce such evidence as would bring
about a conviction, but still it was wellknown that the people who were interned
were the persons who were responsible. What
The
are the facts? On the 22nd May, when our
first internments were made, outrage in this
Province had reached its very highest figure.
From the date of the first internments, and
while the internments were takir place,
crime and outrage decreased propo ionately
until it disappeared altogether. The Government claim that by taking the action it did,
and by making the internments it did, it put
a stop to that particular form of crime.
The suggestion that is made by the hon.
Member (Mr. Coote) is this, that the men
who were responsible for that state of affairs
should be let loose on the community
against the advice of the police. We are
taking the advice of our police, who know
the state of the country, and who give us
reports from time to time, reports on whether
these men or any of them might safely be
released or not. Are we in face of those reports to go and open the jail doors, and to
allow those men out if they go through the
form of taking an oath but do not believe
in the substance of it at all? They will take
the oath in order to get out. One after another, men have stated that they were ready
to take the oath, but it was well-known that
that was done only for the purpose of leaving
them free to commit outrages. We hear
from time to time about the reorganisation
and attempted reorganisation of the I.R.A.
Are we, forsooth, to let out the leaders, the
men who were commanders when particular
outrages took place? Are we to let these men
out to assist in the reorganisation of the
I.R.A. throughout our Six Counties?
I should like the Members of this Committee to know that the question of the
internees is considered, and very carefully
considered, from time to time. The number
in the jail and the internment camp is being
reduced from time to time on the reports
that are given by the police. Restrictions,
no doubt, are sometimes required. Now there
are fewer restrictions, and men very often
get out on their own bail. In getting out
in that way they do acknowledge the
existence of the Northern Government, because no man can sign the form without
recognising his responsibility to the Government and to the King. But I wish to emphasise this point, that the time has not
come when every person who says he is ready
to take the oath of allegiance could be safely
permitted to return to the place where he
had been responsible for a great deal of disorder before.
There is just one other point that I wish
to mention. It has been said that we have
power to put these people outside the country
altogether. We have no power to do that.
We have no power to alienate; we have no
power to deport. We do impose restrictions
when necessary under our own Act: but we
have no power under the Act of 1920, the

Charter of our own Government, to send one
