prevent him going to certain parts, but we
can go no further than that. I think I have
dealt with all the points that have been raised
by the hon. Member for Fermanagh and
Tyrone (Mr. Coote). He, to some extent,
reflects what has been said from time to
time. I assure this Committee that the Ministry of Home Affairs recognise their responsibility. They are desirous of relieving their
internment camps, but up to the present they
find they cannot do so with safety. When
one looks at the state of affairs before the
internments were made, and how one day
eight or ten fires would occur in one city,
doing perhaps £100,000 of damage, what is
£22,000 to the damage that was done by the
firebugs? We believe we are acting for the
safety of the community by the policy we are
adopting, and, while we are desirous of
relieving ourselves from the liability of supporting these men, we believe it is in the best
interests both of the financial position of our
country and of the law and order of the
country itself. (Hon. Members Hear, hear).
Mrs. CHICHESTER: May I say a few
words in regard to this Estimate, and strike
perhaps rather a different note from my
neighbour, the hon. Member for Tyrone and
Fermanagh (Mr. Coote)? I would like most
heartily to congratulate the Minister of Home
Affairs on the Estimate which he has put
before us. I think when he is subjected to
so much criticism in this House, and certainly
outside this House, that he may be glad to
hear the views of some of the Members within the House who do not wish to criticise but
who wish to congratulate him. I think that
he should be greatly congratulated on the
Estimate, particularly on the condition of
affairs which has led up to the reduction
in the amount asked for. I think that
we have rather short memories, and that we
are very much inclined in the country to forget the conditions which have been recalled to
us by the hon. and learned Gentleman who
has just sat down, the Parliamentary Sec-
-retary, the terrible conditions which were
reigning not only in Belfast but throughout
the Six Counties comparatively recently. The
fact that conditions are so different is due
largely and I want to emphasise this, because I do not think the country realises it
as it should-to the firmness and the courage
which has been displayed by the Minister of
Home Affairs in dealing with these matters,
and, as in an instance which he gave us
to-day, in facing the tremendous pressure
brought upon him by both parties to release
men whom he knew to be a danger to the
community. I think if we congratulate him
on nothing else we should congratulate him
on the firmness and courage which he displayed in that instance and I know in many
others. The Government have exercised a wise
discretion in the past with regard to these
internees, and I should have thought that
we could feel assured we could leave this
question of letting the internees out safely
in their hands.
I cannot understand the attitude adopted
in this instance by the hon. Member for
Tyrone and Fermanagh, because it does not
seem to me to be quite consistent with the
attitude which he adopts outside this House
in his own constituency. I would remind
him that the fact that, as he stated here today, he was able to go about with no other
protection than a blackthorn is largely due,
entirely due I might say, to the efforts of
the Minister whom he takes great pleasure
in, shall I say, criticising. I wish again to
congratulate the Minister of Home Affairs on
the Estimates he has presented.

Mr. COOTE: I know it will not depend
on the question, because it is a very vague
question and it is capable of any construction
but I think it is hardly worth while bothering

says that in the Act of 1920 we have no power

Mr. COOTE: Are there no prisoners in
England?
Mr. BEST: They are not internees.
Mr. COOTE: Then I will change the word
and say criminals, because an ordinary
criminal is in my opinion a far more estimable person than an internee, who may be an
unconvicted murderer. You have power
to deport a man convicted of petty theft,
and you have no power to deport a
man who may lead a murder gang.
Really the argument will not hold water. It
is like an argument the Government will
resort to when they want to appear wise.
They say such and such a thing is not in
the Act of 1920 and we are bound by its
provisions. We are administering the law in
our own area and the Government of a State
has a right to do what it likes within that
State. If there are citizens in the State who
will not obey the laws of that State, who will
not comply with any loyal sentiment or with
any oath to be good citizens of the State, the
Government has the right to ask them to
leave the State, and I submit that you have
done it. I will give you the case of Sweeney,
the Postmaster of Omagh, a rabid Sinn
Feiner. He was such a notorious Sinn
Feiner that he was suspect and his house was
raided. With the British Government you
entered into an agreement whereby that man
was sent into Southern Ireland and a man
from Southern Ireland was sent into your
area and took the oath. Yet you say you
cannot do anything. If you have the
resources and the courage and determination
to do it you will do it, and the
people will respect you for doing it.
You took this man Sweeney out of the Post
Office at Omagh in agreement with the British
Government and transferred him to Southern
Ireland, and you get a gentleman from
Southern Ireland to serve at Omagh. All this
is done within the last couple of years, and
yet you come in with this sort of religious
tone. You say the thing is debarred by the
Act of 1920. It is all humbug, with great
respect to my hon. Friend (Mr. Megaw). He
is a lawyer and I am not a lawyer. It is not
common sense, and the law is common sense.
We must have a right to protect our area
and we are protecting it. I submit that there
is nothing in the argument whatever.
That is all I wish to make plain. I wish
to make it absolutely plain that we have the
machinery of administration in the Home
Office. The right hon. Gentleman is the head
of it, and right down through it-in every
fibre and every muscle and indeed the whole
network of the machinery-we have men who
can be relied upon. They will not interfere with

see that they do play the game. I can assure

you need not be afraid of the internees. They
will deal with them. The internees who came
home are behaving themselves. If they behave
themselves and obey the law subject to the
permission and to the control of these men.
we shall try to release as many as possible

there is one remedy, and if you have not

The CHAIRMAN: I might explain to the
hon. Member that the ordinary prison
system for short time prisoners is one thing.
The whole regime of the prison is entirely
different from that of a convict prison.
Where the prisoner has to serve a long sentence the whole conditions of the prison are
made to conform to it.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Then bring the Derry
prisoners to Belfast. We have room enough,
and make Derry Prison a place for convicts.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have tried to explain that it would not be economical to
convert Derry jail into a convict prison.
What we propose to do is to convert one
wing of Belfast jail into a convict prison.
We cannot treat convicts in Northern Ireland any worse than they are treated in
England and Scotland and elsewhere. With
regard to the proceeds of prison labour all
the articles manufactured at present are sold
to other Government Departments. I do not
think it has been suggested for one moment
that that is competition with labour outside.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Is that in every instance
the case? Is it only for Government purposes that this manufacture takes place in
prison?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It is so, with the
exception of mats. I am informed that
there is no local manufactory for mats, and
I do not think we go into competition with
our prison mats.
Mr. MEGAW: I think it is necessary, perhaps, that I should reply to some of the
observations made on this question. The
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr.
Grant) has raised points that certainly
require an answer. The first point that was
made was there were occasions on which internees were released on £10 bail, and on
other occasions some have to give sureties as
well as their own personal bail. Perhaps I
can answer that question and the question
of the other hon. Member for North Belfast
by telling them the system that has been
adopted by the Government in regard to release from internment. First of all no
person could be released who did not come
before the Advisory Committee and get recommended by the Advisory Committee for
release. Latterly it was felt that the condition of affairs enabled the position to be
somewhat relaxed, and we have revised the
procedure from time to time. The police
themselves send us reports as to the various
internees and the conditions on which each
particular internee whom they recommend
for release ought to be released. We in a
great many instances adopt that. It was
felt that the time had come-that was in the
latter part of last year when relaxations
could be made. The state of the country
permittted. The police were consulted-not
only the Royal Ulster Constabulary but the
officers in the county of the Special Constabulary. Each Internee in each county was
considered by himself in the presence of the
County Inspector of the Royal Ulster Constabulary and in the presence of the County
Commandant of the Specials. Every case was
considered, and the report on each of these
men by the intelligence officers who were
also present, was considered, and the cases
that were marked down, in which release
might be safely granted and on what conditions, were there and then determined.
In a number of cases it was felt from these
reports that we might make an experiment
of releasing some persons on their own bail.
That brought about a system by which
some of the less aggravated cases were released on their own bail. That was on the
advice of the Constabulary, not only the
Royal Ulster Constabulary, but the other
Constabulary. When a statement is made
here about the Constabulary-the position of
the Constabulary here I can assure this
Committee that nothing has been done by
this House or by the Government without
the advice and without the assistance of the
Constabulary in its various branches. Thus
it was thought prisoners might be released
on their own bail. Certain cases were felt
to be more difficult. The police recommended
that certain releases might be made on bail,
perhaps on their own and certain sureties
being given. In these cases security has
been given and sureties have been given.
Each case depends upon its own respective
merits. There is no general system. Each
police report is considered and the man
is released where it is felt he can be
released if he complies with the conditions
laid down.

Up to

was felt that perhaps that system might be

character that their bond could not be taken,
and who could not be let loose at this stage.
The police reports on these men are of such
a character that to take their bond would
be running a risk that the Government have
no right to run. I can assure the Committee
that the position with regard to each internee
is reviewed very carefully from time to time,
and is considered in consultation with the
police. The Government will do its best to
have the persons who are interned released
at as early a stage as is consistent with the
safety of the community. One thing I want
to make absolutely plain is that these powers
under the Civil Authorities Act still exist,
and it is important that from time to time

10 APRIL, 1924.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 10th April, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answers to Questions.
DISCHARGE OF TEMPORARY OFFICIALS
1. Major SHILLINGTON asked the Minister
of Finance if he will state how many temporary officials have been discharged from the
different Government offices during the last
six months; and if it is a fact that all these
officials whose services have been dispensed
with were ex-Service men.
FINAN-
The PARLIAMENTARY AND
CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): As with very few
exceptions all temporary appointments in Government Departments are given to ex-Service men, it follows that those temporary
officials whose services have from time to time
to be dispensed with are of necessity almost
all ex-Service men.
The total number of temporary officials
discharged during the last six months is 76
men and 22 women, of whom 71 men and 1
woman fall within the category of ex-service.
All these employees were engaged either for
seasonal or
emergency work or to meet
pressure at the Labour Exchanges where
their services are no longer required owing
to the reduction in unemployment.
COST OF UNEMPLOYMENT FUND.
2. The following question stood on the Paper
in the name of Colonel Woods:
To ask the Minister of Finance whether he
can state the amount chargeable per head of
insurable population in respect of the Unemployment Fund, as at the end of the financial
year.
Colonel WOODS: I beg leave to postpone
question number 2.
CLAIMS UNDER INTOXICATING
LIQUOR ACT.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister
of Finance whether he is aware that an
order, published in the local Press, by the
authority dealing with compensation claims
under the Intoxicating Liquor Act, states
that all claims must be received on or before
the 14th inst., and if he is aware that it is
necessary for claimants to furnish with
their claims an Income-tax assessment certificate, and if he can assist in any way to
facilitate qualified claimants in obtaining
these certificates within the limit of time
allowed by the administration.
Mr. BARBOUR: The answer to the first
portion of the hon. and gallant Member's
question is in the affirmative. As regards the
latter portion of the question I would refer
the hon. and gallant Member to the reply
to the question addressed by him to my right
hon. Friend the Minister of Finance on the
8th inst.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, is the hon. Gentleman aware that
spirit grocers, who have perhaps been assessed
at £300, have been able to show cause for an
abatement, and therefore, if they have not
been served with notices, and cannot get them
when it is necessary, they are particularly
hard hit in not being able to get a certificate
from the Income-tax people?
Mr. BARBOUR: The first part of the
question raises a matter referred to an
authority which was constituted by our own
Act-namely, the authority dealing with
compensation claims; and, while it is desirable to proceed as rapidly as possible in the
adjudication of these claims, I am sure the
Committee will only be following the wishes
of this House if they take such measures as
will ensure justice being done. They have
power to extend the period during which
those claims may be put in. Of course, the
notice given in the Rules and Regulations
was published as long ago as 14th March.
So reasonable time has been given. Where
just cause can be shown, I am sure the
Claims Tribunal will take into consideration
such difficulties as my hon. and gallant
Friend's friends have met with.
SUPERANNUATION FOR TEACHERS
IN TECHNICAL SCHOOLS.
4. Mr. DONALD (on behalf of Mr.
MCMULLAN) asked the Minister of Finance
whether he intends to prepare a scheme of
superannuation for teachers in technical
schools, and if so will he produce it at the
same time as that now being considered for
teachers in secondary schools; and whether
he is aware that a complete official register
of the services of such teachers was kept by
the Department of Agriculture and Technical
Instruction, Dublin, from the time of the
inauguration of technical education, in
1899, and latterly by the Ministry of Education for Northern Ireland, and that, in the
case of these servants of the public, complicated questions of private financial interests in their schools do not arise.
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Mr. BARBOUR: It is the intention of my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance,
in accordance with Section 70 of the Education Act (Northern Ireland), 1923, to frame
a superannuation scheme, in consultation
with the Ministries of Education and Home
Affairs, in respect to teachers in technical
schools, but he is unable to undertake that
such scheme will appear simultaneously with
that now being considered for teachers in
secondary schools.
The Minister is aware that a register of
the services of technical teachers was kept
by the Department of Agriculture and Technical Instruction for Ireland, and is now
kept by the Ministry of Education; but the
register is by no means complete, as it only
includes whole-time service in technical
schools, and contains no complete details of
educational service that may have been rendered in other directions either in Ireland or
in Great Britain. He recognizes that some
of the complicated considerations which
arise in dealing with secondary teachers are
absent, but it is feared that when the details
in the case of technical teachers have been
fully explored, other difficulties almost as
great will emerge before a satisfactory scheme
can be framed.
ASSISTANCE FOR LOCAL INVENTORS.
5. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he is prepared to render
financial assistance or other encouragement to
local inventors.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I regret to inform the
hon. and gallant Member that no Government
funds are available out of which financial
asistance can be given. (Laughter).
My Department is, however, always ready
to assist inventors by securing for them information as to manufacturers amongst whom
their inventions would be likely to find acceptance, and to render to them such further
assistance as properly falls within its sphere.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, I would like to know from the right
hon. Gent. if when he considers that he already made advances to encourage agricultural projects he might consider arranging
for something like what is suggested in the
question.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman if he is prepared to consider the
claim of an inventor when I point out he is
a Member of this House?
Mr. DONALD: May I ask my right hon.
Friend if he is prepared to supply motor-cars
with these inventions on them to each Member of this House?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I am aware that our
mutual Friends, the hon. and gallant Gentleman (Colonel Woods) and the hon. Member
for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin) and myself
are inventors-(hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
-and, therefore, I would be inclined to do all

of money being given for that purpose
PARTICULARS AS TO
INTERNEES."
6. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the names
and home addresses, charges or sentences
against each, and the present whereabouts of
those persons known as "internees."
The MINISTER of HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): There are in round numbers
280 persons who have been interned by my
order as suspected of being about to act in a
manner prejudicial to the preservation of the
peace and maintenance of order in Northern
Ireland. The majority of these persons are
confined in Larne internment camp-the
balance being confined in Londonderry and
Belfast Prisons. As the numbers decrease
from day to day owing to the releases which
are being effected, any return of the nature
asked for by the hon. and gallant Member
would be misleading, and in any case I do
not consider it would be expedient in the
public interest to publish any such return.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, would it be possible for anyone calling at the Ministry of Home Affairs to see a
list such as is mentioned in the question?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I cannot add any
thing to the answer already given.
COMPENSATION FOR DEPENDANTS OF
FALLEN SPECIALS.
7. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether compensation has been
paid to the families or dependants of the men
of the Royal Ulster Special Constabulary who
were killed, or to the constables who were injured, at Clones in 1922, and if so, was this
compensation a charge against the Northern
Government, or was it paid by the Free
State Government.

CONSTABLE FRANCIS MORTESHED'S
BRAVERY.
8. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state what
action, if any, has been taken by the Inspector-General, Royal Ulster Constabulary,
or the Government, to recognise the conspicuous bravery and devotion to duty
displayed by Constable Francis Morteshed,
College Square Barracks, Belfast, when effecting the arrest of an armed raider at Belfast,
on the 7th March last?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Cases where members of the Force display conspicuous bravery
and devotion to duty are dealt with by the
grant to the member of the Force concerned
of a reward in accordance with the Regulations made under sub-Section (5) of Section
4 of the Constabulary Act (Northern Ireland)
1922, or by some other suitable mark of recognition.
The case referred to by the hon. and
gallant Member has, however resulted in a
criminal prosecution, which is still sub
judice, and it would, therefore, be improper
and contrary to established practice to consider as yet any award to the member of the
Force referred to, until the criminal proceedings have been finally disposed of in the
Courts.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, does the right hon. Gentleman not
consider that it is not a matter whether a
person is guilty or not guilty, but whether an
immediate reward should be given when a
person who is armed is arrested?
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
The reward is not given, and does not depend
on the result of the trial. I must, however,
deprecate with all the force at my command
the putting of a question in reference to a
criminal case which is still pending. That
case was pending until this morning when the
jury found the accused guilty of murder, and
he was sentenced to death. But I think for
the use of hon. Members in future it is a
matter that ought to be taken into account.
No question ought to be put in reference to a
case actually pending and at hearing.
Colonel WOODS: It is not a matter of
criminal proceeding. Is the right hon.
Gentleman not aware that this is a matter of
gallantry on the part of a constable?
Mr. SPEAKER: I must say that it would
have been my duty to disallow the question if
I had thought it right, but I considered this
was a matter of recognition of immediate gallantry, and it certainly did not occur to me
that it was in any way dealing with a case
that was sub judice.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask is there to be no
limit to the number of questions asked in this
House?
Mr. SPEAKER: Absolutely none at present.
The position is that up to date we have never
got within ten minutes of the time in which
there were sufficient questions to cause a
block, and that being so I see no reason to
prevent hon. Members asking as many questions as they like. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.)
MUD-SPLASH GUARDS FOR MOTOR
LORRIES.
9. COLONEL WOODS asked the Minister
of Home Affairs whether he will consider the
advisability of granting permission to local
inventors of mud-splash guards to affix their
inventions to Government motor lorries,
and, if so, will he at the termination of a
two months' wet weather test, call for official
reports upon each device so used?
Sir DAWSON BATES: The proposal
suggested by the hon. Member would not
solve this problem as it would not be a sufficiently comprehensive test.
At the recent tests held by the Royal Automobile Club the appliances submitted for
examination and report were subjected to
all essential tests, including kerb tests,
stability tests, mud-splashing tests, tests
regarding interference with the maintenance
of the vehicle, tests for simplicity, ease of
fitting, first cost, upkeep, amount of projection, noise and appearance.
It would not be possible by the means suggested by the hon. Member to ensure that
the appliances submitted for examination
complied with these various tests, and the
only method by which the test of an effective
mud-splash guard could be ascertained would
be on the lines indicated in the recent tests
held by the Royal Automobile Club.

granted to his Majesty to complete the

will come in course of payment during the
year ending on the 31st March, 1925, to
provide for grants to local authorities in

aid."
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Estimates
submitted to the Committee for the service
of the financial year 1924-1925 under the head
of Grants to Local Authorities have been
prepared on bases which I trust are now
familiar to the Members of the Committee.
They show a net decrease of £122,121, but
that is largely accounted for by the temporary grant in relief of rates on agricultural
land which was passed by the Committee for
the service of the financial year 1923-24 and
which is not included in the present estimates. Accordingly, excluding this item, it
may be stated that the amount which the
Committee is asked to Vote by way of grants
to local authorities under the heading of
Local Government Services approximates to
the amount granted by the Committee for
the financial year 1923-24. At the same
time there are increases on some of the subheads and decreases in others which I will
explain when dealing with the particular
sub-heads. I would also draw attention to
the fact that in preparing the estimates
under this particular class, we have shown
the various housing grants in a group by
themselves. All the remaining grants, including Public Health, Poor Law, and general
grants have been grouped under the head of
Miscellaneous Grants." There is one
special grant included in the current year's
estimates which has not appeared before and
which is of a temporary nature. That is the
grant under sub-head S, which is in aid of
the Belleek Boundary Road and which I will
deal with later.

deficit not exceeding twenty-five shillings

Committee voted the sum of £27,500. This
amount is payable to the Belfast Corporation and four urban authorities which had
adopted the Act in the Six Counties. Hon.
Members will recollect that an agreement
was arrived at between the Government and

Corporation with a view to cutting these

payable to the Belfast Corporation or any
other of the local authorities which had

Turning to sub-head S, hon. Members are

HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Duff]
The matter that I rose particularly about
refers to Sub-head P, the welfare of the
blind. I am sorry to notice a decrease in the
estimate of £600. Last year £4.000 was allocated; this year only £3,100. The reason I
am sorry about this is that there are liabili
ties which ought to be met by the Ministry of
Home Affairs under this classification that do
not seem to have been included in the estimate. I allude particularly to the Homes for
the Blind at Cliftonville. The Blind Persons
Act Committee of our local government body
at the end of 1922 determined to do something
to further the interests of the blind, and they
thought they could not serve those interests
in a more direct or more beneficial way than
in offering to the Homes for the Blind sufficient encouragement to proceed with the
building of a new wing to house the blind
workmen who were practically homeless in
the city of Belfast. That institution with
commendable public spirit at once agreed to
take the responsibility of carrying on that
work if this additional accommodation was
provided, and a resolution of the Belfast
Corporation passed the County Borough
Council municipal meeting on 1st January,
1923, undertaking to pay half of the cost as
under the Blind Persons Act, and expecting
that the other half would be paid by the
Ministry of Home Affairs. Several interviews took place in the Ministry of Home
Affairs, and I, as Chairman of that Committee, was the medium. The matter was
gone ahead with. Now the building is practically completed. It has been completed
by a separate building overdraft on the bank.
We have received a letter from the Ministry
of Home Affairs to some extent repudiating
responsibility for half of this expense.
reason given for this repudiation is that an
arrangement was made with the Ministry of
Labour whereby this building would be carried out by green card labourers. and the
amount of the allowance under that head has
been sent to the Homes for the Blind 1egularly and credited to the building account,
thereby reducing the liability of the Ministry
of Home Affairs and the Belfast Corporation.
If it is the law of the Medes and Persians
that such allowance from the Ministry of
Labour debars the Ministry of Home Affairs
from carrying out their original bargain,
then I suggest to the Homes for the Blind
that they return the money received from the
Ministry of Labour-

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): Hear, hear.
Mr. DUFF: And thereby increase the
liability of the Ministry of Home Affairs. It
seems to me that the situation is somewhat

Mr. ANDREWS: It created much-needed

Mr. DUFF: It did create employment. I

by benefiting the greatest number and bene
fiting them in the best way possible. I

cause when the Belfast Corporation encouraged the Homes for the Blind in this we
did it in perfect good faith, carrying out the
provisions of the Blind Persons Act, and we
fixed a sum that would cover not only the
building but the equipment of the building.
I expect the figure of the actual building contract will still enable that to be done. It
must not be forgotten that this is a charitable
institution and that they have had a very heavy
responsibility in taking on over fifteen or
twenty residents. They have got to raise
money by private charity to enable those
men to live, and all that has been asked and
all that has been provided out of publio funds
is the actual building and the equipment.
For that reason I regret that this Estimate
has apparently been reduced when I expected
to see it greatly enlarged, because if there is
any work that any public body, whether
local or rural or Parliamentary, can take up
it is to develop the Blind Persons Act and
bring brightness and a certain measure of
comfort to those who are absolutely or practi
cally helpless and dependent on the good will
and good spirit of their fellow-men.

who know the conditions that exist in the
large centres of population will look upon
this almost with feelings of despair. Thousands of people are without housing accommodation of any kind. Some are living under
conditions that are not at all desirable and
want to be improved at the earliest possible
moment. Where is the difficulty in connection with this matter?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): Bricklayers.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Home
Affairs charges bricklayers with the whole
trouble
Mr. DONALD: It was Labour unfortunately.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Then if that is
so he as a representative of Labour ought
to do something.
Mr. GORDON: I would like to correct the
har hon. Member for Londonderry. I did not
charge the bricklayers with being responsible
for the shortage of houses.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Oh!
Mr. GORDON: He wanted to know who
was responsible for the shortage of housing.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Who was to
blame?
Mr DONALD: The Minister of Labour.
Mr. GORDON: What I wanted to communicate to him by the word "bricklayers"
was that a shortage of bricklayers meant a
shortage of houses.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: I have no desire whatever to put the Parliamentary Secretary in a false position, and I congratulate
him upon his dexterity in getting out of a
difficult position. Surely there are sufficient
bricklayers throughout the country to build
500 houses for local authorities in a period of
twelve months. That really cannot be the
explanation of the whole trouble. Whereever the difficulty arises this question must be
grappled with in some way, and how it is
going to be done I do not know. One of the
local authorities, I see by the papers which
have been issued, have come up against the
Ministry of Home Affairs in connection with
this whole question. I understood when the
Housing Act was going through the House
that we were going to have some thousands of houses erected in any case in
the largest centre of population in our
area, namely in the city of Belfast.
It is clear the Minister anticipates that the
Act is not going to be availed of, and that
his Department will not be called upon to pay
the £60 subsidy to local authorities for more
than 500 houses. Really something must be
wrong somewhere, and I would like to have
some further information upon this particular
point. I was hoping that we would have had
an estimate here to-day that would have
amounted to £40,000 or £50,000, so that this
question would have been seriously tackled.
If the local authorities cannot erect these
houses then something must be done in
another direction. I am sure I would be out
of order in touching on questions of policy in
connection with this Vote. The only thing I
do is I express my regret that it has not been
necessary to make a large provision in the
Estimates for subsidies, and whether the
blame rests with the local authority, or with
the bricklayers, or with those who provide the
building materials, the question cannot remain as it is, because it cries for solution in
some way. Undoubtedly the Minister is not
to blame for lack of provision.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: I wish to
refer to the question of housing, but I do not
intend to enter generally into the discussion
at all. I wish to allude to that item of
£17,108; that, I take it, has reference to the
sum of £227,500, and in that connection I
think the Government will save money instead of losing it, because the annual payment
would have been something like £20,000, instead of £17,000, if the Government had not
settled with the Corporation. But the important matter is the statement that it is estimated there will be 2,500 houses built by
private individuals, and only 500 by local
authorities. When the Act of 1923 was going
through the House I ventured to suggest that
it would not bring forward a sufficient number of local builders to put up the houses
necessary. However, the Government thought
otherwise, and I think it has now been demonstrated beyond the shadow of a doubt that
we will not get the number of houses that we
require in Ulster.
My right hon. Friend referred to the Corporation, and it is chiefly on that account that
I got up, because I would like to explain the

[Sir Crawford McCullagh].
position so far as the Corporation is concerned. When the Government passed this
Act they made it retrospective, and I think
they were quite right to do so. I think they
were entitled to take that step, because at
an early date they published a statement in
which they said they would subsidise any
builder who would go on and erect houses.
Consequently, I think they were entitled to
pay the subsidy to any builder who did not
wait until the Bill was passed, but who went
on and took the risk of erecting houses. As
the Act says, the subsidy from the Government applies to those houses, and I take it
that if any local authority passes a resolution
the subsidy will also be available in respect
of any houses it may build. The Corporation had no promise whatever, and I will
explain what they objected to. I know a case
of a builder who had erected four houses.
He sold two of them at a substantial profit.
and he came into the Corporation and said "I
want £40 from you, and £60 from the Government." That was, for the houses already
sold, he wanted £100 each.
Mr. DONALD: They made it a free gift.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: The Corporation take this view-the Government may
do what they like, but the £40 to be paid by
the Corporation, or some part of it, should go to
the party who either rents or buys the house.
That is the policy of the Corporation. I
quite see the difficulty. After giving the
matter careful consideration, I look upon it
this way-Government subsidies were absolutely necessary as a war measure, but I
think the sooner we get back to the old conditions the better. For the moment, unfortunately, private enterprise cannot provide
the houses that are necessary. I go so far as
to say that if the Government are going to
give £60 the Corporation ought to give
the £40 on the same conditions as the Government are giving the £60. That is to say,
if a man is plucky enough to come forward
and build a house or a number of houses he
is entitled to £100 for each house. That is
my opinion, but let me tell you that even
that will not bring the houses that are
needed. I think the sooner public bodies
stop building houses the better for all concerned, but as private enterprise cannot meet
the demand I think the Act of 1923 ought
to be given a chance. It ought to be supported by the Government and by the local
authorities, and I think the builder ought to
get the £100 without any restrictions.
Here is how it will work out in my opinion.
Assuming that a builder comes forward with
plans for a number of houses, he will get £60
in respect of each house from the Government without any conditions. But the £60,
as I have said, is absolutely no good; it
will not provide you with the houses that
are wanted. The additional £40 from the
Corporation will help. If you are going to
say to the builder, "When you get these
houses up, you must go to the Corporation,
and they will fix the price at which you may
sell or let them," you will see at once you are
creating difficulties and that no builder will
take that risk. I am sorry that there has
been so much letter-writing between two such
good penmen, if I may so describe them, on
behalf of the Government and the Corporation. The offices of both are not so far
apart that the one official could not walk
round and see the other and settle the matter
in that way. I mentioned that on the last
occasion, and I was told that that was not
the proper way, as the matter had to be put
on record; but I do not think the existing
state of affairs is creditable to either party,
and I think this letter-writing should stop.
If I understood my right hon. Friend aright,
he has said that he cannot sanction the resolution of the Corporation. Then, for goodness sake, let him write back and say so, and
leave it to the Corporation. In my opinion,
the Corporation would be well advised to
pass the resolution giving the £40 subsidy in
respect of a house that will qualify the
builder to get the £60 from the Government.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. Member, but I think if he
will look at the correspondence he will find
that the attitude of the Government is that
it is ultra vires for the Corporation to tack
on conditions to the resolution.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: I am with
my right hon. Friend. Personally I say he is
right, and my advice to the Corporation will
be to pass the resolution giving the £40.
Then I want to tell the House that even
that will not bring the houses that are
necessary. You say the Corporation should
stop building, but who is going to build?
What is going to happen? The cost of building is too high; but timber is rising; materials are rising; everything required in the
building trade is rising; and wages are going
up on the 1st May-I think there is no
doubt about that. What is going to happen?
My opinion certainly is that this Act should
be given a fair trial; but I know it will not
bring the houses. In my opinion, the Government will have to take the matter into consideration, and they can solve it only on the
lines of getting labour to co-operate in the
turning-out of the houses more quickly than
is being done at the present time.

a muddle from beginning to end, and the Act

selves are looking forward to the erection of

There is one thing at any rate I would like
to say and that is, I am absolutely in favour
of the attitude adopted by the Corporation
in this matter. That may be a surprise. It
is due to the fact that they wanted to control
the sale price of the house as well as the
rental. I think it is desirable that there
should be control in both cases. They can
get a grant on condition that they impose
no conditions themselves except as the Act
is constituted. I think it was a necessary
provision and one that should have been
inserted in the Act. There should have been
limitation in regard to the sale price and the
rent demanded for a house on which a subsidy
had been paid. I sympathise with the Corporation. They are beginning to see the
necessity of controlling the rents and sale
prices of these houses, because it is leading
to a terrible anomaly. We find that in one
district a house is bought at £150 less than
in another district and the one house is as
good as the other. It seems rather strange to
inflate prices and exploit the purchaser in
this way. The sooner we drop all Government
interference in this matter the better.
Mr. DONALD: Hear, hear.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I did not sympathise
with my hon. Friend the Member for East
Belfast (Mr. Donald) when he suggested noninterference in industrial matters. I say it

go too far in that. (Laughter). It is by way

As I understand it, the point that
raised with regard to the Ministry of Labour
is somewhat of a misconception. The debate
has chiefly turned upon the housing question.
The position of the Government with
regard
that was made
clear
when the Housing Act was before
it. The desire of the Government
was as far as possible to put an end to anything in the nature of these restrictions that
have affected building so long, and to encourage the private builder as much as could
be done. In other words, it was to have the
largest number of houses built, and to take
precautions to have as many houses built as
possible. Some criticism was made by the
hon. Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin)
that private builders should be let alone, and

Of
he said that if they were let alone the houses
would be produced. The idea of this Measure
was to encourage private builders by giving
them £100 extra. We thought it would be
more likely to produce houses if we gave a
subsidy of £100, partly from the Government,
and partly from the local authority.
course, the underlying idea about all this is
that there is naturally unrest by reason of
so many restrictions and so many conditions
being introduced in the housing question from
time to time. I really think that the Restric
tion of Rents Act is probably at the bottom
of a great deal of the difficulties that have
arisen.
Builders have no security, or they feel very
doubtful whether they will get a proper re
turn for their money. I think this has
been lost sight of by some who were criticising. As regards houses built now, there
is no restriction under the Act so that,
however much it may cost to build them,
there is freedom as to the rent that may be
charged. Some hon. Members have raised
the point that the rent of houses built ought
to be controlled. That would merely add to
the evil; it would go round in a vicious circle
if a man was encouraged to build and then
care was taken that his rent would not be
what he considered it ought to be. If a
house is built and produced, we believe that
the real attitude to-day should be that there
be an absolutely free contract, that is, that
a man may sell the house for what he can
get for it or that he may let it at whatever
rent he can, because if there
are to be
perpetual restrictions on rent in regard to
new houses there can never be any confidence
on the part of the men who are setting
about building.
A point was discussed to some extent with
regard to the attitude of tuis Government
towards the Corporation. When the Housing
Act was going through there was mention of
settlements and of having a talk.
We did
have talks, and the matter, we thought, was
settled. Subsequently when it came to be
finally discussed in this House some of the
points of difference. were never raised at all.
but when the administration of the Act came
into force we found the thing was not
settled, and now we are asked to talk again.,
The only thing that is left to the Government
is to administer the Act as it is. It is an Act
that enables £100 to be given to the builder,
that is, £60 by the Government and £40 by
the Local Authority, and that has got to be
done under the Act. The terms of the Act
are absolutely precise and the Ministry of
Home Affairs cannot vary and cannot allow
the Corporation to vary them because it is not
a question of two authorities coming together
and discussing how they are to evade an Act

CLASS II. No. 8.
CRIMINAL INJURIES.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum, not exceeding £250,000, be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1925, to provide
recoupment to Local Authorities in Northern
Ireland in respect of payments made by them
on foot of Criminal Injury Decrees."
Sir DAWSON BATES: This Estimate needs
very little explanation on my part.
Hon.
Members will recollect that as a result of
efforts on the part of the Prime Minister
this Government succeeded in getting a grant
of one and a half millions to cover decrees
that had been obtained for malicious injuries
which had occurred during the period of June,
1920, and January, 1922. Unfortunately the
injuries continued, and as a result of further
representations on the part of the Prime
Minister another half million was obtained
from the Imperial Parliament. This has enabled us to make a grant of 60 per cent. to
the local authorities in respect of the decrees
obtained from June, 1920, to October, 1922.
I beg to move.

NEW CLAUSE (Mirrors on Char-a-bancs):
Every char-a-banc shall be fitted with a
mirror, fixed in such a position that the driver
can see, as he is driving, the road immediately
behind him on the right hand side."
Brought up, and read the First time.
Mr. GRANT: I have been asked on behalf
of the hon. Member for Londonderry (Mrs.
Chichester) to move that this Clause be now
read a Second time. I think the Clause
explains itself, and I hope the Government
will see their way to accept it. I think it
is very necessary to have provision of this
kind when these char-a-bancs are going along
the roads and making so much noise that the
drivers cannot hear any cars approaching from
behind. If these mirrors are fitted on the
vehicles they will give the drivers an opportunity of seeing what is coming behind.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I think this Amendment is entirely unnecessary, because the
Ministry have ample powers under the Locomotives and Highways Act and the Motorcar Act to make regulations which cover the
point raised. The question of whether or not
a mirror is a suitable instrument to put on
these vehicles is one which has been engaging
the attention of the Advisory Committee, and
I am at the present time considering their
report. While I do not desire to give any
undertaking in regard to it, I can assure the
hon. Member that, if he withdraws the Clause,
I will give the matter very careful consideration with a view to seeing whether or not
we can really devise something better than
is proposed here. It is proposed in this
Clause that the mirror should be put on the
right-hand side, but I am sure the hon.
Member is aware that certain vehicles have
the left-hand drive, and the passing of a
Clause of this kind would penalise some motor
traders very severely. I hope that under the
circumstances the hon. Member will see his
way to withdraw the Clause.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I happened to. express
approval of this suggestion of the hon. Member
for Derry (Mrs. Chichester), and I am still
of the opinion that provision of this sort
should be made. It is not enough to assure
the Committee that the County Council, or
whatever authority is involved, has it within
its power to make a by-law to regulate the
matter. It is not mandatory, and that can
only be accomplished by inserting this Clause
in the Bill.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am sorry the
hon. Member did not understand me. I tried
to explain that the Ministry have power to
make a regulation compelling owners to provide whatever appliances are thought suitable
and necessary for the vehicle.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Pardon me: I have mistaken the right hon. Gentleman. With that
assurance I would not urge any opposition,
but I am still of opinion that provision of this
sort is necessary, and I hope there will be
no delay in putting the most approved system
in operation, It is essential in the interests
of the public.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: It will be quite
apparent to the Committee that it would be
a somewhat dangerous thing to insert a clause
of this character in the Bill, for this reason,
that it stipulates mirrors, while perhaps in
another three months something much

Mr. MILLER: If an improved thing came
along you could amend your Act of Parliament. I would support this Clause for this
reason, that I do not like orders in council
or by-laws. The Government might forget

Perhaps the Minister of Home Affairs was
perfectly right when he said there might
come some other idea for these motors. We
do not have char-a-bancs in our part of the
country but we have motor lorries, sometimes a motor lorry with a trailer after it.
I can give you one instance which perhaps
will interest the Minister of Home Affairs of
how a very distinguished general got over the
difficulty. He was driving myself and an
officer through the country and one of these
big lorries filled with petrol tins came in
front of us. We went on for over a couple
of miles and blew the horn until we were
tired. It was no good. We could not get
past. Then, tho general got a brain-wave,
and, seeing a heap of stones on the road,
pulled up the car. "Jump out" he said to
me, and we filled up with stones, then rushed
after the car, and let fly the stones on top
of the petrol tins, with the result that we
got past. I do not know whether the Minister of Home Affairs will consider that
-

Mr. GRANT: It was necessary to move

Mr. McGUFFIN: I have only got a word
or two to say in regard to the matter of the
mirror that should be attached to these
machines. What I want to ask the right
hon. Gentleman is will he agree to put in
the best possible provision for the purpose
of observing vehicles coming along from the
rear. There is a real danger here. I have
been in a situation of an exceedingly
dangerous character in that respect, and I
am quite convinced that if a mirror were
attached to the vehicle, the danger could be

Member for the University (Mr. Johnstone)
that if you wait for a perfect arrangement
or invention it may never happen. Is the
matter to be deferred until you get that? I
would ask you to put in a provision of some
kind until something better comes along.
It is better to have vehicles with some protection against inevitable danger where
motors and char-a-bancs are in question.
Mr. DONALD: It is only fair to say that
the Advisory Committee have the whole
matter under consideration. A mirror does
not meet the case. When you have a load
projecting the mirror is no use. The mirror
would have to be attached to the vehicle on
a universal joint so that you would be able
to see when in any position. These mirrors
are being tried at the present on private
cars and other vehicles.

Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard to the

Sir DAWSON BATES: With regard to the

this Bill, perhaps the House does not
clearly understand that we as a Ministry have
ample power to make regulations to cover

Oral Answers to Questions
LIMITATION OF PROFITS.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has received copies
of resolutions passed by the County Armagh
Agricultural Committee and other public
bodies, calling for legislation to limit the
exorbitant profits of middlemen traders,
between the producer and the consumer, and
whether he proposes to take any steps in the
matter; and whether he will introduce a Bill
at an early date for the control of prices of
necessities of life.
The MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): I have been asked to reply. My
right hon. Friend has received copies of the
resolutions to which the hon. and gallant
Member refers.
I would point out to the hon, and gallant
Member that experience has shown that the
measure which he suggests could only be
made effective by the complete control of
foodstuffs, and that even when this has been
attempted the resultant benefit to the consumer has been problematical, and the cost
to the State considerable. The Government
accordingly do not contemplate introducing
legislation of the type proposed by the hon.
and gallant Member at the present stage.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask if the Ministry of Home

Affairs is prepared to follow out the recom
mendations of the Departmental Committee
which was set up to inquire into the cost of
living?
Mr. ARCHDALE: I can add nothing to the
reply which I have given to the hon. and
gallant Member.

ALLOCATION OF MOTOR TAXES.
2. Mr. JOHNSTONE asked the Minister
for Home Affairs whether he can state what
proportion of the receipts from motor taxation for 1923 has been expended in road improvement, and what is being done with the
unexpended balance, if any?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw): The gross receipts from licence duties
on mechanically propelled vehicles for the
year 1923 were £215,420. The grants indicated
to road authorities for the financial year 1923-
24 were £198,542. Payments have already
been made during the financial year amount
ing to £140,377, and the Ministry have at
present under examination claims for the
final instalments of the grants payable to the
road authorities on the basis of the grants
indicated.
SECONDARY TEACHERS' INCREMENT
GRANT.

3. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parlia
mentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education if he is aware that the sums of money
due to the Secondary Teachers as increment
grant have been paid to the Governors of the
Schools as a subvention to aid them in paying
the covenanted salaries; that in many cases
the Teachers have received no money whatever as increment grant; if it is a fact that
the Ministry have sent out a form to the
Headmasters of Schools which the Teachers
are being asked to sign, stating that the
Teachers have duly received the grant, and
if, in fact, the Teachers have received only
the salary which the Governors have covenanted to pay them; and if this diversion of
funds from the purpose for which they were
clearly intended by Parliament has been
authorised by the Ministry.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): The Increment Grant payable
under the Regulations for the Payment of
Salaries to Teachers in Preparatory, Intermediate and Secondary Schools is in accor
dance with Regulation 4 paid to the Governors of the school. The Governors are,
however, required to produce receipts from
the teachers showing that each authorised
teacher has received not only the increment
paid in respect of that teacher, but also in
addition the minimum of the scale salary
which in accordance with the Regulations

ASSESSING OF RATES ON SMALL
PROPERTIES.
4. Major SHILLINGTON asked the Minister of Home Affairs if he has received a
request from the principal Urban Authorities
in Northern Ireland to introduce legislation
which would enable Urban Rating Authorities, if they so desire, to assess all rates on
the owners of property below a certain
valuation, instead of on the occupiers, and
if it is his intention to comply with this
request.
Mr. MEGAW: The answer to the first part
of the hon. and gallant Member's question is
in the affirmative.
The question has carefully been considered
by the Ministry, and I regret that the Ministry are unable to accede to the representations made.
The principle involved by the suggested
change carries with it serious objections on
the ground of policy.
Major SHILLINGTON: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the hon. and learned
Gentleman if it is a fact that Belfast Corporation have power to assess owners of property below a certain valuation instead of
the occupiers?
Mr. GRANT: Arising out of the reply of
the hon. and learned Gentleman, I would like
to know have the Home Office taken into consideration the fact that quite a number of
these occupiers in urban districts are persons
who are unemployed, and whenever this rate
is struck it is not possible for them to find
the amount of money required to be paid in
rates? If it were added, however, to the
weekly rent it would come much easier on
these people. I personally have been asked
by a good many people-
Mr. SPEAKER: Order, order. The hon.
Member must confine himself to a question.
Dr. MORRISON: Arising out of the answer,
may I ask if it is a fact that the Portadown
Urban Council have lost several hundred
pounds through the absence of this suggested
legislation during the last year in rates?
Mr. DONALD: May I ask the hon. and
learned Gentleman, before he replies, if any
request has come from persons other than the
local authorities in regard to this matter?
Mr. MEGAW: I am not altogether acquainted with the position of the Belfast
Corporation, but I understand that they have
private Acts under which their assessments
can be made on the owners of property. The
Local Government Act, 1898, has adopted a
principle which I think is a good one, namely.
that those who ara electors should know what
the rates are for which they are to be
assessed. That is the principle that has been
adopted, and it is felt to be the best principle
that can be adopted.
MIRRORS ON MOTOR VEHICLES.
5. Major SHILLINGTON asked the Minister
of Home Affairs if he is prepared to issue
a regulation compelling all heavy mechanically propelled vehicles using the roads in
Northern Ireland to carry a mirror in such
a position that the driver will be able to
see vehicles coming from behind and desirous
of passing.
Mr. MEGAW: The question of issuing
Regulations requiring heavy motor vehicles
to be fitted with mirrors is at present under
consideration, but having regard to the
growing use on the roads of enclosed light
commercial and private vehicles, the
Ministry require to be satisfied before issuing
any Regulations whether it is justifiable to
promulgate a Regulation applying only to
the heavy vehicles, i.e. the vehicles over two
tons. The matter has been referred again
to the Roads Advisory Committee and the
Ministry await the recommendation of that
Committee before taking definite action in
the matter.
SPEED AND WEIGHT OF MOTOR
LORRIES.
the
6. Major SHILLINGTON asked
Minister of Home Affairs if he is contemplating making any change in the speed at
which heavy motor lorries are permitted to
travel, or in the weight of the loads which
they are allowed to carry.
Mr. MEGAW: It is not proposed to make
any change in the Regulations regarding the
speed or the weights of heavy motor vehicles.
In accordance with the undertaking given
by the Minister of Home Affairs recently in
this House, special instructions have been
issued to the Police Authorities in regard
to taking action in cases where it is found
that these heavy vehicles are exceeding the
speed limit on the public roads in Northern
Ireland.
Prime Minister's Statement. 712
The Boundary Question- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
The Boundary Question.
STATEMENT BY PRIME MINISTER.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: Would I
be in order in asking if the Prime Minister
intends to make a statement on the recent
negotiations which took place when he was
across in London?
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
Mr. Speaker, with your permission and with
the leave of the House I would be very glad
to meet my hon. Friend by making a statement in connection with what has happened
during the past week. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear). Before I do so, as this is the
first time we have met since the very serions
illness of my right hon. Friend, the Minister
of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates), I
would like to say-and I am sure I speak
on behalf of all the members present
here how deeply we sympathise with him in
his illness and how we all wish him a speedy
restoration to full health and the strength
which has enabled him to
such trying times. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear).
carry on through
Own
In making the statement-the grave statement-which I propose to do to the House today, I wish to convey to those outside our
walls in the first instance a message of comfort and encouragement-(hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-because I do not believe that
one's full vigour can be put into any controversial question or one's best be accomplished if you face the difficulty feeling pessimistic and feeling depressed in your
mind. I am far otherwise. I am, as I said
last Thursday, quite undismayed by this new
attack upon our liberties. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I am not quite certain whether
it was Mr. Lloyd George-I believe it waswho spoke so feelingly on one occasion about
refreshing fruit. Therefore, if I begin my
remarks to-day by quoting one of Mr. Lloyd
George's refreshing letters on this subject
perhaps it will supply adequately the text
for anything I have got to say. Writing on
the 20th July, 1921, to Mr. de Valera, who
was then supposed to be the leader of the
Southern Irish people, he said:
The British Government are actuated by
an earnest desire to end the unhappy divisions between Great Britain and Ireland.
Then follow a page and a half, after which
we come down to the following sentence:
The form in which the settlement is to
take effect must allow for full recognition
of the existing powers and privileges of
the Parliament and Government of
Northern Ireland, which cannot be abrogated except by their own consent.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That is the
beginning of my first few words to-day and
it will be the end. Nothing can be done
without the Government in the first instance,
and the representatives of the people sitting
in this House and in the other House, constituting the Parliament of Northern
Ireland.
The question of our Boundary and the
Boundary of Southern Ireland has been
revived again in its intensive form, after
having rested in abeyance for three years, and
as is usual in matters of vast importance
which lie in abeyance for a long time, there
is a sort of scramble, a hurry, a beating up of
everything, and a sudden rush at the end as
though something absolutely necessary must
propel those who have waited and thought so
long into a rash and sudden determination.
I believe that if this matter of the Boundaries
were allowed to peter out, if it were allowed
to remain in the oblivion in which it has
rested for three years, it would be far better
for the people not only of Northern Ireland,
but of Southern Ireland and the Empire as a
whole. The written word, the bond, the
Treaty, the pact, or whatever it may be
called, may possibly tide over a day or two,
and may cause rejoicing; but we have seen
rejoicing turned into sorrow and depression
in a very short time. If you want permanence in the good feeling between the people of
Ireland, then these settlements and pacts and
agreements and Treaties must be entered into
in the heart, and not only by pen upon paper.
I have fought, and fought valiantly, for
a settlement by agreement. What is it that
stands in the way? Clause 12 of the Articles
lays it down that a Boundary Commission is
to be established. It says nothing more. It
has got to be established. But the establishment of a Boundary Commission depends
upon all three Great Britain, Southern Ireland and ourselves appointing representatives. Southern Ireland appointed theirs
some little time ago. The British Government have announced their intention within
the last few days of appointing a Chairman,
and I have received an official intimation from the Government asking me to
appoint a representative for Northern Ire
land. My answer will be in accordance with
the policy of this Government throughout-
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-that is, that it
is impossible to accede to any such request.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) What I want
to ask the lawyers especially is this-The
letter of the Treaty having been carried out
what do people mean by the spirit of the
Treaty? I hold that I have placed already
the true and perfect interpretation on the
spirit of the Treaty. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) The spirit of the Treaty can only be
carried out in the way I have indicated, and
that is in the hearts of the people, coming
together and agreeing that such and such
shall be the boundary between North and
South. There we stand to-day, and I take

The next point I come to is that between
now and the next stage-the next step taken
by the British Government-there may be
some little flutterings upon the political
horizon. There may be some little ups and
downs. To use an expression that is often
indulged in at Westminster, the Government
stock may go down, or, on the other hand,
it may rise. Whether the bulls or the bears,
about which they talk in this connection,
have spasmodic triumphs from hour to hour,
my answer at the end of it all will be
exactly the same answer as I gave on Thursday (Hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and I
desire to take this opportunity of saying
a few words to the people outside, once more
simply to reassure them on that important
subject, and to tell them to pay attention
to practically nothing that they see in the
Press, especially from across the water, or
hear from people who are anxious to cause
dissension in our ranks, but loyally to follow
those representatives whom they sent here
and those of the Government who at the
present moment are in charge of this serious
and important matter. If they do that they
will be best serving Ulster and the Empire.
We have sometimes to do things that are
difficult to do with the greater object in view
at the end. I well know that people, not
alone here but across the water, think that
they can offer a solution of this difficulty
off hand. Why, to hear some people talk, you
would think that we were merely selling a
pound of sugar or a pound of tea, and that
the real difference between us was whether
the abatement of fourpence in the pound on
the tea and three halfpence on the sugar
should come into operation to-day or the
day after to-morrow. That is the mentality
of some persons with regard to this critical
question at present looming upon the horizon.
that If they would only pause before they send
their suggestions to the papers, and still
better, if they would only keep quiet, instead
of disseminating their false opinions, it
would be easier for the leaders to come to a
proper conclusion. I had occasion the other
day to find very serious fault with Lord
Birkenhead. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Yes, hon. Members can cheer, but they only
cheer, and quite rightly cheer, because he
happens to be a particularly prominent man
who has done this wrong thing; but how
often have others, perhaps not bearing quite
so high a title or name, written and made
suggestions which in every instance gravely
embarrass the Government and those in whose
hands are charged the weighty conduct of
such important affairs? Therefore, shortly,
I pray and beg that people may have patience
and trust and hold themselves in, at all
events, till this great crisis is over.
I think it only right to say that in our
negotiations with the present Labour
Government my colleagues, the Marquess of
Londonderry and the right hon. the Attorney-
General (Mr. Best), as well as myself, have
been treated with the utmost courtesy and
consideration. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
It is due to the British Government to say
that throughout the whole of this difficult
problem they have spent themselves in
endeavouring to secure an agreement by
consent, and they have shown activity in
every quarter in order to probe to the very
bottom the various channels, the various side
issues, with which the whole question is
surrounded. Of course, it is obvious to all
here that this question, which has engaged
the attention of Mr. Lloyd George's Government, of Mr. Bonar Law's Government, of
Mr. Baldwin's Government, and now of Mr.
Ramsay MacDonald's Government, is one of
first-class Imperial importance. We must
maintain the attitude towards British
Governments that this subject is not a
political subject, but is a matter for the
Empire and a matter of life and death to the
people here in Ulster. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) I cannot emphasise sufficiently that
it should be raised from out of the political
arena into an arena where only statesmen
should be asked to deal with it.
I would like to go a step further and assure
the House that they need not despair that
the contribution promised by the late
Government towards assisting our Special
Constabulary has been turned down by the
present Government. I still have hopes that
that pledge to us will be amply and properly
fulfilled, and that we need have no hesitation
in saying that the honour of the present Labour Government is as high as
that of any other Government in
carrying out pledges so definitely given. May
I pass to another phase? Whether that
pledge is carried out or not, Ulster will see
that her Special Constabulary are maintained
in the highest state of efficiency, even if we
have to pay every shilling of the cost ourselves. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) I
remember very well when our Parliament first
assembled assuring the people that the safety
of the Borderland and peace within the land
itself were the primary objects of the Government. I went pretty far. I think I used the
words that we would become bankrupt rather
than see chaos and murder and disturbance
inside our area. Therefore, we look forward,
it is true with less satisfaction, but at all
events we look forward with absolute confi-

[The Prime Minister]
dence, to the fact that the people of Ulster
will rise to the occasion and keep that
splendid Force in full power and proper discipline, and in full and complete accord with
its past traditions in order to maintain the
peace, whatever may possibly lie ahead.
In that connection some people have been
heard to say: "You told your audience on
Thursday that the Free State, although
charged as it was in 1920 with the duty of
contributing ten millions a year towards
Great Britain's Imperial services, had not
paid one shilling of that contribution.
Ulster was still paying something between
five millions and six millions a year
towards the maintenance of the Army
and Navy, and other Imperial services,"
and they say: "Why do you not
keep that money yourselves; why do you
allow a situation to arise in which you pay
an enormous sum on the one hand and then
beg and implore the Government on the other
to pay you a comparatively small amount to
carry out what, after all, is an Imperial
service the maintenance of law and order
throughout every corner of the British
Empire?" I think in justice to those who
make that statement I ought to make it clear
to the House and to the country that the
obligation to pay the contribution towards the
Imperial services is one in which I gladly
acquiesce, and it is one in which I hope the
people of Ulster will always gladly acquiesce.
For our contribution to Great Britain we
have several privileges which we never could
do without, in my opinion, without going to
the wall, without sinking into the seventh
or eighth class. We never could do without
those services and those compensations. What
are they? Let me run through a small list
of the services for which we pay our contribution.
I would, naturally, put in the forefront the
safety of our Province, because whatever else
is in doubt there is no doubt at all that the
boundary of Ulster is the boundary of the
Empire. (Hon Members: Hear, hear). No
Government at Westminster could stand for
twenty-four hours if it did not protect its
boundary if it was ever in danger. Therefore,
we have a call on his Majesty's Navy if
necessary. Think for a moment what that
means. The whole great British Fleet can be
and must be directed to its defence by the
Imperial Authorities if ever there is a threat
upon the boundary of our beloved Empire.
and that boundary stretches wherever the sea
stretches, and Ulster is part of that boundary.
And the Army. The Army has already vindicated the position to which I have just
drawn attention. The Army can be employed
to protect our boundary. Therefore, we have
a call on what is perhaps the finest unit of
fighting men in the whole wide world-you have
that for your contribution. And the Air Force,
the new Force, which with the Army and the
Navy goes to make our fighting Services.
The Air Force is at our disposal certainly if
ever there is a threat from across the Border.
But over and above that there is the representation in the Mother of Parliaments. I
dare say it is impossible to translate the value
of that into £5 notes. It is the one bond be
tween us and Great Britain that can be seen
by everyone, our members passing freely to
and fro to voice Ulster in that great Parliament, just as those who have been honoured
in past days and present days by elevation to
the Lords can represent Ulster in the Upper
House. It is that representation which is of
invaluable assistance to us when questions of
Imperial importance crop up.
Then, to get down to the financial side
there is the credit of our Province which,
under this arrangement, is exactly the same as
the credit in Lombard Street, which is the
great financial centre in the City of London.
We can, I believe-my right hon. Friend (Mr.
Pollock) will correct me if I am wrong-borrow money here, and business men can contract
business here, on equally favourable terms to
those that obtain in any other part of the
Empire, even in the centre of the City of
London itself.
The

FINANCE (Mr.
The PRIME MINISTER: That question is
involved. Then what about the trade of the
world? From the port of Belfast steamers of
gigantic tonnage go to every corner of our
Dominions, to every corner of the world, and
when they get to their destination, colonial or
foreign, they meet the flag that ensures the
trade, they meet at the other end those
Ministers of Great Britain, and they meet the
Consular Service who deal with all that vast
interchange of trade between one country and
another forming the Empire. All that is involved in our contribution to Great Britain,
and I say solemnly here that if, as was at one
time suggested, we should have only to pay
what would be a voluntary contribution, I be
lieve that it would be my duty to stand at this
box and say that the amount should be about
the contribution we now make in order to
maintain the Services and to be able to claim
the beneficent consideration which we receive
as part and parcel of Great Britain-Services
that otherwise would be denied us if we were
a small State on the map by ourselves.
That is the explanation of that point, and
when some thoughtless critics on the other
side try to minimise the efforts that we have
made, may I just say that during the past two
years and four months we have paid to Great
Britain in this connection a gross sum of no
less than £13,524,000? I glory that we were
able to pay that amount. I am delighted to

think that my right hon. Friend the Chancellor has been able to give us a balance on the
