a
Having explained that matter as far as it is
in my power, I would like to come down to
the question of our future here in the realms
of legislation. I think it was my hon. Friend.
the Member for West Belfast-not the one
who is present at the moment (Colonel Woods)
-who one day said in a little petulant manner
that there was far too much legislation going
on. I think that remark pleased the
Government more than anything else
that has ever been said in this House,
although the hon. Member may not have
intended it. Legislation is always
grave anxiety to a Government, and it is
also a grave anxiety to all those who have to
make the necessary preliminary inquiries and
to the staff engaged. Therefore I think
the House will be pleased, and the hon.
Member who voiced those sentiments will be
pleased to hear that the Government propose
to have very little legislation this year. The
reason is that we think it necessary that the
Imperial Members should have an opportunity of being constantly in attendance at
Westminster until this crisis is over. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.) It is, of course,
obvious to any one that our case may require
to be stated there at any moment either day
or night,
and We can only ensure
that if we allow this House to get
its legislation through quickly, and release
those members to look after our interests on
the floor of the House at Westminster. If we
adjourn this House for a considerable period
we will reserve under the usual custom in
such matters the right to call the House
together again if it is necessary to consult
with regard to the Boundary or any other
serious matter. That course will necessitate
postponing to the autumn the Redistribution
Bill, which we might have had ready at an
carlier date, but as we have still two years
to run there is no need to put it through so
early as we thought, and therefore we propose
to have the Bill cut and dry for presentation
to this House in the autumn.
Before I part from these various topics 1
would like to make an announcement which is
intended to secure the sympathy not only of
the Members here representing other constituencies, but to secure the sympathy of the
people in every quarter of Ulster who may
think that one part of the area is being a
little bit favoured over another part. The
members are aware of the great difficulties
that have arisen owing to the breakdown of that historic bridge in Derry, and
the Cabinet have had a series of meetings-1
think no fewer than four-at which this
subject of the repair of the Carlisle Bridge
has been brought up for discussion. It may
be asked, "How does that matter affect the
Cabinet?" Well, it affects the Cabinet in just
exactly the same way as the Fermanagh
Triangle affects every man, woman, and
child in Ulster, and as our contribution towards the Bridge at Boa Island, interests
them so does this main artery, this important connection, this Bridge across the Foyle,
interests every man and woman throughout
Northern Ireland. It is a link between those
on the Northern sido and those on the
Southern and you must have a bridge of sufficient strength to carry whatever is necessary.
We have therefore determined that as this is
moro an 'Ulster matter than a purely local
matter we will ask this House to grant
£100,000 towards assisting them in erecting a
bridge which will meet every necessity of the
case, and I trust that Members will allow this
to go through as a tribute, if I may say so,
from the rest of Ulster to that historic city of
Londonderry which for so many centuries has
maintained its own.
Before I close I would just like to make one
further remark. We have been through very
many troublesome times together, and
although there has been, and continually will
be a difference of opinion between certain
members of this House, and other members of
the House as well as the Government, I wish
to say in public, as I had an opportunity of
saying earlier in the day in private, that I
do not believe that any other community of
persons situated in exactly the same position
as we have been during these three trying
years, could have conducted themselves in a
more fitting or proper manner than have the
members of the Parliament of Northern
Ireland. I refer to the other Chamber as
well as to this House, and I want the people
in Ulster to understand that their representatives hold that high position not only
in my estimation but in the estimation of
the people on the other side of the Channel.
What have we accomplished here without a
legitimate opposition, and the absence of a
legitimate opposition is always held up as the
greatest danger of a Parliament. They talk
about corrosion and say, "Your institution
will fade away before your eyes, and you will
find it impossible to carry on." That has
not been the case and I can only say
that I have the deepest trust in the good
common sense of the Ulster people.
Ulster people's trusted representatives in the
House have done their duty during these
trying years and have carried us through.
They ought to be proud of themselves as I

ORDERS OF THE DAY.
Public Libraries Bill (8.)
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
Mr. MEGAW: I regret that it becomes my
duty to propose here the Second reading of
this measure, which was introduced in the
Senate by my right hon. Friend the Minister
of Home Affairs. We have all already expressed our sympathy with him, and I assure
the House that his absence from the duties
of the Ministry of Home Affairs has been a
very serious matter, and has placed the
Ministry in very serious difficulties indeed.
The Bill of which I have the honour to
propose the Second reading is not one that
introduces any new principle. The advantages
of reading facilities are generally recognised.
One is not called upon here to discuss the
importance of libraries either from the
education point of view or from the standpoint of providing innocent enjoyment for the
people who favour the lighter side of literature. The principle of providing or assisting
public libraries in Ireland has been recognised for the towns as far back as 1855. By
an Act passed in that year Urban authorities
were empowered to levy a rate of not exceeding 1d in the pound for the purpose of
libraries within their district. It was not
supposed that the countryman had need
for like facilities-whether it was thought
that the rustic could provide his
literature, or whether there was
venient machinery to put libraries in
operation, I cannot say.
Own
no con-
In 1894 a step forward was taken by an
Amending Act. By the adoption of the
machinery specified in that Act the limitation to the penny rate might be removed, and
two or more authorities might be entitled to
combine their forces for the purpose of more
efficient administration. Now the principle
adopted in that Act was the germ of cooperation, which is the gist of the present
measure, as it is pretty evident that a combined rate of 1d in the £ on two areas will
administratively treble or quadruple the
benefit of the expenditure by a single township. Up to that time the provision of
libraries was still confined to urban areas.
A few years later, in the year 1902, Parliament became alive to the fact that the
countryman might take advantage of the
facilities that had been provided, and that
the use of public libraries might be developed,
and it provided by an Act passed in that year
that the facilities already given to the towns
should be put into operation also in the
country. Of course all these measures were
voluntary. There was nothing mandatorynothing to compel any urban or rural area
to take advantage of the Act. But where the
Act was adopted the Rural District Council
became the Library Authority. That briefly
is how the law stands to-day.
As a matter of fact very few Rural Councils
have put the Act into operation, but I am
glad to say that my own county has set an
example to others in this respect. At least
five rural districts of that county have taken
advantage of the Act. This county, too, has
taken advantage of the Carnegie United
Kingdom Trust, and, despite many difficul
ties, a very energetic Committee has shown
that there is a recognised want for the circulation of books in the country districts. Lack
of time-not lack of interest-has prevented
me from being so well-informed in regard to
the results of this enterprise as I might be,
but I know that those who have devoted much
time and energy to the scheme are satisfied
that their work has not been without fruit.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
The Bill now before the House is an
endeavour to bring a recognised system up to
date, that is, to take advantage of local assist
ance, while not leaving it to be dealt with by
a variety of bodies. The system we are
endeavouring to introduce in this measure is
to co-ordinate central administration with the
local. Suggestions are made that our legisla
tion has adopted a policy of crabbing or
hampering the administration of local bodies.
Nothing is farther from the fact. The Gov
ernment desires to utilise the public work of
these local bodies to the best advantage, and
this Bill as it is framed, I think, will effect
that object. Under the Education Act the
County Council is the Education Authorityit was already the rate raising authority. It
is closely in touch with each of the Rural
District Councils, and is elected by the same
electorate. The aims of the County and the
721 Public Libraries Bill-

Second Reading. 722
& S
Rural District are the same, and I should be
sorry to see any jealousy between them, except a public-spirited rivalry for the common
good.
In the measure before the House the
isolated endeavour of each of the bodies that
are already administering the existing Acts
can be co-ordinated and they work
harmoniously. So far as I can judge
the Rural will have the preponderating
voice. If Members look at the schedule
of the Bill as introduced they will
see how it is proposed to constitute the
new County Library Committee. Two members of the County Council are in the first
instance compulsorily put on the County
Library Committee. Two members of each
Rural District will be members of the body,
and besides that one member of every Urban
District and a commissioner of every town
will also be joined in the administration of
the provisions of the Measure, while an additional number of members of the County
Council-one for each Urban and Rural District-will form members of the Library Committee. But the effect of that is that the
Rural Council, or members from the Rural
Council, will really have the preponderating
voice. It seems to me that this County
Library Committee is a very representative
body indeed, and I think the form of it,
which was a new provision introduced during the passage of the Measure through the
Senate, will commend itself to those who
approach the subject with an open mind.
I should say before I sit down that there is
nothing mandatory about the provisions of
this Measure. It leaves it to every County
Council to adopt the Measure or not to adopt
it, as it pleases. The Government hope that
the provisions will be largely taken advantage of and that the County Councils will
show themselves alive to the importance of
providing library facilities for the population
of their respective counties. This Measure
preserves all the facilities that exist in the
Acts that are already capable of being put
into operation. I do not think there is anything new in it except the principle of coordination in using the existing facilities,
and perhaps introducing a few improvements
in the administration, but there is
nothing extra in the way of expense included in the Measure. It
preserves all the existing facilities of the
Acts, and enables the Urban Authorities
either to carry on by themselves or to sink
their operations in the county systems. That
again is optional; if they find they were
doing better before they can revert to their
own system after having tried their connection with the county system. I do not think
it is necessary for me to go into the specific
provisions of the Bill. They are really all
that I mentioned in the general terms that
I have used I now have the honour to move
the Second Reading of this Bill.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I do not rise to attempt to
take in any sense of the word what the Prime

I am in entire sympathy with this Libraries
Bill, but I cannot agree with the hon. and
learned Gentleman opposite (Mr. Megaw),
who is my colleague in the representation of
the County of Antrim, that the Government

Mrs. CHICHESTER: It seems to me that
the chief purpose that this Bill will serve
will be to bring the advantages of the public

and to encourage the various County Councils

force him to drink. We have had an example

Evidently we are prepared to be optimistic

Council is the education authority, it is the
rating authority; and so it does seem to me
it is only right that it should be given the
opportunity at any rate of carrying out the
provisions of this Bill. I fear, however, that
it is not realised how very busy the average
County Councillor is, how many committees
are associated with the County Councils, and
that the average County Councillor considers
himself a very hard-worked man; in fact, he
considers himself-many have told me so-to
be much more hardworking than the ordinary
Member of Parliament and he gets nothing
for his labours. In this Bill we are giving
him a new committee, new work, and-this
is a point I wish to make-placing the whole
burden or a great burden on his shoulders.
In this I agree with the hon. Member (Mr.
Crawford) who has just spoken, and, I am
afraid, disagree with the hon. and learned
Gentleman opposite (Mr. Megaw). It seems
to me we are placing that burden on his
shoulders without providing very much outside help, and that sufficient representation
is not being given to the Rural District
Councillors. In the case where the chairman
and a member of each Rural District Council
are to be members of this new committee, 1
am not quite sure whether my hon. Friend,
the Member for Antrim (Mr. Crawford)
pointed out that the chairman of each Rural
District Council is a County Councillor exofficio, so that that body would have the
power to nominate him. I do consider that it
is a considerable blot on the Bill that
sufficient representation is not given to the
Rural District Councillors, and I would urge
the Government most strongly to amend the
schedule and to give larger representation on
these committees to the Rural District
Councillors.
It also seems to me a great pity that where
an enterprising, public-spirited Rural District
Council, like several which have been mentioned in the County Antrim, has worked
successfully the Act of 1902 it should be
necessary to take away their powers and give
those powers to another body. I am not
absolutely clear on reading the Bill as to
what will happen if the County Council of a
particular County does not take up these
powers. I am sure I will be reassured on this
point later on. Will the library fall between
two stools, or will the Rural District Council
carry on for that particular area? I hope so.
I am afraid I have to agree with my hon.
Friend (Mr. Crawford) when he referred to
the tendency to discourage Rural District

Commissions of the Peace Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:

Mr. MEGAW: This is a short Bill, and like
the one I had the honour of proposing a short
time ago it does not introduce anything in
the nature of a new principle. It is a Bill
for simplifying the procedure with regard to
appointments to the Commission of the Peace,
and prescribes the fees that are to be paid by
Justices of the Peace in respect of their
727 Commissions of the Peace Bill.
Adjournment.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

[Mr. Megaw]
appointments. The existing practice in
making appointments is very cumbrous and
costly as every time a new magistrate is
appointed for any county it is necessary to
make out a fresh Commission involving a
vast mass of what scems to be rather useless
scrivenery.
The Commission of the Peace
that is now issued for any county recites the
name of every person who already holds the
Commission and to some extent the duties
that are to be discharged by him. The form
in existence is really the survival of centuries.
The office of Justice of the Peace itself is one
of the oldest offices in England. Its history
extends as far back as some 550 years, and I
am not sure whether the method of appointment has changed very much during that
time. In England the procedure for creating
new Magistrates was very largely simplified
by an Act in 1877. That Act has been held
not to apply to Ireland, at least there was
some doubt as to whether that Act, which
was apparently a general Act, applies to
Ireland, and, as a matter of fact, it never has
been put into force in Ireland. Under that
Act rules have been made by which one
Commission is issued for every county and a
schedule is attached to the Commission giving
the names of the Justices as they are
appointed from time to time.
We found very great difficulty when we
took over the Government here with regard
to the appointment of Justices of the Peace.
It will be remembered that the Clerk of the
Crown and Hanaper used to have control of
the Great Seal and all the Commissions were
issued under the Great Seal. The Clerk of
the Crown and Hanaper had his office in
Dublin, and it was no easy task to get him
moved to have magistrates appointed when it
was thought necessary. A greater difficulty,
however, arose at the time of the burning of
the Four Courts, because in that burning the
Great Seal itself disappeared and it took considerable time to have it replaced. After
that the Treaty Act rather changed the
whole system of Government in Ireland, and
there was also the abolition of the office of
Lord Lieutenant.
Now it is thought right to adopt a system
that is pretty much the same as that in
existence in England, which will only require
the issue of one Commission on which the
names can be added from time to time as
they are made. It certainly will be very
much more economical, and it will be at
least equally effective to the method of the
past. It will not require the use of the Great
Seal, so that appointments can be made much
more expeditiously, while the question of
fees on appointment will be settled upon a
satisfactory basis, because there is some
doubt as to the legality of the footing upon
which they are at present charged. The form
of the Commission is settled by the Bill itself.
It is set out in the First Schedule and retains generally the wording of the old Commission; but we have shortened the
language; it does not contain all the archaic
forms that were in existence, and the Bill
itself provides that rules will be made for
the proper working out of the methods of
appointment. I beg to move.
Question put, and agreed to.

whole House for to-morrow.

Illegitimate Children (Affiliation
Orders) Bill.
As amended, considered.
Mr. SPEAKER: May I point out that the
amendments on the Paper are in the wrong
order, in one respect, namely, that on the
Report Stage of a Bill a new Clause must be
taken first. Therefore, I will call on the hon.
and learned Member in charge of the Bill to
nove his new Clause first. It appears last on
the paper.
NEW
CLAUSE.-(COMMUTATION OF
WEEKLY SUMS).
"(1) Any weekly sums payable under an
Affiliation Order may, on the application of
the putative father of an illegitimate child,
be commuted by the Court by which the
Affiliation Order was made for a lump sum,
if that Court is satisfied-
(a) that arrangements have been made for
the proper administration of the lump sum
for the maintenance and education of the
child, and
(b) that the lump sum is sufficient to afford
to the child benefits at least equal to those
which would be afforded by the payment of
weekly sums.
Such lump sum shall be paid to the collecting officer or to such other person or body of
persons as may be designated by the Court,
and shall be invested and applied for the
maintenance and education of the child in
such manner as the Court may direct.
"(2) All sums applicable under this section
for the maintenance and education of an
illegitimate child shall if default is made by
any person in the payment thereof, be recoverable in like manner as sums payable by the
putative father under an Affiliation Order."
Brought up, and read the First time.

THE
SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS

we have endeavoured in the new Clause to
adapt as far as possible the proper administrative methods. I do not think there is
anything in the Clause of a controversial
nature so I will simply move it.

THE MINISTER OF AGRICULTURE (Mr.
Archdale): The object of this Bill is
to try to help the egg industry, which
is a very large one in this country.
Hon. Members may not know that there
and a half million hens in
Ulster, and last year the money brought in
by the export of eggs was about £3,300,000.
That is a very considerable sum to come
into the pockets of people in this country.
We have been trying to help that on in the
Ministry in various ways. We have given
advice in grading and packing, and have sent
instructors into the country, and in other
ways we have been trying to help. The
Charlemont Commission, which sat the other
day, passed a unanimous resolution in favour
of bringing in, a Bill of this sort. For about
six or seven months we in the Ministry have
been making ground for the Bill. We have
had meetings with egg merchants, and we
have also had meetings with farmers in the
different districts. The egg merchants are
practically unanimous in favour of a Bill of
this sort. (Hon Members: Hear, hear.)
What we want to do is to concentrate on the
quality of our exports and try to get better
prices. It is very disheartening for anyone
connected with the Ministry to go to England
and find out that the large importers of eggs
from Ireland are giving up using Irish eggs
altogether, because they cannot depend on the
eggs when they open the case being what
they purport to be. Hundreds of times they
have told me they have opened cases supposed
to contain fresh eggs and have found coldstored eggs, in some cases boiled eggs, and in
very many cases dirty eggs and badly packed
eggs. These are things which we hope this
Bill will prevent. We do not intend that the
measure should act viciously on anyone, but
we want, as hon. Members will see on reading
the Bill, to licence all exporters. We have
nothing to do with the retail merchants. We
have only to do with the wholesale merchants.
Under Clause 1 we want to make it necessary for all wholesale egg merchants to take
out a licence, for which they will pay 20s.
That licence will last them until we see reason to recall it, or as long as they continue
to deal properly in eggs. We want to make
regulations from time to time so as to see that
the eggs are properly graded. That is one
thing necessary on the other side. Danish
and New Zealand eggs which come in fetch
the highest prices. All the eggs are of equal
Marketing of Eggs Bill-
Second Reading.
7 MAY 1924

L

size, and are packed together. You grade the
eggs of a certain size in one case, and the
eggs of a smaller size in another case. We
want to have our eggs packed in that way.
We also want to have them clean. Hens walk
about and dirty the eggs.. We do not want
any dirty eggs offered for sale.
Clause 2 provides that all premises where
cold-stored or pickled eggs are preserved shall
be registered with the Ministry. The trade
in cold-stored eggs is perfectly reasonable to
carry on, and it is very necessary, but we
want to register every place where such a
trade is carried on, so that we can examine
the eggs when they come from a certain district. The owners of such premises have to
keep a record, so that it will be easy for our
officials to see what is going on.
eggs
Clause 3 provides that every person dealing
in preserved, cold-stored, or pickled
must have a brand on the box itself in letters
not less than two inches long, so as to make it
clear that the eggs are not fresh eggs, but
cold stored or pickled eggs. In that way they
will not be palmed off on the public as they
were before.
Clause 4 makes it imperative on the market
authority in places where they collect tolls to
have covered places for the packing of eggs.
We find that one of the worst things in
connection with the buying of eggs in our
various country towns. The buyers pack them
out on the streets without any cover. The
rain comes down and makes the straw musty,
and the eggs do not sell as they should at
the proper price in London.
Clause 5 extends the Public Health Acts
Amendment Act and makes it compulsory
on every urban and rural district to carry
out that Act. Up to the present only a
certain proportion of the Urban and Rural
Councils are carrying out the Act. I am
glad to say that Dungannon Urban Council
was the first one to do so. A good many
Councils have now taken it on. Although
the Ballymoney Council had a picture of me
throwing eggs at someone with a cock crowing, I believe that when asked to take this
matter on they did so and found it very
useful.
Clause 6 gives power to any officer of the
Ministry to enter and examine the place
where eggs are kept and being packed to
1 test them and see that they are what they
are supposed to be.
Clause 7 makes it eligible for us to make
rules and regulations. At first we cannot
say exactly what will be required. We do not
want to make a long Bill with too many
clauses. We want to make it open to us if
we like to make rules for testing and grading
! so that we can bring our eggs to the market
and have them in the same condition as the
Danish eggs which obtain the higher prices.
Clause 8 deals with the fines. The penalty
for the first offence is a fine not exceeding
£20, for the second offence a fine not
exceeding £50, and for the third
offence a fine not exceeding £100. We
find it is necessary to impose considerable
fines. It is wonderful how many cases there
are of the public being defrauded as regards
eggs. I heard the other day of one buyer
getting 200 cases of eggs from a part of
Northern Ireland, and every single one was
condemned by the officer of health in Belfast,
so I think a fine of £50 is not too much for
that kind of thing. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.) Clause 10 deals only with the title of
the Bill.
This Bill is opening new ground so far as
Great Britain is concerned, and I am proud
to think that we in Northern Ireland are the
first to bring in a Bill of this kind to help the
consumer to get eggs of the quality that he
is paying for. We do not intend to carry out
the provisions of this Measure in a hard way.
Hon. Members will remember that the Live
Stock Act also broke new ground in Great
Britain. When that Measure was passed a
large number of people thought they would
be ruined by the refusal of licences for their
bulls; but as a matter of fact we took it so
easily at the start that a great many people
said we were not half severe enough. As time
goes on we intend to become a little tighter
in the application of that Act. We intend to
administer this Bill in a very easy way at
first, and then to become firmer in insisting
on the carrying out of the various provisions.
We know that in order to carry out this Bill
in a proper way we must have the sympathy
of the people of our own country, and we
hopo to have the assistance of all the buyers,
small and great. As I said before, practically
all the egg merchants have agreed to the provisions of this Bill. We had several meetings
with them, and we showed them the draft of
the Measure which we proposed to bring in.
I beg to move.
Mr. COOTE: I am sure we have all listened
with a
great amount of interest to the
Minister of Agriculture trying to explain this
Bill; but, if I may be allowed to say so, he
has failed to show us how he is going to
eliminate the stale egg, and to deal with the
cgg that has arrived at ૧ certain stage.
Nothing in this Bill does that directly, many
things will do it indirectly: but I submit it
is impossible for any Minister or any country
to eliminate the stale egg at once by means
of an Act of Parliament. The industry is so
large and diversified and the commodity
passes through so many hands that it will
require the greatest patience, care, sympathy
and attention to arrive at the stage when you
2A
Marketing of Eggs Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Second Reading.

can say that you are properly directing the
egg industry. What we are afraid of-when
I say "we" I speak of the people in the
country, because probably I have better
means of knowing what the people are saying
than the Minister-is that the Government
will try to control this industry. My criticism
of this Bill on the second reading will be
sympathetic, and I want to say at once that
the people all over the Six Counties are
anxious to have some sort of proper reform.
We had experience of Government control
during the war, and our people do not want
any more interference on the part of Governments with any industry in our country or
for that matter in any other country. Speaking for our own country, I may say that the
people fear there will be too much fussing
and meddling with this industry, and that
fantastic and unnecessary measures will have
the effect of depreciating the value of the
industry. In other words we are afraid that
this Act will resolve itself into a mere official
piece of interference, instead of giving fairplay all round to the producers and the consumers of the eggs, and that officials who
know nothing and care less about the conditions, or at any rate who are not anxious
about them, may do things that are not
above-board. That sort of thing will do great
harm, and will cause an outcry. We wish to
avoid that.
In the first place, I object to the grounds
of the Charlemont Report, on which the Bill
is based. I am sorry I have not the Report
with me, but if you will look at that document you will find in the appendix that only
about half-a-dozen interested people were
summoned as witnesses before the Charlemont Commission. There were some twenty
representative men on the Commission, but
there was very little information given to
them. There were one or two wholesale
people examined, and that was practically
the whole thing; but the people who keep the
fowl, the people who collect the eggs, the
people who live by this means, were not
brought there in order to voice their
difficulties. Something that was pigeon-holed
in the offices of the old department in Dublin,
and that was tried on many a time before,
was brought down and was tried on Ulster.
It was probably thought that we were now
of a more gullible temperament than in the
old days when North and South were together. I hope they are not making a mistake of that sort, because it would be a very
serious thing if they did so.
As to the tone of the Minister in moving
the Second Reading of this Bill, I thought it
was pitched in rather a doleful key. He told
us that Danish eggs fetch the highest price
in the British market. I would like to ask
him does he know the facts? Was it his officials that gave him these figures? Is that so?
We shall see. He told us that the Irish trade
has practically gone. Is he aware that the
trade has increased threefold in the last five
or six years? The value of eggs exported
from Ireland in 1913 was, I think, £3,000,000
odd.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I said so in my speech.
Mr. COOTE: Well, it was an unfortunate
thing to say that the trade has practically
gone. It is better to look at the situation in
its proper perspective, and to deal fairly with
the producers as well as the consumers, and
with those who market the commodity, because this is one of the largest and most re
munerative industries that we have in the
Province of Ulster. It touches a great number of people who are voters, and we ought
not to trifle with them, but we should deal
sympathetically with them and try to evolve
a system that will meet with public approval.
When we have the public behind us we will
eliminate very largely the stale eggs. The
imposition of a small fine here and there is
not enough; you must have the people with
you; they must feel that this measure is for
the betterment of the industry and for the
benefit of the people all round.
I wish to draw the attention of the House
to Clause 1, which deals with the licensing of
wholesale dealers in eggs. It says:-
(1) The Ministry of Agriculture for Northern Ireland (in this Act referred to as
"the Ministry ") shall grant a licence to
carry on business in Northern Ireland as a
wholesale dealer in eggs to any person
applying for such licence who complies or
undertakes to comply with such conditions
in relation to the preparation for sale and
the consignment of eggs as may be prescribed from time to time by the Ministry,
with respect to any class of such business,
in order to secure-
(a) the proper testing, grading and
packing of such eggs; and their freshness
and fitness for the food of man;
and so on. I submit that we have a right to
see this licence. There may be some very
irksome conditions laid down in connection
with it. Parliament is asked to give the
Ministry a blank cheque. It has never been
given a blank cheque before, and for my part
I refuse to give it. We ought to see this
licence, and to know the conditions. We are
willing to support the Government in carrying out any order they may make, if it is a
proper order, and if it is not an irksome one;
but I submit that between this and the final
stages of this Bill, before the Third Reading,
the licence ought to be laid upon the table
of this House. I think that is a reasonable
request, and that that is the way to get the
co-operation of everybody concerned.

I:

Some things are disclosed, and others are
not; of course the officials keep them back.
There are two things that they intend to do,
3 but they have not the manliness to say so
here. They intend to exclude the use of boxes
made from native Irish timber, to eliminate
the use of straw, and to bring about the use
of Swedish wood. I believe that is the goal
which they wish to attain-the use of wood
not grown in Ireland, the use of Swedish
timber and wood-wool. Those are two of
the principal factors, but they are not in the
Bill, and they are trying to get a blank
cheque so that they can exercise those powers.
As to wood-wool, this Ministry of Agriculture
is very careful to refrain from the use of anything that might carry Foot and Mouth
Disease. But this wood-wool comes from the
continent, and is dumped down in Liverpool,
one of the areas prescribed under the Foot
and Mouth Diseases Order. They will bring
that wood-wool over to Ireland; it does not
matter if our cattle get Foot and Mouth
disease; not at all. In fact they are insisting on the use of wood-wool in the egg
competition at the agricultural show, for
which they are offering a prize of £50. They
are trying to make the ratepayers provide
that premium of £50, and at the same time
to eliminate the purchase of their straw.
They will not allow straw to be used, but
they will take material brought from
infected districts, and bring it to the largest
show in the Province of Ulster, with the result that our cattle may become infected
with the disease.
Take another item in connection with that
interesting competition. They tell us
about the conditions in Sweden, and that
farmers here can have such a monopoly, but
they will not allow the Irish boxmaker-the
Ulster boxmaker-to make boxes from native
wood. Your fir cannot be used in connection
with the competition. Under this Order that
is coming in, the Ulster farmer will not be
able to sell his timber. If you will pay a
visit to my constituency, I will show you a
very interesting and excellent series of boxmaking places, and I will not be ashamed to
compare their work with anything that the
foreigner can turn out. Why should they be
precluded from sending their work to Belfast,
their own Belfast that they are paying for?
Why should they be excluded and Swedish
stuff brought in in competition? The thing
is ridiculous. It is only in a Government
office that this could happen. It is not the
fault of the Minister. I am not blaming
the Minister. He knows the value of
timber. His great-grandfather grew excellent timber, and he knows the value of it.
To cut this timber out of our own market
from doing a thing which it can do exceedingly well is simply ridiculous. But it is the
officials who are doing this thing. This is
an officials' Bill. It is not the Minister's
Bill. I do not blame the Minister, but I
hope that on the Committee stage he will
give his attention to these matters to which
I am now drawing attention.
As to the reason for using these two items,
-wood-wool and imported timber-first of
all may I ask, in reply to the doleful
explanation of the Minister, what is the best
test of the excellence of eggs? Is not the
best test of the excellence or non-excellence
of Irish eggs the prices they obtain in the
British market? I challenge the Minister
to say that we do not obtain in many places
as fine a price for Irish eggs as is paid for
English home-grown eggs. When we reach
the price of English home-grown eggs we
are satisfied. I am not here to besmirch
Ulster or the egg producers of the Province.
I say the production of eggs has improved
all along the line, both in quantity and in
quality. The egg trade never was as well in
the history of Ireland.
Mr.
ARCHDALE: Hear, hear. The
Ministry did that.
Mr. COOTE: Then what is complained of?
Where is the necessity for the setting up of

Danish eggs are the finest eggs that are imported into England because they are imported in wood-wool. The inference is that

"Glad to hear your very latest quotations. Danish to-day are 17s to 17s 6'd free

That is per great hundred. Take another

would be simply sending in eggs and the

things from the minds of the people.
Then everything will be right. We want to
stand behind the Government for better
markets. We want to eliminate damp and
the necessity for people packing eggs on a
wet street when the straw will get wet and
among all that muck and dirt. It is disgraceful. If we eliminate all that we have the
finest district for eggs in the United Kingdom. We have our eggs growing in the
estimation of the British market as you can
see by these letters. We are beating the
Dane; we are beating Europe. Now we should
have a make-up of our own. The Government should get a make-up of their own and
try to use as much Irish raw material as
they can. That should be the object instead
of looking into musty cupboards of ten years
ago when somebody or other up in Dublin
did not know what he was talking about.
We want a real, practical scheme which will
give our own people employment. If the
Government give that, you will have one of
the most popular schemes it would be possible
for them to evolve. I do say that one little
mistake one way or another will send
hundreds and thousands of people on the
wrong side. Therefore, it will require more
careful handling.
That is all I have got to say, except that I
want to point out finally to the Minister that
in all these arrangements we should be very
careful that we do not put on unreasonable
expense, because all that will come eventually

or mere fantastic elements into your trade or
appoint a number of inspectors and make the

plenty of expense and all that. The

Ireland. We are not going to make the work
of getting rid of the eggs any more difficult
to the farmer. There is no difficulty
in going round and collecting the
eggs. We cannot put "shipper" on them,
because that would be against the law of
Great Britain. We have to put "dealer." A
wholesale egg dealer is a man who does not
sell by retail; that is the only thing about
it. It does not do away with the lorry which
goes about the country collecting eggs. The
hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh was
also down on the Ministry-I do not think he
was down on me personally-because I said
that Irish eggs were not valued in England
as much as English eggs
Mr. COOTE: Continental eggs.
Mr. ARCHDALE: I do say that Irish eggs
are more valued in England than English
eggs. The quality of Irish eggs is supreme.
No eggs equal them; tney are a long way
better than English eggs, and the English
people would be only too glad if they could
get them in boxes, knowing that when they
opened the boxes they would find the real
Irish eggs. I think as the hon. Member for
Derry (Mrs. Chichester) said the hon. Member
for the University (Dr. Morrison) like
Balaam got up to curse but remained to bless.
At the end of his speech he seemed to be
satisfied with almost everything in the Bill.
My hon. and g allant Friend behind
(Major Shillington) spoke about the regu-
'lations. The men who will receive the
licences will know that we in the Ministry
are not going to behave like lunatics, and are
not going to make idiotic regulations. I will
look into the matter, as far as I can, to see if
anything can be done about laying the

me
regulations on the Table; but we have to
change the regulations now and then both in
regard to grading and selling by weight. We
hope to introduce selling by weight, but we
cannot do so in a hurry. I can assure the
bon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh that
we have no wish at all to bring in rules and
regulations that will operate harshly on the
dealers in eggs. We are certainly not going
to limit the number of wholesale dealers;
there will be as many as ever before; but I
daresay we may crush out some of those
dealers about whom the Member for Derry
spoke, those who keep the eggs for a fortnight
and then send them somewhere else where
they are kept for another fortnight, with the
result that by the time they get to England
they take away the character of Irish eggs.
I feel very grateful to hon. Members for the
way they have spoken about the Bill, and I
can assure them it will be the fault neither
of the Ministry nor of myself, if this measure
does not do good to the Irish egg industry.
Mr. CRAWFORD: May I ask if it is the
intention of the Government to put something into this Bill dealing with selling by
weight?
Mr. ARCHDALE: No, we are not putting
that into the Bill. That would make a great
change too suddenly. We hope to be able to
get the people to buy by weight. A great
many dealers are in favour of buying by
weight, but we will have to wait while we
educate the people gradually.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
There is practically no change from the
Estimate of last year. Our business goes on
from day to day, and from week to week,
on a very level standard, and therefore the
variations are comparatively trifling. There
is only one item of real importance which
will be dropped in this coming year, and that
is the item which is printed in italics at
the bottom, entitled "Special Inquiries,"
£1,000, a non-current charge. That was to
pay for the services of an expert from the
Royal Navy who came over here to launch for
us the new scheme of the Ulster Division
of the Royal Naval Volunteer Reserve.
I would like to take this opportunity of
stating to the Committee the deep obligation
we are under to Captain Hartland Mahon
for having carried through what is known
to us as a very difficult operation, and for
having secured for us H.M.S. "Caroline,"
which was present at the battle of Jutland,
and which is at present in the lough, as our
drill ship. I believe that the tenders for
reconditioning and reconstruction are now
in, and, consequently, we trust that within
a short time there will be some work at all
events in the yards making that ship proper
for drill purposes. The Marquess of
and Ava has been appointed
Captain of the Division, and when the
vessel is ready recruiting will be begun, and
I have no doubt that the city of Belfast and
our entire district will make the Division
one of the best Divisions in the Royal Naval
Volunteer Reserve.
Dufferin
With the exception of that sum there is
no substantial variation in the Estimate.
Like other departments we are limiting the
expenses as far as we possibly can, so that
there shall be no extravagance if it can be
prevented. If hon. Members care to go back
to the earlier Votes they will observe that
there has been a steady decline in the Estimates put forward. Even on this year, over
and above that £1,000 to which I have referred, there is a saving of £232, and we
hope that next year, if the political waters
are unruffled by any unlooked-for incident,
we may be able to effect further economies.
I beg to move.

Oral Answer to Question.
NORTHERN IRELAND'S CONTRIBUTION
TO THE IMPERIAL GOVERNMENT.
Mr. DUFF: Might I ask a question of the
Minister of Finance, of which I have given
private notice? It is to ask the Minister of
Finance whether his attention has been
drawn to the reply given in the Imperial
House of Commons by the Financial Secretary to the Treasury on the 6th instant to a
question addressed to him by Mr. Cahir Healy
regarding the amount of contribution paid by
Northern Ireland during the years 1922-23 and
1923-24, and the grants-in-aid voted by the
Imperial Government to Northern Ireland
during those years; whether there is not a
discrepancy between these figures and those
given on the floor of this House; and, if so,
whether he will make a statement on the
matter?
The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINAN-
CIAL SECRETARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): On behalf of my
right hon. Friend the Minister of Finance, I
may say that he is grateful for the opportunity that has been afforded him to make the
following statement on the matter. It has to do
with the reply given by Mr. Graham to Mr.
Cahir Healy. The official report indicates
that the sums of £6,213,700 and £4,500,000 Spectively, and not £5,213,700 and £4,500,000, as
stated in the Press, were provisionally deducted from the Northern Irish Residuary
Share of Reserved Taxes in respect of the
two years in question. The total contribution, therefore, for the two years is
£10,713,700, to which may be added the contri-
-bution paid in the four months between the
22nd November, 1921, and the 31st March,
1922, amounting to £2,820,800. The gross contribution, therefore, from the date upon
which full financial responsibility rested upon
the Northern Government to the 31st March
last was, as stated by my right honourable
Friend the Prime Minister in his statement
to the House on Tuesday, the sum of
£13,534,500.
With regard to the total grants-in-aid paid
by the Imperial Government in the year
1923-24, I find that there is a discrepancy between the figures published in Mr. Graham's
reply and the accounts of my Department.
This discrepancy-which involves a sum of
£552,534-represents payments for Special
Constabulary and Malicious Injuries voted by
the Imperial Government last year, but
which did not reach the Ministry of Finance
until after 31st March last, and therefore
only appear in our current year's accounts.
The total grants-in-aid paid by the Imperial
Government between the 22nd November,
1921, and the 31st March, 1924, amounted to
£6,780,800, including the sum of £552,534
which came to account in the year 1921-25.
Deducting these grants from the gross amount
of contribution of £13,534,500, a net contribution of £6,753,700 is left.
I have given the net figure for the full
period since the Northern Government was
established. Mr. Graham's net contribution
figure for the years 1922-3 and 1923-4 is
£3,532,840, but in my view the figure should
really be slightly over £4,000,000.
I am
investigating this discrepancy, which I
imagine to be largely due to book-keeping
adjustments in the Treasury accounts which
have resulted in an understatement of the
actual position.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer
I think it would be far better that this House
should await the statement of the Minister
of Finance in introducing the Budget before
we take any notice of these questions.

which I wish to emphasise. These duties
will be particularly onerous during the
first few years of the operation of the
Act, when the local Education Authorities
may reasonably expect to receive suggestions
and advice from the Ministry on any doubtful and difficult points which may arise.
The Accountant to the Ministry has been
assigned the important duties of Controller
of Finance of Local Education Schemes, and,
in consideration of the greatly increased responsibility thus placed upon him, he has
been allowed a special personal rate of salary
which, however, will be liable to reconsideration in the event of a material change in circumstances. The staff of the Ministry has
been further strengthened by the appointment
of a principal clerk to fill a vacancy which
has existed since the formation of the
Ministry, two superintending officers, three
junior executive officers, eight clerks, two
typists, and a comptometer operator. Two
posts an assistant principalship and a
higher grade clerkship-have, however, been
removed from the establishment, so that the
net increase in the office clerical staff, as
compared with the clerical staff provided for
in last year's estimate, is fifteen, and I may
point out that eleven of the fifteen are in the
lower clerical and typing grades. I should
also say that this staff has not all been
engaged up to the present, but will be
engaged as required. Although the increase
of staff as thus set forth is due mainly to the
additional work devolving upon the Ministry
under the operation of the Education Act,
it is not entirely attributable to this cause.
Even apart from the Act, there has been a
steady expansion of the work of the Department since the transfer of services to Belfast,
and part of the additional staff is required
for work which is not directly due to the
operation of the Act. The increase in the
staff, as thus outlined, was decided on in
consultation with the Ministry of Finance,
and after full and careful consideration, and
the Minister is satisfied that the nature and
volume of the additional work to be discharged by the Department is such that it
cannot be adequately performed by any lesser
staff. It will be observed that the subhead
has now been classified so as to show the
staff engaged in each of the main divisions of
the Ministry. I am sure hon. Members will
agree with me that this is a distinct advantage, because at later periods when we wish
to compare it will make that operation much
easier.
The increases under other subheads do not
call for much comment. Subhead C3 (Maintenance and Repairs) shows an increase of
£30, and subhead C4 (Furniture and Fittings)
an increase of £200. The requirements
under these subheads are estimated by the
technical officers of the Works Branch of the
Ministry of Finance, which is responsible for
seeing that the office buildings and equipment
are maintained in a suitable condition.
increases of £200 for Printing (subhead D) and
£100 for Incidental Expenses (subhead G) are
due to the general expansion in the activities
of the Ministry under the operation of the
Education Act.

where this

CLASS IV. No. 2.
EDUCATIONAL SERVICES.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That a sum, not exceeding £1,400,539, be
granted to His Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st March, 1925, to provide for
Educational Services, including Grants-in-
Aid of the Teachers' Pension Fund, Northern
Ireland, (10 and 11 Geo. V. c. 67; 12 and 13
Geo. V., c. 13 [N.I.], and Grants under 13
and 14 Geo. V. c. 21 [N.I.]."- -(Note.-
£500,000 has been voted on account.)
Mr. McKEOWN: This Vote 2 is a very substantial one, amounting to almost £2,000,000,
and I shall endeavour to the best of my
ability to elucidate and explain the necessity
for such a large sum. Hon. Members will
note that the net amount which will be required by the Ministry of Education to provide for the cost of Educational Services
during the current financial year is estimated
at £1,900,539, as compared with £1,845,805
voted for 1923-24, an increase of £54,734.
It is to be observed, however, that this
latter figure does not represent the true increase in estimated expenditure on
educational services in the current year, but
merely the increase in the net amount which
Parliament is being asked to vote. The
capital outlay on the building and equipment
of the new Training College and Hostels for
elementary teachers at Stranmillis exhibits
a very large increase over the corresponding
expenditure last year, but as it is offset by an
equivalent receipt from the special grant of
£400,000 which has been made by the
Imperial Government, it does not increase
the net amount which Parliament is now
being asked to vote.
To arrive at the real increase in estimated
expenditure we must compare, not the net
estimates for the two years, but the gross
estimates-that is, the estimates as they
appear before allowance is made for the re
ceipts which will be appropriated in aid of
the Vote. It will then be seen that it is
anticipated that the gross expenditure in the

place, the cost of living was rapidly increasing, and, in the month in which the Agreement was signed, it reached its highest point,
176 per cent. above the figure for July, 1914,
the standard month. When it is considered
that the corresponding figure for February
last was 79 per cent., it will be realised how
hich greatly circumstances have altered since
that Agreement was signed.

undergoing training for the position
teachers in public elementary

completing their final year at the Church
of Ireland Training College in Dublin, under

which will terminate at the close of the
current session; 77 are in St. Mary's Training

new Training College at Stranmillis.
In the course of the past year, a large
amount of work has been carried out in
connection with the new Training College.
Temporary hostels, providing accommodation
for about 100 women students, have been
erected, and the entire hostel accommodation
is now sufficient for about 125 students. It
is hoped that the hostel accommodation
which will be available at the beginning
of the next training session, will be

The sum of £35,509 is provided under subhead A6 in connection with the superannuation of elementary teachers. Of this
amount, £1,000 is to provide retiring
gratuities to teachers who were in the service
at the time of the passing of the National

in regard to pension on retirement. The

which are paid into that Fund with a view

The sum of £6,380 is provided under subhead B3 to meet the cost of the maintenance and repairs of the Model schools and
certain Public Elementary Schools which are
vested in the Ministry. The responsibility
of the Ministry for maintaining these
schools in suitable repair will continue until
they are transferred to the education
authorities of the areas in which they are
situated.
The estimate for furniture and fittings
(subhead B4) shows a decrease of £4,180.
This decrease is principally due to the fact
that the capital outlay on furniture and
fittings for the new college and hostels at
Stranmillis is expected to amount to only
£3,100 this year, as against £7,000 last year.
The sum of £97,180 is provided for New
Works, Alterations and Additions (subhead
A5) as against £45,400 last year, an increase
of £51,780. It is expected that the capital
outlay on the works in connection with the
new college and hostels at Stranmillis will
amount to £80,000, as against £34,500 last
year, an increase of £45,500. The provision
under this subhead and under the furniture
and fittings subhead in respect of the capital
outlay on this institution thus amounts to
£83,100, but this is offset entirely by an

from the Imperial Government, for which

The grants which will become payable in
respect of the building of new Public Elementary Schools and the enlargement of
existing schools are estimated at £17,000, as
against £10,000 in 1923-24. When the new
Education Act is in full operation throughout the Six Counties, the building and enlarging of schools will be a matter for the
Local Education Authorities, but in the
meantime, such grants as have been
sanctioned by the Ministry must be paid as
the works are completed.
I come now to Intermediate Education. It
is estimated that the expenditure on Intermediate Education this year will amount to
£135,000, which is an increase of £37,775
over last year's figure. It would not, however, serve any useful purpose to institute
a comparison between the estimates, as last

payments to the schools were made partly
on the basis of the new regulations and

arrears of increment grant in respect of the
service of a large number of teachers whose
claims to recognition were still under investigation when the financial year closed.
Neither year, therefore, can be considered
normal as regards expenditure.
Hon. Members will remember that the revised regulations which were framed by the
Ministry last year, and presented to Parlia
ment, provided for the payment of two

Secondary Schools, viz.:-
an incremental grant towards the
salries of recognised teachers serving on
the authorised staffs of the schools, including a special allowance for principal
teachers, and
a capitation grant replacing the several
grants previously paid to the Intermediate
Schools.
I would like specially to draw the attention of hon. Members to this matter of
Intermediate Education. They will see in
the Estimate that on former occasions there
were special grants-grants under the Intermediate Education Act, 1914, a capitation
grant, an interim grant, the normal

simplifies the whole position, and at the

matters which were considered not proper
in connection with these schools For
instance, there were grants in connection
with examinations and hon. Members are
aware that there was certain cramming and
so on in order to receive these grants. Now
I think you will agree that the existing

I am sure hon. Members will recall that
at the time when the educational services
were taken over by the Government of
Northern Ireland there was a special outcry
regarding the deplorable condition of secondary education. There is no doubt it was in
a bad condition, and I remember deputations
coming to the Minister at that time, and I
remember the Minister pointing out that ic
was his intention, as far as the resources of
this country would permit, to endeavour to
put secondary education on a sound and
proper basis commensurate with Northern
Ireland. Hon. Members will, I am sure,
agree that a great step forward has been
taken in this direction, and I think that we
can now state that this class of school in
Northern Ireland, under the new regulations,
will compare favourably with the same class
of school in any other part of the United
Kingdom. A scheme dealing with superannuation allowances for teachers in

I know that there is some uneasiness owing

some little delay at this time, because certain

For various reasons it was thought desirable

brought into force on 1st October, 1924, and

regulations for the payment of the grants,

Education and approved by the Minister of
Finance, and have been duly presented to

authority in the current financial year shall

defined in these rules, incurred in accordance
with a financial scheme approved by the
Ministry and disbursed within the year.
The maximum grant may not exceed two-thirds

which the grant is payable.

is to enable even the poorest boy or girl to go
to a University, if possible; but if the
parents cannot purchase the books for the
children to study at the elementary schools
there is very little prospect of the Act being
of any assistance to those for whose benefit it
was passed. I have had it brought to my
notice on a good many occasions that there
are children sitting in these schools without
books, owing to the fact that their parents
are unable to find the money necessary to
pay for the books. I am afraid the Education Act is going to fail in the object that
we all hoped it would attain if we are not
able to provide books for the children
attending the schools.
There is also the question of the principals
of the schools claiming the right to sell
books to the children. We find in a great
many cases that cheaper books can be bought
outside the schools, but the pupils are not
allowed to buy outside. I remember when I
was attending school that in the case of large
families it was possible to transfer the books
of the older children to the younger after
the annual examination, the younger ones
going into the class that the older ones were
leaving. But we find under the present
system that the books are continually changing, and instead of one pupil being able to
hand over his books to another it is necessary
in some cases to get five or six different sets
of books during the year. I hope that when
the Parliamentary Secretary is replying to
these questions he will be able to assure the
parents of the poorer class of children that
the Ministry does intend to do something
for those who are not in a position to pay
the very high charges that are made for
education at present, and to see that there
will be some prospect of their being able to
take advantage of this new system of education which we hope will be beneficial to all
our people.

Mr. MOLES in the Chair.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That it is expedient to authorise a charge
upon moneys provided by Parliament of all
such sums as may be required in respect of
the expenses of the Ministry of Agriculture,
under any Act of the present Session,
making provisions for the licensing of wholesale dealers in eggs, the registration of
premises where eggs are preserved, the better
testing, grading, and packing of eggs, and
the better prevention of the sale of eggs

The PARLIAMENTARY AND FINANCIAL
SECRETARY OF THE MINISTRY OF
FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): With reference to
the Bill dealing with the Marketing of Eggs,
which received a Second Reading yesterday,
it will be perfectly obvious to the Members
of the Committee that there will be a certain charge upon public funds in order to
carry out the provisions of that Measure.
For instance, inspectors will have to be
appointed in order to see that the Act is
properly carried out, and suitable inspection
will have to take place. On the other hand
there will be a slight income in the way of
fees charged for licences.
Mr. McGUFFIN: But that will not recur;
you will only, have it once.
Mr. BARBOUR: It will recur, because
after all people will die, and when the new
generation come forward to take up the
business they will have to take out licences.
In order that the Committee may not think
they are being asked for a blank cheque in
this way, I may say it is expected that at
the start there will be one chief inspector and
two assistant inspectors, who will of course
have to cover the area of the Six Counties.
There may be a recurring charge of about
£1,000 in order to carry out this work of
expansion. Of course any appointments that
may be made will be subject to the usual
control of the Ministry of Agriculture, and p
also subject to the sanction of the Ministry
of Finance. I beg to move.

Ministers (Temporary Exercise
of Powers) Bill.
Order for Second reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
This Bill, as the title imports, is a Bill to
make provision for the temporary exercise
of the powers of Ministers of Northern
Ireland. Hon. Members are aware of the
emergency which necessitates this legislation.
The Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson
Bates) is unfortunately laid up with a
serious illness. Certain things can only
be done by the Minister in person.
but
Accordingly it becomes necessary to make
provision not only for this case
also in reference to the inability for any
reason of any other Minister to act. The
Bill is made quite general and it gives to
his Grace the Governor of Northern Ireland
power where a Minister is unable to act to
་་
designate any Parliamentary Secretary of
the Ministry or Department of which such
Minister is the head, or any other Minister
of Northern Ireland, to act for such firstmentioned Minister during such period
as the said Governor may think fit; and,
during the said period, references in any
enactment to such first-mentioned Minister
shall be construed as references to the
Parliamentary Secretary or Minister so
designated to act."
Mr. McGUFFIN: Might I ask the right hon.
and learned Gentleman (Mr. Best) is there a
precedent for this in the Imperial House?
Is it necessary there, and is it observed?
Mr. BEST: In answer to that, it is
generally the Ministry that is specified in
the Acts of the Imperial House and so the
difficulty would not arise.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I see.
Mr. BEST: Take, for example, those regulations under the Civil Authorities (Special
Powers) Act. Take internment orders; all these
things can be done by the Minister and by the
Minister only, and, accordingly, if we wish
to intern a person, or to make a new regulation, or anything of that kind, it cannot
be done except by the Minister. The
Minister of Home Affairs (Sir Dawson Bates)
is quite unable to transact business
present, and, therefore, it is absolutely
necessary that provision of this sort should
be made. I do not know whether there is
a precedent in the Imperial Parliament,
but there is a precedent established by this
Parliament under the office of Attorney-
General Act of 1923. Section 2 of that Act
gave power to appoint a substitute in case
the Attorney-General were unable to act.
Colonel WOODS: No, no.
at
Mr. BEST: The hon. and gallant Member
says No, no." I do not exactly know
what the meaning of that observation is. It
seems to have no relevance to any observation I have made, or to any observation
anyone could even think of. There was power
taken to nominate a deputy to the Attorney-
General, because in his case there are many
things which can be done only by him. There
are many statutory obligations which he has
to carry out, and if power had not been
taken to enable a substitute to be appointed
then, if the Attorney-General for the time
being were suddenly to be ill, or for some
reason he had to be absent, that particular
work could not be done. Accordingly, Clause
2 of the Office of Attorney-General Act, 1923,
provided for the nomination of a substitute.
This does precisely the same thing for any
Minister who for any reason may be unable
to act.
Mr. McGUFFIN This Bill seems quite
innocent. It hardly challenges criticism, and

Mr. BEST indicated dissent.
Mr. McGUFFIN: It has some relevance to
it at any rate. Are we to take it that, during

Secretary would be acting as locum tenens,

Mr. BEST: No.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Nothing of that sort takes

mentioned it. That is all I have to say.

point.
Mr. DONALD: We quite recognise that

If this temporary Minister gets into a diffculty will he take the full responsibility?

Minister. I think the House could have
carried on well without the Bill. The House N
has made no complaint and has not asked th

Mr. POLLOCK: My hon. Friend who has
just spoken is under a grave misappre
hension with regard to this matter. This
refers to purely administrative matters where

quired, and in the absence of the Minister

immemorial. It requires a Statute here to

that is to say in the absence of a Minister
where a signature has to be made some other
person shall be endowed with the necessary

mation I wanted from my right hon. Friend.
This only refers to cases where a signature

fore him, and I hope he will not be vested

when they put anything up to him.
Colonel WOODS: I want to ask the right
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Pollock) one question.
If a temporary Minister takes full responsibility for the office does he also get the pay
and emoluments of that office?

Oral Answers to Questions.
R.U.C. GUARD FOR ULSTER PAVILION
AT WEMBLEY.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has now decided to
furnish a guard from the Royal Ulster Constabulary for the Ulster Pavilion, British
Empire Exhibition, at Wembley.
:
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS (Mr.
Megaw) This matter has been carefully considered, and it has been ascertained that
before members of the Ulster Constabulary
could exercise the powers of police officers at
the British Empire Exhibition they would
have to be sworn in as special constables in
London. Apparently Canada is the only Colonial Government which has sent a detachment of police to the Exhibition.
In all the circumstances of the case, the
Northern Government does not consider it
would be justified in incurring the heavy expense which sending a party of the Ulster
Constabulary to the Exhibition would entail.
MANAGEMENT OF THE ULSTER
PAVILION AT WEMBLEY.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Commerce whether he can now state if an
assistant manager has been appointed for the
Ulster Pavilion, British Empire Exhibition,
at Wembley.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
McKeown): I am replying for my right honourable Friend. The reply is in the negative.
I should add, for the information of the hon.
and gallant Member, that it is not intended
to make the appointment to which he refers.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask if it is possible for the
Ulster Pavilion to be properly carried on
without a manager?
Mr. McKEOWN: We have an official of the
Ministry of Commerce there, and he is able
to deal with any matters that arise.
ADMINISTRATION AND DISCIPLINE OF
THE C1 SPECIALS.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will consider the
adoption of certain sections of the Army Act
to apply to the administration and discipline
of the C1 Force, Royal Ulster Special Constabulary, or whether he will lay down definite
regulations for the guidance of the adminis
trators and commanders of that Force.
Mr. MEGAW: The question of supplement
ing the disciplinary powers for this branch
of the Constabulary is under consideration.
Such disciplinary powers must be framed
with regard to statutes and regulations
governing the Police Forces in Northern Ireland.
PRIVATE WORK BY GOVERNMENT
ARCHITECTS.
4. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Finance whether any of the whole-time
architects employed and paid by the Northern
Government are allowed to do, or are doing,
private work outside their official duties.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock) I have no information concerning
the manner in which members of the
Northern Civil Service occupy their time
outside official hours, and it would be improper for me to institute any inquiry on
the subject.
The general principle governing questions
of this nature is that a Civil Servant must
not accept any employment which is likely to
interfere with the proper discharge of his
official duties. The conditions obtaining in
the Imperial Civil Service, which have been
adopted as far as possible for the Civil Service
of Northern Ireland, are generally defined in
the Order in Council of 10th January, 1910.

Mr. POLLOCK: There are now engaged on

Mr. ANDREWS: The document to which

UNOCCUPIED COASTGUARD COTTAGES.
9. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of Agriculture whether he will state the number of
houses at present unoccupied at the various
coastguard stations in Northern Ireland, and
what is the policy of the Government with
respect to these houses.
Mr. POLLOCK: I have taken this question
in the regrettable absence of my right hon.
Friend. As the hon. Member is aware, the
Coastguard Service is an Imperial one, and
therefore not within the jurisdiction of this
House. The Ministry of Finance acts as
agent for the Imperial Government in respect
of the letting of coastguard cottages, and I am
therefore enabled to acquaint the hon. Member that the number of houses at present
unoccupied at the various coastguard stations
in Northern Ireland is twenty-of which nine
are available for letting. Unfortunately, in
the case of these nine no applications have
been received, due, doubtless to their isolated
position. The remaining eleven are
undergoing certain structural alterations,
upon the completion of which the cottages will
be occupied by members of the Coastguard
Service.

In
Mr. McKEOWN: I am replying for my
right honourable Friend. Under an agreement entered into between the Postmaster-
General and the British Broadcasting Company, the latter secured the sole right of
establishing wireless broadcasting stations in
Great Britain and Northern Ireland.
December last the Postmaster-General informed the Ministry of Commerce that he had
received an application from the company for
permission to establish a broadcasting station
in Belfast, and inquired whether the Government of Northern Ireland would desire to
impose on such permission any special conditions. After consultation with the Ministry
of Home Affairs, the Ministry of Commerce
replied specifying certain conditions which,
in the opinion of the Government of Northern
Ireland, should be attached to the Postmaster-
General's permission. It is understood that
the company has been able to proceed with
the erection of the station subject to those
conditions, and, while I am unable to make
any definite pronouncement on the point, I
am informed that it is expected that the
station will be completed and ready for
operation by the middle of July next.

Mr. McKEOWN: One of the conditionsand a very important one-is the right to stop
the transmission, at any time that such a
course is considered necessary or desirable in
the public interest. That right is reserved
to the Northern Government.

CLASS III. No. 2.
NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum, not exceeding £110,100, be
granted to His Majesty, to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will
come in course of payment during the year
ending on the 31st day of March, 1925, in
respect of the contributions and grants in aid
of the cost of benefits and expenses of administration under the National Health
Insurance Acts, 1911-1922."-(Note-£35,000
has been voted on account.)
Mr. ANDREWS: The figures shown in this
Estimate are few, and by themselves require
little explanation. They disclose a decrease.
as compared with 1923-24, of £4.175. which I
think the Committee will consider satisfactory, especially having regard to the fact that
the Estimate is made on the advice of Sir
Alfred Watson. who probably is the chief
authority in the United Kingdom on such
matters. Sub-head A (£145,000) provides for
grants in aid of benefits. That is the State
share of two-ninths of all benefits paid by
approved societies. The reduction of £1,100
is partly due to closer estimating, and partly
due to a reduction in administration allowances to approved societies, from 4s 10d to
4s 5d per insured person per annum.
Under
Sub-head B a sum of £100 only is provided,
the same as last year, to meet belated claims
relating to the period prior to the 1st April,
1922, when the cost of medical certification
was paid for by the State. The Estimate for
expenses of members of Insured Committees
will in future be charged in the ordinary
administration fund of these committees.
I may say that since the Ministry of Labour
took over control of National Health
Insurance we have been able to introduce a
considerable number of economies. In the
first place, there were in Dublin-and I think
are still-three Commissioners. We have
been able to get on without any Commissioner
here. In addition, there are three medical
advisers, and, for so far, any little work of
that kind we have required to be done has
been done for us by the Home Office, at a very
moderate cost. Then, again, there is in
Dublin, I understand, a legal adviser, with his
staff. So far, we have not required to seek
advice of that kind. We have also been able
to introduce savings by means of having a
combined Health Insurance inspector. All
these savings, it is estimated, have amounted
to about £16,000.

Approved societies, the Committee will be
interested to know, have distributed during the
past financial year in sickness benefit £196,150;
disablement benefit, which I would prefer to
call, for the sake of clearness, continuous
sickness benefit, £113,750; maternity benefit,
£44,700; sanatorium benefit, £21,000, or in all
£376,000. It is gratifying to know that in
benefits paid directly to our sick
workers more than the total amount
collected in contributions from Our employers and workers has been paid,
and that the cost of administration and
creating these large, reserves, which it is esti
mated by those who are responsible is
necessary in order to keep the fund solvent
through future years, has been paid out of
the State contribution of two-ninths of the
benefits actually paid. It is estimated that
about 40,000 persons drew sick benefit and
disablement benefit in Northern Ireland dur
ing the past year. This works out at an
average of sixteen weeks per person claiming
benefit or an average of slightly over two
weeks for all our insured persons per annum.
I quote these figures because it is often
held, I think by people who do not
fully understand the position, that of all the
contributions actually paid a large sum does
not go into the pockets of the insured
sick persons. I think the figures I have
quoted show that that is not really so,
be
cause when you remember that 40,000 of our
people have actually drawn benefit during the
year it shows the splendid work which is
being done by means of this fund. And it is
especially gratifying to me to know that this
fund is in a sound financial position. I wish
I could say exactly the same in connection
with the other insurance fund, for adminis
tering which my Department is responsible,
namely, Unemployment Insurance.

I have heard it said that some of our
approved societies are not as generous in paying claims as they ought to be, and sometimes
delays occur which are regrettable, and held
by some to be unnecessary. I really do think,
as regards straight cases, payment is made
almost immediately. There are, of course,
involved cases which require a great deal of
investigation; but where a doctor certifies
that his patient is not in a position to work,
the insured person may feel reasonably satisfied that in a very short time he will get the
benefit to which by statute he is entitled.
Personally speaking, I do not think the medical profession can be accused of harshness.
On the contrary, I think I can say from personal experience I have always found them
to be overflowing with the milk of human
kindness. They are not likely to refuse a certificate to any insured person on other than
proper grounds. In fact, I have heard it
said that on occasions they are so sympathetic
that they are inclined to stretch a point to
meet the insured person beyond which the
approved societies think is fair to them.
However that may be, I do not know exactly
myself, but I do feel, as I have already said,
that this is a great social benefit to our
people, and I have the greatest pleasure in
moving.

2D
