HOUSE OF COMMONS

[Dr. Morrison]
Committee to a case which I have already
brought before the Minister of Labour (Mr.
Andrews) a case that happened in this city
of Belfast. This girl, who is now employed
in a Government office in Belfast, was insured
on the 23rd January, 1917, and she paid her
contributions from 1917 till the 21st January,
1920. She was out of work through illness
from December, 1920, down to the 31st of
October, 1921. She was ten months out of
work, and her contribution from the
society in that time was £4 11s. She continued under treatment and got her certificate
from her doctor-a recognised medical man in
Belfast-and she says that, on the calculation
of her father, the society owes her thirteen
months' benefit, which they decline to pay.
What happened was this-and it is an example
of the technicalities that surround this question-she got a notice from the society that
she should go and be examined by the doctor
of the society. She was ill in bed and unable
to go, and did not go. She had no information
and did not know anything except that after
that her benefit stopped. She did not know
that she should write and say that she was
unable to go. I maintain that it was the
duty of the society to find out whether the
girl was able to go to be examined or not.
At any rate she did not go, and because she
did not go she was struck off, and for her
ten months' sickness the total contribution she
got from this beneficent Act was £4 11s 6d.
Mr. GORDON: Did she continue to send
her weekly certificate?
Dr. MORRISON: She did, but it had not
the effect of getting her any money. The
laws of the Medes and Persians are nothing
compared to the administration of these
friendly societies. Worse than all, she was
not then considered to be in receipt of
benefit. When you are sick you are not expected to contribute, but they did not hold
that she was free from contribution. Again
she got treatment, and they then had a big
pile of arrears against her about which the
poor girl knew nothing at all. In the administration of a great Act like this instruction and direction should be clear and distinct,
so that even the most illiterate person would
be able to read them and to know what to
do, while the names of the different inspectors,
whose duty it is to look after these things,
should be shown in the Post Offices or on the
backs of the cards, so that people may
know that they can go to these persons for
advice in any difficulty. I have known people
to do that, and the society at once cleared
the matter up. Very often the difficulty
arises from a little technicality. Many of
these people cannot write. What I urge upon
the Committee is that they should insist that
something is done to simplify the administration, and that something is done also to give
these people an easy Court of Appeal, instead
of this useless thing which they have at present, and which is like the protection afforded
to the unmarried woman in the past. They
should have some protection from the law
which is supposed to be of such advantage to
them. Even the poorest and humblest in our
community should have this protection.
I have dealt at some length with this
matter, but I have done it in a friendly spirit.
I quite know that the Minister of Labour,
and his deputy, and the officials under them,
have very difficult cards to play. I know
their object is my object, and the object
this Committee, and of every well-disposed
and philanthropic person in Ulster. I urge
upon them that now, after three years'
administration, something should be done to
get rid of these technicalities and to make
the law such that when persons get a doctor's
certificate they can go and obtain their benefit
without any restrictions or obstacles being
placed in their way.

dat Tyrone has referred to homes of rest and

Britain what is known as the Rural Workers'
National Health Insurance Society, which
has accumulated very large reserves, having
the
regard to the fact that the claims are very

in
In regard to the complaints made by hon.
Members of unfair treatment to insured
persons, I have been very largely in touch
with this matter myself, and I have written
many letters to insurance societies for people
who came to me seeking my aid, possibly in
a legal way. So far as the Northern Ireland
Insurance Societies are concerned, I have no
very serious complaint to make against them,
and I think that is possibly because they
are under a good Minister of Labour; but I
have come across some very serious cases
from London in which people have got very
bad treatment. An old lady who had been
an agricultural labourer all her life got a
peremptory letter from London to present
herself for examination before a doctor some
miles away.
She could not walk to the
station. She sent her brother in to pay the
doctor a special fee if he would come to see
her, but the brother had to get a motor-car
and take the old woman, accompanied by her
niece, to the doctor, this putting them to the
expense of from 25/- to 30/-. She did this be
cause she was told that if she were not there
on a certain day at a fixed hour no further
benefit would be paid. A similar case was
given by the hon. Member for the University
(Dr. Morrison) to-day. Because a young lady
did not present herself at the time and place
specified in the notice, all payments were
refused notwithstanding the fact that she
had sent in a medical certificate.
Quite recently the same question was
brought before me and I wrote a letter to
London pointing out the difficulties of the
case and stating they had asked this lady
before to attend. I got a reply that they
would not ask her to attend on this occasion.
I know that these London societies have a
headquarters. They are amalgamated
together and are all in the same pot,
all going in the same way and along the
same lines. I am sure we have only to
direct the attention of the Ministry of
Labour to this matter to have fair play
meted out to these workers. Unfortunately,
the poor people in remote country districts
do not know we have a sympathetic Minister
of Labour, and they do not know how to

CLASS V. No. 2.
AGRICULTURAL SERVICES.
Motion made, and
Question proposed :
That a sum not exceeding £51,029 be
granted to his Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during the
year ending on the 31st March, 1925, in
respect of the expenses of the Ministry of
Agriculture in respect of Agricultural
Institutions, Improvement of Live Stock,
Agricultural Research and Development,
Agricultural Statistics and Sundry Grantsin-Aid. (Note-£24,900 has been voted on
Account).
Mr. POLLOCK: I feel sure that every
Member of the Committee deplores as deeply
as I do the circumstances under which it
is my duty to submit this Estimate for the
Agricultural Services. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) I feel that our hearts go out
to our Colleague (Mr. Archdale) in the very
dark cloud that has overshadowed his life.
In submitting this Estimate I would call
the attention of the Committee to the fact
that there is an increase of £10,419. This is
accounted for by the fact that it arises from
a special grant made under somewhat unusual circumstances in the interest of
agriculture last year. The objects for which
the grant was made are shortly those of
agricultural education, of milk-recording
associations, the development of the poultry
industry, and the improvement in the
character and standard of mountain sheep.
I think it would be convenient if I spoke
of the incidence of that grant as the items
arising out of it appear from time to time
in subheads, and it may be, therefore, informative to hon. members if I recall the
fact that it arose out of a special grant
that was made to agriculture, following the
Report of a Committee which I appointed
and of which Viscount Pirrie, it will be
remembered, was the Chairman. A grant
of £128,000 was made in relief of rates on the
recommendations of that Committee. I do.
not say I was quite in agreement with that
recommendation because I felt that if that
very large sum of money had been devoted
to reproductive purposes-(Hon. Members:
Hear, hear)-it would have accomplished
very much more valuable results than the
comparatively small advantage that accrued
from the reduction that was made in the rates
of agricultural holdings. But the Committee
made a very important recommendation in
deferring to the wishes of the agricultural
community in which they urged upon the
Government the propriety of adopting the
considerations that were submitted by the
Secretary to the Ministry of Agriculture.
The result of that was that the Government
felt it was imposed upon them as an obligation that some grant should be made
that would be applied to matters of a reproductive character in the Province. The
result of that decision was that it was agreed
that a sum of £54,000, spread over four
years, should be devoted to the purposes
I have indicated, and a part of that sum
amounting to £14,925 will be spent during
the coming year and will be devoted to these
purposes.
I now come to the first sub-head, that is,
agricultural research. This Estimate shows
a decrease of £2,236, which is explained by a
reduction in the provision for initial capital
expenditure on new buildings and equipment.
The equipment of the Plant Breeding and
Poultry Divisions has been now practically
completed. You will see from the sheet on
page 49 we are asking for a re-vote of a
sum of £500 in respect of the former Division
being approximately the balance still due
to the contractors at the close of last
financial year for work almost completed.
There is also on the same sheet a more important sum of £3,500, intended for the
adaptation and equipment of buildings at
Stormont for the purpose of an Animal
Diseases Division. Some
provision was
made for this Service last year, but it was
not found practicable in that period to set
the work in motion. The necessary buildings, however, are now being put in hand
and, we hope, will be completed at an early

date. I should like to make it clear that the to which this work is being taken advantage

of.
year in connection with Research Stations

2 and agricultural education establishments
will be defrayed in full out of the special
grant of £400,000 which was made by the
Imperial Government for various objects,
one of which was scientific purposes. Agriculture rightly claimed that a share of that
£400,000 should be devoted to the object
which I am now discussing, and the costs of
the Diseases of Animals Division to which I
have referred will be paid out of that grant.

The decrease in the total provision for
Agricultural Research is due to reductions
in capital expenditure, and is to some extent counter-balanced by minor increases in
the Estimate for the upkeep of the various
Divisions. These minor increases were anticipated and are necessary to the development
of our research organisation. Provision
has been made for a second assistant to the
head of the Chemical Division. The work
of this officer will be in connection with
matters relating to animal nutrition, that
is "baby" beef experiments, which hon.
Members may have noticed took place some
time ago, and the feeding of ensilage to milch
cows instead of roots. It is interesting to
notice that during 1922 and 1923 of the recorded cows, about 50 to 60 samples of milk
a week were tested. At present the number
is 550 per week, showing, of course, a very
remarkable advance in the development of
this side of the Division.
In regard to research work I should like
to refer particularly to one small item of
£150 concerned with zoology. Hon. Members
must not assume that this is the initiation
of a zoological gardens scheme. It is intended for experimentation in respect of the
suppression of insects and those pests which
are so destructive to crops of all descriptions.
It should be of interest to the Committee
to know, for example, that the ravages of
the warble fly alone are estimated to reduce
by no less a sum than £1,000,000 annually
the value of the hides of animals slaughtered
in Ireland. There are other pests-parasites
in poultry, worms in pigs, gapes in fowl,
and so on, and there are also pests which
do much damage to fruit. These will all
be dealt with, at any rate initial arrangements will be made by this small grant of
£150 to proceed with the work of discovering
whether it will be possible to eliminate these
pestiferous insects. It may be of interest
to the Committee to know that the seedtesting station work is being largely availed
of. Last year the samples of seeds received
for testing were 250, this year they amount
to 1,700, which is an indication of the extent
A
We come now to agricultural education,
and under this sub-head hon. Members will
see that there are included three separate
educational institutions, one at Cookstown,
one at Strabane, and one at Antrim.
capital provision of £5,100 has been inserted
to cover an extension of the farm buildings
at the North-West Agricultural School,
Strabane, so as to render the farm an
economic proposition. Provision for this
extension was made in previous years, but
it was not found practicable to put the work
in hands. I should mention that the
capital expenditure for Greenmount and
also for the North-West School are
met out of the grant of £400,000
made by the Imperial Government on the
recommendation of the Colwyn Committee.
The number of pupils at each of the
Institutions is in the aggregate 85, and they
are being trained in the science of agriculture
and farming. Then there are the Queen's
University scholarships that come under
this head. By means of these scholarships
the Ministry hopes to have available a sufficient number of pupils to justify the
establishment of a Faculty of Agriculture
at Queen's University. The total number
of pupils at present at Queen's taking out
the Agriculture Course is twelve. Four are
under the Gibson scheme, that is the scheme
of grants given by the late Mr. Gibson for
County Down students.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask the right
hon. Gentleman are fees paid with respect
to these students, or do they get this education
free?
Mr. POLLOCK: You mean the students in
the University?
Mr. McGUFFIN: Yes.
Mr. POLLOCK: To what extent they contribute I am not prepared to say, but the
presumption is that they contribute in much
the same way as do students of our training colleges, by scholarships and exhibitions.
That is the common practice, but later on
I can let my hon. Friend know definitely the

I come now to the building
grant of £15,000 to the University. This
is part of the total expenditure of £42,000
which will be undertaken in connection with
the University and of which £15,000 will be
spent this year. The total estimated expenditure, as I have just mentioned, is
£42,000 of which the Government provide
£31,000, the University itself £6,000, while
£5,000 is provided by the bequest of the late
Miss Riddell. This grant of £31,000 is also
part of the award of £400,000 made by the
Colwyn Committee, and hon. Members will
realise that the object of the expenditure

which, as I have mentioned, was made by

and on

course this is only a beginning, and, with the

I come
now to sub-head D-Live Stock
Breeding Acts. This is a gradually decreasing sum, as hon. Members will see from
a perusal of the Estimates. Compared with
last year it shows a reduction of £375 in a
total of £900. The ultimate aim is to have
the whole of the inspection of bulls, to
which this item is devoted, done by our own
inspectors, so that it will not be necessary
to incur any additional expense over and
above the ordinary administration of the
department.
The next sub-head-Grants to County Committees is a much more pretentious item.
It follows what has been the custom for
many years in the past, and the amount is
practically the same as last year with tha
exception of a very important item of £5,400
for agricultural development, which is
devoted to providing increased facilities for
agricultural education generally. The County
Committees are provided with this money
because it is felt that it is a great advantage
to decentralise the work and to place most
of these duties upon the County Committers
rather than upon the Ministry itself. There
were only eight instructors and one agricultural Overseer at work in Northern
Ireland in the past, and, in view of the fact
that there are 130,000 farms scattered over the
Six Counties, it will be understood that it
would be quite impossible for these officers
to cover the whole of that area and to keep
in constant touch with all farmers, more
especially those in far away or backward
districts which it was more difficult to get
at. The Ministry is, therefore, arranging
that, in addition to the instructors at present
employed, ten overseers and two instructors
will be provided. The ten overseers will be
placed in backward districts to which in the
past the instructors have not been able to
give adequate attention. The cost of this
additional work for the current year is
estimated at £4,200.

The next item concerns the improvement
of pastures. In reply to the question which
was put some little time ago by the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin),
scholarships to the value of £100 each are
provided, and this is expected to defray the
cost of these students to whom reference was
made earlier. Then we come to Grants to
Agricultural Societies. Following the grant
which was
made by the Department in
Dublin to the Irish Agricultural Organisation Society, last year the Committee passed
an Estimate for £1,000 as Northern Ireland's
share of what had been done in the past It
was found, however, in operation that the
grant was not made use of to the extent
which was contemplated, and, therefore, th's
year it is decided to discontinue that grant
of £1,000 to this society for the organisation
of co-operative societies. There are many
arguments that I might use in relation to
that, but I think probably the main argument
that weighed with the Ministry was that in
the North of Ireland there are sufficient
co-operative societies at the present time
for the conversion of milk into butter, and
any increase in the number might possibly
embarrass the existing societies. In order
to counter-balance this to some extent, and
to assist the educational work of the Ulster
Farmer's Union amongst the farmers, it is
suggested that a grant of £1,000 be made to
that body, and the Ministry are prepared
to justify that from the great assistance
they have had from the Farmer's Union in
carrying on the agricultural development of
the Province. The Ministry also believe that
until the machinery necessary to deal with
the maketing of agricultural produce, that
is eggs, has been developed, it would be unwise to undertake the organisation of other
forms of co-operative societies for the
disposal of agricultural produce.
I come now to sub-head G. which is concerned with assistance to the flax and potato
industries. Experimental work in connection
with those industries will be carried out as
heretofore, and, consequently, the Estimate
is practically the same as last year. On

With regard to the quarantine station,

more
I come now to Forestry, perhaps a
important part of the work of the Ministry
of Agriculture than we are accustomed to
assume. I doubt very much whether the oxtent of the work that has been done in that
section is fully appreciated, but it may interest hon. Members to know that, since we

500,000 trees have been planted in areas

which that work has been done will be fully
appreciated when it is realised that, though
we may not see it in our day and generation, thirty years hence it will be productive
of great benefit to those who come after us.
Thirty years I believe is the maturing period
for the softer woods.

Mr. GRANT: I join with other hon. Members in regretting the circumstances which
prevent the Minister of Agriculture (Mr.
Archdale) from presenting his own estimates
this afternoon. I want to join with the hon.
Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin) in
protesting against this grant of £1,000 to the
Ulster Farmers' Union. The hon. Member
for Derry (Mr. Mark) states that we should
not call them a Union. It does not really
matter what we call these people. In the
eyes of the public they should be called "the
Ulster Farmers' ring "--because it is used as
a ring for fixing prices-and, after all, that
is as bad as calling them a Union. They are
a trading Union for the farmers and protect
the farmers' interests. Very often in this
House we hear Members of the Ulster
Farmers' Union congratulating the Minister
of Agriculture. I belong to a Union, though
they do not call it a Union-they call it an
association, just as the hon. Member for
Derry (Mr. Mark) would call his Union-and
if we got a subsidy of a thousand pounds
from the Minister of Agriculture we would
congratulate him too, and have every right
to do so.
The hon. Member (Mr. Mark) points out
the educational advantages they get for this
money. That is not paying very much of a
tribute to the other educational departments
of the Ministry of Agriculture. There is
another side to the Ulster Farmers' Union.
They are a trading Union just as well as
being a farmers' protective union, and I do
not think that the Government should subsidise the Union to which I belong any more
than they should the Ulster Farmers' Union.
It seems very absurd that the consumers or
ordinary individuals in the community
should have to contribute their share of this
£1,000 for the very purpose of giving this
Union an opportunity of charging whatever
prices they like for whatever commodities
they grow.
On behalf of the consumers of
Northern Ireland I strongly protest against
this £1,000 being given to the Ulster Farmers'
Union.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I regret exceedingly
that I did not hear the earlier part
of this discussion, as I was detained on other
business in another room in the House. I do
hope that no hon. Member of this Committee
will seriously object to this miserable grant
of £1,000 for the education of the young
farmers of the country. Some people forget
that the farmers are the most important
people in the Six Counties. They are the
only producers. They are the only people
who sell their produce at the cheapest end,
and buy all their produce at the dearest.
Mr. GRANT: They are well paid for it at
any rate.
Mr. CRAWFORD: I see no reason to find
fault with them at all, and I think it is right
that the young farmers of the country should
know the proper qualities of seed or the
proper quantities of manure to use, so as, if
possible, to show an increased production of
food in the country. There is another aspect
of this matter, which the Committee will
have to consider very seriously, and that is
that, if something more is not done for
agriculture than was done in the past, the
young people will go away out of the country
and leave us very much the poorer. The
other day I was in the farmstead where I was
brought up. Within a very small area round
that house there used to be twelve or thirteen
houses with families in them. Now there is
not a single person in any of those houses.
The country is getting depopulated because
greater attention is being paid to the artisan
than to the farming population. I would
make a special appeal to the Minister not to
listen to anyone who says that this sum of
£1,000 is wasted. It is doing good work, and
I hope the farmers will get far more encouragement from this House in the future
than they have done in the past.
Mr. LLOYD CAMPBELL: I do not intend
to enter into the controversy about the Ulster
Farmers' Union, but I hope that next year
the Ministry of Commerce will allocate £1,000
for the linen industry.
Mr. POLLOCK: I would like to deal
in the first place with the remark
of my hon. Friend (Mr. Lloyd Campbell) and to say that the linen industry
is subsidised and has been fully subsidised, and therefore I do not think
there is any ground for complaint. It
must be remembered that agriculture is the
most important industry in the Province and
the marked improvement that has been
shown in the condition of agriculture, and
the increased value of the products of agriculture during recent years have been largely
the result of the grants made for agricultural education. I would like to define what
education means in respect of this estimate,
because it assumes two or three forms.
There is the practical agricultural education
given in the three farming institutions in the
Northern area, education in practical farming to the students, young men who are
housed in the institutions and who thus en
gage in farming operations on farms. It is
hoped that these institutions will become
self-supporting and I believe it will not be
very long before they are. They will have
the advantage of giving education to the sons
of farmers, and particularly small farmers,
and imparting knowledge in farming which
it is not possible for them to acquire on the
small 20 or 30 acre patches their fathers
occupy. Then there is the education conducted by the County Committees which is
much more distributed, and which is directed

There were various points raised by different hon. Members with regard to the triparty conference that was held, and which
imposed no financial obligation whatever on
the Government. It was simply a friendly
conference for the purpose of discovering to
what extent the development of the flax area
for this reason could be improved with
advantage to the community, and to
that extent it seems to have succeeded.
The Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone
(Mr. Coote) criticised the
action of
the Government in not allocating grants
for the testing of flax seed of a special
description. He must not overlook the fact
that the Government has subsidised the Research Department for the production of
special seed.
The Lambeg Institution has
largely been maintained by the Government.
The Imperial Government gave a grant in
one year of £5,000 on condition that the
Northern Government did likewise, and the
Northern Government did so in order to
secure the Imperial grant of £5,000 and at
the same time to have the advantage
of improved research work in regard
to the development of a flax seed which
it was understood could be developed
and would yield increased production. During
the present year the research work has
been developed on a large scale in Somersetshire out of seed provided by the Research
Department at Lambeg. This is a very important subject and I thought it worth while
detaining the Committee a few minutes while
I shortly explained what had been done.
My hon. Friend (Mr. Coote) decried the
value of forestry. One of the largest and
most important landowners in Northern Ireland informed me that on all the large areas
of land he owned forestry gave a better
return than if he had attempted to cultivate
the land, so that even on the ground of
practical monetary results forestry on certain
coarse mountain land is a paying proposi
tion. It is for that reason the Government
have thought it right to acquire such large
areas of land, not in one patch, but in various
parts of the country, so far distant as Newcastle in the south to the northern part of
Tyrone in the north, where these trees have
been planted for the use of coming generations.
The Faculty of Agriculture was also
criticised by the Member for Fermanagh and
Tyrone (Mr. Coote), who complained that the
education provided for the students simply
fitted them for going elsewhere to take up
positions. I would remind the hon. Member
that when we require technical lecturers for
the purpose of imparting agricultural in
formation we have got to go to Great Britain
to obtain them, and it is because we feel it is
necessary to develop our own talent and
employ our own people for this work that
assistance is given to this Department. Hon.
Members should not also overlook the fact
that it was on the ground of such necessity
that we were able to claim through the Colwyn
Committee money that would represent the
work done by the Royal College of Science
in Dublin. If it had not been for that we
would not have received the money we now
propose to devote to the University.

different
species of weeds, and their
peculiarities, which a policeman would require to know, and they include ragwort,
charlock, docks, etc.

CLAUSE 3 (New Clause) (Expenses of
County Councils and limit on rate.)
(1) The expenses of a County Council
under the Public Libraries Acts shall be defrayed out of the county fund, and the
amount required shall be raised by means
of the poor rate equally over so much of
the county as comprises the county districts
and towns as respects which the County
Council is for the time being carrying the
Public Libraries Acts into execution.
(2) The amount to be raised as aforesaid
for defraying any such expenses shall not
exceed in any one local financial year a sum
equal to a rate of one penny in the pound
on the rateable value, at the beginning of
that year, of the county districts and towns

SCHEDULE.
Constitution of County Library Committee.
The County Library Committee shall consist of the following persons:—
(a) The chairman and vice-chairman of
the County Council:
(b) Two members of the council (of
whom the chairman shall be one) of each
rural district, as
respects which the
County Council are carrying the Public
Libraries Acts into execution;
(c) One member of the council of each
urban district and one commissioner of
each town the council or commissioners of
which have relinquished their powers and
duties under the Public Libraries Acts in
favour of the County Council;
(d) An additional number of members
of the County Council equal to the number of rural and urban districts and
towns as respects which the County Council are carrying the Public Libraries
Acts into execution.
The County Library Committee may
choose in addition to the aforesaid members
further members (not being members of
any local authority in the county), not exceeding in number one for each rural and
urban district and town as respects which
the County Council is carrying the Public
Libraries Acts into execution.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: I beg to move in the
Schedule, paragraph (b), to leave out "two"
("Two members of the council") and insert
"three."
I put down this amendment because I was
of opinion, as I stated on the Second Reading,
that there are not sufficient numbers given
to the rural district councils in the constitution of the County Library Committees according to this Bill. The figures, it seems to
me, have been to a certain extent doubled,
and although the rural district councils have
been given a representation of two members,
in reality they have only been given a representation of one, because it is laid down that
the chairman of the Rural District Council
should be one of those members, and the
chairman of the Rural District Council is, by
virtue of his office a member of the County
Council. Consequently, he could have been
nominated by the County Council on this
committee, quite apart from the fact that it
is suggested or laid down that he should be
nominated by the Rural District Council. It
would appear that the rural district councils
should have a say in this matter of the Library Committee in, at any rate, equal numbers with the County Council; if not, and
this is a debatable question, in preponderating numbers, because a very important duty,
quite apart from the ordinary functions of
the Library Committee lies with those original county councillors and rural district
councillors who form that committee, and
that is the selection of the outside members
provided for in the last Clause of the Schedule. My suggestion that three members
should be selected from the Rural District
Council is, I think, a right and proper one.
Rural district councils, as I pointed out, on
the Second Reading, have been somewhat
overlooked, at least, they have the impression
that they have been overlooked, not only in
this Bill, but in other Measures which have
been before the House. I do not in any way
suggest there should be any mistrust of the
county councils or the county councillors, but
I do think, and I make this suggestion to the
Public Libraries Bill-
Committee.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mrs. Chichester]
are
Government, that the rural district councils
should be considered in this matter, that their
wishes and their views should be met, and
that it should be, perhaps, shall I say, a matter of courtesy? without going any deeper
into the question. They are feeling very hurt
and they are very sore, certainly in some districts. I know they feel in County Antrim,
where five out of eight rural district councils
have been working the public libraries, and
have been doing it satisfactorily, that their
powers are being taken from them,
they think somewhat arbitrarily, and
being transferred to another body. In the
case of the County Council of Antrim it has
shown itself very interested in this particular subject, and has given
every
facility for the Carnegie Library scheme.
But the same thing does not apply to the
other County Councils, and those who
sympathise with the Rural District Councils,
and are, like myself, Rural District Councillors, are not quite sure that the
County Councils throughout the Six
Counties will take up the attitude
adopted by the County Councils of
Antrim and Derry. I suggest that we ought
to show to the Rural District Councils, which
feel themselves somewhat aggrieved by this
Bill, some little consideration. We ought to
meet them half-way at any rate. They do
not think they are being given enough representation. I had a letter from the Antrim
Rural District Council enclosing a resolution,
which, I fancy, has been handed in in manuscript, and perhaps may be discussed later on.
They make use of a few sentences here which
I think I might read to the Committee. They
say :-
"It is the considered opinion of the Association that the County Council is already
an overloaded machine, the members having
manifold duties to perform, and they do not
believe the management of the scheme will
be satisfactory unless local interests are
predominantly represented."
I do not wish to say very much more on this
question, but before I sit down I want once
more to put as strongly as I can before the
Government the fact that these District
Councils must be considered more than they
have been in the past. They, perhaps, have
a feeling that they are the House of Commons
and that the County Council is the House of
Lords, and they feel a little jealous and
resent this donation of their privileges to
another body-privileges which they have had
in the past. I suggest that that resentment
can be wiped away and their feelings soothed
over if they are given larger representation on
the County Library Committee. For that
reason I move that three members of the
Rural District Councils should be nominated
instead of two.
Mr. CRAWFORD: Might I just say a word
or two in support of the Amendment proposed by the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester)? The idea is not in any way to
wreck this Bill. We are entirely at one with
the idea of the Bill. We want simply to see
an arrangement made so that it will be carried out smoothly throughout the county.
This would be a very small concession to make
to the Rural District Councils. The Committee cannot close its eyes to the fact that
since the way in which it was intended to
constitute the Committee
was made known
no fewer than five Rural District Councils in
Antrim have said that they would withdraw
from the scheme. It is not that they do not
want the library scheme. They do want it,
and are prepared to carry it out, but they
think that the way the Committee is constituted is a slight upon them.
If this Committee passes legislation in such
a way it will not be kindly received in the
country, and in doing so they would be acting, in my opinion, in a very foolish way.
By making a concession such as is proposed
here you would smooth the feelings of the
people, as the hon. Member for Derry (Mr.
Chichester) has said, and let them see that
you are not trying to slight them in any way.
By adopting this Amendment you would be
doing good work. Remember that these Rural
District Councillors are unpaid men put in
that position and trying to do their best for
the country. They have considerable in
fluence in their different localities, and if they
go round saying that the whole library scheme
is a concoction of the Government, that they
are trying to take the power out of the hands
of the people in every way possible, that it
is for Belfast and Belfast alone, and that the
representatives of Belfast want to have all
the power in their hands it will do the scheme
a great deal of harm. The Parliamentary
Secretary (Mr. Megaw) shakes his head as if
I were talking nonsense. I know what the
Parliamentary Secretary
means, but I am
living in the country and I know what the
people are thinking and saying, and I know
what the result will be if you do not yield
something in this respect. It is a mistake
to appoint the Committee in this way, and
I strongly support the Amendment that has
been proposed by the Member for Derry (Mrs.
Chichester.) If you read the Press you
will
see that resolutions are being passed by Rural
District Councils outside County Antrim, and
the burden of their complaint is that the
Government is taking away power from the
Rural District Councils
We do not want
that. We want to take the people with us,
and if there is any way we
can do that let us
do it and not turn the people against legis
lation passed in this House. I hope the Gor
ernment will yield in this small and com
paratively unimportant matter. It may be
sentiment, but sentiment has a good deal to
do with the dour Ulsterman, and even if it is
sentiment I think you ought to yield to it.

Ministers (Temporary Exercise of

CLAUSE 1 (Temporary Exercise of Powers
of Minister.)
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That Clause 1 stand part of the Bill."
Mr. McGUFFIN: I intervene only to say
that I still continue my opposition to the
application of this Measure to all the Ministries. I can quite recognize the necessity
of it in this particular case, where a Minister
has been laid aside through serious illness,
and may not be in this House or in attendance at his Ministry for a considerable time.
I recognize that provision of that sort is
necessary under the circumstances, but to
think of applying the Bill to every Ministry,
and to say that where a Minister happens
to be indisposed for a short time his Parliamentary Secretary shall take his position is
creating a precedent that, I think, will prove
very awkward for us. I recognize the
necessity for the Bill in this particular
instance, but really I think it is absurd to
apply it to all the Ministries, and to say that
where a Minister is absent his Parliamentary
Secretary is to function on his behalf. That
is the only protest I have to make. Otherwise the Bill is acceptable to me.
The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
I have frequently appealed to my hon.
Friend opposite to read the Bills before he
starts to criticize them.

the Schedule as it stands at present the
tRural
District Councils are being given

It was suggested to me that, although
O you may give the County Council a larger
representation than you give to the Rural

will have the preponderating vote. That

gentleman who is greatly interested in this
Bill, and it seems to me to provide an argument against the Schedule as it now stands.
Why give to an authority such large powers
that even the greatest sympathiser with
that authority recognizes will not be used?
Again, I would like to ask why, if it were the
intention of the Government to consider so
much the interests of the Rural District
Councils, did they go out of their way to
choose one of the members to be nominated
by the Rural District Councils? They have
laid it down in the Schedule that the Chairman of the Rural District Council shall be
one of the members nominated. I am not
going to go into the question now of whether
it is wise, or whether it is right that the
Rural District Councils are not able to choose
their own members and have to be dictated
to in this matter, but I would point out
that the Chairman of the Rural District
Council is a County Councillor pro tem, and,

of their way in preparing this Schedule to

make it obligatory on the Rural District
Councils to appoint a County Councillor as

point. It is obvious, and it seems to me
to be completely overlooked, that the County
Councils would have the power to select
and might probably have selected that gentleman, who is already a County Councillor,
when they were selecting their own nominees.
As I have said, nothing that has been said
by the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr.
Megaw) has convinced me that I am wrong
in moving this Amendment. I do not wish
to say, as might have been said by other
hon. Members, that I will divide the Committee on this question. We all know that
it is quite useless, but I believe that at any
rate those hon. Members who represent
country constituencies would go into the
Lobby with me. I do not wish in any way
to emphasize that point, but I would like to
ask the Ministry if they would not sometimes consider it wise to meet the wishes of
those who are not anxious to press matters
to extremes. I beg to move.

Mr. MEGAW: I cannot quite understand
either the heat or the persistence with which
this question is being treated. The hon.
Member for Derry (Mrs. Chichester) said
that the Rural District Councils were being
crippled by the Government. My view is
that they are being very largely crippled
by their friends on the opposite side, who call
the Chairman of the Rural District Council
a County Councillor and assert that he
ceases to exist as a Rural District Councillor
when he becomes an ex officio member of
the County Council. He is only a member
of the County Council because he is Chairman of the Rural District Council. He
must represent the Rural District Council.
If he does not represent the Rural District
Council they can, as I said yesterday, turn
him out at the end of the year and put in
another Chairman who will represent their
views.
What the Government want is an Act that
will be workable. The County Council is
the authority that has got to raise the rates
and work the Act. The fact that the Chairman of the Rural District Council is a mem
ber of the County Council is one of the most
important factors in the working of the
Act, because he recognizes the points of view
of both sides. He is a connecting link
between the central administration of the
County Council and the Rural District
Council, and he will represent the views of
the Rural District Council who have put him
where he is. In that sense he is absolutely
a representative of the Rural District
Council, and must be considered as such.
It has been said that the Government have
been tremendously obdurate in this matter.
As a matter of fact they have given it the
closest consideration. This Schedule was
not in the Bill at the start. It was adopted
in this form as a result of representations
and conferences. It was felt to be a fair
form, and was accepted as such by the
representatives of the Rural District
Councils.
What we want is a Bill that can be worked
and that will appeal to the people. This Bill
will appeal to the people. The representatives of the County Councils are as much,
and more, the representatives of the people
as the Rural District Councillors. I do not
want to create any antagonism or rivalry
between the two bodies. They are all repre
sentatives of the one electorate and they will
all be naturally influenced in the working of
the measure. But the broad fact has got
to be remembered that the Rural District
Councils for the past twenty years have had
an opportunity of working this libraries
scheme. This Bill is not a new measure in
any way. It simply tries to put in better
form a measure that has been operative for
the last twenty years, and the persons who
had the right to operate for that time
were the Rural District Councils. They
could have come together at any time for
the last twenty years and have had powers
to work the scheme. With the exception of
one county the measure has hardly been in
force at all. Now the Government have
thought it well to give it, if possible, a
fresh start and to give it a start by the
education authority of the county, the persons who are liable for the raising of the
rates. In spite of all that has been said,
they will work in harmony with the Rural
Public Libraries' Bill-

sat down has told the Committee that he

discussion to-day and proposed this Amendment which they wish the Committee to
accept. Some of us might say that we cannot
understand the tenacity and persistence of
the Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Megaw) in
maintaining the position which he has tried
to maintain in the speech which he has
just delivered. In the competition and
comparison I think my hon. and learned
Friend will not come off second best. He
has certainly made it clear that he is not
Ra very easy to move.
Jors.
Mr. GRANT: Hear, hear.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: We occasionally, indeed very often, admire him for it.
People of that type have been the strength
of Ulster for a good many years, but there
are always people who are extra tenacious
and extra stubborn. Sometimes by their
policy of unyielding they find themselves
up against difficulties and by their actions
they may tend to antagonize interests that
ought to be conciliated. I wonder does the
Parliamentary Secretary realize what the
feeling in the country is in regard to actions
taken by this Committee during the past
six months in connection with Rural District
Councils ? Rural District Councils are
beginning to feel that no confidence is going
to be placed in them, that a whole lot of
matters of administration are going to be
taken out of their hands, and that things
are going to be centred in future in the
County Councils. The County Councils, I
take leave to say, have more work than they
are able to do. They do it effectively. The
matter of education and other questions
that are going to be handed over
to them to be dealt with will give
them, I think, sufficient work to do
that may eventually entitle them to
be paid for their services just as Members
of Parliament and Senators are paid by this
Government. I am really surprised that the
modest proposal of my Colleague in the
representation of Derry (Mrs. Chichester)
cannot be accepted, and accepted handsomely
by the Government. It is merely the
substitution of "three" for "two," an extra
one from the District Council. I cannot see
that a proposal of that kind is revolutionary.
I cannot see that it is going to upset their
Bill. I cannot see that it is going to interfere with the working of the Libraries Act
in any way whatever. My hon. Friend the
Parliamentary Secretary has made wonderful
play about the Chairman of the District
Council in his capacity as such and as a
representative to the County Council. He
tries to separate him in the most wonderful
way possible. No matter how ingenious he
is he cannot get over the fact that the
Chairman must be a member of the County
Council, and the District Council concerned
has no part in the matter whatever. I think
the Government should realize that the
District Council ought to have a little power
of their own and ought to get permission
to send to this Libraries Committee the man
woman they think best qualified to
represent them. It has nothing to do with
the County Council as a whole. I think
they ought to get the right to send whatever
individuals they prefer, and the difference
between two and three is not such a material
thing that we are going to have the
Libraries Act inefficiently worked or the
whole machinery turned upside down.

that on reflection and on consideration the
Government will see that the proposal of
the hon. Member for Derry (Mrs.

Vote will be found on pages 52 to 58 in the
book of Estimates. Hon. Members will recollect that on the occasion of introducing
the Supplementary Estimates in March last I
drew attention to certain changes in the
form of the Estimates which it has been
desirable to make, so I do not consider it
necessary to refer at any great length to the
changes in form which were made at that
time or the reasons which led to their adoption. It would be sufficient, I think, to
remind hon. Members that the changes we
made in dividing the form of the Estimate
into three sections were in order to show
clearly those expenses which are repayable
by the United Kingdom to the Northern
Ireland Exchequer as compared with those
expenses which are either recoverable or
non-recoverable from public departments in
Northern Ireland, the totals of each of
which are to be found at the foot of the
different sections to which I have referred.
Section 2 deals with those items of expenditure which do not fall either under
those which are recoverable from the United
Kingdom or from those which are chargeable
against Northern Ireland Departments. It
will be seen that on this occasion they
amount to the comparatively small sum of
£1,227.
As regards Section No. 1, hon. Members
will notice that this is expenditure in respect of which the Imperial Government puts us in funds, and the
increase of approximately £65,000 is
due almost entirely to the inclusion
of the large item of £100,000 which is the
estimated amount which will be actually
expended in connection with the new buildings at Stormont during the present
financial year. Hon. Members will regret
that the progress in connection with these
buildings has not been more rapid than it
has been, but there were difficulties in regard to the manner in which the preliminary
work was carried out by the firm of contractors, and the contract has been
cancelled by His Majesty's Office of Works
in London. The work has now been entrusted to a Belfast firm, and I am glad to
say that fairly satisfactory progress is being
made. Under Section 2 hon. Members will
notice that the principal item is dropped
out of the sum which was voted last year-
£26,000-which was principally in connection
with the approach road to Stormont.
was completed some time ago, and is now in
regular use. There is a small item of £250
under sub-head E, which is a contribution
towards the cost of the electric installation
necessary in connection with the buildings

sum of £250 has been fixed as
our share

Section 3 calls for rather more de
tailed explanation, and in particular re
garding the progress which it is hoped to
make on the various works provided for. I

engaged in an abnormal amount of building

ment of Ireland Act. The comparatively

ferring to it at the present time is to give

lecture hall, and, further,

Mr. McGUFFIN: Might I ask the hon.
Member is this expenditure recoverable from

Mr. BARBOUR: I was coming to that
later on. This also comes out of the Colwyn
award. It comes out of the £400,000 Colwyn
Committee grant. In other words it will not
fall on our annual revenue. As regards the
item of £17,000 I would like hon. Members
to realise that there always must be a certain
transition period between the working out of
a previous Act and the coming into force of
a new Act. The building grants have been
made in the past towards the cost of the
erection or improvement of National schools,
and a considerable time has elapsed since
they were originally authorized and approved
by the Ministry of Education. After the
building is actually put in hand some time
must elapse before the work is completed
to such an extent as to enable the promoters
of the school to receive payment of money
from the grant authorized. This £17,000
represents almost entirely previous commitments towards building grants, to receive
which different bodies are qualified under the
new Education Act.
Provision is made for this new construction
work being done by local education authorities,
but we will continue to give two-thirds of
the annual charge. Pending the operation of
the new Act in the country districts it has
been found necessary to include this provision for grants made under the old system.
As regards Belfast I understand the local
Education Committee are already directing
their attention to the need for schools
in their areas, and sites have already
been selected on which these new schools are
to be erected.

Another matter arising out of this Vote is
with regard to our new schools. My attention
was drawn to the fact and I hope my hon.
Friend the Parliamentary Secretary will take
note; I am sorry the Chairman of the Local
Education Committee is not present that we
have now got our director appointed and the
attention of the Local Education Committee is
naturally directed towards where to place our
new schools. My attention was drawn to
what is practically a new school which was
built not very many years ago, and could
be easily altered to suit the requirements. It
is not in the centre of the City; it is in one
of the districts. What is happening?
There
was half an acre of land right behind the
school which could have been extended into
beautiful playgrounds and the school brought
up to our requirements. The land has been
taken quite recently. Now, the foundations of
working-class houses have been cut, and houses
are being built right up behind the school. I
think these are matters worthy of attention,
because there was land that could have been
acquired and saved our Education Authorities
from building an entirely new school in a
district that is growing tremendously. Over
500 houses are under construction right round
this school, and this school is full up. Now it
does appear to me that our Education Authorities should centre their minds on a matter of
that description That school could be enlarged
without building another school in that area.
And here the ground has been taken up quite
recently. I only noticed this week that the
foundations for these houses were being cut.
I refer to Glandore Avenue, a beautiful site
and a healthy district. I know of no better
in the City of Belfast. My attention was
drawn to it. What are the Education Authorities doing? Here is a school that with
little money could be extended to meet the
requirements of the new regulations, and you
find foundations being cut for houses to be
built right up against the school. That is a
matter if it cannot be remedied in that district
is surely worth looking into in some other
districts. I thought it only right to put
these matters before the Government.

-but they are not receiving as much as they

those of us who are connected with this

days that are happily past, and we were very

very peaceable the very fact of the Crossley
cars being in front of the building serves

those cars were removed and if the men were
taken away the feelings of the people would

to restore the building to the condition it

That a sum not exceeding £2,179 be

Mr. BARBOUR: This Vote will be found on
page 64, and I should like to explain to hon.
Members that although the sum stated there
is £3,000, I hope that very little of this
amount will be actually called upon during
the present year. I think this Committee
has already in previous years passed sums of
approximately the same amount as is now
asked for, and yet I believe the actual expenditure the year before last only amounted
to about £32, while the expenditure last year
amounted to £4, if my memory serves me.
Under the Government of Ireland Act the
position of those officers who were transferred
to the Northern Ministries was safeguarded by
the Imperial Parliament to the extent that
the Imperial Parliament made itself responsible for the payment of their gratuities,
retiring allowances, and pensions. The
Imperial Parliament recoups itself by deducting the amount required from our residuary share. That arrangement still continues
in force so far as the officers transferred
under the 1920 Act are concerned, but we have
to make provision in our own Estimates for
any retiring gratuities or pensions that may
be payable to those specially appointed
officers, that is to say those members of the
Civil Service whom we have selected and appointed to the different posts which they hold,
or to our newly-recruited staff. Of course,
having regard to their recent appointment,
it is not likely that many of them will be
retiring for some years to come, but still,
should any, by sickness or other cause,
or wish to become qualified for pension it is
necessary that we should have a certain sum
of money on hand to meet such gratuity
should it become due.

ave been a few necessary additions to the

The work of the Ministry of Home
ffairs is very complicated. It is also very
stensive work, indeed. and the tendency
eems to be to increase the amount of work
hat has got to be done. rather than to
iminish. The successive Acts of Parliament
assed here have very largely to do with the
york adminstered by the Ministry of Home
ffairs. However, the only additional posts

the estimate of a man who was doing temporary duty prior to the appointment. I
may say that this medical inspector not only
discharges the duty of acting as surgeon to
the Police Force, which is a statutory duty,

spections and looking after cases in connection with the administration of the Old Age
Pensions.
We have also found it necessary to appoint
a principal auditor. The accounts of the
Police when the Force was first established
were somewhat improvised, and a good deal
of difficulty arose in regard to them, through
not having a proper staff. We have now
added to that staff a principal, whose appointment has. I think, already resulted in

to. We have also added an inspecting officer
in the same branch, whose duty it is to see
after all the stores in connection with the
Police Force. There is a vast quantity to be
examined, and he has to see that the stores
are kept on a regular footing
I should say that a considerable staff has

a great deal of work in connection with the

more or less on an emergency basis up to the

passed during the year. This falls under the

This Act involves a great deal of work, such

come within the provisions of the Act, and seeing that the plans are of the proper character,
so that the proper financial aid can be given.

very often the magistrates seem to think

I was very much interested in the figures
given by the hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. McGuffin), who certainly has taken a

administration. I assure the Committee I

various schools. We have one Protestant
school here which is struggling to keep going,
and which is very much crippled at present because of want of funds. The whole matter is
engaging the serious attention of the Ministry of Home Affairs. We realize the importance of the work. We are not ignorant of the
fact that crime has not ceased amongst the
juvenile population of our Province. We recognize that fully, but, as I said at the beginning, the magistrates have been rather
disposed to take lenient views with respect to
youthful offenders instead of dealing with
them in a way that might be very much
better for the community.

with during the forthcoming year. Remember

never suggested for one moment that the

The Education Act, 1923.
EXPENSES OF EDUCATION AUTHORI-
TIES IN BELFAST AND LONDONDERRY.
the Parlia-
1. Dr.
MORRISON asked
mentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can state the approximate amount of money respectively allocated,
or applied for, by the Education Committees
of Belfast and Londonderry up to date, for
expenses incurred in connection with the
Education Act.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): The actual expenses incurred by
the Education Authority for the County
Borough of Belfast under the operation of
the Education Act (Northern Ireland), 1923,
in the financial year ended 31st March, 1924,
amounted to £528 6s 11d, towards which the
Ministry has made a payment on account of
£300.
The estimated expenditure of this
Education Authority under the operation of
the Education Act in the current financial
year is £55,700; the Ministry of Education
has undertaken to provide two-thirds of
this amount, or of such smaller sum as may
be properly incurred and disbursed within
that year, but no actual payment has yet
been made by the Ministry in respect of the
current year's expenditure.
The Education Authority for the County
Borough of Londonderry has not yet completed its scheme for carrying out the
provisions of the Education Act within the
area under its control, and no payment has
been made by the Ministry to this Authority
up to the present.
NEW SCHOOLS FOR BELFAST AND
LONDONDERRY.
2. Dr.
MORRISON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education, whether he can state the approximate estimated cost in respect of new schools
required for Belfast and Londonderry.
Mr. McKEOWN : With regard to ner
school buildings and enlargements and
structural improvement of existing school
buildings as required in case of the Belfast
County Borough, the Education Authority
estimate the total capital expenditure on
this work as not likely to be less than
£500,000, and as possibly reaching as large
a sum as £750,000. These figures must,
however, be taken merely as approximations.
There are not sufficient data available at
present to enable an estimate to be prepared
which could be relied
upon to show the
probable expenditure with any close approach
to accuracy.
No estimates have yet been submitted to
the Ministry of Education in regard to the
estimated cost of providing 1 CW school
houses which may be required in the Lendonderry County Borough.
SELECTION OF SITES FOR NEW
SCHOOLS.
3. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parlia
mentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether he can give any assurance
that the boards of management and teachers
in existing schools will not be penalized by
unreasonable selection of sites and attrac
tions offered to children by provided schools.
Mr. McKEOWN: Under Section 8 of the Act
the Education Authority is empowered to provide such schools as may be determined by the
Ministry to be necessary for the education
of all the children residing within the
education area for whose elementary
education sufficient and suitable provision
is not otherwise made. The selection of
suitable sites for the erection of new schools
is, accordingly, a matter for the Education
Authority in the first instance, and the Act
further provides that the Education Autho
rity shall take into account the accommodation available in existing schools.
If by "attractions" the hon. Member
refers to meals, books and scholarships, be
will find that under the Act there is no
discrimination in favour of children attending provided or transferred schools.

MEALS FOR NECESSITOUS CHILDREN.
4. Dr. MORRISON asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education whether the cost of meals for
necessitous children is met from the school
rate or from a grant by the Ministry.
Mr. MCKEOWN: Expenditure incurred by
an Education Authority under Sections 49
to 52 of the Education Act, 1923, in providing
meals for necessitous school children will
form part of the general expenses of the
Education Authority, which will be defrayed
by the Authority out of the funds available
for that purpose, as specified in Section 73
of the Act.
Under Section 76 of the Act, the Ministry
may make a grant in aid of such expenditure
if it has been properly incurred in accordance
with a scheme previously approved by the
Ministry.
Mr. DONALD: May I ask my hon. Friend
if any money was expended for this purpose
during the past year?
Mr. MCKEOWN: We are not aware of any
money having been spent up to the present
time.

F. MORTESHED.
8. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will now consider
the recognition of the services rendered to
the State by Constable Francis Morteshed,
Royal Ulster Constabulary.
Mr. MEGAW: This matter was brought
under notice in the ordinary course on the
conclusion of the criminal proceedings involved, and it has afforded me much pleasure
to approve of the recommendation of the
R.U.C. Reward Board that Constable Francis
Morteshed should be awarded a First Class
Record and a Reward of £20, in recognition
of his very gallant conduct on the occasion
referred to.
THE FAIR WAGES CLAUSE.
10. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the Government have
instructed local authorities to continue to
carry out the "Fair Wages Clause" when
placing contracts, and whether the members
of a local authority can be surcharged if
they place contracts with the lowest tender
who may refuse to carry out the "Fair Wages
Clause."
Mr. MEGAW: The instructions issued by
the Local Government Board on the 29th
November, 1911, in regard to the inclusion
of "Fair Wages Clauses" in contracts
entered into by local authorities are still in
operation, and, SO far as the Ministry
is aware, these instructions are generally
complied with.
The power of surcharge is of course confined
to payments which have already been made
by a local authority, and does not extend to
directing a local authority to make payments
in the future.
Mr. DONALD: I would like to ask my hon.
Friend if he is aware that the Home Office
was applied to for instructions, and that the
answer given was most indefinite? That is
why I put the question. The answer given
to me to-day is definite.

GRANT TO ULSTER
AGRICULTURAL
ORGANIZATION SOCIETY.
Mr. GRANT (by private notice) asked the
Minister of Finance whether the reasons
which he gave in Committee of Supply for the
discontinuance of the grant to the Ulster Agricultural Organization Society in the current
year do not appear to reflect upon the work
of that organization, and whether it is not
a fact that the discontinuance of the grant
was based on other considerations.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am glad the hon. Member has given me this opportunity of making
a statement to the House on the question
of the discontinuance of the grant to the
Ulster Agricultural Organization Society.
During the past year the Ministry of Agriculture was in close touch with that organization, and has always been and still is in
entire sympathy with its objects.
The grant of £1,200 which was voted by
this House last year was discontinued, as the
work of the organization of Co-operative
Societies did not appear to require any
further assistance from Government funds.
It was felt, therefore, that the work of supervising the existing Co-operative Societies
should be carried on at the expense of the
Societies themselves.

ROYAL ULSTER CONSTABULARY.
Motion Made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £598,041 be
granted to His Majesty to complete the
sum necessary to defray the charge which
will come in course of payment during the
year ending on the 31st March, 1925, in
respect of the Salaries and Expenses of the
Royal Ulster Constabulary, including
Police Women and Temporary Inspectors
of Weights and Measures."-(Note-
£215,000 has been voted on account).
Mr. MEGAW: In introducing the Royal
Ulster Constabulary Estimates for 1924-25,
I would like first of all to bring to the notice
of Members of this House the work done
by the Royal Ulster Constabulary in conjunction with the other sections of the Constabulary in Northern Ireland. I should
like, first of all, to draw the attention of
hon. Members to the very harmonious way
in which the different sections of our Constabulary Forces are working together. When
we took over control of the police things
were not in so satisfactory a condition.
There was then really a great lack of harmony and co-operation between the regular
police and the Special Constabulary. AU
this has changed and I am glad to say that
when the Inspector-General, who was then
in command of the Special Constabulary,
took over control of the R.I.C., he brought
about a completely different spirit. The
Royal Ulster Constabulary is largely
recruited from the Special Constabulary.
The figures of recruitment in the
Royal Ulster Constabulary are very
eloquent in this respect. The members of the
old R.I.C. and the members of the Special
Constabulary who have been recruited to
the Force are approximately equal, the
advantage being with the members of the
Special Constabulary. The actual figures
are, 1,378 members of the Special Constabulary are now in the Royal Ulster Constabu
lary, 1,362 members of the old Royal Irish
Constabulary. That has brought about the
happiest results, for just as the R.U.C. and
the Special Constabulary now work together
so has their efficiency increased, and the
rivalry between the various branches of our
police is now a healthy rivalry.
Attention has lately been drawn to the
magnificently courageous act of a constable
of the R.U.C.-indeed, it formed the subject
of a Question in the House to-day-in the
arrest of an armed murderer. It was a fine
act and was worthy of all the commendation
it received, but I should like to
say
that I think the same courage
that was displayed in a case which has come

With regard to recruiting for the police,
the total numbers of the Royal Ulster Constabulary are now in their last hundred,
that is they are over 2,900 out of a normal
force of 3,000. Recruiting has gone on

Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask the hon and
learned Gentleman if the arrangement for
their segregation according to religion has
been observed in the proportions laid down?
Mr. MEGAW: I am not sure that I can go
into that at the moment. There was a report made by the Committee, I know, about
the segregation of the Force according to
religion. Of course we have endeavoured to
carry out that recommendation as far as
possible, but it was impossible to do so
entirely by reason of the lack of recruits
from one section. As I have said, the number
that is in the Force is very largely made up
of recruits from the old Royal Irish Constabulary, of whom we have over 1,300, and
from the Special Constabulary, who number
a few more. The training of the new recruits
goes on in the Newtownards Camp and is
very successful indeed. The quality of the
recruits is very good, their training is very
fine, and I think anyone who pays a visit
to that camp will see that a very great state
of efficiency is reached before the recruit
is sent out to do ordinary duty. Of course
at the beginning we had to use the police
without the same training as they are getting
now. When the Royal Irish Constabulary
were dissolved we just had to improvise a
Force and use the best material we could get.
It proved very good indeed, but it had not
perhaps the same training in actual police
duties as one naturally would have desired.
With regard to the pay of the Police Force,
that is still at the rates laid down in the
Constabulary Act of Northern Ireland and
the R.U.C. Pay Order dated November 6,
1922. In our present Estimates we have
estimated for the full strength of the Force
-that is 3,000--and it is hoped that within
a few months the Force will be up to that
strength. The increase in the amount shown
here is mainly due to the ordinary increments, and partially to the increase in the
number of sergeants. Fifteen sergeants are
used in connection with the Customs patrols
along the Border. During the past year the
Customs duties that are levied on the
Border required continuous patrols, and
fifteen sergeants are employed on that duty.
Our Government receives a refund in respect
of the services of those fifteen sergeants,

not to be assumed that if I had not taken
up this attitude no other person would have
done so.
I have the assurance of the hon.
Gentleman the Member for West Belfast (Sir
Robert Lynn) that if his health had permitted

to-day. The House will realize, therefore,
that I do not stand alone in respect of the

I am afraid the Government cherish the
illusion at the present time that things are
more satisfactory in regard to the Royal
Ulster Constabulary than is really the case.

finding fault with the Government from the
highest to the lowest because of some unfortunate happening in the Force at a later date
-for instance, that discipline had got lax and
things had become careless. I can picture a
debate in this Committee, in which my
friends and myself are pilloried for allowing
discipline in its Police Force to get low down,
for allowing people to get into the Force who
are not the proper custodians of the honour
of the Force and of the great responsibilities
which Ulster placed upon its shoulders.
Therefore with us as a Government, so long
as we are a Government, this holds true. We
must from start to finish, from top to bottom,
rely upon a Force which will not only equal
but surpass the traditions of the old R.I.C.
When discussing this question, do let us, if
we can, dissociate ourselves from personality,
let us even dissociate ourselves from friendship, because it should not arise where either
a military or constabulary force is concerned.
My hon. Friend (Mr. McGuffin) tried to
draw an analogy between some teachers and
the case in point. It is impossible to get an
analogy to a Force like this. What do we get
down to? First of all, a great deal of this
trouble has arisen from the fact that Mr.
Nixon was an Orangeman. Many of us in
this Committee are Orangemen, and we treasure the reputation of that loyal Institution
as much as anyone outside this Committee
What a splendid thing it was for us as a
Government to be able to say to those who
belong to the R.U.C.-" You need not any
longer stay outside the ranks of the Lyal
Orange Institution. You can come in. You
can have your own lodges." But when you
give a great privilege like that, it is up to
every man to honour it, and to see that no
discredit falls upon it, because it is always
the case that the majority suffer for the indiscretions of the minority. You find, however,
that privilege after privilege is taken advantage of by ill-advised persons, with the result
that the privilege has to be withdrawn. The
Ulster Government do not desire to withdraw
from either the members of the R.U.C. or the
Specials the privilege of being Orangemen
and having their own Orange Lodges, but it
can only be done if there is strict adhesion
to the orders issued from the Inspector-General's Department, and it can only be done by
each and all those members, like ourselves,
obeying the laws and ordinances of the Institution on the one hand, and of the R.U.C. on
the other hand.

[The Prime Minister]
And may I say how very unfortunate it is
that this has taken place at a time when we
are particularly anxious that we should have
no friction and no difficulties?
How very
unfortunate it also is that the case has
occurred with a member of the old R.I.C. and
our own R.U.C., an old member who knows
the old Regulations from A to Z. If he did
not, he could not have risen to the position
which he attained. He must have known of
the existence of this Rule, which is one of
the guiding rules of the old R.I.C. No. 6 of
the Code reads:-
"As the character and efficiency of the
Royal Irish Constabulary would be seriously injured even by a suspicion of
partizanship, the expression or manifestation of political or sectarian opinions on
the part of any member of the Force is
strictly forbidden."
That is a very old and a very proper Rule
in the Code, and superimposed upon that was
the direct order which was issued not as some
people think by the Inspector-General alone,
but after, I think, it was considered and
thought out by the Home Office and by the
Government itself-an order to prevent a
disaster of this kind occurring, and it was
disobeyed within a very few days. What are
we to expect if these specific orders are immediately disobyed? Why, at a critical
moment, we might find that the morale of
the Force had gone down, and that some
other instructions that were issued had been
equally disobeyed. You would say, "You
passed that one over, why not pass over this
one?" Gradually, our Force instead of being
the magnificent Force it is, would become of
no value.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Might I ask if the Code
existed, or was a special Code issued for the
instruction of the Force?
The PRIME MINISTER: If my hon.
Friend will only listen to me he will learn
that this is the old Code, which has been
incorporated in the new Code; in other words,
the Code of the R.I.C. is applicable to the
R.U.C. The point is this: The officer in
question knew, though my hon. Friends did
not know, and a great many people outside
did not know, that it was one of the principal
rules of the Code of the R.I.C.
Mr. McGUFFIN: He knew about the
R.I.C. all right.
The PRIME MINISTER: And he knew
also of the distinct and very proper caution
issued by the Inspector-General to prov-nt
this sort of thing occurring. It was a disobedience of orders which could not be overlooked by any Government which proposed to
carry on in Ulster.
Let me come, now, to another aspect of the
case. The outside world and this Committee
might possibly imagine that since the esta
blishment of our Royal Ulster Constabulary,

the Force. That is, unfortunately, not the

have had friends who could come here and
present their cases. But there are more than
100 cases.
Mr. McGUFFIN: For public speeches?
The PRIME MINISTER: For disobedience
of orders.
Mr. McGUFFIN: We are referring to public
speeches.
The PRIME MINISTER: A man may
transgress one order, and not another, but
the offence is equal. If this one-hundred-odd
officers and men were to have their cases pre
sented by hon. Members in this House I think
it would be almost impossible to carry on. Is
this House to decide that the case of every
person in a country district who is dismissed
for theft or for disobedience of orders ought
to be brought up here by his friends? That
will not hold water when you come to analyse
it. I myself was presiding over my County
Grand Lodge the other day, and I had to sign
two or three expulsions from the Order; but
when I did so I did not expect Antrim or
Derry immediately to call meetings and say,
"There is the Grand Master of County Down
expelling Orangemen from the Order." No;
I do not expect that. Why? Simply because
they know well enough what the rules and
ordinances of the Orange Institution are
Therefore they say. If you expelled them
from County Down we expect that they have
broken the rules, and they deserve to be
expelled," and that is the end of it. You

Then we have the subsequent action taken
by the Government or officials of the Police.
Mr. Nixon was asked to attend a conference,
and a set of questions was put to him. He
was only allowed to answer
Yes" or "No."
We all know that there is a form of question
to which one cannot answer "yes" or "no,"
without incriminating oneself. Suppose you
ask a man has he stopped drinking. If he
says "yes" there is an acknowledgment that
he had been drinking. If he says "no," it
implies he is still drinking. It was not a fair
explanation if it was absolutely necessary to
say "yes" or "no," and Mr. Nixon was not
allowed to make an ordinary explanation.
I would like to draw the Prime Minister's
attention to that, before he absolutely decides
that there is no case for Mr. Nixon at all,
because I take it, it was the fault of the
Government. There are three faults against
the Government and one indiscretion against
Mr. Nixon. That he allowed the publication
of his speech is accounted for by the fact that
he was not in Belfast and knew nothing about
the publication of the speech and the photograph until he returned too late to stop it.
