Colonel WOODS: If I am in order now, 1
want to draw attention to compare the Headquarters' Staff of the R.U.C. with the Headquarters' Staff of the old R.I.C. in Dublin
Castle. Dublin Castle Headquarters' Staff
consisted of five officers, who administered
11.000 men, over 32 counties. The R.U.C.
Headquarters' Staff consists of 10 officers, who
administer less than 3,000 men. over
six counties. I do not know whether there
is an increase of efficiency equal to the
proportion shown by the figures. I hope so.
Taking the Force as a whole, it works out
roughly that every policeman on the street
costs the taxpayer £300. He is pretty costly,
ornamental but very expensive. Of course
that is not what the men get. They get little
more than half, less than two-thirds, in their
pay. The rest goes in administration, which
is excessive. We have nine County Inspectors, and really they only administer five
counties, because I understand County Derry
has not got a County Inspector at all. The
Commissioner of Londonderry receives an
extra allowance for doing the job of the
County Inspector.
coma
I would like to say, especially after the result of the last Division, that the
manders of the R.U.C. are not getting
chance. They are being interfered with by
politicians, and are not allowed a free hand
to carry on and get the best out of the Force.
If you turn the Police Force into a political
body you can do nothing but impair its
efficiency and subvert discipline to the
point of disobedience.
Another point that I wish to bring forward
is that this expensive Force has not added
much to the joy of life of the Ulster people,
especially after Curfew. The Curfew restrictions have now been in force for four years.
We are told how peaceful things are. We are
told of the decrease in crime, and the reduction in the number of police cases. A few
days ago in Portadown we had a prosecution
against people who were holding a prayermeeting and were curfewed. I think the hon.
Member for Portadown was not there; I am
not sure. If he had I am sure he would have
got them home peacefully. People in this
Committee and officials know they can always
get a permit that will enable them to get
home. If they have not got a permit it is
their own fault, it is due to their own lariness, but the people cannot do that. I went
down one night to the headquarters in
Chichester Street, and at twenty minutes to
twelve I asked for a permit to enable a friend
of mine to get home to Bangor in his ar.
There was no officer there, or I am sure!
would have had no difficulty. The sergeant
in charge said "No." and he said it in such
a way that it was almost insulting. After
some trouble I did get it-I got it from a
head-constable-but it was only because I was
a Member of Parliament that I was able to
get it. I do not think that is fair. I know
that a few minutes after I had gone another
gentleman went into the office to get a permit. His son had been injured and had been
taken to the Royal Victoria Hospital. This
gentleman asked for a permit to enable him
to go to the hospital and to get home again
after twelve o'clock. but his request was not
complied with. That is an undue annoyance
and is hardly fair to the law-abiding citizens
of Belfast who are subscribing £300 per man
to keep up a sort of Prussian guard.
I would ask the Home Office to take into
consideration the feelings of the ordinary
people who cannot get permits. I think
there should be more men employed on
night duty. They have plenty of men
do it. They have more men than they had
in the old R.I.C. There was a statement
made about the clothing by the hon. and
learned Gentleman (Mr. Megaw). I believe
that this clothing is not produced under
trade union rates, and that it emanates
from one of the industrial homes. You will
find that is the case if you make a few
inquiries. I think that is how it happens.
I appeal to the Minister of Home Affairs
to have Curfew removed before the country
is ruined. The tourist season is now on.
Who is coming to Belfast and the seaside
towns in Ulster when they hear Curfew is
on? They do not want to see policemen in
the streets with revolvers. They will say:
"What kind of a country have we come to?
You will get shot, or if you are not shot
you will be arrested after twelve o'clock."

Mr. DONALD I just want to speak for a
few minutes. In the first place I would like
to emphasize the point put by my hon. Friend
(Mr. Grant) about the Fair Wages Clause.
This is a difficult matter for our local
authorities. I read a letter the other day
regarding two contracts that were given out
on the distinct understanding that the work
would be carried out under the Fair Wages
Clause. As I understand it all local authorities in Northern Ireland just as in Great
Britain, when giving out contracts, make a
stipulation that the work must be carried out,
under the Fair Wages Clause. It has not
been done. It has not, unfortunately, been
carried out, but I hope it will be in
the future. My right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) knows perfectly well that
a specific case was referred to him
in which the contractor was only paying 10d.
an hour and the wages under the Fair Wages
Clause was 1/- an hour.
Mr. POLLOCK: I pointed out here yesterday that there were two cases in evidence
such as referred to by my hon. Friend and
they were dealt with drastically by the
Department and remedied.
Mr. DONALD: I quite agree. My right
hon. Friend has given his answer that these
two cases were dealt with, but thanks are
not due to our Government.
Mr. POLLOCK: Oh!
Mr. DONALD: My right hon. Friend says
"Oh." Is he aware that it was a letter from
Mr. Wheatley, the Minister of Health, that
got the 1/- per hour? No thanks are due to
this Government. I can verify that statement.
It is not to this Government the credit is due.
The credit is due to the Imperial Authorities.
That shows that there is something wrong.
With regard to the clothing I want to
cmphasize another point. When these contracts are given out care should be taken to
see that the contractor is enrolled on the
King's National Roll. My right hon. Friend
(Mr. Pollock) has helped us up to now. I give
him credit for that. He has given every
assistance to the Local Employment Committee
who are working strenuously on behalf of
disabled ex-Service men. Where contracts
are given out, whether for clothing or anything
else, it is imperative that the Government see
that the contractors are on the King's National
Roll. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) That
meets with the unanimous approval of the
Committee.

CLASS III. No. 3.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That a sum not exceeding £219,000 be
granted to his Majesty to complete the sum
necessary to defray the charge which will come
in course of payment during the year ending on
the 31st day of March, 1925, in respect of contributions to the Unemployment Fund and to
special schemes under the Unemployment
Insurance Acts (1920-23)."
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): In asking the Committee to vote
£219,000 as the State contribution to the Unemployment Fund for the financial year
1924-25, I may point out that this is an increase of £24,000. It is one of the few
increases which I think we can look upon as
gratifying because it shows that unemployment is gradually becoming less. Hon.
Members are no doubt aware that the State
contribution is about one-third of the combined contributions paid by workers and
employers, and that as unemployment lessens
these contributions consequently increase.
The State share increases in proportion. It
is a fact that cannot be well altered that
as the drain upon our Unemployment Fund
increases the income of the Fund from all
three contributors falls. This may appear
to violate a very sound business principle
and it undoubtedly involves a great deal of
financing, but in the end it comes to very
much the same thing, because as the drain
upon the fund becomes less the income of
course increases, as is the case, I am thankful to say, at the present moment. Last year
we estimated upon the basis of 16 per cent.
unemployment and this year we feel that we
are justified in estimating upon the basis of
13 per cent. or a reduction of 3 per cent.
The menace of unemployment can only, I
feel convinced, be entirely removed by
the return of normal trade conditions and
the development through private enterprise
of our natural and industrial resources
Unfortunately our Government has little
power over the situation due to the fact
that the present industrial depression is
brought about not by local but by
national and international causes By
the restoration and the maintenance of
law and order and by endeavouring to preserve industrial peace in our midst we have
created a confidence and security which 1
hope will tend to a revival of trade. The
Development Commission over which Lord
Charlemont so ably presides and in which
all the members are taking such a keen and
useful interest is seeking for new avenues of
employment for our people and, as hon.
Members know, the linen trade towards the
closing months of last year showed signs of
very great improvement. In the early
months of this year that improvement was
fully realised. In fact in some quarters it
exceeded our most sanguine expectations,
and up to the present, I am happy to say,
I feel it has been sustained.
Again, it is very pleasing to feel that our
great farming industry is also in a better
position, and I hope sincerely, and the
Government hope sincerely, that the in
creased prices which our farmers are getting
for their produce will encourage them to till
more land, and consequently give more en
ployment to our people. Unfortunately, the
shipbuilding industry has been lagging be
hind, but I am informed that it has passed
the low water mark, and it is felt that it is
now on a slowly rising tide. I am very glad
to be able to say that negotiations have now
been proceeding for some time between two
well-known shipowning companies and one
of our local shipbuilding companies, the
Imperial Trade Facilities Committee and our
Northern Ireland Loans Guarantee Committee, as a result of which the two latter
bodies have recommended assistance by way
of guarantee towards the construction of four
large vessels in Belfast. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) My latest information
with this Government assistance the nego
tiations are likely to reach a satisfactory
termination before very long.
Mr. GRANT: Hear, hear.

of administration and loan interest amounted
Ento £165,000, making in all a total of £2,687,000.

Against this we received income from employers during the year £373,000, from the
workers £336,000, and from the State £254,000,
a total income during the year of £963,000,
eaving a deficit on the 31st March of
£1,724,000, against which it will be remembered that our Prime Minister obtained from
the Imperial Treasury £477,000 to help us in
starting, and which is still available for that
purpose if required. I think I ought to say
in this connection that in the administration
of this fund our local Employment Committees have been giving the most valuable
for assistance.
They have taken an energetic
interest in getting firms to join the King's
tri National Roll of Honour, and have
assisted in obtaining work for many of
t. people. They have also helped to decide
claims for benefit and they have stimulated
where necessary local authorities to undertake
useful works. It is a sad and regrettable
fact, however, that in Belfast, there are still
700 disabled ex-Servicemen out of employment.
I have said before, and I repeat to-day, that I
think this blot could be removed from our
city if there was only a pull and a pull
all together by employers to this end.

Mr. ANDREWS: I very willingly bow to

position, and I hope it will be a great advantage in the administration of this important fund. In speaking of insurance
in general, it is often held that there
are grievances because everybody does
not gain. Of course, it is not in the order of
things that everybody who contributes to an
insurance scheme will draw as much out as
he pays in. The principle upon which every
insurance scheme is worked is that the strong
shall help the weak and the fortunate help
the unfortunate. In this connection I read a
story which illustrates the point. A domestic
servant went to her mistress the other day
and said she had been reading in the papers
about the sufferings our unemployed people
were enduring, and that she would like to
help. Her mistress said, "You are not an
insured person, and, therefore you cannot
help." "I feel," she replied, "that we ought
to be insured, because those of us who are
not subiect to unemployment ought to be
prepared to help those who are."
Mr. GRANT: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: That is the spirit which
will make Ulster in the future, if it will
only permeate all classes in our community.
I beg to move.

I would like also to say a word or two in
connection with the Local Employment Committees. These Committees have done a
great deal of useful work, and have assisted

his responsibility. I would also like to say

much the great services the Belfast Corporation have rendered to the Ministry of Labour

Mr. MARK: There was just one matter
that struck me as the Minister was moving

The question of flax scatchers has been referred to, and the idea that although they
only work, it has been said, on the average of
23 weeks in the year. they can run about all
summer and do nothing is quite wrong. As a
matter of fact, they do not stand on the same
basis as ordinary insured people at all. They
are looked upon as casuals. It is a seasonal
occupation, and they are only entitled to
draw covenanted benefit strictly on the stamp
basis; that is, for every six contributions
they pay they are entitled to get one week's
benefit, and they are entitled in addition
to get uncovenanted benefit during the
scutching season between the months of October and April, but they are in no way entitled to draw uncovenanted benefit right
through the summer in the same way that
other workers might be entitled to do.
Dr. MORRISON: Might I ask the Minister
how much uncovenanted benefit can they
draw for these seven or eight months?
Mr. ANDREWS: The provision in reference
to that is this: that a man is entitled, we will
say, to draw five or six weeks on stamp contributions. The maximum time for which he
can get benefit of any kind during the period
of October to April is six months, and he
cannot draw uncovenanted benefit during
the time that there is no scutching
being done. The position is that he
may draw uncovenanted benefit during
the scutching season, not
during the
time of year when there is no scutching to
be done. He must, therefore, outside the
scutching season, look for work somewhere
else or in some other trade, or else do without
uncovenanted benefit. It is just one of these
things about which reports are circulated
that are really not founded on fact. I have
heard exactly the criticism outside this
House that my hon. Friend (Dr. Morrison)
has made here. I can assure him-
Dr. MORRISON: You have not told us
what the uncovenanted benefit they may have
for six months is. What amount is it? What
is it per week?
Mr. ANDREWS: One of these men can
draw exactly the same as a man engaged in
any other occupation can draw, namely, 15
a week if he is a single man; if he is
married man he can draw in addition to that
sum 5s for his wife and 1s for each child,
which is certainly not over generous.
Mr. MORRISON: They are quite happy on
that in the country.

nothing. Again, the hon. Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone referred to the question
of drainage. That is a most difficult problem
which affects practically every county in
the Northern area, and the Government
would not have been justified in hastily
subsidizing a scheme here and a scheme
there without giving the matter most careful
consideration. Therefore, they appointed the
Development Commission, and one of the
responsibilities with which that Commission
is charged is to inquire into the question
of drainage throughout the whole of our

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO

McKeown): I am glad to be able to inform
the Committee that the Estimates of the
Ministry of Commerce for 1924-25 show a net
decrease of £863 as compared with those of
the preceding year. During the past year
the statutory work of the Ministry, comprising the administration of Companies, Friendly
Societies, Trade Unions and Business Names
Acts, etc., and also the administration of the
Acts relating to Electricity, Gas, Water
Power, Mines and Quarries, Canals, Harbours, Docks and Piers, and Weights and
Measures has proceeded smoothly.
has been a continuous development, 1 ain
glad to be able to report, in the work of the
Commerce and Economic Department of the
Ministry. The efforts of this Department
of the Ministry were, during the first eighteen
months of its existence necessarily focussed
upon establishing contact with firms and
manufacturers throughout the Province, and
to ascertaining the channels into which its
activities could most usefully be directed.
The results of this preliminary work have
substantially materialised, and this Department is now actively discharging the functions for which it was created. The Committee will
measure of
appreciate the
development which this Department of the
Ministry has attained when I tell them that
the average aggregate number of firms supplied during each of the first three months
of the present year with commercial intelligence was 1,062, as compared with 654 during
the corresponding months of 1923.
figures, I may point out, do not include the
information supplied by the Ministry in response to specific inquiries made by firms, of
which, I am glad to state, there is now an

maintained those close and friendly relations
with Trade Associations and Chambers of
Commerce which it has from the outset
sought to establish, and I am glad to say that

These
Amongst additional duties, two items, perhaps, call for special mention, namely, the
reconstitution of the records of the joint
stock companies in Northern Ireland, and the
organization of the Ulster Pavilion at the
British Empire Exhibition. As hon. Members
are already aware, the reconstruction of the
files of joint stock companies involves some
1,300 Northern Ireland companies whose records were destroyed in the Dublin Custom
House fire of 1921. You will recollect that
legislation was obtained in this House and
the work was commenced some eight months
ago, and has made very satisfactory progress.
The organization of the Ulster Pavilion at
the British Empire Exhibition, as Members
of the Committee will readily appreciate, has
also involved a very great amount of detailed
work. Sub-heads "B" to "H" of the Vote,
on page 158, represent the ordinary overhead
working expenses of the Department, and do
not call for any comment, as the total of
these charges remains substantially the same
as for 1923-24.
Under Sub-head I" (Special Enquiries)
provision of £500 is again made for the necessary expenses of the Commission on the
Natural and Industrial Resources of Northern
Ireland under the chairmanship of Lord
Charlemont. The secretarial work of the
Commission is jointly undertaken by the
Ministry of Labour and the Ministry of Commerce, but the total expenditure in connection
with this service is borne on the Ministry of
Commerce Vote.
I would draw special attention to the receipts appropriated in aid of the Ministry's
Vote. These show an increase of almost
£800 as compared with the preceding year.
This increase is attributable to contributions
from statutory electricity and gas under-
These contributions
takings.
consist of
payments made by the undertakings towards

Morrison) raised some point about lack of
courtesy. Of course in a big force there
must be occasional cases in which men are
discourteous. Some people "drest in a little
brief authority" are sometimes disposed to
exercise it in a way that would not commend
itself to anybody. I am happy to say there
are not many such cases, and they are
frowned on when they come to the notice
of the officers. The officers desire above all
things that authority shall be exercised in as
courteous a way as possible, and certainly
that is the view of the Ministry. I have no
knowledge of the complaints made from Newtownards, but if the hon. and gallant Member (Colonel Woods) comes into the Ministry
of Home Affairs I will try to find out, and
will give him any satisfaction I can on the
subject.
Mr. COOTE: I had not hoped to have the
privilege of being here, and I did not
consider any criticism of the Force, but there
are one or two matters I should like to
mention. In the first place, I want to join
issue with the hon. Member for the University (Dr. Morrison) and to state here publicly
that I have not had the same experience
in Tyrone as he may have had in Derry.
He said that there is extravagance in the
working of the Force, especially in the
driving of transport and in the use of petrol.
I can assure the hon. Member and the Committee that, so far as we have experience of
the working of the Constabulary in the
County Tyrone, they do all that can be desired in the way of economy, and fully discharge all their duties in the interests of
the taxpayers. We have not any very outstanding cases of disrespectful conduct on the
part of the Force. When you take a Force
such as the Royal Ulster Constabulary, you
have got to consider that it is made up of
divers units, some of them absolutely trained
and amenable to discipline, and others
voluntary "B" men who may give in their
rifles at a moment's notice and walk off.
Mr. COOTE: It is the desire to have law
and order observed, and to play the game,
as they try in every branch of the Force to
play the game. We should congratulate the
country upon having such an excellent lot
of officers and men in every branch of the
service. They try to do their very best for all
parties and creeds, to maintain the law, to
make the law respected, and to settle the
country; and they have succeeded. Some
little trouble will arise now and then in
every administration. I merely hint at a
matter what happened in a neighbouring
county, a want of dicipline in the "B" Force,
to which exception has been taken by a great
number of the "B" men themselves. I confess at once I have not carried it where I
should have carried it-to headquarters—
because I had hoped that the matter would
be settled locally, and I hope it will be
settled locally. We always wish to give as
little trouble as we can to the men at the
top who have so much trouble to keep the
whole Force going. This is a matter of detail
in administration, and I am taking it up
with the Commandant of the county concerned.
I wish to refer to a matter which touches
some members of the Force. I think it was
brought up here by way of a question. It
is the disability under which some men suffer
through having to pay two or three years'
income-tax in one year. I have the correspondence in my bag, but unfortunately I
have not got it here. I have been written
to by men on the subject. Now they
are asked to pay all the arrears.
That is quite right, but they ought to get
a little extra time.
Mr. MEGAW: I think that the Minister
of Finance stated he would make things as
easy as possible for them. Time is being
given to enable them to pay by instalments.
Mr. COOTE: 1 am sorry for interjecting the
question, but I lost sight of the fact that an
answer had been given. It is only what we
would expect from the Minister of Finance.
A man with a wife and small family, who
has spent money in the years of plenty may
not find it so easy to get along in what we
may call the years of famine. The reply of
the Minister that this matter has been sympathetically met and settled will now go out
to the public. In casting my mind along the
whole Force, I say that the men are as capable, as watchful, as sympathetic and as
attentive to their duties as any human beings
1029 National Health Insurance Bill-

Second Reading.
could possibly be. We expect the R.U.C. to
attend to their duties, and be on the job,
but I say that the "B" men, the men who
sit out at night and get little or no sleep,
and return to their work the next day, ought
to be the object of honour, sympathy
and respect. I am sure this Committee agree
that we should all hold them in respect, that

National Health Insurance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed: "That
the Bill be now read a Second time."
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr.
Gordon): In moving that this Bill be now
read a Second time, I am not unmindful of
the fact that any matter dealing with Health
Insurance in this House is one of considerable interest to Members. On account of the
valuable advice and assistance which we
have received from the Consultative Committee of Approved Societies operating in
Northern Ireland, which Committee is in
agreement with the main features of the Bill,
I feel sure that hon. Members will see the
necessity of giving it a speedy passage through
this House. The object of the Bill is to
provide money to meet the cost of medical
certification. Might I remind the House that
the cost of medical certification was originally
borne entirely by Exchequer Grants. As a
result of the recommendations of the. Geddes
Committee, it was decided that the grant
should be withdrawn and the charge met
from Health Insurance Funds. Owing, however, to an arrangement with the Approved
Societies, the money is to be found without
prejudicing the rights of insured persons to
the benefits provided by the Societies. This
Bill is intended for a period of three years.
A Royal Commission is being set up by the
Imperial Government, as announced by my
right hon. Friend, the Minister of Labour,
in this House, to inquire into the whole
Health Insurance Scheme, and as Northern
Ireland participates in the scheme in operation in the United Kingdom, we have made
a request to be represented on that Commission. It is expected that the Commission
will have issued a Report in time for legislation to be introduced into the Imperial
Parliament to carry out its recommendations
as from the 1st January, 1927.
I think it only right to say that from the
1st April, 1922, till 31st December, 1923, the
approved societies have borne a large proportion of the expenses of medical certification. The total cost of the service is estimated
at approximately £30,000 per annum, or 2s.
per insured person per annum. Of this
amount it is proposed that the State should
continue to contribute 2-9ths, under Section 3
of the National Health Insurance Act, 1911,
leaving 7-9ths to be met from other sources.
Owing to the fact that the scheme is international and that approved societies operate
freely both in Great Britain and in Northern
Ireland, it is deemed essential to follow as
closely as possible the lines of Imperial legislation. We propose to draw on certain
sources to find the money to add to the 7-9ths
of 2d. which the approved societies will be
called upon to pay. It is expected that with
the funds which we will call upon to assist
us in paying this certification the approved
societies will pay 7-9ths of 2d. towards the
amount that we will be able to call upon. I
rather think it advisable that I should briefly
explain how these sources were brought into
being and maintained :-
There is the Central Fund. This fund was
built up from Exchequer Grants and from
deductions from contributions of insured
persons, and also 9-10ths of sums unclaimed
in Stamp Sales Account. This fund is used
chiefly to help societies which incur
deficiency.
a
Then we have the Unclaimed Stamp Sales
Account. This account receives its strength
from stamps which have been sold and paid
for and have gone astray or have been destroyed. The difference between what has been
sold and what has been claimed goes to swell
this fund.
Next we have the Investment Account. A
proportion of the funds of approved societies
is invested, under statute, by the National
Debt Commissioners, and the societies have
the right to invest the remaining amount.
The Commisioners give a guaranteed rate of
interest, which at the moment is 43 per cent.,
and any excess beyond 4 per cent. is placed
to a reserve account. This reserve is used
to meet any losses on the realization of Stock
and to pay interest at a prescribed rate to
the approved societies, even although the
dividend on the funds invested may be lower.
We
The method we are going to adopt to pay
this money which is required for medical
certification is that we propose that the State
will pay 2-9ths of the whole amount.
are going to ask the approved societies to
pay 7-9ths of 2d., the Central Fund to pay
7-9ths of an amount not exceeding 1s. 4d.,
and the residue of the balance will be taken
1031 National Health Insurance Bill- HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Second Reading.
[Mr. Gordon.]
out of the Investment Account reserves.
The Irish Free State upon its establishment decided to separate entirely
from the United Kingdom Insurance
system, and arrangements were made
to give effect to this decision in July,
1923. The operations in connection with the
apportionment of Health Insurance Funds
rendered necessary by this separation are
proceeding, but have not yet been carried to
completion. In the circumstances, the exact
condition of the proceeds of the Stamps Sales
Account and the Income Account of the
National Health Insurance Fund (Investment) Account is not known. The Government Actuary's Department, which is charged
with most of the work connected with the
apportionment in question, estimates that
there will be sufficient balances in the two
funds, taken together, to supply the amount
required for medical certification after the
sums to be provided by the State and by the
approved societies have been paid. When the
exact position of the funds has been ascertained, the proceeds of Stamp Sales Account
will be made, by regulations, to bear an
amount up to the limit of 7-9ths of 1s. 4d.
per insured person per annum, and the
balance, which will be not less than 7-9ths
of sixpence, will be provided from the Income
Account. The doctors are performing their
work, and the money will have to be found
to meet the cost of their service, and that is
our reason for proceeding with this Bill. It
will in no way affect the benefit of the insured
contributor or the additional benefits subscquently given by many of the societies, which
through good management were able to show
substantial surpluses. This, I am sure, will
give great satisfaction to insured persons to
know that their rights are not being infringed in any way, and that the funds of
societies are not being imperilled.
Clause 2 re-enacts as from the 1st January,
1923, the provisions of Section 11 of the Health
Insurance Act, Northern Ireland, of 1922,
under which assistance was given to Approved
Societies from the unclaimed proceeds
of Stamp Sales to enable them to
pay a portion of the arrears of their
members who were suffering from prolonged unemployment and could not
pay their weekly contributions to the funds.
This contribution from the Fund will amount
to £8,000 approximately per annum and we
purpose making provision from 1st January,
1923, to 31st December, 1925-a period of
three years.
In Clause 3 of the Bill, proposals are made
which will bring the health insurance statutes
into line with those for unemployment insurance. An employer who is convicted for
refusing to fulfil his obligations may be required, as a result of such conviction, to pay
all contributions which he has failed to pay
under either set of statutes during the year
preceding the date when the information was
laid. The unemployment insurance statutes
confer the further right on the Ministry of
Labour of recovering summarily as a civil
debt contributions unpaid prior to that year.
This power is now sought for the Ministry
under the health insurance scheme.
Clause 4 and the Schedule propose the repeal of certain provisions in the original
health insurance statutes which are no longer
necessary, as follows:-Paragraph (b) and the
proviso to Sub-section (2) of Section 16 of the
National Insurance Act, 1911. This Subsection provided for the payment out of Parlimentary moneys of one penny per annum
in respect of each insured person for purposes of research. No research work is being
done. This provision was repealed for Great
Britain by the Ministry of Health Act, 1919,
but was allowed to stand for Ireland at the
time. No money was allocated by the
Imperial Parliament for Ireland and the provision has since 1919 been regarded as a dead
letter-consequently we propose to repeal it.
Section 58 of the National Insurance Act,
1911, makes provision for the appointment
of an Advisory Committee for the purpose
of giving the Ministry advice in connection
with certain matters affecting Health Insurance. The Ministry has found it more
satisfactory to consult independent representatives of the various interests involved.
A
Consultative Committee of Approved
Societies has been set up and has been
functioning since the establishment of the
Ministry. A dental Advisory Committee is
also in being, and the Ministry is in touch
with the Medico-Political Committee representing the medical profession in regard to
all matters which affect them. In the
circumstances, it is desired to repeal the
Section in question.
With reference to part of Sub-Section (1) of
Section 31 of the National Insurance Act,
1923, under the early Health Insurance Acts
satisfactory provision was not made for the
administrative expenses of Insurance Committees and it was found necessary for
Parliament to come to the assistance of such
Committees. The 1913 Act provided for the
establishment of schemes by the Committees
for the payment to members of subsistence
allowances and compensation for loss of remunerative time and for the recoupment of
the Committees for the expense involved.
The ordinary allowance to Insurance Committees has been increased by successive
steps and has now reached a point when
it may be regarded as sufficient for all
charges, Insurance Committees were informed by the Ministry some time ago that
this special grant out of Parliamentary funds
would be withdrawn, and power is now
1033 National Health Insurance Bill-

20 MAY 1924
Second Reading.

sought to repeal the provision. The Schedule
shows the extent of the repeal. The Bill is
urgent and I hope the House will give the
Minister and myself all possible help in
passing this measure.
Dr. MORRISON: I would like to draw the
attention of the Minister to sub-clause (3) of
Clause 1 which reads:
"For the purposes of this section the expression 'medical certification' means any
arrangement made by the Ministry for the
provision, for the purposes of the enactments relating to National Health Insurance,
of medical evidence of incapacity for work
in the case of insured persons."
It is not an easy thing for an ordinary member of the community to understand the
wording of a Clause in an Act of Parliament,
and I think this would be an ideal Clause
if it had been drafted by the Parliamentary
Draughtsman with the object of obscuring the
meaning. There is no doubt that, if it has
any meaning at all to me, it means that the
Minister may alter as he thinks well any
rules that govern certification.
He may
make any arrangements he likes.
He may
alter the payment. He may appoint a special
man for the work. He may take the matter
out of the hands of the ordinary medical attendant and put it into the hands of a wholetime officer. He has absolute power to do as
he likes in regard to that.
The Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Gordon),
no doubt, understood the Bill, but from the
way in which he put it before the House I
did not understand it, and I think very few
hon. Members were able to understand it.
He said there was a Consultative Committee
representing the insurance societies and that
they were in agreement with the Ministry
with regard to this thing. I have no doubt
about that. My complaint is that up to now
it was the societies in the main who consulted
with the Ministrv, and the medical profession
was ignored. The Minister of Labour (Mr
Andrews) does not know anything about these
facts, because they are more or less ancient
history. The biggest controversy that ever
agitated medical surgeons was over this question of certification, when the whole profession in Ireland refused to accept the terms
offered, and when provision was made for
whole-time officers to do this job. The Parliamentary Secretary (Mr. Gordon) tells us
that the Minister has got in touch with the
TTlster Society which can sneak on behalf of
Tster. So far as I know this Ulster Medical
Committee was not appointed until a week
ago-at least it was not in touch with him
until a week ago and, if he has laid these
facts and this Bill before them, and if they
are satisfied, I am perfectly satisfied. If he
has not done this I would ask him to consult
this representative Committee of the doctors
and act on their advice in so far as he
thinks well.
I would like to point out that the National
Health Insurance Act added one-third additional work to every dispensary doctor in
Ireland-I give that as my own experienceand they got no extra pay except what small
sum they got for certification. If you take
that away from them you put a burden on
them for which you give no remuneration
whatever. That is the fact so far as I know.
There is this further fact in favour of having
the family or dispensary doctor, who is a
public officer, acting in this matter. He
knows the poor. He has no bias one way or
the other. He is an independent and, in the
main, an honest man. If you appoint a paid
certifier he has no interest except to protect
the societies and to favour the societies. The
mere fact of his appointment makes him independent of the local doctor or of the people.
He is practically a paid agent, and the result
will be that the unspeakably scanty protection that the poor already have under this
Insurance Act will be absolutely wiped out,
they will be at the mercy of paid men, who
do not want to be troubled, and who, perhaps,
know but little about the family history or
diseases, and the result will be that injustice
will be done. I have no desire at all to
obstruct the Minister in this matter, but I
think if he were wise he would follow the
advice I have given him and have a meeting
with the Committee appointed by the Ulster
Medical Society, which speaks for Ulster, and
put the facts before them. It is quite possible
that I may be a member of that Committee.
Mr. ANDREWS: We hope you are.
Dr. MORRISON: In any case it will come
before them, and if they are satisfied then,
so far as I am concerned, and the medical
profession in this House, we will give the Bill
our blessing and facilitate and help the
Ministry in every way we can.
no

used
I may say that it has been

but not

Second Reading.
for the benefit of Approved Societies in Northern Ireland just in the same way as it is
available to help crippled Societies in Great
Britain. On other occasions it has been used

to raid it to some extent to help to provide

Then the hon. Member for North Belfast
also referred to the question of whether the

apart altogether from what this investment
may happen to yield. It is the intention to

much higher, and this money was used for the

Account, which is also being used, as I have

regarding the cost of Medical Certification.
Of course this National Insurance Act is
extremely complicated. It has often been
said that the reserves were more than are
necessary. Whether that is so or not I do not
profess to be able to say, but hon. Members
will recognize that there is bound to be in
connection with any insurance schemes unascertainable liabilities which it is absolutely
necessary to provide for in case a breakdown
would occur in future years. In other words,
I think it is the duty of those who are charged
with the grave responsibility of administering
this Fund for the time being, to see that we
do not leave a legacy of liability which would
be embarrassing to those who may come after
us.

THE BUDGET.
Statement by the Minister of Finance.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That this House approves the proposals
of the Government for meeting the financial
requirements of the year."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): In presenting the financial state
ment for the year 1924-25 I hope not to exhaust the patience of the House to too great
an extent, but I think it would be an advantage if I traced, very shortly, the evolution of
our financial relations with Great Britain
in order that the House may clearly
understand our present position,
When I presented the financial statement of
the Province a year ago, I was unable to do
more than indicate in one sum the amount
which was available to provide a contribution to the services of the nation, and any
resulting surplus after that contribution had
been paid. This amount was, in effect, the
balance of revenue remaining after provision
was made for all the normal expenditure on
the services of the Province.
At that time the Colwyn Committee, which
had undertaken the work of apportioning our
liability to the national services, had not
reached a decision as regards any genera'
principle on which this liability could be
based, and it was only at a later period that
a provisional award was made covering the
first two complete financial years of our
autonomous life, leaving the determination
of the future method of apportionment to be
decided when the additional knowledge gained
by two years of practical experience of the
operation of Local Government might assist
in the solution of this rathor difficult problem.
The decision of the Committee, which was
accepted by the Joint Exchequer Board in
respect of the last financial year, therefore,
settled that the contribution of the Province
to Imperial necessities should be based on
the difference between normal revenue and
the normal expenditure on our local services,
leaving the produce of the Land Purchase
Annuities, approximately £650,000, to bear
those charges which could only be regarded as
outside the category of normal service expenditure.
If reference is made to my financial statement of last year it will be seen that I
estimated the amount available for Imperial
purposes and a reasonable surplus on the
accounts as £4,456,000.
The amount which was eventually found to
be available as a contribution under the
decision of the Colwyn Committee was
£4,770,000, which included the small balance
of the contribution due for the year 1922-23:
and, in addition, there was a surplus of
£47,000, which automatically goes to Sinking
Funds. This contribution of £4,770.000
added to the amounts contributed in the first
16 months of our Local Government makes a
total of £13,534,570 which the Province has
provided toward the upkeep of the Imperial
services since the transfer was made.
I think it must be admitted that this is a
very creditable result for a small State called
into existence in the midst of quite unprecedented political turmoil and disturbance.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
As there appears to have arisen some misunderstanding as to the basis upon which the
contribution has been calculated, I hope hon.

The original contribution provided by the

the rate of £7,920,000, but was to be subject to
reduction if the Joint Exchequer Board
thought that it should justly be of less
amount. Owing to the alterations, since the
contribution was fixed at £7,920,000 chiefly in
regard to revenue raised, the Board made an
Order on the 5th July, 1922, fixing the provisional contribution for 1922-23 at £6,000,000.
This contribution was calculated by reference
to a total expenditure on Imperial Services of
the very large sum of £548,000,000, and was to
be re-assessed when the actual Imperial expenditure for 1922-23 was known. This total
was later estimated at £616,000,000, and, therefore, on the Joint Exchequer Board formula
the Northern Ireland contribution for 1922-23
amounted to £6,700,000. That is £700.000 more
than the original order of the Board.
On the basis of the Colwyn Committee's recommendation, however, it is now found on
the audit of the accounts for the year 1922-23
that the actual contribution for that year is
about £6,480,000-we have already paid itwhile for the year which has closed, it is estimated that after the accounts have been
finally dealt with, a contribution of about

I have on many occasions reminded the
House of the vital importance to the whole
future prosperity of the Province of the
various matters which have been and are
being discussed before the Arbitration Committee. We have succeeded during the past
two years in balancing our Budgets, but it
has only been possible by refusing to authorise a good many items of expenditure
which indeed I should have liked to
have met, but for which I was unable
to raise the necessary ways and means, and
by the recommendations of the Colwyn Committee which involved a departure from the
faulty premises of the White Paper on which
the finances of the Government of Ireland
Act were founded. .
It is proposed to hold a sitting of the
Colwyn Committee early next month to consider further the question of a principle on
which our contribution to national services
may be permanently based, involving a claim
that our essential social services should be
admitted on a standard relative to that
adopted in Britain. (Hon. Members: Hear,
hear.")
Before leaving this question I would like to
place on record my testimony to the valuable
services which have been rendered to the
Province by the efforts which were put forward by Sir Ernest Clark not only in the preparation of our case for which he was entirely responsible, but also in the conduct of
it before the Colwyn Committee. I attribute
the successful outcome of the past two years
to the wonderful work which he has done,
and having in mind the extraordinary complexity of the matters which were discussed
before that Committee I feel that the House
is with me when I say that we are proud to
have associated with us one who has been
untiring in his devotion to the interests of
this Province.
Having made this preliminary survey of
matters of more general interest it may be
informative at this stage if I compare the
details of the estimates of revenue and expenditure of last year with the actual outcome. I am sure hon. Members will find
the comparison of some interest in view of
our present position.
1923-24.
TRANSFERRED REVENUE.
I shall deal first with the question of transferred revenue, that is to say, those sources
of revenue over which we have control. If
honourable Members will refer to Table 3 of
the White Paper in their hands they will see
that the total tax revenue last year was originally estimated to yield £870,000, while the
actual receipts were £840,000.
There is very little that calls for comment
in these figures. Estate Duties, which show
a reduction of £26.000, are difficult to estimate, while Excise Revenue, which comprises
Entertainments Duty Tax, Liquor and other
Licences, yielded £14.000 less than the estimate, although in point of fact the actual
collection in the year by the Customs and

The Budget-
[Mr. Pollock]
Excise Department, which acts as our agents,
was only about £7,000 less than the estimate.
Motor Vehicle Duties, which, as is known,
are collected by local authorities and paid to
the Exchequer Account at stated intervals,
yielded a return of £50,000 in excess of the
estimate, but the whole of the receipts from
this source of revenue, as the House is aware,
go to the benefit of the Road Fund, and do
not affect the Exchequer Account of the year.
There is still another type of revenue to
be considered in this connection, viz., nontax revenue, such as Land Purchase Annuities, Church Temporalities Rent Charges, and
the item termed "Miscellaneous," which comprises various receipts like interest on loans
and investments and small fee stamps. Here
the actual yield was just £3,000 more than
the Estimate, but I should remind hon.
Members that under the Exchequer and
Financial Provisions Act, the receipts from
Land Purchase Annuities and Church Temporalities are reduced by payments into the
Sinking Funds which will accumulate to
maintain in perpetuity what would otherwise be varying and terminable revenues. I
think the House will agree that it is only
sound finance that these important contributions to our revenue should be maintained in perpetuity.
RESERVED REVENUE.
I turn now to our major source of revenue,
namely, those duties which are retained by
the Imperial Government, consisting of
Customs and Excise Duties, Income and Super
Tax, Corporation Profits Duty, and the
postal revenue.
The yield of the Customs and Excise duties
was estimated, on information received from
the Imperial Treasury, of course, at
£5,792,000, but only £4,822,000 was realized.
I informed the House last year of the difficulty which was experienced by the Customs
and Excise Department of the Imperial
Government in framing these Estimates
which had, until last year, been made merely
on returns many years out of date. Events
have fully borne out my statement, as the
reduction from these duties amounts to
nearly one million pounds. The main heads
under which the Estimates show a reduction
are Beer and Tobacco Duties, which, together,
practically account for the whole of the
diminished yield.
The return from Income Tax and Super
Tax shows an increase of over £700,000 compared with the Estimate, which is largely
due to the speeding-up which has taken place
in the collection.
The total yield from reserved tax revenue,
that is excluding the Post Office, was £264,000
less than the Estimate.
With regard to the postal Services, I estimated that last year the administration
would involve a loss of £118,000, but in point
of fact the revenue has gone up by £51,000,
and the cost of the Post Office shows a reduction, compared with the Estimate, of
£42,000, or a net difference in favour of
Northern Ireland of £93,000. Instead of the
loss of £118,000, therefore, the Postal Service
only shows a loss of £25,000 during the year,
which is a record. This I regard as a very
satisfactory result of the year's working,
particularly when it is realized that in the
preceding financial year the Post Office involved us in a loss of £112,000.
I cannot avoid the conclusion that this
important improvement in the financial results of the Post Office, taken in conjunction
with the increase in motor revenue, furnishes
evidence I think important evidence of
gradually increasing prosperity in the Province. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The
Post Office results are specially significant.
The Estimate of the total normal revenue
was £12,378,000, while the actual receipts
amounted to £12,178,000, or a total reduction
of £200,000. If these figures are compared
with the revenue receipts appearing on Tables
1 and 2, hon. Members will see that I have
excluded in both cases the provision made by
the Imperial Government under the Government of Ireland Act, towards the erection
and equipment of public buildings, as it
does not in any sense affect our revenue.

CAPITAL ACCOUNT.
Hon. Members will see that I have
made a slight alteration in the form of the
Capital Budget. Owing to the difficulty in

because they are very uncertain, and to confine the printed statement to showing only
the borrowings which will be necessary to

well as for financing the construction of new
police barracks. As provision for the repayment of these borrowings has been made in
the normal Budget, I think the present
form, as it appears in this White Paper,
gives a more logical statement of the general

I anticipate, however, that the total demands on Capital Account during the year
will probably be considerably in excess of
£1,000,000, included in which I estimate that

The proceeds from Ulster Savings Certificates are expected to yield nearly £500,000.
and the balance will have to be raised by

These Certificates-which came into being

Finance Minister's Statement. 1052
The Budget-
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mr. Pollock]
-were continued in their original form
until December last, when, having regard
to the lower rates of interest prevailing, we
decided to reduce the interest yield by extending the duration of the Certificate from
ten years to twelve years. The issue price
still remains as before (namely 12/6), but

I have also made another change by reducing the maximum holding of any one
person from £500 to £400. As the Certificates are free of any liability to Income-
Tax, it is not the policy of the Government
to encourage the more wealthy classes of the
community to invest in the Certificates.
They are intended primarily as an investment for the poorer classes of our population,
and as such are a most convenient form of
investment for those who can only subscribe
in small amounts.
Backed as they are by the security of the
British Government, the Certificates are an
excellent investment for the small investor,
and I have every hope that, with a revival
in trade-which possibly may eventuate before a long time-an even greater effort
will be made by the people of the Province
to invest in this security.
I have now discussed the estimated revenue
and expenditure of the Province for this year
in which we stand, and I shall now for
a very few moments endeavour to bring into
relief some of the outstanding services
which in my judgment from the financial
point of view call for special note.
EDUCATION.
The House has doubtless observed the increase relatively small-in the Vote for
educational services. It is necessary, however, to point out that the recent Act will
not become fully operative during the present financial year.
Many new features of our educational
system have still to develop, and these will
entail very considerable additional expenditure.
It is well known that the Belfast education
authority contemplate a very extensive and
exceedingly costly scheme of school building
operations, on which the major portion of
the expenditure is expected to be borne by
the State. At present it is impossible oven
to approximate the liability under this head.
For the present year we have appropriated
£40,000, but this amount is relatively insignificant compared with that which will be
required when the full effect of the scheme
is felt.
It must also be borne in mind that increased enforcement of school attendance
presumes increased teaching staffs, and this,
of course, means enhanced expenditure. At
present there are only 330 young persons in
training for the position of teachers, whereas
it is estimated that fully 400 will ultimately
be required to satisfy the needs of the schools
in Northern Ireland.
The cost of intermediate education-the
claims of which have been so frequently
pressed in this House-may be expected to
increase during the coming years, when the
full effect of the improved salary scales, etc.,
are felt.
A superannuation scheme for Intermediate
Teachers is at present under consideration,
and will be submitted to Parliament in the
near future. This may probably involve an
expenditure of £70,000 a year.
Increased salary scales for teachers in
technical schools are also being discussed.
I have deliberately detailed these various
features of our education scheme, in order
that the Committee may realise, and be prepared for the financial results which will
before long begin to make their appearance.
In regard to Primary Education, my hon.
Friend the Parliamentary Secretary to the
Ministry indicated a few days ago that an
inter-departmental inquiry is contemplated
to investigate whether under existing circumstances any revision of present salary scales
is appropriate.
And when touching on this matter, I wish
to remove a misapprehension which appears
to exist in the minds of some teachers, judging from recent correspondence I have seen
in the Press. Any saving which can be
effected in any department of this service
accrues to the benefit of the Province, and
not to the Imperial Treasury, as seems to be
assumed. It seems to be assumed by the
writers of some of these letters, that any
saving that may be effected do:s not touch
upon the finances of our Province, but goes
to benefit the Imperial Authority. There is
no doubt that such is not the case, and there
need be no doubt on the subject.
Edu-
The total estimated cost of our
cational System for the present year is
approximately £2,000,000, of which teachers'
emoluments account for about £1,500,000.
I cannot leave this subject of Education
without offering my testimony to the very
efficient work done by the financial officer
of this Department with whom, in my dual
capacity of Minister of Finance, and Chairof the Training College Committee, I necessarily come into frequent relationship.
UNEMPLOYMENT INSURANCE FUND.
I
now come to another subject which,
I think, the House should hear something
1053 The Budget-
Finance Minister's Statement, 1054
21 MAY 1924
about-that is, the Unemployment Insurance
Fund. The position of this Fund is giving
me no little uneasiness. The debit balance
still continues to accumulate. This is mainly
due to the fact that our shipbuilding
industry remains in a parlous condition.
We have made every effort, through the
machinery of our Loans Guarantee Act to
induce shipowners to prosecute their building programmes, with only very partial
success; industrial strife, rising wages and
high cost of materials are all deterrents, I
am sorry to say.
It is some small encouragement that we
have been able this week to advertise the
gratifying news, to which my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Labour, referred
yesterday, that orders have been definitely
placed in one of our local yards for two
steamers of very considerable dimensions,
while satisfactory arrangements have now
been made for placing orders for two
additional steamers within the
course of
next week. That is to say, a total provision of
four large steamers for one of our yards.
When work gets advanced on these orders
there should be a welcome relief to great
numbers of the different shipbuilding trades
which are at present unemployed.
The cost of these four steamers is expected
to be as much as £3,000,000.
I am glad to be able to say that these
orders have been rendered possible through
the machinery of the Loans Guarantee
Committee, and that the small Act we
passed early last
year has more than
justified itself in its results.
We have already advanced £1,800,000 to
the Insurance Fund. This advance has been
provided by the sales of Saving Certificates
and temporary borrowings, and it must be
obvious that this continually increasing
burden cannot go on indefinitely.
The British Fund is in a much healthier
condition by reason of the fact that the
area of contribution is so much greater.
When acute industrial depression develops,
a small area such as ours containing only a
comparatively sparse industrial element,
cannot be expected to have the same elasticity as the wider area of Great Britain,
with its many diversified industries, most of
which have recovered to normal conditions
at the present time.
The present Government in Britain proposes to make some radical changes in the
working of the Unemployment Insurance
Fund, and I entertain the hope that some
arrangement may be made with the British
authorities whereby the burden upon our
resources may be somewhat lightened.
HOUSING.
I leave that subject now, and I touch upon
Housing, with which my Department has
had some intimate relations during the year.
The survey of our present year's financial
responsibility would be incomplete without
a reference to the important subject of
housing.
The Committee is aware that the Government commuted its liability to the Belfast
Corporation under the Housing Act of 1919
for a capital payment of £227,500. This
arrangement, whilst entailing a burden on
the taxpayers of the Province had a very
distinct advantage in releasing the Corporation from the embarrassment of Government
control, and enabling that body, as I understand, to realise the houses-I do not know
how many-without any loss to the ratepayers. I have arranged to finance this
payment by the provision of annuities
extending over a term of 20 years.
But the completion of this transaction has
hardly touched even the fringe of the Housing
problem in Belfast. A very acute shortage
of houses, principally of the class suitable
for the wage-earners' still exists.
Mr. DONALD: Hear, hear.
Mr. POLLOCK: Last year we followed the
lead given by Britain in Mr. Neville
Chamberlain's Housing Act, which was
mainly intended to assist and encourage
private builders. Towards this end We
offered a subsidy in the form of a capital
grant of £60 for each house built up to the
Government standard. The Belfast Corporation adopted our suggestion and supplemented this Grant with a subsidy of £40,
thus making a total grant of £100 to the
builder of a working man's house which
before the War could have been constructed
for well under £150.
This substantial subsidy, I am sorry to
say, has failed in its object for two reasons:
1st. Because the Corporation appears to
have hedged its grant of £40 with conditions
which the small builder could not or would
not comply with.
2nd. Because the small building speculator
of the past who helped so greatly to provide
Belfast with houses, has not, I am sorry to
soy, sufficient capital to undertake small
house-building on any considerable scale.
That is the information in my possession.
I understand the Belfast Corporation has
now relaxed its restrictions on this subsidy
of £40, and it is to be hoped that this will
give a stimulus to the work of the small
speculative builder, or to those who desire
to purchase houses for their own occupation.
The Budget-
Debate.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

[Mr. Pollock]
I think it may be taken for granted that
this problem can never be finally solved
until house-building and house-investment
are freed from all restrictions and free play
is given to private enterprise.
Mr. DONALD: Why were these put on?
Mr. POLLOCK: I am not responsible for
that. Public Authorities may engage on
house-building schemes when heavily subsidised by State grants, because the loss, if
any, is made good from the pockets of the
ratepayers, but private builders can take no
such risks so long as the lack of security in
respect of the letting of houses exists.
Mr. DONALD: Lack of confidence.
Mr. POLLOCK: Lack of security or confidence. I have completed my general survey
of the financial position of the Province.
There are still several important problems
to be solved, involving our financial relations
to the Central Authority.
In 1920 I ventured to predict that the
experiment of the creation of a Federal State
within the Kingdom was such a departure
from our historical constitutional relationships, it could not be expected that a probationary period of less than five years
would solve the novel problems which would
arise.
The experiment has now extended to thre
years, and whilst I contend that its success,
in many respects, may be regarded as phenomenal, we have yet to settle a number of
matters, of both a political and a financial
character.
Whilst political questions remain undetermined, it would be idle to predict our future
financial requirements further than I have
done. But in the domain of our ordinary
internal necessities for social and other local
services, we can if we exercise ordinary economy, make both ends meet. I observe,
however, a growing tendency to expect the
State to meet every financial want of the
community. This tendency, if I may say so,
is destructive of our old Ulster spirit of selfreliance, and it is only by a realisation of
the fact that the State means the people,
and that everything must be paid by the
people, that we shall develop our Province
into a self-respecting and prosperous unit
within the Kingdom. I beg to move. (Hon.
Members: Hear, hear.)
Mr. McGUFFIN: It would seem almost
a presumption for one with my limited experience in finance to intervene at this
stage in the presentation of a very important Budget. I do so, however, because of
the unrepresentative character of the House.
Those who have been accustomed to lead in
criticisms of finance are unfortunately
absent to-day, and the duty devolves upon
some person, at least, to open the debate
with regard to the matter. My confidence
in the matter is not inspired by a special
knowledge of the subjects under discussion,
but, my effort rather is to initiate the
Debate in the first instance, and in the course
of my remarks to compliment the right hon.
Gentleman on the very lucid way in which
he has presented what on the whole appears
to me to be a very complicated statement.
It is not an easy matter for one who is
untried in questions of finance to initiate a
criticism on the subject. I observed while
I was a Member of the Imperial House that
the duty was generally undertaken by ex-
Chancellors, men of experience, and after
they had broken ice in the matter and had
opened the case it was then for the juniors
or less experienced Members to come in and
offer some criticism. On the whole the
Budget is an assuring one, and considering
the difficulties with which the Chancellor
had to contend, I think it is a very satisfactory one, too.
I think, however, by way of passing that
we should have had a notification of the
date when this Budget was expected to be
introduced. I was more than amazed when
I heard it was to be introduced to-day. As
a rule one takes the opportunity of looking
up the previous Budget and comparing notes.
I had not the opportunity of doing so as I
was present here to-day in another capacity
and am, therefore, at a disadvantage in
speaking now. The amount of contribution
that we are expected to pay this year is, if
I have taken a note of it correctly, £3,312,000.
Have we an assurance that that sum, or
something approximate to that, may be the
amount that we may be expected to pay in
future? I am sorry to hear from the statement this evening that the question is still
sub judice and that we have no final assurance as to what our contribution is likely
to be. I think the Chancellor, speaking on
a former occasion, said that until we have
some stability and some assurance in regard
to this matter we could have no confidence
with regard to our financial position. I
think that is realised by every person
here. I do not think it would be advisable to say at the moment what one thinks,
but I do feel that even a smaller contribution would be as much as would be
expected of us as a self-governing State.
I have an idea that the whole thing was in
a very confused way when the apportionment
of our contribution was first made. If I recollect properly the amount was in the
vicinity of £8,000,000. It is now reduced,
and will probably be £3,312,000. It shows
how unstable the condition of affairs
is, and it shows moreover, the lack
of knowledge there was with regard

what the real financial possibilities of our State were when our contribution was fixed in the first instance. With
regard to other portions of the Budget statement I come in the first case to the question
of the Entertainment tax. I understand that
the Chancellor said that to follow the example
of the Imperial Parliament would mean a
reduction of £45,000, and that he is not prepared to undertake it. I am very sorry, because when speaking on this question on
previous occasions I have insisted that it is
a most undemocratic tax and one above all
others that should disappear as
possible. The Chancellor is accepting the conditions that obtain with regard to the motor
licences across the water. Of course that
will not cost him anything, and, therefore,
there is no concession so far as that is concerned, but in this particular case, where it
was within his power to remit the tax provided he had the financial resources, he
passes it over and practically says to those
who are contributing through this tax, “I
can do nothing for you." I want him to
understand that this tax is in a large degree
paid by the industrial classes, and if a remission is possible, I would appeal to him
to take it into consideration, and see what
he can do in the matter. When this tax
was originally imposed wages were very
high; they were 100 per cent. higher than
to-day, and the people did not feel the
burden of it, but although there is the
same desire for amusement, the same taxation exists. If the Chancellor can
do anything in the matter, I think
the industrial classes in the city would be
very much obliged.
I am rather surprised that the Chancellor
proposes to reduce the amount that can be
invested in connection with Savings Certificates, from £500 to £400. He has the example
of the Belfast Savings Bank, which puts no
limitation on the amount, and in a degree
represents industrial investments. I do not
see how by reducing the amount from £500
to £400 he is in any sense accommodating
the working classes by the exclusion of the
upper classes. He might let it go on as it
was and keep it at £500. I am not sure,
but I believe that even the Co-operative
Society are committed to an investment of
£500, and I do not see why any change should
be made in respect of this matter. On the
question of Education, I am at one with the
Chancellor, because I think we are in a very
grave situation in regard to the matter. We
have accepted the statutes of Education
practically obtaining across the water with
all the commitments in connection therewith,
and I am afraid it is going to involve us in
more than we are able to meet.
With regard to the provision that the
Chancellor hopes to make for Housing, I am
at one with him, too, in thinking that the
sooner private enterprise is introduced into
this matter, and that Parliament ceases to
interfere, the better for all concerned. We
find that houses can be built much more
rapidly by private enterprise than by local
authorities. We find that. houses built by
local authorities are costing even mora. I
had the opportunity of inspecting one in a
certain district in the city very recently,
and it does not reflect very much credit on
the Corporation to say that it was put up
under their ægis. A worse house, perhaps,
I never looked at. The equipment is ridiculous. It reflects very little credit on this
House and the Corporation, both of which
contributed towards them, to think that they
have been helping in the building of these
houses. I do not suppose any private builder
would turn out such a house, and I do hope
and trust we will not hear any more of interference on the part of the Government in
regard to subsidies for the erection of
buildings.
The unemployment question is a serious
one, and we are grateful to the Chancellor
and the Government for the action they have
taken in the provision of these ships that, in
all probability, will go far to relieve unemployment. Unemployment is rampant
here, particularly amongst the shipbuilding
classes. It is sad to think that 50 per cent. of
those formerly employed in the shipbuilding
industry in this city are at present unemployed and walking the streets. We are
gratified to know that the textile industry is
improving, and in that degree believe it is
due to the right hon. Gentleman who presides
over the Ministry of Labour and is responsible for these things. I am more than
pleased with the statement that was submitted by the right hon. Gentleman. The
House is entitled to feel gratified. I am
sure that so far as the House can it will
facilitate him in all the projects he has in
view with regard to the question of revenue
and expenditure.
Mr. DUFF: I have very few remarks to
make, but first, I desire to compliment the
Minister of Finance on the method he
adopted in placing these figures before us.
We have all been able to get a grasp of the
situation. I think, perhaps the most ominous
fact he has disclosed to us to-day is that
small item of £45,000, because here we have,
I believe, the first difference between the
benefits which our colleagues in Scotland
and England have and those which we are
able to give in this State. It is, perhaps, a
little bit unfortunate that the first sacrifice
that has been demanded from us as a
Parliament is going to fall on the lowest

[Mr. Duff]
Those
standard of any in this Province.
of us who know Belfast know that the great
masses of our industrial people go to entertainments that do not reach a higher figure
than sixpence. Of course, it is a moot
question as to whether the benefits of the
reduction on the entertainment tax would
have been given, to the people, but, I think,
if I know the Belfast people at all, they
would have made sure that they did get the
benefit of it if this benefit had been
available.
The next point I would like to refer to is
the prospect of the expenses of Education.
My hon. Friend, the Member for North
Belfast (Mr. McGuffin) seems to have been
impressed very seriously because he imagines
that a very grave position will develop.
Well, this whole question of the expenses
of education and the development of the cost
of it hinges on practically one point, and
that is whether you are going to follow out
the Act or whether you are going to
continue the conditions that at present
exist. Why do I say that is the hinge or
pivot of the whole question? The Act states
that the compulsory age is from six to
fourteen years, and at present you allow
schools to be crammed with children from
3 up to six years, and a considerable
addition to your expenses is on that account.
Now, if the conditions were such that those
children of 3 to five years of age could be
effectively taught even small questions of
discipline then it might be worth while, but
I challenge any Member of this House to
take me to any school in the city of Belfast
where children of 3 to five years are under
conditions where they can benefit even in
the elementary principles of discipline far
less education. It seems to me that in
justice to the Local Government bodies,
whose expenditure will be enormously
increased by this position of affairs, the
whole question should be reconsidered on a
broad basis. The Province would benefit
far more by children of from five to fourteen
being educated properly than by perpetuating a condition of affairs under which
children from three and a half years are
mixed up with those of older ages and the
whole position so congested that neither
teachers nor scholars can get the utmost
benefit available.
Now there is another point why this
should be considered by the Minister of
Finance on a broad basis. Medical inspection, school meals, and many other things
are compulsory or are unavoidable-while
the child attends school, because, although
the Act only makes it compulsory for you
to do certain things for a child from six
to fourteen years, in actual practice you
have got to do the same for the child of
three and a half, if it is in the school, as
you are compelled to do for the child of
six. It seems to me that this whole question
of the shortage of teachers is involved in
this matter, and there are other matters
also that when they are thoroughly investigated will show that this point of the
school attendance age is the pivot upon which
your expenses and the expenses of the Local
Government bodies will develop and be a
great burden. Again I say that if the conditions were such that the child of from
three and a half to five could be really
educated during the period then I would
take a different view of the matter, but no
school that I have visited is in such a condition that that object can possibly be
attained, no matter what effort is made by
the teacher or no matter what effort is made
by the child.
It is a serious matter, but I do not think
that the possible development of education in
Belfast need be a financial menace if a clear
policy is thought out and defined. I am sorry
that I have had to put this matter so
stringently or so strongly, but the more I
think on this question-the provision of
schools, medical treatment, the provision of
meals for school children, the provision of
teachers and everything else, and recollect
that the number of chilren under school age
is about 25 per cent. at least in Belfast-the
more I am convinced that if that 25 per cent.
were dealt with in some other way you would
relieve a considerable congestion and at the
same time put your financial affairs in a
more solidly and clearly defined position.
These are the points which I thought it my
duty to put clearly before the House. Not
only is the Ministry of Finance involved
but the Local Government bodies are involved, and when you tell the Local Government bodies to adopt the latest methods of
education it will not encourage them if in this
House the whole development of education
from a financial standpoint is taken to be a
grave menace to the future. I do not share
that view at all, but I do say that, even at
the sacrifice of discouraging the attendance
of children, say up to the age of five, if
that were done then your financial stringency
would be relieved; there would be room for development, and there would be no financial
menace in my opinion. Again I wish to
compliment the Minister of Finance for
putting the position before us in such a
way that some of us can get up and speak on
the matters with which he has so clearly dealt.

Mr. COOPER: I am sorry the Minister of
Finance has not been bold enough in his
Budget statement to tackle the question of
motor vehicle duties. That is one of the
transferred services, and it is a duty which I
think this House has the power of collecting
in its own way. Everyone in this Province
knows at the present time that the system of
collecting and imposing motor taxes is verv
unfair. Take a car like a Ford car, which is
the cheapest car on the market, and is run
by a noor clergymen or somebody in a country
parish. He cannot run that car unless he
pays a tax of £24. He has a small salary, and
is not able to run that car for more than
100 or 200 miles in the year. On the other
hand, we have a car, with half the taxes on
it, coming out of Belfast every day in the
week. tearing un the roads in the country.
Sometimes it is five or six, or up to fifteen.
tons in weight. That car gets off with a
comparatively small tax. The only system on
which the motor tax can be fairly imposed
is by nutting a tax on petrol. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The whole of the people
of Ulster want the tax put on the petrol.
There are members of this House here who
told me they only drive their cars for a few
hundred miles in the year, and they have to
pay this big tax. I was struck with some

share of taxation,
Mr. McGUFFIN: That is another question.

pay up.
There is just one other thing. Is the

[Mr. Crawford.]
was greatly pleased to hear the Minister of

would get the same social service as in other
parts of the Empire, and I sincerely hope he
