to give us in Northern Ireland the same
social service as they have in other parts of
the country.
I understand that in one of the reserved
services the Chancellor said he had a marked
saving the postal service. Although it is a
reserved service I think there could be more
savings on it. I believe there are deliveries
of letters in some parts of the country much
too frequent for the number of letters to be
delivered. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Indeed, I understand that on one occasion
it cost 81d each to deliver the letters in
certain parts of the country. That being so,
there should be less frequent deliveries in
places where letters are so scarce, and where
the delivery costs so much. I mention that
simply as a way in which money could be
saved. I have a distinct recollection when
people in the country had to go to the Post
Office for their letters, and it would be no
injustice in those districts where the population is sparse and the correspondence very
scarce, to have less frequent deliveries than
in the towns.
The Minister deserves to be congratulated
on the marvellous success that has attended
the Ulster Savings Certificates. It is a great
sum of money to be invested, and it is a real
sound proof that the people of Northern
Ireland have absolute confidence in this
Government, and in the way it is managing
the affairs of the Province. The Minister
deserves congratulations on that. I am
sorry that while he said the people are
anxious they should have the same advantages as other parts of the Empire, he did not
apply that same logic to the question of the
Entertainment Tax. I am not a great man for
entertainments, but I think if we are to have
the same social advantages as they have in
England, he is scarcely so logical as he
usually is when he could not see his way to
give us the same advantages as they have on
the other side. He has made concessions in
regard to motor duty, but unfortunately the
effect of that is that anything he loses in that
way will come off the Road Board, and if the
expenses of the roads are kept up the balance
will fall on the ratepayers.
The poor
people through the country will have to pay
for this concession, provided the money is
spent on the roads the same as hitherto.
There are two or three things that the
Minister did not mention. I regret exceedingly he made no reference to agriculture.
Nothing is being done to show that the policy
of the Government is one to try to help the
people and keep them in the country. Not
only scores but hundreds of thousands are
going away from this land, and the Government should do something to prove that they
are trying, in the words of the Prime Minister
a few years ago, to stabilise agriculture and
to make it possible for the farming
population to remain at home.
There is another point in connection with
housing that I think is an injustice. The
Minister made no mention of giving farmers
the same facilities as are given to people in
the towns and within the radius of towns. I
see no reason why a farmer who wants to
improve his house and cannot do so at present
should not have the same advantages in the
matter of borrowing money. Whatever he
would do to the house would increase the
value of the place and increase the rating
capacity. It would be a good thing if farmers
got the same advantages as other people in
that respect. The right hon. Gentleman
made no mention either of old-age pensions.
and I was hopeful that he would reduce the
age to 65 years. The time has arrived when
people of 65 years of age should get pensions.
If the Minister had devoted that marvellously
quick brain of his to the old age pension
business and tried to devise means whereby
the frauds perpetrated at present could be
done away with, he would have sufficient
money to give people who really deserved it
the pension at 65 years of age. I hold that
no man has a right to make રી will and
leave his wife worse off than the law allowed
him if he made no will. We all know there
are people who make wills and leave women
in such a state that they are bound to apply

into the hands of the children. It is not fair

not devise some means whereby if that man

Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH: No, not

House I would like to reply to some of the
points raised by my hon. Friends. My hon.
Friends have ranged over a very wide variety
of subjects, and many of them are very
important, so important that if I devoted my

will endeavour to go through them as quickly

Member for North Belfast (Mr. McGuffin),
i.n a particularly complimentary speech,
spoke of the surplus of three million odd
pounds that accrued, and inquired whether
I had any definite knowledge that this sum
would be expected by the Imperial authorities. Such, I understood, was the question
that was put to me. I. of course, cannot
answer that question, but I can say this that
there is something that the House should
know, or, rather, something that should be
impressed upon them, and that is this fact
that when we took over the services our
revenue was £14.000.000. To-day it is only
£9,000,000, a reduction of £5,000,000. That
reduction is determined by two causes. The
first was faulty calculation originally, but
the more important is the reduction in
taxation, so that when my hon. Friend (Sir
Crawford McCullagh), who has just sat down,
speaks of the maintenance of taxation I
would remind him that through the action
of the Imperial Parliament a very material
reduction has taken place in the commodities
of life and also in income tax. That is the
. explanation of why our revenue is reduced
by £5,000,000, and why our contribution concurrently is reduced from £8,000,000 to
£3,000,000. That is the position we occupy
to-day and that is the reply I make to the
hon. Member for North Belfast.
A considerable amount of discussion
ranged round the entertainment tax, and a
final appeal was made to me by my hon.
Friend (Sir Crawford McCullagh) not to refuse to follow the action of the Imperial
Chancellor in respect of this tax. No one
would be more desirous than I am that
taxation should be reduced. I am perfectly
well aware that taxation at present generally
is a very serious burden, and particularly
a heavy burden on industry. This tax, however, is not understood to touch industry. As
my hon.
Friend reminded me it was a
democratic tax, that is to say, a tax imposed
upon a class that very largely frequent such
places as picture houses. But I would remind
my hon. Friend also that possibly that is Lot
the largest part of the population who become
liable to this tax. There are football matches
where vast crowds of people assemble, and
other entertainments of a similar nature to
which the same arguments do not apply. The
principal reason which influenced me in the
decision I came to was that we stand to-day
politically in a very difficult and uncertain
position. The circumstances are familiar to
the House, and I do not wish to enlarge upon
them or to go into any detail with regard
to them, but I think that the gravity of the
position is sufficient to warrant the opinion
being held by every hon. Member that, no
one, and no Government, and no Finance
Minister responsible for the finances of this
Province can give away any money he can
possibly retain in the coffers of the Government. I want to say no more on this subject,
but that is the main reason actuating me.
Another argument introduced was that we
should go on parallel lines with Great Britain
equally in expenditure and in revenue-on
both sides of the account. I admit the force
of that argument. That is to say that we
claim on the one hand equal terms in respect
of expenditure and social service with Great
Britain, and that on the other side we should
also keep on parallel lines in respect of our
taxation. That is true. but we have not
established the principle yet that the
Imperial Treasury or the Imperial Government will recognise our right to equality
in expenditure and social services.
I think if that principle had been settled
probably we should have approached this
question of the entertainments tax from a
different point of view. I think that probably
it will be settled before a great while. I do
not desire to give any undertaking. I cannot
possibly give any undertaking in view of the
financial position of the Province. Still at
the same time the question might be approached from a different angle.

Mr. McGUFFIN: You encouraged investment at the out-set.
Mr. POLLOCK: It was primarily in the interests of the working-class community, to

and at the same time to develop a sense of

of principle.

The motor vehicle duties were referred to
by the hon. Member for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Cooper) and others. The imposition of the motor vehicle tax was determined, as I understand it, after investigation
by a very important committee, and the
difficulties of imposing the tax upon spirit
were so great it was found that the present
system, while not at all
an equitable
principle in its entirety, was still one exceedingly difficult to discontinue for the reason
that there are so many different types of
motors. They use not only petrol, on which
no difficulty would be presented in imposing
Custom duties on importation, but benzol,
which is of home manufacture,
petroleum which, I understand, is used considerably in heavy vehicles. Then there are
other forms of propulsion, such as electricity
and steam. All these matters enter into a
tax upon motor vehicles. Therefore the
Committee which has recently been sitting in
London-a most important committee
which Belfast was represented-has, I believe,
come to some conclusions, although I am not
in a position to state their nature, but I
believe there is something of a middle course
being recommended. As to whether it will
be adopted or not by the Government on the
other side I cannot tell. We at the present
time can only remain in our present position
until we see the position more clearly defined.

Education whether he can give any information as to the probable date when the
proposed new scale of safaries for technical
teachers will be published, and further,
whether the salaries laid down in that scale
will be retrospective.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): In reply to the first part of the
question, I regret that it is still impossible
for me to say when the new scale of salaries
for technical teachers will be available. The
drafting of regulations to give effect to the
proposed scale is receiving constant attention,
but it is a matter of very great difficulty
to find a simpler method of payment to take
the place of the complicated system at present in force. I can assure my hon. Friend,
however, that there will be no avoidable
delay.
As regards the second part of the question,
the Ministry of Education and the Ministry
of Finance have agreed to accept the recommendation of the Committee that the scales
should have retrospective eflect.

Gentleman state whether there is any
likelihood of the scale being published within
a reasonable time, say a month or six
weeks?
Mr. McKEOWN: I can give my hon.
Friend the assurance that in all probability
the scales will be published within six weeks.
Mr. McGUFFIN: May I ask the hon.
Gentleman if the Inter-Departmental Committee has actually been called together and
is functioning in respect of this matter?

DEMAND FOR WORKERS IN GREAT
BRITAIN.
4. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Labour whether he will state the position
arising out of the demand for workers in
England and Scotland.
Mr. ANDREWS: There is at present a demand for particular classes of skilled tradesmen in shipbuilding centres in Great Britain.
A demand for joiners, principally from the
Clyde, has been notified to the Belfast Employment Exchange, and the available
employment has been offered in the ordinary
course to unemployed joiners in Belfast. I
may say that, after consultation with the
local representatives of the Trade Union concerned, I satisfied myself by a special
inquiry made in Glasgow by an officer of
my Department that this particular demand
could not be filled by suitable labour in the
Clyde district, and also we took care to
offer the work first to single men where in
most cases there would be less domestic
difficulty than would ordinarily exist. Unfortunately a sufficient number of men did
not accept the available employment. As this
is apparently suitable employment within
the meaning of the Unemployment Insurance
Acts, unemployment benefit is disallowed
under the provision of the Statutes.
men concerned are, however, entitled to urge

MOTOR VEHICLE LICENCES.
5. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance if he will state the total number
of Motor Vehicle Licences granted during
the years 1923-24 in Northern Ireland, and
whether the Government propose to introduce legislation to reduce the tax on motor
vehicles and put the increased charges on
consumption.
Mr. ANDREWS: I have been asked to
take this question for my right hon. Friend.
31,367 Motor Vehicle Licences were issued
in Northern Ireland during the year 1923.
Of that number 17,339 were Annual Licences
and 14,028 were quarterly and part year
Licences.
The latest figures available for the year
1924 show a total of 21,906 licences issued to
the end of March, 15,739 being annual
licences, and 6,167 quarterly and part year
licences.
As regards the second part of the question
I would refer the hon. Member to the statement made by the Minister of Finance in
his speech in the House yesterday.

6. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Finance whether he will state whether spirit
grocers who were unable to fulfil the requirements of the Intoxicating Liquor Act would
be compensated for the period between the
date of the surrender of the licence, 16th,
17th, 18th January, 1924, and the date of the
decision of the claims by the Court, seeing
that expenses are incurred although these
houses are closed.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The question of the amount of compensation to be awarded in individual cases

question, but I should explain that the principles governing the grant of awards are
contained in Part II of the First Schedule
to the Intoxicating Liquor Act. I cannot
see, however, that any running expenses are
likely to be incurred by the closure of the
spirit side of a spirit grocery establishment.

whether something could not be done to
assist about sixty working men who purchased a house each some four or five years
ago, but who have failed to obtain possession
of their own houses owing to the house

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
No, Sir; I do not think it would be possible

PRIVATE TIME OF CIVIL SERVANTS.
8. Dr. MORRISON asked the Prime
Minister whether it is the considered opinion
of the Government that highly-paid officials
of the Northern Government who belong to
the professional class, and who also have the
security of Civil Service pensioners, may
compete with their professional brethren for
outside work; and if he is aware that the
ordinary professional man and the taxpayers
generally resent this action.
Mr. POLLOCK: I take this question for
my right hon. Friend.
I would refer the hon. Member to a reply
given to the hon. Member on the 13th
instant. So long as a Civil Servant discharges satisfactorily and efficiently the
official duties entrusted to and required of
him, the direction in which he occupies his
private time is not a matter with which
the Government considers that it has any
concern. I am not aware of the existence
of the feeling to which the hon. Member
refers in the latter part of the question.
It may perhaps be some information to
my hon. Friend if I read to him the restrictions which are imposed by the Imperial
Government on Government servants of a
professional class:-
1. An officer must not have an office in his
own name.
2. He must not exhibit a notice plate at
his house, giving his name, profession, and
professional degrees.
3. He must not use information he has
obtained during the course of his professional
work in the Department for private practice.
4. He must not do private work during
official hours.
Subject to these regulations, the Imperial
authorities hold the view that an officer is
entitled to spend his private time according
to his own desires, and do work by taking
leave or working out of office hours.

The PRIME MINISTER: Perhaps as I
was the only person present when the
original arrangement with the British
Government was made in regard to the voting
of £500,000 to assist in meeting the grave
situation regarding unemployment at that
particular time I might be able in a few
words to explain to my hon. Friend and to
the House generally how we stand with regard to it to-day. An agreement was entered
into. It was one of the portions of that
agreement that fell upon the British Government to carry out that a sum of £500,000
should be granted to Northern Ireland in
order to meet to some extent the situation
then existing. When the grant was
sanctioned by the British Ministry I myself
immediately put forward a claim that the
ex-servicemen should have first call upon
the two-thirds of the fund to be allocated
to Protesant workers, and the other side put
forward a claim that those who were at that
time, I think, upon the White Cross should
have the first claim upon the one-third of
the £500,000 that would naturally fall to
Roman Catholics employed in the city of
Belfast.
So matters went on, and this portion of
the agreement was faithfully fulfilled by his
Majesty's Ministers until commitments were
entered into to the extent at all events of
some £300,000. There, therefore, remained
still a sum of £200,000 to be granted by the
Imperial Authorities to us to carry on in
order to complete the £500,000. At that time, it
will be within the memory of hon. Members,
a very large number of questions were outstanding between the British Government and
this Government, and a suggestion was made
by Mr. Stanley Baldwin that a small committee should be set up to go into all outstanding financial matters. I acquiesced in
that arrangement, being anxious to get many
things settled that were still hanging over
our heads. The personnel suggested was
Lord Colwyn as Chairman, Sir Josias Stamp
and Sir Laming Worthington Evans. To that
personnel I readily agreed.
My right hon. Friend the Minister of
Finance and his advisers put forward the
whole case from our point of view of these
outstanding financial commitments. It is a
very valuable document and it sets forth in
review practically all the points which remained to be settled up to the date on which
the Committee was established. After hearing the evidence on the various points decisions were given, and to my horror and
astonishment instead of saying that this
£500,000 was a pledge beyond their interference in any way they held for some reason
best known to themselves and never explained
to us that £300,000 was sufficient, and that
£200,000, therefore, would have to be cut off
the original amount of £500,000. Now the
difficulty we were in as a Government was
this, that we could not agree to the setting
up of and leaving to this small Committee the
decision of such weighty matters unless both
sides were prepared to agree to the findings.
We agreed to that naturally enough, and
consequently as this £500,000 was reduced by
£200,000 we had to acquiesce. But I would
like to say this, in order that there should
be no shadow of misunderstanding, that
taking the report as a whole and taking the
adjudications of these three gentlemen as a
whole Ulster was not unfairly treated in
the aggregate. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
Then the difficulty with which my right
hon. Friend (Mr. Pollock) and I were confronted was that we had led the House and
the country to believe, and especially the
city of Belfast, that we were going to get
£500,000. To them it was really not a matter
of the source but of the fact. With the
assistance of my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Labour, very large commitments
swallowing up the £500,000 had not only
then been entered into, but the
work which meant entering into them
was well under
Therefore,

right hon. Friends and
my
myself

The question, I hope, has been elucidated

other ways we can get a quid pro quo for

Mr. ANDREWS: This Bill, which I have
now the honour to ask the House to consider
and to give a Second Reading, is one of
very great importance to our industrial
classes, and, in a lesser degree, it affects
almost our entire community. Hon. Members
are probably aware of the fact that
Tuesday last the Imperial Minister
Labour introduced a new Unemployment
Bill in the Imperial Parliament. It was not
in its main provisions criticized by any
portion of the House, but after a certain
amount of friendly discussion it was given
a Second Reading with the approval of both
the Conservative and the Liberal Parties.
It is a most important Measure, but I do
not think that it is necessary that I should
take up the time of this House by going into
all its Clauses. At the same time I feel
that I ought to tell hon. Members something
of its main provisions. In the first place
it proposes to increase the benefit payable
to men from 15s to 18s per week, and to
women from 12s to 15s per week. It leaves
girls and boys between sixteen and eighteen
years of age and dependant wives exactly as
they are, and it increases the dependants'
allowances per child from 1s to 2s per week,
which is not, I think, an extravagant sum.
Mr. DONALD: Hear, hear.
Mr. ANDREWS: The Bill also goes into
quite a number of other matters. For instance, it proposes to do away with the
refunds at 60. One reason given for this
proposal is that these refunds are inconsistent with the principle of insurance. It
also avoids an enormous amount of clerical
work in computing the acutal amounts
accruing to men and women under this
Section from the day they enter an insurable
occupation to the day they leave it at 60
years of age. The Bill is drafted in such
a way as not to do an injustice so far as
it can be avoided. It is proposed that
this compensation Clause should have
effect, so far as I understand it, for one year,
and that, in addition, compensation will be
given to those who are 50 years of age and
over and who have up to now acquired certain rights which are admitted. The Bill
does not affect contributions at the present
time in any way. It may be argued that this
is a Socialistic Measure because it is introduced by a Government which calls itself a
Socialistic Government. Now, I really do
not think the political colour of a
Government that introduces a Bill of
this kind is a factor which should influence us; it is the Bill we have got to
consider apart altogether from who its
sponsors are. The Bill, in my opinion, and
in the opinion of the Government, is not a
Socialistic Measure in any sense or form,
and we feel that we are not justified in departing from legislation of the kind which
passes the Imperial Parliament, and for this
reason: We do not see why our people here
should be deprived of benefits which they
would have received automatically if we had
not made the political sacrifice of having a
Parliament of our own.


this

making of loans, and for other purposes

I. To authorise a charge upon the Consolidated Fund and the growing produce
thereof in respect of the payment of (a)

connection with the provision of improvement of buildings for the use or
modation of the Royal Ulster Constabulary;
(b) such sums as may be required for the

of moneys provided by Parliament, and

provided by Parliament in respect of the

Ministry of Finance aforesaid.
Mr. BARBOUR: The Financial Resolution
now before the Committee requires some explanation from me, having regard to the
necessarily technical language in which it is
framed, and, in order that the Committee
may know exactly what machinery is contemplated in the Bill of which it is the
forerunner. It can hardly be said that any
controversial matters are raised, and hon.
Members are, I think, already familiar with
the main purposes-the carrying out of which
necessitated this machinery.
In the first place reference has been made
on several occasions to the sum of £400,000
which has been made available by the
Imperial Government under the Colwyn
Award and which, generally speaking, was
granted with the object of making good any
defect or insufficiency in the buildings or
equipment used for Irish Services in

Committee.
Northern Ireland. Some of these buildings
are in course of construction, and the items
of expenditure
have appeared on the
Estimates which have been passed by this
House. The items which have reached this
stage are the Training College and Hostel
for Student Teachers at Stranmillis, and
certain Agricultural Institutions, with which
bon. Members are familiar, at Strabane,
Greenmount, and Cookstown. In addition to
that reference has been made in the House
to the out-and-out grant to Queen's University
of Belfast of a sum which will eventually
amount to £31,000 for the establishment of
a Faculty of Agriculture at the University.
Hon. Members will remember that the
University itself is contributing towards this
end a free site for the buildings which it will
be necessary to erect, and they are also finding out of their own funds £11,000 to enable
this work to be started. Of the £31,000 which
this Government is granting,
£15,000 has already been voted
Estimates this year as being the amount of

a
of
a sum
in the
The other objects to which the Colwyn
Award will be devoted will be the provision
of a Police Depot, a Convict Prison, a Borstal
Institution, and a Criminal Lunatic Asylum.
The Resolution contemplates the establishment of special capital fund into
which this sum of £400,000 will bg
paid and out of which payments will
be made from time to time to the
Votes bearing the expenditure in the
first instance. It is possible, however, that
this sum of £400,000 will prove insufficient
for the various improvements I have indicated, and, in order that an additional sum
may be available if required, it is proposed
to empower the Ministry of Finance to raise
by means of terminable annuities or other
securities a further sum not exceeding £75,000.
It will be clear, therefore, that before the
special Capital Fund now to be established
can be drawn upon, the approval of this
House must be given to the detailed items of
expenditure which will appear from time to
time in the Estimates. I wish to draw the
particular attention of hon. Members to the
fact that when this expenditure comes to be
incurred estimates will be submitted in the
usual way and will require to be voted by
the House, and at the same time the attention
of hon. Members will be drawn to the effect
of the amount appropriated in aid from this
fund which it is now proposed should be
established. I think hon. Members will
appreciate that this sum of £400,000 is
distinctly of a capital nature and should not
be mixed up with the ordinary funds arising
from our annual revenue and expenditure.
It is well to keep track of this sum and to see
that it is devoted to the particular institutions for which it was awarded.
The second important object of the Bill
which will give effect to this Resolution is
concerned with the provision of money to
enable land and buildings to be acquired
for the use or accommodation of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary. I referred a few days
ago to the very important expenditure that
it has been considered necessary to incur to
bring the different Barracks of the Royal
Ulster Constabulary up-to-date, to put them
into a proper sanitary condition, and generally to bring them into line with those in
England and Scotland. I would remind hon.
Members that it is not proposed to charge
against the revenue
year by year the
large outlay that will be involved in
carrying out these improvements, but
it is proposed that this also should
be regarded as an outlay of a capital
nature and should be met by means
of a Sinking Fund which will be charged in
the estimates, and over a period of years will
wipe out the initial expenditure. It is proposed that in the first place the money should
be paid out of the Consolidated Fund and
then that the Consolidated Fund should be
reimbursed by means of an annuity. Hon.
Members will remember that in the Royal
Ulster Constabulary Vote this year, the first
annual instalment, or portion thereof, was in-
Icluded in the estimates towards this end. It
is proposed that the capital outlay should be
repaid to the Exchequer over a period not exceeding 25 years. Part 2 of the Resolution
is necessary in order to carry this out.
It will be observed that the Resolution
refers to the extension of the powers of the
Ministry of Finance with respect to the investment of moneys. This is not a very big
matter. As hon. Members will understand,
this sum of £400,000 will be paid over to us
at an early date, whereas the expenditure of
it may extend over some time. Therefore,
it is necessary to have power to make use
of the money until it is actually required
to be spent on the purposes for which it is
provided. We may require to make loans
to Local Authorities, and it is proposed to
use this money temporarily for such purposes as power is sought to use it. I have
indicated the main changes which are contemplated, and the subsidiary changes may
conveniently be dealt with in connection
with the Bill. I beg to move.

Colonel WOODS: With reference to my
question to-day and the answer returned, I
am sorry the Government is not taking any
steps in regard to this pamphlet which was
published and circulated on Sunday, 4th
inst. The pamphlet makes the statement:-
"The rum-sodden British were defeated
by the comparatively sober Germans."
I doubt if there is any Member of this
House who will agree that that is a fit and
proper publication to be allowed to be circulated in this loyal State. I am quite
unable to express my feelings in regard to
this scandalous libel on the British Army,
and on the ex-Servicemen of the Six
Counties. It applies to yourself, Mr.
Speaker, if I may say so; it applies to the
Prime Minister, to the hon. and gallant
Member for Armagh (Major Shillington),
and to the hon. and gallant Member for
Down (Captain Mulholland), and if it is
allowed to pass-

of the hon. and gallant Member for Armagh
(Major Shillington).

before it can be discussed?

is it. I am sorry for causing delay. It does
not matter who issued it so much as-

Colonel WOODS: I will read it.

I O.G.T.
I did not want to state whether or not
this pamphlet was circulated by the Prohibitionists or anybody else. The thing is
a scandal, and it was circulated in Belfast
on Sunday, 4th inst. It does not matter to
me who was responsible for the original
article. Its intention is quite obvious. It
is to libel the men who went out to the
front to keep these people alive. I resent
this more than I can say as a deadly insult,
and if the Minister of Home Affairs, or
whoever is responsible at the moment for
the Ministry of Home Affairs, does not take
action at once-
Mr. POLLOCK: Against whom?
Colonel WOODS: Against the distributors
of this insult-he no longer represents his
constituents, and he should resign. There is
precedent for action by the Government, because in 1916 one gentleman called Greenfield,
I believe, had the temerity to say that the
Ulster Division went over the top drunk on
the 1st July, 1916. That gentleman was fined
£50, and he left the country, I do not know
whether because of the action of the Government or of his own volition. It is a good
thing for him that he did. I suggest-in fact
I demand-that the Government take instant action in this case in defence of the
character of the men who went out from here
to serve their country without any thought of
reward. They certainly never thought at
that time of a reward like this. I would like
to know if there is any Member in this House
who could defend an insult like this to ex-
Servicemen. I demand that the Government
take instant action.

SPEED LIMIT OF MOTOR VEHICLES.
.
1 Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the laws governing
the speed limits of motor vehicles are the
same in the Six Counties as in England.
The
PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw): The laws governing the speed
of motor vehicles in England and in
Northern Ireland are identical except as
regards heavy motor cars fitted with pneumatic tyres or tyres of a soft or elastic
material. Since 1st June, 1922, a maximum
speed of 12 miles per hour is permitted in
Great Britain for any heavy motor
fitted with tyres made of a soft or elastic
material when not drawing a trailer.
car
In Northern Ireland a heavy motor car
not drawing a trailer may travel at 12 miles
per hour only if the vehicle is fitted with
pneumatic tyres or tyres of a soft or elastic

NATIONAL HEALTH INSURANCE.
2. Dr. MORRISON asked the Minister of
Labour whether, seeing that it is a fact
that Inspectors are acting all over the
Northern area to see that employers are
complying with the law in regard to
National Health Insurance, it would not
be possible to use them to enforce the law
in another respect, that is by advising the
insured how to act if they experience delays
or refusals to pay when they claim benefits
under the Act.
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): In reply to my hon. Friend, I
may say that my Department's Inspectors,
and also the Headquarters of the Ministry,
do frequently give advice to persons insured
under the National Health Insurance Acts.
At the same time, I fully recognize the importance of the matter to which my hon.
Friend refers in his question, and I will
take an early opportunity of bringing it
before a joint meeting of the representatives
of the Approved Societies and the Ulster
Medico-Political Committee, which I think
my hon. Friend will agree is the best
method of determining the wisest course to
pursue in the first instance.
Dr. MORRISON: Thank you, very much.
QUESTION OF SPECIAL PROTECTION.
Mrs. CHICHESTER (by private notice)
asked the Minister of Home Affairs for what
reason special protection is being afforded
to Thomas Devlin, of Drumallan, Co.
Derry; whether the Government is aware
that the man is strongly suspected of
having taken part in outrages in the past;
whether he went to the Free State and
joined the Army there in order to avoid
arrest. Will the Government make a statement on the subject?
Mr. MEGAW: Devlin was recently subjected to maltreatment by some unknown
and ill-disposed persons, and to prevent the
possibility of further attack, protection has
been temporarily afforded him. As regards.
the second part of the question, I have not
been able to obtain sufficiently definite information to enable the Government to take
action, but inquiries on this point are being
actively prosecuted.

Mr. DONALD: I only want to say one or
two words with regard to this Bill. It is a
very comprehensive Measure indeed and it
brings about very great changes in the
administration of Unemployment Insurance.
I desire to say a few words with regard to
one particular Clause. This Bill is introduced to conform with the Bill which is now
going through the Imperial House of Commons. The original Act of 1911 provided for
fifteen weeks benefit in the year. The Act
of 1920 provided for twenty-six weeks benefit in the year, and the Act of 1923 provided
for forty-four weeks benefit in the year. The
present Bill makes provision for fifty-two
weeks benefit in the year, and that means
continuous benefit for the whole of the year.
In the Bill I notice one Clause with which
I do not agree. It is proposed to abolish the
Clause whereby a member who has contri--
buted all his life on reaching the age of 60
was able to get a refund of the money he
had paid into the Society, with 2 per cent.
compound interest. I am sorry to see in
this Bill that it is proposed to abolish that
provision, because in my opinion it tends to
do away with the encouragement of thrift.
In another Bill which will come before the
House this afternoon-the Belfast Corporation Bill-there is a Superannuation Clause
which deals with this very point-that where
a man has contributed voluntarily to a fund
he shall, when he retires from the service,
get a refund of that money. That is perfectly legitimate. This Bill has passed
through the Committee Stages and I only
want to enter my protest against the abolition
of the Clause to which I refer. In my judg
ment it is very unfair to abolish a Clause of
that description. However, we have not yet
had the full scope of the Bill before us, and

Constabulary (Acquisition of Land)
Bill.

Mr. BEST: The Ministry of Home Affairs
have met with certain difficulties in the
acquisition of certain sites on which to erect
new barracks for the R.U.C., and attempts
to acquire sites by agreement have unfortunately proved to be abortive. It has therefore
become necessary to ask Parliament to confer
Compulsory Powers on the Ministry of Home
Affairs to acquire such sites. The method by
which it is proposed to secure such powers is
to enable the Ministry to make in the first
instance a provisional order in the case of
any specific site or sites to be acquired, and
having made such Order notice is to be given
to the owners, lessees or occupiers. A month
is allowed in which such owners, lessees or
occupiers
may make objections and the
Ministry then proceed to consider such
objections, and in the light of such objections
they may either modify the Order or confirm it as originally made.
This procedure follows that which was
adopted in the case of the Irish Land for
Sailors and Soldiers Act, of 1919. As regards
the settling of the price to be paid, an arbitrator will be appointed in accordance with
the provisions of the 2nd Schedule of the
Housing of the Working Classes Act, 1890.
Some modifications, however, in that Schedule
are proposed. Under that Schedule appeal is

not allowed except the amount of Award

It is therefore proposed in this Bill to give

I beg to move.

The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews): The dispute in Londonderry
between the Corporation and its employees
was reported to the Ministry of Labour by
the Secretary of the Municipal Employees'
Association on April 25th. In accordance
with the provisions of the Industrial Courts
Act, my Department endeavoured to bring
about a settlement of the matters in dispute.
A meeting of the Corporation had already
been held to consider the workers' demand
for an increase of 2/- per week in wages, and
my Department was subsequently able to
arrange for a postponement of the threatened
strike for one week. During that week, a
further meeting of the Corporation was held
and was attended by an officer of the
Department at the Council's request. The
Corporation decided to adhere to its decision
taken at the previous meeting to refuse to
entertain the workers' demand or to agree
to refer the matter to arbitration, and I
regret that the strike began on May 9th.
Stoppages of work have also unfortunately
occurred in the building trade and the porkcuring trade in Londonderry. I am informed,
however, that although these strikes are
causing inconvenience and loss to the City,
the interests of the general community are
being safeguarded as far as possible, and,
having given the matter careful consideration, I am of opinion that no further
opportunity for Government intervention
has yet arisen. The parties concerned are,
however, aware of the fact that, should they
desire it, the assistance of my Department
is readily available.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman
if he is prepared to persist in his efforts and
have either a representative of the Ministry
of Labour in Derry, or be present himself,
for the purpose of securing negotiations to
bring to an end this unfortunate and
disastrous strike?
Mr. ANDREWS:
I can assure my hon.
Friend that I am keeping in close personal
touch with the situation and that I will do
everything possible, as soon as the opportunity arises, to help matters in any way I
can.

Mr. BARBOUR: I think it will be obvious
to those hon. Members who have had the
opportunity of glancing through the provisions of this Bill that there is really no new
feature introduced in it. The proposals have
already been mentioned before in this House.
So far there has not been any adverse opinion
expressed in connection with them. There
are two main questions covered by the Bill.
The first is the application of the sum of
£400,000 paid to the Northern Government
on the recommendation of the Colwyn Committee in final satisfaction of certain claims
preferred under the Government of Ireland
Act, with the object of making good any
defect or insufficiency in the buildings or
equipment used for Irish services in Northern
Ireland; and the second main object of the
Bill is the machinery for carrying out the
construction and adaptation of Police
Barracks for the Royal Ulster Constabulary.
Hon. Members will see if they refer to
Clause (1) that it is proposed to establish a
Capital Fund No. 2 from the £400,000 grant.
That will be the style of the fund as we have
already a Capital Fund No. 1. It is proposed
to apply this fund to the several purposes
mentioned in Sub-sections (1), (a), (b) and (c)
of that Clause. I should point out, however,
that before this fund can be so applied the
authority of the House must be sought in
the annual Votes, and accordingly my
Department will be unable to embark upon
any expenditure under the Bill for which
Parliamentary approval is not given.
Clause 1 (3) is introduced to deal with expenditure which has been incurred during
the two financial years, 1922-23 and 1923-24,
on purposes for which this capital fund has
been set up, and it is thought more proper

that as this expenditure has been met during
these years from revenue, the fund should
be drawn upon to an equivalent amount.
Clause 1 (4) authorizes the Ministry of
Finance to borrow a sum not exceeding
£75,000 if the £400,000 proves insufficient for
the various purposes of the Act. This sum
will be repaid by terminable annuities or
other securities.
Clause 2 deals with the provision of capital
expenditure on police barracks, and authorizes the Ministry of Finance to borrow a
sum not exceeding in all £375,000 for the
acquisition of land and buildings and the
making of structural alterations to existing
premises. Repayment of the sum borrowed
will be effected by means of terminable annuities or other securities spread
period not exceeding 25 years.
over રી
Hon. Members will see that the main
difference between these two first objects is
that one has regard to expenditure which is
met out of money furnished to us by the
Colwyn Committee, and the second deals with
expenditure which we will have to face out
of our own resources. The expenditure for
constabulary barracks is more or less of a
capital nature, and so instead of charging
each year the outlay that might be made in
any one year it is proposed to establish this
fund to meet such expenditure, and that
expenditure will be repaid by annuities
spread over 25 years, so that there will be
no exceptionally heavy charge for any one
year.
Clause 3 provides that the capital fund
which was established under the Exchequer
and Financial Provisions Act of 1923 shall
be made available for the purpose of borrowings if necessary.
This Clause also provides (Sub-section 4)
that the Capital Fund No. 2, to which I have
already referred, may be temporarily invested
until it is drawn upon for the purposes of
the Bill. It is perfectly obvious that we
should make use of this money if it is not
immediately required for the purpose for
which it is ultimately intended.
Clause 4 deals with the proceeds of the sale
and disposition of property acquired under
the Bill. In this connection it is proposed
that the borrowing of £75,000 on Capital
Fund No. 2 shall be reduced by the proceeds
of any such sales, and that any sums
borrowed for police barracks expenditure
shall likewise be reduced if the proceeds
arise from the sale of police barracks. Such
transactions may or may not arise, but in
any case this Clause makes provision that
should we find it necessary to dispose of a
police barracks in one place and establish a

new police barracks in another, the sum
realized by the sale of the first should be

Clause 5, Sub-section (1), seeks to clarify
the existing lending authority of the Ministry
of Finance, and empowers the Ministry to
lend money to any Council or Board of
Guardians, etc., for any purposes for which
they have power to borrow under any enactment. In previous legislation dealing with
the powers to lend it is, I think, perfectly
obvious that such power is implied as every
power is given to the Ministry to borrow
money in order to make its loans, but it
does not seem to have been expressed anywhere that the Ministry will have the power
to make these loans. This Clause is simply
introduced to clarify the previous Act, and
make it perfectly clear that the Ministry of
Finance have statutory power to lend moneys
in this way.
Sub-section 2 of that Clause makes a few
drafting Amendments to the Exchequer and
Financial Provisions Act of 1923 in connection
with the disposal of the annual surplus.
These Amendments do not call for any
comment.
Sub-section 3 provides that repayment of
advances made out of the voted moneys shall
be treated as capital repayments in the
accounts to be kept by the Ministry of
Finance.
I beg to move.

Authorities, should give preference to firms

I am quite sure that I am expressing the
feelings of every Member of this House
when I say that our gratitude and sympathy
still go out to the ex-Servicemen, and in
particular to the disabled ex-Servicemen.
It may be said that the Government are
fulfilling their obligation with regard to
contracts. That may be so up to a point, but
it has come to our knowledge that contracts
have been given out to people who do not
come under the King's National Roll of
Honour. What I feel more than anything
else is the fact that some of these contractors
have been exploiting ex-Servicemen. I have
in my mind one case in which disabled ex-
Servicemen were dismissed, because they
sought the standard rate of wages, and they
have not been reinstated. That is not the
right thing-we should not exploit our ex-
Servicemen in that way-but that is not the
question that I am going to deal with here
to-day. I am going to put it as plainly as
I can in the form of an appeal not only to
this House but to the country in general. I
would like to take the minds of the Members
back a little, because after all it is just as
well that we should not lose sentiment in
this matter. According to the War Cabinet's
Committee's Report of 1918, the total strength
of our fighting Forces, including Reserves,
was 7,130,280, white races; other races, including white, 1,524,187, making a grand
total of 8,654,467. Of these, 666,833 made the
supreme sacrifice, and 2,040,520 were disabled
and wounded. It is for the last-mentioned
that I am making this appeal to-day. That
was a great achievement, and, in the words
of our old leader, was there ever a greater
achievement than that of the men who
joined up from this Province in defence of
their country? It is for those men that this
Motion has been tabled, in order that they
may get employment as early as possible.
It has been estimated that over four millions
of those who were fortunate enough to come
home have returned to civil life, but there
are a great number who unfortunately are
still unemployed.
I wish to deal now with the local side of
the question. I will take the Government
first. A report submitted to us on the 11th
April last showed that the total of the male
staff employed by the various Government
Departments, other than the Ministry
of Labour, was 769, the figure for the
Ministry of Labour being 466. The total
number of disabled ex-Servicemen employed
in the Government Departments at that time
was 1.235. In those Departments there are
253 seriously disabled ex-Servicemen, and 51
of those have a disability of 50 per cent. and
over. I offer no criticism of those figures
further than to say we are entitled to know
whether the Government themselves are
showing a good example to those outside who
may employ disabled men. If we segregate
the figures, we find that the total male staff
employed by the Ministry of Labour on the
24th March last was 466, as I have already
said. Of that number, 134 were disabled ex-
Servicemen, and 22 had a disability of 50 per
cent. and over. Then in all the other
Departments, out of a total of 769, 29 have
a disability of 50 per cent. and over. Figures
were also submitted which showed that the
number of severely disabled ex-Servicemen
on the books of the Appointments and Training Branch of the Ministry of Labour was 47,
and I regret to say there are still 700 disabled
ex-Servicemen unemployed in the city of
Belfast to-day. Although we have 700 today, it must be remembered that some two
years ago we had double that number, and
in this connection I must pay tributes to the
right hon. Gentleman, the Minister of
Labour, to the Minister of Finance, who has
given every assistance in his power, and to
the King's National Roll Committee, the
chairman of which is Mr. Godfrey Ferguson,
J.P. That gentleman has given his time
freely in connection with propaganda work,
and the committee have met frequently in
order to approach employers with a view to
getting those men into employment. It may
undoubtedly be said that bad trade had
something to do with the fact that these men
did not obtain employment earlier. We are
just in the same position as the people of
Great Britain with regard to this matter.
In Great Britain, as you see from the Press,
a Bill has been introduced to make it compulsory to employ these men. What brought
about that state of affairs? A Select Committee was set up by the Imperial Government some time ago, and they made certain
recommendations. I will read their final
recommendation:-
So urgent is the problem that your Committee recommend that their proposals
should be carried into effect forthwith, and
the necessary legislation passed during the
Autumn Session; but should the figures
show that the problem has not, by the 1st
of May, 1923, been successfully dealt with
on the lines proposed, recourse should then
be had to a form of compulsion modified
in character and scope, as circumstances
inay dictate.
A Bill has been introduced in the Imperial
House to make it compulsory, and the
Second Reading has been passed. I do not
know what the ultimate decision on that
Bill will be, but I hope that, after the great
achievements, after the number of men who
volunteered from our Province, it will never
be said that the employers of Northern Ire-

land had to be compelled to employ the men

These men come under three classified heads,
Firstly, there are those whose disabilities
would not prevent them from returning to
their usual occupations, or to another occupation, under ordinary industrial conditions,
after training if necessary. Secondly, there
are those whose disabilities would prevent
them from returning to the usual occupations,
but would not preclude them from employment under ordinary industrial or commercial conditions on what may be described as
light jobs. Thirdly, there are those whose
disabilities render it difficult for them to be
employed under ordinary industrial or commercial conditions except in some institution
specially designed for ex-Servicemen suffering
from very severe occupational disabilities.

I need not further detain the House.
thought it my duty to bring forward this

example. I read some of the speeches in

accusation cannot be levelled at the Belfast
Corporation. I am informed that seventyfive per cent. of their employees are ex-

number, which is five per cent. The Belfast
Water Board and the Poor Law Board have
also qualified, but there are a great number
of our employers who have not yet come
under the scheme. I make this special appeal
to the employers to-day to come under the
scheme. It is an obligation on every one of
us who can, including the employers, to do
something for our disabled ex-Servicemen. I
trust this appeal will have the desired effect,
and that these 700 men will get into employment at an early date. I beg to move.

motives-motives of humanity. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The basis of justice should

nation or the world a promise that there

It would be most disastrous if such a thing
were to come again. But supposing such a
thing through the workings of Providence
visited our nation afresh upon what ground
would you appeal to ex-Servicemen if you
ignore your duty now in reference to a
verbal agreement which you entered into
when they went forth to do their duty to
their country? Let us do what is just to
them now. Let them see by our attitude in

our obligation so that not only we may be

bound to think that is the case, but let us

a Government.

Now just for a few moments let me deal
with some of the opportunities of ex-Servicemen, because this matter is an important one
and has been referred to on more than one
occasion in this House. The hon. Member for
East Belfast (Mr. Donald) classified ex-Servicemen. The first class are those eligible for
their original, occupation because their disablement was of a very negligible quantity,
and therefore the probability is that they
would automatically merge into their former
Occupation. The second class are men disabled to the extent that it did not preclude
them from taking light jobs, and the third
class, the most important of all,
were those who
So heavily
handicapped that they should learn
special handicrafts suited to their disablement. The Imperial Government, inspired by
our action here. has established a very large
instructional establishment. and men of
the third class have been largely, and
are being, trained for special handicrafts.
At present there are nearly 400 in that
institution. and there are a great many
others spread over the Province; but I am
sorry to say that a large number are still
waiting their turn in this establishment and
elsewhere before they can be enrolled for
their training. The difficulty described by
my hon. and learned Friend, the Member for
the University, does arise. When they
emerge from the Training Establishment,
and are presumably fitted to engage in the
crafts in which they have been trained, and
become what is known as "improvers." there
is a great deal of difficulty in absorbing
them into industry. The duty of the
Government, through the Appointments and
Training Branch of the Ministry of Labour,
does not end when the man is trained.
When he emerges from the Training Institution, where he is turned into a jeweller, a
tailor, or a roadmaker, it is the business of
the Appointments and Training Branch of
the Ministry of Labour to see that that man
is entered for some job with some employer.
The employer has a difficulty, because there
are trade union limitations. Therefore,
when complaints are made here about the
number of disabled ex-service men that are
still unemployed, it must be recognised that
the entire fault does not lie either with the
Government or with the employer, but that
some part of the liability must necessarily
fall upon their companions in labour. That
difficulty must be overcome if the men are to
be quickly absorbed, after their training,
into their future employment. Now, the
Government not only maintain them during
their period of training, but during their
period of improvership; that is, during the
period following their training, when they
are employed in a workshop and do not receive full wages, the Government supplements the wages that they receive so as to
bring their wages up to the proper normal
standard. That is what the Government is
doing in respect of ex-service men.

I may say at once that the principle underlying the notice of motion has the full
approval of the Ministry of Home Affairs.
It is a standing rule in this Ministry that
all advertisements inviting tenders must
state that preference will be given to firms
on the King's National Roll of Honour.
(Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) So far as the
contracts of the Ministry itself are concerned
we have that set out on the forefront of the
advertisements asking for tenders. The extent to which preference should be given,
however, is a matter that is not easy to lay
down by way of general rule, and the circumstances of
every case have got to be
considered. Of course, the matter of great
importance is that we are dealing here with
public funds, and we are trustees to that
extent. We have got to deal with these funds
in a very careful way, but the position with
regard to preference being given to those on
the Roll is complicated by a matter that has
already been touched upon by the Minister of
Finance, that is that the Ministry make it
a practice of giving the preference to the
extent of five per cent. to Ulster firms in
contracts in which the purchase of materials
is concerned, and where the material is
manufactured in Ulster. That gives extra
employment here, and that is a matter that
cannot be lost sight of.
I should like to call the attention of hon.
Members to this. because it shows the danger
of going too far in some of these matters.
It has, in fact, happened in one case that
none of the firms tendering at reasonable
prices from Ulster were on the King's
National Roll of Honour, and that a firm
tendering from across the water was on the
Roll. If the principle laid down in the
resolution, as it was originally framed, had
been strictly adhered to, the Ulster firm
would have lost the contract and the contract would have had to go to the English
firm.
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: Hear, hear.

Mr. MEGAW: Take the case where the

the conditions on which preference is given
to firms on the National Roll of Honour are

must be approximately equal to the others.
I think it will be agreed by the House that
we should not accept an inferior article to

that the periods of delivery are similar and
that the abilities of the firms to carry out

Honour that they are and should be able
to compete, at least, on fair equal terms

The hon. Member for Londonderry (Sir
Robert Anderson) raised a very important
point in regard to local authorities. The
contracts entered into by local authorities
are very largely governed by statutory
enactments, and these cannot be interfered
with unless there is something in the way of
fresh legislation. Local authorities are
bound by statute under ordinary circumstances to accept the lowest tender, that is
if the conditions set out in the form inviting
tenders are observed. Members of local
bodies will be held personally liable if they
accept a higher tender, unless there is some
very important circumstance attached to it.
where a lower one has been submitted. Of
course, there are great difficulties about laying down general rules. I have stated that
the principle that our own Ministry has
followed is the setting out in the advertisement that preference will be given to firms
on the King's National Roll of Honour. So
far as the local authorities are concerned,
except there is special legislation we could
not interfere. We could not allow breaches
of the law. Some mention was made of the
question of surcharges. It would be a very
dangerous thing to say that surcharges
generally would be remitted, and the
Ministry of Home Affairs certainly could
not do that unless it had the express sanction
of this House to do so.
Mr. GORDON: I would not have intervened in this discussion had it not been that the
hon. Member for the University (Dr. Morrison)
seemed to challenge me across the floor of
the House. I was listening with much interest as I always do-to the hon. Member
and I fear that I involuntarily expressed myself. He challenged that expression and

thought that I was in agreement with a certain statement he had made. When I said
No " he again challenged me and asked was
I on the opposite side, and I again said "No,"
because I was in this position that by either
saying "No" or "Yes" I was in a difficulty,
and consequently I felt it would be better-
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: To say nothing.

Mr. GORDON: Probably. I thought it
would be better if I rose in the House and
replied to what was an allegation, or, perhaps,
I should say a slander, upon the trade unions
of the country. He made a statement to the
effect that the trade unions refused to absorb
these men in their trade organisations and
that as a result men were to-day unemployed.
I do not know whether it is a slander or
not, but it is an exaggerated expression that
I wish to repudiate. I would like to repeat a
few words that were given utterance to by
the Minister of Finance. He said there was
considerable difficulty in absorbing these
men. That is not the fault of the trade
unions. Every hon. Member of this House
has an opportunity of examining the balance
sheets of every trade organization, and he
has only to do so to find there is wide-spread
unemployment amongst the skilled workers
represented by these particular trainees.
Dr. MORRISON: Bricklayers.
Mr. GORDON: I have never heard of any
disabled men who were trained as bricklayers. There are plumbers, shoemakers,
barbers-
Sir ROBERT ANDERSON: And Members
of Parliament. (Laughter).
Mr. GORDON: They have not trained any
yet. (Laughter.) Some of the men have
been absorbed into the particular trades I
have mentioned, and the trade unions have
offered no objection. But, when you take
into consideration some of the highlyskilled trades, where a man has to serve an
apprenticeship of from five to seven years,
it is not likely that a man going into a
Training Factory and being kept at one
specific job, will be able to learn all connected with the particular handicraft or
trade that he is being trained for. Consequently, it is not the fault of the trade
unions. The employer will not employ him.
Why? Because the market is overstocked
with labour. For every job that is available
there are dozens of skilled tradesmen. I do
not say that these men are not skilled, but
they are not skilled to the same extent as the
men who have served an apprenticeship and
probably have been employed in a particular
trade for quite a number of years.

I would like to say this from my own
personal experience: I have found the Trade
Unions most sympathetic. I have gone
round the various Local Employment Committees throughout the Six Counties, and I
found that in almost every Committee of the
King's National Roll of Honour there were
representaties of the trade unions, and that
they were most sympathetic to the claims of
the disabled ex-service men. Some hon.
Members in this House referred to how
little has been done. I would like to inform
the House of what has been done in many
of the provincial towns that I have visited
since I became Parliamentary Secretary.
Some of the employers in provincial towns
have undertaken to train disabled ex-service
men as sheeting weavers. In other cases the
Local Employment Committees have found
there was a great opportunity of starting
window-cleaning. They bought the entire
outfit and started the ex-service men in the
work of window-cleaning. Quite recently I
visited the home town of my hon. Friend and
colleague in the representation of the
County of Antrim (Mr. Crawford), and I
found that an effort was being made by the
Local Employment Committee to start
several ex-service men as window-cleaners.
I have nothing more to say, except that there
are 712 disabled ex-service men in the city of
Belfast, and between 1,100 and 1,200 in the
Six Counties, and I think that a great effort
should be made by the employers of labour
on behalf of those men. I think I am safe
in saying that in what little has been done,
not only in Belfast, but throughout the Six
Counties, great credit is due to the trade
union representatives on the Local Employment Committee. They have given great
assistance to the Ministry of Labour. I have
much pleasure in supporting the Resolution
before the House.

PENSION SCHEME FOR SECONDARY
TEACHERS.
1. Mr McGUFFIN asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of Education
if, in view of the fact that unless the Pension Scheme for Secondary Teachers is ratified before Parliament adjourns, teachers
who have served for forty-five years and
upwards, and who are anxious to retire,
will be unable to do so with any certainty
as to what their pensions are likely to be,
he can arrange to have the Pension Scheme
for Secondary Teachers submitted to the
House before its rising, so that it may come
into force, and that the teachers whose long
service entitles them to retire may be enabled to do so at the end of the summer
term.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): As the Ministry of Finance is,
under the provisions of the Education Act,
responsible for framing Pension Schemes
for teachers, I have arranged with my hon.
Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary to the
Ministry of Education, to reply to this question.
The Departmental Committee entrusted
with the investigation of the subject of a
Pension Scheme for Secondary Teachers
have submitted their report, but the consideration of the details has not yet been
undertaken by the Minister of Education
and myself. My hon. Friend will therefore
understand that at this stage of the Session
it is not possible to comply with his request
to present Rules forthwith.
I can, however, say that I will endeavour
during the course of the summer to place
teachers in possession of the general scope
of the proposed scheme, and if I can do so
it should be possible for those who, through
age, desire to retire to come to a decision
with the full facts before them.

Mr. McGUFFIN: Might I ask the right
hon. Gentleman if the report will be circulated amongst the Members of this House
in order that they may have an opportunity of considering it, seeing that the House
is about to adjourn, and that we shall have
no opportunity of discussing it?
Mr. POLLOCK: I assume my hon. Friend
means that the report, whatever form it
may take, will be circulated among the
Members of this House in the interval.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Yes.
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not think there is any
objection to that, but I do not like to ente.
into any undertaking, until I consult the
Minister of Education who, obviously, must
have something to say on a matter of that
kind.
Mr. MCGUFFIN: Will the decision
arrived at by the Ministry of Education
and the Ministry of Finance have to be submitted to this House before it can be put
into force?
Mr. POLLOCK: It is doubtful whether
legislation will be required. I hope not. I
hope it will be sufficient by Order to make
the necessary provisions for proceeding with
it, but as to that, it must be understood I
am not dogmatic.
Mr. JOHNSTONE: I should like to ask
the right hon. Gentleman if he could give
an assurance in this House that the provisions of the Pensions Bill will be retrospective. I think that would save a great
deal of anxiety in the minds of the teachers.
Mr. POLLOCK: I do not think it is
desirable for me to enter into any detail in
regard to this report, which, in itself,
ranges over a great variety of matters. It
would be wiser until I can meet the Minister of Education and settle these details
that I should make no definite statement
on the subject. I am sure my hon. Friend
will realize the importance of that decision.

THE GOVERNMENT HOUSING GRANT.
2. Mr. JOHNSTONE asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the conditions which must be fulfilled by prospective private builders of small houses, in
order to obtain the Government grant of
£60, sanctioned by this House; whether the
payment of this grant is conditional upon
the payment of any grant by a local authority; whether the financial position of the
prospective builder is regarded as a possible
bar to the payment of the grant, and how
many grants have already been sanctioned
either actually or provisionally.
The
PARLIAMENTARY
SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw): The conditions which must
be fulfilled are those prescribed by the
Housing Act (Northern Ireland), 1923,
which are generally as follow:-That the
houses must be of the kitchen or small
parlour type, with a minimum of 600 and
a maximum of 950 superficial feet. That
the houses must have been commenced on
or after the 24th day of October, 1922, and
completed before the 1st day of April, 1925.
In addition, the houses must satisfy the
Ministry as to structural stability and
proper sanitation, and be certified to have
been completed in a proper and workmanlike manner.
The payment of this grant is not conditional upon the payment of any grant by
a local authority. It is only subject to
the conditions in the Act as specified above.
The financial position of the prospective
builder is no bar to the payment of the
grant; the grant being payable on the completion of the houses.
Certificates have been transmitted to the
Ministry in respect of 793 houses which
have been already completed or which will
qualify for grants on certificates being received as to completion in a proper manner.
Of these 63 are already actually completed.
Mr. DONALD: Could my hon. and learned
Friend tell us the position now in view of
the crisis that has arisen with the local
authorities in regard to house building
under the Act?
Mr. MEGAW: I am not aware that any
crisis has arisen so far as the application
of the Act generally is concerned. I know
there is one body which has declined to put
it into operation.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Might I ask the hon.
and learned Gentleman if the Government
will continue to pay this subsidy irrespective of whether the Corporation does or
not?
Mr. MEGAW: Yes.
FLAG DAY COLLECTIONS.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether full inquiry is made
into every organization to which permission
is granted to collect money on the streets
by means of 'flag days," and what
measures can he adopt to prevent the total
or a large percentage of funds so collected
from being absorbed in "administration."

Mr. MEGAW: I would refer the hon. and
gallant Member to the provision of Article
16 of the Regulations made pursuant to 6
and 7 Geo. V, c. 31, sec. 5, relative to collections in streets or public places. The
main provision of that article is to the
effect that the persons responsible for such
collections are required to submit to the
Commissioner, R.U.C., in the case of a
County Borough, and elsewhere to the
County Inspector a detailed account in a
prescribed form of all receipts and expenditure, certified by two officials of the society
and duly audited by its auditor or other
responsible person not connected with the
fund, and must be prepared to satisfy the
Commissioner as to the due and proper
application of the proceeds. The provisions
of this article are being complied with.
Colonel WOODS: What would be the
action of the Ministry of Home Affairs if
an organization was known to pay £5 each
to the committee men employed in helping
to collect on flag days?
Mr. DONALD: I think in all fairness my
hon. and learned Friend should refute those
allegations.
Mr. SPEAKER: I was just going to say
that one cannot allow hypothetical questions
as to what would be the action of the
Minister in certain events. Questions must
deal with specific facts.
Colonel WOODS: This has taken place.
Mr. SPEAKER: I beg your pardon.
Mr. MEGAW: I am not aware of it.

Home Affairs whether he will state the

CONSTITUTION OF POOR LAW
COMMISSION.
5. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he has received copies
of resolutions from the Moira Rural District Council, the Lurgan Board of Guardians, and other public bodies, protesting
against the constitution of the Poor-Law
Commission, appointed to inquire into
Local Government administration, and if
he will consider the inclusion on the Commission of representatives from District
Councils and Boards of Guardians outside
Belfast.
Mr. MEGAW: Resolutions have been received from some authorities on the lines
indicated in the hon. and gallant Member's
question.
The resolutions, however, appear to have
been passed under a misapprehension, as the
Commission includes in its numbers two
representatives of District Councils and
Boards of Guardians outside Belfast.
A Warrant for the constitution of the
Commission has been signed, and it has
already held its first meeting.
In view of the above and the fact that
it is fully representative of all interests.
and already has 39 members, it is not proposed to add any additional members.
DISTRICT
INSPECTOR'S
ALLOWANCES
RENT
6. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the
reason for the difference of twenty pounds
in the rent allowance paid to District-
Inspectors of the Royal Ulster Constabulary
and the rent allowance paid to District-
Inspectors of the Special Constabulary.
Mr. MEGAW: The rent allowances granted
to members of the police forces vary according to the status of the different ranks, and
in some instances with the local conditions.
The difference between the rent allowance
of ranks named in the Question is correctly
stated. It may be pointed out that there is
no rank of District-Inspector in the Special
Constabulary.
BOUNTY TO SPECIAL
CONSTABLES.
7. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the "bounty" in lieu
of pension granted to Special. Constables on
demobilisation is not the "bonus" paid
monthly to the Special Constabulary; and
if any extra grant or compensation was paid
to the Special Constables who were demobilised with four days' notice in September.
1922.
Mr. MEGAW: A bounty for approved
service is payable to members of the "A"
Class Special Constabulary in lieu of pension
rights. This bounty was paid up to 1922.
quarterly, but is now paid monthly; this
course being more convenient for the men
than the former quarterly system. On discharge from the force the men receive the
amount of bounty due at date of discharge.
The Special Constables who were demobilised
in September, 1922, were discharged on the
expiry of their contracts. They received the
bounty then due to them, but no claim for
any extra grant or compensation arises.
ARREST OF JAMES CASSIDY.
8. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the full
facts regarding the arrest, on Saturday. 24th
inst.. of the ex-Serviceman. James Cassidy.
3 Ardilea Street. Oldpark Road, Belfast.
Mr. MEGAW: Cassidy was interned in
October. 1922. In July, 1923, he was before
the Advisory Committee and undertook to
them that he would leave Northern Ireland
if released. He was released and an order
was made by the Minister of Home Affairs
excluding him from entering certain parts of
Northern Ireland including Belfast. He was
arrested in Belfast in the 24th instant. and
proceedings have been instituted against him
under the Civil Authorities Act.

11. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of

Ulster Pavilion at the Wembley Exhibition
adequately represents the importance of our

The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE (Mr.
McKeown): I am replying for my right hon.
Friend. I am glad to be able to assure the
hon. and gallant Member that the Ulster
Pavilion at Wembley is as representative of
the industries of the Six Counties as it has
been possible for the Department to make it.
The hon. and gallant Member is probably
unaware of the fact that in November, 1922,
every trade association and every Chamber
of Commerce in Northern Ireland was invited
to nominate a representative to serve on a
Central Committee to determine the nature
of Northern Ireland's participation in the
British Empire Exhibition. Out of this
Committee an Executive Committee of
traders and manufacturers was formed, and
in consultation with this Committee invitations to participate in the exhibit were
subsequently transmitted to upwards of 30
associations, bodies and individual firms representing the whole field of Ulster industry
in all its branches, great and small. In
addition to this, in order that no avenue of
participation might be left unexplored,
advertisements were on three occasions inserted in all the leading newspapers throughout the Six Counties.
The Exhibit made in the Ulster Pavilion
comprises, amongst other things, Linen, Shipbuilding, Rope, Tobacco, Whisky, Aerated
Waters, Shirts and Collars, Bacon and
Manufactured Foodstuffs, Soap, Woollen
Goods, Pottery, and Engineering Models, so

THREATENED STRIKE IN LURGAN.
13. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Labour whether he has taken, or proposes
to take, steps to avert the threatened strike
of operatives in the linen industry at
Lurgan?
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY
TO THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR (Mr
Gordon): I have been asked by the Minister
of Labour to reply. Information of a
threatened stoppage in connection with the
demand for increased piece-rates in certain
cases in the Punch Hemstitching Branch of
the Linen Trade in Lurgan was received by
the Ministry on the 9th May. On inquiries
being made, it was found that the matters
in dispute were still under consideration by
the parties. Subsequently, following on a
letter from the Manufacturers' Association,
which has appeared in the Press, the Union
decided to issue a strike notice on the
expiration of 14 days. They held a meeting
of the workers on Monday evening last, and
after further consideration, confirmed the
formal notice given for a strike on the 28th
inst. The Ministry again on Tuesday communicated with the parties with a view to
seeing whether a stoppage of work could be
avoided. I regret that this has not been
found possible, but I can assure the House
that we are keeping in close touch with the
parties, and shall not fail to take such steps
as are practicable with a view to securing
resumption of work at the earliest possible
moment.

SALARIES OF TECHNICAL TEACHERS.
Mr. GRANT (by private notice) asked the
Parliamentary Secretary to the Ministry of
Education, whether the answer given to the
hon. Member for North Belfast on Thursday
of last week, to the effect that the scales of
salaries for Technical Teachers would, in all
probability be published within six weeks,
when taken in conjunction with the answer
given to the hon. Member for Queen's University, to the effect that this House will
have an opportunity of considering these
scales before they become operative, and when
taken in conjunction with the further fact
that this House is to rise in the course of
a week, means that the scales will not become operative until the Autumn Session;
and if so, whether the Ministry of Education
has taken into consideration the injurious
effect upon Technical Education, of this
further postponement of the Teachers' claim
to fair and just treatment.
The PARLIAMENTARY SECRETARY TO
THE MINISTRY OF EDUCATION (Mr.
McKeown): It is the fact that, having regard to the terms of Section 99 of the Education Act, the new salary scales for
Technical School Teachers cannot become
operative until after the lapse of ten days
on which either House of Parliament shall
sit, counted from the date on which the regulations relating thereto have been laid
before both Houses of Parliament.
In the circumstances, and in view of the
suspension of the current Session of Parliament this week, this necessarily implies
that it will not be possible to make actual
payment to the teachers of any arrears of
salary accruing to them under the new regulations until some time after the commencement of the Autumn sitting.
But I might add that it is the intention
of the Government to publish the proposed
scales shortly for the information of teachers
and all concerned on the understanding that
they are subject to review by Parliament
before becoming operative.
