Mr. GRANT: I do not rise to criticise
this Resolution. I just want to say that I
happen to be the father of one of those
brilliant scholars to whom the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Barbour) has referred, and I want
to say on his behalf, and on behalf of the
others who were successful, that they
appreciate very much the efforts put forward
by the Ministry of Education to send them
to Wembley. The only appeal I hear when
I go home is:-When is the Minister of Education going to have another excursion to
Wembley? I can truly say that the whole
undertaking was very much appreciated by
the parents who were able to send their boys
or girls to Wembley, and on their behalf I
beg to thank the Minister.
Mr. McGUFFIN: I am not in the happy
position of the hon. Gentleman who has just
resumed his seat. I can neither claim
brilliance myself nor transmit it to others
if I had it. I think it was a very courteous
act on the part of the hon. Gentleman (Mr.
Grant) to make this acknowledgment to the
Committee, and I congratulate him on
having a son who was successful. This Vote,
of course, is a small matter. £2,800 has
been laid out. £1,000 was paid by the
Government, and the remainder was raised
by voluntary contributions, notably that
made by the Minister of Education himself,
the munificent gift of £500. For that he is
entitled to the thanks of the community. As
I understood it, when this proposal was made
the object was to be educative, but when
I was in Wembley-I had the temerity to
cross there; I do not know whether it argues
lack of wisdom or not-I saw some children.
They were brought there in a rush, and
they did not appear to me to halt at any
particular place. Their chief objective
seemed to be the outdoor attractions, such
as-I am not familiar with them-the switchback and things of that sort. I had not
the opportunity of seeing the Ulster children,
but I am assured by the statement of the
hon. Gentleman (Mr. Barbour) that they
were under good guidance, and that, where
it was possible, instruction was given with
regard to those things that they had before
their view. I would suggest that, if it is
possible, we should to some extent test the
effect of the undertaking. That could easily
be done if the Ministry of Education would
arrange to distribute a few prizes to those
who would write the best essays on their
impressions of Wembley. It would be a
test. It is being done every day in the
schools, I understand, with regard to less
important matters, and some excellent essays
have been written. I myself would be disposed to give a prize, although I have not
very much money, to give the boys an opportunity of putting their impressions on paper
in the form of a short essay. Then the
House could judge of what the effect had
been. The teachers, who are the examiners,
would be the best judges of what had been
done. It is not a mere matter of composition
I want to test, but rather if the children
got an intelligent impression of the places
they were brought to visit, and if they
were under instruction which gave them at
least an idea of the importance of the great
Empire of which they are subjects, of its
widespread power, its commerce, and So
forth. I would suggest, if I am permitted,
that the Education Department should be
the means or instrument of instituting a
competition of this description. Of the 900
children who attended, at least a proportion
would be able to show that excellence of
intelligence and acquisition which has been
the result of their visit to Wembley. I leave
the suggestion at that, but I think that
without this we would not be assured of
the success we were entitled to expect from
the visit of these children to London.

SALE OF FIREWORKS TO CHILDREN.'
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That this House do now adjourn."-
(Mr. Burn.)
Mr. GRANT: There is one matter to
which I would like to draw the attention of
the right hon. the Minister of Home Affairs.
Within the past few weeks there have been
in the local police courts a considerable
number of prosecutions of children for
throwing fireworks, and squibs and crackers
in picture palaces and on the public streets.
I recognise that owing to the trouble we
had in the city a few years ago these things
are an absolute nuisance and cause great disturbance in the minds of people, but on the
other hand it seems to me rather unfair
that the parents of children of tender years
should be fined in sums of 20s and 40s and
costs when the people who sell them are
allowed to do so without interference. I
recognise that the police are doing their
duty in bringing up these cases, and I recognise also that the magistrates are doing
all they can to put a stop to it by inflicting
these heavy penalties, but it certainly is a
hardship to a man who has been unemployed
for a considerable time to have to pay such
a heavy penalty if the children are summoned for using these particular crackers.
I was on the Bench this morning and I was
asked by some of the magistrates to bring
this matter forward as Hallowe'en is coming
on and there will be a considerable amount
of these fireworks used. I would like to know
from the right hon. Gentleman if it is not
possible for the Home Office to bring into
effect immediately some Order prohibiting
the sale of these crackers and fireworks. I
think it is very necessary that something
should be done.
Mr. LAVERY: I would like to support
the hon. Gentleman (Mr. Grant), who has
just sat down, in this connection. I was on
the Bench this forenoon also in my town,
and there were four cases brought forward
of a similar kind, the children being from
seven to ten years of age. We could not
see or feel that we would be justified as
magistrates in fining the parents of these
children. We simply let them off with costs
of court, believing that those who sell should
be punished. I hope that the Minister of
Home Affairs will see if it is possible that
this sale of fireworks should be stopped
immediately.
Sir DAWSON BATES: May I suggest to
my hon. Friends that there really must be
a limit in the State controlling the movements of children? I do not see that the
State should relieve the parent of the responsibility of looking after his child. The
suggestion is that the sale of fireworks should
be prohibited. Under the Explosives Act all
these shops have to be registered with the
local authority, and it is an offence for a
shopkeeper to sell any explosives, fireworks,
or things of that sort to any child under
the age of thirteen, and I think it is not
fair to impose further restrictions in peaceful times on shopkeepers. I would like to
emphasise again that there is far too much
tendency to grandmotherly legislation. The
whole tendency among a certain class of
parents appears to be to throw the entire
responsibility upon the Government.
I hope these prosecutions that have recently taken place will have the effect of
putting an end to a most objectionable
practice. Children must realise that they
cannot behave in the way some of them did
in the past. I heard a case not very long
ago of a child throwing a lighted squib on
a lady's dress, where it exploded. If anyone
looks at the Press he will see constant complaints. I think the Government are doing
the right thing in strictly enforcing the
law. I am only sorry that the Member for
Down (Mr. Lavery) has taken the attitude
he has. I would commend my hon. Friend
who sits opposite me (Mr. Grant) for sitting
on the Bench and having the courage to
enforce the law.
Mr. GRANT: I must say I am exceedingly
disappointed at the reply of the right hon.
Gentleman-

Sir DAWSON BATES: The governing
body in connection with the medical profession in Great Britain and Northern Ireland
is the General Medical Council established
by the Medical Act of 1858. In that body
is vested the duty of registration of members
of the medical profession and of general
control and supervision of the profession.
Arrangements have recently been entered
into between the General Medical Council
and the Irish Free State Government under
which the Council will continue for a year to
register holders of medical degrees conferred
in the Free State on the same terms and conditions as obtained prior to the establishment
of the new regime in Southern Ireland.
As regards the question of nurses:-
Negotiations are still pending between the
Nursing Council of Northern Ireland and
the Irish Free State Nursing Council with
a view to the establishment of reciprocal
arrangements between the two Councils
under which nurses registered by one Council
would be recognised as eligible for registration by the other Council and vice versa.
The arrangements have not yet been formally completed.
Colonel WOODS: May I ask the right hon.
Gentleman, if, in the meantime, nothing can
be done for nurses who have taken out
certificates in the Free State and wish to
register in Northern Ireland?
Sir DAWSON BATES: I am afraid not.

aware of the serious inconvenience and loss

Sir DAWSON BATES: Every effort has
been made to obtain alternative accommodation for the Constabulary at present
in occupation of the Co-operative Hall,
Frederick Street, but I regret no suitable
alternative building is available. I need
scarcely point out that the locality was a
very troublesome one during the period of
recent outrages in the city. The presence
of a platoon in Frederick Street Hall has
done much to bring about the present
peaceable state of affairs. It is, however,
regarded as imperative to maintain a platoon
in the area so as to preserve this satisfactory
condition of affairs.
Efforts are still being made to obtain
other premises at reasonable cost for adaptation, etc., but many difficulties have been
experienced.
As soon as Frederick Street Hall can be
vacated, either by securing alternative
accommodation, or by withdrawal of the
platoon, if conditions permit of it, steps
will be taken accordingly.

OFFENCES AGAINST LICENSING LAWS.
5. Mr. CRAWFORD asked the Minister
of Home Affairs, if he can state the number
of offences against the Licensing Laws and
the number of cases of drunkenness in Belfast and each of the Six Counties of Northern
Ireland during the first six months of 1923
or 1924 respectively; also the number of
offences and cases of drunkenness on Sundays
in the same districts and for the same
periods?
Sir DAWSON BATES: It would be difficult, within the compass of an oral answer,
to give in detail the particulars asked for
by the hon. Member, but the totals are as
follows:-
Offences against the Licensing Laws by
Publicans and Spirit Grocers during the
first six months of 1923 and the corresponding period of 1924 were 436 and 121
respectively.
Cases of Drunkenness during the same
two periods were 3,650 and 3,177 respectively.
Offences on Sunday by Publicans and
Spirit Grocers during these periods were
164 and 73 respectively.
Cases of Drunkenness on Sunday during
the same periods were 234 and 59 respectively.
I am circulating with the official report a
Return giving the full details asked for by
the hon. Member.

a
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr. Pollock): As the Ministry of Finance is, under
the provisions of the Education Act, responsible for framing Pension Schemes for all
classes of teachers, I have arranged with my
hon. Friend, the Parliamentary Secretary of

organisations representing the teachers concerned.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
This matter has been rather sprung upon
me, but I will endeavour to the best of my
ability to meet the arguments of my hon.
Friend. First of all, it would be an ungracious thing to divide the House on a Vote
to pay the fees of Counsel, who was engaged
by the Government to put up their case
before the Judicial Committee of the Privy
Council, in view of the fact that the findings
of the Judicial Committee were all in favour
of Ulster, that is to say, they confirmed the
opinion upon which I stood from the very
beginning with regard to the Commission
and supported all through, as I was, by a
unanimous Cabinet, and this House.
Douglas Hogg's duties there were to defend
Ulster's case, and our own Attorney-General
was associated with him, also junior counsel
and solicitors who were acting in London
under instructions from our Attorney-
General. Having won his case Sir Douglas
Hogg's remarks may possibly be read in two
ways. I myself understood what he meant
by the remarks to which the hon. Member
(Mr. Donald) refers, to be that legislation
in the British House of Commons could be
introduced, defining the duties of the Commission under Article XII of the Treaty;
and both in the House of Commons and in
the House of Lords on the other side, an
attempt was made so to define the duties of
the Commission, that it would have been
possible for us to consider favourably the
appointment of a Commissioner. But the
energies of our friends in both Houses unfortunately, were not rewarded with success.
Consequently we are faced with the position
in which we now find ourselves. I certainly
think that whatever learned cousel, in
a case of this sort, may say or do, so long as
he wins his case it would be very inappropriate for us to cast any aspersions upon him
for language he may use in what he considers the best way of conducting his case.

Economic Conditions in Rural Ulster.
Dr. MORRISON: I beg to move:
That this House views with grave concern
the Economic Conditions existing in rural
Ulster, especially as regards the farmers
and agricultural labourers, which are deplorable, and not to be remedied by Grants
in Aid of Local Rates; and calls upon the
Government to formulate a policy which
will give both farmers and workers a fair
opportunity to develop the resources of the
greatest industry in Ulster, thereby relieving the pressure of congestion and unemployment in urban centres.
The immediate cause of the Motion, which
is on the Order Paper, and which hon.
Members can see for themselves, is the little
discussion we had the other day with regard
to the egg industry. But I would have raised
this question, and indeed I have raised it,
on many occasions since I came into this
House. Some people, I believe, ask what
business it is of mine to interfere with duties
that belong to ordinary Members and farmers
generally. My excuse is that I have for
thirty years lived amongst a population of
farmers and labourers, and have attended to
them medically-5,000 people. I know their
wants and I know their difficulties.
Perhaps I
know them better than
Members of this House,
and it is simply because I respect
do many
and admire their independence and pluck
under most distressing circumstances, and
sympathise with them for the hard and
distressing conditions under which many of
them carry on their work, that I support
them in every claim that is just and fair. I
think I also have the right to speak for them,
considering that I represent the University,
and that in every parish in Northern
Ireland there are four or five graduates from
that University, who are directly or indirectly
affected by the prosperity of the farming
community. Therefore, I think it is my duty
to interfere in everything that has a tendency
to promote the welfare of the community,
and consequently the welfare of those people.
I hope, and I believe that everybody in
this House is as sympathetic on this matter
as I am. I regret to say that on one occasion,
and on one occasion only, I have noticed
that the Labour Members of the House were
inclined to criticise the grant the Agricultural Department gave to the Farmers'
Union. I know these Labour Members well,
and I consider them fair, reasonable, moderate men.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Hear, hear.
Dr. MORRISON: If they knew the conditions under which the agricultural labourer
carries on his work, and the distressing
conditions that have governed agriculture
for the last three years, I think that instead
of cavilling and raising objections they would
give every assistance they could.
I confess at once that the Cabinet has done
everything it could. I have no fault to find
with anything the Cabinet has done or with
what it has not done. Many of the conditions
to which I have referred are legacies handed
over to this Government from the British
Parliament, and reforms cannot be effected
in a day. To the Prime Minister especially
I would pay a tribute for what he has done.
I quite understand that the Minister of
Finance and the different heads of the
Departments here are friendly, but for the
special grant we got to relieve the distress
of secondary teachers, the grant to the Derry
Bridge, and the grant of £128,000, which we
have got for two years, I think that, while
everybody else deserves credit, the Prime
Minister is the to whom it is really due.
man

Conditions in Rural Ulster 1306
14 OCTOBER 1924

I want to stress this policy the Prime
Minister has adopted. I want also to point
out that so far as I can judge we as a Government should go further. As many of the
Members of this House know, the present
year is the worst within living memory for
the agricultural community. People talk
about the labourers in Belfast, but I can
tell you for a fact that the majority of the
farm labourers, and many of the farmers,
were on three days out of six all through
this summer wet to the skin, when they were
at their work. They went into the house,
but there was no turf brought home from
the bog, and how they managed to dry their
clothes and carry on their work under the
conditions that prevailed would be a puzzle
to the town dweller.
I propose to deal with what I call the
injustice done to the agricultural industry
in the incidence of rates and taxes, and when
I speak of the agricultural industry 1 mean
farmers and labourers and the people who
carry on industry in rural Ulster. To my
mind the interests of the farmer and the
labourer are closely allied, and what affects
the prosperity of the farmer affects the prosperity of the labourer, and vice versa. Going
down from the House last Thursday I came
across a gentleman who is perhaps one of the
most experienced local government administrators in the Six Counties. I refer to
Senator Long. He is the chairman of the
Londonderry Asylum Board, chairman of the
Londonderry County Council, and he has
been for thirty years chairman of the Limavady Rural District Council. We were
talking about these conditions, and Senator
Long said:
"The questions you raised have been very
prominently before us in connection with
the Asylum, and I can get you figures to
show how the legislation presses unduly
on the ratepayers. I will call with the
clerk and ask him to send them to you."
I have the figures here, supplied by the
clerk of the Londonderry Asylum, and they
bear out what I say is the injustice done
in the administration of the finances of the
Asylum by British legislation. But what I
want to deal with is something in addition
to that, namely the whole administration of
Local Government affairs in Ulster in
addition to the asylums-the whole administration, not a part such as is covered by
the asylums. The asylums were established
in 1821. At first all the expense of running
the asylums fell on the local rates raised
by the Grand Jury Acts. In 1874
Treasury paid their first contribution, and
that first contribution was half the cost of
maintenance or four shillings a week,
whichever was tho lesser.
the
This continued until the passing of the
Local Government Act of 1898 when a
special grant was made by the Treasury to
uneet past moral liabilities, and the year
1897 was fixed as the standard
year for
their contribution. All further additions
to the expenditure were in future to come
wholly from local sources. This also
applied to the Medical Charities Act and
all Local Government Board administration
except in one little respect, and that was
the payment of salaries for the Medical
Officers of the Unions. The medical profession, the Poor Law officers scattered
over Ireland could not get holidays. The
position was that, owing to existing arrangements, the whole of the cost of the
holidays came off the ratepayers. Representations were made to the Treasury with
the object of their paying half of that.
The Treasury consented, with the result that
all Boards of Guardians in Ireland and in
Ulster gave the doctors a four-weeks holiday;
but that was a special case. How did this
system work out, and how did it affect the
local ratepayers-that is in the main the
farmers? The grant in aid in 1874 paid half
the cost of the eight shillings a week, but
long before 1898 it had ceased to do so. An
asylum that has to provide new accommodation suffers in the Capitation Grant. Inspectors and public opinion demand considerate treatment and every facility for the
care of these lunatics. Londonderry Asylum,
as well as all other bodies in Ulster.
approved of special consideration being given
to these afflicted people, and consequently an
auxiliary asylum has been built at Gransha
costing £51,381. The original Londonderry
Asylum was built to accommodate 120
patients, and was to serve the counties of
Tyrone and Donegal. The cost was £27,500.
Additions were made to accommodate
337 patients at a cost of £29,000.
Tyrone and Donegal got an asylum each of
their own and the patients were transferred
in 1853 and in 1866. Notwithstanding this
relief of the congestion the auxiliary asylum
had to be built at Gransha to accommodate
64 patients. There is a total deficiency in the
grant in aid of maintenance since 1910, that
is taking the year 1897 as the standard year
-from 1910 up to the present time there is
a total loss, which comes on the ratepayers,
of £7,950. This has to be made good from
local taxation, which, as I maintain, comes
in the main from the agricultural industry.
What I would like to know is when is this
to stop? We have been demanding increased
caro and increased comfort for everybody
who is distressed, and rightly demanding it,
and if this thing goes on I can see that the
burden of taxation will grow indefinitely.
The grant in aid for the last four years represented 16 per cent. instead of 50 per cent.
of the capitation grant. The total amount of
rates raised in County Derry-and this illu-
1307 Conditions in Rural Ulster
Conditions in Rural Ulster 1309
HOUSE OF COMMONS
[Dr. Morrison]
strates what happens all over the county in
connection with different Local Government
bodies, such as the rural councils and the
urban councils; and County Derry, as I have
said before, is fairly representative of the
other counties in Ulster-has risen steadily
from 1897. In 1905 the rate amounted to
£40,000. In 1918 it amounted to £56,000. In
1920 it was £77,000, that is an increase of
£37,000 as compared with 1905. Now I take
1920 with its £30.000 of an increase as a fair
sample. We had some troubles afterwards
which probably increased the rate, but they
should not be counted. At any rate in 1923
the amount raised by rates in the county
was £100,000, and in 1924 it was £110,000.
This obviously affects every farmer and
labourer in the county. The average man
who occupies a. district council cottage pays
his rates. It has been decided as a policy
by the farmers in many cases where they
let houses to ask the tenant to be liable for
the rates. Previous to twenty or thirty years
ago the rates were a negligible quantity. No
farmer bothered about paying them. If he
got the rent the thing was all right. Now
the bargain is always made for the working
man to pay the rates. I had a woman in
my house yesterday morning doing some
work. She lives in a district council cottage,
and that woman tells me that her rates when
she first got the cottage were less than 10s
a year. Two years ago, she says, they were
close on 30s. For the last two years
they have been reduced, but these reductions
are due not to the system under which she
lives so much as to the special grant given
by this House.
We would like to see if something could
be done to meet the difficulties. Work,
such as is carried on in an asylum for the
treatment of lunatics, medical treatment for
the poor, the prevention of disease. I maintain, are matters of national moment as well
as local matters, and the Government have
recognised that fact by paying this grant.
That being so, I think we should demand
that we should get the half of all the expenditure that is incurred in regard to these
matters. In olden days, in my young days,
the question of the rent was the serious
thing. To-day it is the question of taxation.
The labourers pay their share of indirect
taxation. They pay taxes on whisky and
tobacco and other dutiable articles, and they
can surely in justice claim relief from direct
taxation when it is a matter of promoting
the national well-being.
In connection with the question of National
Health Insurance, I would like to sayand I do it freely-that, of all the
Ministers with whom I have had to deal,
the most friendly, if I can make a distinction
at all, is the Minister of Labour. He meets
me if it is at all possible, and I think he
has got some ideas from me that have been
helpful to him. I think that with my assistance he will be able to straighten things out.
Everybody knows that this matter of health
insurance causes a heavy tax on the farmer
and on the labourer. I have pressed again
and again to find out how this money has

The total amount paid in cash benefit
to members since the inception of the Act,
up to the 31st December, 1922, exceeded
£172,000.
That is a very large sum, but I would like

quite as big a sum as we would be inclined

no matter how long he may be sick. Here

I want to take the question of education,

be penalised if they do not transfer their

rule how many schools are unnecessary?"

Ulster has been injured and endangered by

up because they were forced to pay trade

I put this matter before the House, and

But it is for you to supply the County
Councils with the necessary legal enactments
and give them force.
I pass over the Trade Boards because they
have been dealt with, but I do implore the
Ministry to consider this question of tillage.
There are millions of acres of good land
going to loss and the crops are being destroyed. There are so many small holdings
and there is such a hunger for land that in
the spring time the people will till their
low-lying land because it is in their blood to
do so.
Then the Autumn comes with its
floods and destroys it all. The Minister
ought to take this question into serious consideration. I am sure that in his heart he
says he will, but he must take the rock out
of the road and he must give the people the
power to develop their own land and protect
them in the development of it. It is quite
an easy matter to place the power in the
hands of the people so that they can do it
for themselves. Of course, there is the
question of finance in the way, but that is-
Mr. POLLOCK: A secondary matter.
Mr. COOTE: That is a detail. I have
known several cases where people were
willing to provide the necessary funds for
this purpose if they were given the powers,
but while there will be credit required it
is worth it all. It will give you millions of
acres of land that is not developed to-day.
Do something on a well-considered scale instead of answering questions here to-day
about £128,000. That is a mere bagatelle.
We want something that will give us
millions instead of thousands. We want the
right to till our own land. You may sneer,
but you cannot sneer at Denmark, and a
man who sneers at his own country when
he has not done anything to help it is not
playing the game fairly. We have a country
that can, if it is well looked after, be brought
to as high a state of perfection as Denmark or
any other country. We have the people
willing to do it, and we appeal to the Ministry to take steps to bring it about at once.
There is no good in waiting for another
year, and then another year. I tell you
Nemesis is on the track of the Minister of
Agriculture if there is not something done
with regard to this flooding very soon.

Sir ROBERT LYNN: I only want to intervene in this debate for a few moments, because sometimes I think a feeling gets
abroad that we in Belfast take no interest
in the rural districts. I do not think there
is an hon. Member of this House, whether
he represents, as I do, an industrial seat or
a rural seat, who is not keenly interested
in our premier industry. After all agriculture is the premier industry in this
country-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and
we are grateful to the two hon. Members
who in very moderate and very wise language have brought this matter before the
House to-day. Agriculture is
through a very terrible time.
years to
come it will want the fostering
care of a sympathetic Government, and, I,
as representing an industrial seat, would
appeal most sincerely and most heartily to
the Members of the Government to help
agriculture at this time, and in helping
agriculture they are going to help the whole
of Ulster, because if the agricultural industry is prosperous it will keep a great
many people on the land who would otherwise leave it. Believe me there is nothing
in which we hon. Members of this House
could take part that would do greater good
to our country than in keeping the people
on the land. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
We hear a great deal of talk about "Back
to the land." It is a very difficult thing to
get people back to the land once they have
left it, and, therefore, our business ought to
be to concentrate on keeping them there.

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

[Sir Robert Lynn]
I agree with the hon. Momber for the
University (Dr. Morrison) and the hon.
Member for Fermanagh and Tyrone (Mr.
Coote) that the burden of taxation does fall
with undue weight upon the agricultural
districts, and I think the Government might
consider the whole question of the incidence
of taxation. We could have no better man
to go into that subject than my right hon.
Friend, the Minister of Finance (Mr.
Pollock). We know his sympathy as well as
his ability and his all-round knowledge of
the conditions that prevail in Ulster. I do
agree with my hon. Friend, the Member for
the University (Dr. Morrison) that the time
has come when the whole cost of local
government services should be gone into and
revised. Parliament for the last twenty
years has been imposing enormous burdens
on local councils, without ever thinking for
a moment of how the money is going to be
raised. It is all very well for members of
Parliament to shout vote for things, and
then leave other people to pay for them. I
am in the position that I have always
preached economy, and I hope I shall continue to do so. I think we have got to go
into the whole of the services of Northern
Ireland, not with the object of seeing how
much more we can spend, but with the
object of seeing how much we can really
save. I think our whole local government
system-roads and quite a number of other
things that I am not going to deal with now
-might be remodelled on lines that would
take a very heavy burden off the shoulders
of the unfortunate ratepayers.
There is just one other point that I should
like to stress, so far as the Minister of
Agriculture is concerned, and that is in
regard to afforestation. I really think there
is no part of the United Kingdom that calls
out more for afforestation than Ulster does.
Those of us who know Ulster well know that
you can grow trees in every part of the
Province, and grow them successfully. Unfortunately, it is one of the things that you
find difficulty in getting the smaller people
to engage in, though, I think that the
Minister of Agriculture might do a great deal
in that regard through schools, and also by
placing grants of young trees at the disposal of farmers for nothing, or, if that is
not possible, at a very small cost indeed. I
think that a very excellent scheme of afforestation might be introduced in this Province.
I do not say that it is going to bring its reward immediately, but as my hon. Friend
for Tyrone and Fermanagh (Mr. Coote) says
we ought to take a long view in these matters, and we ought to think of the benefit
it would be to the whole community.
Then another thing is, can we do anything
to get cheap power? I was greatly interested
in the last Session of Parliament when I
thought there was going to be cheap power
introduced in the district in which my hon.
Friend was interested-I mean on the Bann
-because if we could get cheap power in
the rural districts I believe we would reestablish those small rural industries which
we all regret to see disappearing. We know
they are disappearing because of the
economic laws that are in force. But I see
no reason in the world why, with cheap
power in the rural districts, we could not
re-establish those industries and create new
ones in very many places. As I said before, I am sure that the Members who represent industrial cities are just as anxious,
every one of them, as I am to do what they
can to help the agricultural class.
realise their loyalty, we realise their industry, we realise the difficulties through

There are one or two things I would like

exhibits says they are not to be beaten by
Denmark or any other country. We are

can depend upon us.
I was over in London and saw, as I said

We have an
egg trade now. We get

As regards Education, the Ulster Dairy

It has had a very remarkable progress.

Expiring Laws Continuance Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed:
"That the Bill be now read a Second time."
The
ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
This Bill continues temporarily certain
enactments whether of the Parliament of the
United Kingdom or of this Parliament which
may be regarded as still being experimental
or liable to revision. A certain date is fixed
for their continuance, namely, 31st December.
1925. The Bill has been framed so as to fit
in with the corresponding Imperial Bill of
the present year. That Bill applies to
Northern Ireland. The Expiring Laws Continuance Bill of Great Britain or of the
United Kingdom applies to Northern Ireland
in so far as it deals with any enactments relating to a subject with respect to which the
Parliament of Northern Ireland has not the
power to make laws, and the present Bill
supplements this provision by dealing with
enactments in respect of which
we have
power to make laws. The two measures,
therefore, taken together deal with all tem
porary laws applicable to Northern Ireland
according as they come within the one
category or the other.
Expiring Laws Bill- 15 OCTOBER 1924
Second Reading.

I think possibly hon. Members might like
me to make some few remarks about some
of the measures that are contained in the
Schedule to the Bill. It will be quite a subject for their curiosity as to why some of the
measures are being continued and as to why
they are not being dealt with in other ways.
If you would turn to the Schedule to the
Bill, the first one I would draw attention
to is the Labourers (Ireland) Act, 1833. The
original Labourers Act, 1883, was of a temporary character covering a period of ten
years only, but as will be seen from part
one of the Schedule to this Bill that Act has
been modified and continued up to date and
it is necessary for us to carry on its provisions year to year under the Expiring Laws
Continuance Act, as long as the Housing conditions in Rural Districts remain what they
are and until the Government and Parliament are satisfied that no further facilities
for providing Labourers' Cottages in Rural
Districts are required.
The next one I want to make some
observations upon is the Statutory Undertakings (Temporary Increases of Charges)
Act, 1908. Hon. Members will find it at the
bottom of page 4. This Act was passed dur
ing the War in consequence of inflation of
prices to enable Local Authorities who had
under their jurisdiction Statutory Undertakings, e.g., Gas Undertakings, Tramway
Undertakings, etc., to increase their Statutory Scale of Charges in order to
increased costs of working due to rise in
prices. The continuance of the Act is
essential for the present as prices are still
considerably in excess of those in operation
prior to the War and several of the undertakings of this description are finding it difficult to balance income with expenditure.
meet
The next Act I wish to refer to is the
Housing (Ireland) Act, 1919, Section 21. Hon.
Members will find it at the top of page 5.
This Section which is being continued for
another year was originally framed with the
view to relaxing some of the restrictions in
regard to building, in order to meet the
urgent demand for houses. It enables Local
Authorities to assent to departures from their
building By-Laws in regard to the planning
and construction of houses in their respective districts, but it does not compel the
local authorities to agree to such departures.
It merely gives them leave to agree if so
minded.
•
The next Act is the increase of Rent and
Mortgage Interest Restrictions Act, 1920.
Hon. Members will have it in recollection
that the Prime Minister informed this House
on the 9th inst.-last Thursday-that it was
the intention of the Government to introduce
a Bill this Session dealing with the question
of restriction of rent, and the modification
this
of the Act of 1920. However, this is a very
short and full Session, and in view of the
critical period during which the Government
of this Province are passing it was felt that
it would be impossible to do full justice to
a Measure of this kind, which will require
such careful consideration and which will
involve so many perplexities and so much
conflict of interests. In all the circumstances
it has been decided, and I am sure
House will agree, that it is a wise decision
to postpone the introduction of the Bill and
to carry on the Act of 1920 for the present
until a more suitable opportunity arises for
dealing with this very thorny and intricate
subject. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.) The
fact that we take power to extend the Act
to December, 1925, by no means implies that
the other Bill I have referred to will not
be introduced before that date. I think I
have the authority of the Prime Minister
for saying that it was the intention to introduce it an an early date.
The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig)
indicated assent.
Mr. McGUFFIN: But it will not come into
operation.
Mr. BEST: Once it comes into operation
then by its terms this particular one can be
put an end to. The next Act is the Summer
Time Act, 1922, which is mentioned on page
5. A Bill is being introduced which will
lay down that the period of summer time
in Northern Ireland is to be the same in
future as the period in force in Great
Britain. I think the House will probably
agree to pass this Bill, as everyone must
recognise the intolerable confusion which
would be caused if our period of Summer
Time differed from that on the other side
of the Channel. It is, however, possible
in existing circumstances that the passage
of this Bill into law may be delayed, and
I think it is therefore safer to include the
Act of 1922 in the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill SO that if our present Bill
is held up for
any reason we shall
still have provision made for Summer Time
next year. If the Bill referred to becomes
law this Session we can then delete the
reference to the 1922 Act in the Expiring
Laws Continuance Bill.
The next Act to which I want to draw
attention is on page 6-the Local Government (Emergency Fowers) Act, 1921, (Northern Ireland). Hon. Members will recollect
that this Act was passed in 1921 to enable
the Ministry to cope with the very serious
state of affairs that had arisen in Northern
Ireland on the transfer of powers owing
to the refusal for political reasons of certain
local authorities to recognise the jurisdiction
of the Government of 'Northern Ireland.
This Act empowers the Minister of Home

The next Act to which I wish to refer
is the Civil Authorities (Special Powers)
Act (Northern Ireland), 1922. I hope hon.
Members will agree with the Government
that the time has not yet come when we
can do without the powers conferred by
this Act, which, as we all know, has largely
contributed to the immense improvement is
in the condition of Northern Ireland from
the point of view of law and order during
the last two years. We think it right to
continue this Act, hoping that it will not
be necessary to put it into operation, but
holding it in reserve in case it should be
necessary.
The next measure to which I would direct
the attention of hon. Members is the Inspectors of Weights and Measures Act
(Northern Ireland), 1923. I think it would be
desirable to recall to the memory of hon.
Members the circumstances under which it
became necessary to introduce the Weights
and Measures Act of 1923, which is included
in the Expiring Laws Continuance Bill now
before the House. The Constabulary Act
(Northern Ireland), 1922, establishing the
R.U.C. provided for the continuance of the
system formerly in operation in Ireland,
under which the duty of inspection of
Weights and Measures was imposed upon
members of the police force in possession of
a certificate of qualification from the Board
of Trade as prescribed by Statute. It was
subsequently found that the number of R.I.C.
possessing this prescribed certificate of
qualification who joined the R.U.C., was entirely inadequate for the efficient discharge
of this important duty and it, therefore, became necessary to obtain statutory authority
to enable the work to be carried out by
persons other than members of the Force.
The Weights and Measures Act, 1923, gave
the Government the required authority to
avail ourselves of the services of ex-members
of the R.I.C. who possessed the Board of
Trade Certificate and who were qualified to
undertake the work.
ex-
This arrangement as hon. Members are
aware, was regarded as a temporary
pedient only, and the House will remember
that last year the mover of this Bill-I think
it was myself-expressed the hope that it
would not be necessary to continue this Act
further as it was expected that a sufficient
number of members of the R.U.C. would
obtain the necessary Board of Trade Certificate to do away with the necessity of
employing persons who are not members of
that Force as Inspectors of Weights and
Measures. I regret to say that these expectations have not been realised and at the
examinations held in April last none of the
candidates belonging to the R.U.C. was
successful. I am informed that the standard
required from the candidates is now so high
that it is very difficult for a man who has
police duties to perform to reach it. The
question of whether we should arrange to
release a number of police from their
ordinary duties so that they can prepare
themselves for the next examination, or
whether we should ask the local authorities
to undertake the work is now under consideration, but in the meantime the work of
examining weights and measures must be
carried on, and, therefore, we must continue
last year's Act for another period so that
we may not be left without any Inspectors
whatsoever. I have no further observations
to make on this Measure, and I, therefore,
beg to move.

My next point is in regard to Summer
Time. Well, I do not believe in being in
the humiliating position of saying ditto to
every Act that the British House of Commons
passes. I think it is a great misfortune
that we will not act until the British
authority acts, and then say that they have
set us the example. I hold that the time
has come when we ought to realise that we
control an area of our own, and I think
we ought to take steps to do the best thing
in the interests of that area in the circumstances peculiar to it, and in the many
matters that come up affecting it. Sometimes this Parliament is asked to wait until
it sees what is done across the water.
are a community by ourselves, self-supporting, and, I hope, self-developing. Certainly
we will have to develop ourselves if we are
to develop at all. We must look after the
citizens in our area according to the requirements of the local situation. I want to say
that I object to the application of Summer
Time on behalf of the great farming community who form the largest industry and
probably half the electorate of this Province.
I object for very cogent reasons. The farmers
cannot carry on
their industry properly
because of the conditions of this Act. They
have difficulty in the ingathering of their
crops if you impose upon them a day which
brings them out at an hour in the morning
when the dew is on the crops. They must
attend to other things or walk about until
the sun rises in the heavens. I hold that
you are taking one-eighth of the time of
the husbandman, and that is a very
serious thing in the economic conditions
that prevail in Northern Ireland. I object
for other reasons. I hold that there is something unfortunate in the whole of this
Summer Time business. I hold that it is wrong
from the medical point of view. It is doing
an injustice to childhood. It is disorganising
home life; it is making the children restless
and nervous. You know that children will
not go to sleep contentedly while there is
daylight. All these things are unfortunate
for the child life of the country, and
latterly, whatever the reason, be it divine
or otherwise, while you have tried to improve
the hand of the clock and the circle of
the sun there has been no blessing to agriculture or any other industry either in
Ireland or in Great Britain. You want to
be wiser than your Maker. For these
practical reasons I object to Summer Time.
I know that Ministers may say Why cannot farmers change their hours for
commencing and ending their work?" You
cannot ask a lot of labouring men employed

in a community to adopt a different line

and that it does not matter very much. A

I can assure the House that all we desire

fraud in one shop it may cause the whole
countryside to go wrong. It is apparently
a technical matter to discover whether
scales and weights and measures are of the
high standard they ought to be.

I now pass on to the hon. Member's remarks about the continuance of Summer
Time. I know quite well that the Government has to stand up against harsh criticism
from time to time, but we have faced this
problem on many former occasions. I can
only say for my own part that I believe
that the creation of Summer Time has been
of enormous benefit to the people as a whole,
and I think that if a plebescite was taken
throughout the length of England, Scotland,
Wales, and Northern Ireland it would be
predominantly in favour of getting as much
sunshine as possible during the summer
months, especially for the sake of the
children. The idea of the Government is to
introduce a short Bill, and to say that whatever time is fixed by the Imperial authority,
either by Act of Parliament or Order in
Council, our clocks in Ulster should synchronise with British time. The difficulty
and the trouble that would result from
having times different here and across the
water are such that it makes it impossible
to think of going back to the difference of
27 or 25 minutes-I have forgotten the
exact figure-in the old days. Therefore, it
is proposed to bring in a Bill enacting that
whatever time is fixed by the Imperial
Parliament shall automatically be observed
here. At the same time we shall exercise an
influence in coming to a decision, because

PARLIAMENTARY
SECRETARY
OF THE MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Mr. Megaw): I think a considerable amount
of confusion has arisen during the course
of the debate with regard to the Weights
and Measures Act, and there have been what
I regard as some rather serious misstatements and reflections which should not have
been made. How does the matter stand?
Previous to any legislation on our part the
only persons who could act as inspectors of
weights and measures were the Royal Irish
Constabulary. Prior to 1904 I do not know
that there was anything specially required
of these particular men, but in 1904 an Act
of the Imperial Parliament was passed
which is in force at this date. It says that
The Board of Trade shall provide for the
holding of examinations for the purpose of
ascertaining whether applicants for the post
of inspector.
" England and Ireland both required that the person who is
appointed as inspector shall qualify by a
Board of Trade examination.

That is the position that met us when we
took over office here. There was only one
set of persons required to be inspectors, that
is members of the Royal Irish Constabulary
who had the certificate of the Board of Trade.
Then when the Royal Ulster Constabulary
was formed there was not a sufficient number
in that force who held those certificates. My
recollection is that there were only five who
were qualified to act as inspectors of weights
and measures. Then we passed our Act. I
was entrusted with the duty of proposing the
Second reading of that Act, and there was a
very considerable debate during its progress.
I pointed out, either in Committee Stage or
on the Second reading, that this examination
was not of the trival character that the hon.
Member for North Belfast seemed to think
it was. There seemed to be an idea in the
House that any man in the street who knew
anything about trade-say by going into a
grocer's shop and buying something-could
adjust weights and measures. Weights and
measures like very many other scientific instruments have been greatly changed during
the last number of years. They are very
different as you can see going about the
world. It is not the ordinary balance that
very often has to be adjusted. There aro
other manipulations required in instruments
that are of a very delicate character, at any
rate the Board of Trade has so decided. We
have got to deal in commerce with England
and other parts of the world, and it is of
the highest importance that our weights and
measures should be of a proper standard-
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-and that our
traders should not be accused of fraud
when they are not guilty of that offence,
but when perhaps the mistake arises from
imperfect instruments.

We realised all that. We found it was
absolutely necessary that we should have
inspectors of weights and measures appointed
because during war time that service like
many others was neglected. Hardly any
attention was paid to it during war time.
It became necessary, therefore, to appoint a
proper number of inspectors of weights and
measures through the various counties, and
we took what we considered was the easiest
way. We had men who had the Board of
Trade certificates-men in the R.I.C. They
were the only available men who were qualified prior to the Ulster examination. I do
not think it was an expensive service. Inspectors of weights and measures are paid
at the rate of £150 a year. They are only
able to do the work at that salary because
they have got their pensions. At any rate,
we had no choice. We had to take one or
the other. We had either to abandon the
service altogether or to take the men who
were qualified. The Prime Minister has
already pointed out that we cannot make
any legislation that will infringe on this
question. We have got to take the Board of
Trade Certificate to-day and there is no getting out of it.
What was done was this. We endeavoured
as far as possible in the R.U.C. to have men
trained in the inspecting class who would
get that examination and qualify. Reflections have been made on that school.
When a sufficient number of members of the
R.U.C. did not come forward what did the
Inspector-General do? He invited volunteers
who wished to get into that service to come
forward. All who were thought to have
a chance were given a training in that
school. I am not at all sure that the best
men in the R.U.C., who had better prospects
opening for them in the way of promotion
to Head-constableship and District-Inspectorship, volunteered for that service. Once
inen get into the weights and measures
department they seem to get side-tracked

brought in restriction of rent at a time when

man was earning big wages. You restricted

whether the House sits or not, this thing
will go on. I do not like this continuance
of expiring legislation.

The ATTORNEY-GENERAL (Mr. Best):
We now turn from this interesting question
of weights and measures and various matters
that have been discussed, and come to a
more human matter, that is, to discuss this
Bill which is to remove doubts as to the
application of the Deceased Brothers Widows
Marriage Act, 1921, to Northern Ireland.
The Bill is necessary in order to place the
law relating to marriage with a deceased
brother's widow in the same position as it
has been in Great Britain since 28th July,
1921. On that day the Royal Assent was
given to the Deceased Brother's Widow's
Marriage Act, 1921, and that statute contains
no express words applying it to Northern Ireland. That statute, however, was passed
after the 3rd of May, 1921, which was the
appointed day for the transfer of legislative
power to the Parliament of Northern Ireland, and it relates to a matter in respect
of which the Parliament of Northern
Ireland had at the time of its passing power
to legislate. The Imperial Act, therefore,
has no force in Northern Ireland. It is of
very great importance indeed that the Act
should be declared to be applicable in
Northern Ireland, and to be so applicable
not only from the present date but from
the date of the passing of the Imperial Act-
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-that is, the
28th July, 1921.
In the course of the administration of
the Office of Registrar-General, which is
carried on under the direction of my right
hon. Friend, the Minister of Finance, and
his Ministry, evidence has become available
to show that at least one marriage has taken
place in Northern Ireland between a man
and his deceased brother's widow, in the
belief that such marriage
was valid by
reason of the Act of 1921. Information has
also been received of a case in which it is

ed in August, 1921, and it indicated that

least possible disturbance of present conditions.

Northern Ireland.
It is hereby declared that the Deceased
Brother's Widow's Marriage Act, 1921,
applies to Northern Ireland, and the said
Act shall be deemed to have applied to
Northern Ireland as from the passing
thereof:
The Act of 1921-I have got it here-is itself retrospective. It purports to amend
the Act of 1907, which first legalised marriage
with a deceased wife's sister. As I say the
Act of 1921 is retrospective as from the date
of its own passing, and it achieves this effect
by providing for the insertion of certain
words into the Deceased Wife's Sister
Marriage Act of 1907. The effect of the main
provisions of that Act of 1907 taken in conjunction with the Act of 1921 may be stated
as follows:
"No marriage heretofore or hereafter
contracted between a man and his deceased

Mr. ARCHDALE: This Bill, as the headings say, is
"to amend and remove doubts as to
certain provisions of the Assurance
Companies Act, 1909, as they apply in
Northern Ireland."
an
It is mainly administrative. It is
amending Bill, and it is brought in to remove doubts that have arisen as to people
insured in Northern Ireland under these
Acts. The Bill now under consideration
deals with Assurance matters in general,
while the Industrial Assurance Bill, which we
have already had before the House this afternoon, as its name implies, is confined to a
special class of life assurance. As hon. Members are aware Assurance Companies are required by the Act of 1909 to make a deposit
of £20,000 upon the warrant of the Board
of Trade in respect of certain classes of
business undertaken, such as Fire, Life,
Accident and Employers' Liability Assurance, either in London or in Belfast. The
Order in Council which adapted the provisions of the Assurance Companies' Act of
1909 to Northern Ireland relieved existing
companies which had already made a deposit from any obligation to make in
Northern Ireland a second deposit in respect
of the same class or classes of business,
and, conversely, the one Northern Ireland
company which had made a deposit was relieved of the obligation to make a second
deposit in London.
The Order in Council did not, however,
cover the case of companies which after
the establishment of the Government of
Northern Ireland might be formed to carry
on operations in Great Britain and
Northern Ireland, and as the law stands at
present any such company would be under
the necessity of paying a deposit of £20,000
in Belfast as well as in London. After carefully considering this question my Ministry
and I have come to the conclusion that such
a requirement is not altogether necessary
or advisable, and accordingly Clause 1 of
the Measure now before the House provides
that we in Northern Ireland will recognise
deposits made in London and relieve from
the necessity of making a further deposit
in Northern Ireland any company which
proposes to commence operations in
Northern Ireland and which has made or
makes such a deposit in London. I
should also mention that the concession we
now make would apply to any Dominion
I company which makes a deposit in London.
Clause 2 is designed to facilitate
administrative arrangements, and provides
that the Ministry of Commerce may accept
from an Assurance Company copies of its
accounts and other documents as deposited
with and accepted by the Board of Trade.
As hon. Members are aware, practically all
Assurance Companies carrying on business
in Northern Ireland also operate in Great
Britain. The Board of Trade and the
Government Actuary's Department at Westminster subject the accounts and valuations
of these companies to close scrutiny, and,
accordingly, there is much to be said for
the proposal that copies of these examined
accounts should be accepted in Northern
Ireland, where only a very small portion of
the company's business may actually be
carried on. I beg to move.

be regarded as absolute law in the absence

by the Government is this: that there was
no legislation affecting the opening of yards
in the Act of 1923. There was undoubtedly
an extra prohibition as regards the opening
of licensed premises for the sale of intoxicating liquor, but it did not go further
than that. Anything done by the Act of

had taken place. In other words, while the
opening of a yard, accompanied by other
circumstances, might be evidence that an
offence was committed, the opening of the
yard in itself could not be interpreted in
any way as an infringement of the Act.
That matter was brought before the
Ministry of Home Affairs by the Associated
Chambers of Commerce, and a reply was
given to the Associated Chambers of Commerce in the same terms as the letter referred to by my hon. and learned Friend
(Mr. Hanna.) An instruction was issued
to the police of the same character, stating
what was the view of the Government in
regard to that matter, namely, that there
was no offence in the opening of yards, but
that there would be an offence in the opening of any licensed premises for sale.
Another matter has been raised by my
colleague. It is one of which I have had
no notice beforehand, and on which I
should not like to commit the Government
in any way. It is in respect of the dual
business. This is the first time it has been
brought to my attention, but I cannot say it
has not occurred to me already as a matter
that might give rise to some ambiguity.
Up to the present I am not aware
that there have been any prosecutions
based on the double business. I am quite
aware that it is only since 1st October that
the double business has been involved, and
it would be out of place for me to make

It is easy
onough for me to say-and I can do so
without any hesitation-that if a yard is
structurally separated from the rest of the

carrying on of a dual business, but if the

of the law. At any rate the matter has not

questioning Orders made by authoritative

enactment. We have given our view
with regard to it and it is the view we are

considered that there is any injustice done
to anyone by the administration of the law
in this matter.

Mr. DUFF: I wish to apologise for not

HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Thursday, 16th October, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock,
Mr. SPEAKER in the Chair.
PAPER PRESENTED.
Ministry of Education.-Regulations for
the Payment of Salaries to Teachers in Preparatory, Intermediate, and Secondary
Schools. (By Act.)
Oral Answers to Questions.
HIRING OF POLICE MOTORS.
1. Mr. COOTE (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs, if he will state
who is responsible for the hiring of motor
cars for the use of the police at Lisnaskea,
Co. Fermanagh; why the work has been
taken from the man who did it in troublesome times; whether he received any notice
of the transfer, and who has the work now,
and on what terms?
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): As a rule the police
use their own transport, and do not ´hire
cars, but when the necessity arises for such
hiring the District-Inspector is the officer
responsible for making the arrangements.
No contract is entered into, but in the
ordinary course the man who is most convenient is employed, provided his charge is
within the authorised maximum rate, viz.:
10d per mile-within the last two years
three persons have been employed in this
way at various times at Lisnaskea, and I
am not aware that there is any foundation
for the allegation that the work has been
taken away from any individual.
COTTAGES FOR EX-SOLDIERS IN
FERMANAGH.
2. Mr. COOTE (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Minister of Home Affairs, if he can now
say whether any cottages for ex-soldiers are
to be built at Lisbellaw and Ballinamallard,
County Fermanagh, and if he can give the
reason why none of the cottages have been
so far allocated to these very loyal villages
in County Fermanagh, seeing that a large
number of applications have been made by
ex-soldiers in both villages?
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): This is a matter which comes
under the survey of my Ministry, and
therefore I reply to my hon. Friend.
I would refer him to the reply given to
his question on the 20th May last. Owing
to the restricted number of cottages which
are to be erected in Northern Ireland it is
unfortunately inevitable that cottages
cannot he built in every locality from
which applications have been received
from ex-Service men.
REAR LIGHTS ON BICYCLES.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether he intends to follow
the recommendation of the Roads Advisory
Committee in regard to rear lights on
bicycles, in the interests of the safety of
cyclists and motorists.
Sir DAWSON BATES: I have carefully
considered the recommendation of the Roads
Advisory Committee, and also of the Special
Committee appointed by the Imperial
Government on the subject of rear lights on
pedal cycles.
While there is much to be said for the
proposal that these cycles should be fitted
with rear lights, it is also bound up with
the larger question of rear lights on all
horse drawn vehicles.
The matter, as the hon. and gallant
Member no doubt realises, affects a very
considerable section of the community at
large, and is, accordingly, not one for hasty
or ill-considered legislation. I am carefully
considering the whole question in all its
bearings, and will be prepared to deal with
it as soon as a suitable opportunity arises.
MARRIED SPECIALS' SEPARATION
ALLOWANCE.
4. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether married members of
the Special Constabulary stationed at Newry
have had their separation allowance of 2/-
per diem deducted from their pay.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The only cases in
Newry in which payment of separation
allowance to married members of the Special
Constabulary has been discontinued, are
those in which the families of the men concerned have accommodation in the town, and
permission has been given to the men to
reside with their families. In such circumstances separation allowance is not payable.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
reply, are there no cases where married
constables are compelled to sleep in the
barracks?
Oral Answers.
Oral Answers.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Sir DAWSON BATES: Where there are
cases of a constable being ordered to sleep
in the barracks of course he is entitled to
separation allowance.
Colonel WOODS: That is the point.
THE BELFAST-LISBURN ROAD.
5. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether his attention has
been drawn to the condition of the road
surface on the Belfast-Lisburn Road, and
whether he intends to take any action in
the matter.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Antrim County
Council are at present engaged on work of
reconstruction on the Belfast-Lisburn Road,
partly in concrete and partly in asphaltic
cement. These works form part of a general
scheme for the reconstruction of the Class 1
roads in the county, for which a loan of
£115,000 has been sanctioned, and for which
the Ministry of Home Affairs have accepted
financial responsibility up to the extent of
60 per cent. Naturally during the progress
of these important works it is necessary to
close to traffic certain specified portions of
the road-(hon. Members: Hear, hear)-but
every effort is made to reduce as far
as possible inconvenience to the travelling
public. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)
MOTOR TAXATION INQUIRY.
6. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether any report had been
received from the Commission appointed by
the Northern Government to work in conjunction with the Commission set up by the
Imperial Government to inquire into the
system of Motor Taxation.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The hon, and gallant
Member appears to be under a misapprehension regarding the appointment of a
Commission by the Government of Northern
Ireland to inquire into the system of motor
taxation. The situation is as follows:-
In view of the desirability of keeping in
close touch with the Imperial Government
on questions of taxation of motor vehicles,
arrangements were made by permission of
the Ministry of Transport, Whitehall,
whereby three representatives of the Government of Northern Ireland were enabled to
attend the meetings of the Imperial Government's Departmental Committee on Motor
Taxation, with a view to their being in
a position to assist and advise the Government of Northern Ireland in the event of
the question of the introduction of new
legislation dealing with the Taxation of
Motor Vehicles being considered.
The Departmental Committee submitted
their Report to the Imperial Government
rocently, and the recommendations may be
said briefly to fall under three heads:-
In the first place they recommended that
immediate legislation should be enacted, remedying existing defects in the system of
Motor Taxation in relation to the surrender
of licences and to the surcharge payable on
quarterly licences.
These recommendations have been accepted
by the Imperial Government, and also, on
the recommendation of the representatives
referred to above, by the Government of
Northern Ireland, and it will be found that
the proposals in question are embodied in
the Finance Bill, which comes before this
House for Second Reading to-day.
The second and main recommendation was
to the effect that a tax on petrol is not at
present practicable, and consequent on that
was the third recommendation that the question of the revision of the present Treasury
Horse Power Rating of Motor Vehicles
should be referred to a special Technical
Committee.
The Government of Northern Ireland are
keeping in close touch with developments in
this connection, but pending the findings of
that Technical Committee consideration of
the whole question must be necessarily deferred.
OBSTRUCTIONS IN THE SILLIES RIVER.
7. Mr. COOTE (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Prime Minister if he is aware that the
Ministry of Labour agreed to give the Fermanagh County Council £1,000 towards the
cost of removing shoals and obstructions in
the Sillies river, on condition that such sum
would be 60 per cent. of the cost of labour
spent on such work, but that the County
Council were unable to proceed with the
work owing to the absence of statutory
power to raise the remaining 40 per cent.
in any manner whatever, and whether the
Government is prepared to introduce a short
Bill to enable the County Council to carry
out this work, and if he can now state the
intentions of the Government regarding the
general question of drainage, which has become more acute owing to the recent very
wet seasons.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am taking this question
on behalf of the Prime Minister.
As regards the first part of the question,
I am aware that a scheme of the nature
suggested by the hon. Member was approved
at a total estimated cost of £1,000, but that
it could not be proceeded with owing to the
statutory difficulty. I may perhaps correct
Oral Answers. 1402

三
the hon. Member's figures. The amount of
the unemployment relief grant sanctioned
was not £1,000, but 60 per cent. of the labour
cost of £800, i.e., a total grant of £480.
As regards the latter part of the question,
the Government have had the the whole
drainage problem, including the effectiveness
of the existing law relating to Drainage
Boards, under serious consideration for some
time past. I am, to-morrow, meeting a deputation from the farmers of County Fermanagh, who have advocated the introduction of a Bill as suggested by the hon.
Member, and after our exchange of views
I hope to be in a better position to bring
the matter before the Cabinet, with a view
to deciding on the general course of action
to be taken. I need not remind the hon.
Member that the general question of drainage is not one to be lightly resolved, having
been the subject of no fewer than nineteen
Commissions of Inquiry in the course of the
last 150 years.
Mr. COOTE: Arising out of that answer,
and in view of all the discussion that has
taken place in regard to this matter, is the
Government not yet prepared to propound a
policy to aid the development of agriculture
by a drainage scheme, or are they still
merely theorising in the matter? What is
their policy? That is the question the
country is asking, and will the Minister not
soon be able to give an answer?
Mr. POLLOCK: The Government is not
theorising. It is taking advantage of all the
practical advice that is procurable, and as
soon as such practical advice is sufficiently
matured to enable the Government to act, I
have no doubt action will be taken.
NEW SCHOOL FOR LISBELLAW.
8. Mr. COOTE (for Mr. Cooper) asked the
Parliamentary Secretary of the Ministry of
Education, if a new Protestant school is
urgently required at Lisbellaw, Co. Fermanagh; how long the people have been
agitating for the work to be carried out;
what is the cause of the delay, and if he will
undertake to have matters put right.
Mr. POLLOCK: The premises at present
used for the Lisbellaw Public Elementary
School have been reported by the inspectors
to be old and generally unsuitable for school
purposes, and an application for a grant
towards the erection of a new building under
the management of the Reverend Canon
McTighe, LL.D., rector of Lisbellaw, was
under consideration by the Commissioners of
National Education prior to the war. In
view, however, of the total suspension of
grants during the war and the restrictions
placed by the Imperial Treasury on such
grants in the years that followed, the Commissioners were unable to proceed with the
case.
When the Ministry of Education took over
control of the Educational Services for
Northern Ireland, in February, 1922, the
consideration of the case was re-opened, and
in November, 1923, the Ministry sanctioned
grants towards the erection of the new house
to accommodate boys and girls only. Following the sanction of this grant, the manager
suggested the erection of a larger house than
that which the Ministry was empowered
under the regulations to allow, and as a
result of the manager's proposal the Ministry had the case further investigated by the
senior inspector in charge of the district.
As the result of this investigation the
Ministry decided that the proper course in
the educational interests of the district was
to provide accommodation in the new house
for the pupils of the infant school as well as
of the senior school, especially as the principal of the infant school is due to retire at
an early date. The manager has agreed to
this course, and plans of the new house on
this basis are in preparation. It is hoped
that these plans will be ready in a few days.
The Ministry of Education is endeavouring
to expedite the case as much as possible.
PUNCH HEMSTITCHING PIECE RATES.
9. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Labour, whether he can state the result of
the recent investigation into the yield of
the piece rates as fixed by the Trade Board
on punch hemstitching, as the result of a
strike which took place in Lurgan during
May of this year.
:
The MINISTER OF LABOUR (Mr.
Andrews) At the request of the Linen and
Cotton Handkerchief Trade Board, my Department carried out the investigation to
which the honourable and gallant Member
refers. The inquiry consisted of inspections
in a number of firms selected by the Trade
Board, and the resulting particulars were
furnished to the Board in accordance with
their request. On the 7th August the Board
informed me that having regard to the
returns so submitted and to all the circumstances of the case, the Board are of opinion
that no sufficient cause has been shown for
an alteration in the present general minimum piece rates for punch hemstitching,
which the Board are satisfied yield to a
worker of ordinary skill and experience in
the trade the existing piecework basis time
rate of 7d. per hour."

Colonel WOODS: As this is rather an important matter, I give notice that I will
bring it up on the Motion for Adjournment.

A GOVERNMENT OFFICIAL'S PENSION.
10. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Agriculture whether he will state the
amount of pension now paid to Mr. Crowe,
late of the Ministry of Agriculture, and
whether Mr. Crowe retired by reason of the
age qualification.
Mr. POLLOCK: I am taking this question
for the Minister of Agriculture, who is absent because of duties elsewhere. The reply
is-Mr. Crowe's retirement was not on
grounds of age, but was voluntary in pursuance of the privilege accorded by the
Government of Ireland Act, 1920, to transferred Irish officers of retiring on special
terms. His superannuation allowances were
fixed by the Civil Service Committee, and
consist of a non-variable pension of £143
15s 0d, a supplemental pension of £52 18s Od,
variable quarterly in accordance with the
fluctuation of the official increased cost of
living figure, and a lump sum additional
allowance of £498 18s 4d.

other

answer that. He receives 10s. a week in
