The PRIME MINISTER: The hon. Member
(Mr. Donald) has, I think, traversed a great
many matters that are outside the immediate ambit of the Bill before the House,
and I would just like to say to him that
the Government are fully alive to their responsibility in the matter of endeavouring
to help the local authorities to build houses
for the working classes. If we keep our
attention closely concentrated upon that
object, I think it really would be better than
discussing the question of rules laid down
by the various trade unions, for instance,
regarding their workpeople-rules that we
have no power whatever to alter. My hon.
Friend opposite (Mr. McGuffin) suggested
that bricklayers might be paid by piecework,
laying bricks at so much for so many bricks,
instead of being paid so much per day.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Lest that statement
should be misrepresented, I would like to
say to the Prime Minister that the opinion
I expressed was in reference to a bonus. I
did not mean to put the men on piecework,
but to pay them a bonus on their turnout,
which is a very different thing.
The PRIME MINISTER: I presume my
hon. Friend really means if they were to take
less wages per day, and to have a bonus for
laying more than a certain number of bricks.
Mr. McGUFFIN: A bonus on their wages.
The PRIME MINISTER: I am not going
into the matter. I am only pointing out
that this Bill is only an expression of an
endeavour on the part of this House
to solve this great problem of supplying
houses for the working classes, and the
moment we get off that, and extraneous
matters are raised, we are involved in arguments which may go on for an interminable
time. So I will pass by, if I may, this excursion into the realm of trade unions and
the various trades which are concerned in the
actual building of houses.
Before I get down to the Bill itself, I would
like to refer to the idea of my hon. Friend,
the Member for the University who comes
from Derry (Dr. Morrison) of voting against
the Third Reading of the Bill on the ground
that this is an unfair allocation of the funds
at the disposal of the Government of
Northern Ireland to the industrial city of
Belfast. Well, I do hope that that is a spirit
which will not creep into the House, that the
House should carefully weigh whether a Bill
should be passed or not, because it is of
greater benefit to the City of Belfast on
account of its size and its problems than it
is perhaps to country districts. Look at the
retaliation, if I may put it that way, that
Belfast Members could make when it comes
to a grant towards the erection of labourers'
cottages throughout the country districts.
Look at the grant that this House unanimously-I think unanimously not only in the
question of voting but also in feeling-gave
for two years towards the reduction of agricultural rates. Look at the assistance that
we are endeavouring most equitably and most
fairly to render towards the erection of
bridges in an outlying part of our counties.
And if the question of drainage is brought
forward at a future date, we may have to
tackle that great problem on rather an extensive scale. It is really for our Chancellor
of the Exchequer, in consultation with his
Cabinet colleagues, to endeavour to maintain
the allocation of whatever funds are at our
disposal in a fair way not alone to Belfast
but to the Six Counties as a whole. I would
just like to remind some hon. Members that
in some respects Belfast is half of Northern
Ireland, and although it may swallow up a
great deal of money which is at our disposal,

Oral Answers to Questions.
SEIZURE OF A GUN IN CO. FERMANAGH.
1. Mr. DONALD (for Mr. Cooper) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs, if he will give
the reason for the seizure of the gun of Mr.
John Cathcart, Kilyven, Monen, County
Fermanagh; if Mr. Cathcart applied for a
permit, and with what result; and if he will
state where the gun now is, and if it will be
returned to the owner; and whether he is
aware that Mr. Cathcart is a large farmer,
and a loyalist, and requires the gun to shoot
foxes on his farm in Knockmore for the
protection of his sheep.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): When Mr. Cathcart applied
for a firearms' certificate on 14th March,
1924, it transpired that he had been in possession of a gun for a prolonged period prior
to that date without having the necessary
permit. The question of prosecuting Mr.
Cathcart for his breach of the law then arose,
but as he had, although at a very late date,
disclosed the fact that he had a gun in his
possession, it was decided that the ends of
justice would be adequately met by the forfeiture of the weapon. The gun is now in
the possession of the police, and I regret I
cannot see my way to order its return.
I am aware that Mr. Cathcart is a large
farmer and a loyalist, and doubtless requires
a gun for the purpose of killing vermin on
his land. These facts do not, however, in
any way excuse him from compliance with
the law.
FERMANAGH POLICE OFFICERS'
MILITARY SERVICE.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether the County Commandant's Adjutant of the Special Constabulary
in County Fermanagh has previously served
in H.M. Forces.
Sir DAWSON BATES: There are two
adjutants of Special Constabulary at Enniskillen. One of these volunteered for service
at the outbreak of war, and was rejected on
medical grounds, but was engaged in
Government work during the war. The
other adjutant served in the Army from 1911
to 1920. The latter has been temporarily
seconded for other duty, and the officer acting
in his place served for 2 years in the Army,
prior to joining the Special Constabulary.
EXPLOITATION OF FOOD STUFFS.
3. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can, under Act of
Parliament, take such steps as will prevent
the exploitation of the public by traders in
essential foodstuffs.
The MINISTER OF COMMERCE (Mr.
Archdale): I have been asked by my right
hon. Friend to reply to this question. 1
infer that the hon. and gallant Member
refers to the possibility of controlling food
prices. There is no existing statute which
gives powers of this nature. If my hon. and
gallant Friend is inquiring whether it will
be possible for the Government to institute
legislation to attain this end, I would refer
him to the answer given to the question
asked by him in the House on 6th May last.

otherwise, and how many were not SO

SUNDAY BROADCASTING IN BELFAST.

asked the Minister of Commerce whether
he is aware that no wireless broadcasting
is being done from the Belfast Station on
Sundays, and whether he can state the
reasons for this?
Mr. ARCHDALE: The answer to the
first part of the question is in the affirmative and to the second part in the negative.
I may add for the information of the hon.
and gallant Member that I understand
that the whole question of Sunday Broadcasting from the Belfast Station is under
the consideration of the Directors of the
Britsh Broadcasting Company in London.
Colonel WOODS: Is the right hon.
Getleman aware that programmes have
already been published for two consecutive
Sundays, but none have been broadcast?

Mr. McGUFFIN: I have only a few words
to say with respect to this matter. In the
first instance I offer congratulations to the
right hon. Gentleman that the Bill has so
smoothly passed through the House without
significant opposition or material alteration.
We are still sorry it has been necessary that
this Bill should be promoted in the House in
order to relieve unemployment. While the
House has accorded perfectly unanimous
support of the measure there is still a point
which I would like to impress upon the right
hon. Gentleman without being discourteous
or offensive to him in any way, as I hold him
above suspicion. Therefore, he may be perfectly at ease in his mind. I have for some
time past been receiving communications
complaining of the administration of the
Act, which is quite a different thing to the
passing of this Bill. It is a very easy matter,
we understand, to pass a Bill here, and
though the Minister is not primarily responsible for the administration, at the same
time a degree of responsibility attaches to
him in his high office if there are any complaints as to the administration.
If I had introduced this matter as early as
I might have done by reason of the correspondence I have received from time to time,
I might have done so several weeks ago,
but this morning I received a letter, which
is only one of a series, setting forth what is
regarded as a great injustice in the administration of the Act. I do not wish to go into
details in the matter, but if the right hon.
Gentleman is anxious to read what is said,
I will place the correspondence at his disposal. I will only say this with respect to
it, that it relates to the transfer of labour
from here to across the water.
The particular instance which I have before my
mind is that of a carpenter, a married man
with a family, who against his will, is being
transferred to a position in Glasgow. The point
is this: he alleges-and I suppose he has some
reason for saying it-that it will be a serious
disadvantage to him as, for instance, wages
across the water are, according to his quotation, from 2s 6d to 2s a week less than are
paid in this area, and while he is informed
he will have £3 10s across the water it is
also stated that that includes overtime.
Overtime can only be worked there to the
extent of thirty hours a month and it is
absolutely at the option of the employer

whether he will give him any or not. Those

What I want to point out to the right

and above all I exonerate the right hon.

am concerned. That does not, however, relieve the public mind of certain opinions
with regard to the matter. I thought it

There is another point I want to put in

I am very glad that the Bill has been expedited through the House, and that it will
now be in operation for the benefit of the
people. It is necessary under the circumstances that it should be. The Bill comes
into operation in fulfilment of a promise
made by the Government that we should be
brought into line industrially with anything

Gentleman will be relieved considerably of

position has been materially improved, and I
also think that in the near future we will be
able to cherish the hope that we will come
right in our embarrassments financially in
connection with State matters.
Dr. MORRISON: I may tell the House

Dr. MORRISON: It is an ameliorative

We have in this Bill contributions from

This Bill proposes to increase the contributions on the part of the State, and seeing

I want to see these people switched off

he came back was kept waiting twenty weeks

As regards the other matters which he
mentioned, I want to refer to the question
of seasonal workers. I know that that is
a very difficult problem. Men are engaged
for part of the year in seasonal occupations
which are insurable. Then for another
portion of the year they are not in insurable
occupations at all, and during that portion
of the year they are not asked to pay contributions. My hon. Friend cited the instance of flax scutchers. I may relieve his
mind on that point, because I have made
an arrangement-in fact, it was made more
than a year ago by which no seasonal
workers in the flax scutching trade will be
entitled to draw unemployment benefit outside the period which can be considered the
scutching season. In other words, they are
entitled to pay contributions for about half
of the year, and they are only entitled to
draw benefit for a similar period, if out of
work. I think that that is quite fair to
the men in this and in other seasonal occupations, and I think it safeguards the fund
from abuses. As I have said on other
occasions, I feel it to be the duty of my
Department to see that everybody who is
entitled to get unemployment benefit gets
is as promptly as possible, but at the same
time it is equally our duty to see that the
fund is not depleted by claims being made
which are not entitled to be made. My
hon. Friend pointed to a case in my own
constituency, where, he said, a man who
was working was drawing benefit. If he
will furnish me with the particulars of that
case I will undertake to have the man
in question brought to book. It is regrettable that sometimes we are obliged to
prosecute persons for drawing benefit while
they are working, but at the same time it
is a public duty which has got to be done,
and, personally, I have not hesitated to take
the course when I found it was necessary.

The PRIME MINISTER (Sir James Craig):
I rise to move the Second Reading of the
Bill dealing with time, as it is affected by
legislation from time to time. I am very
anxious to stabilise this question of summer
time. It is one that I was associated with
at Westminster when it was first introduced.
I think I may say, as a close attendant in
that House for many years, that I heard
all the debates connected with it, and, of
course, since our Parliament has been established we ourselves have had discussions on
the subject. I very seldom hear any new
arguments produced either for or against
summer time. They are merely a repetition,
and, so far as I am concerned, I am prepared
to stand up year by year and defend summer
time. I think that on the whole the country
benefits from having the advantage of the
extra hour's summer sunshine when it can
get it. But my object really in introducing
this Bill to-day is in order not to hold out
false hopes to the farming community that
some new arguments can be produced that
will make us change our minds. I have
always thought that one of the great disadvantages of many Acts of Parliament was
that they are not sufficiently permanent, and
that the community does not grow up with
the feeling that that is the law, and the law
for many years to come, so that they may
adapt themselves to the principle, and become accustomed to it. It may be said that
this is a matter that should be kept entirely
in the hands of the Parliament of Northern
Ireland. If I thought that there was any
chance of this Government or any future
Government deviating from the time that
will be settled for Great Britain as a whole,
then I would not hesitate to say,
"Let us
keep it entirely in our own hands." But we
have now in the Imperial House of Commons
a stronger representation than we have ever
had before, in the sense that we have now
got the whole of the representation in the
hands of our own party, if I may say so-
(hon. Members: Hear, hear)—and they can
voice the sentiments of the Ulster people
in the much larger question of what is the
time to govern the whole of the United
Kingdom and of Northern Ireland. I think
it would really devolve upon them to put
forward the arguments which may be applicable to our locality as against England,
on account of the fact that we lie further
away, and, under ordinary circumstances,
would have a difference of twenty-five
minutes in our time as in the old days.
The Free State, which lies in many parts
further west than we do, has found it suitable to introduce summer time and to
synchronise with Great Britain in that
manner. I really cannot tell what the future
may dictate in regard to the policy of
summer time in the Free State, but I feel
in my own mind that whatever time is considered suitable by the British Parliament
to be the time in Great Britain is good
3C
Time Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[The Prime Minister]
enough for us and more convenient for us
in a hundred ways. The question is really
a very much larger one than it used to be
in its early stages. It has now got to be a
matter of international importance, and the
British Government are endeavouring, if
they can, to secure the same time upon the
Continent as there is in Great Britain at
the period of summer time, in order that
those who are travelling to and from the
Continent may not find a difference in time
and run the risk of missing steamer connections and trains on the other side. It
seems to me that the development of Ulster
-which although in its infancy has already
become quite evident to anyone-in regard
to tourist traffic makes it even more important than ever before that we should keep
the same time as the country from which
the tourists come. I am led to believe that
the traffic during this past summer, bad
and all as the weather was, has been infinitely greater than for many years past,
and that the steamship companies had
waiting lists every night of eighty
and ninety passengers trying to
get
sleeping accommodation, and in
many
instances lines had to be put on two
steamers to bring the passengers to and fro.
That may have been due, of course, to the
Wembly Exhibition, but I believe that that
influx into our Province of visitors from
the other side is going to grow to a very
large extent, and the constant irritation of
having to change one's watch here on one's
arrival to keep the time that would be prescribed in any other way, and to alter it
on going back to the other side is a
mischievous sort of thing which I am sure
our visitors would feel very much and would
wish to avoid.
I do not intend to make a very long speech
on the subject. I intend to point out that
the business men find a great advantage in
having a common time between ourselves and
the other parts of Great Britain. There is
a great advantage in the sending and receipt
of telegrams. You know that if you send one
at a certain time it will reach there before
the office is closed on the other side, without
considering the difference of an hour or an
hour and twenty-five minutes. In the old
days it was very difficult, when you were
sending a telegram, to get at the time when
it would reach its destination having regard
to the difference of the hour or an hour and
twenty-five minutes after it was sent out. As
everybody knows, even to-day, when the time
comes to change the clocks at the beginning
of summer time, one has to think whether it
has to go forward of backward. To remember that all through the period of
summer time is really a nuisance to the
whole community, and I think that with the
experience of the number of years that
summer time has been in operation, and the
fact that the country as a whole is strongly
in favour of it, this Bill will commend itself
to this House, and that the House will allow
us simply to say that the time fixed by Great
Britain will automatically become the time
in Northern Ireland.

therefore good for the farming community to

very small shape, and containing very few
lines, I think I might describe it as a wolf
in sheep's clothing, and although it occupies
such a small space and can be slipped in
so unobtrusively I am afraid that contained
in these lines is material which will be
disastrous to the agricultural interests which
I represent. I had intended to make a request, an appeal to the Government, to ask
them in this matter if they are determined
to go on with this Bill, if nothing that can
be said will alter their decision. I had
intended to ask them if they would take off
the Whips and allow us to vote freely. and
not to put us to the necessity-those of us
who are ardent supporters of the Government
of being obliged to vote against the
Government. However, as I have said, 1
am fighting a forlorn hope, and as I appear
to be practically the only representative of
agricultural interests here it is no use for
me to put forward that request. (Hon.
Members: No, no.) I am only too glad
from the voices I hear to think I am going
to get some support to-day.
To pass from that, I want to make a
protest against the finality contained in this
Measure.. Hitherto, as the Prime Minister
has said, each year the farmer has hoped
and believed that it might be the last year,
that next year might bring release from a
Measure which he looks upon not only as
irksome but as ruinous. To-day we are
faced with a Measure for all time. We
are going to follow the English example,
but we are not putting the Ulster farmer
-and this, I think, one is apt to forgeton an equality with the English farmer.
England has decided to utilise the daylight.
That is well and good, but any disadvantages
accruing to the English farmer, and there
are undoubtedly many, are summed up
in one hour, owing to the difference of one
hour as a result of tampering with the
clocks. The advantages to be reaped by the
industrial works in England are the advantages of one hour. Here in Ulster it is
proposed to place the farmer for all time
on an inferior footing to the English farmer
to the extent of practically another halfhour, that is to say, he is going to work
the hour and a half difference from the
hour set by the sun, which is, after all, the
timepiece which was given to us by the
Creator of all things.
Some people have said in this House that
it is easy for one to find a way out of the
difficulties put in his way by nature, and
that it is easy to find a way to overcome
nature's laws. The hon. Member for North
Belfast (Mr. Grant) a few days ago when
speaking on this subject under the heading
of another Bill asked why should not the
farmer alter his ways, why should he not
rise as heretofore by the time of the sun,
the inference being that he and his labourers
would begin their work, I suppose, an hour
and a half later in the morning, and finish
an hour and a half later in the evening
than those in other industries. I should
like to ask him what would happen if the
milk supply to the city of Belfast was not
received until 10 or 11 o'clock instead of
7 or 8? And what would the workmen in
the city say if the hon. Member for North
Belfast asked them to stay on for an hour
and a half at their work? Would he say to
them when others are enjoying themselves,
going out in the evening with their wives
and families, that they should stay on at
work, not getting home until just time
for their evening meal, when daylight had
gone, and they had no time in which to
till their little plot of ground? Would he
say that to them? Yet that is what he
expects the farmer to say to the labourer
in the country. I would ask him if he
thinks that reasonable. If the farmer does
not ask him to do what I am quite certain
the industrial worker would not be asked
to do, what happens? He cannot carry on.
Time Bill-
Second Reading.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
[Mrs. Chichester]
He loses nine hours in the six days of the
week.
It comes back to this, that it is the farmer
himself who has to suffer, but I cannot help
feeling that in the end if the farmer is made
to suffer in this way it will come to something else, it will mean that it is the worker
in the city who will have to suffer in the
end. The hon. Member for North Belfast
(Mr. Grant) and others have said that the
country cannot exist without the city, that
the farmer depends on the city to get rid
of his surplus produce, but if it comes to
that it seems to me that we must remember
that if bare existence is considered the
farmer can always exist on his own produce.
And what would the city do without that
surplus produce? I know it is a question
of give and take. No section of the community has a right to consider its recreation
at the expense of the existence of another
section of the community. It is not a
question of considering one's own individual
feelings; it seems to me it is a question of
co-operation. I do wish that hon. Members
who come from the city would realise the
sufferings of the farmers at the present
time, and the hardships which they are
enduring. Of course, owing greatly to the
bad season their crops are ruined, their hay
and corn have been washed away, their
potatoes are rotting in the field, and they
have no firing. If the hon. Member could
see all that and realise it, and that the
rates are just as high, if not higher, in the
country as in the city, he would wonder
how the farmer is able to make both ends
meet. He would feel that it was a promise
of help that was required, not a promise of
continued loss which, at any rate in the
eyes of most farmers, this Bill will mean.
You ask him to step with England? Yes,
but why more than England? Already it is
harder for the farmer to manage in Northern
latitudes, where the dews are heavier, and
where the sun is weaker. I know it is
useless almost to talk, but I have the feeling
that I must do my duty by my constituents,
and so I would ask whether, even at this
hour, a compromise of any kind between the
interests of the city and of the country
could not be arrived at. In spite of what
the Prime Minister has said with regard to
the difference of time, I would ask if it
would not be possible not to go on with
this Bill as it stands at the moment, out to
leave it or to consider for the future the
question of a difference of 30 minutes instead
of the whole hour. The half hour would
make an enormous difference to the farmer.
To the industrial worker in Belfast the halfhour would simply mean that he would be
placed on an equal footing with the industrial worker in England, and he would have
nothing in consequence to complain of. It
would not do away with the hardship to the
farmer, but it would lessen it considerably,
and would put him in the sane position as
the English farmer. I know that the difference in time, as the Prime Minister has
pointed out, has its disadvantages, but do
these disadvantages outweigh the material
advantages which it would give to the agricultural districts in the Six Counties, a
difference which would only exist for five
months in the year, an evil which we endured without a murmar before Irish time,
as it was called, was done away with? I
do not want to speak any further on this
subject. I know that every argument that
has been brought forward has been
mentioned before, but I would ask the
Government in this instance to reflect once
more, and see if it would not be possible
to do something which would help the farmer
in this respect, and not put him at a great
disadvantage as compared with the English
farmer.

is going to be impaired the slightest

It is inevitable that this change should
come, and I think it is a pity that this
House should be wrangling over it. My
honest conviction is that the farmer is

sees coming, and that the opposition is
dying. While I would like to meet him I

both in the country and the towns that it
is a change which I think is beneficial, and
one that every person should support. There-

a

Valuation Acts Amendment Bill.
Order for Second Reading read.
Motion made, and Question proposed,
"That the Bill be now read a Second
time."
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The object of this Measure is to
provide a remedy for a state of affairs
which is one of the many difficulties that
arose from and were incident to the war.
The unprecedented rise in the value of property introduced anomalies which became
such an injustice in many cases that it was
necessary that some arrangement should be
made whereby relief in some measure
could be afforded to those to whom injustice was done. I had strong representations made to me from time to time in regard to these matters from persons who
were affected, and it was quite obvious that
it was necessary that immediate action should
be taken if some remedy was to be provided.
So long as the value of property remained
stable, as it was in 1914, none of these
anomalies could arise, but since 1914 such
an extraordinary increase has taken place
in the value of property, and in the
rental value, that these anomalies were
created. I, therefore, thought it right that
a small committee should be appointed to
investigate the whole subject. It is, I
think, clear that the only real way to deal
with an important subject of this kind is
to carry out a complete re-valuation of
property, but as the circumstances of the
moment did not lend themselves to such an
arrangement because of the instability of
values and because of the standard of values,
the Committee recommended, after a comparatively short examination of the subject,
that steps should be taken to provide for an
immediate rectification of the anomalies to
which I have referred.
This Bill, the Second reading of which I
am now moving, embodies the recommendations contained in the Interim Report of
that Committee. As a matter of fact, my
Department has actually been working since
last year according to these recommendations, and it is in order to place the question beyond all legal doubt that the Government now submit this short measure. The
basic principle governing the determination
of the annual value of any house or building
is laid down in the Valuation Act of 1852
and is, briefly, letting value. The Bill does
Valuation Bill-
Second Reading
3 NOVEMBER 1924
not alter that principle, and if hon. Members
will refer to the first paragraph they will
see that what it does is to throw everything
back to the rateable values of 1914 and then
to make an addition of 15 per cent. to
those ascertained values. The year 1914
was selected because of the stability of values
at that period. They were not subject to
the violent fluctuations that took place
subsequently as the result of the war. But
it would not have been consistent to ignore
the general upward trend of values, and so
we have adopted he recommendation that
to the 1914 value should be added this 15 per
cent. This figure was arrived at after very
close and careful consideration and is
approximately the net addition which was
made to standard rents by the Rents Restriction Act.
But this comparatively simple method
requires to be expanded in order to allow of
its application to the several classes of
cases which have to be dealt with. As
far as possible, the valuation officers will
be required to base the revised valuation
of premises on the figures shown in the
lists in force for 1914, as being the valuation
of those particular premises in that
year. In some cases they will have to refer
to what is defined on page three of the Bill
as "comparable valuations." That is to
say, they will require to be guided by the
valuations of property in the neighbourhood
of properties that have been re-valued.
Mr. McGUFFIN: Will that mean in that
case the valuation on a new property that
has never been assessed before?
Mr. POLLOCK: No. I am speaking now
of alterations that have been made in properties that required re-valuation, but it may
be that in the case of new properties, and
probably will be, the valuer will be bound
to have regard to the values of surrounding
properties. You will see that is provided
for in the Bill. At the top of page 2 hon.
Members will see there are three classes
provided for, that is to say, first the new
buildings this is the point my hon. Friend
referred to-which were not on the valuation lists in 1914; secondly, cases in which
the 1914 figures were "stale," and, thirdly,
premises whose utility has changed, whose
character has changed. It is unnecessary
for me to say more about the first-class,
that is valuations of new buildings, but as
to the second, where the valuations are
out-of-date, there are many properties
where the valuations were made sixty
years ago, and, of course, these appear in
the 1914 lists as the 1914 valuations. It
would be merely perpetuating the anomaly
to use the 1914 figures without some
reasonable adjustment in cases like that.
Let me
To turn now to the third or last case,
premises whose utility or character has
changed, we must revert to the foundation
of valuation, that is, the letting value.
Here I may give an example.
assume a second-hand clothes shop is transformed into a theatre. Obviously the
letting value would be very considerably
enhanced, but the valuation officers in such
a case while endeavouring to estimate the
value of such property would necessarily
have to have regard to the standard by
which such property would have been
valued in 1914 instead of 1924.
Paragraph (ii), beginning on line 16 of page
2, will in all likelihood apply to the majority
of revisions, and on that account perhaps
may require special consideration. It deals
with cases in which premises have been
placed on the revision list because of ordinary structural alterations, such as the erection of a garage or a conservatory, or the
minor alterations that are from time to time
made to most buildings. This paragraph
provides that in dealing with a case such as
I have indicated, the valuer will ascertain
the 1914 valuation of the premises and will,
prior to the addition of 15 per cent., adjust it
in order to allow for the value of the alterations, still on the 1914 standard of values.
Mr. DONALD: Plus the 15 per cent.
Mr. POLLOCK: Added afterwards. These
are the fundamental principles of the short
Bill I am now submitting to the House, but
I should mention that its operation is not
extended to houses already protected by the
provisions of the Rent Restriction Act, as we
do not consider it desirable that that Act
should be over-ridden. It would be well, in
order to avoid misunderstanding, also to explain that generally the Bill does not apply
to land. The valuation of land is a most
involved problem, which we propose to deal
with when revising the whole system.
I have gone into the provisions of this Bill
in considerable detail because I think it is
desirable that everybody should have a clear
conception of the whole matter. As I have
said, the subject is by no means a simple
one, but I am convinced that this measure,
to some extent a provisional measure, if
approved by Parliament, will remedy and
prevent any of the injustices which have
been complained of in the past. I beg to
move. (Hon. Members: Hear, hear.)

4 NOVEMBER 1924
HOUSE OF COMMONS.

Tuesday, 4th November, 1924.
The House met at Three of the Clock, Mr.
SPEAKER in the Chair.
Oral Answer to Question.
POLICE TRANSFER ON MARRIAGE.
Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs, whether the Police Code regulations, affecting the transfer of members of
the Constabulary who contract marriages in
their districts or are promoted, have been
applied in the Police District of Newry.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS
(Sir Dawson Bates): There are no regulations
in the Code requiring the transfer of men
on promotion. The Regulation which my
hon. and gallant Friend has possibly in
mind in regard to transfer on marriage is
as follows:
CODE 1075.-When a man obtains permission to marry, if the woman he marries
is a native "of the county in which he is
serving or locally connected therein he will
be liable to be at once removed to another
county."
There have been two cases in the Newry
district where members of the Force
married women locally connected with that
district, but the particular circumstances in
these cases did not render it necessary to
enforce transfers as provided for under the
Regulation which I have quoted.

the fatal gift of fluency, and it occasionally

With regard to the school children, if I
am in order I desire to say that the competition between schools in rural areas, and
I believe in Belfast, for children is so great
that if a desire on the part of the parents
for an earlier hour is insisted upon, and the
parents resenting the order threaten to send
their children to another school, their
wishes will be complied with. The schools
in the country are managed by committees,
and they can alter the school hours at any
time, if they like. I am the manager of a
school. This question has never arisen in
the country, and I believe in all seriousness
that the getting of children out of bed and
beginning the work of washing-up an hour
earlier is a good and wholesome thing.

CIAL SECRETARY TO THE MINISTRY
OF FINANCE (Mr. Barbour): When moving
the Second Reading of the Housing Acts
Amendment Bill my right hon. Friend gave
the reasons which had led the Government to
propose the extension by one
year of the
period of operation of the Housing Act of

Oral Answers to Questions
ULSTER PAVILION AT WEMBLEY.
The following question stood in the Order
Paper in the name of Colonel Woods:-1. To
ask the Minister of Commerce whether he
can state what steps are being taken to dispose of the Ulster Pavilion at Wembley.
Colonel WOODS: This question has been
postponed at the request of the Minister of
Commerce.
EX-SERVICE CIVIL SERVANTS.
2. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Finance whether he will state his intention
as to the ultimate future of ex-Service Civil
Servants who are now employed as temporary" Civil Servants.

The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The position of temporary Civil
Servants in the Government Departments
of Northern Ireland, who are ex-Service
men, has not been lost sight of. The hon.
and gallant Member will, of course, realise
that it is imperative for other sources of
recruitment to be left open in order that
there may be some outlet into the Government Service for youths leaving school, and
also that there may be in the junior ranks
of the Service a certain proportion of the
staff not of mature age.
Colonel WOODS: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman if the ex-Service Civil Servants are
gradually being replaced by boys from
school?
Mr. POLLOCK: If I understand my hon.
and gallant Friend, his question is: Are the
existing temporary ex-Servicemen in the
Civil Service being replaced by the new examination entrants? I am not ready to
answer that question definitely, but so far
as I am aware they are not being replaced
up to the present.
COOKSTOWN SPRING SHOW-PREMIUM
BULLS.
3. Mrs. CHICHESTER asked the Minister
of Agriculture, if he is aware of the representations made by the Mid-Ulster Shorthorn Breeders' Association, requesting that
an allocation of premiums might take place
at the Cookstown Spring Bull Sale-as well
as at Belfast and Derry-and what steps he
proposes to take in the matter.
Mr. POLLOCK: I answer this question for
my right hon. Friend, the Minister of Agriculture, who is unable to be present to-day.
On the 15th ultimo the Minister of Agriculture received a deputation from the Mid-
Ulster Shorthorn Breeders' Association
asking that their Annual Spring Sale at
Cookstown be recognised as a centre for the
provisional selection of bulls for premium.
As Mr. Archdale informed the deputation,
it was not considered advisable to make any
change in the direction suggested, and the
reasons for this decision were fully explained to the deputation.
Mrs. CHICHESTER: Arising out of that
answer, may I ask the right hon. Gentleman if he is aware that out of a total of
only slightly over 600 entries at Balmoral
in 1923, no fewer than 282 came from
within a fifteen mile radius of Cookstown,
and that practically the same percentage
came from within the same radius in 1924,
and does he not think that the Association
is entitled to a special concession in this
matter?
Mr. POLLOCK: Of course, the House will
readily realise that I am not in a position
to argue the merits or the demerits of any
particular place or centre where bulls are
examined for premiums, but I think, even
from my limited knowledge of the subject,
it is not difficult to realise that if the centres
where these examinations are held are extended it will have a tendency to reduce the
standard and character of the animals examined. The natural tendency on the part
of those having high-class animals is to go
to the larger centres. I may say that it is
also an advantage to the Department, because obviously the competition is of a
keener character, and therefore the standard
must necessarily be high before premiums
can be gained. That is the main reason why
the Department found it impossible to fall
in with the suggestion of the Mid-Ulster
Shorthorn Breeders' Association to establish
an additional centre which would involve
not only the difficulties I have mentioned,
but also considerably increased cost to the
Department.

DISPOSAL OF THE "ARGENTA."
5. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he can state the reason
for retaining the ex-prison ship "Argenta,"
and what expenses are being incurred in
consequence of this retention; and if he has
made any arrangements for the disposal of
this ship.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): I beg to refer the hon. and
gallant Member to the answer which was
given to a similar question which he asked
on the 20th May last, and to add that
arrangements are now being made for the
disposal of this vessel. The cost of berthing
the vessel amounts, approximately, to £600
per annum.
SAILORS' AND SOLDIERS' HOUSES AT
COLERAINE.
6. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether any houses have been
erected in the town of Coleraine under the
Irish Land (Provisions for Sailors and
Soldiers) Act, and, if so, how many.
Mr. POLLOCK: I propose to take this
question for my right hon. Friend, the
Minister of Home Affairs.
It has already been intimated to the
House that the Ministry of Finance now acts
as agent for the Irish Land Trust. I will,
therefore, reply to the hon. Member's
question.
No houses have yet been erected in the
town of Coleraine under the Irish Land (Provision for Sailors and Soldiers) Act, 1919.
Mr. DONALD: Arising out of that answer,
may I ask if any request has come to the
Ministry from that district for the allocation
of houses in that neighbourhood?
Mr. POLLOCK: Some cottages have been
provisionally allocated to the Urban District
of Coleraine, and a suitable site has been
provisionally selected for that purpose, but
further action cannot be taken at present
because of the differences that at present
exist between the Trust itself and His
Majesty's Treasury in regard to the maximum provision for the cottages in question.
I referred to this, as my hon. Friend will
recall, in a reply I gave to a question of
the hon. Member for Tyrone. This matter
has not yet been settled.
ROADS ADVISORY COMMITTEE
REGULATIONS.
7. Mr. DONALD asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether the Regulations and
Recommendations of the Roads Advisory
Committee, have been put into operation by
the Local Authorities in Northern Ireland
regarding the cutting of hedges, and the removal of other obstructions at dangerous
corners and cross-roads: whether the Regulations at present governing motor and other
traffic are inadequate, and do not ensure
the safety of the public; and what steps the
Government proposes to take to bring these
up to date.
Sir DAWSON BATES: The Ministry of
Home Affairs has accepted the recommendations of the Roads Advisory Committee in connection with the cutting of
hedges and the removal of obstructions at
dangerous corners.
The first matter, however, involves new
legislation and I am waiting a suitable
opportunity for introducing legislation
dealing with this and other similar matters
in connection with road traffic.
As regards the removal of advertisement
hoardings, etc., at dangerous corners, a
circular letter was issued by the Ministry
conveying to road authorities in Northern
Ireland the recommendations of the Roads
Advisory Committee, and the Ministry are
not aware that these authorities have been
unreasonably negligent in the performance
of their duties in this respect.
With regard to the last part of the hon.
Member's question, I desire to say that instructions have been given to the police
authorities with the view to their exercising
greater control over the speed at which
motor vehicles travel on the roads, and
pending further experience, I am not
satisfied that the existing law in connection
with the speed limits of motor vehicles is
defective.

I would like to express my appreciation of

1587 Illegitimate Children Bill-

HOUSE OF COMMONS. Senate's Amendments.
1.-(1) Where a man is alleged by the
mother to be the father of her illegitimate
child, and has been summoned in accordance with the provisions of this Act to
appear before a court of summary jurisdiction, constitued as hereinafter provided
acting for the petty sessions district or
place in which the mother resides, or in
which the mother
or her illegitimate
child is in receipt of relief from the poor
rates of any poor law union, the court
shall have power, after hearing all the
circumstances of the case, to adjudge the
man to be the putative father of the child,
and to make an order upon him (in this
Act referred to as an Affiliation Order ")
for the payment of-
(a) a weekly sum of money not exceeding
twenty shillings a week in respect of the
maintenance and education of the child;
(b) the expenses incidental to the birth
of the child;
(c) if the child has died before the
making of the Affiliation Order, the funeral
expenses of such child, not exceeding five
pounds; and
(d) the costs of obtaining the Affiliation
Order.

(2) For the purposes of this Act the expression 'the mother" means any single
woman who is with child or delivered of
an illegitimate child, and includes-

from her husband, but who at the time
of her marriage was with child of, or
delivered of, an illegitimate child.
(3) The court shall not make an Affiliation Order unless--
(a) the birth of the child has taken
place;

(5) A court of summary jurisdiction,
when hearing and determining any matter
under this Act, shall be constituted of a

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,
That this House do agree with the Senate
in the said amendment." This is partly a
re-arrangement of the clause as it left this
House. However, there is one important
change, and that is, that when the Bill left
this House it was provided that an Affiliation Order should only remain in force until
the child reached the age of fourteen years,
unless it was subsequently altered by order
of the court. The Senate now propose that
the age should be definitely fixed in the case
of a male at fifteen, and in the case of a
female at sixteen. There is a great deal to
be said for that. Sixteen is a difficult age
in regard to a girl and I think she should
have that protection.
Amendment agreed to.

Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,
"That this House do agree with the Senate
in the said Amendment." The ordinary
procedure, I might explain to the House. is
that the woman applies to the magistrate
for a summons, which is returnable on a
fixed day before the Court. The child may
not be born before the summons is returnable. and, therefore, the mother may not
be in a position to attend the Court. This
Amendment is to enable the Court to have
power to adjourn the hearing of a case
to a subsequent date. Under the Summary
Jurisdiction Act a case can only be
adjourned from Court to Court.
Amendment agreed to.

Senate Amendment:
Clause 3, leave out sub-section (1).
Sir DAWSON BATES: I beg to move,
"That this House do agree with the Senate
in the said Amendment." This is the muchdiscussed subject of the perpetuation of testimony. The Government on further consideration and, may I say, having also heard
the learned discussion which took place in
the other House felt they could not resist the
amendment which was proposed by the
Senate. It was pointed out there that difficulties would arise. Of course, hon. Members
are aware that in the original Bill it is
proposed that the woman could make a small
testimony giving facts as to the father of
the child before the child was born. Hon.
Members will realise that there are many
difficulties in a case of this kind, and that
the shock to a woman of having become
pregnant, might have very serious results
with regard to her health. There is also the
question of blackmail. It is well-known, I
understand, that a woman in that condition
of health very often makes statements
which cannot be at all substantiated. We
have investigated and we find that out of
1.000 births only six resulted in the death of
the mother-I think those are the figures. It
is also rather a new idea under the law;
although the practice exists in regard to
criminal cases, where a deposition made before
can
a person's death
be used in
subsequent proceedings. Hitherto it has
never been known in the law of England
that a depostion should be used in a civil
case after the death of the person making
that deposition. I think it would be undesirable that this House should press the
matter and make what would be an entirely
new addition to the law at the present time.
Dr. MORRISON: This is really the only
controversial question that arises on the
amendments of the Senate. Substantially it
means, as far as I can gather, that, if the
mother of an illegitimate child dies before
she has established her claim-dies in childbirth or from any of the diseases which are
associated with pregnancy-her illegitimate
child, supposing it is living, as in many cases
it frequently is, for whom special care should
be provided above and beyond the ordinary
illegitimate child. this child should be left
absolutely unprotected, a helpless and hopeless waif to be sent to a reformatory or to a
home. It appears to me that that is unfair
-very seriously unfair-and I dispute the
figures that the Minister of Home Affairs
has placed before the house. During the

Reformatory Home in 1922 there were 112

point, and I have made it frequently before

those mothers was 2 in 112, where they were
carefully nursed and had every attendance
that medical skill could give them, what
would it be in the balance of the 1.300 cases
of illegitimate children that are born in
Northern Ireland every year for whom no
such care is provided.

con-
Dr. MORRISON: Before the House adjourns, there is a matter I would like to
bring before the Minister of Finance. It is
connected with the pension scheme which
has been drawn up for Secondary
teachers. I understand that the teachers
had an interview with the Minister of
Education yesterday, and also with the
Minister of Finance, and I was deputed by
the Secondary teachers to arrange a
ference with the University Members, who
naturally are very much interested in this
question. We had the conference last night,
and the decision we came to was that
although the teachers have put their views
before the Minister, it is quite possible, as
the Minister of Finance knows, that having
put their views before him with regard to
the matter of the interim grant, we might
be able to induce the Minister to alter his
views. I had hopes that if we had an
opportunity of putting forward our views,
and also the views of some of the professors
connected with the Technical School and
with the University, we might be able to
show to the Minister that a reasonable
claim has been put forward for further
generosity in dealing with the question of
pensions.
One point I should like to refer to is that
in the question of re-valuation of past
services the one-third instead of full service
is taken into consideration. I think that is
unfair. The second point 1S that the
teacher must be 65 years of age before he or
she gets the pension at all unless in case
of illness. The teachers ask, anl I think
not unreasonably, that this Bill should be
retrospective, in so far as it would go back
to August, 1922, to cover the case of granting pensions to a few old teachers who,
after a long period of service, have retired,
and who under the present system would be
excluded from pensions. I think that is a
reasonable and a gracious thing, and I
put it forward with confidence.
member two old teachers I was interested
in coming and interviewing the right
hon. Gentleman, who has charge of the
finances, and he said it was natural that
there should be economy in the distribution
of public money but he would never be a
party to an injustice.
3E
I re-
1603 Secondary Teachers' Pensious. HOUSE OF COMMONS Secondary Teachers' Pensions. 1604
[Dr. Morrison]
With regard to the refund which they
claim when they cease to teach, in some
mysterious way the Government desire that
that should be paid to the heirs of these
people. I assure the Minister that the
salary is not so princely that these people
will have sufficient accumulated savings
to enable them to do without this
refund which they would rather have given
to themselves. Last year I went back to my
old school, the Coleraine Academical Institution, where I was taught for four years.
Some other Members of this House-distinguished Members-were educated there.
I do not know about the Prime Minister,
but I am certain some of his brothers were
there in my day. I went into the master's
room, and I met there the whole staff of
teachers. They said to me, 'It is a curious
thing that if we are put on the scale of
salaries which the Government have drawn
up we will be losing." Well, that is proof
I think, not perhaps of the inadequacy of the
grant because the teachers in the main say
that it is satisfactory, but it is proof of the
generosity of the governors of the school.
They told me another thing, that the proposal with regard to pensions and increments was to divide it by two-that is, that
the years of service were divided by two and
only one year counted for two. What struck
me as peculiarly cruel about it was that
two men there who had been out in Flanders
and France and had fought for their country
had to serve two years which would only
count as one. That is particularly unfair.
One man who went out never came back,
but these two did come back and they suffer
this penalty for loyalty to their country.
All I ask that the Minister will do in this
matter is that he will wait before finally
making up his mind-that he will wait
until we are able to bring our heavy
artillery on him. While I approve of his
keeping a close fist on the finances of this
State of ours, I would like him to remember
that justice is not to be sacrificed,
or should not be sacrificed in the
interests of economy. (Hon. Members:
Hear, hear.) All I ask is that he
will not commit himself to-day, because if
he does we are down and out, but that he
will wait until he meets not only the distinguished doctors who are Members of this
assembly, but other professors and learned
men whom the Vice-Chancellor will possibly
accompany.
Mr. McGUFFIN: The hon. Gentleman
who has just resumed his seat, the Member
for the University (Dr. Morrison) anticipated me in this matter, but he has put the
case so cogently that I will not trespass
further on the indulgence of the House by
putting forward the views I had intended.
I would like, however, to ask the Minister of
Finance if we would be at liberty to discuss
the proposals in this Report, which has been
laid upon the Table, and which has only
been ready for four days, on the resumption of Parliament next year? If so, will he
give the House an opportunity of discussing
it with the Whips off and leave the decision
to a free vote of the Members? I feel,
as the hon. Member (Dr. Morrison) does,
that a grave injustice is done to these
men, who have served in their Own
-particular capacity in a very efficient
way and maintained secondary education
in this country with but small sympathy and small support from the Imperial
Parliament. If it had not been for the
loyalty of these men in the different schools
I do not know what would have become of
secondary education in this country. They
held out a hope from year to year-and this
hope was always deferred. I would like the
Minister of Finance to hear what 1 am
saying for I really do not intend to occupy
the time of the House for the mere sake of
talking.
I want the Minister to understand that
these men have a particular claim upon us
at the present time. It is probable that
their service will perhaps be overlooked. To
say that it is treating them fairly to grant
them a pension on the basis of only onethird the service is, in my opinion, a
grievous injustice. It would amount in the
maximum, in a case of any teacher who had
forty years' service, to a sum of £120. That
sum would be utterly inadequate to maintain a man, especially one who occupies the
status of a teacher and who would like to
maintain the respectability he has hitherto
done. I would like to know from the Minister whether he will give the House an
opportunity of discussing this Report.
the House had been sitting longer I would
have taken the opportunity of bringing it

been so badly treated in the past that
Over and over again practically every

Colonel WOODS: I would like to impress

Servants who are ex-servicemen. They

Oral Answers to Questions.
SEPARATION ALLOWANCES OF
SPECIAL CONSTABULARY.
1. Colonel WOODS asked the Minister of
Home Affairs whether he will state the
exact conditions under which married members
of the Special Constabulary are paid separation allowances.
The MINISTER OF HOME AFFAIRS (Sir
Dawson Bates): Separation Allowance,
formerly termed Separation Subsistance
Allowance, at 2s a day is granted to a
married member of the Special Constabulary
who is compelled by the action of the
authorities both to sleep and mess apart from
his family, to recoup him for the extra expense which he has to incur by reason of the
fact that he is unable to partake of his meals
with his family.
The grant of the allowance is conditional
on the following provisions:-
(1) that, if married subsequent to 31st
March, 1924, while serving in the Force, he
must have attained two years' service before the allowance can be paid to him;
(2) that a certificate is given by the responsible officer that suitable accommodation is not obtainable for the man and
his family at the place where he is
stationed; or
(3) that he is required both to sleep and
mess in barracks, and is thus unable to
partake of his meals with his family.
SEIZURE OF FERMANAGH FARMER'S
-GUN.
2. Mr. DONALD (for Mr. Cooper) asked
the Minister of Home Affairs, if he will give
the reason for the seizure of a valuable gun
the property of Mr. Simpson, Loughan
Monea; if Mr. Simpson had a permit; if he
will state where the gun now is and if it will
be returned to the owner; and whether he is
aware that Mr. Simpson is a highly respectable loyalist farmer and a man of excellent
character, and requires the gun for the purpose of killing vermin on his land?
Sir DAWSON BATES: Mr. Simpson was
required to surrender his gun to the police
in July, 1922, as he had not obtained a Firearms Permit in accordance with the public
notice issued on the 18th May, 1922. At that
time he held a permit issued by the
competent Military Authority under the
Defence of the Realm Regulations, but that
became obsolete when the provisions of the
Firearms Act, 1920, were put into force in
Northern Ireland. The gun is now at the
R.U.C. Depot at Sprucefield, Lisburn.
a
I am aware that Mr. Simpson is respectable loyalist farmer, and that he requires the gun for the purpose of killing
vermin on his land, and, if he applies for a
Certificate under the Firearms Act, his application will be duly considered. So far no
such application has been made.

PUBLIC TRUSTEE.
Sir CRAWFORD MCCULLAGH
Major Shillington) asked the Minister of
Finance, if he has further considered the
appointment of a Public Trustee for
Northern Ireland, or, if such an appointment
is not considered advisable, would it be
possible to arrange for the Public Trustee
in England to act for people residing
Northern Ireland, who might wish to avail
themselves of his services?
in
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Mr.
Pollock): The hon. Member is no doubt referring to the statement made by me in the
course of the debate on the 28th February,
1923, in reply to a suggestion by the hon.
Member for the University, in which I indicated that I would have the whole subject
of the appointment of a Public Trustee for
Northern Ireland investigated. I may now
say that I followed up this matter and
obtained full facilities for making my inquiries from the English Public Trustee,
and, as a result of this investigation, I will
briefly summarise my conclusions.
I cannot find that there is any insistent
popular demand for the creation of such an
office in this area, and I imagine that if
action were initiated by this Government,
opposition from the legal and accountancy
professions would be likely to result, while
there would be no guarantee that the general
public would make any considerable use of
the office. As the hon. Member is aware,
Scotland is in the identical position of Ireland, as the existing Act only applies to
England and Wales, and I cannot trace that,
when the Act was passed in the year 1906,
there was any demand for its extension to
the other areas.
I may also add that the English experience
was that until the volume of work dealt
with by the office increased considerably, it
was almost impossible for the office to be
self-supporting unless by charging exorbitant
fees. In a small area like Northern Ireland
this difficulty would be ever present, because
it is evident that in the matter of Trusteeship the Government must supply legal and
accounting staff possessing the highest qualifications and who would expect to be paid
accordingly.
I regret that I do not consider that the
proposal to make an arrangement with the
English Public Trustee is at present feasible.
Even if that officer were prepared to undertake the work, I am satisfied that he could
not do so without legislation both in the
Imperial House and in this House.
Mr. DONALD: Hear, hear.

Governor, in the name and on behalf of
His Majesty the King, has been pleased to
give his Assent to the following Acts agreed

PROROGATION.
Message from the Senate.
A message was delivered by the Gentleman
Usher of the Black Rod, as follows:-
Mr. Speaker, his Grace the Governor
of Northern Ireland commands this
Honourable House to attend immediately
in the Senate.
The House went, and having returned,
Mr. SPEAKER (standing in the Clerk's
place at the Table): I have to acquaint the
House that the House has this day been to
the Senate, where his Grace the Governor
delivered his Speech to both Houses of
Parliament as follows:-
KING'S SPEECH.
Members of the Senate and of the
House of Commons.
I have to congratulate you upon the
legislative measures passed this session,
which mark steady progress in the promotion of the general welfare of the people.
I am glad to learn that there are hopeful
signs of a recovery from the acute period
of depression generally experienced, although
I regret that it is less rapid than we all so
earnestly desire. The weather, which has
proved so unfortunate to agriculture-our
greatest industry-and the continued slackness in the Shipyards, have prejudicially
affected conditions in Northern Ireland, but
prices for agricultural produce are showing
an upward tendency which will mitigate
the losses sustained by farmers. I also note
with pleasure that an improvement has
taken place in shipbuilding, where the prospects are now somewhat brighter It is
still necessary to create work specially designed for the relief of unemployment, and
in this regard it is satisfactory to know
that the Government continues to receive
the cordial co-operation of Local Authorities
in whose districts unemployment is serious.
An Act has been passed this session which
has conferred increased rates of benefit for
those who are unemployed, in conformity
with similar legislation by the Imperial
Parliament.
The King's Speech.
Prorogation.
7 NOVEMBER 1924
In other directions by means of the Loans
Guarantee Act, you have promoted the development of private industrial undertakings calculated to relieve unemployment. A
sum of £5,000,000 has been made available
for this purpose and guarantees have already been given of over £4,500,000. A
satisfactory sign in this period of trade depression is the continued popularity of
Ulster Savings Certificates, in which nearly
£1,500,000 has now been invested.
It is with great pleasure that I am able
to state that the maintenance of law and
order has been so satisfactorily continued
and to record the thanks of our people to
officers and men of the Royal Ulster and
Special Constabulary. Their vigilance, tact
and devotion to duty has enabled the whole
community to settle down to a life of
confidence and security.
I am gratified to know that the development of the new system of Educational
Administration under the Act of last
session is proceeding smoothly and rapidly.
Statutory rules and orders have been laid
before Parliament. Negotiations are in progress with the County Councils for the
establishment of the Local Educational
Authorities in the Counties, the 1st day of
October 1924 having been appointed by Order
in Council for the bringing into operation
of those provisions of the Act under which
these Bodies are required to be set up.
Your Housing Act extends the provisions
of last year's measure with a view to affording further opportunity to private
builders and to local authorities to erect
houses with Government assistance.
a
The Exchequer and Financial Provisions
Act which was passed early in the Session,
has provided for the disposal of the sum of
£400,000 granted by the Imperial Government in final satisfaction of the claim for
the provision of buildings in accordance
with the Government of Ireland Act 1920,
excluding Parliamentary Buildings, new Law
Courts and administrative offices. This sum
will be utilised in connection with a Training College and Hostel for School Teachers,
a depôt for the Royal Ulster Constabulary,
a Convict Prison, a Borstal Institution and
Criminal Lunatic Asylum, and Institutions
for agricultural instruction and research.
Members of the House of Commons.
I thank you for the provision of supplics
for the public services.
Members of the Senate and of the
up
House of Commons.
Various Commissions which have been set
are still engaged upon work of farreaching importance and the members are
deserving every praise for the industry
and care with which they are prosecuting
their inquiries.
I am satisfied with the success of the
Ulster Pavilion at the British Empire
Exhibition, which provided a useful link
in connecting Northern Ireland with other
parts of His Majesty's Dominions. Upwards
of 900 children, mainly from elementary
schools, visited the Exhibition, and it is
believed that the effect will be to foster and
encourage Imperial ideals.
Many representatives of the Dominions
and Colonies have visited our shores this
year and will I hope take away with them
recollections of the loyalty of our people
towards the Empire of which they and we
are so proud to form a part.
I pray that the blessing of Almighty God
may rest upon your labours.
After which the Proclamation proroguing
Parliament was read as follows:-
BY HIS GRACE THE GOVERNOR OF
NORTHERN IRELAND.
A PROCLAMATION
Proroguing the Present Parliament of
Northern Ireland.
WHEREAS it is provided by Section
Eleven of the Government of Ireland Act,
1920, as modified by and in pursuance of
the Irish Free State (Consequential Provisions) Act, 1922, that the Governor of
Northern Ireland shall, in His Majesty's
name, Summon, Prorogue and Dissolve the
Parliament of Northern Ireland.
AND WHEREAS it is desirable that this
Ireland
present Parliament of Northern
should be Prorogued to the Tenth day of
March, One Thousand Nine Hundred and
Twenty-five.
NOW I, JAMES ALBERT EDWARD,
DUKE OF ABERCORN, Governor of
Northern Ireland, by this Proclamation do
publish and declare His Majesty's Pleasure
that the said Parliament be, as from the
reading of this Proclamation in the Parliament of Northern Ireland, Prorogued to
Tuesday, the Tenth day of March, One
Thousand Nine Hundred and Twenty-five.
AND I Do Hereby Further Declare His
Majesty's Royal Will and Pleasure to be
that the said Parliament shall, on the said
Tenth day of March, One Thousand Nine
Hundred and Twenty-five, assemble and be
holden for the despatch of divers urgent
and important affairs, and the Senators and
Members of the House of Commons of
Northern Ireland are hereby required to
give their attendance accordingly.
Prorogation.
End of Session.
HOUSE OF COMMONS.
Given at Belfast, this Sixth day of
November, One Thousand Nine Hundred and
Twenty-four.
Signed by his own hand,
ABERCORN.
GOD SAVE THE KING.
End of the Fourth Session (opened

Tuesday,
11th March, 1924) of the First Parliament
of Northern Ireland, in the Fifteenth year
of the Reign of His Majesty King George
the Fifth.
